How to use this course

  1. Have the book open. Each day starts with a "Read first" box naming the sections and pages of the SLAM Handbook (Carlone, Kim, Barfoot, Cremers, Dellaert, eds., Cambridge University Press). Read those pages before the lesson, or right after it if the pages feel hard.
  2. Then do the lesson. It restates the idea in plain words, works through the derivation steps the book leaves out, and uses the book's own notation so you can go back and forth.
  3. Play with every widget. They are small real computations (a Gauss-Newton solver, an ICP loop, a belief-propagation pass), not pictures.
  4. Take the quiz, then mark the day done. Progress is saved on this device only.
  5. Day 6 of each week is a review: a formula sheet, a mixed quiz, and pen-and-paper problems with worked solutions.
  6. Check the page chips. A chip such as §1.3.2 · p. 30 tells you where in the book a statement comes from.

The map

The course follows the book in order: Part I is the estimation machinery (Weeks 1–10), Part II is the sensors (Weeks 11–18), Part III is where the field is heading (Weeks 19–24). Tap a week to see its days.

Week 1 · Day 1

What SLAM is, and how a SLAM system is put together

After today you can state the SLAM problem, split a SLAM system into its front-end and back-end, and explain why loop closures stop drift.

About 60 min · Read §I.1–I.2, pp. 3–8 (6 pages) · No prerequisites

Read first: Prelude §I.1–I.2, pp. 3–8

While you read, look for three things:

  • The two special cases that SLAM reduces to when you already know the map, or already know the pose (p. 3).
  • What the front-end hands to the back-end in Example I.1 (visual) and Example I.2 (LiDAR), on pp. 7–8.
  • The paragraph on p. 8 that says why loop closures matter.

Today's big idea

SLAM estimates two things at once, where the robot has been and what the world looks like, because each one is needed to compute the other. Every system in this book does it in two stages: a front-end turns raw sensor data into a small set of geometric constraints, and a back-end finds the trajectory and map that best satisfy all of them.

1. One problem, two unknowns

A robot in a place it has never seen needs a map (where the obstacles, objects, and landmarks are) and its own pose (position and orientation) inside that map. Simultaneous localization and mapping (SLAM) is the problem of building the map while estimating the pose with respect to it. §I.1 · p. 3

The difficulty is circular. To place a new observation in the map you need to know where the robot was when it made it. To know where the robot is you need to compare what it sees with the map. If someone hands you one of the two, the problem collapses into an easier one:

You already knowYou must estimateThe problem is called
The mapThe poseLocalization
The pose (for example from motion capture or differential GPS)The mapMapping
NeitherBothSLAM

In practice "neither" is the normal case. Motion capture and differential GPS are expensive and cover small areas, consumer GPS is accurate only to meters and fails indoors, and a prior map is often missing, out of date, or too coarse. §I.1 · pp. 4–5 That is why the handbook treats SLAM, and not localization alone, as the core capability.

2. SLAM is an inverse problem

Sensors do not report poses or maps. They report numbers that depend on the poses and the map: a pixel coordinate, a range, an angular rate. Write the unknowns (all poses and all map parameters) as one long vector \(\mathbf{x}\), and each measurement as

\[ \mathbf{z}_i = h_i(\mathbf{x}) + \boldsymbol{\eta}_i , \]

where \(h_i\) is a measurement model that predicts what the sensor should read for a given \(\mathbf{x}\), and \(\boldsymbol{\eta}_i\) is noise. Going from \(\mathbf{x}\) to \(\mathbf{z}\) is easy: it is geometry. SLAM asks for the reverse: given all the \(\mathbf{z}_i\), find the \(\mathbf{x}\) that could have produced them. The book calls this an inverse problem. §I.2 · p. 5 You will write this equation properly in Week 2, where it becomes a least-squares problem.

There are two ways to set it up. Indirect methods first compress the raw data into a few easy-to-model quantities, such as keypoints in an image, and only model those. Direct methods model the raw data itself, such as the brightness of every pixel. Indirect methods are cheaper and lead to simpler math. Direct methods use all the information and can be more accurate, at the cost of heavier computation and a harder optimization problem. §I.2 · pp. 5–6

3. Front-end and back-end

Indirect methods split a SLAM system in two. §I.2 · pp. 6–7

The front-end processes raw data into compact pseudo-measurements, detects when the robot returns to a known place, and supplies a rough initial guess. The back-end takes those pseudo-measurements and solves for the poses and map. The book's two running examples give the two standard problem shapes:

ModelFront-end producesBack-end estimatesBack-end problem
Landmark-based (Example I.1, visual SLAM)Observations of 3D landmarks: matched keypoints across imagesPoses and landmark positionsBundle adjustment (BA)
Pose-graph (Example I.2, LiDAR SLAM)Relative poses: odometry between consecutive scans, loop closures between revisitsPoses onlyPose-graph optimization (PGO)

Where you draw the line is a trade. Handing the back-end only relative poses makes it fast, but it has thrown away the raw observations, so the answer is slightly less accurate than bundle adjustment on the same data. §I.2 · p. 8

In plain words

The front-end is the part that looks. It says things like "I moved about one meter forward" and "that corner is the same one I saw ten minutes ago". The back-end is the part that thinks. It takes all of those statements, which never agree perfectly, and finds the single story of where the robot went that contradicts them the least.

4. Drift, and why loop closures matter

Odometry is the estimate of how the robot moved between two nearby moments. Chaining odometry steps gives a trajectory, but every step carries a small error and the errors add up. The accumulated error is called drift. A loop closure is a measurement that ties the current pose to a pose from much earlier, made when the robot recognizes a place it has visited before. §I.2 · p. 8

Try it: the robot drives a 40-step square and should end exactly where it started. Raise the heading noise, then press "Close the loop".

Notice two things. Heading noise opens a much larger gap than distance noise does. And closing the loop reduces the error along the whole path, not only at the last pose.

Filling the gap: how fast does drift grow?

The book says drift is "bound to" grow but does not say how fast. A one-line model shows it. Suppose each step moves the robot by \(u_k\) and odometry reports \(u_k + \epsilon_k\), with independent errors of variance \(\sigma^2\). After \(n\) steps the position error is the sum \(\epsilon_1 + \dots + \epsilon_n\), and variances of independent errors add:

\[ \operatorname{var}(\text{error after } n \text{ steps}) = n\,\sigma^2 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \text{typical error} = \sigma\sqrt{n}. \]

So pure distance error grows like \(\sqrt{n}\): slowly, but without bound. Heading error is worse. A heading that is off by a small angle \(\theta\) displaces everything that follows sideways, and after driving a further distance \(L\) the position is off by about \(L\,\theta\). Heading errors therefore get multiplied by distance travelled, which is what you saw in the widget: 1° of heading noise per step matters far more than 3% of distance noise.

A loop closure adds one equation that odometry alone can never supply: "pose 40 equals pose 0". The back-end then adjusts every pose a little so that all odometry steps and this new equation are satisfied as well as possible. In the widget, with equally trusted steps, that spreads the end gap evenly over the 40 steps.

Common mistakes

  • "SLAM is localization plus mapping, run one after the other." The two are solved together. An error in a pose corrupts the map points seen from it, and the corrupted map then misleads later poses.
  • "A loop closure only fixes the pose where it happens." It is a constraint between two poses, and the back-end redistributes the error along the entire loop between them.
  • "Landmark-based SLAM has no loop closures." It has them implicitly: seeing an old landmark again is a loop closure. §I.2 · p. 8

Check yourself

Q1. A warehouse robot is given an accurate floor map and must work out where it is. Which problem is this?

With the map known, only the pose is unknown, which is localization. SLAM is needed when neither is known.

Q2. In a LiDAR pose-graph system, what does the back-end receive from the front-end?

Scan matching turns pairs of scans into relative-pose measurements. The back-end optimizes the trajectory from those alone (pose-graph optimization).

Q3. Each odometry step has an independent position error with standard deviation 2 cm. Roughly how large is the typical error after 100 steps?

Variances add, so the standard deviation grows like the square root of the number of steps: 2 cm × √100 = 20 cm.

Q4. Why is pose-graph optimization usually a little less accurate than bundle adjustment on the same data?

The relative poses are an abstraction of the original observations. The back-end is faster but no longer sees the raw measurements, so small modeling errors remain.

Recap

  1. SLAM estimates the robot's trajectory and the map together, because each is needed to compute the other.
  2. It is an inverse problem: measurements are functions of poses and map plus noise, and we solve for the poses and map.
  3. The front-end turns raw data into pseudo-measurements (landmark observations, odometry, loop closures). The back-end optimizes.
  4. Landmark-based models lead to bundle adjustment. Pose-graph models lead to pose-graph optimization.
  5. Odometry drifts without bound. Loop closures are what keep the error bounded and the map globally consistent.

Sources

  1. SLAM Handbook, Prelude to Part I, §I.1 "What is SLAM?" and §I.2 "Anatomy of a Modern SLAM System", pp. 3–8.
  2. The drift model in "Filling the gap" is the standard random-walk argument (variances of independent errors add).

Week 1 · Day 2

Where SLAM sits in a robot, and the probability you need

After today you can explain why a SLAM system runs a fast loop and a slow loop, judge when a robot needs SLAM at all, and combine a Gaussian prior with a Gaussian measurement using Bayes' rule.

About 60 min · Read §I.3, pp. 9–12 (4 pages) · Needs Week 1 Day 1

Read first: Prelude §I.3 and §I.3.1, pp. 9–12

While you read, look for:

  • The two feedback loops in Figure I.4 (p. 9): a small one through the motion controller and a large one through motion planning. Note which part of SLAM feeds each.
  • What separates SLAM from structure from motion (p. 10).
  • The three questions Q1–Q3 (pp. 10–12) and the short answer to each.
  • The Office 1 / Office 3 story of Figure I.5 (pp. 11–12), and the term "perceptual aliasing".

Today's big idea

SLAM is a service for the rest of the robot, and its two customers have different deadlines: the controller needs odometry within milliseconds, the planner can wait seconds for a globally corrected map. The language the back-end uses to do its job is probability. A belief is a density, usually a Gaussian, and Bayes' rule says how a measurement turns a prior belief into a sharper one.

1. One system, two loops, two deadlines

SLAM exists to serve downstream tasks. The pose estimate lets a controller hold the robot on a planned trajectory. The map, together with the current pose, lets a planner find a path. §I.3 · p. 9 Figure I.4 shows that these are two separate feedback loops, both passing through SLAM, and they run at very different speeds.

LoopCustomerWhat SLAM suppliesDelay it can tolerate
Inner (control)Motion controllerOdometry from the front-endMilliseconds for a fast drone
Outer (planning)Motion plannerGlobally corrected trajectory and map from the back-endSeconds

This is why a real SLAM system is several processes running in parallel and not one function from sensor data to a map. §I.3 · p. 9 The processes also talk in both directions. The back-end periodically corrects the odometric trajectory that the controller uses, and it can tell the loop-closure detector which candidate matches are plausible. §I.3 · p. 10

"Slow" does not mean "offline". The back-end must stay online: its runtime may not grow without bound as data keeps arriving, and it has to fit on the robot's own computer. That requirement is what historically separated SLAM from structure from motion (SfM), the computer-vision problem of reconstructing a 3D scene from images. SfM typically takes an unordered pile of photos and may spend hours on a cluster. SLAM receives its data in order, as the robot moves, and must answer in seconds. The book adds that the border has blurred, and many people now use "visual SLAM" and "SfM" interchangeably. §I.3 · p. 10

2. Do we really need SLAM?

The book asks this in three steps. §I.3.1 · pp. 10–12

QuestionShort answerThe argument
Q1. Is SLAM needed for every task?NoKeeping a target in view, moving a short distance, or working where localization infrastructure exists can all be done without it. Long-term operation without infrastructure needs memory, and the map is that memory.
Q2. Does the map have to be metrically accurate?For long-term use, yesOdometry alone drifts, so two rooms that share a wall can end up far apart in the estimate, and the robot misses the short path between them.
Q3. Do we need a map at all?Open, but maps helpA network can map sensor data straight to actions, but its internal representation cannot be queried or inspected. Maps transfer across tasks, and in some applications the map is the product.

Q2 has a tempting middle road. A topological map is a graph whose nodes are places and whose edges mean "you can get from here to there". It stores no distances or angles, so it needs no optimization: add an edge when the robot drives between two places or when place recognition says two views show the same place. The weakness is perceptual aliasing: two different places that look alike. If Office 1 and Office 3 look the same, a purely topological map merges them into one room (Figure I.5d). A metric map has geometry to check the claim against. §I.3.1 · p. 12 Section 4 below puts a number on how misleading a look-alike can be.

3. Random variables and Gaussians

The rest of today is background that Chapter 1 assumes. A random variable is a quantity whose value we are unsure of. Its probability density \(p(x)\) says how plausible each value is and integrates to 1. The book writes \(p(\mathbf{a})\) for a density and \(p(\mathbf{a}\mid\mathbf{b})\) for the density of \(\mathbf{a}\) once \(\mathbf{b}\) is known. Notation · p. xiv Two numbers summarize a density: the mean \(\mu = \E[x]\) and the variance \(\sigma^2 = \E[(x-\mu)^2]\). The square root \(\sigma\) is the standard deviation, in the same units as \(x\).

The Gaussian (normal) density with mean \(\mu\) and variance \(\sigma^2\) is

\[ p(x) = \frac{1}{\sigma\sqrt{2\pi}}\,\exp\!\left(-\frac{(x-\mu)^2}{2\sigma^2}\right). \]

About 68% of its probability lies within \(1\sigma\) of the mean, 95% within \(2\sigma\), and 99.7% within \(3\sigma\). A range sensor with \(\sigma = 0.05\) m reads within 0.10 m of the true range about 95% of the time.

For a vector \(\boldsymbol{\theta}\in\R^n\) the mean becomes a vector \(\boldsymbol{\mu}\) and the variance becomes the covariance matrix \(\boldsymbol{\Sigma} = \E[(\boldsymbol{\theta}-\boldsymbol{\mu})(\boldsymbol{\theta}-\boldsymbol{\mu})\T]\), an \(n\times n\) symmetric matrix with the variances on its diagonal. You will meet the multivariate Gaussian in the book as equation (1.9):

\[ \N(\boldsymbol{\theta};\boldsymbol{\mu},\boldsymbol{\Sigma}) = \frac{1}{\sqrt{|2\pi\boldsymbol{\Sigma}|}}\exp\!\left(-\tfrac12\norm{\boldsymbol{\theta}-\boldsymbol{\mu}}^2_{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}\right), \qquad \norm{\mathbf{e}}^2_{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}} = \mathbf{e}\T\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{-1}\mathbf{e}. \]

§1.2.2 · p. 27 It has the same shape as the scalar formula: \((x-\mu)^2/\sigma^2\) has become \(\mathbf{e}\T\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{-1}\mathbf{e}\), a squared distance measured in units of standard deviation.

A worked reading of a covariance matrix. Suppose a landmark's position \((x, y)\) has

\[ \boldsymbol{\Sigma} = \begin{bmatrix} 4 & 1.2 \\ 1.2 & 1 \end{bmatrix}\ \text{m}^2 . \]

Then \(\sigma_x = \sqrt{4} = 2\) m and \(\sigma_y = \sqrt{1} = 1\) m. The off-diagonal entry is the covariance of \(x\) with \(y\). Dividing it by both standard deviations gives the correlation \(\rho = 1.2/(2\times 1) = 0.6\): when \(x\) is above its mean, \(y\) tends to be above its mean too. The curves of constant density are ellipses, tilted when \(\rho\neq 0\). You will draw them tomorrow.

4. Bayes' rule

Write the joint density of a state \(x\) and a measurement \(z\) in the two possible orders, \(p(x,z) = p(x\mid z)\,p(z) = p(z\mid x)\,p(x)\), and divide by \(p(z)\):

\[ \underbrace{p(x\mid z)}_{\text{posterior}} = \frac{\overbrace{p(z\mid x)}^{\text{likelihood}}\ \overbrace{p(x)}^{\text{prior}}}{p(z)} \ \propto\ p(z\mid x)\,p(x). \]

The prior is what you believed before the measurement. The likelihood is the measurement model read backwards: for the \(z\) you actually observed, how well does each candidate \(x\) explain it? The posterior is what you believe afterwards. The denominator \(p(z)\) does not depend on \(x\); it only rescales the result so that it integrates to 1. The book marks prior quantities with a check, \(\check{x}\), and posterior ones with a hat, \(\hat{x}\). Notation · p. xiv

A worked example with perceptual aliasing. From odometry, the robot gives a 10% chance to being back at a place it has seen before. Its place-recognition module reports a match. The module fires 90% of the time when the place really is the same, and 20% of the time when it is a different place that looks similar. How likely is a true revisit?

\[ P(\text{same}\mid\text{match}) = \frac{0.9\times 0.1}{0.9\times 0.1 + 0.2\times 0.9} = \frac{0.09}{0.27} = \frac13 . \]

The match is wrong two times out of three, although the detector "works 90% of the time". Revisits are rare and look-alikes are common, and the prior carries that fact. This is why a back-end cannot accept every loop closure at face value; the book returns to it in Chapter 3. §I.3.1 · p. 12

5. Two estimators: MLE and MAP

A density is a belief; a robot needs one number to act on. Two standard choices:

\[ x^{\text{MLE}} = \argmax_x\ p(z\mid x), \qquad x^{\text{MAP}} = \argmax_x\ p(x\mid z) = \argmax_x\ p(z\mid x)\,p(x). \]

The maximum likelihood estimate (MLE) picks the state that best explains the measurements and ignores the prior. The maximum a posteriori (MAP) estimate picks the peak of the posterior. They coincide when the prior is flat. Tomorrow's pages name these two as the estimation framework behind modern SLAM, §I.4.1 · p. 15 and Chapter 1 writes SLAM as a MAP problem in equation (1.8). §1.2.1 · p. 27

Try it: a robot in a corridor believes from odometry that it is at 2.0 m, give or take 1.0 m. A range sensor then says 4.0 m, give or take 0.5 m. Move the four sliders.

Notice: at the default settings the MLE is the measurement itself, 4.00 m, and the MAP is 3.60 m. The prior pulls the estimate back, but only a fifth of the way, because the measurement is the more precise of the two. The posterior is narrower than both inputs. Raise the prior σ to 3.0 and the MAP moves to 3.95 m, almost onto the MLE.

Filling the gap: why Gaussian times Gaussian is Gaussian, and where 3.60 comes from

Prior: \(x\sim\N(\check{x},\check{\sigma}^2)\). Measurement: \(z = x + \eta\) with \(\eta\sim\N(0,\sigma_z^2)\), so the likelihood is \(p(z\mid x) = \N(z;\,x,\,\sigma_z^2)\). Take the negative logarithm of likelihood times prior. The exponents add and the constants in front become an additive constant:

\[ J(x) = -\log\big(p(z\mid x)\,p(x)\big) = \frac{(x-\check{x})^2}{2\check{\sigma}^2} + \frac{(z-x)^2}{2\sigma_z^2} + \text{const}. \]

The logarithm is increasing, so the maximum of the posterior is the minimum of \(J\). Set the derivative to zero:

\[ J'(x) = \frac{x-\check{x}}{\check{\sigma}^2} - \frac{z-x}{\sigma_z^2} = 0 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \hat{x} = \frac{\check{x}/\check{\sigma}^2 + z/\sigma_z^2}{1/\check{\sigma}^2 + 1/\sigma_z^2}. \]

\(J\) is a quadratic in \(x\), and a density whose negative log is a quadratic is a Gaussian. Its variance is one over the curvature \(J''\):

\[ \frac{1}{\hat{\sigma}^2} = J''(x) = \frac{1}{\check{\sigma}^2} + \frac{1}{\sigma_z^2}. \]

With the widget's numbers: \(\hat{x} = (2/1 + 4/0.25)/(1/1 + 1/0.25) = 18/5 = 3.6\) m and \(\hat{\sigma}^2 = 1/5\), so \(\hat{\sigma} = 0.447\) m. Rearranging the mean gives the form on the widget's last tile:

\[ \hat{x} = \check{x} + K\,(z-\check{x}), \qquad K = \frac{\check{\sigma}^2}{\check{\sigma}^2+\sigma_z^2} = \frac{1}{1+0.25} = 0.8 . \]

Look at what happened in the first line: maximizing a posterior turned into minimizing a sum of squared errors, each divided by its variance. Chapter 1 does the same thing with thousands of terms.

Common mistakes

  • "p(z | x) and p(x | z) are the same number." In the look-alike example the first is 0.9 and the second is 1/3. Bayes' rule is the conversion between them, and it needs the prior.
  • "The likelihood is a density over x." It is a density over \(z\). Read as a function of \(x\) it need not integrate to 1.
  • "MAP is always better than MLE." MAP is only as good as its prior. Set the prior σ to 0.2 in the widget: a confident, wrong prior drags the estimate far from a good measurement.

Check yourself

Q1. A drone's motion controller needs pose updates within a few milliseconds. Which SLAM output can acceptably arrive seconds later?

The control loop runs on odometry and needs low latency. Global planning runs at a lower rate, so the back-end's corrected trajectory and map can lag by seconds, as long as the back-end stays online.

Q2. The prior chance of a revisit is 0.2. A place recognizer fires with probability 0.9 on a true revisit and 0.1 otherwise. It fires. What is the probability of a true revisit?

Bayes' rule: 0.9 × 0.2 / (0.9 × 0.2 + 0.1 × 0.8) = 0.18 / 0.26 ≈ 0.69.

Q3. Prior: position 10 m with σ = 2 m. Measurement: 13 m with σ = 1 m. What is the MAP estimate?

Weights are 1/σ²: 1/4 for the prior and 1 for the measurement. (10 × 0.25 + 13 × 1) / 1.25 = 15.5 / 1.25 = 12.4 m. Equivalently K = 4/(4+1) = 0.8 and 10 + 0.8 × 3 = 12.4.

Q4. A 2-D position has covariance with rows (9, −3) and (−3, 4). What is the correlation between its two coordinates?

The standard deviations are √9 = 3 and √4 = 2. Correlation = covariance / (σ₁σ₂) = −3 / 6 = −0.5.

Q5. With a Gaussian prior and a Gaussian measurement of the same scalar, when does the MAP estimate equal the MLE?

The weight on the measurement is K = σ̌² / (σ̌² + σ_z²). It tends to 1 as the prior σ grows, and then the MAP estimate equals z, which is the MLE. With equal σ the MAP is the midpoint.

Recap

  1. SLAM feeds a fast control loop (odometry, milliseconds) and a slow planning loop (corrected trajectory and map, seconds), so it runs as parallel processes, and even the slow one must stay online.
  2. Not every task needs SLAM, but long-term operation without infrastructure needs a consistent map. Odometry drifts, and topological maps are fooled by perceptual aliasing.
  3. A Gaussian is fixed by a mean and a covariance. The exponent \(\mathbf{e}\T\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{-1}\mathbf{e}\) is a squared distance in units of σ.
  4. Bayes' rule: posterior ∝ likelihood × prior. MLE maximizes the likelihood, MAP maximizes the posterior.
  5. For Gaussians, MAP is a least-squares problem: inverse variances add, and the mean is the inverse-variance-weighted average.

Sources

  1. SLAM Handbook, Prelude to Part I, §I.3 "The Role of SLAM in the Autonomy Architecture" and §I.3.1, pp. 9–12; Notation, p. xiv; equations (1.9)–(1.10), p. 27, quoted ahead of Week 2.
  2. Thrun, Burgard, Fox, Probabilistic Robotics, 2005, Chapter 2 (Bayes' rule, priors and posteriors).
  3. Barfoot, State Estimation for Robotics, 2017, Chapter 2 (Gaussian densities, combining Gaussian estimates).

Week 1 · Day 3

From Kalman filters to factor graphs, and how Gaussians fuse

After today you can say why SLAM moved from filters to factor-graph optimization, fuse two Gaussian estimates by adding their information, and show on a three-pose example why the information matrix is sparse while the covariance is dense.

About 60 min · Read §I.4–I.5, pp. 13–18 (6 pages) · Needs Week 1 Day 2

Read first: Prelude §I.4–I.5, pp. 13–18

While you read, look for:

  • The three practical problems of EKF-SLAM (bottom of p. 13 and p. 14).
  • What particle filters fixed, and the failure called particle depletion (p. 15).
  • The sentence on p. 15 about the covariance matrix being dense while its inverse is sparse. It is the most important sentence of the Prelude.
  • What Spatial AI adds to SLAM (pp. 16–17, Figure I.7). Skim §I.5 (pp. 17–18): it is the table of contents in prose.

Today's big idea

SLAM back-ends went through three designs: the extended Kalman filter, particle filters, and optimization over a factor graph. The third won because of one structural fact: the inverse of the covariance matrix, the information matrix, is sparse. Information is also the quantity that behaves simply: when independent measurements are combined, their information adds.

1. Three generations of back-ends

Estimating a map from noisy measurements is much older than robotics. Gauss triangulated the Kingdom of Hannover in the 1820s, and Cholesky invented the matrix factorization that carries his name while surveying, before the First World War. §I.4.1 · p. 13 You will use that factorization on Day 5.

In robotics, the early work reached two insights. To avoid drift in an unknown environment you must estimate the robot poses and the positions of fixed external things (landmarks) together. And an existing tool, the extended Kalman filter (EKF), can do it if you stack the robot pose and all landmark positions into one long state. An EKF keeps a single Gaussian belief over that state, a mean and a covariance matrix, and updates both after every measurement, using a linear approximation of the motion and measurement models. The acronym SLAM dates from 1995. §I.4.1 · p. 13

ApproachBelief is stored asWhat it gaveWhat limited it
EKF-SLAMOne Gaussian: mean and dense covariance over pose and landmarksSLAM with standard estimation theoryGross errors from outliers and wrong data association; linearization around drifting odometry, which can make it diverge; cost growing quadratically with the number of state variables
Particle filters (early 2000s)A set of trajectory hypotheses, the particlesMany landmarks, dense maps such as 2-D occupancy grids, no linearization, less sensitivity to outliersAccuracy needs thousands of particles; if none is near the true trajectory the filter diverges (particle depletion), and 3-D makes this worse
Factor-graph optimization (2005–2015, dominant today)The maximum likelihood or MAP estimate of the trajectory and map, found by optimizationNear-linear cost thanks to sparsity, online operation, and a setting that allows deeper analysisThe topic of this book

§I.4.1 · pp. 13–15 Data association means deciding which landmark or place a measurement refers to; an association error is the look-alike problem from Day 2. Two remarks in the text are worth keeping. First, optimization was proposed in the early days of SLAM and set aside as too slow; sparsity is what brought it back. Second, an EKF with suitable linearization points can be understood as a single iteration of a nonlinear optimization solver, so the optimization view contains the filtering view. §I.4.1 · p. 15 The book's focus on factor graphs is a choice of scope: EKF-based methods remain popular for visual-inertial odometry. §I.4.1 · p. 16

2. Where the field is heading, and how the book is laid out

SLAM estimates geometry. That is enough for "go to position (x, y, z)" and not enough for "pick up the clothes in the bathroom and take them to the laundry room", which needs the robot to know what a bathroom is. Spatial AI is the name for a perception system that reasons about geometry, semantics, and possibly physics together, with SLAM as the submodule that handles geometry. It closes a third, slower loop over task planning, on top of the two loops from Day 2. §I.4.2 · pp. 16–17

The handbook has three parts. Part I (Chapters 1–6) is foundations: factor graphs and optimization, poses on manifolds, outliers, differentiable optimization, map representations, and advanced solvers. Part II (Chapters 7–12) is the state of practice, one sensor per chapter: cameras, LiDAR, radar, event cameras, inertial sensors, and wheel and legged odometry. Part III (Chapters 13–18) covers trends, from learned components and new map representations to Spatial AI and foundation models. §I.5 · pp. 17–18 The history above is the history of the back-end, which is why Part I comes first.

3. Fusing two Gaussians: information adds

Yesterday's result for a prior and a measurement was \(1/\hat{\sigma}^2 = 1/\check{\sigma}^2 + 1/\sigma_z^2\). The quantity that adds is not the variance but its inverse. Give it a name: the information (or precision) of a scalar Gaussian is \(\lambda = 1/\sigma^2\). Give the numerator of the mean a name too: \(\eta = \mu/\sigma^2 = \lambda\mu\). Then fusing two independent estimates of the same quantity is two additions and one division:

\[ \lambda = \lambda_1+\lambda_2, \qquad \eta = \eta_1+\eta_2, \qquad \mu = \eta/\lambda . \]

Example: two range readings of the same wall, 10.0 m with \(\sigma = 0.3\) m and 10.4 m with \(\sigma = 0.4\) m.

EstimateMeanStd. dev.Information, 1/varianceInformation × mean
Reading 1μ = 10.0σ = 0.30λ = 11.11η = 111.1
Reading 2μ = 10.4σ = 0.40λ = 6.25η = 65.0
Fusedμ = 176.1 / 17.36 = 10.14σ = 1/√17.36 = 0.24λ = 17.36η = 176.1

The fused value sits closer to the better reading, and its σ of 0.24 m beats both.

For vectors the same rule holds with matrices. The information matrix is \(\boldsymbol{\Lambda} = \boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{-1}\) and the information vector is \(\boldsymbol{\eta} = \boldsymbol{\Lambda}\boldsymbol{\mu}\). The pair \((\boldsymbol{\mu},\boldsymbol{\Sigma})\) is the covariance form of a Gaussian and \((\boldsymbol{\eta},\boldsymbol{\Lambda})\) is its information form. They describe the same density.

TaskCovariance formInformation form
Fuse two independent estimates\(\boldsymbol{\Sigma} = (\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_1^{-1}+\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_2^{-1})^{-1}\), then \(\boldsymbol{\mu} = \boldsymbol{\Sigma}(\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_1^{-1}\boldsymbol{\mu}_1+\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_2^{-1}\boldsymbol{\mu}_2)\)\(\boldsymbol{\Lambda} = \boldsymbol{\Lambda}_1+\boldsymbol{\Lambda}_2\), \(\boldsymbol{\eta} = \boldsymbol{\eta}_1+\boldsymbol{\eta}_2\)
Say "I know nothing about this direction"An infinite varianceA zero
Read off the mean and the uncertainty of one variableDirectly: \(\boldsymbol{\mu}\) and the diagonal of \(\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\)Needs a linear solve, \(\boldsymbol{\Lambda}\boldsymbol{\mu} = \boldsymbol{\eta}\)

Filling the gap: why information adds

Let two estimates of the same \(\mathbf{x}\) have independent errors, so that the joint likelihood is the product of the two Gaussian densities. Multiplying densities adds exponents. Expand one exponent, using \(\boldsymbol{\Lambda}_1 = \boldsymbol{\Sigma}_1^{-1}\) and the symmetry of \(\boldsymbol{\Lambda}_1\):

\[ -\tfrac12(\mathbf{x}-\boldsymbol{\mu}_1)\T\boldsymbol{\Lambda}_1(\mathbf{x}-\boldsymbol{\mu}_1) = -\tfrac12\mathbf{x}\T\boldsymbol{\Lambda}_1\mathbf{x} + (\boldsymbol{\Lambda}_1\boldsymbol{\mu}_1)\T\mathbf{x} - \tfrac12\boldsymbol{\mu}_1\T\boldsymbol{\Lambda}_1\boldsymbol{\mu}_1 = -\tfrac12\mathbf{x}\T\boldsymbol{\Lambda}_1\mathbf{x} + \boldsymbol{\eta}_1\T\mathbf{x} + \text{const}. \]

So in information form a Gaussian is \(\exp(-\tfrac12\mathbf{x}\T\boldsymbol{\Lambda}\mathbf{x} + \boldsymbol{\eta}\T\mathbf{x})\) up to a constant factor: \(\boldsymbol{\Lambda}\) is the quadratic coefficient and \(\boldsymbol{\eta}\) the linear one. Add the second exponent:

\[ -\tfrac12\mathbf{x}\T(\boldsymbol{\Lambda}_1+\boldsymbol{\Lambda}_2)\mathbf{x} + (\boldsymbol{\eta}_1+\boldsymbol{\eta}_2)\T\mathbf{x} + \text{const}. \]

This is again a quadratic in \(\mathbf{x}\), so the product is a Gaussian, and reading off its coefficients gives \(\boldsymbol{\Lambda} = \boldsymbol{\Lambda}_1+\boldsymbol{\Lambda}_2\) and \(\boldsymbol{\eta} = \boldsymbol{\eta}_1+\boldsymbol{\eta}_2\). The covariance-form formulas in the table are these two additions with every \(\boldsymbol{\Lambda}\) written as \(\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{-1}\).

4. See it in two dimensions

A worked example first. Estimate A of a landmark is \(\boldsymbol{\mu}_A = (0, 0)\) with \(\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_A = \diag(4,\ 0.25)\): vague in \(x\) (σ = 2), sharp in \(y\) (σ = 0.5). Estimate B is \(\boldsymbol{\mu}_B = (2, 1)\) with \(\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_B = \diag(0.25,\ 4)\): the other way round.

\[ \boldsymbol{\Lambda} = \diag(0.25,\ 4) + \diag(4,\ 0.25) = \diag(4.25,\ 4.25), \qquad \boldsymbol{\eta} = \begin{bmatrix} 0 \\ 0 \end{bmatrix} + \begin{bmatrix} 4\times 2 \\ 0.25\times 1 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 8 \\ 0.25 \end{bmatrix}. \] \[ \boldsymbol{\mu} = \boldsymbol{\Lambda}^{-1}\boldsymbol{\eta} = \begin{bmatrix} 8/4.25 \\ 0.25/4.25 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 1.88 \\ 0.06 \end{bmatrix}, \qquad \boldsymbol{\Sigma} = \diag(0.235,\ 0.235),\quad \sigma = 0.49 \text{ in both directions}. \]

The fused estimate takes its \(x\) almost entirely from B and its \(y\) almost entirely from A: each is trusted where it is sharp.

Try it: drag the centres A and B, and turn the two ellipses with the sliders. Each ellipse is the 1σ contour of a Gaussian with half-axes 1.5 and 0.4.

Notice: at the default settings the two ellipses are at right angles and the fused ellipse is a circle of radius 0.39, tighter than the short axis of either input and a quarter of A's area. The fused mean is not midway between A and B; it sits near the point where the two long axes cross. Set both sliders to the same angle and the fused ellipse stays long (1.06 × 0.28), because neither estimate knows that direction. Drag A or B: the fused mean moves, but the fused ellipse never changes size.

Intuition

An elongated ellipse says "the landmark is somewhere along this line". Two such statements along different lines pin down a point, the way two bearings fix a ship's position. The last thing you noticed is a general property of linear-Gaussian fusion: the fused covariance depends on how good the measurements are, not on what they read.

5. Why the information matrix is sparse

The book's key sentence: the EKF's covariance matrix is dense, but its inverse, the information matrix, is very sparse with a predictable pattern, as long as past robot poses are kept in the state. §I.4.1 · p. 15 The smallest example shows why. A robot moves along a line through poses \(x_0, x_1, x_2\). There is a prior on \(x_0\) and two odometry measurements, \(u_1 = x_1 - x_0 + \text{noise}\) and \(u_2 = x_2 - x_1 + \text{noise}\), all with \(\sigma = 1\).

Each measurement is a Gaussian factor, and by Section 3 their information adds. The odometry factor \(u_1\) has exponent \(-\tfrac12(x_1-x_0-u_1)^2\). Its quadratic part is

\[ (x_1-x_0)^2 = x_0^2 - 2x_0x_1 + x_1^2 = \begin{bmatrix} x_0 & x_1 \end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix} 1 & -1 \\ -1 & 1 \end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix} x_0 \\ x_1 \end{bmatrix}, \]

so it adds the block \(\begin{bmatrix} 1 & -1 \\ -1 & 1 \end{bmatrix}\) to the rows and columns of \(x_0\) and \(x_1\), and nothing anywhere else. The prior adds 1 to the \((x_0,x_0)\) entry. Summing the three factors:

\[ \boldsymbol{\Lambda} = \underbrace{\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 \end{bmatrix}}_{\text{prior}} + \underbrace{\begin{bmatrix} 1 & -1 & 0 \\ -1 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 \end{bmatrix}}_{u_1} + \underbrace{\begin{bmatrix} 0 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & -1 \\ 0 & -1 & 1 \end{bmatrix}}_{u_2} = \begin{bmatrix} 2 & -1 & 0 \\ -1 & 2 & -1 \\ 0 & -1 & 1 \end{bmatrix}, \qquad \boldsymbol{\Sigma} = \boldsymbol{\Lambda}^{-1} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 1 & 1 \\ 1 & 2 & 2 \\ 1 & 2 & 3 \end{bmatrix}. \]

Check the inverse by multiplying: the first row of \(\boldsymbol{\Lambda}\) times the first column of \(\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\) is \(2 - 1 + 0 = 1\), times the second column is \(2 - 2 + 0 = 0\), and so on.

Read the two matrices. \(\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\) is full: every pose is correlated with every other, because an error in \(x_0\) is inherited by all later poses. Its diagonal, 1, 2, 3, is the random-walk drift from Day 1: one unit of variance per step. \(\boldsymbol{\Lambda}\) has a zero between \(x_0\) and \(x_2\) because no measurement involves both. For a chain of \(n\) poses, \(\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\) has \(n^2\) non-zero entries and \(\boldsymbol{\Lambda}\) has \(3n-2\). With \(n = 10{,}000\) that is \(10^8\) numbers against about 30,000. An EKF stores and updates \(\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\), which is the third EKF problem in the table of Section 1; a factor-graph solver works with \(\boldsymbol{\Lambda}\).

The condition "as long as past poses are kept" matters. A filter removes old poses from the state, and removing a variable from a Gaussian connects all the variables it was connected to, so the zeros of (oldsymbol{Lambda}) fill in. Keeping the whole trajectory makes the state larger but keeps (oldsymbol{Lambda}) sparse.

Common mistakes

  • "Fusing means averaging the covariances." Covariances never add when fusing estimates of the same quantity. Information matrices add; the fused covariance is smaller than either input.
  • "A zero in Λ means the two variables are uncorrelated." \(x_0\) and \(x_2\) have a zero in \(\boldsymbol{\Lambda}\) and covariance 1 in \(\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\). The zero means only that no factor links them directly.
  • "Filters are obsolete." The book's scope is factor graphs, but it says plainly that EKF-based estimators are still popular in visual-inertial odometry. §I.4.1 · p. 16

Check yourself

Q1. Which of these is NOT one of the three practical problems of EKF-SLAM listed in the book?

The EKF does represent landmark uncertainty: its covariance covers the robot pose and every landmark. That dense covariance is the source of the cost problem.

Q2. Two independent measurements of the same length have σ = 3 cm and σ = 4 cm. What is the σ of their fusion?

Information adds: 1/9 + 1/16 = 25/144, so σ² = 144/25 and σ = 12/5 = 2.4 cm. It is smaller than both inputs.

Q3. Estimate A has covariance diag(4, 1) and estimate B has covariance diag(1, 4). What is the covariance of their fusion?

Λ = diag(1/4, 1) + diag(1, 1/4) = diag(1.25, 1.25), so Σ = diag(0.8, 0.8). Better than the best input (variance 1) in both directions.

Q4. In the three-pose chain of Section 5, the robot adds a loop-closure measurement of x₂ − x₀ with σ = 1. How does Λ change?

The new factor adds the block [1 −1; −1 1] to the rows and columns of x₀ and x₂. A factor creates entries exactly between the variables it involves, so the zero fills in.

Recap

  1. EKF-SLAM suffered from outliers, from linearizing around drifting odometry, and from a dense covariance. Particle filters eased these but need many particles.
  2. Factor-graph optimization became dominant because the information matrix is sparse when the whole trajectory is kept.
  3. Information form: \(\boldsymbol{\Lambda} = \boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{-1}\), \(\boldsymbol{\eta} = \boldsymbol{\Lambda}\boldsymbol{\mu}\). Independent estimates fuse by adding \(\boldsymbol{\Lambda}\) and \(\boldsymbol{\eta}\).
  4. Each factor adds information only between the variables it touches. That is where the zeros of \(\boldsymbol{\Lambda}\) come from.
  5. Spatial AI extends SLAM's geometry with semantics. The book covers foundations (Part I), sensors (Part II), and trends (Part III).

Sources

  1. SLAM Handbook, Prelude to Part I, §I.4 "Past, Present, and Future of SLAM, and Scope of this Handbook" and §I.5 "Handbook Structure", pp. 13–18.
  2. Thrun, Burgard, Fox, Probabilistic Robotics, 2005, Chapter 3 (the information form of a Gaussian and the information filter).
  3. Barfoot, State Estimation for Robotics, 2017 (fusing Gaussian estimates; sparsity of the inverse covariance for a chain of poses).

Week 1 · Day 4

Linear least squares

After today you can set up a linear least-squares problem, derive and solve its normal equations by hand, weight measurements by their noise, and explain why the result is the Gaussian maximum likelihood estimate.

About 60 min · Re-read the Notation pages, pp. xiv–xv (2 pages) · Needs Week 1 Day 3

Read first: the Notation pages, pp. xiv–xv

There are no new pages today. Skim the notation tables at the front of the book for:

  • The three fonts (p. xiv): italic \(a\) is a scalar, bold lower-case \(\mathbf{a}\) a column vector, bold upper-case \(\mathbf{A}\) a matrix. Today's \(\mathbf{A}\), \(\mathbf{x}\), \(\mathbf{b}\) follow this.
  • \(p(\mathbf{a}\mid\mathbf{b})\), \(\N(\boldsymbol{\mu},\boldsymbol{\Sigma})\), and the L2 norm \(\norm{\mathbf{x}}_2 = \sqrt{\sum x_i^2}\) (p. xiv). Every norm today is an L2 norm.
  • The 3-D geometry table (p. xv): frames, rotation matrices, SO(3), SE(3). Only glance at it. You will need it when the course reaches Chapter 2.

Today's big idea

Almost every computation in a SLAM back-end ends in the same small problem: find the \(\mathbf{x}\) that makes \(\mathbf{A}\mathbf{x}\) as close as possible to \(\mathbf{b}\). The answer solves the normal equations \(\mathbf{A}\T\mathbf{A}\,\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{A}\T\mathbf{b}\). Dividing each equation by its noise level first turns this into the maximum likelihood estimate under Gaussian noise.

1. More equations than unknowns

A robot drives along a line at constant speed. Its position is measured at four times:

Time t (s)Measured position y (m)Prediction of guess (1, 1)ResidualPrediction of (1.5, 1)Residual
01101.5−0.5
13212.50.5
24313.50.5
34404.5−0.5

The model is \(y = x_1 + x_2\,t\), with two unknowns: the start position \(x_1\) and the speed \(x_2\). Each measurement gives one linear equation, \(x_1 + x_2 t_i = y_i\). Stack them:

\[ \underbrace{\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 1 \\ 1 & 2 \\ 1 & 3 \end{bmatrix}}_{\mathbf{A}} \underbrace{\begin{bmatrix} x_1 \\ x_2 \end{bmatrix}}_{\mathbf{x}} = \underbrace{\begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 3 \\ 4 \\ 4 \end{bmatrix}}_{\mathbf{b}} . \]

Four equations, two unknowns: the system is overdetermined, and because the measurements are noisy no \(\mathbf{x}\) satisfies all four. For any candidate \(\mathbf{x}\) the residual \(\mathbf{r} = \mathbf{b} - \mathbf{A}\mathbf{x}\) lists how far each equation is from holding. The least-squares solution is the candidate with the smallest sum of squared residuals:

\[ \mathbf{x}^\star = \argmin_{\mathbf{x}}\ \norm{\mathbf{A}\mathbf{x}-\mathbf{b}}_2^2 = \argmin_{\mathbf{x}}\ \sum_i r_i^2 . \]

In the table, the guess \((1, 1)\) has cost \(0+1+1+0 = 2\). The line \((1.5, 1)\) has cost \(4\times 0.25 = 1\), and the next section shows that nothing does better. The book writes this problem as equation (1.24b), with the unknown called \(\boldsymbol{\delta}\) because there it is a correction to a current guess. §1.3.2 · p. 31

2. The normal equations

The minimizer satisfies a square linear system, the normal equations, which is the book's equation (1.25): §1.3.3 · p. 31

\[ \mathbf{A}\T\mathbf{A}\,\mathbf{x}^\star = \mathbf{A}\T\mathbf{b}. \]

For the example,

\[ \mathbf{A}\T\mathbf{A} = \begin{bmatrix} 4 & 6 \\ 6 & 14 \end{bmatrix}, \qquad \mathbf{A}\T\mathbf{b} = \begin{bmatrix} 12 \\ 23 \end{bmatrix}. \]

The entries have plain meanings: 4 is the number of points, 6 is \(\sum t_i\), 14 is \(\sum t_i^2\), 12 is \(\sum y_i\), and 23 is \(\sum t_i y_i\). Solve \(4x_1+6x_2 = 12\) and \(6x_1+14x_2 = 23\): multiply the first by 1.5 and subtract it from the second to get \(5x_2 = 5\), so \(x_2 = 1\) and then \(x_1 = (12-6)/4 = 1.5\). The best line is \(y = 1.5 + 1.0\,t\).

Filling the gap: where the normal equations come from

Write the cost as a function \(f(\mathbf{x})\) and expand the square. The two cross terms are equal because each is a scalar and a scalar equals its transpose:

\[ f(\mathbf{x}) = (\mathbf{A}\mathbf{x}-\mathbf{b})\T(\mathbf{A}\mathbf{x}-\mathbf{b}) = \mathbf{x}\T\mathbf{A}\T\mathbf{A}\mathbf{x} - 2\,\mathbf{b}\T\mathbf{A}\mathbf{x} + \mathbf{b}\T\mathbf{b}. \]

Two differentiation rules are all you need: \(\nabla_{\mathbf{x}}(\mathbf{c}\T\mathbf{x}) = \mathbf{c}\) and, for a symmetric matrix \(\mathbf{Q}\), \(\nabla_{\mathbf{x}}(\mathbf{x}\T\mathbf{Q}\mathbf{x}) = 2\mathbf{Q}\mathbf{x}\). They are the vector versions of \((cx)' = c\) and \((qx^2)' = 2qx\). With \(\mathbf{Q} = \mathbf{A}\T\mathbf{A}\) and \(\mathbf{c} = \mathbf{A}\T\mathbf{b}\):

\[ \nabla f(\mathbf{x}) = 2\,\mathbf{A}\T\mathbf{A}\mathbf{x} - 2\,\mathbf{A}\T\mathbf{b} = \mathbf{0} \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \mathbf{A}\T\mathbf{A}\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{A}\T\mathbf{b}. \]

Is this stationary point a minimum, and the only one? The second derivative of \(f\) is the constant matrix \(2\mathbf{A}\T\mathbf{A}\). For any direction \(\mathbf{v}\), \(\mathbf{v}\T\mathbf{A}\T\mathbf{A}\mathbf{v} = \norm{\mathbf{A}\mathbf{v}}_2^2 \ge 0\), so \(f\) curves upward everywhere. If the columns of \(\mathbf{A}\) are linearly independent (\(\mathbf{A}\) has full column rank), then \(\mathbf{A}\mathbf{v}\neq\mathbf{0}\) whenever \(\mathbf{v}\neq\mathbf{0}\), the curvature is strictly positive in every direction, and \(f\) is a bowl with exactly one lowest point. If the columns are dependent, a whole line of \(\mathbf{x}\) values gives the same cost. That happens in SLAM when nothing anchors the map: with odometry only and no prior, shifting every pose by the same amount changes no residual.

The normal equations also have a geometric reading. Move everything to one side: \(\mathbf{A}\T(\mathbf{b}-\mathbf{A}\mathbf{x}^\star) = \mathbf{0}\). Each row of \(\mathbf{A}\T\) is a column of \(\mathbf{A}\), so this says that the residual is perpendicular ("normal") to every column of \(\mathbf{A}\).

Check it on the example: \(\mathbf{r} = (-0.5,\ 0.5,\ 0.5,\ -0.5)\). Its dot product with the first column \((1,1,1,1)\) is 0, and with the second column \((0,1,2,3)\) it is \(0.5+1-1.5 = 0\).

3. Weights: trusting some measurements more

Plain least squares treats every equation alike. If measurement \(i\) has noise standard deviation \(\sigma_i\), a residual should count in units of its own \(\sigma_i\). Weighted least squares minimizes \(\sum_i r_i^2/\sigma_i^2\). With the covariance matrix \(\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\) of the measurement noise (diagonal with entries \(\sigma_i^2\) when the noises are independent) this is

\[ \norm{\mathbf{A}\mathbf{x}-\mathbf{b}}^2_{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}} = (\mathbf{A}\mathbf{x}-\mathbf{b})\T\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{-1}(\mathbf{A}\mathbf{x}-\mathbf{b}), \qquad\text{solved by}\qquad \mathbf{A}\T\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{-1}\mathbf{A}\,\mathbf{x}^\star = \mathbf{A}\T\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{-1}\mathbf{b}. \]

The quantity \(\norm{\mathbf{e}}^2_{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}} = \mathbf{e}\T\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{-1}\mathbf{e}\) is the squared Mahalanobis distance, the book's equation (1.10). §1.2.2 · p. 27 It measures an error in standard deviations. Example: \(\mathbf{e} = (3, 1)\) with \(\boldsymbol{\Sigma} = \diag(9,\ 0.25)\) gives \(9/9 + 1/0.25 = 1 + 4 = 5\). The first component is 3 units off where \(\sigma = 3\): one sigma. The second is 1 unit off where \(\sigma = 0.5\): two sigma, so it contributes four times as much, although it is the smaller number.

You never need a separate weighted solver. Divide row \(i\) of \(\mathbf{A}\) and entry \(i\) of \(\mathbf{b}\) by \(\sigma_i\) (in general, multiply both by \(\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{-1/2}\)) and the weighted problem becomes a plain one. This is whitening, and the book does it once in equations (1.22)–(1.23) and then drops the covariances from the notation. §1.3.1 · p. 30 Whitening also removes units, so rows that came from ranges in metres and rows that came from angles in radians can sit in the same \(\mathbf{A}\).

Try it: the amber measurement disagrees with the other five. Change how much noise you believe it has. You can also drag any point.

Notice: at σ = 1 the weighted line and the equal-weight line coincide, and the single amber point tilts the fit a long way because it sits far out at the right end. Raise its σ to 5 and the solid line swings back onto the other five points, while the amber residual, though large, is under one of its own σ. Lower σ to 0.2 and the line passes almost through the amber point.

In plain words

Six witnesses describe the same event. Least squares finds the story that disagrees with all of them as little as possible. Weights say how reliable each witness is. A witness you barely trust (large σ) can be far from the final story without it counting for much.

4. Why squares? Gaussian maximum likelihood

Squaring the residuals is not a matter of taste. It is what Gaussian noise implies.

Filling the gap: weighted least squares is the MLE

Let \(\mathbf{a}_i\T\) be row \(i\) of \(\mathbf{A}\), and suppose \(b_i = \mathbf{a}_i\T\mathbf{x} + \eta_i\) with independent noises \(\eta_i\sim\N(0,\sigma_i^2)\). Independence makes the likelihood of all the measurements a product:

\[ p(\mathbf{b}\mid\mathbf{x}) = \prod_i \frac{1}{\sigma_i\sqrt{2\pi}}\exp\!\left(-\frac{(b_i-\mathbf{a}_i\T\mathbf{x})^2}{2\sigma_i^2}\right). \]

Take the negative logarithm. The product becomes a sum and the factors in front become a constant that does not depend on \(\mathbf{x}\):

\[ -\log p(\mathbf{b}\mid\mathbf{x}) = \tfrac12\sum_i \frac{(b_i-\mathbf{a}_i\T\mathbf{x})^2}{\sigma_i^2} + \text{const} = \tfrac12\norm{\mathbf{A}\mathbf{x}-\mathbf{b}}^2_{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}} + \text{const}. \]

Maximizing the likelihood is minimizing its negative log, so \(\mathbf{x}^{\text{MLE}}\) is the weighted least-squares solution. A Gaussian prior on \(\mathbf{x}\) contributes one more squared term of the same kind, as in the function \(J(x)\) of Day 2, so MAP estimation is least squares with a few extra rows.

The same matrix tells you how good the answer is. The solution \(\mathbf{x}^\star = \boldsymbol{\Lambda}^{-1}\mathbf{A}\T\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{-1}\mathbf{b}\), with \(\boldsymbol{\Lambda} = \mathbf{A}\T\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{-1}\mathbf{A}\), is a linear function of \(\mathbf{b}\), and \(\mathbf{b}\) has covariance \(\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\). A linear map \(\mathbf{M}\) turns a covariance \(\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\) into \(\mathbf{M}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\mathbf{M}\T\), so

\[ \cov(\mathbf{x}^\star) = \boldsymbol{\Lambda}^{-1}\mathbf{A}\T\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{-1}\,\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\,\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{-1}\mathbf{A}\boldsymbol{\Lambda}^{-1} = \boldsymbol{\Lambda}^{-1}\boldsymbol{\Lambda}\boldsymbol{\Lambda}^{-1} = \boldsymbol{\Lambda}^{-1}. \]

So \(\boldsymbol{\Lambda} = \mathbf{A}\T\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{-1}\mathbf{A} = \sum_i \mathbf{a}_i\mathbf{a}_i\T/\sigma_i^2\) is the information matrix of Day 3: every measurement row adds its own piece of information. The book gives \(\mathbf{A}\T\mathbf{A}\) (after whitening) exactly this name in equation (1.26). §1.3.3 · p. 31

In the example with every \(\sigma_i = 1\) m:

\[ \boldsymbol{\Lambda} = \begin{bmatrix} 4 & 6 \\ 6 & 14 \end{bmatrix}, \qquad \boldsymbol{\Lambda}^{-1} = \frac{1}{20}\begin{bmatrix} 14 & -6 \\ -6 & 4 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 0.7 & -0.3 \\ -0.3 & 0.2 \end{bmatrix}. \]

The start position is known to \(\sqrt{0.7} = 0.84\) m and the speed to \(\sqrt{0.2} = 0.45\) m/s. Four measurements of 1 m quality give an estimate better than any one of them.

Common mistakes

  • "Least squares minimizes the perpendicular distance from the points to the line." It minimizes the error in the measured quantity, here the vertical distance. The perpendicularity in the figure is in the space of measurement vectors, not in the plot of the data.
  • "A larger σ gives a measurement more weight." The weight is \(1/\sigma^2\). Doubling σ quarters the weight.
  • "The subscript in \(\norm{\mathbf{e}}_{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}\) means multiply by Σ." The subscript names the covariance; the formula uses its inverse.
  • "If \(\mathbf{A}\T\mathbf{A}\) is singular, the software is at fault." A singular \(\mathbf{A}\T\mathbf{A}\) means the measurements do not determine \(\mathbf{x}\). The cure is another measurement or a prior.

Check yourself

Q1. Three equally good measurements of one unknown x read 2, 3, and 7. What is the least-squares estimate?

A is a column of three ones, so AᵀA = 3 and Aᵀb = 12. The estimate is 12/3 = 4, the mean. The mean is the least-squares answer to "one number that fits them all".

Q2. Two measurements of one unknown: 10 with σ = 1 and 16 with σ = 2. What is the weighted least-squares estimate?

Weights are 1/σ²: 1 and 0.25. (10 × 1 + 16 × 0.25) / (1 + 0.25) = 14 / 1.25 = 11.2. This is the fusion rule of Day 3.

Q3. At the least-squares solution, what is true of the residual r = b − A x?

The normal equations are Aᵀr = 0: the residual has zero dot product with each column of A. It is zero only if the equations happen to be consistent.

Q4. An error e = (4, 1) has covariance diag(4, 1). What is its squared Mahalanobis distance?

eᵀΣ⁻¹e = 16/4 + 1/1 = 5. The value 17 is the plain squared length, and 3 comes from dividing by σ instead of σ².

Q5. One row of a least-squares problem reads x₁ + 2x₂ = 5, from a sensor with σ = 0.1. What is the whitened row?

Whitening divides the row and its right-hand side by σ, here multiplying by 10. Squaring the whitened residual then gives the 1/σ² = 100 weight.

Recap

  1. Least squares picks the \(\mathbf{x}\) that minimizes \(\norm{\mathbf{A}\mathbf{x}-\mathbf{b}}_2^2\), the sum of squared residuals.
  2. The minimizer solves the normal equations \(\mathbf{A}\T\mathbf{A}\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{A}\T\mathbf{b}\), and is unique when \(\mathbf{A}\) has full column rank. The residual is orthogonal to the columns of \(\mathbf{A}\).
  3. Weighted least squares minimizes the Mahalanobis norm \(\norm{\mathbf{A}\mathbf{x}-\mathbf{b}}^2_{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}\). Whitening (dividing each row by its σ) reduces it to the plain problem.
  4. Under independent Gaussian noise the weighted least-squares solution is the maximum likelihood estimate.
  5. \(\boldsymbol{\Lambda} = \mathbf{A}\T\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{-1}\mathbf{A}\) is the information matrix of the estimate, and \(\boldsymbol{\Lambda}^{-1}\) is its covariance.

Sources

  1. SLAM Handbook, Notation, pp. xiv–xv; equation (1.10), p. 27, and equations (1.22)–(1.26), pp. 30–31, quoted ahead of Week 2.
  2. Strang, Introduction to Linear Algebra, 2016, Chapter 4 (projections, least squares, the normal equations).
  3. Barfoot, State Estimation for Robotics, 2017 (least squares as Gaussian maximum likelihood; covariance of the estimate).

Week 1 · Day 5

Cholesky, QR, SVD: the factorizations behind every solver

After today you can test a matrix for positive definiteness, solve normal equations by Cholesky factorization and by QR, read a condition number from singular values, and explain why solvers never form a matrix inverse.

About 60 min · Re-read two paragraphs on pp. 13 and 15 · Needs Week 1 Day 4

Read first: two paragraphs you have already read, pp. 13 and 15

There are no new pages today. Re-read, with yesterday's least squares in mind:

  • The geodesy paragraph on p. 13. Cholesky was a surveyor. His factorization came out of map-making, and Section 2 below is that method.
  • The paragraph on p. 15 that begins "Between 2005 and 2015". Optimization was once "too slow", and sparsity made it practical. Today shows what solving means, and Section 5 shows why sparsity survives it.
  • Optional preview: §1.3.3 on pp. 31–32 states today's material in half a page. You will read it properly in Week 2.

Today's big idea

A solver never computes \(\boldsymbol{\Lambda}^{-1}\). It factors a matrix into triangular or orthogonal pieces and then substitutes. Cholesky factors the information matrix \(\boldsymbol{\Lambda} = \mathbf{A}\T\mathbf{A}\). QR factors \(\mathbf{A}\) itself and is more accurate. The SVD tells you, through the condition number, how much accuracy there is to lose.

1. Positive definite matrices

A symmetric matrix \(\boldsymbol{\Lambda}\) is positive definite if \(\mathbf{v}\T\boldsymbol{\Lambda}\mathbf{v} \gt 0\) for every \(\mathbf{v}\neq\mathbf{0}\), and positive semidefinite if \(\mathbf{v}\T\boldsymbol{\Lambda}\mathbf{v}\ge 0\). You proved yesterday that \(\mathbf{A}\T\mathbf{A}\) is always positive semidefinite, since \(\mathbf{v}\T\mathbf{A}\T\mathbf{A}\mathbf{v} = \norm{\mathbf{A}\mathbf{v}}_2^2\), and positive definite exactly when \(\mathbf{A}\) has full column rank. Covariance and information matrices are of this kind. For a symmetric matrix these statements are equivalent:

TestOn [4 6; 6 14]On [1 3; 3 1]
All eigenvalues are positive16.81 and 1.19: yes4 and −2: no
For a 2 × 2: top-left entry and determinant are positive4 and 20: yes1 and −8: no
Cholesky factorization runs to the end (Section 2)YesFails at √(1 − 9)

For the second matrix, \(\mathbf{v} = (1,-1)\) gives \(\mathbf{v}\T\boldsymbol{\Lambda}\mathbf{v} = 1 - 6 + 1 = -4\). Positive definiteness is what makes a least-squares cost a bowl with one lowest point.

2. Cholesky: a triangular square root

Every symmetric positive definite matrix can be written as

\[ \boldsymbol{\Lambda} = \mathbf{R}\T\mathbf{R}, \qquad \mathbf{R}\ \text{upper triangular with a positive diagonal.} \]

\(\mathbf{R}\) is the Cholesky factor. This is the book's equation (1.26); many other texts use the lower-triangular \(\mathbf{L} = \mathbf{R}\T\) instead. §1.3.3 · p. 31 Triangular systems are solved by substitution, one unknown at a time, so the normal equations \(\mathbf{R}\T\mathbf{R}\,\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{A}\T\mathbf{b}\) split into two easy solves, equations (1.27) and (1.28):

\[ \mathbf{R}\T\mathbf{y} = \mathbf{A}\T\mathbf{b}\ \ \text{(forward substitution, top row first)}, \qquad \mathbf{R}\,\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{y}\ \ \text{(back substitution, bottom row first)}. \]

Filling the gap: computing R by matching entries

Multiply out a general 2 × 2 factor and compare with \(\boldsymbol{\Lambda}\), entry by entry:

\[ \mathbf{R}\T\mathbf{R} = \begin{bmatrix} r_{11} & 0 \\ r_{12} & r_{22} \end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix} r_{11} & r_{12} \\ 0 & r_{22} \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} r_{11}^2 & r_{11}r_{12} \\ r_{11}r_{12} & r_{12}^2+r_{22}^2 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 4 & 6 \\ 6 & 14 \end{bmatrix}. \]

Top-left: \(r_{11} = \sqrt4 = 2\). Top-right: \(r_{12} = 6/2 = 3\). Bottom-right: \(r_{22} = \sqrt{14-3^2} = \sqrt5 \approx 2.236\). Each entry of \(\boldsymbol{\Lambda}\) gave one new entry of \(\mathbf{R}\), in an order where everything else was already known. The general algorithm does the same, row by row:

for i = 1 … n:
    r[i][i] = sqrt( Λ[i][i] − Σ_{k<i} r[k][i]² )        # fails here if Λ is not positive definite
    for j = i+1 … n:
        r[i][j] = ( Λ[i][j] − Σ_{k<i} r[k][i]·r[k][j] ) / r[i][i]

Now solve yesterday's normal equations with it. Forward: \(2y_1 = 12\) gives \(y_1 = 6\); then \(3y_1 + \sqrt5\,y_2 = 23\) gives \(y_2 = 5/\sqrt5 = \sqrt5\). Back: \(\sqrt5\,x_2 = \sqrt5\) gives \(x_2 = 1\); then \(2x_1 + 3x_2 = 6\) gives \(x_1 = 1.5\). The same answer as yesterday, with no inverse in sight.

For a dense \(n\times n\) matrix the factorization costs about \(n^3/3\) operations §1.3.3 · p. 31 and each substitution about \(n^2\). The factorization is the expensive part, and Section 5 explains why sparsity makes it cheap in SLAM.

3. QR: factor A, not AᵀA

The QR factorization writes the tall matrix itself as \(\mathbf{A} = \mathbf{Q}\mathbf{R}\), where the columns of \(\mathbf{Q}\) are orthonormal (\(\mathbf{Q}\T\mathbf{Q} = \mathbf{I}\)) and \(\mathbf{R}\) is \(n\times n\) upper triangular. Two consequences follow in one line each:

\[ \mathbf{A}\T\mathbf{A} = \mathbf{R}\T\mathbf{Q}\T\mathbf{Q}\mathbf{R} = \mathbf{R}\T\mathbf{R}, \qquad\qquad \mathbf{R}\T\mathbf{R}\,\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{R}\T\mathbf{Q}\T\mathbf{b}\ \Longrightarrow\ \mathbf{R}\,\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{Q}\T\mathbf{b}. \]

The first says that the \(\mathbf{R}\) of QR is the Cholesky factor of \(\mathbf{A}\T\mathbf{A}\) (up to the signs of its rows), which is the book's equation (1.33). The second says that the least-squares solution needs one back substitution, and \(\mathbf{A}\T\mathbf{A}\) is never formed. §1.3.3 · p. 32

The easiest way to compute a QR by hand is Gram–Schmidt: make the columns of \(\mathbf{A}\) orthonormal one at a time. For yesterday's \(\mathbf{A}\), with columns \(\mathbf{a}_1 = (1,1,1,1)\) and \(\mathbf{a}_2 = (0,1,2,3)\):

StepComputationResult
Normalize the first column\(r_{11} = \norm{\mathbf{a}_1}_2 = 2\), \(\mathbf{q}_1 = \mathbf{a}_1/2\)\(\mathbf{q}_1 = (0.5,\ 0.5,\ 0.5,\ 0.5)\)
Measure how much of the second column lies along it\(r_{12} = \mathbf{q}_1\T\mathbf{a}_2 = (0+1+2+3)/2\)\(r_{12} = 3\)
Remove that part\(\mathbf{v} = \mathbf{a}_2 - 3\,\mathbf{q}_1\)\(\mathbf{v} = (-1.5,\ -0.5,\ 0.5,\ 1.5)\)
Normalize what is left\(r_{22} = \norm{\mathbf{v}}_2 = \sqrt{2.25+0.25+0.25+2.25}\), \(\mathbf{q}_2 = \mathbf{v}/r_{22}\)\(r_{22} = \sqrt5\)
Rotate the right-hand side\(\mathbf{q}_1\T\mathbf{b} = 12/2\), \(\ \mathbf{q}_2\T\mathbf{b} = (-1.5-1.5+2+6)/\sqrt5\)\(\mathbf{Q}\T\mathbf{b} = (6,\ \sqrt5)\)

\(\mathbf{R} = \begin{bmatrix} 2 & 3 \\ 0 & \sqrt5 \end{bmatrix}\) is the Cholesky factor from Section 2, and \(\mathbf{Q}\T\mathbf{b} = (6, \sqrt5)\) is the vector \(\mathbf{y}\) found there by forward substitution. Back substitution again gives \(\mathbf{x} = (1.5,\ 1)\).

The book uses a full \(m\times m\) matrix \(\mathbf{Q}\) and splits \(\mathbf{Q}\T\mathbf{b}\) into a top part \(\mathbf{d}\) (our \((6,\sqrt5)\)) and a bottom part \(\mathbf{e}\), with \(\norm{\mathbf{e}}_2^2\) equal to the least-squares cost; this is equations (1.29)–(1.32). §1.3.3 · p. 32 You can check that without finding \(\mathbf{e}\): an orthogonal \(\mathbf{Q}\) preserves length, so \(\norm{\mathbf{e}}^2 = \norm{\mathbf{b}}^2 - \norm{\mathbf{d}}^2 = 42 - (36+5) = 1\), which is yesterday's cost. Real libraries build \(\mathbf{Q}\) from Householder reflections, which are more stable than Gram–Schmidt, and never store it. The book states that QR is more accurate and more stable than Cholesky on the normal equations, and about twice as slow when there are many more rows than columns. §1.3.3 · pp. 31–32 Section 4 shows where the accuracy comes from.

4. The SVD and the condition number

The singular value decomposition (SVD) writes any \(m\times n\) matrix as \(\mathbf{A} = \mathbf{U}\mathbf{S}\mathbf{V}\T\), where \(\mathbf{U}\) and \(\mathbf{V}\) have orthonormal columns and \(\mathbf{S} = \diag(s_1,\dots,s_n)\) holds the singular values \(s_1\ge s_2\ge\dots\ge s_n\ge 0\). (Most texts call the middle matrix \(\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\); here that letter is taken by covariances.) In words: \(\mathbf{A}\) rotates, stretches each axis by \(s_i\), and rotates again. The number of non-zero singular values is the rank. The ratio of the largest stretch to the smallest is the condition number:

\[ \kappa(\mathbf{A}) = \frac{s_{\max}}{s_{\min}} . \]

Filling the gap: why κ is the error amplifier

Take a square system \(\mathbf{A}\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{b}\) and disturb the right-hand side by \(\delta\mathbf{b}\). The solution moves by \(\delta\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{A}^{-1}\delta\mathbf{b}\). The inverse stretches by at most \(1/s_{\min}\), so \(\norm{\delta\mathbf{x}} \le \norm{\delta\mathbf{b}}/s_{\min}\). And \(\mathbf{A}\) stretches by at most \(s_{\max}\), so \(\norm{\mathbf{b}} = \norm{\mathbf{A}\mathbf{x}} \le s_{\max}\norm{\mathbf{x}}\), that is \(1/\norm{\mathbf{x}} \le s_{\max}/\norm{\mathbf{b}}\). Multiply the two inequalities:

\[ \frac{\norm{\delta\mathbf{x}}}{\norm{\mathbf{x}}} \ \le\ \frac{s_{\max}}{s_{\min}}\,\frac{\norm{\delta\mathbf{b}}}{\norm{\mathbf{b}}} = \kappa(\mathbf{A})\,\frac{\norm{\delta\mathbf{b}}}{\norm{\mathbf{b}}}. \]

A relative error in the data can grow by a factor of up to \(\kappa\) in the answer. Computer arithmetic makes relative errors of about \(10^{-16}\) in double precision and \(10^{-7}\) in single precision at every step, so as a rule of thumb you lose about \(\log_{10}\kappa\) of your digits.

Now the key fact. Substituting the SVD, \(\mathbf{A}\T\mathbf{A} = \mathbf{V}\mathbf{S}\mathbf{U}\T\mathbf{U}\mathbf{S}\mathbf{V}\T = \mathbf{V}\mathbf{S}^2\mathbf{V}\T\). The eigenvalues of \(\mathbf{A}\T\mathbf{A}\) are the squares \(s_i^2\), so

\[ \kappa(\mathbf{A}\T\mathbf{A}) = \frac{s_{\max}^2}{s_{\min}^2} = \kappa(\mathbf{A})^2 . \]

Forming the normal equations squares the condition number and doubles the digits you lose. QR works on \(\mathbf{A}\) and avoids the squaring. For yesterday's \(\mathbf{A}\): the eigenvalues of \(\mathbf{A}\T\mathbf{A}\) are \(9\pm\sqrt{61}\), that is 16.81 and 1.19, so \(s = 4.10\) and \(1.09\), \(\kappa(\mathbf{A}) = 3.76\), and \(\kappa(\mathbf{A}\T\mathbf{A}) = 14.1\). That problem is harmless. The next one is not.

Try it: two poses \(x_1, x_2\) with a precise odometry measurement \(x_2 - x_1 = 1\) and an imprecise GPS fix on each. After whitening, the GPS rows are multiplied by the small number ε = (odometry σ)/(GPS σ):

\[ \mathbf{A} = \begin{bmatrix} -1 & 1 \\ \varepsilon & 0 \\ 0 & \varepsilon \end{bmatrix}, \qquad \mathbf{A}\T\mathbf{A} = \begin{bmatrix} 1+\varepsilon^2 & -1 \\ -1 & 1+\varepsilon^2 \end{bmatrix}, \qquad \kappa(\mathbf{A}) = \frac{\sqrt{2+\varepsilon^2}}{\varepsilon}. \]

Notice: at the default ratio of 100, κ(A) is 141 and κ(AᵀA) is about 20,000. Single precision carries about 7 digits. The normal equations are already wrong in the fourth digit (relative error near 2 × 10⁻⁴), and QR is right to 7 digits. Move the slider to the right: the pink curve rises like κ², and beyond a ratio of about 4,000 Cholesky fails, because 1 + ε² rounds to exactly 1 and AᵀA becomes singular. QR is unaffected all the way.

The exact answer tends to \((0.25,\ 1.25)\) as the GPS gets worse: the difference is the odometry's 1 and the midpoint is the GPS's 0.75. The information about the midpoint is the \(\varepsilon^2\) in \(\mathbf{A}\T\mathbf{A}\), and once rounding erases it the normal equations have lost the GPS completely. In double precision the same thing happens near a ratio of \(10^8\), and at a ratio of \(10^4\) the normal equations already give up 8 of 16 digits.

5. Never invert

The formula \(\mathbf{x} = \boldsymbol{\Lambda}^{-1}\mathbf{A}\T\mathbf{b}\) is for paper. In code, three things are wrong with it.

Problem with the inverseWhat factor-and-substitute does instead
Cost: computing \(\boldsymbol{\Lambda}^{-1}\) means solving \(n\) systems, one per columnSolves one system
Accuracy: multiplying by a computed inverse adds rounding errorSubstitution is backward stable
Sparsity: the inverse of a sparse matrix is usually denseThe triangular factor of a sparse matrix can stay sparse

The third is the one that matters in SLAM, and you have already seen it. On Day 3 the chain of three poses had a tridiagonal \(\boldsymbol{\Lambda}\) and a completely full \(\boldsymbol{\Lambda}^{-1}\). Its Cholesky factor is

\[ \boldsymbol{\Lambda} = \begin{bmatrix} 2 & -1 & 0 \\ -1 & 2 & -1 \\ 0 & -1 & 1 \end{bmatrix} = \mathbf{R}\T\mathbf{R}, \qquad \mathbf{R} = \begin{bmatrix} 1.414 & -0.707 & 0 \\ 0 & 1.225 & -0.816 \\ 0 & 0 & 0.577 \end{bmatrix}. \]

The zero survived. For a chain of \(n\) poses \(\mathbf{R}\) has \(2n-1\) non-zeros, against \(n^2\) for the inverse, and both the factorization and the substitutions take time proportional to \(n\). This is the "close-to-linear complexity" of the history on p. 15. §I.4.1 · p. 15

FactorizationFormWorks onUse it for
Cholesky\(\boldsymbol{\Lambda} = \mathbf{R}\T\mathbf{R}\)Symmetric positive definite matricesThe fastest solve of the normal equations
QR\(\mathbf{A} = \mathbf{Q}\mathbf{R}\)Any \(\mathbf{A}\) with full column rankLeast squares without squaring κ
SVD\(\mathbf{A} = \mathbf{U}\mathbf{S}\mathbf{V}\T\)Any matrixRank, condition number, diagnosing a badly posed problem; the most expensive of the three

Common mistakes

  • "A tiny determinant means the matrix is ill-conditioned." The matrix \(0.001\,\mathbf{I}\) has a tiny determinant and κ = 1. Conditioning is about the ratio of singular values, not their size.
  • "QR and Cholesky give different answers." In exact arithmetic they give the same \(\mathbf{R}\) and the same \(\mathbf{x}\). They differ only in how rounding error enters.
  • "Ill-conditioning is a bug in the solver." It is a property of the problem: some direction of \(\mathbf{x}\) is barely measured. A better solver loses fewer digits, but only better measurements fix it.

Check yourself

Q1. What is the Cholesky factor R (upper triangular, RᵀR = Λ) of the matrix with rows (9, 6) and (6, 5)?

r₁₁ = √9 = 3, r₁₂ = 6/3 = 2, r₂₂ = √(5 − 2²) = 1. Check: RᵀR has rows (9, 6) and (6, 4 + 1).

Q2. Which of these symmetric matrices is NOT positive definite?

Its determinant is 3 − 4 = −1, so one eigenvalue is negative. Cholesky would fail at r₂₂ = √(3 − 2²). The others have a positive top-left entry and a positive determinant.

Q3. A has singular values 20 and 0.02. Roughly how many decimal digits do the normal equations lose, compared with QR?

κ(A) = 20/0.02 = 1,000, costing about 3 digits. The normal equations work with κ(AᵀA) = κ(A)² = 10⁶, costing about 6.

Q4. A 3 × 3 matrix has singular values 10, 2, and 0. Which statement is right?

Two non-zero singular values means rank 2. One direction is mapped to zero, κ is infinite, and Ax = b cannot have a unique solution.

Q5. Why does a SLAM solver factor Λ instead of inverting it?

The inverse exists and gives the same x in exact arithmetic. The point is cost: the inverse of the sparse information matrix is the dense covariance, with n² entries.

Recap

  1. \(\mathbf{A}\T\mathbf{A}\) is positive definite when \(\mathbf{A}\) has full column rank; then it has a Cholesky factor, \(\boldsymbol{\Lambda} = \mathbf{R}\T\mathbf{R}\).
  2. Cholesky solves the normal equations with one factorization and two triangular substitutions.
  3. QR factors \(\mathbf{A} = \mathbf{Q}\mathbf{R}\) and solves \(\mathbf{R}\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{Q}\T\mathbf{b}\). Its \(\mathbf{R}\) is the Cholesky factor of \(\mathbf{A}\T\mathbf{A}\).
  4. The condition number \(\kappa = s_{\max}/s_{\min}\) bounds how much relative error grows. The normal equations square it.
  5. Never form an inverse: factor and substitute. The factor of a sparse matrix can stay sparse; the inverse cannot.

Sources

  1. SLAM Handbook, §I.4.1, pp. 13 and 15; §1.3.3 "Matrix Factorization for Least Squares", equations (1.25)–(1.33), pp. 31–32, quoted ahead of Week 2.
  2. Trefethen and Bau, Numerical Linear Algebra, 1997 (QR by Gram–Schmidt and Householder, conditioning of least squares, stability of the normal equations).
  3. Golub and Van Loan, Matrix Computations, 2013 (Cholesky factorization, the SVD, condition numbers).

Week 1 · Review

Week 1 review: the SLAM problem and its toolkit

After today you can describe a SLAM system and its history in a few sentences, fuse Gaussian estimates in information form, and solve a small weighted least-squares problem by hand with a Cholesky factorization.

About 60 min · No new pages

The week in one paragraph

SLAM estimates a robot's trajectory and a map together. A sensor-specific front-end turns raw data into odometry, landmark observations, and loop closures; a back-end finds the trajectory and map that fit them best. Odometry alone drifts, and loop closures bound the drift. The back-end serves a fast control loop and a slow planning loop and must stay online. Its history runs from the EKF through particle filters to factor-graph optimization, which won because the information matrix is sparse. The math underneath is short: beliefs are Gaussians, Bayes' rule combines them, independent information adds, and the MAP estimate under Gaussian noise is a weighted least-squares problem, solved by factoring a matrix and never by inverting it.

1. Formula sheet

What it isFormulaWhere
Measurement model\(\mathbf{z}_i = h_i(\mathbf{x}) + \boldsymbol{\eta}_i\)§I.2, p. 5 · Day 1
Bayes' rule, MAP, and MLE\(p(x\mid z)\propto p(z\mid x)\,p(x)\); \(\ x^{\text{MAP}} = \argmax_x p(z\mid x)p(x)\); \(\ x^{\text{MLE}} = \argmax_x p(z\mid x)\)Named in §I.4.1, p. 15 · Day 2
Gaussian density\(\N(\boldsymbol{\theta};\boldsymbol{\mu},\boldsymbol{\Sigma}) = \frac{1}{\sqrt{|2\pi\boldsymbol{\Sigma}|}}\exp\!\big(-\tfrac12\norm{\boldsymbol{\theta}-\boldsymbol{\mu}}^2_{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}\big)\)Equation (1.9), p. 27 · Day 2
Scalar prior plus measurement\(\hat{x} = \check{x} + K(z-\check{x})\), \(K = \frac{\check{\sigma}^2}{\check{\sigma}^2+\sigma_z^2}\), \(\ \frac{1}{\hat{\sigma}^2} = \frac{1}{\check{\sigma}^2}+\frac{1}{\sigma_z^2}\)Day 2
Information form and fusion\(\boldsymbol{\Lambda} = \boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{-1}\), \(\boldsymbol{\eta} = \boldsymbol{\Lambda}\boldsymbol{\mu}\); fusing: \(\boldsymbol{\Lambda} = \boldsymbol{\Lambda}_1+\boldsymbol{\Lambda}_2\), \(\boldsymbol{\eta} = \boldsymbol{\eta}_1+\boldsymbol{\eta}_2\)Information matrix: §I.4.1, p. 15 · Day 3
Information added by one measurement \(\mathbf{a}\T\mathbf{x}\) with noise σ\(\mathbf{a}\mathbf{a}\T/\sigma^2\), so \(\boldsymbol{\Lambda} = \mathbf{A}\T\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{-1}\mathbf{A}\)Day 3, Day 4
Normal equations\(\mathbf{A}\T\mathbf{A}\,\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{A}\T\mathbf{b}\); weighted: \(\mathbf{A}\T\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{-1}\mathbf{A}\,\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{A}\T\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{-1}\mathbf{b}\)Equation (1.25), p. 31 · Day 4
Mahalanobis norm and whitening\(\norm{\mathbf{e}}^2_{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}} = \mathbf{e}\T\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{-1}\mathbf{e} = \norm{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{-1/2}\mathbf{e}}_2^2\)Equations (1.10), p. 27, and (1.22), p. 30 · Day 4
Cholesky solve\(\boldsymbol{\Lambda} = \mathbf{R}\T\mathbf{R}\); \(\ \mathbf{R}\T\mathbf{y} = \mathbf{A}\T\mathbf{b}\), then \(\mathbf{R}\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{y}\)Equations (1.26)–(1.28), p. 31 · Day 5
QR solve and condition number\(\mathbf{A} = \mathbf{Q}\mathbf{R}\), \(\mathbf{R}\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{Q}\T\mathbf{b}\); \(\ \kappa(\mathbf{A}) = s_{\max}/s_{\min}\), \(\kappa(\mathbf{A}\T\mathbf{A}) = \kappa(\mathbf{A})^2\)Equations (1.29)–(1.33), p. 32 · Day 5

2. Mixed quiz

Check yourself

Q1. Which of these is a loop closure?

A loop closure ties the current pose to a much earlier one. The first option is odometry, which only links neighbours and therefore drifts.

Q2. The book says the back-end "must remain online". What does that require?

The back-end may lag the front-end by seconds, but it has to keep up with the data stream on embedded hardware. That requirement is what set SLAM apart from offline structure from motion.

Q3. Prior: x = 0 m with σ = 2 m. Measurement: z = 5 m with σ = 2 m. What is the posterior?

Equal information on both sides gives the midpoint. Information adds: 1/4 + 1/4 = 1/2, so σ² = 2 and σ ≈ 1.41 m.

Q4. What made optimization-based SLAM practical between 2005 and 2015?

The covariance is dense, but its inverse is sparse with a predictable pattern, which allows solvers with close-to-linear cost (p. 15).

Q5. Two poses x₀, x₁ on a line. A prior on x₀ has σ = 1 and one odometry measurement of x₁ − x₀ has σ = 0.5. What is Λ?

The prior adds 1/1² = 1 to the top-left entry. The odometry adds (1/0.5²) × [1 −1; −1 1] = [4 −4; −4 4].

Q6. Three measurements of one unknown: 4 (σ = 1), 8 (σ = 1), and 9 (σ = 0.5). What is the weighted least-squares estimate?

Weights 1/σ² are 1, 1, 4. (4 + 8 + 4 × 9) / (1 + 1 + 4) = 48/6 = 8. The plain mean would be 7.

Q7. A QR factorization of A gives R with rows (3, 1) and (0, 2). What is AᵀA?

AᵀA = RᵀQᵀQR = RᵀR = [3 0; 1 2][3 1; 0 2] = [9 3; 3 5]. The second option is RRᵀ, the wrong order.

Q8. In double precision (about 16 digits), a least-squares problem has κ(A) = 10⁵. Roughly how many correct digits can you expect from the normal equations, and from QR?

You lose about log₁₀ κ digits. The normal equations work with κ² = 10¹⁰ and keep about 6. QR works with κ = 10⁵ and keeps about 11.

3. Pen-and-paper problems

  1. From odometry, a robot gives a 2% chance to being back at a known place. A place recognizer fires with probability 0.9 on a true revisit and 0.05 otherwise. (a) It fires. What is the probability of a true revisit? (b) A second, independent recognizer with the same rates also fires. What is it now?

    Solution

    (a) Bayes' rule: \(\dfrac{0.9\times 0.02}{0.9\times 0.02 + 0.05\times 0.98} = \dfrac{0.018}{0.067} \approx 0.27\). Still more likely a look-alike than a revisit.

    (b) The posterior from (a) becomes the new prior: \(\dfrac{0.9\times 0.269}{0.9\times 0.269 + 0.05\times 0.731} = \dfrac{0.242}{0.278} \approx 0.87\). Independent evidence compounds: two agreeing checks are worth far more than one.

  2. Two independent estimates of a landmark position: \(\boldsymbol{\mu}_1 = (0, 0)\) with \(\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_1 = \diag(1, 9)\), and \(\boldsymbol{\mu}_2 = (2, 3)\) with \(\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_2 = \diag(4, 1)\). Find the fused mean and covariance.

    Solution

    Information matrices: \(\boldsymbol{\Lambda}_1 = \diag(1,\ 1/9)\), \(\boldsymbol{\Lambda}_2 = \diag(1/4,\ 1)\). Sum: \(\boldsymbol{\Lambda} = \diag(1.25,\ 1.111)\).

    Information vectors: \(\boldsymbol{\eta}_1 = (0, 0)\), \(\boldsymbol{\eta}_2 = (2/4,\ 3/1) = (0.5,\ 3)\). Sum: \(\boldsymbol{\eta} = (0.5,\ 3)\).

    Mean: \(\boldsymbol{\mu} = (0.5/1.25,\ 3/1.111) = (0.4,\ 2.7)\). Covariance: \(\boldsymbol{\Sigma} = \diag(0.8,\ 0.9)\). In \(x\) the result stays near estimate 1, which is the sharper one there; in \(y\) it goes most of the way to estimate 2.

  3. Fit the line \(y = x_1 + x_2 t\) to the points \((t, y) = (0, 0),\ (1, 1),\ (2, 4)\) by least squares. Form the normal equations, solve them with a Cholesky factorization, and verify that the residual is orthogonal to both columns of \(\mathbf{A}\).

    Solution

    \(\mathbf{A}\) has rows \((1,0), (1,1), (1,2)\) and \(\mathbf{b} = (0,1,4)\). So \(\mathbf{A}\T\mathbf{A} = \begin{bmatrix} 3 & 3 \\ 3 & 5 \end{bmatrix}\) and \(\mathbf{A}\T\mathbf{b} = (5,\ 9)\).

    Cholesky: \(r_{11} = \sqrt3\), \(r_{12} = 3/\sqrt3 = \sqrt3\), \(r_{22} = \sqrt{5-3} = \sqrt2\).

    Forward, \(\mathbf{R}\T\mathbf{y} = (5, 9)\): \(y_1 = 5/\sqrt3\); \(\sqrt3\,y_1 + \sqrt2\,y_2 = 9\) gives \(y_2 = 4/\sqrt2 = 2\sqrt2\).

    Back, \(\mathbf{R}\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{y}\): \(x_2 = 2\sqrt2/\sqrt2 = 2\); \(\sqrt3\,x_1 + \sqrt3\cdot 2 = 5/\sqrt3\) gives \(x_1 = 5/3 - 2 = -1/3\). The line is \(y = -\tfrac13 + 2t\).

    Residual: \(\mathbf{r} = \mathbf{b}-\mathbf{A}\mathbf{x} = (\tfrac13,\ -\tfrac23,\ \tfrac13)\). Against \((1,1,1)\): \(\tfrac13-\tfrac23+\tfrac13 = 0\). Against \((0,1,2)\): \(-\tfrac23+\tfrac23 = 0\). The cost is \(\tfrac19+\tfrac49+\tfrac19 = \tfrac23\).

  4. A robot moves along a line through poses \(x_0, x_1, x_2\). There are four measurements, all with \(\sigma = 1\): a prior \(x_0 = 0\); odometry \(x_1 - x_0 = 1\) and \(x_2 - x_1 = 1\); and a GPS fix \(x_2 = 2.6\). (a) Write \(\mathbf{A}\) and \(\mathbf{b}\). (b) Form \(\boldsymbol{\Lambda} = \mathbf{A}\T\mathbf{A}\) and solve for the poses. (c) How is the 0.6 m disagreement between odometry and GPS shared out?
