A factor touches exactly the unknowns its measurement depends on. The measured value is a known number inside the factor, not a node.

Q3. A scalar factor has error 0.3 and σ = 0.1. How much does it add to the cost (1.18)?

The squared Mahalanobis distance is (0.3/0.1)² = 9: the error is three standard deviations.

Q4. You double the σ assigned to one sensor. What happens to the weight of its squared errors in the cost?

The weight is 1/σ². Doubling σ divides it by 4, and the estimate moves toward what the other factors say.

Q5. Two direct measurements of a scalar x: 2 with σ = 1, and 5 with σ = 0.5. After whitening, A is the column (1, 2) and b = (2, 10). What is the least-squares estimate?

AᵀA = 1 + 4 = 5 and Aᵀb = 2 + 20 = 22, so x = 22/5 = 4.4, four fifths of the way toward the more precise measurement.

Q6. Back substitution: R has rows (2, 1) and (0, 3), and d = (5, 6). What is δ* in Rδ* = d?

Bottom row first: 3δ₂ = 6 gives δ₂ = 2. Then 2δ₁ + 2 = 5 gives δ₁ = 1.5.

Q7. In which case is the Gauss-Newton matrix 2AᵀA exactly the Hessian of J, so that one step reaches the minimum?

The dropped term contains second derivatives of the measurement functions. For linear functions they are zero, the cost is exactly quadratic, and GN is the linear solve of Day 3.

Q8. One unknown, A = 3 and b = 6. What is Marquardt's step (1.38) with λ = 1?

(A² + λA²)δ = Ab gives (9 + 9)δ = 18, so δ = 1: half the Gauss-Newton step 18/9 = 2.

3. Pen-and-paper problems

  1. A planar robot has poses \(\mathbf{p}_1,\mathbf{p}_2,\mathbf{p}_3\) and sees one landmark \(\boldsymbol{\ell}\) by bearing from \(\mathbf{p}_1\) and from \(\mathbf{p}_3\). There is a prior on \(\mathbf{p}_1\), odometry between consecutive poses, and a loop closure between \(\mathbf{p}_3\) and \(\mathbf{p}_1\). Write the factorization \(\phi(\mathbf{x})\), and give the number of columns and rows of \(\mathbf{A}\).

    Solution

    One factor per piece of information, each a function of the variables it involves:

    \[ \phi(\mathbf{x})=\phi_1(\mathbf{p}_1)\,\phi_2(\mathbf{p}_1,\mathbf{p}_2)\,\phi_3(\mathbf{p}_2,\mathbf{p}_3)\,\phi_4(\mathbf{p}_3,\mathbf{p}_1)\,\phi_5(\mathbf{p}_1,\boldsymbol{\ell})\,\phi_6(\mathbf{p}_3,\boldsymbol{\ell}). \]

    Columns: \(3\cdot3+2=11\) unknown numbers. Rows: the prior, the two odometry factors, and the loop closure measure 3 numbers each (12 rows), and each bearing measures 1, so \(\mathbf{A}\) is \(14\times11\). The graph is one unary factor on \(\mathbf{p}_1\), a triangle of pose-pose factors, and two factors reaching up to \(\boldsymbol{\ell}\).

  2. A scalar \(x\) has a Gaussian prior with mean 1 and \(\sigma=2\). One direct measurement gives \(z=4\) with \(\sigma=1\). Find the MAP estimate by whitening and solving the normal equation, with linearization point \(x^0=0\).

    Solution

    Both factors have Jacobian \(H=1\). Dividing each row by its \(\sigma\): the prior row is \(A_1=1/2=0.5\), \(b_1=(1-0)/2=0.5\). The measurement row is \(A_2=1\), \(b_2=4\).

    \(\mathbf{A}\T\mathbf{A}=0.25+1=1.25\) and \(\mathbf{A}\T\mathbf{b}=0.25+4=4.25\), so \(\delta^*=4.25/1.25=3.4\) and \(x^{\text{MAP}}=x^0+\delta^*=3.4\).

    Check with weights \(1/\sigma^2\): \((0.25\cdot1+1\cdot4)/(0.25+1)=3.4\). The estimate sits between prior and measurement, four times closer to the measurement.

  3. A robot on a line has two unknown positions \(x_1,x_2\). Three factors, all with \(\sigma=1\): a prior \(x_1=0\), odometry \(x_2-x_1=2\), and an absolute measurement \(x_2=3\). Build \(\mathbf{A}\) and \(\mathbf{b}\), then solve by Cholesky factorization and the two substitutions. What cost is left?

    Solution
    \[ \mathbf{A}=\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0\\ -1 & 1\\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix},\quad \mathbf{b}=\begin{bmatrix}0\\2\\3\end{bmatrix},\quad \mathbf{A}\T\mathbf{A}=\begin{bmatrix}2 & -1\\ -1 & 2\end{bmatrix},\quad \mathbf{A}\T\mathbf{b}=\begin{bmatrix}-2\\5\end{bmatrix}. \]

    Cholesky: \(r_{11}=\sqrt2=1.414\), \(r_{12}=-1/1.414=-0.707\), \(r_{22}=\sqrt{2-0.707^2}=\sqrt{1.5}=1.225\).

    Forward, \(\mathbf{R}\T\mathbf{y}=\mathbf{A}\T\mathbf{b}\): \(y_1=-2/1.414=-1.414\), \(y_2=(5-(-0.707)(-1.414))/1.225=4/1.225=3.266\).

    Back, \(\mathbf{R}\boldsymbol{\delta}^*=\mathbf{y}\): \(\delta_2=3.266/1.225=2.667\), \(\delta_1=(-1.414+0.707\cdot2.667)/1.414=0.333\).

    So \(x_1=1/3\) and \(x_2=8/3\). The three residuals are \(1/3\), \((8/3-1/3)-2=1/3\), and \(8/3-3=-1/3\): the disagreement of 1 between "0 + 2" and "3" is shared equally by the three equally trusted factors. The cost left is \(3\cdot(1/3)^2=1/3\).

  4. A robot is on the \(x\)-axis at unknown position \(x\). A beacon at \((0,3)\) reports range \(z=5\) with \(\sigma=1\), so \(h(x)=\sqrt{x^2+9}\) and the true answer is \(x=4\). Start at \(x^0=1\). (a) Compute \(A\), \(b\), and \(J\). (b) Take one Gauss-Newton step and evaluate \(J\). (c) Take instead one Levenberg step (1.37) with \(\lambda=0.1\). (d) Compute the gain ratio of the step in (c).

    Solution

    (a) \(dh/dx=x/\sqrt{x^2+9}\). At \(x=1\): \(A=1/\sqrt{10}=0.316\), \(b=5-\sqrt{10}=1.838\), \(J=b^2=3.377\).

    (b) \(\delta^{\text{gn}}=b/A=5.811\), so \(x=6.811\). There \(h=\sqrt{46.39+9}=7.443\) and \(J=(5-7.443)^2=5.97\). The cost went up: the slope of \(h\) at \(x=1\) is only 0.316, but it grows toward 1 as \(x\) grows, so the straight-line model demanded far too long a step.

    (c) \(A^2=0.1\), so \(\delta^{\text{lm}}=Ab/(A^2+\lambda)=0.581/0.2=2.906\), and \(x=3.906\). There \(h=\sqrt{15.25+9}=4.925\) and \(J=(5-4.925)^2=0.006\). Lower than 3.377: accept, and reduce \(\lambda\).

    (d) Predicted: \(L(0)-L(\delta)=b^2-(A\delta-b)^2=3.377-(0.919-1.838)^2=3.377-0.844=2.533\). Actual: \(3.377-0.006=3.371\). So \(\rho=3.371/2.533=1.33\), above 0.75: the model was pessimistic, and a trust-region method would enlarge its region.

You are ready for next week if you can

  • Draw the factor graph of a small SLAM problem and write the posterior as a product of factors.
  • Explain why Gaussian factors turn MAP inference into the cost (1.18).
  • Linearize and whiten a factor, and say which columns of \(\mathbf{A}\) its rows occupy.
  • Solve a 2- or 3-unknown normal equation by Cholesky factorization and substitution.
  • State the SD, GN, and LM steps, and explain what \(\lambda\) and the trust region are for.

Next week looks inside \(\mathbf{A}\), \(\mathbf{A}\T\mathbf{A}\), and \(\mathbf{R}\): why they are sparse, how the order of the variables decides how sparse \(\mathbf{R}\) stays, and how the factorization can be updated as new measurements arrive.

Sources

  1. SLAM Handbook, Chapter 1, §1.1–§1.4, pp. 19–35.
  2. Nocedal and Wright, Numerical Optimization, 2006 (Gauss-Newton, Levenberg-Marquardt, dogleg, gain ratio).
  3. Golub and Van Loan, Matrix Computations, 2013 (Cholesky and QR).

Week 3 · Day 1

Why SLAM is sparse: the Jacobian, the information matrix, and their graphs

After today you can read the nonzero pattern of the Jacobian and of the information matrix straight off a factor graph, and explain why the variable ordering changes the cost of a factorization but not its answer.

About 60 min · Read §1.5, pp. 35–39 (4 pages) · Needs Week 2 Day 3

Read first: §1.5, from the bottom of p. 35 to p. 39

The top of p. 35 is the end of last week's dogleg method. Start at the heading "1.5 Factor Graphs and Sparsity". While you read, look for:

  • The counting argument on p. 36: how many factors the simulated example could have, and how many it has.
  • Figure 1.7 on p. 37. Match each block-row to one factor of the toy example and each block-column to one variable.
  • Figure 1.8 on p. 37. Check that a block of \(\boldsymbol{\Lambda}\) is filled exactly where the graph next to it has an edge.
  • The two numbers in Figure 1.9 on p. 39: 9399 and 4168 nonzeros for the same problem.

Today's big idea

Each measurement in SLAM involves only a few variables, so almost every entry of the matrices we factor is zero. The factor graph is a drawing of those zeros: a factor is a block-row of \(\mathbf{A}\), a variable is a block-column, and two variables share a nonzero block of \(\boldsymbol{\Lambda} = \mathbf{A}\T\mathbf{A}\) exactly when they share a factor. Solvers that skip the zeros handle millions of unknowns, and how many zeros survive the factorization depends on the order of the variables.

1. Count the factors

The solvers of Week 2 · Day 3 treated \(\mathbf{A}\) as a full table of numbers. For the book's simulated example (Figure 1.5, about 100 poses and 20 landmarks) that already wastes most of the work. Count what could be there and what is: §1.5 · p. 36

  • Pose to pose. About 100 odometry factors in a chain, where 100² pairs would be possible.
  • Pose to landmark. About 400, where 100 × 20 = 2000 would be possible: a landmark is seen from nearby poses only.
  • Landmark to landmark. None. Nothing measures one landmark relative to another.

The reason is physical: a sensor has a limited range and a robot moves a short distance per step, so one measurement can only relate things that are close in space or time. The book calls this structure typical of most SLAM problems.

Ignoring it gets expensive fast. Dense Cholesky costs about \(n^3/3\) operations (Week 2). For the \(n = 333\) unknowns of Figure 1.9 that is 12 million operations and no trouble. For \(n = 10^5\) it is \(3.3 \times 10^{14}\), about four days at a billion operations per second, and a dense \(\boldsymbol{\Lambda}\) of \(10^{10}\) numbers would fill 80 GB. Real problems have "thousands or even millions of unknowns", §1.5 · p. 36 and they are solvable only because the zeros are never stored or touched.

2. The factor graph is the pattern of the Jacobian

Recall the linear problem inside every Gauss-Newton step, equation (1.40):

\[ \boldsymbol{\delta}^* = \argmin_{\boldsymbol{\delta}} \sum_i \norm{\mathbf{A}_i \boldsymbol{\delta}_i - \mathbf{b}_i}_2^2 . \]

Here \(\boldsymbol{\delta}_i\) holds only the variables that factor \(i\) touches. Stack the terms and you get one big matrix \(\mathbf{A}\) in which every factor is a block-row and every variable is a block-column. A block is nonzero only where the factor touches the variable. §1.5.1 · p. 36 The book then drops the \(\boldsymbol{\delta}\) and writes the unknowns as \(\mathbf{x}\), because nothing below depends on where the linear problem came from.

Filling the gap: why the other blocks are exactly zero

A factor comes from a measurement model \(h_i\) that reads only its own variables. Factor \(\phi_8\) of the toy example predicts a measurement from \(\mathbf{p}_2\) and \(\boldsymbol{\ell}_1\) and from nothing else. Its row of the Jacobian holds the derivatives of that prediction with respect to all five variables, and the derivative with respect to a variable that does not appear in \(h_8\) is zero. No approximation is involved.

The size of a block is (number of measured values) × (size of the variable). With planar poses (3 numbers) and point landmarks (2 numbers), \(\mathbf{A}\) for Figure 1.5 has \(3 \times 95 + 2 \times 24 = 333\) columns, and its 1126 rows are the scalar measurements. Fig. 1.9 · p. 39

All week we use a version of the toy example of Figure 1.3 that you can compute by hand. Put the robot on a line, so every pose and landmark is one number, and give every measurement unit noise. The nine factors become nine rows:

FactorWhat it saysℓ₁ℓ₂p₁p₂p₃b
ϕ₁ prior on p₁p₁ = 010
ϕ₂ odometryp₂ − p₁ = 1−111
ϕ₃ odometryp₃ − p₂ = 1−111
ϕ₄ prior on ℓ₁ℓ₁ = 0.610.6
ϕ₅ prior on ℓ₂ℓ₂ = 2.412.4
ϕ₆ absolute fix of p₁p₁ = 0.210.2
ϕ₇ p₁ sees ℓ₁ℓ₁ − p₁ = 0.51−10.5
ϕ₈ p₂ sees ℓ₁ℓ₁ − p₂ = −0.31−1−0.3
ϕ₉ p₃ sees ℓ₂ℓ₂ − p₃ = 0.51−10.5

The filled cells sit where Figure 1.7 has its blocks \(\mathbf{A}_{13}, \mathbf{A}_{23}, \mathbf{A}_{24}, \dots\) (first index the factor, second the column, with columns ordered \(\boldsymbol{\ell}_1, \boldsymbol{\ell}_2, \mathbf{p}_1, \mathbf{p}_2, \mathbf{p}_3\)). Only 14 of the 45 cells are filled, and no row has more than two.

3. The information matrix and its graph

Cholesky works on the information matrix \(\boldsymbol{\Lambda} = \mathbf{A}\T\mathbf{A}\), also called the Hessian. Strictly it is the Gauss-Newton approximation of the Hessian (Week 2 · Day 4). It is symmetric, and positive definite when the MAP solution is unique. §1.5.2 · pp. 36–37 For the toy problem on a line, multiply out the table above:

\[ \boldsymbol{\Lambda} = \mathbf{A}\T\mathbf{A} = \begin{bmatrix} 3 & 0 & -1 & -1 & 0 \\ 0 & 2 & 0 & 0 & -1 \\ -1 & 0 & 4 & -1 & 0 \\ -1 & 0 & -1 & 3 & -1 \\ 0 & -1 & 0 & -1 & 2 \end{bmatrix} \qquad \text{rows and columns } \ell_1, \ell_2, p_1, p_2, p_3 . \]

Compare with Figure 1.8(a): the zeros are in the same places.

Filling the gap: which blocks of \(\mathbf{A}\T\mathbf{A}\) are nonzero

Write \(\mathbf{A}_{ij}\) for the block of factor \(i\) in the column of variable \(j\). Block \((j,k)\) of the product is a sum over the rows:

\[ \boldsymbol{\Lambda}_{jk} = \sum_{i} \mathbf{A}_{ij}\T \mathbf{A}_{ik} . \]

A term survives only if factor \(i\) touches both variable \(j\) and variable \(k\). So \(\boldsymbol{\Lambda}_{jk} \neq \mathbf{0}\) needs at least one factor that contains both. In the toy example \(\boldsymbol{\Lambda}_{14} = \mathbf{A}_{81}\T\mathbf{A}_{84}\) comes from \(\phi_8\) alone (in numbers, \(1 \cdot (-1) = -1\)), and \(\boldsymbol{\Lambda}_{15} = \mathbf{0}\) because no factor joins \(\boldsymbol{\ell}_1\) and \(\mathbf{p}_3\).

The diagonal block \(\boldsymbol{\Lambda}_{jj} = \sum_i \mathbf{A}_{ij}\T\mathbf{A}_{ij}\) collects every factor on variable \(j\): the 4 in the \(p_1\) position is \(\phi_1, \phi_2, \phi_6, \phi_7\), one unit each. A unary factor such as a prior adds to the diagonal and to nothing else.

This gives a second graph. Draw one node per variable and join two variables if they ever appear in the same factor. Call it \(G\). At the block level, the nonzero pattern of \(\boldsymbol{\Lambda}\) is the adjacency matrix of \(G\). A factor on three or more variables joins all of them pairwise (a clique). §1.5.2 · p. 37 The book notes that \(G\) is the graph of a Markov random field and leaves it there; we will use \(G\) on Days 2 and 3 to predict where a factorization creates new nonzeros.

In plain words

Think of each measurement as a short sentence that mentions two or three names. The Jacobian is the list of sentences. The information matrix is the table of who has been mentioned together with whom. In a town where everybody only talks about their neighbours, that table is almost empty.

4. Sparse factorization, fill-in, and the ordering

Both routes from Week 2 have sparse versions: Cholesky on \(\boldsymbol{\Lambda}\) and QR on \(\mathbf{A}\). They skip the zeros and so need far fewer operations than the dense counts. The book names the libraries most packages call (CHOLMOD and SuiteSparseQR) and reports that on sparse problems Cholesky or LDU beats QR by more than a constant factor. §1.5.3 · p. 38

There is a catch. The triangular factor \(\mathbf{R}\), with \(\mathbf{R}\T\mathbf{R} = \boldsymbol{\Lambda}\), can have nonzeros where \(\boldsymbol{\Lambda}\) has zeros. These extra entries are called fill-in, and their number depends on the variable ordering, the order of the columns. In Figure 1.9 the natural order (poses, then landmarks) gives an \(\mathbf{R}\) with 9399 nonzeros. Reordering the columns with the COLAMD heuristic (column approximate minimum degree) gives 4168. Back-substitution returns the same estimate from both. §1.5.3 · p. 38

Try it: the widget builds a small problem, draws \(\mathbf{A}\) and \(\boldsymbol{\Lambda}\), and computes the pattern of \(\mathbf{R}\) for the ordering you pick. Switch the ordering from "poses, then landmarks" to "minimum degree", then try the others.

Notice that Λ has 91 nonzeros out of 361. With poses first, R has 109 nonzeros, 54 of them fill-in. Minimum degree brings that down to 70 with 15 fill-ins, and a random order lands in between. Nothing about the problem changed, only the order of the columns.

Filling the gap: a four-variable example of fill-in

Take one "hub" variable tied to three others that are not tied to each other. Put the hub first and factor (work through the Cholesky recipe of Week 1 · Day 5):

\[ \boldsymbol{\Lambda} = \begin{bmatrix} 4 & 1 & 1 & 1 \\ 1 & 4 & 0 & 0 \\ 1 & 0 & 4 & 0 \\ 1 & 0 & 0 & 4 \end{bmatrix} \;\Rightarrow\; \mathbf{R} = \begin{bmatrix} 2 & 0.5 & 0.5 & 0.5 \\ 0 & 1.936 & -0.129 & -0.129 \\ 0 & 0 & 1.932 & -0.138 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 1.927 \end{bmatrix} . \]

Three zeros of \(\boldsymbol{\Lambda}\) became nonzero: \(\mathbf{R}\) is completely full. Now move the hub to the last position, which only renames the variables:

\[ \boldsymbol{\Lambda}' = \begin{bmatrix} 4 & 0 & 0 & 1 \\ 0 & 4 & 0 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 & 4 & 1 \\ 1 & 1 & 1 & 4 \end{bmatrix} \;\Rightarrow\; \mathbf{R}' = \begin{bmatrix} 2 & 0 & 0 & 0.5 \\ 0 & 2 & 0 & 0.5 \\ 0 & 0 & 2 & 0.5 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 1.803 \end{bmatrix} . \]

No fill-in at all. Removing the hub first forces its three neighbours to account for each other; removing it last never does. Day 3 turns this into a rule you can apply to a graph.

Why the answer cannot change. Reordering is a permutation matrix \(\mathbf{P}\): \(\mathbf{A}\mathbf{x} = (\mathbf{A}\mathbf{P})(\mathbf{P}\T\mathbf{x})\), because \(\mathbf{P}\mathbf{P}\T = \mathbf{I}\). The cost \(\norm{\mathbf{A}\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{b}}^2\) is the same function, written with its unknowns in a different order, so its minimizer is the same vector with its entries shuffled.

Finding the ordering with the least fill-in is NP-hard, so solvers use heuristics such as COLAMD. §1.5.3 · p. 38 The book also mentions iterative solvers (preconditioned conjugate gradient, and power iterations in visual SLAM) as alternatives, and says sparse factorization remains the method of choice for most SLAM problems.

Common mistakes

  • "Sparse means there are few measurements." It means each measurement involves few variables. Figure 1.9 has 1126 measurement rows and is still very sparse.
  • "A better ordering gives a better estimate." Every ordering gives the same MAP estimate. The ordering only changes how much work and memory the factorization needs.
  • "If Λ is sparse, its inverse is sparse too." The covariance \(\boldsymbol{\Lambda}^{-1}\) is usually completely full: every variable is correlated with every other through chains of measurements. Sparsity lives in the information matrix and its factor, which is why we solve with them and never form the inverse.

Check yourself

Q1. A problem has 50 planar poses (3 numbers each) and 30 point landmarks (2 numbers each). How many columns does A have?

One column per unknown number: 50 × 3 + 30 × 2 = 210. The number of rows depends on the measurements, not on the variables.

Q2. In the toy example, which block of Λ is zero?

No factor contains both ℓ₁ and p₃, so every term of the sum for that block vanishes. The other three pairs share ϕ₇, ϕ₃, and ϕ₉.

Q3. You add one factor on three variables, ϕ(p₁, p₂, ℓ₂), to the toy example. How many new edges does G get?

A ternary factor joins all three pairs. The pair p₁–p₂ is already joined by ϕ₂, so the new edges are p₁–ℓ₂ and p₂–ℓ₂.

Q4. One variable shares factors with all others, which share none among themselves. Where should it go in the ordering to avoid fill-in?

This is the hub example. Eliminated first, the hub ties all its neighbours together and R fills completely. Eliminated last, it creates no new nonzero.

Recap

  1. SLAM is sparse because a measurement relates only things that are close in space or time. There are no landmark-to-landmark factors at all.
  2. Every factor is a block-row of A and every variable a block-column. A block is nonzero only where the factor touches the variable.
  3. \(\boldsymbol{\Lambda}_{jk} = \sum_i \mathbf{A}_{ij}\T\mathbf{A}_{ik}\) is nonzero only if some factor contains both variables. The pattern of Λ is the adjacency matrix of the graph G.
  4. The factor R can have fill-in: nonzeros where Λ has zeros. How much depends on the variable ordering.
  5. All orderings give the same estimate. Finding the best one is NP-hard, so solvers use heuristics such as COLAMD.

Sources

  1. SLAM Handbook, §1.5 "Factor Graphs and Sparsity", pp. 35–39, with Figures 1.7–1.9 and equation (1.40). The dense operation count is from §1.3.3, p. 31.
  2. Golub and Van Loan, Matrix Computations, 4th edition, 2013 (the Cholesky factorization used in the four-variable example).
  3. Davis, Direct Methods for Sparse Linear Systems, 2006 (fill-in, the hub example, minimum-degree orderings).
  4. The toy problem on a line and its numbers are this course's own construction, with the same graph as the book's Figure 1.3.

Week 3 · Day 2

Variable elimination: from a factor graph to a Bayes net

After today you can eliminate a variable from a factor graph by hand, on the graph and as a partial QR step on the matrix, and say what the resulting conditional and new factor mean.

About 60 min · Read §1.6.1–1.6.2, pp. 40–44 (5 pages) · Needs Week 3 Day 1

Read first: §1.6.1–1.6.2, pp. 40–44 (stop at the heading 1.6.3 on p. 45)

While you read, look for:

  • The three objects in equation (1.43) on p. 40: the product factor \(\psi\), the conditional \(p(\mathbf{x}_j \mid \mathbf{s}_j)\), and the new factor \(\tau(\mathbf{s}_j)\).
  • Figure 1.10 on p. 41. In each of the five panels, find the shaded variable, the arrows that now point at it, and the red factor that was created.
  • Equation (1.47) on p. 42: which three block-rows of Figure 1.7 were taken out, and why those.
  • Equations (1.48)–(1.49) and Figure 1.11 on pp. 42–43: the one row above the line, and the red rows below it.

Today's big idea

Elimination removes one variable at a time. Collect the factors that touch the variable, multiply them, and split the product into a conditional density of that variable given its neighbours and a new factor on the neighbours alone. When every variable is gone, the factor graph has become a Bayes net that hands you the MAP estimate by back-substitution. For linear-Gaussian factors each split is a small QR factorization, and the whole procedure is sparse QR.

1. Where we are going: a product of small conditionals

A factor graph stores the unnormalized posterior as a product of factors, \(\phi(\mathbf{x}) = \phi(\mathbf{x}_1, \dots, \mathbf{x}_n)\), equation (1.41). The variable elimination algorithm rewrites it, for a chosen ordering \(\mathbf{x}_1, \dots, \mathbf{x}_n\), as equation (1.42):

\[ p(\mathbf{x}) = p(\mathbf{x}_1 \mid \mathbf{s}_1)\, p(\mathbf{x}_2 \mid \mathbf{s}_2) \cdots p(\mathbf{x}_n) = \prod_j p(\mathbf{x}_j \mid \mathbf{s}_j) . \]

A product of conditionals in which each variable depends only on variables that come later is a Bayes net: a directed graph with an arrow into \(\mathbf{x}_j\) from each variable it is conditioned on. The set \(\mathbf{s}_j\) of those variables is the separator of \(\mathbf{x}_j\). §1.6.1 · p. 40 The \(p(\mathbf{x})\) here is the posterior \(p(\mathbf{x} \mid \mathbf{z})\) of Week 2; the measurements are fixed numbers inside the factors, so the book stops writing them.

Any density can be written as a chain, \(p(x_1 \mid x_2, \dots, x_n)\, p(x_2 \mid x_3, \dots, x_n) \cdots p(x_n)\), by the chain rule of probability, but in general the first conditional depends on all the other variables. A sparse factor graph gives small separators: in the toy example no conditional depends on more than two variables.

Why want this form? The last conditional \(p(\mathbf{x}_n)\) depends on nothing, so you can maximize it alone. Then \(p(\mathbf{x}_{n-1} \mid \mathbf{s}_{n-1})\) has all its parents known, and so on backwards. The book adds that sampling and marginalization are easy in this form too.

2. Eliminating one variable

The algorithm keeps a factor graph on the variables not yet eliminated, and repeats one step. §1.6.1 · p. 40

for each variable x_j, in the chosen order:
    1. remove every factor that touches x_j
       separator s_j = all the other variables in those factors
    2. multiply them into one product factor   psi(x_j, s_j)
    3. split it:   psi(x_j, s_j) = p(x_j | s_j) * tau(s_j)      (1.43)
    4. keep p(x_j | s_j) for the Bayes net
       put the new factor tau(s_j) back into the graph

Filling the gap: what the split in step 3 is

It is the product rule \(p(a, b) = p(a \mid b)\,p(b)\), applied to a function that is not normalized. Define the new factor by integrating the eliminated variable out, and the conditional as what is left:

\[ \tau(\mathbf{s}_j) = \int \psi(\mathbf{x}_j, \mathbf{s}_j)\, d\mathbf{x}_j , \qquad p(\mathbf{x}_j \mid \mathbf{s}_j) = \frac{\psi(\mathbf{x}_j, \mathbf{s}_j)}{\tau(\mathbf{s}_j)} . \]

By construction the conditional integrates to 1 over \(\mathbf{x}_j\) for every value of \(\mathbf{s}_j\), so it is a proper density, and the product of the two pieces is \(\psi\) again. Nothing is lost or approximated. The factor \(\tau\) is a summary: everything the removed factors implied about the separator once \(\mathbf{x}_j\) itself is no longer asked about.

Only the factors touching \(\mathbf{x}_j\) are involved. Every other factor is a constant as far as \(\mathbf{x}_j\) is concerned and stays in the graph untouched. This locality is the whole reason elimination is cheap on a sparse graph.

For the toy example and the ordering \(\boldsymbol{\ell}_1, \boldsymbol{\ell}_2, \mathbf{p}_1, \mathbf{p}_2, \mathbf{p}_3\), the five steps of Figure 1.10 are:

StepFactors removedSeparatorConditional keptNew factor
1. Eliminate ℓ₁ϕ₄, ϕ₇, ϕ₈p₁, p₂p(ℓ₁ | p₁, p₂)τ(p₁, p₂)
2. Eliminate ℓ₂ϕ₅, ϕ₉p₃p(ℓ₂ | p₃)τ(p₃)
3. Eliminate p₁ϕ₁, ϕ₂, ϕ₆ and τ(p₁, p₂) from step 1p₂p(p₁ | p₂)τ(p₂)
4. Eliminate p₂ϕ₃ and τ(p₂) from step 3p₃p(p₂ | p₃)τ(p₃)
5. Eliminate p₃τ(p₃) from step 2 and τ(p₃) from step 4emptyp(p₃), a priornone

Multiply the fourth column and you have equation (1.44): \(p(\boldsymbol{\ell}_1 \mid \mathbf{p}_1, \mathbf{p}_2)\, p(\boldsymbol{\ell}_2 \mid \mathbf{p}_3)\, p(\mathbf{p}_1 \mid \mathbf{p}_2)\, p(\mathbf{p}_2 \mid \mathbf{p}_3)\, p(\mathbf{p}_3)\). §1.6.1 · p. 41 Notice step 3: the separator of \(\mathbf{p}_1\) is found in the graph as it is at that moment, including the factor made in step 1.

Try it: with the book's ordering selected, press "Eliminate next" five times and compare each state with the matching panel of Figure 1.10. The numbers are those of the toy problem on a line from Day 1.

Notice that each step deletes the factors around one variable and leaves at most one new factor (pink) on its neighbours. With the book's ordering no new edge is ever needed, so the fill-in stays at 0, and after five steps the estimate reads p₁ = 0.076, p₂ = 0.984, p₃ = 1.956, ℓ₁ = 0.620, ℓ₂ = 2.428.

3. With Gaussian factors, the product factor is a small least-squares problem

So far nothing assumed Gaussians. Now let every factor be \(\phi_i(\mathbf{x}_i) = \exp\!\left(-\tfrac12 \norm{\mathbf{A}_i\mathbf{x}_i - \mathbf{b}_i}_2^2\right)\), which is what linearization gives. Multiplying exponentials adds their exponents, and a sum of squared norms is the squared norm of the stacked vector. That is all of equation (1.45):

\[ \psi(\mathbf{x}_j, \mathbf{s}_j) = \prod_{i \in \mathcal{N}_j} \phi_i(\mathbf{x}_i) = \exp\!\left(-\tfrac12 \sum_i \norm{\mathbf{A}_i\mathbf{x}_i - \mathbf{b}_i}_2^2\right) = \exp\!\left(-\tfrac12 \norm{\bar{\mathbf{A}}_j [\mathbf{x}_j; \mathbf{s}_j] - \bar{\mathbf{b}}_j}_2^2\right) . \]

\(\mathcal{N}_j\) is the set of factors adjacent to \(\mathbf{x}_j\), \(\bar{\mathbf{A}}_j\) stacks their rows, and \([\mathbf{x}_j; \mathbf{s}_j]\) stacks the eliminated variable on top of its separator. §1.6.2 · p. 42 In matrix terms: pull out of \([\mathbf{A} \mid \mathbf{b}]\) the rows that have a nonzero in column \(j\).

For \(\boldsymbol{\ell}_1\) in the toy problem these are the rows of \(\phi_4, \phi_7, \phi_8\), equation (1.47). On a line, with columns \(\ell_1, p_1, p_2\):

\[ \bar{\mathbf{A}}_1 = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 1 & -1 & 0 \\ 1 & 0 & -1 \end{bmatrix}, \qquad \bar{\mathbf{b}}_1 = \begin{bmatrix} 0.6 \\ 0.5 \\ -0.3 \end{bmatrix} . \]

4. Partial QR does the split

Equation (1.48) factorizes the stacked matrix, with its right-hand side attached, as

\[ [\bar{\mathbf{A}}_j \mid \bar{\mathbf{b}}_j] = \mathbf{Q} \begin{bmatrix} \mathbf{R}_j & \mathbf{T}_j & \mathbf{d}_j \\ \mathbf{0} & \tilde{\mathbf{A}}_\tau & \tilde{\mathbf{b}}_\tau \end{bmatrix} , \]

with \(\mathbf{Q}\) orthogonal and \(\mathbf{R}_j\) upper-triangular. It is called partial because only the columns of \(\mathbf{x}_j\) are made triangular; the separator columns are carried along. §1.6.2 · p. 42

Filling the gap: why this factors \(\psi\), and the toy step by hand

An orthogonal matrix does not change lengths: \(\norm{\mathbf{Q}\T\mathbf{v}}^2 = \mathbf{v}\T\mathbf{Q}\mathbf{Q}\T\mathbf{v} = \norm{\mathbf{v}}^2\). Apply \(\mathbf{Q}\T\) inside the norm of the exponent and read off the two block-rows of (1.48):

\[ \norm{\bar{\mathbf{A}}_j [\mathbf{x}_j; \mathbf{s}_j] - \bar{\mathbf{b}}_j}^2 = \norm{\mathbf{R}_j\mathbf{x}_j + \mathbf{T}_j\mathbf{s}_j - \mathbf{d}_j}^2 + \norm{\tilde{\mathbf{A}}_\tau\mathbf{s}_j - \tilde{\mathbf{b}}_\tau}^2 . \]

The exponential of a sum is a product, so \(\psi\) splits into a term that contains \(\mathbf{x}_j\) and a term that does not. The second is \(\tau(\mathbf{s}_j)\). The first is a Gaussian in \(\mathbf{x}_j\) whose width does not depend on \(\mathbf{s}_j\), so it integrates to the same constant for every \(\mathbf{s}_j\): it is the conditional \(p(\mathbf{x}_j \mid \mathbf{s}_j)\) up to that constant. This is equation (1.49).

Now the numbers. We need an orthonormal basis whose first vector points along the first column of \(\bar{\mathbf{A}}_1\), which is \((1,1,1)\). One choice is

\[ \mathbf{q}_1 = \tfrac{1}{\sqrt3}(1, 1, 1), \qquad \mathbf{q}_2 = \tfrac{1}{\sqrt2}(0, 1, -1), \qquad \mathbf{q}_3 = \tfrac{1}{\sqrt6}(2, -1, -1) . \]

Check that they are orthogonal to each other and have length 1. The rows of \(\mathbf{Q}\T[\bar{\mathbf{A}}_1 \mid \bar{\mathbf{b}}_1]\) are the three vectors applied to the three rows, for example \(\mathbf{q}_1\): \(\tfrac{1}{\sqrt3}(1+1+1,\; -1,\; -1 \mid 0.6+0.5-0.3)\). All three:

\[ \mathbf{Q}\T[\bar{\mathbf{A}}_1 \mid \bar{\mathbf{b}}_1] = \left[\begin{array}{ccc|c} 1.732 & -0.577 & -0.577 & 0.462 \\ 0 & -0.707 & 0.707 & 0.566 \\ 0 & 0.408 & 0.408 & 0.408 \end{array}\right] . \]

Read each row as a sentence:

  • Row 1, the conditional. \(1.732\,\ell_1 - 0.577\,p_1 - 0.577\,p_2 = 0.462\). Divide by 1.732: \(\ell_1 = (0.8 + p_1 + p_2)/3\). That is the average of the three things said about \(\ell_1\): it is at 0.6, at \(p_1 + 0.5\), and at \(p_2 - 0.3\). Its precision is \(1.732^2 = 3\), three unit measurements.
  • Row 2, new factor. Multiply by \(\sqrt2\): \(p_2 - p_1 = 0.8\), with variance 2. Two sightings of the same landmark, subtracted, act like an odometry measurement: \((\ell_1 - p_1) - (\ell_1 - p_2) = 0.5 - (-0.3)\).
  • Row 3, new factor. Multiply by \(\sqrt6\): \(p_1 + p_2 = 1.0\), with variance 6. It comes from \(2\ell_1 - (\ell_1 - p_1) - (\ell_1 - p_2)\), which is \(2(0.6) - 0.5 + 0.3\).

The landmark is gone from rows 2 and 3, and what it told us about the two poses is still there. Any other orthonormal \(\mathbf{q}_2, \mathbf{q}_3\) gives a different-looking pair of rows that describes the same factor. The widget makes them triangular as well, so it shows \((0.82, -0.41 \mid -0.29)\) and \((0, 0.71 \mid 0.64)\). Both pairs have the same \(\tilde{\mathbf{A}}_\tau\T\tilde{\mathbf{A}}_\tau\) and \(\tilde{\mathbf{A}}_\tau\T\tilde{\mathbf{b}}_\tau\).

In plain words

To remove a landmark from the problem, first write down how you would compute it if someone told you the poses (the conditional). Then write down what the landmark's measurements imply about the poses alone (the new factor). Put the first note aside for later and keep working with the second.

5. Do it for every variable and you have sparse QR

Each step moves one finished row \([\mathbf{R}_j \;\, \mathbf{T}_j \mid \mathbf{d}_j]\) to the top part of the matrix and returns the rows \([\tilde{\mathbf{A}}_\tau \mid \tilde{\mathbf{b}}_\tau]\) to the pool. Figure 1.12 shows the remaining four steps. At the end the finished rows form an upper-triangular \(\mathbf{R}\) with the same pattern as the Bayes net: row \(j\) has a nonzero in column \(k\) exactly when \(\mathbf{x}_k\) is in the separator of \(\mathbf{x}_j\). The elimination algorithm with partial QR is sparse QR factorization, and the book states that sparse Cholesky is a special case of the same algorithm. §1.6.2 · pp. 42–44 Tomorrow's Schur complement is its Cholesky form.

Because each variable here is a block of several numbers (a pose, a landmark), every step eliminates a group of scalar columns at once. The book identifies this as multi-frontal QR, and notes that sparse linear algebra libraries form such groups on their own for speed; in SLAM the groups come for free from the meaning of the variables. §1.6.2 · pp. 44–45

Common mistakes

  • "Eliminating a variable discards it." Its conditional is kept, and \(\psi = p(\mathbf{x}_j \mid \mathbf{s}_j)\,\tau(\mathbf{s}_j)\) holds exactly. Elimination reorganizes the information; it loses none.
  • "The new factor is an extra measurement." It is a summary of measurements that were already there. In the worked step, "p₂ − p₁ = 0.8" was implied by ϕ₇ and ϕ₈ all along.
  • "The separator is the set of neighbours in the original graph." It is the set of neighbours at the moment of elimination. Factors created by earlier steps count, which is how new edges (fill-in) appear.

Check yourself

Q1. With the ordering ℓ₁, ℓ₂, p₁, p₂, p₃, which factors are multiplied together when p₁ is eliminated?

ϕ₇ was used up when ℓ₁ was eliminated. What remains around p₁ is its two unary factors, the odometry factor ϕ₂, and the new factor on (p₁, p₂).

Q2. Eliminate ℓ₂ from the two rows "ℓ₂ = 2.4" and "ℓ₂ − p₃ = 0.5" (unit noise). What is R for ℓ₂?

The ℓ₂ column of the stacked rows is (1, 1), and R is its length, √2 = 1.414. Its square, 2, is the precision of ℓ₂ given p₃: two unit measurements.

Q3. In the same step, what does the new factor τ(p₃) say?

Apply q₂ = (1, −1)/√2 to both rows: 0.707 p₃ = (2.4 − 0.5)/√2. So p₃ = 1.9, the prior on ℓ₂ minus the sighting, and the variances of the two add to 2.

Q4. Suppose you eliminate p₂ first in the toy graph. What is its separator?

p₂ appears in ϕ₂ (with p₁), ϕ₃ (with p₃) and ϕ₈ (with ℓ₁). The new factor then ties those three together, which creates two edges that were not in the graph. Check it in the widget with the "p₂ first" ordering.

Recap

  1. Elimination turns the product of factors \(\phi(\mathbf{x})\) into a Bayes net \(\prod_j p(\mathbf{x}_j \mid \mathbf{s}_j)\), one variable at a time.
  2. One step: remove the factors touching \(\mathbf{x}_j\), multiply them into \(\psi(\mathbf{x}_j, \mathbf{s}_j)\), split it as \(p(\mathbf{x}_j \mid \mathbf{s}_j)\,\tau(\mathbf{s}_j)\), and return \(\tau\) to the graph.
  3. With linear-Gaussian factors, \(\psi\) is a small stacked least-squares term and the split is a partial QR factorization.
  4. The first row block \([\mathbf{R}_j \; \mathbf{T}_j \mid \mathbf{d}_j]\) is the conditional. The remaining rows are the new factor on the separator.
  5. Repeating the step for all variables is sparse (multi-frontal) QR, and the finished rows form \(\mathbf{R}\).

Sources

  1. SLAM Handbook, §1.6.1 "Variable Elimination Algorithm" and §1.6.2 "Linear-Gaussian Elimination", pp. 40–45, equations (1.41)–(1.49), Figures 1.10–1.12.
  2. Koller and Friedman, Probabilistic Graphical Models, 2009 (variable elimination and the definition of the new factor as a marginal).
  3. Dellaert and Kaess, Factor Graphs for Robot Perception, 2017 (elimination of Gaussian factor graphs by partial QR).
  4. Golub and Van Loan, Matrix Computations, 4th edition, 2013 (QR factorization and orthogonal invariance of the 2-norm).

Week 3 · Day 3

The Cholesky factor is a Bayes net: back-substitution, fill-in, and the Schur complement

After today you can read each row of R as a Gaussian conditional, solve for the MAP estimate by back-substitution, predict fill-in from the graph for a given ordering, and marginalize a Gaussian variable with the Schur complement.

About 60 min · Read §1.6.3, pp. 45–46 (2 pages), and p. 38 again · Needs Week 3 Day 2

Read first: §1.6.3, p. 45 to the top of p. 46, then the second paragraph of p. 38 again

While you read, look for:

  • The sentence on p. 45 that links "directed acyclic graph" to "upper-triangular".
  • Equations (1.51)–(1.52): the mean and the covariance of one conditional, written with \(\mathbf{R}_j\), \(\mathbf{T}_j\), \(\mathbf{d}_j\).
  • Equation (1.53) and the paragraph before it: in which order back-substitution visits the variables, and why that order always works.
  • On p. 38: the definition of fill-in. Today explains where it comes from.

Today's big idea

The triangular factor \(\mathbf{R}\) and the Bayes net are the same object. Row \(j\) of \(\mathbf{R}\) is the Gaussian conditional of variable \(j\) given its separator, so solving \(\mathbf{R}\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{d}\) from the bottom up is MAP inference in the Bayes net. Eliminating a variable ties its neighbours together; in matrix form that tie is the Schur complement, which is also how a Gaussian variable is marginalized out.

1. Reading R as a Bayes net

Yesterday each elimination step produced one finished row \([\mathbf{R}_j \;\, \mathbf{T}_j \mid \mathbf{d}_j]\). Stack them in elimination order and you get an upper-triangular matrix. For the toy problem on a line with the book's ordering (run the Day 2 widget to the end to see it):

\[ [\mathbf{R} \mid \mathbf{d}] = \left[\begin{array}{ccccc|c} 1.732 & 0 & -0.577 & -0.577 & 0 & 0.462 \\ 0 & 1.414 & 0 & 0 & -0.707 & 2.051 \\ 0 & 0 & 1.915 & -0.696 & 0 & -0.540 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 1.477 & -0.677 & 0.129 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0 & 1.021 & 1.996 \end{array}\right] \quad \begin{array}{l} p(\ell_1 \mid p_1, p_2) \\ p(\ell_2 \mid p_3) \\ p(p_1 \mid p_2) \\ p(p_2 \mid p_3) \\ p(p_3) \end{array} \]

The off-diagonal nonzeros of row \(j\) sit in the columns of its separator: they are the arrows into \(\mathbf{x}_j\). A Bayes net is a directed graph without cycles, and "no cycles" means the variables can be ordered so that every arrow points from a later variable to an earlier one. In matrix terms nothing lies below the diagonal. The book's one-line summary: a factor graph is the picture of a sparse Jacobian, and a Bayes net is the picture of a Cholesky factor. §1.6.3 · p. 45

You can check that this is the Cholesky factor of Day 1's \(\boldsymbol{\Lambda}\): for instance entry \((3,3)\) of \(\mathbf{R}\T\mathbf{R}\) is \(0.577^2 + 1.915^2 = 4.00\) and entry \((3,4)\) is \((-0.577)(-0.577) + (1.915)(-0.696) = -1.00\).

2. Each row is a Gaussian, and back-substitution is MAP inference

Equation (1.51) writes the conditional as \(p(\mathbf{x}_j \mid \mathbf{s}_j) = k \exp\!\left(-\tfrac12 \norm{\mathbf{R}_j\mathbf{x}_j + \mathbf{T}_j\mathbf{s}_j - \mathbf{d}_j}_2^2\right)\), and (1.52) says this is a Gaussian in \(\mathbf{x}_j\). A Bayes net made of such conditionals is a Gaussian Bayes net. §1.6.3 · p. 45

Filling the gap: from (1.51) to mean and covariance

Pull \(\mathbf{R}_j\) out of the expression inside the norm. It is square and invertible:

\[ \mathbf{R}_j\mathbf{x}_j + \mathbf{T}_j\mathbf{s}_j - \mathbf{d}_j = \mathbf{R}_j\left(\mathbf{x}_j - \boldsymbol{\mu}_j\right), \qquad \boldsymbol{\mu}_j = \mathbf{R}_j^{-1}(\mathbf{d}_j - \mathbf{T}_j\mathbf{s}_j) . \]

Then \(\norm{\mathbf{R}_j(\mathbf{x}_j - \boldsymbol{\mu}_j)}^2 = (\mathbf{x}_j - \boldsymbol{\mu}_j)\T \mathbf{R}_j\T\mathbf{R}_j (\mathbf{x}_j - \boldsymbol{\mu}_j)\). Compare with the exponent of a Gaussian, \((\mathbf{x} - \boldsymbol{\mu})\T\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{-1}(\mathbf{x} - \boldsymbol{\mu})\): the information matrix is \(\mathbf{R}_j\T\mathbf{R}_j\), so \(\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_j = (\mathbf{R}_j\T\mathbf{R}_j)^{-1}\). The mean moves linearly with the separator; the covariance does not depend on it at all. The constant is \(k = |2\pi\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_j|^{-1/2}\), the usual Gaussian normalizer.

Why maximizing one conditional at a time gives the joint maximum. The joint density is the product of the conditionals. Each one, whatever its parents are, can reach its peak value \(k\) by setting \(\mathbf{x}_j = \boldsymbol{\mu}_j\), and \(k\) does not depend on the parents. So no variable has to compromise: go through the variables in reverse elimination order, set each to its conditional mean given the values already chosen, and every factor of the product is at its maximum at once.

That procedure is equation (1.53), \(\mathbf{x}_j^* = \mathbf{R}_j^{-1}(\mathbf{d}_j - \mathbf{T}_j\mathbf{s}_j^*)\), and it is ordinary back-substitution on \(\mathbf{R}\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{d}\). The last variable has an empty separator, so it comes first. For the toy problem, carrying more digits than printed above:

\[ \begin{aligned} p_3^* &= 1.996 / 1.021 = 1.956 \\ p_2^* &= (0.129 + 0.677 \times 1.956)/1.477 = 0.984 \\ p_1^* &= (-0.540 + 0.696 \times 0.984)/1.915 = 0.076 \\ \ell_2^* &= (2.051 + 0.707 \times 1.956)/1.414 = 2.428 \\ \ell_1^* &= (0.462 + 0.577 \times (0.076 + 0.984))/1.732 = 0.620 \end{aligned} \]

The diagonal carries uncertainty as well. The last conditional has no parents, so it is the marginal of \(p_3\): its variance is \(1/1.021^2 = 0.96\). For the other variables \(1/R_j^2\) is the variance given the separator, which is smaller than the marginal variance.

3. Fill-in, seen on the graph

The new factor \(\tau(\mathbf{s}_j)\) touches every variable of the separator. In the graph \(G\) of Day 1 this means: eliminating a variable joins all of its current neighbours to each other. An edge that had to be added is a fill-in, and it becomes a nonzero of \(\mathbf{R}\) where \(\boldsymbol{\Lambda}\) had a zero. Row \(j\) of \(\mathbf{R}\) has one diagonal entry plus one entry per separator variable, so the size of \(\mathbf{R}\) is the sum of \(1 + |\mathbf{s}_j|\) over all variables.

Try it: choose "poses first" and step through. Watch the pink factor after eliminating p₂ and after p₃.

Notice that eliminating p₂ creates a factor between p₃ and ℓ₁, and eliminating p₃ then ties ℓ₁ to ℓ₂, two landmarks that no measurement ever related. R ends with 12 nonzeros and 2 fill-ins instead of 10 and 0, and the estimate is the same to the last digit. The "reversed" ordering is worse still: 13 nonzeros.

The minimum-degree idea follows directly: at each step eliminate the variable that has the fewest neighbours, because its separator, and so its row of \(\mathbf{R}\) and the factor it leaves behind, is smallest. It is greedy and not optimal, but cheap and usually good. COLAMD, the heuristic behind the 4168 of Figure 1.9, is an approximate minimum-degree ordering that works from the columns of \(\mathbf{A}\) directly. §1.5.3 · p. 38 In landmark SLAM it tends to eliminate landmarks early: a landmark seen from two poses has two neighbours, while a pose in the middle of the trajectory has many.

4. The Schur complement: elimination in information form

The same step can be done on the normal equations \(\boldsymbol{\Lambda}\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{g}\), with \(\mathbf{g} = \mathbf{A}\T\mathbf{b}\). Split the variables into the block \(a\) to eliminate and the rest \(b\):

\[ \begin{bmatrix} \boldsymbol{\Lambda}_{aa} & \boldsymbol{\Lambda}_{ab} \\ \boldsymbol{\Lambda}_{ba} & \boldsymbol{\Lambda}_{bb} \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} \mathbf{x}_a \\ \mathbf{x}_b \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} \mathbf{g}_a \\ \mathbf{g}_b \end{bmatrix} . \]

Filling the gap: block elimination

Solve the first block-row for \(\mathbf{x}_a\): \(\mathbf{x}_a = \boldsymbol{\Lambda}_{aa}^{-1}(\mathbf{g}_a - \boldsymbol{\Lambda}_{ab}\mathbf{x}_b)\). This is the conditional mean of \(\mathbf{x}_a\) given \(\mathbf{x}_b\), the information-form twin of (1.53). Substitute it into the second block-row and collect \(\mathbf{x}_b\):

\[ \underbrace{\left(\boldsymbol{\Lambda}_{bb} - \boldsymbol{\Lambda}_{ba}\boldsymbol{\Lambda}_{aa}^{-1}\boldsymbol{\Lambda}_{ab}\right)}_{\text{Schur complement of } \boldsymbol{\Lambda}_{aa}} \mathbf{x}_b = \mathbf{g}_b - \boldsymbol{\Lambda}_{ba}\boldsymbol{\Lambda}_{aa}^{-1}\mathbf{g}_a . \]

This smaller system no longer contains \(\mathbf{x}_a\). It is what the remaining factors plus the new factor \(\tau\) add up to. The correction \(\boldsymbol{\Lambda}_{ba}\boldsymbol{\Lambda}_{aa}^{-1}\boldsymbol{\Lambda}_{ab}\) is nonzero in position \((j,k)\) when both \(j\) and \(k\) are neighbours of \(a\): the "join all neighbours" rule again.

Numbers: eliminate \(\ell_1\) from Day 1's \(\boldsymbol{\Lambda}\). Here \(\boldsymbol{\Lambda}_{aa} = 3\), and \(\ell_1\) is linked to \(p_1\) and \(p_2\) with \(-1\) each, so the correction is \(\tfrac13\) in the four positions of the \((p_1, p_2)\) block:

\[ \begin{bmatrix} 4 & -1 \\ -1 & 3 \end{bmatrix} - \frac13 \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ 1 & 1 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 3.667 & -1.333 \\ -1.333 & 2.667 \end{bmatrix} . \]

The next pivot is \(\sqrt{3.667} = 1.915\) and the entry beside it \(-1.333/1.915 = -0.696\): row 3 of \(\mathbf{R}\) above. Cholesky factorization is this step repeated, with a square root taken each time.

For a Gaussian, the Schur complement has a second meaning. It is the information matrix of the marginal \(p(\mathbf{x}_b)\), the distribution of \(\mathbf{x}_b\) when \(\mathbf{x}_a\) is integrated out. Conditioning on a known value of \(\mathbf{x}_a\) is the other way to remove it. The two operations swap roles between the two forms of a Gaussian:

To getCovariance form (Σ)Information form (Λ = Σ⁻¹)
Marginal p(x_b): forget x_aKeep the block Σ_bb. Delete the rest.Schur complement: Λ_bb − Λ_ba Λ_aa⁻¹ Λ_ab
Conditional p(x_b | x_a): x_a is knownSchur complement: Σ_bb − Σ_ba Σ_aa⁻¹ Σ_abKeep the block Λ_bb. Delete the rest.

The marginal row follows from the block elimination above. Solve \(\boldsymbol{\Lambda}[\mathbf{u}; \mathbf{v}] = [\mathbf{0}; \mathbf{w}]\): the reduced system gives \(\mathbf{v} = \mathbf{S}^{-1}\mathbf{w}\) with \(\mathbf{S}\) the Schur complement. But \([\mathbf{u}; \mathbf{v}] = \boldsymbol{\Sigma}[\mathbf{0}; \mathbf{w}]\), so \(\mathbf{v} = \boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{bb}\mathbf{w}\). Hence \(\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{bb} = \mathbf{S}^{-1}\): the covariance of the marginal is the inverse of the Schur complement.

Try it: three numbers in a chain, so \(x_1\) and \(x_3\) share no factor. Remove the middle one both ways, then remove an end instead.

Notice that Λ has a zero between x₁ and x₃, and marginalizing x₂ puts −0.50 there: fill-in. Conditioning on x₂ leaves the zero, and its ellipse is not tilted: once x₂ is known, the two ends are independent. Remove x₁ or x₃ and no new entry appears, because an end has only one neighbour.

Going deeper (optional): why smoothing stays sparse and filtering does not

A filter keeps only the current pose and marginalizes each old pose out as soon as the robot moves on. By the rule above, every such step joins all landmarks seen from that pose to each other and to the next pose. After a while the information matrix over the landmarks is full. Keeping the whole trajectory in the problem, as this chapter does, means no pose is marginalized, and \(\boldsymbol{\Lambda}\) keeps the sparse pattern of the factor graph. More variables, but far fewer nonzeros.

Common mistakes

  • "To marginalize a variable, delete its row and column of Λ." That conditions on it. Deleting rows and columns marginalizes only in covariance form.
  • "Fill-in is round-off error." It is structural. The entries are real dependencies created by removing a variable that connected its neighbours.
  • "Back-substitution needs the inverse of R." For scalar variables each step is one division. For block variables it is a small triangular solve.

Check yourself

Q1. A row of [R | d] for scalar variables reads 2·x₁ − 1·x₂ = 3, and back-substitution has already found x₂ = 1. What is x₁?

x₁ = (d − T·x₂)/R = (3 − (−1)(1))/2 = 2.

Q2. For the same row, what is the variance of x₁ given x₂?

Σ = (RᵀR)⁻¹ = 1/2² = 0.25. It does not depend on the value of x₂.

Q3. G is a path a – b – c – d. Which variable, if eliminated first, creates a fill-in?

b has two neighbours, a and c, which are not joined. Eliminating b adds the edge a – c. The ends a and d have one neighbour each, so nothing needs joining.

Q4. Two scalars have Λ = [[2, −1], [−1, 2]]. What is the information (inverse variance) of the marginal of x₂?

Schur complement: 2 − (−1)(1/2)(−1) = 1.5. Check through the covariance: Σ = Λ⁻¹ = (1/3)[[2, 1], [1, 2]], so the variance of x₂ is 2/3 = 1/1.5.

Q5. Same Λ. What is the information of x₂ once x₁ is known?

Conditioning in information form keeps the block: Λ₂₂ = 2. Knowing x₁ can only help, and indeed the variance 1/2 is smaller than the marginal variance 2/3.

Recap

  1. Row \(j\) of \([\mathbf{R} \mid \mathbf{d}]\) is the conditional \(p(\mathbf{x}_j \mid \mathbf{s}_j)\): mean \(\mathbf{R}_j^{-1}(\mathbf{d}_j - \mathbf{T}_j\mathbf{s}_j)\), covariance \((\mathbf{R}_j\T\mathbf{R}_j)^{-1}\). Upper-triangular means acyclic.
  2. Back-substitution in reverse elimination order sets each variable to its conditional mean. That is the MAP estimate.
  3. Eliminating a variable joins all its current neighbours. New edges are fill-in. Minimum-degree orderings keep separators small.
  4. In information form, elimination is the Schur complement \(\boldsymbol{\Lambda}_{bb} - \boldsymbol{\Lambda}_{ba}\boldsymbol{\Lambda}_{aa}^{-1}\boldsymbol{\Lambda}_{ab}\), which is the information matrix of the marginal.
  5. Marginalizing is easy in covariance form and costs a Schur complement in information form. Conditioning is the reverse.

Sources

  1. SLAM Handbook, §1.6.3 "Sparse Cholesky Factor as a Bayes Net", pp. 45–46, equations (1.50)–(1.53); §1.5.3, p. 38, for fill-in and COLAMD.
  2. Barfoot, State Estimation for Robotics, 2017 (marginals and conditionals of a joint Gaussian, the Schur complement).
  3. Davis, Direct Methods for Sparse Linear Systems, 2006 (elimination graphs, minimum degree, COLAMD).
  4. Thrun, Burgard, Fox, Probabilistic Robotics, 2005 (information-form filters and what marginalizing poses does to sparsity).

Week 3 · Day 4

The Bayes tree, and why a new measurement touches only part of it

After today you can group the conditionals of an eliminated factor graph into a Bayes tree, name the frontal and separator variables of each clique, and predict which cliques a new factor forces you to recompute.

About 60 min · Read §1.7 to §1.7.2, pp. 46–49 (4 pages) · Needs Week 3 Day 3

Read first: §1.7, §1.7.1 and §1.7.2, pp. 46–49

While you read, look for:

  • The reason on p. 46 why updating a matrix factorization is not enough for SLAM.
  • The definition of "chordal" on p. 46, and the cycle the book points to in the toy Bayes net (p. 47).
  • Figure 1.13 on p. 47: the three cliques, and which rows of \(\mathbf{R}\) carry which colour.
  • The two properties of the Bayes tree in the last paragraph of p. 48.
  • Figure 1.14 on p. 49: which clique is left alone when a factor between \(\mathbf{p}_1\) and \(\mathbf{p}_3\) is added.

Today's big idea

The conditionals of a Bayes net that came from elimination can be grouped into cliques, and those cliques form a tree. During elimination, information only travels from the leaves up to the root. A new factor can therefore change only the cliques that hold its variables and the cliques above them. Take that part of the tree apart, eliminate it again, and hang the untouched sub-trees back on.

1. The problem: measurements never stop

A robot wants a fresh estimate every time a measurement arrives. Refactoring \(\boldsymbol{\Lambda}\) from scratch each time costs more and more as the trajectory grows, although one new measurement changes very little. For a linear problem there are classical ways to update an existing factorization (tomorrow shows one). But SLAM is nonlinear: when the estimate moves, old factors must be linearized again, old rows of \(\mathbf{A}\) change, and it is not clear how to do that without factoring everything again. The book's answer is to stop thinking of \(\mathbf{R}\) as a matrix and to store it as a graphical model that can be edited locally, the Bayes tree. §1.7 · p. 46

2. Elimination gives a chordal Bayes net, and chordal graphs have cliques that form a tree

A graph is chordal (or triangulated) if every cycle of more than three nodes has a chord, an edge joining two nodes that are not consecutive on the cycle. Ignoring arrow directions, the Bayes net produced by the elimination algorithm is always chordal. §1.7.1 · p. 46

Filling the gap: why elimination always produces a chordal graph

Take any cycle in the Bayes net and let \(v\) be the variable on it that was eliminated first. Its two neighbours on the cycle, \(u\) and \(w\), were eliminated later, so the edges \(v\)–\(u\) and \(v\)–\(w\) mean that both were in the separator of \(v\). Yesterday's rule says eliminating \(v\) joins all members of its separator, so \(u\) and \(w\) share a factor from then on, and whichever of the two is eliminated first gets the other in its separator. The Bayes net therefore has the edge \(u\)–\(w\). If the cycle has more than three nodes, \(u\) and \(w\) are not consecutive on it, and this edge is a chord.

The same argument shows that each variable together with its separator is a clique, a set of variables that are all joined pairwise.

The toy Bayes net (last panel of Figure 1.10) has the cycle \(\mathbf{p}_1\)–\(\mathbf{p}_2\)–\(\boldsymbol{\ell}_1\), so at the level of single variables it is not a tree. §1.7.1 · p. 47 But its largest cliques are \(\{\boldsymbol{\ell}_1, \mathbf{p}_1, \mathbf{p}_2\}\), \(\{\mathbf{p}_2, \mathbf{p}_3\}\) and \(\{\boldsymbol{\ell}_2, \mathbf{p}_3\}\), and these three overlap like a tree: the first and the third each share one variable with the middle one and nothing with each other. For chordal graphs this always works. The book states it without proof. The undirected version is known as a clique tree or junction tree.

3. The Bayes tree

A Bayes tree is a directed tree whose nodes are the cliques \(\mathbf{c}_k\) of the chordal Bayes net. For each clique: §1.7.1 · p. 47

  • the separator \(\mathbf{s}_k = \mathbf{c}_k \cap \boldsymbol{\varpi}_k\) is what the clique shares with its parent clique \(\boldsymbol{\varpi}_k\);
  • the frontal variables \(\mathbf{f}_k = \mathbf{c}_k \setminus \mathbf{s}_k\) are the rest;
  • the node stores one conditional \(p(\mathbf{f}_k \mid \mathbf{s}_k)\), and the clique is written \(\mathbf{f}_k : \mathbf{s}_k\).

The joint density is the product over the cliques, equation (1.55): \(p(\mathbf{x}) = \prod_k p(\mathbf{f}_k \mid \mathbf{s}_k)\). The root has an empty separator and stores a prior \(p(\mathbf{f}_r)\). Every variable is frontal in exactly one clique.

Filling the gap: building the tree from the Bayes net

The book says the cliques can be "identified". The procedure, from the iSAM2 paper, visits the conditionals in reverse elimination order. For \(p(\mathbf{x}_j \mid \mathbf{s}_j)\): if \(\mathbf{s}_j\) is empty, start a root clique. Otherwise find the clique in which the first-eliminated variable of \(\mathbf{s}_j\) is frontal. If that clique's variables are exactly \(\mathbf{s}_j\), add \(\mathbf{x}_j\) to it as another frontal variable. If not, start a new clique \(\mathbf{x}_j : \mathbf{s}_j\) as its child. For the toy example:

ConditionalClique foundSame variables as the separator?Tree afterwards
p(p₃)none, the separator is emptyroot: p₃
p(p₂ | p₃)root, {p₃}yes, join itroot: p₂, p₃
p(p₁ | p₂)root, {p₂, p₃}no, new childadds p₁ : p₂
p(ℓ₂ | p₃)root, {p₂, p₃}no, new childadds ℓ₂ : p₃
p(ℓ₁ | p₁, p₂)p₁ : p₂, which is {p₁, p₂}yes, join itthat clique becomes ℓ₁, p₁ : p₂

Each clique is a small dense piece of \(\mathbf{R}\): the rows of its frontal variables, with nonzeros only in the columns of the clique. The book calls the Bayes tree "a deeply meaningful sparse storage scheme" for the square-root information matrix. §1.7.2 · p. 48 Rows of different branches overlap only in columns that belong to a common ancestor: in Figure 1.13(c), the rows of the two child cliques meet only in the root's columns.

4. Updating: only the path to the root

Two facts about how the tree was made explain everything. §1.7.2 · p. 48

  1. Information flows upward only. A clique is computed from its own factors and from the new factors \(\tau\) passed up by its children. Nothing computed in a parent is ever used in a child.
  2. A factor enters at the first of its variables to be eliminated, that is, in the clique where that variable is frontal.

So a new factor \(\phi(\mathbf{x}_j, \mathbf{x}_{j'})\) changes the cliques where \(\mathbf{x}_j\) and \(\mathbf{x}_{j'}\) are frontal and every clique above them, up to the root. Sub-trees hanging below or beside these paths were computed from factors that have not changed. The update is an edit of the tree:

1. detach the affected cliques (the paths from the new factor's variables to the root)
2. turn each of them back into a factor on its variables f_k and s_k
3. add the new factor
4. eliminate this small factor graph, in any convenient order -> a new top of the tree
5. re-attach the untouched sub-trees ("orphans") below it

Figure 1.14 adds a factor between \(\mathbf{p}_1\) and \(\mathbf{p}_3\). \(\mathbf{p}_1\) is frontal in the left clique and \(\mathbf{p}_3\) in the root, so those two are detached. They become a factor on \((\boldsymbol{\ell}_1, \mathbf{p}_1, \mathbf{p}_2)\) and a factor on \((\mathbf{p}_2, \mathbf{p}_3)\). Add \(f(\mathbf{p}_1, \mathbf{p}_3)\) and eliminate in the order \(\boldsymbol{\ell}_1, \mathbf{p}_1, \mathbf{p}_2, \mathbf{p}_3\):

  • \(\boldsymbol{\ell}_1\): separator \(\{\mathbf{p}_1, \mathbf{p}_2\}\), as before.
  • \(\mathbf{p}_1\): its factors are \(\tau(\mathbf{p}_1, \mathbf{p}_2)\) and the new \(f(\mathbf{p}_1, \mathbf{p}_3)\), so its separator is now \(\{\mathbf{p}_2, \mathbf{p}_3\}\) and not just \(\{\mathbf{p}_2\}\).
  • \(\mathbf{p}_2\): separator \(\{\mathbf{p}_3\}\). Then \(\mathbf{p}_3\), with none.

Run the tree-building procedure on these four conditionals and you get a root \(\mathbf{p}_1, \mathbf{p}_2, \mathbf{p}_3\) with a child \(\boldsymbol{\ell}_1 : \mathbf{p}_1, \mathbf{p}_2\). The clique \(\boldsymbol{\ell}_2 : \mathbf{p}_3\) is hung back under the root unchanged. §1.7.2 · p. 49

Intuition

Why is \(\boldsymbol{\ell}_2 : \mathbf{p}_3\) untouched although the new factor involves \(\mathbf{p}_3\)? Because \(\mathbf{p}_3\) is only its separator. The clique stores "how to place \(\boldsymbol{\ell}_2\) once \(\mathbf{p}_3\) is known", and that rule was built from \(\phi_5\) and \(\phi_9\) alone. The new measurement changes what we believe about \(\mathbf{p}_3\), which is stored in the root. The value of \(\boldsymbol{\ell}_2\) will still move when back-substitution runs again; its conditional does not.

Try it: the tree on the right was built by the steps on the left. Press "Add next pose" and watch which cliques turn pink. Go on to step 11, where the robot returns to its start.

Notice that an ordinary step redoes only 3 or 4 variables next to the root, however long the trajectory already is. Step 11 adds a loop closure to x1, which sits at the very bottom of the tree, so the path to the root is the whole tree and all 14 variables are redone. Step 12 sees landmark l1 again and costs almost as much. Steps 13 and 14 are cheap again. Over the run the incremental updates re-eliminate 67 variables, against 135 for refactoring everything at every step.

Figure 1.15 shows the same effect at a larger scale: the Bayes tree at step 400 of a simulated Manhattan-world sequence, with only a small part recalculated. §1.7.2 · pp. 49–50

Common mistakes

  • "The root is where the robot started." The root holds the variables eliminated last. A good incremental ordering puts the most recent poses there, because that is where the next factors will arrive.
  • "The Bayes tree is a different, approximate model." It is the same density and the same \(\mathbf{R}\) as the Bayes net, grouped by clique.
  • "A factor between two variables changes two cliques." It changes their cliques and all the ancestors of both. If one of the variables is deep in the tree, that can be most of it.

Check yourself

Q1. In the clique written ℓ₁, p₁ : p₂, which variables are frontal?

Frontal variables are written before the colon and the separator after it. The clique stores p(ℓ₁, p₁ | p₂).

Q2. A cycle a – b – c – d – a has no other edges. Is the graph chordal?

Chordal means every cycle longer than three has a chord. Elimination would add one: whichever node goes first, its two neighbours are joined.

Q3. In the toy Bayes tree a second prior factor on ℓ₂ alone arrives. Which cliques must be recomputed?

The factor enters where ℓ₂ is frontal, and the new factor that clique passes upward changes its parent, the root. The clique ℓ₁, p₁ : p₂ is on no path from ℓ₂ to the root.

Q4. With ordering ℓ₁, ℓ₂, p₁, p₂, p₃, which rows of R belong to the root clique?

The root's frontal variables are p₂ and p₃, the last two eliminated, so its conditionals are the last two rows. Row 3, p(p₁ | p₂), went into the left child.

Q5. Why can the sub-trees that are not on a path to the root be reused as they are?

Information flows upward during elimination, so a clique depends only on its own factors and its descendants. The estimates of its variables may still change, through the separator, when back-substitution is run.

Recap

  1. Batch refactoring wastes work, and plain incremental matrix updates do not handle relinearization. The Bayes tree is \(\mathbf{R}\) stored so it can be edited.
  2. Elimination yields a chordal Bayes net. Its cliques form a tree.
  3. Each clique \(\mathbf{f}_k : \mathbf{s}_k\) stores \(p(\mathbf{f}_k \mid \mathbf{s}_k)\); the separator is what it shares with its parent; \(p(\mathbf{x}) = \prod_k p(\mathbf{f}_k \mid \mathbf{s}_k)\).
  4. Information flows from leaves to root, and a factor enters at its first eliminated variable.
  5. A new factor affects only the cliques of its variables and their ancestors. Detach them, add the factor, re-eliminate, re-attach the orphans.

Sources

  1. SLAM Handbook, §1.7 "Incremental SLAM", §1.7.1 "The Bayes Tree", §1.7.2 "Updating the Bayes Tree", pp. 46–50, equations (1.54)–(1.55), Figures 1.13–1.15.
  2. Kaess, Johannsson, Roberts, Ila, Leonard, Dellaert, iSAM2: Incremental smoothing and mapping using the Bayes tree, 2012 (the procedure that builds the tree from the chordal Bayes net).
  3. Koller and Friedman, Probabilistic Graphical Models, 2009 (chordal graphs and clique trees).

Week 3 · Day 5

iSAM and iSAM2: incremental smoothing and mapping

After today you can describe how iSAM1 and iSAM2 keep a SLAM solution up to date, including incremental reordering, partial back-substitution and selective relinearization, and say when an update is cheap and when it is not.

About 60 min · Read §1.7.3 and §1.8, pp. 50–52 (2 pages of text) · Needs Week 3 Day 4

Read first: §1.7.3 and §1.8, from the bottom of p. 50 to p. 52

Most of p. 50 is Figure 1.15, so this is a short reading. Look for:

  • p. 50: how iSAM1 handled linearization, and what iSAM2 uses in place of the matrix.
  • p. 51, first paragraph: which variables are forced to the end of the ordering, and why.
  • p. 51, second paragraph: when back-substitution may stop early.
  • p. 51, third paragraph: why relinearizing a variable affects more cliques than adding a factor does.

Today's big idea

Incremental smoothing and mapping keeps the whole trajectory in the estimate but does only the work a new measurement calls for. iSAM1 updates the matrix \(\mathbf{R}\) directly and starts over from time to time. iSAM2 edits the Bayes tree and is lazy in three places: it reorders only the variables it re-eliminates, re-solves only where the answer moved, and relinearizes only the factors whose variables moved.

1. iSAM1: add a row to R without refactoring

The first version, iSAM1, used the incremental matrix factorization methods of Golub and Van Loan. §1.7.3 · p. 50 The book does not show them, so here is the basic one.

Filling the gap: updating R with Givens rotations

We have \([\mathbf{R} \mid \mathbf{d}]\), so the current cost is \(\norm{\mathbf{R}\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{d}}^2\) plus a constant. One new scalar measurement, already whitened, adds a term \((\mathbf{a}\T\mathbf{x} - \beta)^2\). The new problem is the least-squares problem of the stacked matrix

\[ \left[\begin{array}{c|c} \mathbf{R} & \mathbf{d} \\ \mathbf{a}\T & \beta \end{array}\right] , \]

which is upper-triangular except for its last row. A Givens rotation is a rotation in the plane of two rows. To zero entry \(a_c\) of the new row against row \(c\) of \(\mathbf{R}\), set \(r = \sqrt{R_{cc}^2 + a_c^2}\), \(\cos = R_{cc}/r\), \(\sin = a_c/r\), and replace the two rows by

\[ \begin{aligned} \text{row } c &\leftarrow \cos \cdot (\text{row } c) + \sin \cdot (\text{new row}) , \\ \text{new row} &\leftarrow -\sin \cdot (\text{row } c) + \cos \cdot (\text{new row}) . \end{aligned} \]

The new diagonal entry is \(r\) and the new row's entry in column \(c\) is \((-a_c R_{cc} + R_{cc} a_c)/r = 0\). A rotation is orthogonal, so by the argument of Day 2 the cost function is unchanged. Repeat for each column from the first nonzero of \(\mathbf{a}\) to the last. What remains of the new row is a single number in the right-hand-side column, which only adds to the residual.

Two things to notice. Rows of \(\mathbf{R}\) above the first nonzero of \(\mathbf{a}\) are never touched. And mixing in row \(c\) can put nonzeros into later entries of the new row that started as zeros, so one rotation is usually not enough.

Try it: \(\mathbf{R}\) belongs to five poses in a chain. Rotate in a loop closure to the first pose, then switch to the measurement that touches only the newest pose.

Notice that the loop closure x₅ − x₁ = 4.6 needs 5 rotations and changes every row of R, and the estimate moves from (0, 1, 2.1, 3, 4) to (0, 1.12, 2.34, 3.36, 4.48). The measurement x₅ = 4.4 needs one rotation and changes one row. Yet it also moves every estimate, because back-substitution passes the change in x₅ on to all the others.

This is yesterday's tree rule in matrix clothing. For a chain, the rows from the first nonzero down to the last are the path to the root. The tree is more precise for general graphs, because it also skips branches that lie between the two in the ordering but are unrelated.

iSAM1 had two weak spots. The column order was the order in which variables arrived, so loop closures produced growing fill-in. And all of \(\mathbf{R}\) was built on one linearization point. Its remedy was a periodic batch step: linearize the full factor graph again, at fixed intervals or when fill-in became unwieldy. §1.7.3 · p. 50 The work between two batch steps was small, but the batch steps themselves grew with the map.

2. iSAM2: edit the tree, and be lazy three times

iSAM2 stores the posterior as a Bayes tree and applies the update of Day 4 for every new measurement. §1.7.3 · p. 50 Three practical questions remain, and the book answers each on p. 51.

Which ordering for the part that is re-eliminated? Only the variables of the affected cliques are eliminated again, so only they can be reordered. Running COLAMD on them alone is one option. iSAM2 does better with constrained COLAMD: it forces the most recently accessed variables to the end of the ordering, which puts them in the root clique, and orders the rest well. The reason is a bet about the future. The next factors will almost surely involve the newest pose, and if that pose is already in the root, the path to the root is as short as it can be. The book expects later updates to be efficient "in most cases, except for large loop closures". §1.7.3 · p. 51

Which variables need a new value? Back-substitution in the tree starts at the root and moves towards the leaves, each clique using the values of its separator. A clique's solution changes only through its separator, so if the values handed down have changed by less than a small threshold, there is no need to descend further. §1.7.3 · p. 51 The widget above shows why this matters: an update that changes one row of \(\mathbf{R}\) can still shift every estimate a little, and the threshold decides how far down the tree those shifts are followed.

Which factors are linearized again? Only those containing a variable whose estimate has moved away from its linearization point by more than a threshold. §1.7.3 · p. 51 The iSAM2 paper calls this fluid relinearization: there are no batch steps any more.

Filling the gap: why relinearization reaches further than a new factor

Adding a factor leaves all old factors as they were. The affected cliques can be turned back into factors as they are, and only cliques where the new factor's variables are frontal, plus their ancestors, are redone.

Relinearizing variable \(v\) is different: every factor that touches \(v\) gets a new \(\mathbf{A}_i\) and \(\mathbf{b}_i\). Such a factor entered the tree at the clique where the first of its variables was eliminated, and \(v\) may be only a separator variable there. So every clique that contains \(v\) at all, as frontal or as separator, holds outdated numbers and must be redone, together with all ancestors. The cliques cannot simply be recycled either. The method has to go back to the original nonlinear factors, and the contributions of the untouched sub-trees must have been cached during elimination. The book's verdict: this affects larger parts of the tree, but is in most cases still much cheaper than recomputing all of it. §1.7.3 · p. 51

Put together, one iSAM2 step looks like this (a summary of pp. 50–51, not the paper's exact listing):

when new factors (and new variables) arrive:
  1. mark the cliques on the paths from the new factors' variables to the root
  2. mark every clique containing a variable that has moved past the
     relinearization threshold, and the paths from those to the root
  3. turn the marked part back into a factor graph: relinearized original
     factors where needed, cached summaries of the sub-trees below, the new factors
  4. order its variables with constrained COLAMD (recent variables last)
     and eliminate: this is the new top of the Bayes tree
  5. re-attach the untouched sub-trees
  6. back-substitute from the root; stop going down a branch where the
     change is below the threshold
QuestioniSAM1iSAM2
How is the factor stored?As the sparse matrix RAs a Bayes tree
A new measurementIncremental matrix factorization updateRe-eliminate the affected cliques
RelinearizationThe full graph, periodically or when fill-in growsPer variable, when it moves past a threshold
Variable orderingImproved only at the periodic batch stepsUpdated at every step for the affected variables, recent ones last
Solution updateBack-substitutionBack-substitution from the root, stopped early by a threshold

3. When is an update cheap?

Go back to the Day 4 widget with today's vocabulary. While the robot explores, each new factor involves the newest pose and something recent. Those variables are in or next to the root, so 3 or 4 variables are re-eliminated, independent of how long the trajectory is. That is the regime in which incremental smoothing gives a full-trajectory estimate at a nearly constant cost per step.

A loop closure ties the newest pose to an old one that sits deep in the tree. The whole path between them is redone, and for a large loop this can be most of the tree. No ordering trick removes that cost, since the new measurement really does change what is known about everything on the loop. Afterwards the old variable is near the root and the following steps are cheap again.

In plain words

Keep your notes in a binder with the newest pages on top. A new observation about today only needs the top pages rewritten. Discovering that today's place is the same as a place from chapter one means rewriting everything in between. Once that is done, you are back to rewriting only the top pages.

Both algorithms are implemented in the GTSAM library, and the book reports that they have been applied to many robotics estimation problems, at sizes that reach into the millions. §1.7.3 · p. 51

4. Where the chapter leaves you

Section 1.8 is a short reading list. For factor graphs and elimination in more detail the book recommends the longer article by Dellaert and co-authors that it cites, and for the Bayes tree the iSAM2 paper by Kaess and co-authors. §1.8 · p. 51 It then names what the plain version of this chapter left out and the rest of the handbook supplies: state variables that live on manifolds, such as rotations (next week), many kinds of sensors, outlier measurements (Week 6), and the outputs of learned models. §1.8 · pp. 51–52

The path of Chapter 1, in one line each:

ObjectAs a graphAs linear algebra
The problemFactor graphSparse Jacobian A and right-hand side b
Who is related to whomGraph G (Markov random field)Pattern of Λ = AᵀA
SolvingVariable eliminationSparse QR or Cholesky
The resultBayes netUpper-triangular R and d
The estimateMAP inference in the Bayes netBack-substitution
Keeping it up to dateEditing the Bayes treeIncremental factorization

Common mistakes

  • "Incremental means approximate." For the linear problem the updated tree is exactly what a batch factorization would give. The approximations are the two thresholds, which trade a little accuracy for speed.
  • "iSAM is a filter." It is a smoother: every past pose stays in the estimate and can still be corrected, as a loop closure shows.
  • "A loop closure is cheap because it is one factor." The cost depends on where its variables sit in the tree, not on the number of factors.

Check yourself

Q1. A row of R reads (3, …) in column c and the new row has 4 in column c. After the Givens rotation, what is the diagonal entry R_cc?

r = √(3² + 4²) = 5. The rotation moves all the weight of the two entries into the row of R and leaves zero in the new row.

Q2. R has 100 columns in arrival order. A new measurement row has its first nonzero in column 97. How many rows of R can change?

Rotations start at the first nonzero and move right. Rows above it are never mixed with the new row.

Q3. Why does iSAM2 force the most recently used variables to the end of the elimination ordering?

Variables eliminated last form the root clique. New factors usually involve recent variables, so the affected path to the root stays short.

Q4. Variable v is frontal in clique C₁ and a separator variable in its child C₂. Its estimate has moved past the relinearization threshold. Which cliques are redone?

Relinearization changes the factors on v, and some of them were absorbed in C₂, where v is a separator. All cliques containing v are redone, plus everything above them.

Q5. During back-substitution a clique receives separator values that changed by far less than the threshold. What does iSAM2 do?

A clique's solution depends on the rest of the tree only through its separator. If that input has barely changed, neither will the outputs further down.

Recap

  1. A new measurement row can be rotated into \(\mathbf{R}\) with Givens rotations. Rows above its first nonzero are untouched. This is the matrix view of "only the path to the root".
  2. iSAM1 updates \(\mathbf{R}\) this way and relinearizes the full graph in periodic batch steps.
  3. iSAM2 edits the Bayes tree: re-eliminate the affected cliques, with recently used variables ordered last so they sit in the root.
  4. It back-substitutes only as far as the solution changes, and relinearizes only variables that moved past a threshold. Relinearization redoes every clique containing such a variable.
  5. Exploration costs a few variables per step. A large loop closure can cost most of the tree.

Sources

  1. SLAM Handbook, §1.7.3 "Incremental Smoothing and Mapping", pp. 50–51, and §1.8 "Further Readings & Recent Trends", pp. 51–52.
  2. Golub and Van Loan, Matrix Computations, 4th edition, 2013 (Givens rotations and updating a QR factorization when a row is added).
  3. Kaess, Ranganathan, Dellaert, iSAM: Incremental smoothing and mapping, 2008 (iSAM1: Givens updates, periodic reordering and relinearization).
  4. Kaess, Johannsson, Roberts, Ila, Leonard, Dellaert, iSAM2: Incremental smoothing and mapping using the Bayes tree, 2012 (fluid relinearization, constrained ordering, partial solution updates).

Week 3 · Review

Week 3 review: sparsity, elimination, and the Bayes tree

After today you can go from a factor graph to its matrix patterns, eliminate it by hand into a Bayes net and a Bayes tree, marginalize with the Schur complement, and say what an incremental update has to recompute.

About 60 min · No new pages

The week in one paragraph

A SLAM least-squares problem is sparse because each factor touches few variables: factors are block-rows of \(\mathbf{A}\), variables are block-columns, and \(\boldsymbol{\Lambda} = \mathbf{A}\T\mathbf{A}\) has a nonzero block only between variables that share a factor. Variable elimination removes one variable at a time, leaving a conditional (a row of \(\mathbf{R}\)) and a new factor on its neighbours; with Gaussian factors this is sparse QR or Cholesky, and the result is a Bayes net solved by back-substitution. Removing a variable joins its neighbours, which is fill-in on the graph and the Schur complement in the matrix, so the ordering decides the cost. Grouping the conditionals into cliques gives the Bayes tree, in which a new factor affects only the path from its variables to the root. iSAM2 uses that to update the solution incrementally.

1. Formula sheet

What it isFormulaWhere
Blocks of the information matrix\(\boldsymbol{\Lambda}_{jk} = \sum_i \mathbf{A}_{ij}\T\mathbf{A}_{ik}\), nonzero only if a factor contains both \(j\) and \(k\)§1.5.2, p. 37 · Day 1
One elimination step\(\psi(\mathbf{x}_j, \mathbf{s}_j) = p(\mathbf{x}_j \mid \mathbf{s}_j)\,\tau(\mathbf{s}_j)\)(1.43), §1.6.1, p. 40 · Day 2
The same step as partial QR\([\bar{\mathbf{A}}_j \mid \bar{\mathbf{b}}_j] = \mathbf{Q}\begin{bmatrix} \mathbf{R}_j & \mathbf{T}_j & \mathbf{d}_j \\ \mathbf{0} & \tilde{\mathbf{A}}_\tau & \tilde{\mathbf{b}}_\tau \end{bmatrix}\)(1.48), §1.6.2, p. 42 · Day 2
A row of R as a Gaussianmean \(\boldsymbol{\mu}_j = \mathbf{R}_j^{-1}(\mathbf{d}_j - \mathbf{T}_j\mathbf{s}_j)\), covariance \(\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_j = (\mathbf{R}_j\T\mathbf{R}_j)^{-1}\)(1.51)–(1.52), §1.6.3, p. 45 · Day 3
Back-substitution\(\mathbf{x}_j^* = \mathbf{R}_j^{-1}(\mathbf{d}_j - \mathbf{T}_j\mathbf{s}_j^*)\), in reverse elimination order(1.53), §1.6.3, p. 45 · Day 3
Size of Rnonzeros \(= \sum_j (1 + |\mathbf{s}_j|)\); fill-in = edges added when neighbours are joinedDay 3
Schur complement: marginal of \(\mathbf{x}_b\) in information form\(\boldsymbol{\Lambda}_{bb} - \boldsymbol{\Lambda}_{ba}\boldsymbol{\Lambda}_{aa}^{-1}\boldsymbol{\Lambda}_{ab}\)Day 3 (not in the book)
Conditional of \(\mathbf{x}_b\) given \(\mathbf{x}_a\) in covariance form\(\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{bb} - \boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{ba}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{aa}^{-1}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{ab}\)Day 3 (not in the book)
Bayes tree\(p(\mathbf{x}) = \prod_k p(\mathbf{f}_k \mid \mathbf{s}_k)\), with \(\mathbf{s}_k = \mathbf{c}_k \cap \boldsymbol{\varpi}_k\) and \(\mathbf{f}_k = \mathbf{c}_k \setminus \mathbf{s}_k\)(1.55), §1.7.1, p. 47 · Day 4

2. Mixed quiz

Check yourself
