The odd powers of the series collect into \(\tfrac{\phi}{2!} - \tfrac{\phi^3}{4!} + \dots = \tfrac{1-\cos\phi}{\phi}\) and the even ones into \(\tfrac{\phi^2}{3!} - \tfrac{\phi^4}{5!} + \dots = 1 - \tfrac{\sin\phi}{\phi}\). At \(\phi = 0\) both coefficients vanish and \(\mathbf{J} = \mathbf{I}\): for small rotations, vectors simply add.

Right Jacobian. If the second rotation is the small one, the mirror-image formula holds: \(\Exp(\boldsymbol{\theta}_1)\Exp(\boldsymbol{\theta}_2)\approx\Exp\big(\boldsymbol{\theta}_1 + \mathbf{J}_r(\boldsymbol{\theta}_1)^{-1}\boldsymbol{\theta}_2\big)\) with \(\mathbf{J}_r(\boldsymbol{\theta}) = \mathbf{J}(-\boldsymbol{\theta}) = \mathbf{J}(\boldsymbol{\theta})\T\).

Kinematics. The book introduces \(\mathbf{J}\) through \(\dot{\boldsymbol{\theta}} = \mathbf{J}^{-1}(\boldsymbol{\theta})\,\boldsymbol{\omega}\), equation (2.33). In words: the rate of change of the rotation vector is not the angular velocity, unless the axis stays fixed. \(\mathbf{J}\) converts between the two. In the plane \(\mathbf{J} = 1\) and \(\dot\theta = \omega\).

Try it: compare the plain sum and equation (2.34) against the exact answer.

Notice that at the default settings (θ₁ of size 0.1 rad, θ₂ of 60°, axes at right angles) the plain sum is off by 0.053 rad, about 3°, and equation (2.34) by 0.0009 rad. Each time θ₁ shrinks by a factor of 10, the error of the sum shrinks by 10 and that of (2.34) by 100: first order against second order. Set the angle between the axes to 0° and both errors drop below the bottom of the chart.

Poses have a Jacobian too, written \(\mathbf{J}(\boldsymbol{\xi})\), and the book reuses the symbol. §2.1.5.4 · p. 62 These Jacobians return in Week 7 when poses are differentiated inside a network.

Common mistakes

  • "\(\mathbf{T}\ominus\mathbf{T}^0\) is \(\mathbf{T}-\mathbf{T}^0\)." The matrix difference is not in the Lie algebra. ⊖ is Log of a relative transformation.
  • "\(\Ad(\mathbf{T})\) has the size of \(\mathbf{T}\)." It multiplies tangent vectors: 6 × 6 in 3D, 3 × 3 in the plane.
  • "The adjoint identity is a small-angle approximation." (2.31) is exact for any \(\boldsymbol{\xi}\). The Jacobian formula (2.34) is the approximate one.
  • "(2.34) treats θ₁ and θ₂ alike." Only the small one is multiplied by \(\mathbf{J}^{-1}\), and the Jacobian is evaluated at the large one. Left factor small: left Jacobian. Right factor small: right Jacobian.

Check yourself

Q1. In \(\SO(2)\), \(\mathbf{R}^0\) is a rotation by 30° and \(\mathbf{R}\) a rotation by 75°. What is \(\mathbf{R}\ominus\mathbf{R}^0\)?

\(\Log\big((\mathbf{R}^0)\T\mathbf{R}\big)\): the relative rotation is by \(75^\circ - 30^\circ = 45^\circ\), and its Log is that angle. The answer is a tangent vector (here a single number), not a matrix.

Q2. A planar robot is at \(\mathbf{t} = (3, 0)\) with heading 0. It turns on the spot: \(\boldsymbol{\xi} = (0, 0, 0.1)\). Which left perturbation \(\boldsymbol{\epsilon} = \Ad(\mathbf{T})\boldsymbol{\xi}\) describes the same motion?

With \(\mathbf{R} = \mathbf{I}\): \(\boldsymbol{\epsilon} = (-\theta\,\mathbf{S}\mathbf{t},\ \theta) = (0.1\,(t_2, -t_1),\ 0.1) = (0, -0.3, 0.1)\). A turn about the origin by 0.1 rad would lift the robot by 0.3. The translation −0.3 cancels that, so the robot stays put and only turns.

Q3. Which expression equals \(\big(\mathbf{T}^0\,\Exp(\boldsymbol{\xi})\big)^{-1}\)?

Equation (2.26). Inverting a product reverses the order, and the inverse of \(\Exp(\boldsymbol{\xi})\) is \(\Exp(-\boldsymbol{\xi})\). The perturbation moves to the left and changes sign.

Q4. In the widget, \(\boldsymbol{\theta}_1\) is made 10 times smaller. By about what factors do the errors of \(\boldsymbol{\theta}_1+\boldsymbol{\theta}_2\) and of equation (2.34) shrink?

The plain sum misses terms that are linear in \(\boldsymbol{\theta}_1\), such as \(\tfrac12\boldsymbol{\theta}_1\times\boldsymbol{\theta}_2\), so its error scales with \(\norm{\boldsymbol{\theta}_1}\). Equation (2.34) keeps all linear terms and misses only quadratic ones, so its error scales with \(\norm{\boldsymbol{\theta}_1}^2\).

Recap

  1. \(\mathbf{T}\ominus\mathbf{T}^0 = \Log\big((\mathbf{T}^0)^{-1}\mathbf{T}\big)\) is the tangent vector from \(\mathbf{T}^0\) to \(\mathbf{T}\). With ⊕ it gives differences, errors, and interpolation.
  2. \((\mathbf{T}^0\,\Exp(\boldsymbol{\xi}))^{-1} = \Exp(-\boldsymbol{\xi})(\mathbf{T}^0)^{-1}\): inverting swaps the side and flips the sign.
  3. \(\mathbf{T}\,\Exp(\boldsymbol{\xi}) = \Exp(\Ad(\mathbf{T})\boldsymbol{\xi})\,\mathbf{T}\), exactly. \(\Ad(\mathbf{T})\) re-expresses a local tangent vector in the global frame.
  4. \(\Exp(\boldsymbol{\theta}_1)\Exp(\boldsymbol{\theta}_2)\approx\Exp(\boldsymbol{\theta}_2+\mathbf{J}(\boldsymbol{\theta}_2)^{-1}\boldsymbol{\theta}_1)\) for small \(\boldsymbol{\theta}_1\): the BCH series cut after the terms linear in \(\boldsymbol{\theta}_1\).
  5. \(\mathbf{J}(\boldsymbol{\theta}) = \sum(\boldsymbol{\theta}^\wedge)^n/(n+1)!\) equals \(\mathbf{I}\) at zero, and is the same matrix that turns \(\boldsymbol{\rho}\) into a translation.

Sources

  1. SLAM Handbook, §2.1.5 "Lie Group Extras", pp. 60–62, equations (2.24)–(2.35).
  2. Barfoot, State Estimation for Robotics, 2017 (adjoint of SE(3), BCH formula, closed form of the SO(3) Jacobian and its inverse series, left and right Jacobians).
  3. Solà, Deray, Atchuthan, A micro Lie theory for state estimation in robotics, 2018 (⊕ and ⊖, the SE(2) adjoint, covariance of a composition, interpolation).
  4. Barfoot and Furgale, Associating Uncertainty with Three-Dimensional Poses for Use in Estimation Problems, 2014 (compounding uncertain poses).

Week 4 · Review

Week 4 review: Lie groups and optimization on manifolds

After today you can move between a pose and its tangent vector, run one Gauss-Newton step on a group by hand, state what a covariance of a pose means, and use the adjoint to change the side of a perturbation.

About 60 min · No new pages

The week in one paragraph

Rotations and poses are matrices tied by constraints, so they form curved manifolds, \(\SO(d)\) and \(\SE(d)\), not vector spaces. They are also groups, and each has a flat companion, its Lie algebra, with one coordinate per degree of freedom. The exponential map turns a vector of the Lie algebra into a group member, and the logarithm goes back. That is enough to rebuild everything Week 2 did with vectors: a perturbation \(\mathbf{T}^0\,\Exp(\boldsymbol{\xi})\) replaces "guess plus step" in Gauss-Newton, \(\bar{\mathbf{T}}\,\Exp(\boldsymbol{\delta})\) with Gaussian \(\boldsymbol{\delta}\) replaces "mean plus noise", and \(\Log\) of a relative transformation replaces subtraction. Because order matters in a group, two more tools are needed: the adjoint, which moves a perturbation across a transformation exactly, and the Jacobian, which combines two exponentials approximately.

1. Formula sheet

What it isFormulaWhere

2. Mixed quiz

Check yourself

Q1. How many degrees of freedom does a planar pose in \(\SE(2)\) have?

Two for translation and one for the heading: \(3(d-1)\) with \(d=2\). The 3 × 3 matrix has nine entries, but most are fixed.

Q2. You know \(\mathbf{T}^b_a\) and \(\mathbf{T}^c_b\). Which product converts coordinates from frame \(a\) to frame \(c\)?

The matrix nearest the point acts first, and adjacent indices must match: \(\mathbf{T}^c_a = \mathbf{T}^c_b\mathbf{T}^b_a\). The other order does not have matching indices, and poses do not commute.

Q3. What is \(\Exp(\pi)\) in \(\SO(2)\)?

\(\cos\pi = -1\) and \(\sin\pi = 0\), so the matrix is \(-\mathbf{I}\): a half turn. Its determinant is \((-1)^2 = 1\), so it is a proper rotation.

Q4. Which description of \(\boldsymbol{\xi}\) for a 3D pose matches the book?

Equation (2.7b): \(\boldsymbol{\xi} = (\boldsymbol{\rho},\boldsymbol{\theta})\in\R^6\). \(\boldsymbol{\rho}\) is not the position, which is \(\mathbf{J}(\boldsymbol{\theta})\boldsymbol{\rho}\), and \(\boldsymbol{\theta}\) is an axis times an angle, not Euler angles.

Q5. In Gauss-Newton on \(\SE(3)\), what is the approximation \(\mathbf{T}^0(\mathbf{I}+\boldsymbol{\xi}^\wedge)\) used for?

The first-order form makes the model linear in \(\boldsymbol{\xi}\) so that \(\mathbf{H}_i\) can be read off. The residual uses the exact current pose, and the update (2.19) uses the exact exponential, which keeps the pose in the group.

Q6. A point is at \(\boldsymbol{\ell} = (0,0,2)\). The perturbation is \(\boldsymbol{\rho} = (1,0,0)\), \(\boldsymbol{\theta} = (0,0.5,0)\). What are the top three entries of \(\tilde{\boldsymbol{\ell}}^{\odot}\boldsymbol{\xi}\)?

\(\boldsymbol{\rho}+\boldsymbol{\theta}\times\boldsymbol{\ell} = (1,0,0) + (0,0.5,0)\times(0,0,2) = (1,0,0)+(1,0,0) = (2,0,0)\). A turn about y pushes a point on the z-axis in the x direction, and the translation adds to it.

Q7. One-step model of Day 4 with \(L = 10\) m and heading noise \(\sigma = 0.1\) rad. What is the standard deviation of the sideways tangent coordinate \(\rho_2\)?

The covariance is \(\sigma^2(0,L,1)\T(0,L,1)\). Its middle diagonal entry is \(\sigma^2L^2 = 1\ \text{m}^2\), so the standard deviation is \(L\sigma = 1\) m.

Q8. Which of these identities is exact for every \(\boldsymbol{\xi}\), not only for small ones?

The adjoint identity (2.31) follows from \(\mathbf{T}\exp(\mathbf{A})\mathbf{T}^{-1} = \exp(\mathbf{T}\mathbf{A}\mathbf{T}^{-1})\) with no terms dropped. The first is false unless the wedge matrices commute, and the other two are first-order approximations.

3. Pen-and-paper problems

  1. A planar transformation \(\mathbf{T}^b_a\) has \(\theta = 90^\circ\) and \(\mathbf{t}^b_a = (1, 2)\). (a) Write \(\mathbf{T}^b_a\) as a 3 × 3 matrix. (b) Convert the landmark \(\boldsymbol{\ell}^a = (3, 0)\) to frame \(b\). (c) Write \((\mathbf{T}^b_a)^{-1}\) and use it to convert your answer back.

    Solution

    (a) \(\cos 90^\circ = 0\), \(\sin 90^\circ = 1\):

    \[ \mathbf{T}^b_a = \begin{bmatrix} 0 & -1 & 1 \\ 1 & 0 & 2 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix}. \]

    (b) \(\mathbf{R}\boldsymbol{\ell}^a = (0, 3)\). Adding \(\mathbf{t}\) gives \(\boldsymbol{\ell}^b = (1, 5)\).

    (c) \(\mathbf{R}\T = \begin{bmatrix} 0 & 1 \\ -1 & 0 \end{bmatrix}\), so \(\mathbf{R}\T\mathbf{t} = (2, -1)\) and the translation of the inverse is \(-\mathbf{R}\T\mathbf{t} = (-2, 1)\):

    \[ (\mathbf{T}^b_a)^{-1} = \begin{bmatrix} 0 & 1 & -2 \\ -1 & 0 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix}. \]

    Back: \(\mathbf{R}\T(1,5) = (5,-1)\), and \((5,-1) + (-2,1) = (3, 0)\). This is \(\boldsymbol{\ell}^a\) again.

  2. Use Rodrigues' formula to compute \(\mathbf{R} = \Exp(\boldsymbol{\theta})\) for \(\boldsymbol{\theta} = (0, \tfrac{\pi}{2}, 0)\). Check your answer in two ways: apply it to \((1,0,0)\), and recover the angle from the trace.

    Solution

    The axis is \(\mathbf{a} = (0,1,0)\) and the angle \(\phi = \pi/2\), so \(\sin\phi = 1\) and \(1-\cos\phi = 1\). From (2.6b),

    \[ \mathbf{a}^\wedge = \begin{bmatrix} 0 & 0 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 \\ -1 & 0 & 0 \end{bmatrix}, \qquad \mathbf{a}^\wedge\mathbf{a}^\wedge = \mathbf{a}\mathbf{a}\T - \mathbf{I} = \begin{bmatrix} -1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & -1 \end{bmatrix}. \] \[ \mathbf{R} = \mathbf{I} + \mathbf{a}^\wedge + \mathbf{a}^\wedge\mathbf{a}^\wedge = \begin{bmatrix} 0 & 0 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ -1 & 0 & 0 \end{bmatrix}. \]

    Check 1: \(\mathbf{R}(1,0,0) = (0,0,-1)\). A quarter turn about y by the right-hand rule takes the x-axis to minus z. Check 2: \(\tr\mathbf{R} = 1 = 1 + 2\cos\phi\), so \(\cos\phi = 0\) and \(\phi = 90^\circ\).

  3. Verify the adjoint identity (2.31) in the plane. Let \(\mathbf{T}\) be the pose at \(\mathbf{t} = (2, 0)\) with heading 90°, and \(\boldsymbol{\xi} = (\rho_1,\rho_2,\theta) = (0, 0, \tfrac{\pi}{2})\), a quarter turn on the spot. Compute \(\mathbf{T}\,\Exp(\boldsymbol{\xi})\) directly. Then compute \(\boldsymbol{\epsilon} = \Ad(\mathbf{T})\boldsymbol{\xi}\) with the planar adjoint of Day 5, and \(\Exp(\boldsymbol{\epsilon})\,\mathbf{T}\).

    Solution

    Left side. \(\Exp(\boldsymbol{\xi})\) is a pure rotation by 90° with no translation. Composing it on the right keeps the position and adds the headings: \(\mathbf{T}\,\Exp(\boldsymbol{\xi})\) is at \((2,0)\) with heading 180°.

    Adjoint. \(\Ad(\mathbf{T})\boldsymbol{\xi} = (\mathbf{R}\boldsymbol{\rho} - \theta\,\mathbf{S}\mathbf{t},\ \theta)\). Here \(\boldsymbol{\rho} = \mathbf{0}\) and \(-\mathbf{S}\mathbf{t} = (t_2, -t_1) = (0, -2)\), so \(\boldsymbol{\epsilon} = (0, -\pi, \tfrac{\pi}{2})\).

    Right side. \(\Exp(\boldsymbol{\epsilon})\) has rotation 90° and translation \(\mathbf{V}\boldsymbol{\rho}_\epsilon\) with both coefficients of \(\mathbf{V}\) equal to \(2/\pi\) (Day 2):

    \[ \mathbf{V}\boldsymbol{\rho}_\epsilon = \tfrac{2}{\pi}\begin{bmatrix} 0 \\ -\pi \end{bmatrix} + \tfrac{2}{\pi}\,\mathbf{S}\begin{bmatrix} 0 \\ -\pi \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 0 \\ -2 \end{bmatrix} + \begin{bmatrix} 2 \\ 0 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 2 \\ -2 \end{bmatrix}. \]

    Now compose: the position of \(\Exp(\boldsymbol{\epsilon})\,\mathbf{T}\) is \(\mathbf{R}(90^\circ)(2,0) + (2,-2) = (0,2) + (2,-2) = (2, 0)\), and the heading is \(90^\circ + 90^\circ = 180^\circ\). Both sides agree. Seen from the global frame, turning on the spot at \((2,0)\) is a quarter turn about the origin combined with exactly the translation that puts the robot back where it stood.

  4. Gauss-Newton on \(\SO(2)\), by hand. A robot with unknown heading \(\mathbf{R}\in\SO(2)\) observes one known landmark \(\boldsymbol{\ell} = (1,0)\) and measures \(\mathbf{z} = \mathbf{R}\boldsymbol{\ell} + \boldsymbol{\eta} = (0.6, 0.8)\), with \(\boldsymbol{\Sigma} = \mathbf{I}\). Start from \(\mathbf{R}^0 = \mathbf{I}\) and perturb on the right, \(\mathbf{R} = \mathbf{R}^0\Exp(\theta)\). (a) Find the Jacobian of \(\mathbf{R}\boldsymbol{\ell}\) with respect to \(\theta\). (b) Do two Gauss-Newton iterations. (c) Compare with the exact answer.

    Solution

    (a) To first order \(\mathbf{R}^0\Exp(\theta)\boldsymbol{\ell}\approx\mathbf{R}^0(\mathbf{I}+\theta\mathbf{S})\boldsymbol{\ell} = \mathbf{R}^0\boldsymbol{\ell} + \mathbf{R}^0\mathbf{S}\boldsymbol{\ell}\,\theta\). So \(\mathbf{H} = \mathbf{R}^0\mathbf{S}\boldsymbol{\ell}\), a 2 × 1 matrix, with \(\mathbf{S}\boldsymbol{\ell} = (0,1)\). It is a unit vector for every \(\mathbf{R}^0\), so \(\mathbf{H}\T\mathbf{H} = 1\) and the normal equations reduce to \(\theta^* = \mathbf{H}\T\mathbf{r}\).

    (b) Iteration 1. \(\mathbf{R}^0 = \mathbf{I}\): prediction \((1,0)\), residual \(\mathbf{r} = (0.6,0.8)-(1,0) = (-0.4, 0.8)\), \(\mathbf{H} = (0,1)\), so \(\theta^* = 0.8\). Update: \(\mathbf{R}^0\leftarrow\Exp(0.8)\), a rotation by 0.8 rad.

    Iteration 2. Prediction \(\mathbf{R}^0\boldsymbol{\ell} = (\cos 0.8, \sin 0.8) = (0.6967, 0.7174)\). Residual \(\mathbf{r} = (-0.0967, 0.0826)\). \(\mathbf{H} = \mathbf{R}^0(0,1) = (-0.7174, 0.6967)\). Then \(\theta^* = (-0.7174)(-0.0967) + (0.6967)(0.0826) = 0.0694 + 0.0576 = 0.1269\). Update: \(\mathbf{R}^0\leftarrow\mathbf{R}^0\Exp(0.1269)\), a rotation by \(0.9269\) rad in total.

    (c) The measurement is a unit vector, so the exact answer is the heading with \(\cos\theta = 0.6\), \(\sin\theta = 0.8\): \(\theta = 0.9273\) rad (53.13°). Two iterations are within 0.0004 rad. At every iteration the estimate was a rotation matrix. An additive update of the four matrix entries would have left the circle after the first step.

You are ready for next week if you can

  • Read \(\mathbf{T}^b_a\) as "from \(a\) to \(b\)", compose two transformations, and invert one.
  • Write \(\boldsymbol{\theta}^\wedge\) and \(\boldsymbol{\xi}^\wedge\), and compute \(\Exp\) and \(\Log\) for \(\SO(2)\) and \(\SE(2)\) by hand.
  • Explain each line of the loop "linearize in \(\boldsymbol{\xi}\), solve, \(\mathbf{T}\leftarrow\mathbf{T}\,\Exp(\boldsymbol{\xi})\)".
  • Say where the mean and where the covariance of a Gaussian on \(\SE(3)\) live.
  • Use \(\ominus\) to form a difference of two poses and to interpolate between them.
  • State what the adjoint and the Jacobian are for, and which of the two is exact.

Sources

  1. SLAM Handbook, Chapter 2, §2.1 "Optimization on Manifolds", pp. 53–62.
  2. Barfoot, State Estimation for Robotics, 2017.
  3. Solà, Deray, Atchuthan, A micro Lie theory for state estimation in robotics, 2018.

Week 5 · Day 1

Why continuous time, and trajectories built from splines

After today you can say when a trajectory is better stored as a function of time than as a list of poses, build a B-spline curve from its basis functions, and name the coefficients that one measurement touches.

About 60 min · Read §2.2 (opening) and §2.2.1, pp. 62–65 (3 pages) · Needs Week 3 Day 1

Read first: §2.2 opening and §2.2.1, pp. 62–65

Start at the heading "2.2 Continuous-Time Trajectories" near the bottom of p. 62 and stop at the heading "2.2.2" on p. 65. While you read, look for:

  • The three kinds of time that the last paragraph before §2.2.1 tells you to keep apart (p. 63).
  • Equation (2.36) and the phrase "local support" (p. 63).
  • In Figure 2.3 (p. 64), how many coefficient variables each black measurement dot is connected to.
  • What you need from the solver to put an uncertainty on a queried pose (top of p. 65).

Today's big idea

Instead of estimating one pose per measurement, estimate a small set of coefficients that define a smooth function \(\mathbf{p}(t)\), and evaluate that function at whatever instant a sensor fired. If the function is a sum of basis functions that are each nonzero for only a short time, every measurement still touches only a handful of unknowns, so the factor graph stays sparse.

1. One pose per measurement does not scale

Until now every measurement was attached to a pose variable at its own time stamp. That works when a camera delivers a few frames per second. It breaks down in three situations the book lists. §2.2 · pp. 62–63

  • High-rate sensors. Suppose an inertial measurement unit reports 200 times a second. One minute of driving would need 12,000 pose variables for that sensor alone.
  • Asynchronous sensors. A camera and a lidar rarely fire at the same instants, so each would need its own poses.
  • Motion-distorted sensors. A spinning lidar, a radar, or a rolling-shutter camera collects one "frame" over a stretch of time while the robot moves. Every point or pixel row has its own time stamp, and strictly each one was taken from a different pose.

A continuous-time trajectory is a function \(\mathbf{p}(t)\) that returns the pose at any time \(t\). It is defined by far fewer variables than there are measurements. It also lets you ask for the pose at times when nothing was measured: between measurements (interpolation) or, with caution, after the last one (extrapolation). §2.2 · p. 63

2. A trajectory as a weighted sum of basis functions

The parametric way to build \(\mathbf{p}(t)\) is to fix \(K\) known functions of time, the temporal basis functions \(\boldsymbol{\Psi}_k(t)\), and add them up with unknown weights, the coefficients \(\mathbf{c}_k\):

\[ \mathbf{p}(t) = \sum_{k=1}^{K} \boldsymbol{\Psi}_k(t)\,\mathbf{c}_k . \tag{2.36} \]

The coefficients are the estimation variables. The basis functions are chosen once and never change. For now \(\mathbf{p}\) is an ordinary vector, such as a position. Poses on a Lie group come on Day 5. §2.2.1 · p. 63 In the simplest case every component of \(\mathbf{p}\) uses the same scalar function \(\psi_k(t)\), so \(\boldsymbol{\Psi}_k(t) = \psi_k(t)\,\mathbf{I}\). The book makes that simplification itself in equation (2.53).

Here is the smallest useful example. Put knots at \(t = 0, 1, 2, \dots\) seconds and let \(\psi_k\) be a "hat" that is 1 at knot \(k\), falls linearly to 0 at the two neighbouring knots, and is 0 everywhere else. At \(t = 2.25\) only two hats are nonzero: \(\psi_2 = 0.75\) and \(\psi_3 = 0.25\). With \(c_2 = 4\) and \(c_3 = 8\),

\[ p(2.25) = 0.75 \cdot 4 + 0.25 \cdot 8 = 5 . \]

That is linear interpolation between the coefficients. The curve is continuous but has corners at the knots, so its velocity jumps. Smoother basis functions fix that.

3. B-splines and local support

A spline is a function made of polynomial pieces joined at knots. A basis function has local support if it is zero outside a short interval. §2.2.1 · p. 63 The standard family with both properties is the B-spline. The book names it but does not construct it, so here is the construction.

Filling the gap: the B-spline recursion

Measure time in knot intervals, so the knots are the integers. The B-spline of degree 0 that starts at knot \(k\) is a box:

\[ B_{k,0}(t) = \begin{cases} 1 & k \le t \lt k+1 \\ 0 & \text{otherwise.} \end{cases} \]

Each higher degree is a blend of two neighbours of the degree below, with weights that are linear in \(t\). This is the Cox–de Boor recursion, written here for evenly spaced knots:

\[ B_{k,d}(t) = \frac{t-k}{d}\,B_{k,d-1}(t) + \frac{k+d+1-t}{d}\,B_{k+1,d-1}(t) . \]

Do one step by hand with \(k=0\), \(d=1\): \(B_{0,1}(t) = t\,B_{0,0}(t) + (2-t)\,B_{1,0}(t)\), which equals \(t\) on \([0,1)\) and \(2-t\) on \([1,2)\). That is the hat from section 2. Each step makes the function one interval wider and one derivative smoother:

Degree dNonzero overFunctions nonzero at any timeWhat is continuous at the knots
01 interval1nothing (the curve jumps)
1 (linear)2 intervals2position
2 (quadratic)3 intervals3position, velocity
3 (cubic)4 intervals4position, velocity, acceleration

Two more facts hold for every degree: the functions are never negative, and at any time the nonzero ones add up to exactly 1. So \(\mathbf{p}(t)\) is always a weighted average of the nearby coefficients.

For the cubic case, write \(u \in [0,1)\) for the fraction of the current knot interval that has passed. Running the recursion three times gives the four weights, from the oldest active coefficient to the newest:

\[ w_0 = \tfrac{1}{6}(1-u)^3,\quad w_1 = \tfrac{1}{6}(3u^3-6u^2+4),\quad w_2 = \tfrac{1}{6}(-3u^3+3u^2+3u+1),\quad w_3 = \tfrac{1}{6}u^3 . \]

Worked example. Take four active coefficients \(0, 3, 6, 3\) and the middle of the interval, \(u = 0.5\). The weights are \(0.0208,\ 0.4792,\ 0.4792,\ 0.0208\) (they sum to 1), so

\[ p = 0.0208\cdot 0 + 0.4792\cdot 3 + 0.4792\cdot 6 + 0.0208\cdot 3 = 4.375 . \]

Try it: move the time slider and watch which basis functions light up. Then drag a coefficient up and down. Change the degree and repeat.

Notice that at degree 3 exactly four basis functions are nonzero at any time (0.057, 0.590, 0.348, 0.004 at the starting position) and they sum to 1. Dragging a coefficient changes the curve only inside the shaded band, four knot intervals wide. The widget shifts each function so that function \(k\) peaks at \(t = k\).

In plain words

Think of a row of people holding a long flexible rod. Each person can lift or lower only the part of the rod near them. The coefficients are how high each person holds their hands. The rod is the trajectory. No single person decides the shape anywhere, and no person affects the rod far away.

4. What one measurement touches

Suppose the robot observes landmark \(\boldsymbol{\ell}\) at time \(t_i\). The measurement model is the same as before, except that the pose is read off the trajectory at that instant: §2.2.1 · pp. 63–64

\[ \mathbf{z}_i = \mathbf{h}_i\big(\mathbf{p}(t_i), \boldsymbol{\ell}\big) + \boldsymbol{\eta}_i = \mathbf{h}_i\Big(\sum_{k=1}^{K} \boldsymbol{\Psi}_k(t_i)\,\mathbf{c}_k,\ \boldsymbol{\ell}\Big) + \boldsymbol{\eta}_i . \tag{2.37, 2.38} \]

The sum looks like it involves all \(K\) coefficients. It does not: with local support, \(\boldsymbol{\Psi}_k(t_i)\) is zero for all but a few \(k\). Collect those active coefficients and the landmark in \(\mathbf{x}_i\), and the model is again \(\mathbf{z}_i = \mathbf{h}_i(\mathbf{x}_i) + \boldsymbol{\eta}_i\), equation (2.39), which is the form every factor has had since Week 2 · Day 2. With cubic B-splines a landmark measurement becomes a factor on five variables: four coefficients and one landmark. The book calls it a quinary factor (Figure 2.3).

Filling the gap: the Jacobian with respect to a coefficient

To linearize you need the derivative of the residual with respect to each \(\mathbf{c}_k\). The chain rule gives it in one line. Let \(\mathbf{H}_i = \partial \mathbf{h}_i / \partial \mathbf{p}\) be the Jacobian you would have used for a pose variable. Since \(\mathbf{p}(t_i)\) is linear in the coefficients,

\[ \frac{\partial \mathbf{h}_i}{\partial \mathbf{c}_k} = \mathbf{H}_i\,\frac{\partial \mathbf{p}(t_i)}{\partial \mathbf{c}_k} = \mathbf{H}_i\,\boldsymbol{\Psi}_k(t_i) . \]

For a cubic B-spline this is \(\mathbf{H}_i\) times one of the four numbers \(w_0,\dots,w_3\), and zero for every other coefficient. Nothing else in the Gauss-Newton machinery changes.

5. Velocity and queries come for free

Because the coefficients do not depend on time, differentiating the trajectory only differentiates the basis functions: §2.2.1 · p. 64

\[ \dot{\mathbf{p}}(t) = \sum_{k=1}^{K} \dot{\boldsymbol{\Psi}}_k(t)\,\mathbf{c}_k . \tag{2.40} \]

So a sensor that measures velocity, or acceleration, gives a factor on the same coefficients. For the cubic weights above, with knot spacing \(T\) seconds, \(\dot w_0 = -\tfrac{1}{2T}(1-u)^2\), \(\dot w_1 = \tfrac{1}{2T}(3u^2-4u)\), \(\dot w_2 = \tfrac{1}{2T}(-3u^2+2u+1)\), \(\dot w_3 = \tfrac{1}{2T}u^2\). In the worked example (\(T = 1\) s, \(u=0.5\)) these are \(-0.125, -0.625, 0.625, 0.125\), and the velocity is \(3\cdot(-0.625) + 6\cdot 0.625 + 3\cdot 0.125 = 2.25\) units per second.

After MAP inference you can evaluate (2.36) or (2.40) at any time. The uncertainty follows too. Stack the active weights at the query time in a row \(\boldsymbol{\Psi}(t)\) and let \(\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_c\) be the marginal covariance of the active coefficients. Because the map from coefficients to pose is linear, the rule for a linear function of a Gaussian from Week 1 · Day 2 gives

\[ \boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{p}(t) = \boldsymbol{\Psi}(t)\,\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_c\,\boldsymbol{\Psi}(t)\T . \]

Only the marginal over the few active coefficients is needed, not the whole covariance. §2.2.1 · p. 65 Example with the hats of section 2: at the midpoint the weights are \((0.5, 0.5)\). If the two coefficients each have variance 0.04 and covariance 0.01, the queried value has variance \(0.25\cdot0.04 + 0.25\cdot0.04 + 2\cdot0.25\cdot0.01 = 0.025\).

Common mistakes

  • "The coefficients are poses on the trajectory." Only for the linear hat functions. A cubic B-spline does not pass through its coefficients: at a knot (\(u = 0\)) the weights are \(\tfrac16, \tfrac46, \tfrac16\), so the curve is a blend of three of them.
  • "Continuous time means infinitely many unknowns." The unknowns are the \(K\) coefficients. The function is continuous; the list of variables is finite and usually shorter than in discrete time.
  • "Local support is only a convenience." It is what keeps each factor small. With basis functions that are nonzero everywhere, such as sines, every measurement would touch every coefficient and the sparsity of Week 3 · Day 1 would be lost.

Check yourself

Q1. A trajectory is a cubic B-spline. One landmark is observed at one time stamp. How many variables does the resulting factor connect?

Four basis functions are nonzero at any time, so four coefficients are active, plus the landmark: a five-way factor, as in Figure 2.3.

Q2. At a knot of a cubic B-spline (u = 0) the three active coefficients are 1, 4, and 7. What is the value of the curve there?

At u = 0 the weights are 1/6, 4/6, 1/6 (the fourth is 0). So p = (1 + 16 + 7)/6 = 4.

Q3. A cubic B-spline has knots every 0.5 s. You change one coefficient. Over how long a stretch of time can the trajectory change?

A cubic basis function is nonzero over four knot intervals: 4 × 0.5 s = 2 s. Outside that window its weight is zero.

Q4. A rolling-shutter camera exposes each image row at a slightly different time. What does a continuous-time trajectory let you do that one pose per image does not?

Each pixel's residual uses p(t) at that pixel's time. The unknowns are still the same few coefficients.

Q5. A wheel encoder measures speed. To use it with a spline trajectory you need

Equation (2.40): the velocity is the sum of the differentiated basis functions times the same coefficients.

Recap

  1. Continuous-time trajectories separate measurement times, estimation variables, and query times.
  2. Parametric form: \(\mathbf{p}(t) = \sum_k \boldsymbol{\Psi}_k(t)\,\mathbf{c}_k\), equation (2.36). The coefficients are the unknowns.
  3. B-splines of degree \(d\) come from the Cox–de Boor recursion. Exactly \(d+1\) are nonzero at any time, and they sum to 1.
  4. Local support means a measurement at \(t_i\) is a factor on the few active coefficients; its Jacobian is \(\mathbf{H}_i\boldsymbol{\Psi}_k(t_i)\).
  5. Derivatives and queried covariances come from the same coefficients, through \(\dot{\boldsymbol{\Psi}}_k\) and \(\boldsymbol{\Psi}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_c\boldsymbol{\Psi}\T\).

Sources

  1. SLAM Handbook, §2.2 "Continuous-Time Trajectories" (opening) and §2.2.1 "Splines", pp. 62–65, equations (2.36)–(2.40), Figure 2.3.
  2. The B-spline recursion, the partition-of-unity property, and the uniform cubic weights follow de Boor, A Practical Guide to Splines, 1978.
  3. The sensor rates in section 1 are illustrative numbers chosen for the example, not figures from the book.

Week 5 · Day 2

From splines to kernels: the nonparametric view

After today you can explain why the number of basis functions is hard to choose, derive the kernel form of the normal equations from the spline form, and build a kernel matrix from a kernel function.

About 60 min · Read §2.2.2, pp. 65–66 (2 pages) · Needs Week 2 Day 3 and Week 5 Day 1

Read first: §2.2.2, pp. 65–66

Read from the heading "2.2.2 From Parametric to Nonparametric" to the heading "2.2.3". While you read, look for:

  • The two ways a spline fit goes wrong, in the first paragraph (p. 65).
  • The regularizer term in equation (2.43) and what it prefers (p. 65).
  • The phrase "with a little bit of algebra" between (2.44) and (2.45) (pp. 65–66). Today's lesson is that algebra.
  • What the last paragraph of the section says looks expensive (p. 66).

Today's big idea

The regularized spline problem can be rewritten so that the basis functions appear only through one matrix, \(\mathbf{K} = \boldsymbol{\Psi}\boldsymbol{\Psi}\T\), whose entry \((i,j)\) says how strongly the trajectory at time \(t_i\) is tied to the trajectory at time \(t_j\). Once only \(\mathbf{K}\) matters, you can fill it in directly from a kernel function and never write down a basis function or a coefficient.

1. Too many basis functions, or too few

A parametric method makes you pick the type and number of basis functions before you see the data. Pick too many and the curve has enough freedom to follow the noise: it overfits. Pick too few and the curve cannot bend as much as the real trajectory did: it is too smooth. §2.2.2 · p. 65

Try it: the dots are noisy position measurements (noise standard deviation 0.25) taken at irregular times, with nothing between 5.2 s and 7 s. First shrink the knot spacing to 0.4 s and set λ to 0.001. Then set the spacing to 3 s. Then try 0.4 s with λ = 0.

Notice the two error numbers. At the start (knots every 1 s, 12 coefficients for 24 measurements) the residual is 0.21, about the noise level, and the error against the true curve is 0.16. With knots every 0.4 s and λ = 0.001 the residual drops to 0.06, far below the noise, while the true error rises to 0.39: the curve is fitting noise and wanders in the gap. With knots every 3 s both numbers are near 0.4: the curve is too stiff. With λ = 0 and close knots the problem has no unique solution at all.

2. The spline problem as regularized least squares

To keep the algebra short the book drops the landmarks for this section and keeps only the trajectory. §2.2.2 · p. 65 Recall the linear problem that one Gauss-Newton iteration solves (Week 2 · Day 3): stack the whitened Jacobians in \(\mathbf{A}\) and the whitened residuals in \(\mathbf{b}\), and find the pose update \(\boldsymbol{\delta}\) that minimizes \(\norm{\mathbf{b} - \mathbf{A}\boldsymbol{\delta}}^2\). Its solution satisfies the normal equations \(\mathbf{A}\T\mathbf{A}\,\boldsymbol{\delta} = \mathbf{A}\T\mathbf{b}\), equation (1.25).

With a spline the pose at a measurement time is a linear function of the coefficients, so a change \(\boldsymbol{\delta}_c\) in the coefficients changes the poses at the measurement times by

\[ \boldsymbol{\delta} = \boldsymbol{\Psi}\,\boldsymbol{\delta}_c . \]

Here \(\boldsymbol{\Psi}\) is a tall matrix with one block row per measurement time and one block column per coefficient. Row \(i\) holds the basis functions evaluated at \(t_i\), so it is zero except at the few active coefficients. For one measurement this is the term the book writes as equation (2.41), with \(\mathbf{H}_i\boldsymbol{\Psi}_i\) as the Jacobian. It is the chain rule you used on Day 1. Substituting \(\boldsymbol{\delta} = \boldsymbol{\Psi}\boldsymbol{\delta}_c\) and adding a penalty on large coefficients gives

\[ \boldsymbol{\delta}_c^* = \argmin_{\boldsymbol{\delta}_c} \Big( \norm{\mathbf{b} - \mathbf{A}\boldsymbol{\Psi}\boldsymbol{\delta}_c}^2 + \norm{\boldsymbol{\delta}_c}^2 \Big) . \tag{2.43} \]

The second term is the regularizer. It prefers coefficients near zero, and it is what stops the overfitting you saw in the widget. In the language of Week 2 · Day 2 it is the negative log of a Gaussian prior \(\N(\mathbf{0}, \mathbf{I})\) on the coefficients, so (2.43) is still a MAP problem.

To solve it, set the gradient to zero. The gradient of the first term is \(-2\boldsymbol{\Psi}\T\mathbf{A}\T(\mathbf{b} - \mathbf{A}\boldsymbol{\Psi}\boldsymbol{\delta}_c)\) and of the second is \(2\boldsymbol{\delta}_c\). Setting the sum to zero and moving the unknown to the left:

\[ \big( \boldsymbol{\Psi}\T\mathbf{A}\T\mathbf{A}\boldsymbol{\Psi} + \mathbf{I} \big)\,\boldsymbol{\delta}_c^* = \boldsymbol{\Psi}\T\mathbf{A}\T\mathbf{b} . \tag{2.44} \]

These are the normal equations with \(\mathbf{A}\boldsymbol{\Psi}\) in place of \(\mathbf{A}\), plus \(\mathbf{I}\) from the regularizer. The widget solves exactly this system, with the regularizer scaled by a factor λ so that you can turn it up and down.

3. From coefficients to poses

The coefficients are a means to an end. What you want is the pose update \(\boldsymbol{\delta}^* = \boldsymbol{\Psi}\boldsymbol{\delta}_c^*\). The book states the equation it satisfies and leaves the steps out. §2.2.2 · pp. 65–66

Filling the gap: the "little bit of algebra" from (2.44) to (2.45)

Step 1. Move the first term of (2.44) to the right and factor:

\[ \boldsymbol{\delta}_c^* = \boldsymbol{\Psi}\T\mathbf{A}\T\mathbf{b} - \boldsymbol{\Psi}\T\mathbf{A}\T\mathbf{A}\boldsymbol{\Psi}\boldsymbol{\delta}_c^* = \boldsymbol{\Psi}\T\mathbf{A}\T\big( \mathbf{b} - \mathbf{A}\,\boldsymbol{\Psi}\boldsymbol{\delta}_c^* \big) . \]

Step 2. Multiply both sides by \(\boldsymbol{\Psi}\) from the left. Wherever \(\boldsymbol{\Psi}\boldsymbol{\delta}_c^*\) appears write \(\boldsymbol{\delta}^*\), and name the product \(\mathbf{K} = \boldsymbol{\Psi}\boldsymbol{\Psi}\T\):

\[ \boldsymbol{\delta}^* = \underbrace{\boldsymbol{\Psi}\boldsymbol{\Psi}\T}_{\mathbf{K}} \mathbf{A}\T\big( \mathbf{b} - \mathbf{A}\boldsymbol{\delta}^* \big) . \]

Step 3. Collect the terms with \(\boldsymbol{\delta}^*\) on the left:

\[ \big( \mathbf{I} + \mathbf{K}\mathbf{A}\T\mathbf{A} \big)\,\boldsymbol{\delta}^* = \mathbf{K}\mathbf{A}\T\mathbf{b} . \]

Step 4. Multiply by \(\mathbf{K}^{-1}\) from the left:

\[ \big( \mathbf{A}\T\mathbf{A} + \mathbf{K}^{-1} \big)\,\boldsymbol{\delta}^* = \mathbf{A}\T\mathbf{b} . \tag{2.45} \]

The coefficients are gone. Compared with the plain normal equations (1.25), the only new thing is \(\mathbf{K}^{-1}\) added on the left.

Check with numbers. Two measurement times, two basis functions, and for simplicity \(\mathbf{A} = \mathbf{I}\):

\[ \boldsymbol{\Psi} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 1 \end{bmatrix},\quad \mathbf{b} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 2 \end{bmatrix},\quad \mathbf{K} = \boldsymbol{\Psi}\boldsymbol{\Psi}\T = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ 1 & 2 \end{bmatrix},\quad \mathbf{K}^{-1} = \begin{bmatrix} 2 & -1 \\ -1 & 1 \end{bmatrix} . \]

Coefficient route (2.44): \(\boldsymbol{\Psi}\T\boldsymbol{\Psi} + \mathbf{I} = \begin{bmatrix} 3 & 1 \\ 1 & 2 \end{bmatrix}\) and \(\boldsymbol{\Psi}\T\mathbf{b} = (3, 2)\), so \(\boldsymbol{\delta}_c^* = (0.8, 0.6)\) and \(\boldsymbol{\delta}^* = \boldsymbol{\Psi}\boldsymbol{\delta}_c^* = (0.8, 1.4)\). Pose route (2.45): \(\mathbf{I} + \mathbf{K}^{-1} = \begin{bmatrix} 3 & -1 \\ -1 & 2 \end{bmatrix}\) and the right side is \((1, 2)\), so \(\boldsymbol{\delta}^* = \tfrac15(2\cdot1 + 1\cdot2,\ 1\cdot1 + 3\cdot2) = (0.8, 1.4)\). The two routes agree.

Going deeper (optional): when does the inverse of K exist?

\(\mathbf{K} = \boldsymbol{\Psi}\boldsymbol{\Psi}\T\) has as many rows as there are measurement times but rank at most the number of coefficients. With more times than coefficients, which the book notes is the usual case, this \(\mathbf{K}\) is singular and step 4 cannot be taken literally. Step 3 is always valid. The issue disappears in the next section: there \(\mathbf{K}\) is built from a kernel function and, for the kernels used in practice and distinct times, it is positive definite.

4. The kernel trick

Look at what \(\mathbf{K}\) contains. Its entry \((i,j)\) is row \(i\) of \(\boldsymbol{\Psi}\) times row \(j\):

\[ K_{ij} = \sum_{k=1}^{K} \psi_k(t_i)\,\psi_k(t_j) , \]

an inner product of the basis functions evaluated at two times. It is large when the same basis functions are active at both times, and zero when no basis function covers both. The matrix \(\mathbf{K}\) is called the kernel matrix. §2.2.2 · p. 66

Filling the gap: K is a prior covariance

The regularizer said the coefficients have prior \(\mathbf{c} \sim \N(\mathbf{0}, \mathbf{I})\). The trajectory values at the measurement times are \(\mathbf{p} = \boldsymbol{\Psi}\mathbf{c}\), a linear function of a Gaussian, so they are Gaussian with mean zero and covariance

\[ \E[\mathbf{p}\mathbf{p}\T] = \boldsymbol{\Psi}\,\E[\mathbf{c}\mathbf{c}\T]\,\boldsymbol{\Psi}\T = \boldsymbol{\Psi}\boldsymbol{\Psi}\T = \mathbf{K} . \]

So \(K_{ij}\) is the covariance, before any measurement, between the trajectory at \(t_i\) and at \(t_j\). Its inverse \(\mathbf{K}^{-1}\) is the information matrix of that prior (Week 1 · Day 3), and (2.45) says: information from the measurements, \(\mathbf{A}\T\mathbf{A}\), plus information from the prior, \(\mathbf{K}^{-1}\). A penalty on coefficients has turned into a prior directly on the trajectory.

Equation (2.45) needs the basis functions only through these inner products. The kernel trick is to skip the basis functions and choose a function of two times, the kernel function \(\mathcal{K}(t,t')\), that returns the inner product directly. The kernel matrix is then filled in by evaluating it at every pair of measurement times: §2.2.2 · p. 66

\[ \mathbf{K} = \big[\, \mathcal{K}(t_i, t_j) \,\big]_{ij} . \]

The method is now nonparametric: there are no spline coefficients to estimate. What remains to choose are the kernel's hyperparameters. The book's example is the squared-exponential kernel, whose usual form is

\[ \mathcal{K}(t,t') = \sigma_f^2 \exp\!\Big( -\frac{(t-t')^2}{2\ell^2} \Big) , \]

with a length scale \(\ell\) (how far apart in time two poses can be and still be strongly tied) and a magnitude \(\sigma_f^2\). For \(\sigma_f = 1\), \(\ell = 1\) s, and times \(0, 1, 3\) s:

\[ \mathbf{K} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & e^{-1/2} & e^{-9/2} \\ e^{-1/2} & 1 & e^{-2} \\ e^{-9/2} & e^{-2} & 1 \end{bmatrix} \approx \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0.607 & 0.011 \\ 0.607 & 1 & 0.135 \\ 0.011 & 0.135 & 1 \end{bmatrix} . \]
QuestionParametric (spline)Nonparametric (kernel)
What is estimatedK coefficientsThe trajectory at the M measurement times
What you chooseType, number, and spacing of basis functionsThe kernel function and its hyperparameters
Linear system(2.44), size set by K(2.45), size set by M
What sets the smoothnessHow many basis functions there areThe kernel, for example its length scale

Intuition

A spline says "the trajectory is one of the shapes I can build from these pieces". A kernel says "any shape is allowed, but values at nearby times must agree". The second statement does not limit how detailed the trajectory can be, which is why the book says nonparametric methods have higher representational power.

5. What this costs

Two things look worse in (2.45). The system is larger, because there are usually more measurement times than coefficients; the book returns to this at the end of §2.2.3, and so do we on Day 4. And it needs \(\mathbf{K}^{-1}\). For a kernel such as the squared exponential every pair of times has a nonzero entry in \(\mathbf{K}\), and in general its inverse is dense too. A dense \(\mathbf{K}^{-1}\) is a factor that ties every pose to every other pose, which destroys the sparsity that made SLAM tractable in Week 3. §2.2.2 · p. 66

Tomorrow's question is therefore: is there a family of kernels for which \(\mathbf{K}^{-1}\) is sparse by construction? You have already seen a hint. In the numeric check above, \(\mathbf{K} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ 1 & 2 \end{bmatrix}\) is full, but its inverse has the pattern of a chain.

Common mistakes

  • "Nonparametric means there is nothing to tune." It means no fixed, finite set of basis-function coefficients. The kernel's hyperparameters still have to be chosen, and they set how smooth the result is.
  • "More basis functions always fit better." They fit the measurements better. They fit the true trajectory worse once they start following the noise, as the widget shows.
  • "K and its inverse have the same sparsity." They generally do not. A full \(\mathbf{K}\) can have a sparse inverse, and that is exactly what the next section exploits.

Check yourself

Q1. You fit a spline with very closely spaced knots and no regularizer to noisy data. The residual at the measurements is far below the sensor noise. What has most likely happened?

A residual below the noise level means the curve is reproducing individual noise values. That is overfitting; between the measurements the curve is usually worse.

Q2. At time t₁ the active basis-function values are (0.5, 0.5, 0) and at time t₂ they are (0, 0.5, 0.5). What is the kernel-matrix entry K₁₂?

K₁₂ is the inner product of the two rows: 0.5·0 + 0.5·0.5 + 0·0.5 = 0.25. Only the shared basis function contributes.

Q3. A squared-exponential kernel has magnitude 1 and length scale 2 s. What is its value for two times 2 s apart?

The exponent is −(2²)/(2·2²) = −0.5, and e^−0.5 ≈ 0.607.

Q4. In equation (2.45), which term plays the role that the regularizer on the coefficients played in (2.43)?

The identity matrix in (2.44) came from the regularizer. After the change of variables it becomes K⁻¹, the information matrix of the prior on the trajectory.

Q5. A trajectory has 500 measurement times and is modelled by a spline with 40 scalar coefficients. Roughly how large are the systems (2.44) and (2.45)?

(2.44) solves for the coefficients, (2.45) for the trajectory at every measurement time. The book points out that the second is larger and deals with it later.

Recap

  1. Too many basis functions overfit, too few oversmooth. A regularizer \(\norm{\boldsymbol{\delta}_c}^2\) helps, and it is a Gaussian prior on the coefficients.
  2. Regularized spline normal equations: \((\boldsymbol{\Psi}\T\mathbf{A}\T\mathbf{A}\boldsymbol{\Psi} + \mathbf{I})\,\boldsymbol{\delta}_c^* = \boldsymbol{\Psi}\T\mathbf{A}\T\mathbf{b}\), equation (2.44).
  3. In terms of the poses \(\boldsymbol{\delta}^* = \boldsymbol{\Psi}\boldsymbol{\delta}_c^*\): \((\mathbf{A}\T\mathbf{A} + \mathbf{K}^{-1})\,\boldsymbol{\delta}^* = \mathbf{A}\T\mathbf{b}\) with \(\mathbf{K} = \boldsymbol{\Psi}\boldsymbol{\Psi}\T\), equation (2.45).
  4. \(\mathbf{K}\) is the prior covariance of the trajectory at the measurement times. The kernel trick fills it in from a kernel function \(\mathcal{K}(t,t')\) with no basis functions.
  5. The open problem is \(\mathbf{K}^{-1}\): dense for a general kernel.

Sources

  1. SLAM Handbook, §2.2.2 "From Parametric to Nonparametric", pp. 65–66, equations (2.41)–(2.45).
  2. The step-by-step derivation of (2.45), the numeric check, and the remark on when the inverse exists are worked out here from (2.44).
  3. The reading of the kernel matrix as a prior covariance (the weight-space and function-space views) and the squared-exponential kernel formula follow Rasmussen and Williams, Gaussian Processes for Machine Learning, 2006.

Week 5 · Day 3

Gaussian-process priors from a stochastic differential equation

After today you can write a motion prior as a differential equation driven by white noise, compute its transition function and kernel matrix, and show why the inverse kernel matrix is block-tridiagonal.

About 60 min · Read §2.2.3, pp. 66–68 (3 pages) · Needs Week 3 Day 1 and Week 5 Day 2

Read first: §2.2.3, pp. 66–68

Read from the heading "2.2.3 Gaussian Processes" to the sentence about STEAM under equation (2.52). The last paragraph of p. 68 is for tomorrow. While you read, look for:

  • What each symbol in equation (2.46) is (pp. 66–67).
  • The two kinds of motion-prior factor in Figure 2.4, and how many variables each touches (p. 67).
  • The difference between the matrices in (2.50) and (2.51): count the nonzero blocks in a row (p. 68).
  • Why the state in (2.52) contains the velocity as well as the pose (p. 68).

Today's big idea

Do not pick a kernel formula. Pick a simple physical model of how the robot moves, driven by random noise, and let the kernel be whatever covariance that model implies. Because the model's state is Markovian (the future depends on the past only through the present), the inverse kernel matrix links each state only to its neighbours in time. The prior over the whole trajectory becomes a chain of small binary factors.

1. A Gaussian process, and the plan

A Gaussian process (GP) is a probability distribution over functions with one defining property: the values of the function at any finite set of times are jointly Gaussian. It is fixed by a mean function and a kernel function \(\mathcal{K}(t,t')\), which gives the covariance between the values at two times. We write \(\mathbf{x}(t) \sim \mathcal{GP}(\mathbf{0}, \mathcal{K}(t,t'))\). Yesterday you saw that the kernel matrix is the prior covariance of the trajectory at the measurement times, so choosing a kernel is the same as choosing a GP prior.

Yesterday also ended with a problem: equation (2.45) needs \(\mathbf{K}^{-1}\), which is dense for a general kernel. The book's plan is to construct kernels whose inverse is sparse by design. §2.2.3 · p. 66

2. A motion model driven by white noise

The construction starts from a linear, time-invariant stochastic differential equation (SDE): §2.2.3 · pp. 66–67

\[ \dot{\mathbf{x}}(t) = \mathbf{A}\,\mathbf{x}(t) + \mathbf{L}\,\mathbf{w}(t), \qquad \mathbf{w}(t) \sim \mathcal{GP}\big(\mathbf{0},\ \boldsymbol{\mathcal{Q}}\,\delta(t-t')\big) . \tag{2.46} \]

Here \(\mathbf{x}(t)\) is the state, \(\mathbf{A}\) says how the state would evolve with no noise, and \(\mathbf{w}(t)\) is white noise: a random signal whose values at any two different times are uncorrelated (that is what the Dirac delta \(\delta(t-t')\) says). \(\mathbf{L}\) selects which components of the state the noise pushes on, and \(\boldsymbol{\mathcal{Q}}\) is the power spectral density, which sets how strong the noise is. The two priors used this week:

PriorState xALIn words
Random walk\(\mathbf{p}\)\(\mathbf{0}\)\(\mathbf{I}\)The velocity is white noise. The pose wanders.
Constant velocity, equation (2.52)\((\mathbf{p}, \mathbf{v})\)\(\begin{bmatrix} \mathbf{0} & \mathbf{I} \\ \mathbf{0} & \mathbf{0} \end{bmatrix}\)\(\begin{bmatrix} \mathbf{0} \\ \mathbf{I} \end{bmatrix}\)The acceleration is white noise. The velocity wanders, so the pose is smooth.

The name "constant velocity" describes the noise-free part: \(\dot{\mathbf{p}} = \mathbf{v}\), \(\dot{\mathbf{v}} = \mathbf{0}\). The noise lets the velocity change, slowly if \(\boldsymbol{\mathcal{Q}}\) is small.

Filling the gap: what white noise does over an interval

White noise is never used on its own, only integrated. Take the scalar random walk \(\dot p = w\) with power spectral density \(Q_c\). The change in \(p\) over an interval is \(\int_s^t w(\tau)\,d\tau\). It has mean zero, and its variance is

\[ \E\Big[ \int_s^t\! w(\tau)\,d\tau \int_s^t\! w(\tau')\,d\tau' \Big] = \int_s^t\!\!\int_s^t Q_c\,\delta(\tau-\tau')\,d\tau\,d\tau' = \int_s^t Q_c\,d\tau = Q_c\,(t-s) . \]

The delta function removes one of the two integrals. So the variance of the accumulated change grows in proportion to elapsed time, and \(Q_c\) is that variance per second. If \(p\) is in metres, \(Q_c\) is in m²/s. Example: \(Q_c = 0.5\) m²/s over 4 s gives variance 2 m², a standard deviation of 1.41 m.

3. The transition function and one discrete step

A linear SDE can be integrated in closed form: §2.2.3 · p. 67

\[ \mathbf{x}(t) = \boldsymbol{\Phi}(t,t_1)\,\mathbf{x}(t_1) + \int_{t_1}^{t} \boldsymbol{\Phi}(t,s)\,\mathbf{L}\,\mathbf{w}(s)\,ds, \qquad \boldsymbol{\Phi}(t,s) = \exp\big(\mathbf{A}(t-s)\big) . \tag{2.47} \]

The transition function \(\boldsymbol{\Phi}(t,s)\) carries a state from time \(s\) to time \(t\) when there is no noise. The integral adds up the noise that arrived in between, each piece carried forward to time \(t\). Since \(\mathbf{x}(t)\) is a linear function of Gaussian quantities, it is itself a GP.

Filling the gap: Φ and the step covariance for the two priors

The matrix exponential is the series \(\exp(\mathbf{M}) = \mathbf{I} + \mathbf{M} + \tfrac12\mathbf{M}^2 + \dots\) from Week 4 · Day 2. For the random walk \(\mathbf{A} = \mathbf{0}\), so \(\boldsymbol{\Phi} = \mathbf{I}\). For constant velocity \(\mathbf{A}^2 = \mathbf{0}\) (multiply it out), so the series stops after two terms. With \(\Delta t = t - s\):

\[ \boldsymbol{\Phi}(t,s) = \mathbf{I} + \mathbf{A}\,\Delta t = \begin{bmatrix} \mathbf{I} & \Delta t\,\mathbf{I} \\ \mathbf{0} & \mathbf{I} \end{bmatrix} , \]

which is "new position = old position + velocity × time, velocity unchanged".

Apply (2.47) between two consecutive times \(t_{i-1}\) and \(t_i\). It reads \(\mathbf{x}_i = \boldsymbol{\Phi}(t_i,t_{i-1})\,\mathbf{x}_{i-1} + \mathbf{w}_i\), where \(\mathbf{w}_i\) is the integral term: a zero-mean Gaussian with the covariance the book defines under equation (2.49),

\[ \mathbf{Q}_i = \int_{t_{i-1}}^{t_i} \boldsymbol{\Phi}(t_i,s)\,\mathbf{L}\,\boldsymbol{\mathcal{Q}}\,\mathbf{L}\T\,\boldsymbol{\Phi}(t_i,s)\T\,ds . \]

Random walk, one axis: the integrand is \(Q_c\), so \(Q_i = Q_c\,\Delta t\), as in the box above. Constant velocity, one axis: \(\boldsymbol{\Phi}(t_i,s)\,\mathbf{L} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & t_i - s \\ 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix} 0 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} t_i - s \\ 1 \end{bmatrix}\). Substituting \(\tau = t_i - s\), which runs from 0 to \(\Delta t\):

\[ \mathbf{Q}_i = Q_c \int_0^{\Delta t} \begin{bmatrix} \tau^2 & \tau \\ \tau & 1 \end{bmatrix} d\tau = Q_c \begin{bmatrix} \tfrac13\Delta t^3 & \tfrac12\Delta t^2 \\ \tfrac12\Delta t^2 & \Delta t \end{bmatrix} . \]

With \(Q_c = 2\) and \(\Delta t = 0.5\) s this is \(\begin{bmatrix} 0.083 & 0.25 \\ 0.25 & 1 \end{bmatrix}\). The velocity variance grows like \(\Delta t\) and the position variance like \(\Delta t^3\): over short intervals the position barely deviates from a straight line.

4. The kernel matrix and its inverse

Assume the initial state has mean zero and covariance \(\mathcal{K}(t_1,t_1)\). Taking the covariance of (2.47) at two times gives the kernel function: §2.2.3 · p. 67

\[ \mathcal{K}(t,t') = \boldsymbol{\Phi}(t,t_1)\,\mathcal{K}(t_1,t_1)\,\boldsymbol{\Phi}(t',t_1)\T + \int_{t_1}^{\min(t,t')} \boldsymbol{\Phi}(t,s)\,\mathbf{L}\boldsymbol{\mathcal{Q}}\mathbf{L}\T\,\boldsymbol{\Phi}(t',s)\T\,ds . \tag{2.48} \]

Read it as two sources of shared randomness. The first term is the uncertain starting state, carried to both times. The second is the noise that arrived before the earlier of the two times: only that noise has reached both states.

For the scalar random walk (\(\Phi = 1\)) the formula collapses to \(\mathcal{K}(t,t') = \mathcal{K}(t_1,t_1) + Q_c\,(\min(t,t') - t_1)\). The book then states that the kernel matrix at all the measurement times has the tidy form \(\mathbf{K} = \boldsymbol{\Phi}\mathbf{Q}\boldsymbol{\Phi}\T\), equation (2.49), and that \(\boldsymbol{\Phi}^{-1}\) is almost empty. Here is why both are true. §2.2.3 · pp. 67–68

Filling the gap: where K = ΦQΦᵀ and its sparse inverse come from

Write \(\mathbf{x}_i = \mathbf{x}(t_i)\) and \(\boldsymbol{\Phi}_{i,j} = \boldsymbol{\Phi}(t_i,t_j)\). Call the initial state \(\mathbf{w}_1 = \mathbf{x}_1\), and use the one-step form from section 3:

\[ \mathbf{x}_1 = \mathbf{w}_1, \qquad \mathbf{x}_i = \boldsymbol{\Phi}_{i,i-1}\,\mathbf{x}_{i-1} + \mathbf{w}_i \quad (i = 2,\dots,M) . \]

The \(\mathbf{w}_i\) are independent, because they integrate white noise over intervals that do not overlap. Their covariances are \(\mathcal{K}(t_1,t_1), \mathbf{Q}_2, \dots, \mathbf{Q}_M\). Stack these on the diagonal of a block-diagonal matrix \(\mathbf{Q}\). (Figure 2.4 labels each step covariance by the index of the interval's first state, so its \(\mathbf{Q}_1\) is the \(\mathbf{Q}_2\) here.)

Forward. Unroll the recursion: \(\mathbf{x}_2 = \boldsymbol{\Phi}_{2,1}\mathbf{w}_1 + \mathbf{w}_2\), \(\mathbf{x}_3 = \boldsymbol{\Phi}_{3,1}\mathbf{w}_1 + \boldsymbol{\Phi}_{3,2}\mathbf{w}_2 + \mathbf{w}_3\), and so on, using \(\boldsymbol{\Phi}_{3,2}\boldsymbol{\Phi}_{2,1} = \boldsymbol{\Phi}_{3,1}\). Every state is a sum over all earlier noises. Stacked, \(\mathbf{x} = \boldsymbol{\Phi}\mathbf{w}\) with the full lower-triangular \(\boldsymbol{\Phi}\) of equation (2.50). The covariance of a linear function of \(\mathbf{w}\) is then \(\mathbf{K} = \boldsymbol{\Phi}\mathbf{Q}\boldsymbol{\Phi}\T\).

Backward. Solve the same recursion for the noises: \(\mathbf{w}_1 = \mathbf{x}_1\) and \(\mathbf{w}_i = \mathbf{x}_i - \boldsymbol{\Phi}_{i,i-1}\mathbf{x}_{i-1}\). Each noise involves only two neighbouring states. Stacked, \(\mathbf{w} = \boldsymbol{\Phi}^{-1}\mathbf{x}\), and you can read off \(\boldsymbol{\Phi}^{-1}\) with no computation: identity blocks on the diagonal and \(-\boldsymbol{\Phi}_{i,i-1}\) just below it, which is equation (2.51).

The prior as factors. With \(\mathbf{K}^{-1} = \boldsymbol{\Phi}^{-\mathsf{T}}\mathbf{Q}^{-1}\boldsymbol{\Phi}^{-1}\), the prior's negative log is

\[ \mathbf{x}\T\mathbf{K}^{-1}\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{w}\T\mathbf{Q}^{-1}\mathbf{w} = \norm{\mathbf{x}_1}^2_{\mathcal{K}(t_1,t_1)} + \sum_{i=2}^{M} \norm{\mathbf{x}_i - \boldsymbol{\Phi}_{i,i-1}\,\mathbf{x}_{i-1}}^2_{\mathbf{Q}_i} . \]

That is one unary factor on the first state and one binary factor between each pair of consecutive states: the motion-prior factors of Figure 2.4. No term couples \(\mathbf{x}_i\) with \(\mathbf{x}_j\) unless \(|i-j| \le 1\), so \(\mathbf{K}^{-1}\) is block-tridiagonal, however long the trajectory.

Worked example: scalar random walk at \(t = 0, 1, 2\) s with \(\mathcal{K}(t_1,t_1) = 1\) and \(Q_c = 1\), so \(\mathbf{Q} = \mathbf{I}\).

\[ \boldsymbol{\Phi} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 1 & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 1 & 1 \end{bmatrix},\quad \mathbf{K} = \boldsymbol{\Phi}\boldsymbol{\Phi}\T = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 1 & 1 \\ 1 & 2 & 2 \\ 1 & 2 & 3 \end{bmatrix},\quad \boldsymbol{\Phi}^{-1} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 & 0 \\ -1 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & -1 & 1 \end{bmatrix},\quad \mathbf{K}^{-1} = \begin{bmatrix} 2 & -1 & 0 \\ -1 & 2 & -1 \\ 0 & -1 & 1 \end{bmatrix} . \]

\(\mathbf{K}\) has no zeros and agrees with the kernel formula, \(K_{ij} = 1 + \min(t_i,t_j)\). Its inverse has a zero in the corner: the first and third states are not directly linked. Check one product: row 3 of \(\mathbf{K}\) times column 1 of \(\mathbf{K}^{-1}\) is \(1\cdot2 + 2\cdot(-1) + 3\cdot0 = 0\).

Try it: set the number of times to 3 to see the matrices above, then raise it. Then switch the prior.

Notice that K is full for every prior. For the random walk at six times, K⁻¹ has 16 nonzero entries out of 36: the diagonal and its two neighbours. For constant velocity with state (p, v) the inverse is block-tridiagonal with 2 × 2 blocks. For "constant velocity, positions only" and for the squared exponential, every entry of the inverse is nonzero.

5. Markov, and why the state carries velocity

The inverse is sparse because the state of the SDE is Markovian: once you know \(\mathbf{x}_{i-1}\), nothing earlier helps to predict \(\mathbf{x}_i\). §2.2.3 · p. 68 In Week 3 · Day 1 you saw that a zero block in the information matrix means "no factor between these two variables". Here it is the same statement, and \(\mathbf{K}^{-1}\) is the information matrix of the prior.

The price is that the state must contain everything the model needs to predict the next step. For the constant-velocity prior a position alone is not enough: to predict where the robot goes next you also need its velocity. So the state is \(\mathbf{x} = (\mathbf{p}, \mathbf{v})\), as in equation (2.52), and the estimator solves for a velocity at every estimation time alongside the pose. The book notes this variant is sometimes called simultaneous trajectory estimation and mapping (STEAM). §2.2.3 · p. 68

The widget's third option shows what happens if you refuse. Dropping the velocities from the constant-velocity kernel is the marginalization of Week 3 · Day 3, and it fills the information matrix in: positions alone are not Markovian, because two earlier positions together reveal the velocity.

In plain words

The prior is a rule of the form "the next state should be close to what the current state predicts". A rule like that only ever compares neighbours. A thousand such rules in a row describe a smooth path of any length, and none of them mentions two states that are far apart.

Common mistakes

  • "A sparse inverse means distant poses are uncorrelated." No. \(\mathbf{K}\) is full: every pose is correlated with every other. The zeros are in \(\mathbf{K}^{-1}\), and mean there is no direct factor between distant poses.
  • "Constant-velocity prior means the robot moves at constant velocity." It means deviations from constant velocity are penalized, with a strength set by \(\boldsymbol{\mathcal{Q}}\). The measurements can still bend the trajectory.
  • "The velocities are extra work." They are what keeps the factor graph a chain. Leaving them out makes the prior dense.

Check yourself

Q1. A scalar random-walk prior has power spectral density 0.5 m²/s. What is the standard deviation of the change in position over 8 s?

The variance is Q_c Δt = 0.5 × 8 = 4 m², so the standard deviation is 2 m.

Q2. Under the constant-velocity model, the state is (p, v) = (1, 3). With no noise, what is the state 2 s later?

Φ = [[1, 2], [0, 1]], so p becomes 1 + 2·3 = 7 and v stays 3.

Q3. A scalar random walk is evaluated at 5 times. How many entries of the 5 × 5 inverse kernel matrix are nonzero?

Tridiagonal: 5 on the diagonal plus 4 above and 4 below, 13 in all.

Q4. A scalar random walk starts at t₁ = 0 with zero initial variance and has Q_c = 1. What is the kernel value K(2, 5)?

K(t, t′) = Q_c · min(t, t′) = 2. Only the noise up to the earlier time is shared by both values.

Q5. Why does the constant-velocity prior use a state with both pose and velocity?

Predicting the next position needs the current velocity. With (p, v) as the state each step depends only on the previous state, which gives the chain of binary factors.

Recap

  1. Motion prior: \(\dot{\mathbf{x}} = \mathbf{A}\mathbf{x} + \mathbf{L}\mathbf{w}\) with white noise of power spectral density \(\boldsymbol{\mathcal{Q}}\), equation (2.46). Its solution is a GP.
  2. One step: \(\mathbf{x}_i = \boldsymbol{\Phi}(t_i,t_{i-1})\mathbf{x}_{i-1} + \mathbf{w}_i\), \(\mathbf{w}_i \sim \N(\mathbf{0}, \mathbf{Q}_i)\). Constant velocity: \(\boldsymbol{\Phi} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & \Delta t \\ 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix}\), \(\mathbf{Q}_i = Q_c\begin{bmatrix} \Delta t^3/3 & \Delta t^2/2 \\ \Delta t^2/2 & \Delta t \end{bmatrix}\) per axis.
  3. \(\mathbf{K} = \boldsymbol{\Phi}\mathbf{Q}\boldsymbol{\Phi}\T\) is dense. \(\mathbf{K}^{-1} = \boldsymbol{\Phi}^{-\mathsf{T}}\mathbf{Q}^{-1}\boldsymbol{\Phi}^{-1}\) is block-tridiagonal.
  4. As factors: one unary factor on the first state and a binary factor \(\norm{\mathbf{x}_i - \boldsymbol{\Phi}\mathbf{x}_{i-1}}^2_{\mathbf{Q}_i}\) between consecutive states.
  5. This needs a Markovian state, so higher-order priors estimate derivatives too (STEAM).

Sources

  1. SLAM Handbook, §2.2.3 "Gaussian Processes", pp. 66–68, equations (2.46)–(2.52), Figure 2.4.
  2. The unrolled-recursion derivation of \(\mathbf{K} = \boldsymbol{\Phi}\mathbf{Q}\boldsymbol{\Phi}\T\) and the closed form of \(\mathbf{Q}_i\) for white noise on acceleration follow Barfoot, State Estimation for Robotics, 2017.
  3. White noise, its integral, and the matrix-exponential solution of a linear SDE follow Särkkä and Solin, Applied Stochastic Differential Equations, 2019. The definition of a Gaussian process follows Rasmussen and Williams, Gaussian Processes for Machine Learning, 2006.

Week 5 · Day 4

Gaussian-process regression and interpolation by hand

After today you can compute a GP posterior mean and variance from a small kernel matrix by hand, interpolate between two estimated states at constant cost, and explain why measurement, estimation, and query times can all differ.

About 60 min · Read §2.2.3 (end), pp. 68–69 (1 page) · Needs Week 3 Day 3 and Week 5 Day 3

Read first: the end of §2.2.3, pp. 68–69

Read from the last paragraph of p. 68 ("This formulation of continuous-time trajectory estimation is really an example of Gaussian process regression") to the heading "2.2.4" on p. 69. It is short; most of today is the math behind it. While you read, look for:

  • What a query costs and which estimated states it involves (top of p. 69).
  • The lidar example of using fewer control points than measurements (p. 69).
  • The reason given for why extra estimation times do not cause overfitting, and the caveat that follows (p. 69).

Today's big idea

The estimator of the last two days is Gaussian-process regression: start from a Gaussian prior over whole trajectories and condition it on noisy measurements. Conditioning returns a mean and a variance at every time, measured or not. With a prior that comes from an SDE, the answer at a query time needs only the two estimated states on either side of it.

1. Regression is conditioning a Gaussian

Work with one scalar coordinate \(p(t)\) and a zero-mean GP prior with kernel \(\mathcal{K}\). Sensors measure the position at times \(t_1,\dots,t_M\) with independent noise of variance \(\sigma^2\): \(z_i = p(t_i) + \eta_i\). We want \(p(\tau)\) at a query time \(\tau\). By the definition of a GP, the measurements and the query value are jointly Gaussian with mean zero:

\[ \begin{bmatrix} \mathbf{z} \\ p(\tau) \end{bmatrix} \sim \N\!\left( \mathbf{0},\ \begin{bmatrix} \mathbf{K} + \sigma^2\mathbf{I} & \mathbf{k}_\tau \\ \mathbf{k}_\tau\T & \mathcal{K}(\tau,\tau) \end{bmatrix} \right), \qquad \mathbf{k}_\tau = \begin{bmatrix} \mathcal{K}(t_1,\tau) \\ \vdots \\ \mathcal{K}(t_M,\tau) \end{bmatrix} . \]

\(\mathbf{K}\) is the kernel matrix at the measurement times, and the noise adds \(\sigma^2\) to its diagonal. Now apply the rule for conditioning one block of a Gaussian on another from Week 3 · Day 3: if \((\mathbf{a}, \mathbf{b})\) are zero-mean and jointly Gaussian, then given \(\mathbf{a}\), \(\mathbf{b}\) has mean \(\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{ba}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{aa}^{-1}\mathbf{a}\) and covariance \(\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{bb} - \boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{ba}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{aa}^{-1}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{ab}\). With \(\mathbf{a} = \mathbf{z}\) and \(\mathbf{b} = p(\tau)\):

\[ \hat p(\tau) = \mathbf{k}_\tau\T\,(\mathbf{K} + \sigma^2\mathbf{I})^{-1}\,\mathbf{z}, \qquad \operatorname{var}\big(p(\tau)\big) = \mathcal{K}(\tau,\tau) - \mathbf{k}_\tau\T\,(\mathbf{K} + \sigma^2\mathbf{I})^{-1}\,\mathbf{k}_\tau . \]

These two formulas are GP regression. The posterior mean is a weighted sum of the measurements. The posterior variance is the prior variance minus what the measurements explained, and it does not depend on the measured values, only on the times and the kernel.

Filling the gap: this is equation (2.45)

The book reaches the same estimator through the modified normal equations \((\mathbf{A}\T\mathbf{A} + \mathbf{K}^{-1})\,\boldsymbol{\delta}^* = \mathbf{A}\T\mathbf{b}\). To see that the two agree, use direct position measurements. The whitened Jacobian is \(\mathbf{A} = \mathbf{I}/\sigma\) and the whitened residual, starting from a zero estimate, is \(\mathbf{b} = \mathbf{z}/\sigma\), so (2.45) reads \((\sigma^{-2}\mathbf{I} + \mathbf{K}^{-1})\,\hat{\mathbf{p}} = \sigma^{-2}\mathbf{z}\). Factor the bracket as \(\sigma^{-2}\mathbf{K}^{-1}(\mathbf{K} + \sigma^2\mathbf{I})\) and invert:

\[ \hat{\mathbf{p}} = (\mathbf{K} + \sigma^2\mathbf{I})^{-1}\mathbf{K}\,\sigma^{2}\cdot\sigma^{-2}\mathbf{z} = \mathbf{K}\,(\mathbf{K} + \sigma^2\mathbf{I})^{-1}\mathbf{z} . \]

(The last step swaps the two factors, which is allowed because both are functions of the same matrix \(\mathbf{K}\).) Row \(i\) of \(\mathbf{K}\) is \(\mathbf{k}_\tau\T\) for \(\tau = t_i\), so this is the regression mean evaluated at the measurement times. MAP estimation with the kernel prior and GP regression are the same computation. The book's version is preferable in SLAM because it works with the sparse \(\mathbf{K}^{-1}\) and never forms the dense \(\mathbf{K}\).

2. A full example by hand

Prior: a random walk that starts at exactly \(p(0) = 0\), with \(Q_c = 1\). From Day 3 its kernel is \(\mathcal{K}(t,t') = \min(t,t')\). Two measurements with noise variance \(\sigma^2 = 1\): \(z = 2\) at \(t = 1\) and \(z = 3\) at \(t = 3\).

\[ \mathbf{K} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ 1 & 3 \end{bmatrix},\quad \mathbf{K} + \sigma^2\mathbf{I} = \begin{bmatrix} 2 & 1 \\ 1 & 4 \end{bmatrix},\quad (\mathbf{K} + \sigma^2\mathbf{I})^{-1} = \frac17\begin{bmatrix} 4 & -1 \\ -1 & 2 \end{bmatrix},\quad (\mathbf{K} + \sigma^2\mathbf{I})^{-1}\mathbf{z} = \frac17\begin{bmatrix} 5 \\ 4 \end{bmatrix} . \]

For each query time, \(\mathbf{k}_\tau = (\min(1,\tau), \min(3,\tau))\). The mean is \(\mathbf{k}_\tau\) dotted with \((5,4)/7\). For the variance at \(\tau = 2\): \(\mathbf{k}_\tau = (1,2)\), \((\mathbf{K}+\sigma^2\mathbf{I})^{-1}\mathbf{k}_\tau = (2,3)/7\), so the variance is \(2 - (1\cdot2 + 2\cdot3)/7 = 6/7\).

Query time τkPosterior meanPosterior variance
1 (a measurement time)(1, 1)9/7 ≈ 1.291 − 4/7 = 3/7 ≈ 0.43
2 (between)(1, 2)13/7 ≈ 1.862 − 8/7 = 6/7 ≈ 0.86
3 (a measurement time)(1, 3)17/7 ≈ 2.433 − 16/7 = 5/7 ≈ 0.71
5 (after the last one)(1, 3)17/7 ≈ 2.435 − 16/7 = 19/7 ≈ 2.71

Four things to read off, all of which hold in general:

  • The estimate does not pass through the measurements. At \(t = 1\) the sensor said 2 and the posterior says 1.29, because the prior (anchored at 0) and the noise both have a say.
  • At a measurement time the posterior variance (0.43, 0.71) is below the sensor's own variance of 1. The other measurement and the prior add information.
  • Between the measurements the mean is the straight line between the two estimates, \((9/7 + 17/7)/2 = 13/7\), and the variance bulges above both ends.
  • After the last measurement the mean stays where it was, because the random-walk prior predicts no change, and the variance grows by \(Q_c = 1\) per second: \(5/7 + 2 = 19/7\). This is the caution the book attaches to extrapolation. §2.2 · p. 63

3. The same thing on a real trajectory

Try it: this is the data from Day 2, now fitted with a GP. Lower the power spectral density Q to 0.001, then raise it to 100. Then switch to the random-walk prior and set Q to 1.

Notice the band. At the start (constant velocity, Q = 10) it is ±0.42 among the measurements and ±1.66 in the middle of the gap. After the last measurement the mean carries on in a straight line at the last estimated velocity, and the band widens quickly. With Q = 0.001 the mean is nearly a straight line, the error rises to 0.70, and the band is narrow and wrong: the prior is too stiff and too sure. With Q = 100 the band in the gap is wider than the plot. With the random-walk prior the mean is made of straight pieces between measurements, as in the hand example.

Q is the hyperparameter the book says must be tuned to get the desired smoothness. §2.2.2 · p. 66 Compare with the spline widget: there, too many coefficients made the problem singular. Here every instant is covered by the prior, so the estimate is defined everywhere and comes with an honest uncertainty where data is missing.

4. Interpolating between two estimated states

The formulas of section 1 use every measurement for every query. With an SDE prior that is unnecessary. The book states that a query costs the same no matter how many measurements there are, because it involves only the estimated states at the two times that bracket it. §2.2.3 · p. 69

Filling the gap: the interpolation formula

Let \(t_k \lt \tau \lt t_{k+1}\). Under the prior, \(\mathbf{x}(\tau) = \boldsymbol{\Phi}(\tau,t_k)\mathbf{x}_k + \mathbf{w}_\tau\) with \(\mathbf{w}_\tau \sim \N(\mathbf{0}, \mathbf{Q}_\tau)\), where \(\mathbf{Q}_\tau\) is the step covariance of Day 3 for the interval from \(t_k\) to \(\tau\). Likewise \(\mathbf{x}_{k+1}\) given \(\mathbf{x}_k\) has covariance \(\mathbf{Q}_{k+1}\), and the covariance between \(\mathbf{x}(\tau)\) and \(\mathbf{x}_{k+1}\) given \(\mathbf{x}_k\) is \(\mathbf{Q}_\tau\boldsymbol{\Phi}(t_{k+1},\tau)\T\). Conditioning \(\mathbf{x}(\tau)\) on \(\mathbf{x}_{k+1}\) as well, with the same rule as in section 1, gives

\[ \mathbf{x}(\tau) = \boldsymbol{\Lambda}(\tau)\,\mathbf{x}_k + \boldsymbol{\Omega}(\tau)\,\mathbf{x}_{k+1} + \text{noise}, \qquad \boldsymbol{\Omega}(\tau) = \mathbf{Q}_\tau\,\boldsymbol{\Phi}(t_{k+1},\tau)\T\,\mathbf{Q}_{k+1}^{-1}, \quad \boldsymbol{\Lambda}(\tau) = \boldsymbol{\Phi}(\tau,t_k) - \boldsymbol{\Omega}(\tau)\,\boldsymbol{\Phi}(t_{k+1},t_k) , \]

where the noise has covariance \(\mathbf{Q}_\tau - \boldsymbol{\Omega}(\tau)\mathbf{Q}_{k+1}\boldsymbol{\Omega}(\tau)\T\). Because the state is Markovian, once the two bracketing states are known no other state or measurement says anything more about \(\mathbf{x}(\tau)\). So the posterior mean at \(\tau\) is \(\boldsymbol{\Lambda}\hat{\mathbf{x}}_k + \boldsymbol{\Omega}\hat{\mathbf{x}}_{k+1}\), and the posterior covariance is \([\boldsymbol{\Lambda}\ \boldsymbol{\Omega}]\) applied on both sides of the joint posterior covariance of the two states, plus the noise covariance. (Barfoot writes \(\boldsymbol{\Psi}\) for our \(\boldsymbol{\Omega}\); we rename it because \(\boldsymbol{\Psi}\) already means a basis function this week.)

Random walk. \(\Phi = 1\), \(Q_\tau = Q_c(\tau - t_k)\), \(Q_{k+1} = Q_c(t_{k+1} - t_k)\). With \(\alpha = (\tau - t_k)/(t_{k+1} - t_k)\) this gives \(\Omega = \alpha\) and \(\Lambda = 1 - \alpha\): linear interpolation. The noise variance is \(Q_c\,(t_{k+1}-t_k)\,\alpha(1-\alpha)\), largest at the midpoint.

Check against section 2. At \(\tau = 2\), between \(t = 1\) and \(t = 3\): \(\alpha = 0.5\). The mean is \(0.5\cdot\tfrac97 + 0.5\cdot\tfrac{17}{7} = \tfrac{13}{7}\). The joint posterior of the two estimates has variances \(\tfrac37, \tfrac57\) and covariance \(\tfrac17\), so the variance is \(0.25\,(\tfrac37 + \tfrac57 + 2\cdot\tfrac17) + 1\cdot2\cdot0.25 = \tfrac{5}{14} + \tfrac{7}{14} = \tfrac67\). Both match the table.

Constant velocity. The same formula with the \(\boldsymbol{\Phi}\) and \(\mathbf{Q}\) of Day 3 gives 2 × 2 matrices whose entries are cubic polynomials in \(\alpha\). The interpolated position is the cubic curve that matches the estimated position and velocity at both ends (cubic Hermite interpolation).

So the choice of SDE decides the interpolation scheme: a random walk gives straight lines, constant velocity gives cubics. The book makes the same point on p. 73.

5. Three kinds of time, and fewer states than measurements

The interpolation formula has a second use. A measurement taken at a time \(t_i\) that falls between two estimation times can be modelled through \(\mathbf{x}(t_i) = \boldsymbol{\Lambda}\mathbf{x}_k + \boldsymbol{\Omega}\mathbf{x}_{k+1}\). Its factor then touches the two bracketing states instead of needing a state of its own. The book's example: one state per lidar scan, while every point in the scan is still used at its own time stamp. It compares the idea to inducing points in the GP literature. §2.2.3 · p. 69

This is the separation of measurement times, estimation times, and query times from Day 1, now for the nonparametric method. One difference from splines matters in practice. Adding more estimation times to a GP does not cause overfitting, because the kernel regularizes every stretch of the trajectory however finely it is divided. You still need enough of them to capture the detail of the motion. §2.2.3 · p. 69

QuestionSpline (Days 1–2)GP with an SDE prior (Days 3–4)
Estimation variablesCoefficientsStates (pose, and derivatives if the prior needs them) at chosen times
A measurement at an arbitrary time touchesThe active coefficients (4 for a cubic)The 2 bracketing states
RegularizationNone unless you add itBuilt in: the motion-prior factors
More variables than neededRisk of overfittingNo overfitting, only more computation
Query at any timeEvaluate the basis functionsInterpolate from 2 states, mean and covariance

Common mistakes

  • "The posterior mean passes through the measurements." Only if the noise variance is zero. Otherwise it is a compromise between the measurements and the prior.
  • "The band shows where the measurements scatter." It is the uncertainty of the trajectory itself. It can be much narrower than the sensor noise where many measurements overlap, and much wider where there are none.
  • "A query needs all the measurements again." With a Markovian prior it needs the two bracketing estimated states and their joint covariance, nothing else.

Check yourself

Q1. Which of these does the GP posterior variance at a query time NOT depend on?

The variance formula contains K, k, and σ² only. The measured values enter the mean, not the variance.

Q2. Random-walk prior with p(0) = 0 and Q_c = 1, so the kernel is min(t, t′). One measurement z = 3 at t = 2 with noise variance 2. What is the posterior mean at t = 2?

K = 2, so the mean is 2/(2 + 2) × 3 = 1.5: halfway between the prior mean 0 and the measurement, because the prior variance and the noise variance are equal.

Q3. Same setup as Q2. What is the posterior variance at t = 2?

2 − 2·(1/4)·2 = 1. Two sources with variance 2 each (prior and measurement) combine to variance 1.

Q4. With a random-walk prior the estimates are 10 at t = 4 s and 14 at t = 6 s. What is the interpolated mean at t = 4.5 s?

α = 0.5/2 = 0.25, so the mean is 0.75·10 + 0.25·14 = 11.

Q5. A trajectory was estimated from 100 measurements, then re-estimated from 10,000. With an SDE prior, how does the cost of one query change?

Constant time with respect to the number of measurements (p. 69). Solving for the states costs more, but each query afterwards does not.

Recap

  1. GP regression: \(\hat p(\tau) = \mathbf{k}_\tau\T(\mathbf{K} + \sigma^2\mathbf{I})^{-1}\mathbf{z}\) and \(\operatorname{var} = \mathcal{K}(\tau,\tau) - \mathbf{k}_\tau\T(\mathbf{K} + \sigma^2\mathbf{I})^{-1}\mathbf{k}_\tau\). It is the same estimator as equation (2.45).
  2. The variance is small near measurements, bulges between them, and grows without bound when extrapolating.
  3. With a Markovian prior, \(\hat{\mathbf{x}}(\tau) = \boldsymbol{\Lambda}(\tau)\hat{\mathbf{x}}_k + \boldsymbol{\Omega}(\tau)\hat{\mathbf{x}}_{k+1}\): constant cost per query. Random walk gives linear interpolation, constant velocity gives cubic.
  4. The same interpolation lets a measurement between estimation times become a factor on two states, so there can be far fewer states than measurements.
  5. More estimation times do not overfit a GP. Too few lose detail.

Sources

  1. SLAM Handbook, §2.2.3 "Gaussian Processes", pp. 68–69 (GP regression, interpolation, control points); §2.2, p. 63 (extrapolating with caution).
  2. The regression mean and variance formulas follow Rasmussen and Williams, Gaussian Processes for Machine Learning, 2006. The worked example is computed here from those formulas.
  3. The interpolation matrices and the fact that the constant-velocity prior gives cubic Hermite interpolation follow Barfoot, State Estimation for Robotics, 2017.

Week 5 · Day 5

Splines and Gaussian processes on Lie groups

After today you can rewrite a spline in cumulative form, interpolate between two poses on SE(d) with Exp and Log, and write the random-walk motion-prior factor between two poses together with its linearization.

About 60 min · Read §2.2.4 and §2.3, pp. 69–74 (6 pages) · Needs Week 4 Day 5 and Week 5 Day 4

Read first: §2.2.4 and §2.3, pp. 69–74

This is the longest reading of the week, and the densest. While you read, look for:

  • First re-read the top of p. 62 (§2.1.5.4, equations (2.33)–(2.35)): the left Jacobian \(\mathbf{J}\) defined there is used on p. 71.
  • Which differences appear in the cumulative form, equation (2.54) (p. 69).
  • In the lower half of Figure 2.5, how many cumulative basis functions are neither 0 nor 1 at a given time (p. 70).
  • Footnote 3 on p. 71: why the perturbation is on the left this time.
  • What the local variable in Figure 2.7 and equation (2.68) is (pp. 72–73).
  • The last sentence of §2.2.4: the one difference between the spline and GP approaches (p. 74).

Today's big idea

Poses cannot be added or scaled, so a weighted sum of poses means nothing on SE(d). The difference between two neighbouring poses, however, can be turned into an ordinary vector with Log, scaled or given a Gaussian prior there, and turned back with Exp. Splines reach this through cumulative basis functions. Gaussian processes reach it through a local variable defined between control points. For the simplest case of each, the result is the same interpolation formula.

1. Why the sum fails on a group

Everything this week has used \(\mathbf{p}(t) = \sum_k \psi_k(t)\,\mathbf{p}_k\) with vectors \(\mathbf{p}_k\). Try it with rotations. The entrywise average of the planar rotations by 0° and by 90° is

\[ \tfrac12\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix} + \tfrac12\begin{bmatrix} 0 & -1 \\ 1 & 0 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 0.5 & -0.5 \\ 0.5 & 0.5 \end{bmatrix}, \]

whose determinant is 0.5, not 1. It is not a rotation: it also shrinks. This is the point of Week 4 · Day 1: \(\SO(d)\) and \(\SE(d)\) are not vector spaces. The sensible answer, a rotation by 45°, comes from taking the relative rotation (90°), halving its angle, and applying that to the first rotation. The rest of today generalizes this recipe. §2.2.4 · p. 69

2. The cumulative form of a spline

With the same scalar basis functions \(\psi_k(t)\) for every component, the spline is \(\mathbf{p}(t) = \sum_{k=1}^{K}\psi_k(t)\,\mathbf{p}_k\), equation (2.53).
