The \(\mathbf{p}_k\) are now called control points. The book rewrites the sum so that only the first control point and differences of neighbours appear: §2.2.4.1 · p. 69

\[ \mathbf{p}(t) = \psi^c_1(t)\,\mathbf{p}_1 + \sum_{k=2}^{K} \psi^c_k(t)\,(\mathbf{p}_k - \mathbf{p}_{k-1}), \qquad \psi^c_k(t) = \sum_{\ell=k}^{K}\psi_\ell(t) . \tag{2.54, 2.55} \]

The \(\psi^c_k\) are the cumulative basis functions.

Filling the gap: deriving the cumulative form

Write each control point as the first one plus the steps that lead to it: \(\mathbf{p}_k = \mathbf{p}_1 + \sum_{j=2}^{k}(\mathbf{p}_j - \mathbf{p}_{j-1})\). Substitute into (2.53):

\[ \mathbf{p}(t) = \Big(\sum_{k=1}^{K}\psi_k\Big)\mathbf{p}_1 + \sum_{k=2}^{K}\psi_k \sum_{j=2}^{k}(\mathbf{p}_j - \mathbf{p}_{j-1}) . \]

In the double sum, the step \(\mathbf{p}_j - \mathbf{p}_{j-1}\) is multiplied by every \(\psi_k\) with \(k \ge j\). Collecting them gives \(\sum_{j=2}^{K}\big(\sum_{k=j}^{K}\psi_k\big)(\mathbf{p}_j - \mathbf{p}_{j-1})\), which is (2.54). The first bracket is \(\psi^c_1\), and it equals 1 wherever the basis functions sum to one.

For a linear spline with knots \(T\) seconds apart, each \(\psi^c_k\) is a ramp: 0 before its segment, rising linearly from 0 to 1 across it, and 1 afterwards (equations (2.58)–(2.59), lower half of Figure 2.5). Write \(\alpha_k(t)\) for the fraction of the segment that has passed. On the segment that ends at control point \(k\), every earlier step has weight 1, every later step has weight 0, and one step is in transition: §2.2.4.1 · p. 70

\[ \mathbf{p}(t) = \mathbf{p}_{k-1} + \alpha_k(t)\,(\mathbf{p}_k - \mathbf{p}_{k-1}) . \tag{2.60} \]

Numbers: control points 2, 5, 4, and a time 30% of the way from the second to the third. The cumulative weights are \(1, 1, 0.3\), so \(p = 2 + 1\cdot(5-2) + 0.3\cdot(4-5) = 4.7\), which is the linear interpolation \(5 + 0.3\cdot(4-5)\).

Reading note: an index shift on p. 70

Equations (2.56)–(2.57) place control point \(k\) at time \((k-1)T\) (check: \(\psi_1 = 1\) at \(t = 0\)). Equations (2.58)–(2.62) are written as if control point \(k\) sat at time \(kT\): in (2.60) the curve reaches \(\mathbf{p}_k\) as \(t \to kT\). The two halves of the page are one index apart. Nothing later depends on it. What matters is the pattern above: on each segment, \(\alpha\) runs from 0 to 1 while the curve goes from one control point to the next.

3. From the vector space to the group

The cumulative form uses only three operations, and each has a group counterpart from Week 4 · Day 2:

Vector spaceLie group
Difference \(\mathbf{p}_k - \mathbf{p}_{k-1}\)\(\Log\big(\mathbf{T}_k\mathbf{T}_{k-1}^{-1}\big)\), a vector
Scale the difference by \(\psi^c_k(t)\)Scale that vector by \(\psi^c_k(t)\)
Add the result to \(\mathbf{p}_{k-1}\)Apply \(\Exp(\cdot)\) and multiply onto \(\mathbf{T}_{k-1}\)

For the linear spline this turns (2.60) into §2.2.4.1 · p. 71

\[ \mathbf{T}(t) = \Exp\!\Big( \alpha_k(t)\,\Log\big(\mathbf{T}_k\mathbf{T}_{k-1}^{-1}\big) \Big)\,\mathbf{T}_{k-1} = \big(\mathbf{T}_k\mathbf{T}_{k-1}^{-1}\big)^{\alpha_k(t)}\,\mathbf{T}_{k-1} . \tag{2.61, 2.62} \]

The power in the second form is shorthand for the first: a matrix raised to a real power means Exp of the scaled Log. Check the ends. At \(\alpha = 0\), \(\Exp(\mathbf{0}) = \mathbf{I}\) and \(\mathbf{T}(t) = \mathbf{T}_{k-1}\). At \(\alpha = 1\), \(\mathbf{T}(t) = \mathbf{T}_k\mathbf{T}_{k-1}^{-1}\mathbf{T}_{k-1} = \mathbf{T}_k\). In between, the result is always a valid pose, because Exp always lands on the group.

Try it: drag the far pose, turn its heading, and slide α from 0 to 1.

Notice that the interpolated pose follows a circular arc while its heading turns at a steady rate. At the starting position, ξ = (15.01, −10.67, 2.09), ordered translation then rotation as in the book, and at α = 0.5 the pose is 2.45 units from the midpoint of the straight line. The first two numbers of ξ are not the displacement between the two positions. The last tile repeats section 1: blending the two rotation matrices entrywise gives determinant 0.25 at α = 0.5.

Two remarks. First, the book perturbs on the left here, where §2.1.3 perturbed on the right. Footnote 3 gives the reason: when the unknown pose maps world coordinates to sensor coordinates, splines are usually applied in the sensor frame, and the perturbation is placed there too. §2.2.4.1 · p. 71 Second, with a higher-order spline more than one step is in transition at a time (three for a cubic), so \(\mathbf{T}(t)\) is a product of several such Exp factors. The active set is still small.

4. Linearizing through the interpolation

The control poses are the estimation variables. Gauss-Newton perturbs each one, \(\mathbf{T}_k = \Exp(\boldsymbol{\xi}_k)\,\mathbf{T}_k^0\), and needs to know how the interpolated pose moves in response: \(\mathbf{T}(t) = \Exp(\boldsymbol{\xi}(t))\,\mathbf{T}^0(t)\), equation (2.63). The book quotes the first-order answer: §2.2.4.1 · p. 71

\[ \boldsymbol{\xi}(t) \approx \big(\mathbf{I} - \mathbf{A}(\alpha_k)\big)\,\boldsymbol{\xi}_{k-1} + \mathbf{A}(\alpha_k)\,\boldsymbol{\xi}_k, \qquad \mathbf{A}(\alpha) = \alpha\,\mathbf{J}\big(\alpha\,\boldsymbol{\xi}_{\mathrm{rel}}\big)\,\mathbf{J}\big(\boldsymbol{\xi}_{\mathrm{rel}}\big)^{-1}, \tag{2.64, 2.65} \]

where \(\boldsymbol{\xi}_{\mathrm{rel}} = \Log(\mathbf{T}_k^0\mathbf{T}_{k-1}^{0\,-1})\) and \(\mathbf{J}\) is the left Jacobian of \(\SE(d)\) from Week 4 · Day 5. (The book writes the group element itself as the argument of \(\mathbf{J}\); it means the Jacobian evaluated at that element's Log.)

Filling the gap: three checks that make (2.65) believable

  • \(\alpha = 0\): \(\mathbf{A} = \mathbf{0}\), so \(\boldsymbol{\xi}(t) = \boldsymbol{\xi}_{k-1}\). At the start of the segment the interpolated pose is control pose \(k-1\).
  • \(\alpha = 1\): \(\mathbf{A} = \mathbf{J}\mathbf{J}^{-1} = \mathbf{I}\), so \(\boldsymbol{\xi}(t) = \boldsymbol{\xi}_k\).
  • Control poses close together: \(\boldsymbol{\xi}_{\mathrm{rel}}\) is small, \(\mathbf{J} \approx \mathbf{I}\), and \(\mathbf{A} \approx \alpha\mathbf{I}\). Then \(\boldsymbol{\xi}(t) \approx (1-\alpha)\boldsymbol{\xi}_{k-1} + \alpha\,\boldsymbol{\xi}_k\): the perturbation is interpolated the same way as the pose. The Jacobians correct this when the two control poses are far apart.

Now take any measurement at time \(t\) whose linearized error is \(\mathbf{e}_i(t) \approx \mathbf{z}_i - \mathbf{h}_i(\cdot) - \mathbf{H}_i\,\boldsymbol{\xi}(t)\), equation (2.66), and substitute (2.64):

\[ \mathbf{e}_i(t) \approx \mathbf{z}_i - \mathbf{h}_i\big(\mathbf{T}^0(t)\,\tilde{\boldsymbol{\ell}}_i\big) - \mathbf{H}_i\big(\mathbf{I} - \mathbf{A}(\alpha_k)\big)\,\boldsymbol{\xi}_{k-1} - \mathbf{H}_i\,\mathbf{A}(\alpha_k)\,\boldsymbol{\xi}_k . \tag{2.67} \]

This is the chain rule of Day 1 again. There a measurement's Jacobian was \(\mathbf{H}_i\) times a basis-function value; here it is \(\mathbf{H}_i\) times \(\mathbf{I} - \mathbf{A}\) for one control pose and \(\mathbf{H}_i\mathbf{A}\) for the other. Each measurement touches two control poses. §2.2.4.1 · p. 72

5. Gaussian processes on Lie groups

The GP needs a vector for its SDE to act on. The book defines one between each pair of control poses, the local variable §2.2.4.2 · pp. 72–73

\[ \boldsymbol{\xi}_k(t) = \Log\big(\mathbf{T}(t)\,\mathbf{T}_k^{-1}\big), \qquad t_k \le t \le t_{k+1} . \]

It is zero at \(t_k\) and equals \(\Log(\mathbf{T}_{k+1}\mathbf{T}_k^{-1})\) at \(t_{k+1}\) (Figure 2.7). The control poses \(\mathbf{T}_k\) are the global variables and remain the things we estimate. Put the simplest SDE on the local variable, a random walk:

\[ \dot{\boldsymbol{\xi}}_k(t) = \mathbf{w}(t), \quad \mathbf{w}(t) \sim \mathcal{GP}\big(\mathbf{0}, \boldsymbol{\mathcal{Q}}\,\delta(t-t')\big) \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad \boldsymbol{\xi}_k(t) \sim \mathcal{GP}\big(\mathbf{0}, \min(t,t')\,\boldsymbol{\mathcal{Q}}\big) , \tag{2.68, 2.70} \]

with time counted from \(t_k\). This is Day 3's result with \(\boldsymbol{\Phi} = \mathbf{I}\): over a segment of length \(T\) the local variable picks up covariance \(T\boldsymbol{\mathcal{Q}}\). The motion-prior factors are then, in terms of the control poses,

\[ \mathbf{e}_1 = \Log\big(\mathbf{T}_1\check{\mathbf{T}}_1^{-1}\big), \qquad \mathbf{e}_k = \Log\big(\mathbf{T}_k\mathbf{T}_{k-1}^{-1}\big) \ \ (k \gt 1), \tag{2.73} \]

the first weighted by the initial covariance \(\mathcal{K}(t_1,t_1)\) around a prior pose \(\check{\mathbf{T}}_1\), the others by \(T\boldsymbol{\mathcal{Q}}\). In words: neighbouring control poses should be close, and \(T\boldsymbol{\mathcal{Q}}\) says how close. It is the same chain as on Day 3 (Figure 2.6), with \(\Log(\mathbf{T}_k\mathbf{T}_{k-1}^{-1})\) in place of \(\mathbf{x}_k - \mathbf{x}_{k-1}\). Querying between control poses by GP interpolation gives equation (2.74), which is (2.62) again: here the linear interpolation is a consequence of choosing a random walk, not a separate choice. §2.2.4.2 · p. 73

Filling the gap: linearizing the prior factor, equation (2.75)

Write \(\mathbf{T}_{\mathrm{rel}} = \mathbf{T}_k^0\mathbf{T}_{k-1}^{0\,-1}\). Perturbing both poses on the left and using \((\Exp(\boldsymbol{\xi})\mathbf{T})^{-1} = \mathbf{T}^{-1}\Exp(-\boldsymbol{\xi})\):

\[ \mathbf{e}_k = \Log\big( \Exp(\boldsymbol{\xi}_k)\,\mathbf{T}_{\mathrm{rel}}\,\Exp(-\boldsymbol{\xi}_{k-1}) \big) . \]

Step 1. Move the right-hand exponential to the left with the adjoint identity \(\mathbf{T}\,\Exp(\boldsymbol{\xi}) = \Exp(\Ad(\mathbf{T})\,\boldsymbol{\xi})\,\mathbf{T}\) from Week 4 · Day 5: \(\mathbf{T}_{\mathrm{rel}}\Exp(-\boldsymbol{\xi}_{k-1}) = \Exp(-\Ad(\mathbf{T}_{\mathrm{rel}})\boldsymbol{\xi}_{k-1})\,\mathbf{T}_{\mathrm{rel}}\).

Step 2. Two small exponentials next to each other combine by adding their arguments, to first order: \(\mathbf{e}_k \approx \Log\big( \Exp(\boldsymbol{\xi}_k - \Ad(\mathbf{T}_{\mathrm{rel}})\boldsymbol{\xi}_{k-1})\,\mathbf{T}_{\mathrm{rel}} \big)\).

Step 3. A small left perturbation \(\boldsymbol{\epsilon}\) changes the Log by \(\mathbf{J}^{-1}\boldsymbol{\epsilon}\) (this is equation (2.34) on p. 62). When neighbouring control poses are close, \(\mathbf{J} \approx \mathbf{I}\), and

\[ \mathbf{e}_k \approx \Log(\mathbf{T}_{\mathrm{rel}}) + \boldsymbol{\xi}_k - \Ad(\mathbf{T}_{\mathrm{rel}})\,\boldsymbol{\xi}_{k-1} . \tag{2.75} \]

So the factor's Jacobian is \(\mathbf{I}\) with respect to \(\boldsymbol{\xi}_k\) and \(-\Ad(\mathbf{T}_{\mathrm{rel}})\) with respect to \(\boldsymbol{\xi}_{k-1}\). The printed (2.75) has no \(\mathbf{J}^{-1}\); reading it as the close-poses approximation is our interpretation.

If measurements fall between control poses, they are handled exactly as for the linear spline, with (2.67), because both methods interpolate linearly between \(\SE(d)\) control poses. The book's summary of the difference: the GP approach adds motion-prior factors that regularize the problem, and the spline approach does not. A footnote adds that such prior terms can also be introduced for splines. §2.2.4.2 · p. 74

Where to read more (§2.3)

The book points to Chirikjian for the theory of uncertainty on manifolds, including global treatments; to Boumal for optimization on manifolds; to Barfoot for estimation on Lie groups when the uncertainty is compact, and for the nonparametric continuous-time methods; and to the survey by Talbot et al. for continuous-time estimation, parametric and nonparametric. §2.3 · p. 74

Common mistakes

  • "The power in (2.62) is taken entry by entry." It is the group power: Log, scale by α, Exp.
  • "Interpolating position and angles separately is the same thing." On \(\SE(d)\) rotation and translation are coupled by Exp. The widget shows an arc where separate interpolation gives a straight line.
  • "The local variable is a new unknown." It is a device for writing the prior as a vector-space SDE. The estimation variables are still the control poses, plus derivatives if the chosen prior needs them.

Check yourself

Q1. Two planar rotations are by 30° and by 90°. What is the group interpolation between them at α = 0.25?

The relative rotation is 60°. A quarter of it is 15°, applied to the first: 30° + 15° = 45°.

Q2. A linear spline has control points p₁, p₂, p₃. At a time halfway between the second and the third, what are the cumulative weights on the steps (p₂ − p₁) and (p₃ − p₂)?

The first step is complete (weight 1) and the second is half done (weight 0.5): p = p₁ + (p₂ − p₁) + 0.5 (p₃ − p₂).

Q3. In equation (2.64), what is the perturbation of the interpolated pose when α = 1?

A(1) = J J⁻¹ = I, so the weight on control pose k − 1 is zero and the weight on control pose k is the identity. At α = 1 the interpolated pose is control pose k.

Q4. A random-walk prior on SE(d) has power spectral density 0.5 I and control poses every 0.1 s. What covariance weights the factor between consecutive control poses?

The local variable accumulates covariance T Q over one segment: 0.1 × 0.5 I = 0.05 I, as in equation (2.71).

Q5. According to the book, what is the main difference between the linear-spline and random-walk-GP formulations on SE(d)?

Both use the same linear interpolation and the same measurement linearization (2.67). The GP's motion-prior factors regularize the problem (p. 74).

Recap

  1. Cumulative form: \(\mathbf{p}(t) = \psi^c_1\mathbf{p}_1 + \sum_{k\ge2}\psi^c_k(\mathbf{p}_k - \mathbf{p}_{k-1})\) with \(\psi^c_k = \sum_{\ell\ge k}\psi_\ell\). Only differences of neighbours appear.
  2. On a group: \(\mathbf{T}(t) = \Exp\big(\alpha_k\Log(\mathbf{T}_k\mathbf{T}_{k-1}^{-1})\big)\mathbf{T}_{k-1}\), equations (2.61)–(2.62).
  3. Perturbations pass through the interpolation as \(\boldsymbol{\xi}(t) \approx (\mathbf{I} - \mathbf{A})\boldsymbol{\xi}_{k-1} + \mathbf{A}\boldsymbol{\xi}_k\), with \(\mathbf{A} \approx \alpha\mathbf{I}\) for nearby control poses.
  4. GP on a group: an SDE on the local variable \(\boldsymbol{\xi}_k(t) = \Log(\mathbf{T}(t)\mathbf{T}_k^{-1})\). The random walk gives factors \(\Log(\mathbf{T}_k\mathbf{T}_{k-1}^{-1})\) with covariance \(T\boldsymbol{\mathcal{Q}}\).
  5. Spline and GP share the interpolation. The GP adds the motion prior.

Sources

  1. SLAM Handbook, §2.2.4 "Spline and GPs on Lie Groups", pp. 69–74, equations (2.53)–(2.75), Figures 2.5–2.7; §2.3 "Further Readings & Recent Trends", p. 74.
  2. The derivation of the cumulative form, the checks on (2.65), and the steps to (2.75) are worked out here from the book's equations and the adjoint identity of §2.1.5.
  3. The formula \(\mathbf{A}(\alpha) = \alpha\,\mathbf{J}(\alpha\boldsymbol{\xi})\,\mathbf{J}(\boldsymbol{\xi})^{-1}\) and the first-order effect of a left perturbation on the Log follow Barfoot, State Estimation for Robotics, 2017.

Week 5 · Review

Week 5 review: continuous-time trajectories

After today you can build a spline or a Gaussian-process trajectory from first principles, work small examples of each by hand, and say what changes when the state is a pose on a Lie group.

About 60 min · No new pages

The week in one paragraph

A continuous-time trajectory replaces "one pose per measurement" with a function of time defined by a few variables, so measurement times, estimation variables, and query times can differ. The parametric version is a spline: a sum of basis functions with local support, so each measurement touches only a few coefficients. Regularizing the coefficients and changing variables turns the spline normal equations into a form where only the kernel matrix \(\mathbf{K}\) appears, and choosing \(\mathbf{K}\) directly gives the nonparametric version, a Gaussian process. If the kernel comes from a white-noise-driven differential equation with a Markovian state, \(\mathbf{K}^{-1}\) is block-tridiagonal and the prior is a chain of binary factors. Conditioning on measurements gives a mean and variance at any time, from the two bracketing states alone. On a Lie group both methods work on differences of neighbouring control poses, mapped to the Lie algebra with Log and back with Exp.

1. Formula sheet

What it isFormulaWhere
Spline trajectory\(\mathbf{p}(t) = \sum_{k=1}^{K}\boldsymbol{\Psi}_k(t)\,\mathbf{c}_k\)(2.36), p. 63 · Day 1
Uniform cubic B-spline weights, \(u \in [0,1)\)\(\tfrac16(1-u)^3,\ \tfrac16(3u^3-6u^2+4),\ \tfrac16(-3u^3+3u^2+3u+1),\ \tfrac16u^3\)Day 1 (not in the book)
Regularized spline normal equations\((\boldsymbol{\Psi}\T\mathbf{A}\T\mathbf{A}\boldsymbol{\Psi} + \mathbf{I})\,\boldsymbol{\delta}_c^* = \boldsymbol{\Psi}\T\mathbf{A}\T\mathbf{b}\)(2.44), p. 65 · Day 2
Kernel form, with \(\mathbf{K} = \boldsymbol{\Psi}\boldsymbol{\Psi}\T\) or \([\mathcal{K}(t_i,t_j)]_{ij}\)\((\mathbf{A}\T\mathbf{A} + \mathbf{K}^{-1})\,\boldsymbol{\delta}^* = \mathbf{A}\T\mathbf{b}\)(2.45), p. 66 · Day 2
SDE prior and transition function\(\dot{\mathbf{x}} = \mathbf{A}\mathbf{x} + \mathbf{L}\mathbf{w}\), \(\ \boldsymbol{\Phi}(t,s) = \exp(\mathbf{A}(t-s))\)(2.46)–(2.47), pp. 66–67 · Day 3
Constant-velocity prior, one axis\(\boldsymbol{\Phi} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & \Delta t \\ 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix}\), \(\ \mathbf{Q}_i = Q_c\begin{bmatrix} \Delta t^3/3 & \Delta t^2/2 \\ \Delta t^2/2 & \Delta t \end{bmatrix}\)(2.52), p. 68 · Day 3
Kernel matrix and its inverse\(\mathbf{K} = \boldsymbol{\Phi}\mathbf{Q}\boldsymbol{\Phi}\T\), \(\ \mathbf{K}^{-1} = \boldsymbol{\Phi}^{-\mathsf{T}}\mathbf{Q}^{-1}\boldsymbol{\Phi}^{-1}\) (block-tridiagonal)(2.49)–(2.51), pp. 67–68 · Day 3
GP regression at a query time τ\(\hat p = \mathbf{k}_\tau\T(\mathbf{K}+\sigma^2\mathbf{I})^{-1}\mathbf{z}\), \(\ \operatorname{var} = \mathcal{K}(\tau,\tau) - \mathbf{k}_\tau\T(\mathbf{K}+\sigma^2\mathbf{I})^{-1}\mathbf{k}_\tau\)Day 4 (the book states the idea, pp. 68–69)
Cumulative form of a spline\(\mathbf{p}(t) = \psi^c_1\mathbf{p}_1 + \sum_{k=2}^{K}\psi^c_k\,(\mathbf{p}_k - \mathbf{p}_{k-1})\), \(\ \psi^c_k = \sum_{\ell=k}^{K}\psi_\ell\)(2.54)–(2.55), p. 69 · Day 5
Pose interpolation, and the random-walk prior factor\(\mathbf{T}(t) = \Exp\big(\alpha_k\Log(\mathbf{T}_k\mathbf{T}_{k-1}^{-1})\big)\mathbf{T}_{k-1}\), \(\ \mathbf{e}_k = \Log(\mathbf{T}_k\mathbf{T}_{k-1}^{-1})\) with covariance \(T\boldsymbol{\mathcal{Q}}\)(2.61), p. 71; (2.73), p. 73 · Day 5

2. Mixed quiz

Check yourself

Q1. A trajectory is a quadratic (degree 2) B-spline. How many coefficients does one measurement at one time stamp involve?

A B-spline of degree d has d + 1 basis functions nonzero at any time: 3 for a quadratic.

Q2. The four active coefficients of a cubic B-spline are all equal to 6. What is the value of the curve at u = 0.37?

The weights are nonnegative and sum to 1 for every u, so a weighted average of four sixes is 6.

Q3. Two measurement times, two basis functions, and Ψ has rows (1, 0) and (1, 1). What is K = ΨΨᵀ?

K₁₁ = 1·1 + 0·0 = 1, K₁₂ = 1·1 + 0·1 = 1, K₂₂ = 1·1 + 1·1 = 2. (ΨᵀΨ, the other order, would give rows (2, 1) and (1, 1).)

Q4. What does the kernel trick replace?

Equation (2.45) needs the basis functions only through K = ΨΨᵀ, so K can be filled in from a kernel function directly.

Q5. Constant-velocity prior on one axis with Q_c = 3 and a step of 1 s. What is the position variance added over the step (the top-left entry of the step covariance)?

Q_c Δt³/3 = 3 · 1/3 = 1. (The velocity variance is Q_c Δt = 3 and the cross term is 1.5.)

Q6. For an SDE prior, K is full but the (1, 4) block of K⁻¹ is zero. What does the zero mean?

Zeros in an information matrix mean no direct factor. The states are still correlated, which is why K has no zeros.

Q7. Random-walk prior with p(0) = 0 and Q_c = 1 (kernel min(t, t′)). One measurement z = 4 at t = 1 with noise variance 1. What is the posterior variance at the query time τ = 3?

k = min(3, 1) = 1 and K + σ² = 2, so the variance is 3 − 1·(1/2)·1 = 2.5. Equivalently: 0.5 at t = 1, plus 1 per second for the 2 s of extrapolation.

Q8. In the linearized random-walk prior factor (2.75), what is the Jacobian of the error with respect to the perturbation of the earlier pose, ξ of k − 1?

e ≈ Log(T_rel) + ξ_k − Ad(T_rel) ξ_{k−1}. The adjoint appears because the earlier pose's perturbation has to be moved through the relative pose.

3. Pen-and-paper problems

  1. A uniform cubic B-spline has knots every \(T = 0.5\) s. On one knot interval the four active coefficients are 2, 4, 4, 0 (oldest first). Find the position and the velocity at \(u = 0.25\).

    Solution

    Weights at \(u = 0.25\): \(w_0 = 0.75^3/6 = 0.0703\), \(w_1 = (3\cdot0.015625 - 6\cdot0.0625 + 4)/6 = 0.6120\), \(w_2 = (-0.046875 + 0.1875 + 0.75 + 1)/6 = 0.3151\), \(w_3 = 0.015625/6 = 0.0026\). They sum to 1.

    Position: \(2\cdot0.0703 + 4\cdot0.6120 + 4\cdot0.3151 + 0 = 3.849\).

    Derivatives of the weights with respect to \(u\): \(-\tfrac12(0.75)^2 = -0.28125\), \(\tfrac12(3\cdot0.0625 - 1) = -0.40625\), \(\tfrac12(-0.1875 + 0.5 + 1) = 0.65625\), \(\tfrac12\cdot0.0625 = 0.03125\). They sum to 0. So \(dp/du = 2\cdot(-0.28125) + 4\cdot(-0.40625) + 4\cdot0.65625 = 0.4375\), and since \(u = t/T\), the velocity is \(0.4375/0.5 = 0.875\) units per second.

  2. A scalar random-walk prior with initial variance 1 and \(Q_c = 1\) is evaluated at \(t = 0\) and \(t = 1\), so \(\mathbf{K} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ 1 & 2 \end{bmatrix}\). The position is measured at both times with noise variance 1: \(\mathbf{z} = (0, 3)\). Find the estimate (a) from the modified normal equations (2.45) and (b) from the GP regression formula, and check that they agree.

    Solution

    (a) With \(\mathbf{A} = \mathbf{I}\) and \(\mathbf{b} = \mathbf{z}\): \(\mathbf{K}^{-1} = \begin{bmatrix} 2 & -1 \\ -1 & 1 \end{bmatrix}\), so \(\mathbf{I} + \mathbf{K}^{-1} = \begin{bmatrix} 3 & -1 \\ -1 & 2 \end{bmatrix}\) with determinant 5 and inverse \(\tfrac15\begin{bmatrix} 2 & 1 \\ 1 & 3 \end{bmatrix}\). Then \(\hat{\mathbf{p}} = \tfrac15(2\cdot0 + 1\cdot3,\ 1\cdot0 + 3\cdot3) = (0.6, 1.8)\).

    (b) \(\mathbf{K} + \mathbf{I} = \begin{bmatrix} 2 & 1 \\ 1 & 3 \end{bmatrix}\), inverse \(\tfrac15\begin{bmatrix} 3 & -1 \\ -1 & 2 \end{bmatrix}\), so \((\mathbf{K}+\mathbf{I})^{-1}\mathbf{z} = \tfrac15(-3, 6)\) and \(\hat{\mathbf{p}} = \mathbf{K}\cdot\tfrac15(-3,6) = \tfrac15(3, 9) = (0.6, 1.8)\). The same.

    Note how the prior shares information: the estimate at \(t = 0\) is pulled up from 0 to 0.6 by the measurement at \(t = 1\).

  3. Constant-velocity prior on one axis, state \((p, v)\), two times one second apart, \(Q_c = 1\), initial covariance \(\mathbf{I}\). Write the prior as two factors and assemble the \(4\times4\) inverse kernel matrix \(\mathbf{K}^{-1}\). If a third time were added, which block of the new \(6\times6\) matrix would be zero?

    Solution

    Factors: \(\norm{\mathbf{x}_1}^2_{\mathbf{I}} + \norm{\mathbf{x}_2 - \boldsymbol{\Phi}\mathbf{x}_1}^2_{\mathbf{Q}_2}\) with \(\boldsymbol{\Phi} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix}\) and \(\mathbf{Q}_2 = \begin{bmatrix} 1/3 & 1/2 \\ 1/2 & 1 \end{bmatrix}\). Its determinant is \(1/12\), so \(\mathbf{Q}_2^{-1} = \begin{bmatrix} 12 & -6 \\ -6 & 4 \end{bmatrix}\).

    Expanding the second factor, the blocks of \(\mathbf{K}^{-1}\) are: bottom-right \(\mathbf{Q}_2^{-1}\); top-right \(-\boldsymbol{\Phi}\T\mathbf{Q}_2^{-1} = \begin{bmatrix} -12 & 6 \\ -6 & 2 \end{bmatrix}\); top-left \(\mathbf{I} + \boldsymbol{\Phi}\T\mathbf{Q}_2^{-1}\boldsymbol{\Phi} = \begin{bmatrix} 13 & 6 \\ 6 & 5 \end{bmatrix}\). So

    \[ \mathbf{K}^{-1} = \begin{bmatrix} 13 & 6 & -12 & 6 \\ 6 & 5 & -6 & 2 \\ -12 & -6 & 12 & -6 \\ 6 & 2 & -6 & 4 \end{bmatrix} . \]

    With a third time the only new factor links states 2 and 3, so the block between states 1 and 3 (and its transpose) is zero. You can check the first two rows and the zero block in the Day 3 widget with "constant velocity" and three times.

  4. On \(\SE(2)\), \(\Exp\big((\rho_1,\rho_2,\theta)\big)\) has rotation by \(\theta\) and translation \(\mathbf{V}(\theta)\,(\rho_1,\rho_2)\) with \(\mathbf{V}(\theta) = \tfrac{1}{\theta}\begin{bmatrix} \sin\theta & -(1-\cos\theta) \\ 1-\cos\theta & \sin\theta \end{bmatrix}\). Let \(\mathbf{T}_{k-1} = \mathbf{I}\) and let \(\mathbf{T}_k\) have rotation 90° and translation \((1, 1)\). (a) Find \(\boldsymbol{\xi} = \Log(\mathbf{T}_k\mathbf{T}_{k-1}^{-1})\). (b) Find the interpolated pose at \(\alpha = 0.5\) and its distance from the midpoint of the straight line. (c) A random-walk prior has \(T\boldsymbol{\mathcal{Q}} = \diag(0.1, 0.1, 0.05)\). What does this factor contribute to the cost, \(\norm{\mathbf{e}_k}^2_{T\boldsymbol{\mathcal{Q}}}\)?

    Solution

    (a) \(\theta = \pi/2\), so \(\mathbf{V} = \tfrac{2}{\pi}\begin{bmatrix} 1 & -1 \\ 1 & 1 \end{bmatrix}\) and \(\mathbf{V}^{-1} = \tfrac{\pi}{4}\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ -1 & 1 \end{bmatrix}\). Then \((\rho_1,\rho_2) = \mathbf{V}^{-1}(1,1) = (\pi/2, 0)\) and \(\boldsymbol{\xi} = (\pi/2,\ 0,\ \pi/2) \approx (1.571, 0, 1.571)\). This is "drive forward while turning at the same rate": a quarter circle of radius 1.

    (b) \(\alpha\boldsymbol{\xi} = (\pi/4, 0, \pi/4)\). The rotation is 45°. The translation is \(\mathbf{V}(\pi/4)\,(\pi/4, 0) = (\sin 45^\circ,\ 1 - \cos 45^\circ) = (0.707, 0.293)\). That point lies on the circle of radius 1 centred at \((0,1)\), as it should. The straight-line midpoint is \((0.5, 0.5)\), at distance \(\sqrt{0.207^2 + 0.207^2} = 0.293\).

    (c) \(\mathbf{e}_k = \boldsymbol{\xi}\), so the cost is \((\pi/2)^2/0.1 + 0 + (\pi/2)^2/0.05 = 24.7 + 49.3 = 74.0\). A prior this tight strongly resists a quarter turn in one segment; measurements would have to pay for it.

You are ready for next week if you can

  • Explain what separating measurement times, estimation variables, and query times buys you, with one sensor example.
  • Evaluate a cubic B-spline and its velocity from four coefficients, and say which coefficients a measurement touches.
  • Go from the regularized spline normal equations (2.44) to the kernel form (2.45) without looking.
  • Write the constant-velocity SDE, its transition matrix, and explain why \(\mathbf{K}^{-1}\) is block-tridiagonal.
  • Compute a GP posterior mean and variance for two measurements by hand, and interpolate between two states.
  • Write the interpolation between two poses on \(\SE(d)\) and the random-walk prior factor between them.

Sources

  1. SLAM Handbook, Chapter 2, §2.2 "Continuous-Time Trajectories" and §2.3, pp. 62–74.
  2. Extra material as cited on Days 1–5: de Boor, A Practical Guide to Splines, 1978; Rasmussen and Williams, Gaussian Processes for Machine Learning, 2006; Barfoot, State Estimation for Robotics, 2017.
  3. The \(\SE(2)\) exponential map in problem 4 follows Solà, Deray, Atchuthan, A micro Lie theory for state estimation in robotics, 2018.

Week 6 · Day 1

Where outliers come from, and why least squares cannot cope

After today you can name the sources of outliers in SLAM, compute how far one bad measurement moves a least-squares estimate, and say what a breakdown point is.

About 60 min · Read §3.1, pp. 75–78 (4 pages) · Needs Week 2 Day 2

Read first: chapter opening and §3.1, pp. 75–78

While you read, look for:

  • The two examples of wrong data association on p. 76: a landmark given the wrong identity, and a loop closure between two places that only look alike.
  • The causes of outliers on p. 76 that are not data-association mistakes.
  • The sentence on p. 77 that says why squaring the residuals is the root of the trouble.
  • Figure 3.1 on p. 77: compare the top row (ground truth) with the bottom row (least squares with outliers).

Today's big idea

Least squares is the right estimator when every error is Gaussian. Real front-ends sometimes match the wrong things, and those measurements are wrong by meters, not by noise. Because the cost squares each residual, a few such outliers outvote all the good measurements and the estimate can be arbitrarily wrong.

1. What least squares silently assumes

In Week 2 · Day 2 you derived the back-end problem from a noise model. If measurement \(\mathbf{z}_i\) equals its prediction \(h_i(\mathbf{x}_i)\) plus zero-mean Gaussian noise with covariance \(\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_i\), then the maximum a posteriori estimate is the nonlinear least-squares problem

\[ \mathbf{x}_{\text{MAP}} = \argmin_{\mathbf{x}} \sum_i \norm{\mathbf{z}_i - h_i(\mathbf{x}_i)}^2_{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_i}, \tag{3.1} \]

where \(\mathbf{x}_i\) is the part of the state that measurement \(i\) involves and \(\norm{\mathbf{e}}^2_{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}} = \mathbf{e}\T\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{-1}\mathbf{e}\). Ch. 3 opening · p. 75 The chapter writes the size of one term as a scalar residual \(r_i(\mathbf{x}) = \norm{\mathbf{z}_i - h_i(\mathbf{x}_i)}_{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_i}\), so the cost is \(\sum_i r_i(\mathbf{x})^2\). A residual is measured in standard deviations: \(r_i = 3\) means "this measurement disagrees with the estimate by 3σ". §3.1.2 · p. 77

The book calls the Gaussian light-tailed: it gives almost no probability to large errors. §3.1.2 · p. 77

Filling the gap: how light is "light-tailed"?

For a Gaussian error \(e\) with standard deviation \(\sigma\), the probability of landing further than \(k\sigma\) from the mean is \(2\,(1 - \Phi(k))\), where \(\Phi\) is the standard normal cumulative distribution. From a table of \(\Phi\):

Error larger thanProbability under the Gaussian modelIn words
1σ0.32one measurement in three
3σ0.0027one in 370
5σ5.7 × 10⁻⁷one in 1.7 million
10σ1.5 × 10⁻²³never, for practical purposes

So a model with only Gaussian noise says that a 10σ error cannot happen. When one does happen, the estimator "believes" the measurement anyway, and the only way to make a 10σ error plausible is to move the estimate a long way toward it.

2. Where the bad measurements come from

The back-end never sees raw data. It sees what the front-end extracted (see Week 1 · Day 1), and the extraction involves a decision: which landmark is this, which earlier pose saw the same place? Deciding what a measurement refers to is the data association problem. A wrong decision gives a measurement that is precise but about the wrong thing. §3.1.1 · p. 76

CauseWhat goes wrongKind
Wrong landmark identityA detection is attributed to landmark \(\ell_j\) but really shows a different landmark, so \(\mathbf{z}_{ij}\) is far from \(h(\mathbf{p}_i, \ell_j)\).Data association
False loop closurePlace recognition links poses \(\mathbf{p}_i\) and \(\mathbf{p}_j\) that did not observe the same scene.Data association
Moving objectThe landmark is identified correctly, but the model assumes it is static and it has moved.Violated assumption
Sensor faultA faulty wheel encoder, dust on the lens.Failure or degradation

False loop closures often have a specific cause, perceptual aliasing: two different places look the same to the sensor, like two classrooms in one building or identical office cubicles. §3.1.1 · p. 76

A false loop closure is the worst kind of outlier. It is not a noisy version of the truth. It is a confident statement, with a small covariance, that two distant poses coincide.

3. Why squaring makes it worse

Evaluate the cost near the true state. Good measurements have residuals around 1 (they are in units of σ), so each contributes about 1 to \(\sum_i r_i^2\). An outlier that is off by 20σ contributes \(20^2 = 400\): as much as 400 good measurements. The optimizer reduces the cost fastest by shrinking that one term, and it does so by bending the estimate away from what the good measurements say. §3.1.2 · p. 77

Try it: the blue points lie near the line \(y = 0.5x + 1\). Drag the pink point around, then change the number of good points.

Notice: with 12 good points, one bad point at (8.5, 1.2) changes the fit from y = 0.52x + 0.82 to y = 0.36x + 1.35, and at the true line it alone carries 98% of the cost. Drag it further and the line follows without limit. With 40 good points the pull is weaker, but it never reaches zero.

Filling the gap: one outlier moves the estimate by error ÷ N

The simplest least-squares problem is estimating one number \(x\) from \(N\) direct measurements \(z_1, \dots, z_N\) with equal noise. The cost is \(\sum_i (z_i - x)^2\). Set its derivative to zero:

\[ \frac{d}{dx}\sum_{i=1}^{N} (z_i - x)^2 = -2\sum_{i=1}^{N}(z_i - x) = 0 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \hat{x} = \frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N} z_i . \]

The least-squares estimate is the mean. Now corrupt one measurement by adding an error \(E\) to it. The sum grows by \(E\), so

\[ \hat{x}_{\text{corrupted}} = \hat{x} + \frac{E}{N}. \]

Two things follow. The shift is proportional to \(E\), so there is no bound on the damage: make \(E\) large enough and the estimate is anywhere you like. And the shift shrinks only like \(1/N\), so adding good data dilutes an outlier but never removes it. Example: nine measurements equal to 2.0 and one equal to 52.0 give \(\hat{x} = (9 \times 2 + 52)/10 = 7.0\), far from every single measurement.

In a line fit, or in SLAM, the same thing happens with one extra twist that the widget shows: a bad point far from the middle of the data has a long lever arm, so it changes the slope as well as the offset.

4. Breakdown point: a number for "how fragile"

Robust statistics measures fragility with the breakdown point of an estimator: the smallest fraction of the measurements that, if replaced by arbitrary values, can move the estimate arbitrarily far. This idea is not in today's pages, but it is the standard yardstick and you will meet it in the papers the chapter cites.

  • The mean (least squares) has breakdown point \(1/N\), which tends to 0: one bad measurement out of any number is enough, as Section 3 showed.
  • The median has breakdown point 50%. To drag the middle value arbitrarily far you must corrupt half of the data.

Example: the data \(\{0.8,\ 0.9,\ 1.0,\ 1.1,\ 1.2\}\) have mean 1.0 and median 1.0. Replace 1.2 by 100. The mean becomes \((0.8 + 0.9 + 1.0 + 1.1 + 100)/5 = 20.76\). The median, the middle of \(\{0.8, 0.9, 1.0, 1.1, 100\}\), is still 1.0.

No estimator can have a breakdown point above 50% without extra information: if most of the data are wrong and they agree with each other, nothing in the data says which group to trust. Remember this limit on Days 3 and 5, where methods tolerate far more than 50% outliers. They can because they are told something extra, for example that the odometry is trustworthy.

In plain words

Least squares runs a vote where each measurement's voice gets louder the more it disagrees with everyone else. One measurement that is wildly wrong shouts down a hundred that are quietly right.

5. What it does to a map, and the plan for the week

Figure 3.1 runs plain least squares on three standard problems. §3.1.2 · pp. 77–78

DatasetTypeSizeOutliers
M3500Simulated pose graph, grid-like3500 2D poses, 8953 measurements15% random outliers added to the loop closures
SubTReal pose graph from a tunnel682 3D poses, 3278 measurementsAlready in the data
Victoria ParkReal landmark SLAM7120 2D poses and landmarks, 17728 measurements15% random outliers added to the landmark measurements

All three estimates are unusable. In SubT the failure has a recognizable shape: two parallel corridors that look alike produce many false loop closures, and the back-end obeys them by folding the two corridors into one. §3.1.2 · p. 78 That is perceptual aliasing written into the map.

The chapter attacks the problem at both ends of the pipeline:

WhereIdeaMethodsDay
Front-end (§3.2)Find and delete gross outliers before they reach the optimizerRANSAC, pairwise consistency maximization2, 3
Back-end (§3.3)Change the cost so that surviving outliers have little pullRobust losses, IRLS, graduated non-convexity4, 5

Common mistakes

  • "An outlier is a very noisy measurement." Usually it is a precise measurement of the wrong thing. Inflating every covariance to cover it would throw away the accuracy of the good data.
  • "With enough good data the outliers average out." The shift is \(E/N\). It is small only if \(E\) is bounded, and a false loop closure can be wrong by the size of the building.
  • "Outliers are random, so they point in random directions and cancel." Perceptual aliasing produces many outliers that agree with each other, as in the SubT corridors.

Check yourself

Q1. Nineteen range measurements read 4.0 m and one reads 44.0 m. What is the least-squares estimate of the range?

The estimate is the mean: the outlier's error is 40 m and N = 20, so the shift is 40/20 = 2 m, giving 6.0 m. Check: (19 × 4 + 44)/20 = 120/20 = 6.

Q2. Evaluated at the true state, 200 good measurements each have residual 1 (in units of σ) and one outlier has residual 30. What fraction of the cost Σr² comes from the outlier?

The outlier contributes 30² = 900 and the good measurements 200 × 1 = 200, so the share is 900/1100 ≈ 0.82. One measurement in 201 owns most of the cost.

Q3. A camera tracks a parked car as a landmark. The car is identified correctly in every frame, then drives off while still in view. Why do its measurements become outliers?

The association is right, so this is not a data-association error. The measurement model assumes a static landmark, and a violated assumption produces large residuals just as a wrong match does (p. 76).

Q4. You have 11 measurements of one quantity. What is the smallest number of them an adversary must corrupt to move the median arbitrarily far?

The median of 11 values is the 6th smallest. With 5 corrupted values, the 6th smallest is still one of the 6 good values, or lies between good values. With 6 corrupted values sent to +∞, the 6th smallest is corrupted. The mean would need only 1.

Recap

  1. Least squares is MAP estimation under Gaussian noise, and a Gaussian says large errors essentially never happen.
  2. Outliers come mostly from wrong data association (wrong landmark, false loop closure, perceptual aliasing), and also from violated assumptions and sensor faults.
  3. Squaring gives an outlier with residual \(k\) the weight of \(k^2\) good measurements.
  4. One corrupted measurement shifts a mean by \(E/N\): unbounded in \(E\). The breakdown point of least squares is zero.
  5. The chapter's answer has two layers: reject outliers in the front-end, and make the back-end cost robust to the ones that remain.

Sources

  1. SLAM Handbook, Chapter 3 opening and §3.1 "What Causes Outliers and Why Are They a Problem?", pp. 75–78, equation (3.1), Figure 3.1.
  2. Rousseeuw and Leroy, Robust Regression and Outlier Detection, 1987 (breakdown point; mean versus median).
  3. The Gaussian tail probabilities are standard normal table values. The \(E/N\) argument is the derivative of a sum of squares, as in Week 1 Day 4.

Week 6 · Day 2

RANSAC: finding the largest set of measurements that agree

After today you can state the consensus maximization problem, run RANSAC by hand on a small example, and compute how many iterations it needs for a given inlier fraction and minimal-set size.

About 60 min · Read §3.2 opening and §3.2.1, pp. 78–81 (4 pages) · Needs Week 6 Day 1

Read first: §3.2 opening and §3.2.1, pp. 78–81

While you read, look for:

  • The two "key insights" on pp. 79–80: inliers obey a geometric constraint, and the inliers are the largest set that obeys it for one common \(\mathbf{x}\).
  • Problem (3.4) on p. 80, and the remark that it involves only a small part of the SLAM state.
  • The three steps of RANSAC on pp. 80–81, and the words minimal set and minimal solver.
  • The two numerical examples on p. 81: \(n = 5,\ \omega = 0.7\) and \(n = 10,\ \omega = 0.1\).

Today's big idea

Inliers are measurements of one physical situation, so they all fit one model. Outliers have no reason to agree with each other. RANSAC guesses the model from the smallest possible random sample, counts how many measurements agree with the guess, and keeps the guess with the most support.

1. Inliers obey geometry

A SLAM front-end first produces a set of candidate measurements that may contain many outliers, then filters it. §3.2 · p. 78 The book's running case (Example 3.1) is feature-based visual SLAM. The front-end matches 2D feature points between the image at time \(k-1\) and the image at time \(k\). Each matched pair is a 2D-2D correspondence, and some matches are wrong. §3.2.1 · p. 79

What makes filtering possible is that correct matches are not free to be anything. If the scene is static, the way pixels move between two images is fixed by the camera's motion. For calibrated cameras, corresponding points \(\mathbf{z}_i(k-1)\) and \(\mathbf{z}_i(k)\) satisfy the epipolar constraint

\[ \mathbf{z}_i(k-1)\T \left( [\mathbf{t}^{k-1}_{k}]_\times\, \mathbf{R}^{k-1}_{k} \right) \mathbf{z}_i(k) = 0, \tag{3.2} \]

where \(\mathbf{R}^{k-1}_k\) and \(\mathbf{t}^{k-1}_k\) are the unknown rotation and translation of the camera between the two times. §3.2.1 · p. 79 Here \([\mathbf{t}]_\times\) is the 3×3 skew-symmetric matrix that performs a cross product: \([\mathbf{t}]_\times \mathbf{v} = \mathbf{t} \times \mathbf{v}\).

Filling the gap: where the epipolar constraint comes from

The book states (3.2) without proof. It takes four lines. For a calibrated camera, \(\mathbf{z}\) is the direction of the viewing ray: the pixel written as a 3-vector \([u, v, 1]\T\) in normalized image coordinates. The 3D point lies somewhere along that ray, at an unknown depth \(d \gt 0\).

Step 1. Write the point's coordinates in both camera frames: \(\mathbf{p}^{k-1} = d_1\,\mathbf{z}_i(k-1)\) and \(\mathbf{p}^{k} = d_2\,\mathbf{z}_i(k)\). The relative pose maps one to the other, \(\mathbf{p}^{k-1} = \mathbf{R}\,\mathbf{p}^{k} + \mathbf{t}\) (dropping the indices on \(\mathbf{R}^{k-1}_k, \mathbf{t}^{k-1}_k\)). So

\[ d_1\,\mathbf{z}_i(k-1) = d_2\,\mathbf{R}\,\mathbf{z}_i(k) + \mathbf{t}. \]

Step 2. Take the cross product of both sides with \(\mathbf{t}\). Since \(\mathbf{t}\times\mathbf{t} = \mathbf{0}\), the last term disappears:

\[ d_1\,[\mathbf{t}]_\times\,\mathbf{z}_i(k-1) = d_2\,[\mathbf{t}]_\times\,\mathbf{R}\,\mathbf{z}_i(k). \]

Step 3. Take the dot product of both sides with \(\mathbf{z}_i(k-1)\). The left side is \(d_1\,\mathbf{z}_i(k-1)\T(\mathbf{t}\times\mathbf{z}_i(k-1))\), which is zero because a cross product is perpendicular to both of its factors.

\[ 0 = d_2\;\mathbf{z}_i(k-1)\T\,[\mathbf{t}]_\times\,\mathbf{R}\;\mathbf{z}_i(k). \]

Step 4. Divide by \(d_2 \gt 0\). That is (3.2). The unknown depths have dropped out, which is the point: the constraint links two pixels and the camera motion, and nothing else.

Why five correspondences. Equation (3.2) is unchanged if \(\mathbf{t}\) is multiplied by any non-zero number, so only the direction of \(\mathbf{t}\) can be recovered: 2 unknowns. The rotation has 3. That is 5 unknowns, and each correspondence gives one scalar equation, so 5 correspondences are the minimum. This is why footnote 4 on p. 80 says the minimal set has size 5 and the pose is found "up to scale".

With noisy pixels the left side of (3.2) is small but not zero, so in practice one asks for \(\left|\mathbf{z}_i(k-1)\T([\mathbf{t}]_\times\mathbf{R})\,\mathbf{z}_i(k)\right| \le \gamma\). In general, each kind of measurement comes with a constraint of the form

\[ C(\mathbf{z}_i, \mathbf{x}) \le \gamma, \tag{3.3} \]

where \(\mathbf{x}\) is the unknown the constraint depends on (here the relative pose) and \(\gamma\) is a threshold tuned to the noise level. §3.2.1 · p. 79

2. Consensus maximization

One correspondence alone can satisfy (3.3) for some \(\mathbf{x}\). The test only bites when many correspondences must satisfy it for the same \(\mathbf{x}\). Let \(\mathsf{M}\) be the set of candidate (putative) correspondences. The inlier set is estimated as the largest subset that one \(\mathbf{x}\) can explain:

\[ \mathsf{S}^\star_{\text{CM}} = \argmax_{\mathbf{x},\ \mathsf{S}\subset\mathsf{M}} |\mathsf{S}| \quad \text{s.t.}\quad C(\mathbf{z}_i, \mathbf{x}) \le \gamma \quad \forall i \in \mathsf{S}. \tag{3.4} \]

This is consensus maximization. \(|\mathsf{S}|\) is the number of elements of \(\mathsf{S}\). §3.2.1 · p. 80 Two properties matter:

  • It is small. \(\mathbf{x}\) is one relative pose between two frames, not the whole trajectory and map.
  • It is still hard. \(\mathsf{M}\) has \(2^{|\mathsf{M}|}\) subsets, so trying them all is hopeless: 100 correspondences give about \(1.3\times10^{30}\) subsets. Front-ends need an answer in milliseconds, so they use a fast heuristic.

Today's widget uses the simplest instance. A measurement is a point \((x_i, y_i)\), the unknown is a line \(y = ax + b\), and the constraint is \(C = |y_i - a x_i - b| \le \gamma\): the point lies within a vertical distance \(\gamma\) of the line.

3. The RANSAC loop

RANdom SAmple Consensus (RANSAC) rests on one assumption: \(\mathbf{x}\) is low-dimensional and can be computed from a handful of measurements. The smallest number of measurements that determines \(\mathbf{x}\) is the size \(n\) of the minimal set, and a fast routine that computes \(\mathbf{x}\) from exactly \(n\) measurements is a minimal solver. §3.2.1 · p. 80

ProblemUnknownMinimal set nMinimal solver
Line through points (the widget)Slope and intercept2The line through two points
Motion from 3D-3D correspondencesRelative pose3Horn's method (footnote 7, p. 82)
Motion from 2D-2D correspondences, calibratedRelative pose up to scale5Nistér's 5-point method (p. 80)
best = empty set
repeat:
    1. sample n correspondences at random          (a minimal set)
    2. x_hat = minimal_solver(sample)
    3. S = { i in M : C(z_i, x_hat) <= gamma }     (who agrees with x_hat?)
       if |S| > |best|:  best = S
until |best| is large enough, or the iteration limit is reached
return best, and the x_hat that produced it

The set kept at the end is the consensus set. §3.2.1 · pp. 80–81 The logic: if all \(n\) sampled measurements happen to be inliers, \(\hat{\mathbf{x}}\) is close to the truth and all the other inliers agree with it. If the sample contains an outlier, \(\hat{\mathbf{x}}\) is wrong and few measurements agree. So the size of the consensus set tells a good sample from a bad one, without knowing which measurements are inliers.

Try it: press Step a few times, then Play. Hollow points are the true outliers, which the algorithm does not know.

Notice: at the default settings the first sample includes an outlier and only 9 points agree with its line. The second sample is two inliers and its consensus set is all 24 inliers and nothing else. A least-squares fit to that set gives y = 0.51x + 0.94, while least squares on everything gives the dashed line y = 0.12x + 2.81. Now set Outliers to 70% and press Play: the largest agreeing group is the second "wall", and RANSAC returns it (20 points, all outliers).

The last experiment is a warning. RANSAC finds the largest group that agrees, and that is the inliers only if the outliers do not form a bigger group of their own.

4. How many iterations?

Let \(\omega\) be the probability that a randomly drawn measurement is an inlier, which is the inlier fraction if sampling is uniform. The book states that the expected number of iterations to draw an all-inlier sample is \(1/\omega^n\). §3.2.1 · p. 81

Filling the gap: the iteration count, derived

One sample. Treat the \(n\) draws as independent (accurate when the set is much larger than \(n\)). The sample is all-inlier with probability \(q = \omega^n\).

Expected number of samples. Each iteration succeeds with probability \(q\), independently. Let \(E\) be the expected number of iterations up to and including the first success. Either the first one succeeds (probability \(q\), cost 1), or it fails and you are back at the start having spent one iteration:

\[ E = q \cdot 1 + (1-q)(1 + E) \quad\Longrightarrow\quad E = \frac{1}{q} = \frac{1}{\omega^n}. \]

For \(n = 5,\ \omega = 0.7\): \(\omega^n = 0.7^5 = 0.168\) and \(E = 5.95\), the book's "less than 10". For \(n = 10,\ \omega = 0.1\): \(E = 10^{10}\).

Iterations for a given confidence. An average is not a guarantee. The probability that \(k\) samples in a row are all contaminated is \((1-\omega^n)^k\). To make that at most \(1 - p\), so that at least one clean sample was drawn with probability \(p\), solve for \(k\):

\[ (1-\omega^n)^k \le 1 - p \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad k \ge \frac{\log(1-p)}{\log(1-\omega^n)}. \]

The inequality flips because \(\log(1-\omega^n)\) is negative. This formula is not in the book. It is the standard stopping rule from the original RANSAC paper. For \(n = 5,\ \omega = 0.7,\ p = 0.99\): \(k \ge \log(0.01)/\log(0.832) = 25.03\), so 26 iterations.

Minimal set nω = 0.9ω = 0.7ω = 0.5ω = 0.3
21.2 expected, 3 for 99%2.0, 74.0, 1711.1, 49
31.4, 42.9, 118.0, 3537.0, 169
51.7, 65.9, 2632.0, 146411.5, 1893
82.3, 917.3, 78256.0, 117715 242, 70 188

Each cell gives the expected number of iterations \(1/\omega^n\), then the number needed for 99% confidence. Read across a row and the count explodes as inliers get rarer. Read down a column and it explodes as the minimal set grows. The exponent \(n\) is why so much research goes into solvers with the smallest possible sample.

5. When RANSAC is the right tool, and when it is not

RANSAC is the default for outlier rejection in landmark-based front-ends because minimal solvers are fast (hundreds of iterations in a few milliseconds), and because it returns an estimate \(\hat{\mathbf{x}}\), for example the camera motion, that serves as an initial guess for the back-end. §3.2.1 · p. 81

It stops being practical in two situations. §3.2.1–3.2.2 · p. 81

  • Few inliers. The book's rule of thumb is that RANSAC works well below about 70% outliers. Strong perceptual aliasing can push the outlier rate far higher.
  • Large minimal sets. A pose graph with \(N\) poses needs at least \(N-1\) relative-pose measurements to determine every pose (a spanning tree), and \(N\) is in the thousands. There is no small sample to draw.

Stopping RANSAC early in those cases does not give a slightly worse answer. It gives a wrong \(\hat{\mathbf{x}}\) and a wrong set of correspondences. Tomorrow's method avoids sampling altogether.

Common mistakes

  • "RANSAC solves consensus maximization." It is a heuristic for (3.4). It returns the best set among the samples it happened to try, with no guarantee that it is the largest one.
  • "A larger sample gives a better model, so sample more than the minimum." Every extra point multiplies the chance of a clean sample by \(\omega\). Accuracy comes afterwards, from refitting to the whole consensus set.
  • "The threshold γ is a detail." Too small, and noisy inliers are rejected so that good samples score badly. Too large, and outliers near the model are accepted. Move γ in the widget to 0.10 and to 1.50 and watch the consensus set.

Check yourself

Q1. Half of the points are inliers and you fit a line (n = 2). What is the expected number of RANSAC iterations until a sample contains only inliers?

One sample is clean with probability 0.5² = 0.25, and the expected number of trials until the first success is 1/0.25 = 4.

Q2. Same setting (ω = 0.5, n = 2). How many iterations make the probability of at least one all-inlier sample 99%?

k ≥ log(0.01)/log(1 − 0.25) = (−4.605)/(−0.2877) = 16.01, so 17. The expected count of 4 is far from a guarantee: after 4 iterations the failure probability is still 0.75⁴ = 0.32.

Q3. Why can the relative pose of two calibrated cameras be estimated from 5 correspondences, and not fewer?

Equation (3.2) is one scalar equation per correspondence. It is unchanged when t is rescaled, so the length of t cannot be found, leaving 3 + 2 = 5 unknowns.

Q4. In step 3 of RANSAC, a sample that contains one outlier usually produces a small consensus set. Why?

The solver cannot know a sample is contaminated. It returns a model that fits the n sampled points exactly and is far from the truth, so most inliers fail C(z, x̂) ≤ γ. The count is what reveals the bad sample.

Recap

  1. Inliers satisfy a geometric constraint \(C(\mathbf{z}_i, \mathbf{x}) \le \gamma\) for one common \(\mathbf{x}\). For two calibrated views it is the epipolar constraint.
  2. Consensus maximization (3.4) asks for the largest subset that one \(\mathbf{x}\) explains. It is combinatorial.
  3. RANSAC samples a minimal set, solves for \(\hat{\mathbf{x}}\), counts who agrees, and keeps the best.
  4. Expected iterations: \(1/\omega^n\). For confidence \(p\): \(k \ge \log(1-p)/\log(1-\omega^n)\).
  5. It fails when inliers are rare or the minimal set is large, as in pose-graph optimization.

Sources

  1. SLAM Handbook, §3.2 opening and §3.2.1 "RANdom SAmple Consensus (RANSAC)", pp. 78–81, equations (3.2)–(3.4), Example 3.1.
  2. Fischler and Bolles, Random Sample Consensus: A Paradigm for Model Fitting with Applications to Image Analysis and Automated Cartography, 1981 (the algorithm and the iteration count for a given confidence).
  3. Hartley and Zisserman, Multiple View Geometry in Computer Vision, 2004 (derivation of the epipolar constraint; RANSAC sample counts).

Week 6 · Day 3

Pairwise consistency maximization and the maximum clique

After today you can write a consistency function for point matches and for loop closures, build the consistency graph, and find the inlier set as its maximum clique.

About 60 min · Read §3.2.2, pp. 81–85 (5 pages) · Needs Week 6 Day 2

Read first: §3.2.2, pp. 81–85

While you read, look for:

  • The two reasons on p. 81 why RANSAC does not fit pose-graph problems.
  • The two consistency functions: (3.5) for 3D-3D correspondences on p. 82 and (3.6) for loop closures on p. 83. Neither contains the state \(\mathbf{x}\).
  • The definition of a clique and the four-step summary on p. 84.
  • The trade-offs between PCM and RANSAC on p. 85, including footnote 11.

Today's big idea

Instead of asking "does this measurement agree with a model?", ask "do these two measurements agree with each other?". That question needs no model and no solver. Draw a graph with an edge for every pair that agrees. The inliers all agree with one another, so they form a group in which every pair is connected, a clique, and the largest clique is taken as the inlier set.

1. Why a second front-end method

RANSAC needs a small minimal set and a fair share of inliers. Loop closures in a pose graph offer neither: the smallest sample that determines \(N\) poses has \(N-1\) measurements, and perceptual aliasing can make most candidate loop closures wrong. §3.2.2 · p. 81 Pairwise Consistency Maximization (PCM) does not sample. It looks for the largest set of measurements that are consistent with one another, and the book reports it sorting through sets with upwards of 90% outliers. §3.2.2 · p. 82

On Day 1 you saw that no estimator survives more than 50% arbitrary outliers. PCM does not contradict that. It relies on an assumption: the wrong measurements are wrong in unrelated ways and so rarely agree with each other, while the right ones always do.

2. Consistency functions

A consistency function \(F\) takes two measurements and returns a number that is small when both could be correct at the same time:

\[ F(\mathbf{z}_i, \mathbf{z}_j) \le \gamma, \tag{3.7} \]

with \(\gamma\) set by the noise level. It is state independent: \(\mathbf{x}\) does not appear, so the test is evaluated directly on the data. §3.2.2 · p. 83 You must design \(F\) for each kind of measurement. The book gives two.

3D-3D correspondences (Example 3.2). An RGB-D camera gives 3D points. Correspondence \(i\) pairs a point \(\mathbf{z}_i(k-1)\) seen at time \(k-1\) with a point \(\mathbf{z}_i(k)\) seen at time \(k\). If \(i\) and \(j\) are both correct matches of static points, the distance between the two points is the same in both frames:

\[ \Big|\ \norm{\mathbf{z}_i(k-1) - \mathbf{z}_j(k-1)} - \norm{\mathbf{z}_i(k) - \mathbf{z}_j(k)}\ \Big| \le \gamma. \tag{3.5} \]

§3.2.2 · p. 82

Filling the gap: why the distance cannot change

Both frames see the same static points, from two camera poses related by an unknown rotation \(\mathbf{R}\) and translation \(\mathbf{t}\). Every correct correspondence obeys \(\mathbf{z}(k-1) = \mathbf{R}\,\mathbf{z}(k) + \mathbf{t}\) with the same \(\mathbf{R}, \mathbf{t}\). Subtract the equation for \(j\) from the one for \(i\). The translation cancels:

\[ \mathbf{z}_i(k-1) - \mathbf{z}_j(k-1) = \mathbf{R}\,\big(\mathbf{z}_i(k) - \mathbf{z}_j(k)\big). \]

A rotation does not change lengths, because \(\mathbf{R}\T\mathbf{R} = \mathbf{I}\): for any vector \(\mathbf{v}\), \(\norm{\mathbf{R}\mathbf{v}}^2 = \mathbf{v}\T\mathbf{R}\T\mathbf{R}\mathbf{v} = \mathbf{v}\T\mathbf{v} = \norm{\mathbf{v}}^2\). So the two distances in (3.5) are equal, up to noise, whatever the camera motion was. The unknown motion has been eliminated, which is why no solver is needed.

Numbers (in 2D for brevity). At \(k-1\): \(\mathbf{z}_1 = (0,0)\), \(\mathbf{z}_2 = (3,4)\), \(\mathbf{z}_3 = (6,8)\). At \(k\): \(\mathbf{z}_1 = (1,1)\), \(\mathbf{z}_2 = (-3,4)\), \(\mathbf{z}_3 = (2,2)\).

  • Pair (1,2): distance 5 at \(k-1\), and \(\sqrt{(-4)^2 + 3^2} = 5\) at \(k\). Difference 0: consistent.
  • Pair (1,3): distance 10 at \(k-1\), and \(\sqrt{1^2 + 1^2} = 1.41\) at \(k\). Difference 8.59: inconsistent for any sensible \(\gamma\).

The test on pair (1,3) says that 1 and 3 cannot both be right. It does not say which one is wrong. That is decided by looking at all pairs together.

Loop closures (Example 3.3). Assume the odometry is trustworthy and only loop closures may be wrong. Take two loop closures, \(\mathbf{T}^a_b\) between poses \(a\) and \(b\) and \(\mathbf{T}^c_d\) between poses \(c\) and \(d\). Together with the odometry they form a cycle, and relative poses composed around a cycle must return to the start:

\[ \operatorname{dist}\!\big(\mathbf{T}^a_b \cdot \bar{\mathbf{T}}^b_c \cdot \mathbf{T}^c_d \cdot \bar{\mathbf{T}}^d_a,\ \mathbf{I}\big) \le \gamma, \tag{3.6} \]

where \(\bar{\mathbf{T}}^b_c\) and \(\bar{\mathbf{T}}^d_a\) are the odometry measurements chained from \(b\) to \(c\) and from \(d\) to \(a\), and dist measures how far a pose is from the identity \(\mathbf{I}\). §3.2.2 · p. 83

A one-dimensional example. In a straight corridor a pose is a position, a relative pose is a signed displacement, composing is adding, and the identity is 0. Suppose the measurements are \(T^a_b = +0.1\) m, \(\bar{T}^b_c = +3.0\) m, \(T^c_d = -0.2\) m, \(\bar{T}^d_a = -3.1\) m. Around the cycle: \(0.1 + 3.0 - 0.2 - 3.1 = -0.2\) m. With \(\gamma = 0.5\) m the pair is consistent. Now replace the second loop closure with an aliased one that claims \(T^c_d = +4.0\) m: the sum is \(4.0\) m, and the pair is inconsistent. In practice \(\gamma\) grows with the length of the loop, because a longer odometry chain accumulates more noise (footnote 9, p. 83).

3. From pairs to a graph, from a graph to a clique

PCM asks for the largest set of measurements in which every pair is consistent:

\[ \mathsf{S}^\star_{\text{PCM}} = \argmax_{\mathsf{S}\subset\mathsf{M}} |\mathsf{S}| \quad\text{s.t.}\quad F(\mathbf{z}_i, \mathbf{z}_j) \le \gamma \quad \forall i, j \in \mathsf{S}. \tag{3.8} \]

§3.2.2 · p. 83 Compare with consensus maximization (3.4): \(\mathbf{x}\) is gone, and all the constraints can be computed once, in advance.

Build the consistency graph: one node per putative measurement, and an edge between \(i\) and \(j\) whenever \(F(\mathbf{z}_i, \mathbf{z}_j) \le \gamma\). A clique is a set of nodes in which every two are joined by an edge. The maximum clique is the largest one. Problem (3.8) is exactly the maximum clique problem on the consistency graph. §3.2.2 · pp. 83–84

By hand. Six measurements A–F have these consistent pairs: A–B, A–C, A–D, B–C, B–D, C–D, D–E, D–F, E–F. That is 9 edges out of \(6\times5/2 = 15\) possible pairs. The set {A, B, C, D} is a clique: all six of its pairs are in the list. {D, E, F} is a clique of size 3. Is there a clique of size 5? Every member of one would have at least 4 neighbours, and only D has that many (A, B, C, E, F). So there is none, and the maximum clique is {A, B, C, D}, and PCM keeps those four and rejects E and F. Note that D is consistent with E and F as well. One edge to an outlier does no harm. What counts is membership of the large mutually consistent group.

Try it: ten point matches between two frames. The widget applies (3.5) to all 45 pairs and searches every subset for the maximum clique.

Notice: at the default γ = 0.15, 22 of the 45 pairs are consistent: the 15 pairs among the six true inliers (1, 2, 3, 4, 9, 10) and 7 chance pairs. The chance edges do not form a large clique, so the maximum clique is exactly the six inliers. Lower γ to 0.05 and two inliers drop out because noise breaks some of their edges. Raise γ to 0.50 and outlier 7 joins the clique. Back at γ = 0.15, set 7 outliers: the three inliers are still found, with 70% outliers.

4. What it costs

The four steps of PCM are: choose \(F\); evaluate it on every pair and build the graph; find the maximum clique; return its measurements. §3.2.2 · p. 84

Filling the gap: counting the work

Building the graph is cheap. \(N\) measurements have \(N(N-1)/2\) pairs: 45 for \(N = 10\), 499 500 for \(N = 1000\). Each test is a few arithmetic operations.

Finding the clique is the hard part. The widget checks all \(2^{10} = 1024\) subsets. That brute force doubles with every added measurement: \(N = 60\) already gives about \(10^{18}\) subsets. The maximum clique problem is NP-hard, and it is also hard to approximate. §3.2.2 · p. 84 In practice two families of algorithms are used:

  • Exact algorithms, usually branch and bound. They explore subsets but discard whole branches that cannot beat the best clique found so far. For example, a node with only 3 neighbours cannot belong to a clique larger than 4, so it is dropped once a clique of size 4 is known. Worst-case time is still exponential.
  • Heuristic algorithms, which are faster and may return a clique that is large but not the largest.

The density of the graph decides which is practical. Recent exact solvers find maximum cliques quickly in large sparse graphs. Dense graphs, where many pairs are consistent, are slow for exact solvers. §3.2.2 · pp. 84–85

5. PCM versus RANSAC

QuestionRANSACPCM
What is tested?Each measurement against a model \(\hat{\mathbf{x}}\) from a minimal solverEach pair of measurements against each other
Needs a minimal solver?Yes, with a small minimal setNo
Needs a consistency function?NoYes, and for some problems (2D-2D correspondences) none is easy to design
Outlier ratesEffective below about 70%Has handled upwards of 90%
Hard stepNumber of samples grows like \(1/\omega^n\)Maximum clique is NP-hard, slow on dense graphs
Also returnsAn estimate \(\hat{\mathbf{x}}\)Only the set of measurements

§3.2.2 · p. 85

Both tests are necessary but not sufficient for a measurement to be an inlier (footnote 11, p. 85). A pairwise test can be too permissive. Here is a concrete case for (3.5): a mirror image. If the points at time \(k\) were a reflection of the points at \(k-1\), every pairwise distance would be preserved and every pair would pass, yet no rotation and translation maps one set to the other. A minimal solver would notice. Pairwise distances cannot. The book makes the general point that (3.5) may accept some outliers that RANSAC would reject. §3.2.2 · p. 85

The quality of PCM rests on the choice of \(F\). The useless function \(F \equiv 0\) makes every pair consistent, the graph complete, and the maximum clique the whole set: nothing is rejected. A function that only inliers can pass rejects every outlier. §3.2.2 · p. 85 Real functions sit in between, and whatever passes goes on to a back-end that must cope with the rest. That is tomorrow.

Common mistakes

  • "A measurement with an edge to an inlier is an inlier." Edges to single inliers happen by chance, and more often as γ grows. Only membership of the maximum clique counts.
  • "An inconsistent pair tells you which measurement is wrong." It says the two cannot both be right. The graph as a whole decides.
  • "PCM beats the 50% limit, so it is strictly stronger than RANSAC." It works when outliers are mutually inconsistent. Outliers that agree with each other, such as many false loop closures between the same two look-alike corridors, can form the largest clique.

Check yourself

Q1. A place-recognition module proposes 20 loop closures. How many pairwise consistency tests does PCM evaluate?

Every unordered pair once: 20 × 19 / 2 = 190.

Q2. In a corridor (1-D), two loop closures measure +0.3 m (a to b) and −0.1 m (c to d). Odometry gives +5.0 m from b to c and −5.4 m from d to a. With γ = 0.25 m, are the two loop closures consistent?

0.3 + 5.0 − 0.1 − 5.4 = −0.2 m. Its distance from the identity (zero) is 0.2 m, within γ. The test uses only measurements, never the estimated poses.

Q3. A consistency graph on nodes 1–6 has edges 1–2, 1–3, 2–3, 3–4, 3–5, 3–6, 4–5, 4–6, 5–6. How large is the maximum clique?

{3, 4, 5, 6} is a clique: all six pairs 3–4, 3–5, 3–6, 4–5, 4–6, 5–6 are edges. A clique of 5 would need two more nodes joined to all of them, but nodes 1 and 2 are not joined to 4, 5, or 6.

Q4. Why can PCM be applied to loop closures in a pose graph with thousands of poses, where RANSAC cannot?

The consistency function (3.6) is state independent and pairwise. RANSAC would have to sample a spanning tree of N − 1 measurements. Maximum clique is NP-hard, and γ is still needed.

Recap

  1. A consistency function \(F(\mathbf{z}_i, \mathbf{z}_j) \le \gamma\) tests whether two measurements can both be correct, without the state.
  2. For 3D-3D matches: rigid motion preserves the distance between two points (3.5). For loop closures: poses composed around a cycle give the identity (3.6).
  3. PCM (3.8) = the maximum clique of the consistency graph.
  4. Building the graph costs \(N(N-1)/2\) tests. Maximum clique is NP-hard, and solved exactly by branch and bound or approximately by heuristics.
  5. Pairwise consistency is necessary, not sufficient, so some outliers reach the back-end.

Sources

  1. SLAM Handbook, §3.2.2 "Graph-theoretic Outlier Rejection and Pairwise Consistency Maximization", pp. 81–85, equations (3.5)–(3.8), Examples 3.2 and 3.3, Figures 3.3 and 3.4.
  2. The proof that rotations preserve length, the mirror-image example, and the subset counts are standard linear algebra and counting, added here.

Week 6 · Day 4

M-estimation: robust losses, IRLS, and Black-Rangarajan duality

After today you can compare robust losses by their influence functions, derive the IRLS weight and run IRLS by hand, and rewrite a robust loss as weighted least squares plus an outlier process.

About 60 min · Read §3.3 opening to §3.3.2, pp. 85–92 (8 pages, 2 of them figures) · Needs Week 6 Day 1 and Week 2 Day 4

Read first: §3.3 opening, §3.3.1, §3.3.2, pp. 85–92

While you read, look for:

  • Equation (3.9) on p. 86, and the requirement placed on \(\rho\) just below it.
  • The six loss shapes in Figure 3.5 (p. 87). Which ones go flat?
  • The weight rule (3.12) on p. 89 and the two gradients it comes from.
  • How (3.14) on p. 90 turns a \(\min\) of two numbers into a minimization over a weight, and the outlier process (3.18) on p. 92.

Today's big idea

Replace the square in the cost by a function that grows more slowly for large residuals, so an outlier's pull is bounded or vanishes. The new problem is no longer least squares, but it can be solved as a sequence of weighted least-squares problems: weight each measurement by how believable its current residual is, solve, and repeat.

1. M-estimation and the influence function

Front-end rejection misses some outliers, so the back-end must tolerate them. §3.3 · p. 85 M-estimation ("maximum-likelihood-type estimation") keeps the residuals \(r_i(\mathbf{x})\) of Day 1 and changes only what is done to them:

\[ \mathbf{x}_{\text{MAP}} = \argmin_{\mathbf{x}} \sum_i r_i(\mathbf{x})^2 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \mathbf{x}_{\text{MEST}} = \argmin_{\mathbf{x}} \sum_i \rho\big(r_i(\mathbf{x})\big). \tag{3.9} \]

The robust loss \(\rho\) must be non-negative and grow less than quadratically for large residuals. §3.3 · p. 86 To see why that is the right requirement, take the gradient of the cost \(f(\mathbf{x}) = \sum_i \rho(r_i(\mathbf{x}))\) with the chain rule:

\[ \frac{\partial f}{\partial \mathbf{x}} = \sum_i \frac{\partial \rho(r_i)}{\partial r_i}\cdot\frac{\partial r_i(\mathbf{x})}{\partial \mathbf{x}}. \tag{3.10} \]

The second factor says in which direction measurement \(i\) wants to move the estimate. The first factor says how hard it pulls. That factor is the influence function \(\psi(r) := \partial\rho(r)/\partial r\). §3.3 · p. 86 For the quadratic loss \(\psi(r) = 2r\): the pull grows without bound, which is Day 1's problem restated. A robust loss has \(\psi(r) \ll 2r\) for large \(r\), and ideally \(\psi(r)\to 0\).

2. The menu of losses

Figure 3.5 shows the common choices as curves. §3.3 · pp. 86–87 Here they are as formulas, each with one parameter \(\beta\) that marks where inliers end. The book gives the formulas for the truncated quadratic (3.13) and Geman-McClure (3.17). Huber and Tukey are the standard definitions, scaled like the book's so that every loss equals \(r^2\) for small \(r\). The last column, \(w = \psi/(2r)\), is explained in Section 3.

Lossρ(r)Influence ψ(r)Weight w(r)
Quadratic\(r^2\)\(2r\)\(1\)
Huber\(r^2\) if \(|r|\le\beta\), else \(2\beta|r|-\beta^2\)\(2r\) if \(|r|\le\beta\), else \(\pm 2\beta\)\(1\) if \(|r|\le\beta\), else \(\beta/|r|\)
Geman-McClure\(\dfrac{\beta^2 r^2}{\beta^2+r^2}\)\(\dfrac{2\beta^4 r}{(\beta^2+r^2)^2}\)\(\left(\dfrac{\beta^2}{\beta^2+r^2}\right)^{2}\)
Tukey's biweight\(\tfrac{\beta^2}{3}\big[1-(1-r^2/\beta^2)^3\big]\) if \(|r|\le\beta\), else \(\tfrac{\beta^2}{3}\)\(2r(1-r^2/\beta^2)^2\) if \(|r|\le\beta\), else \(0\)\((1-r^2/\beta^2)^2\) if \(|r|\le\beta\), else \(0\)
Truncated quadratic\(\min\{r^2,\beta^2\}\)\(2r\) if \(|r|\lt\beta\), else \(0\)\(1\) if \(|r|\lt\beta\), else \(0\)

Try it: pick a loss and move the residual slider. Watch the middle panel.

Notice: for Huber with β = 1, a residual of 2.5 costs 4.00 where the quadratic charges 6.25, and its influence is capped at 2.00 where the quadratic's is 5.00. Capped is not zero: an outlier keeps pulling. Switch to Geman-McClure and the influence rises, peaks, and falls back toward zero. For the truncated quadratic and Tukey it is exactly zero beyond β.

How to choose: §3.3 · pp. 86–87

  • Huber is convex, so the optimization behaves well. It is common in bundle adjustment. The price is the non-zero influence you just saw.
  • Losses that go flat (Geman-McClure, Tukey, truncated quadratic) give distant outliers little or no influence, but they are non-convex, so the optimizer can stop in a bad local minimum.
  • A hard cut-off (truncated quadratic) suits problems where the largest error an inlier can have is known.
  • The maximum consensus loss, 0 for small residuals and 1 for large ones, simply counts outliers. Minimizing it is consensus maximization (3.4) from Day 2. Its influence is zero everywhere, so gradients are useless and it is optimized by sampling: that is RANSAC.

Going deeper (optional): a robust loss is still MAP

Switching to \(\rho\) does not abandon probability. A loss is the negative log of a noise density, and losses that grow slowly correspond to heavy-tailed densities. §3.3 · pp. 88–89 Take the density proportional to \(\max\{e^{-r^2},\ e^{-\beta^2}\}\): Gaussian near zero, a constant floor (a uniform density over the sensor's range) far away. Its negative log is \(\min\{r^2, \beta^2\}\), the truncated quadratic. The floor says "with some small probability this measurement is unrelated to the state".

3. Iteratively reweighted least squares

Problem (3.9) has two costs. The fast solvers of Week 2 · Day 4, Gauss-Newton and Levenberg-Marquardt, need a sum of squares. And non-convex costs make any local solver depend on its starting point. §3.3.1 · p. 89 Plain gradient descent does work on some problems (Figure 3.6) but takes thousands of iterations. §3.3 · p. 88

Iteratively reweighted least squares (IRLS) gets the solvers back. At each iteration it solves a weighted least-squares problem whose weights come from the previous estimate:

\[ \mathbf{x}^{(t+1)} = \argmin_{\mathbf{x}} \sum_i w_i\big(\mathbf{x}^{(t)}\big)\, r_i^2(\mathbf{x}), \qquad w_i\big(\mathbf{x}^{(t)}\big) = \frac{\psi\big(r_i(\mathbf{x}^{(t)})\big)}{2\,r_i(\mathbf{x}^{(t)})}. \tag{3.11, 3.12} \]

§3.3.1 · p. 89

Filling the gap: why this weight, and why the iteration lands in the right place

Freeze the weights at \(w_i\) and differentiate the weighted cost \(\sum_i w_i\,r_i^2(\mathbf{x})\):

\[ \frac{\partial}{\partial\mathbf{x}}\sum_i w_i\,r_i^2(\mathbf{x}) = \sum_i 2\,w_i\,r_i(\mathbf{x})\,\frac{\partial r_i(\mathbf{x})}{\partial\mathbf{x}}. \]

Compare with (3.10), \(\sum_i \psi(r_i)\,\partial r_i/\partial\mathbf{x}\). The two sums agree term by term if \(2\,w_i\,r_i = \psi(r_i)\), that is \(w_i = \psi(r_i)/(2r_i)\). That is (3.12).

Now suppose the iteration has converged: \(\mathbf{x}^{(t+1)} = \mathbf{x}^{(t)} = \mathbf{x}^\star\). Then \(\mathbf{x}^\star\) minimizes the weighted problem built with its own weights, so the weighted gradient is zero at \(\mathbf{x}^\star\). By the matching, the gradient (3.10) of the robust cost is zero there too. A fixed point of IRLS is a stationary point of the M-estimation problem. For a non-convex \(\rho\) it may be a poor local minimum, which is tomorrow's topic.

By hand. Estimate one number \(x\) from \(z = \{1, 2, 3, 14\}\), with \(r_i = z_i - x\) and the Huber loss, \(\beta = 2\). A weighted least-squares fit of a constant is the weighted mean \(x = \sum w_i z_i / \sum w_i\).

IterationResiduals at the current xWeights (1 if |r| ≤ 2, else 2/|r|)New x
start: all weights 11, 1, 1, 15.000 (the mean)
1−4, −3, −2, 90.500, 0.667, 1, 0.2227.944 / 2.389 = 3.326
2−2.326, −1.326, −0.326, 10.6740.860, 1, 1, 0.1872.784
3−1.784, −0.784, 0.216, 11.2161, 1, 1, 0.1782.673
limit1, 1, 1, 0.1768/3 = 2.667

The good measurements alone average 2. Least squares says 5. Huber settles at 2.667: much better, and still pulled, because the outlier keeps a weight of 0.176. You can check the limit directly from \(\sum_i\psi(r_i) = 0\): with the first three residuals in the quadratic zone and the fourth beyond \(\beta\), \(2(1-x)+2(2-x)+2(3-x)+2\beta = 0\) gives \(x = 8/3\).

In SLAM the "solve" inside each iteration is one Gauss-Newton or Levenberg-Marquardt step on the weighted problem. §3.3.1 · p. 89 Try it on the line fit of Day 2: 40% of the points are outliers, most of them on a second line.

Notice: with Huber (β = 0.5), IRLS moves from the least-squares line y = 0.12x + 2.81 to y = 0.37x + 1.44 in about 28 steps and stays there, still dragged by the outliers. Geman-McClure reaches y = 0.51x + 0.94, next to the true line, in about 12 steps. The truncated quadratic stops after 2 steps at y = 0.09x + 2.86: it kept the points that happened to lie near the bad starting line and gave all the others weight zero for good.

The book's experiments agree in outline (Figure 3.7): IRLS converges in tens of iterations and is much faster than gradient descent (under 1.5 s against about 5 s for the Huber loss on M3500), at a slight loss of accuracy, and with non-convex losses it can end in a wrong solution. §3.3.1 · pp. 89–91

4. Black-Rangarajan duality: weights as variables

Rule (3.12) was obtained by matching gradients, and it is undefined where \(\rho\) has a corner, such as \(|r| = \beta\) for the truncated quadratic. Black-Rangarajan (B-R) duality gives the same algorithm a cleaner footing by making the weights unknowns of the optimization. §3.3.2 · p. 90

Start with the truncated quadratic, \(\rho(r_i) = \min\{r_i^2, \beta_i^2\}\) (3.13). The book rewrites it as

\[ \rho\big(r_i(\mathbf{x})\big) = \min_{w_i\in[0,1]}\ w_i\,r_i^2(\mathbf{x}) + (1-w_i)\,\beta_i^2. \tag{3.14} \]

Filling the gap: checking (3.14), and the Geman-McClure case in full

Truncated quadratic. The expression in (3.14) is linear in \(w_i\): it equals \(\beta_i^2 + w_i\,(r_i^2 - \beta_i^2)\). A linear function on \([0,1]\) is smallest at an end. If \(r_i^2 \lt \beta_i^2\) the slope is negative, so \(w_i = 1\) and the value is \(r_i^2\). If \(r_i^2 \gt \beta_i^2\) the slope is positive, so \(w_i = 0\) and the value is \(\beta_i^2\). Either way the result is \(\min\{r_i^2, \beta_i^2\}\). Example: \(r = 3,\ \beta = 2\) gives \(4 + 5w\), minimized at \(w = 0\) with value 4.

Geman-McClure. Example 3.5 claims that \(\rho(r) = \beta^2 r^2/(\beta^2+r^2)\) (3.17) equals \(\min_{w\in[0,1]}\ w\,r^2 + \Phi_\rho(w)\) with \(\Phi_\rho(w) = \beta^2(\sqrt{w}-1)^2\) (3.18), and leaves the algebra out. Differentiate \(g(w) = w\,r^2 + \beta^2(\sqrt{w}-1)^2\):

\[ g'(w) = r^2 + \beta^2\cdot 2(\sqrt{w}-1)\cdot\frac{1}{2\sqrt{w}} = r^2 + \beta^2 - \frac{\beta^2}{\sqrt{w}}. \]

Setting \(g'(w) = 0\) gives \(\sqrt{w} = \beta^2/(r^2+\beta^2)\), so

\[ w^\star = \left(\frac{\beta^2}{r^2+\beta^2}\right)^{2}, \tag{3.20} \]

which lies in \([0,1]\), and is a minimum because \(g''(w) = \tfrac12\beta^2 w^{-3/2} \gt 0\). Substitute back, using \(\sqrt{w^\star} - 1 = -r^2/(r^2+\beta^2)\):

\[ g(w^\star) = \frac{\beta^4 r^2}{(r^2+\beta^2)^2} + \frac{\beta^2 r^4}{(r^2+\beta^2)^2} = \frac{\beta^2 r^2\,(\beta^2 + r^2)}{(r^2+\beta^2)^2} = \frac{\beta^2 r^2}{\beta^2+r^2}. \]

That is (3.17). Notice also that \(w^\star\) is the Geman-McClure weight in Section 2's table: B-R duality and rule (3.12) give the same number.

Substituting (3.14) for every measurement turns M-estimation into a joint problem over the state and one weight per measurement:

\[ \min_{\mathbf{x},\ w_i\in[0,1]}\ \sum_{i} \Big[\, w_i\,r_i^2(\mathbf{x}) + (1-w_i)\,\beta_i^2 \,\Big]. \tag{3.15} \]

The first term is weighted least squares. The second charges \(\beta_i^2\) for every measurement that is switched off, so the optimizer cannot simply discard everything. At the solution, \(w_i = 1\) marks an inlier and \(w_i = 0\) an outlier. §3.3.2 · p. 90

Theorem 3.4 extends this to a family of losses. Write \(\phi(z) := \rho(\sqrt{z})\), the loss as a function of the squared residual. If \(\phi'(z)\to1\) as \(z\to0\), \(\phi'(z)\to0\) as \(z\to\infty\), and \(\phi''(z)\lt0\), then M-estimation (3.9) is equivalent to

\[ \min_{\mathbf{x},\ w_i\in[0,1]}\ \sum_{i=1}^{N} \Big[\, w_i\,r_i^2(\mathbf{x}) + \Phi_\rho(w_i) \,\Big], \tag{3.16} \]

where the penalty \(\Phi_\rho\), called the outlier process, depends on the loss. §3.3.2 · pp. 90–92 For Geman-McClure the conditions are easy to check: \(\phi(z) = \beta^2 z/(\beta^2+z)\), \(\phi'(z) = \beta^4/(\beta^2+z)^2\), which is 1 at \(z = 0\) and tends to 0, and \(\phi''(z) = -2\beta^4/(\beta^2+z)^3 \lt 0\). Tomorrow you solve (3.16) by alternating between \(\mathbf{x}\) and the weights.

Common mistakes

  • "A robust loss removes outliers." It reduces their influence. With Huber the influence never reaches zero, as the worked example shows.
  • "The IRLS weights are tuning parameters." They are computed from the residuals by \(w = \psi(r)/(2r)\). The only parameter is \(\beta\).
  • "IRLS finds the minimum of the robust cost." It finds a stationary point that depends on where it starts. The widget's truncated-quadratic run stops at a cost of 8.04, while the line next to the true one costs about 4.3 under the same loss.

Check yourself

Q1. With the Huber loss and β = 1, what IRLS weight does a measurement with residual r = 4 receive?

Beyond β the weight is β/|r| = 1/4. Check with w = ψ/(2r): ψ = 2β = 2, and 2/(2 × 4) = 0.25.

Q2. For the Geman-McClure loss with β = 2, what are the loss and the weight at r = 2?

ρ = β²r²/(β² + r²) = 16/8 = 2, half of the quadratic loss r² = 4. The weight is (β²/(β² + r²))² = (4/8)² = 0.25.
