Q3. One IRLS iteration with the truncated quadratic loss, β = 3.5, on the scalar data z = {0, 1, 2, 9}, starting from the mean x = 3. What is the new estimate?

Residuals z − x are −3, −2, −1, 6. Those with |r| below 3.5 get weight 1 and the last gets 0. The weighted mean is (0 + 1 + 2)/3 = 1.0.

Q4. Which loss leaves an outlier with a pull that does not shrink as its residual grows?

Huber's influence is constant at ±2β beyond β. Geman-McClure's decays toward zero, and the other two are exactly zero beyond β. Huber accepts this in exchange for convexity.

Q5. In problem (3.15), why does the optimizer not set every weight to zero and make the first term vanish?

The outlier process (1 − w)β² charges β² for discarding a measurement. Discarding pays only when the residual squared exceeds β².

Recap

  1. M-estimation replaces \(r^2\) by a robust loss \(\rho(r)\) that grows sub-quadratically (3.9).
  2. The influence function \(\psi = \rho'\) is how hard a measurement pulls. Huber caps it. Geman-McClure, Tukey, and the truncated quadratic send it to zero and pay with non-convexity.
  3. IRLS solves weighted least squares repeatedly with \(w_i = \psi(r_i)/(2r_i)\) (3.12). Its fixed points are stationary points of the robust cost.
  4. B-R duality writes \(\rho(r) = \min_{w\in[0,1]} w\,r^2 + \Phi_\rho(w)\). For the truncated quadratic \(\Phi_\rho = (1-w)\beta^2\). For Geman-McClure \(\Phi_\rho = \beta^2(\sqrt{w}-1)^2\).

Sources

  1. SLAM Handbook, §3.3 opening, §3.3.1 "Iteratively Reweighted Least Squares", §3.3.2 "Black-Rangarajan Duality", pp. 85–92, equations (3.9)–(3.20), Theorem 3.4, Example 3.5, Figures 3.5–3.7.
  2. Huber, Robust Statistics, 1981 (M-estimators, the Huber loss, influence functions, Tukey's biweight).
  3. Barfoot, State Estimation for Robotics, 2017 (robust cost functions and IRLS in the estimation setting).
  4. Black and Rangarajan, On the Unification of Line Processes, Outlier Rejection, and Robust Statistics with Applications in Early Vision, 1996 (the duality).

Week 6 · Day 5

Alternating minimization and graduated non-convexity

After today you can derive IRLS as alternating minimization, compute the GNC weights for the truncated quadratic and Geman-McClure losses, and explain when graduated non-convexity helps and when it fails.

About 60 min · Read §3.3.3–3.4, pp. 92–100 (9 pages, 2 of them figures) · Needs Week 6 Day 4

Read first: §3.3.3, §3.3.4, §3.4, pp. 92–100

While you read, look for:

  • The two steps (3.22) and (3.23) on p. 93. Which one is a SLAM solve, and which one is \(N\) one-line formulas?
  • The two surrogate losses (3.24) and (3.25) on p. 94, and in Figure 3.8 which way \(\mu\) moves for each.
  • The third step that GNC adds on p. 95.
  • The experiment on pp. 96–98 where GNC fails, and what rescues it.

Today's big idea

IRLS on a non-convex loss slides into whichever valley its starting point belongs to. Graduated non-convexity (GNC) first replaces the loss by a nearly convex version with a single broad valley, solves that, and then reshapes the loss step by step back into the real one, following the minimum as it moves. Each step is still an ordinary weighted least-squares solve.

1. IRLS is alternating minimization

Yesterday ended with the joint problem (3.16): minimize \(\sum_i [\,w_i\,r_i^2(\mathbf{x}) + \Phi_\rho(w_i)\,]\) over the state \(\mathbf{x}\) and the weights \(w_i\in[0,1]\). Optimizing both at once is hard. Optimizing either one with the other held fixed is easy. §3.3.3 · p. 92

  • Variable update. With the weights fixed, \(\Phi_\rho(w_i)\) is a constant and what remains is weighted least squares: \[ \mathbf{x}^{(t)} \in \argmin_{\mathbf{x}} \sum_i w_i^{(t)}\,r_i^2(\mathbf{x}). \tag{3.22} \]
  • Weight update. With \(\mathbf{x}\) fixed, each residual is a known number and the sum splits into \(N\) separate scalar problems: \[ w_i^{(t+1)} \in \argmin_{w_i\in[0,1]}\ \Phi_\rho(w_i) + w_i\,r_i^2(\mathbf{x}^{(t)}), \qquad i = 1,\dots,N. \tag{3.23} \]

§3.3.3 · p. 93 You solved both scalar problems yesterday:

LossOutlier process Φ(w)Weight update
Truncated quadratic\((1-w)\,\beta^2\)\(w = 1\) if \(r^2\lt\beta^2\), \(w = 0\) if \(r^2\gt\beta^2\) (anything in \([0,1]\) at equality)
Geman-McClure\(\beta^2(\sqrt{w}-1)^2\)\(w = \big(\beta^2/(r^2+\beta^2)\big)^2\)

Alternating the two steps is alternating minimization, and it is IRLS. With the Geman-McClure loss it is also the dynamic covariance scaling algorithm from the robust SLAM literature. §3.3.3 · p. 93 The book adds, without proof, that the weight from (3.23) is the same as yesterday's rule (3.12).

Filling the gap: why the two weight rules agree

Write \(z = r^2\) and \(\phi(z) = \rho(\sqrt{z})\), as in Theorem 3.4. B-R duality says \(\phi(z) = \min_{w}\,[\,w z + \Phi_\rho(w)\,]\). Let \(w^\star(z)\) be the minimizer. If it lies inside \([0,1]\), the derivative with respect to \(w\) vanishes there: \(z + \Phi_\rho'(w^\star) = 0\). Now differentiate \(\phi(z) = w^\star(z)\,z + \Phi_\rho(w^\star(z))\) with respect to \(z\):

\[ \phi'(z) = w^\star + \underbrace{\big[z + \Phi_\rho'(w^\star)\big]}_{=\,0}\,\frac{dw^\star}{dz} = w^\star. \]

So the optimal weight is the slope of \(\phi\): \(w^\star = \phi'(r^2)\). On the other hand \(\rho(r) = \phi(r^2)\), so by the chain rule \(\psi(r) = \rho'(r) = 2r\,\phi'(r^2)\), which gives \(\phi'(r^2) = \psi(r)/(2r)\). That is rule (3.12). The two derivations of IRLS produce the same weights.

This also explains the three conditions in Theorem 3.4. \(\phi'(z)\to1\) as \(z\to0\) says small residuals get weight 1. \(\phi'(z)\to0\) as \(z\to\infty\) says huge residuals get weight 0. \(\phi''(z)\lt0\) says the weight decreases as the residual grows, so it stays between 0 and 1.

A useful consequence. Each step minimizes the joint cost (3.16) over one block of unknowns with the other fixed, so neither step can increase it. The cost goes down at every iteration and the iteration settles. Nothing says it settles at the global minimum.

2. Why plain IRLS gets stuck

The first variable update uses all weights equal to 1, so it is least squares, and Day 1 showed how bad that estimate is. The first weight update then judges every measurement by its residual with respect to that bad estimate. With the truncated quadratic the judgment is final: measurements that happen to lie near the wrong estimate get weight 1, the rest get 0, and the next solve sees only the first group. Yesterday's widget stopped after 2 steps for this reason. The book reports that IRLS with the truncated quadratic or Geman-McClure loss can fail with as little as 10% outliers. §3.3.4 · p. 93

Intuition

Picture the robust cost as a landscape with many pits. IRLS only walks downhill. GNC first floods the landscape so that one wide basin remains, lets the walker reach its bottom, then drains the water slowly. As the pits reappear the walker is already standing in the deep one.

3. Surrogate losses with a dial

GNC replaces \(\rho\) by a family \(\rho_\mu\) controlled by one number \(\mu\). At one end of the dial \(\rho_\mu\) is convex, at the other it is the original loss. §3.3.4 · p. 93 The book gives two families. §3.3.4 · pp. 94–95

GNC truncated quadratic (Example 3.6):

\[ \rho_\mu(r) = \begin{cases} r^2 & \text{if } r^2 \in \big[0,\ \tfrac{\mu}{\mu+1}\beta^2\big] \\ 2\beta|r|\sqrt{\mu(\mu+1)} - \mu(\beta^2 + r^2) & \text{if } r^2 \in \big[\tfrac{\mu}{\mu+1}\beta^2,\ \tfrac{\mu+1}{\mu}\beta^2\big] \\ \beta^2 & \text{if } r^2 \in \big[\tfrac{\mu+1}{\mu}\beta^2,\ +\infty\big) \end{cases} \tag{3.24} \]

GNC Geman-McClure (Example 3.7):

\[ \rho_\mu(r) = \frac{\mu\beta^2 r^2}{\mu\beta^2 + r^2}. \tag{3.25} \]
GNC truncated quadraticGNC Geman-McClure
Convex end\(\mu\to0\)\(\mu\to\infty\)
Original loss at\(\mu\to\infty\)\(\mu = 1\)
Each iterationmultiply \(\mu\) by a factor above 1 (1.4 in the paper the book cites)divide \(\mu\) by that factor, down to 1
Outlier process \(\Phi_{\rho_\mu}(w)\)\(\dfrac{\mu(1-w)}{\mu+w}\beta^2\)\(\mu\beta^2(\sqrt{w}-1)^2\)
Weight update (derived below)\(1\) below the band, \(\dfrac{\beta\sqrt{\mu(\mu+1)}}{|r|}-\mu\) inside it, \(0\) above\(\left(\dfrac{\mu\beta^2}{r^2+\mu\beta^2}\right)^{2}\)

Filling the gap: checking the ends of the dial, and deriving the weights

Geman-McClure. Divide top and bottom of (3.25) by \(\mu\beta^2\): \(\rho_\mu(r) = r^2/(1 + r^2/(\mu\beta^2))\). As \(\mu\to\infty\) this tends to \(r^2\), the convex quadratic. At \(\mu = 1\) it is (3.17). In between, differentiating twice with \(c = \mu\beta^2\) gives \(\rho_\mu''(r) = 2c^2(c - 3r^2)/(c+r^2)^3\), which is positive while \(r^2 \lt \mu\beta^2/3\). So \(\mu\) sets the width of the convex zone, and a large \(\mu\) puts most residuals inside it. The surrogate is (3.17) with \(\beta^2\) replaced by \(\mu\beta^2\), so the weight is (3.20) with the same replacement.

Truncated quadratic: the pieces join. At the lower edge \(r^2 = \tfrac{\mu}{\mu+1}\beta^2\), so \(|r| = \beta\sqrt{\mu/(\mu+1)}\), and the middle expression is \(2\mu\beta^2 - \mu\beta^2 - \tfrac{\mu^2}{\mu+1}\beta^2 = \tfrac{\mu}{\mu+1}\beta^2 = r^2\). At the upper edge it is \(2(\mu+1)\beta^2 - \mu\beta^2 - (\mu+1)\beta^2 = \beta^2\). As \(\mu\to\infty\) both edges close in on \(\beta^2\) and (3.24) becomes \(\min\{r^2, \beta^2\}\). As \(\mu\to0\) the band stretches over all residuals and \(\rho_\mu(r)\approx 2\beta\sqrt{\mu}\,|r|\): a shallow V, which is convex.

Truncated quadratic: the weight. The book gives \(\Phi_{\rho_\mu}\) and leaves the weight update (3.27) to the reader. Minimize \(g(w) = w\,r^2 + \mu\beta^2\,\dfrac{1-w}{\mu+w}\) over \(w\in[0,1]\). By the quotient rule,

\[ \frac{d}{dw}\,\frac{1-w}{\mu+w} = \frac{-(\mu+w) - (1-w)}{(\mu+w)^2} = -\frac{\mu+1}{(\mu+w)^2}, \qquad\text{so}\qquad g'(w) = r^2 - \frac{\mu(\mu+1)\beta^2}{(\mu+w)^2}. \]

Setting \(g'(w) = 0\) gives \((\mu+w)^2 = \mu(\mu+1)\beta^2/r^2\), hence

\[ w^\star = \frac{\beta\sqrt{\mu(\mu+1)}}{|r|} - \mu . \]

This is at least 1 when \(r^2 \le \tfrac{\mu}{\mu+1}\beta^2\) and at most 0 when \(r^2 \ge \tfrac{\mu+1}{\mu}\beta^2\), so outside the band the weight is clipped to 1 or 0. Those are exactly the three cases of (3.24). Example: \(\beta = 1,\ \mu = 1,\ r = 1.2\). The band is \(r^2\in[0.5, 2]\) and \(r^2 = 1.44\) is inside, so \(w^\star = \sqrt{2}/1.2 - 1 = 0.18\). The plain truncated quadratic would say 0.

4. The GNC algorithm

Each iteration has three steps. §3.3.4 · p. 95

w_i = 1 for all i;  mu = a value where rho_mu is (nearly) convex
repeat:
    1. variable update:  x = argmin_x  sum_i w_i * r_i(x)^2          (3.26)
    2. weight update:    w_i = argmin_w  Phi_mu(w) + w * r_i(x)^2    (3.27)
    3. control update:   move mu one notch toward the original loss
until rho_mu is the original loss

Steps 1 and 2 are IRLS on the current surrogate. Step 3 is the only addition, and it is why the method is cheap to add to an existing solver.

The book does not say where to start \(\mu\). The widget below uses a common-sense choice: after the first least-squares solve, take the largest residual \(r_{\max}\) and pick \(\mu\) so that no measurement starts with weight zero. For the truncated quadratic that means the upper edge of the band lies beyond \(r_{\max}^2\), and the widget sets \(\mu_0 = \beta^2/(2r_{\max}^2-\beta^2)\), which puts the edge at \(2r_{\max}^2\). For Geman-McClure it sets \(\mu_0 = 2r_{\max}^2/\beta^2\), so every weight starts above \((2/3)^2 = 0.44\).

Try it: the same data as yesterday. Press Step and watch the top plot change shape while the line swings.

Notice: with the truncated quadratic (β = 0.5), least squares leaves a largest residual of 3.53, so μ starts at 0.010 and the surrogate is a wide shallow bowl. In about 7 steps, with μ still below 0.1, the line has swung from y = 0.12x + 2.81 onto the inliers. The remaining steps sharpen the weights to 0 and 1. GNC ends at y = 0.51x + 0.94 with cost 4.33. Plain IRLS on the same loss (dotted line) ends at y = 0.09x + 2.86 with cost 8.04. Now set Outliers to 50%: with the truncated quadratic, GNC ends at the same wrong line as IRLS, while with Geman-McClure it still succeeds where plain IRLS fails.

5. What GNC can and cannot do

On the three datasets of Day 1 (Figure 3.9), GNC with either loss recovers fairly accurate trajectories where gradient descent and IRLS sometimes failed, and in real problems it has tolerated around 80–90% wrong loop closures. §3.3.4 · p. 95 Two limits:

  • No guarantee. GNC is a heuristic. The 50% experiment in the widget is a small example. Its performance depends on the problem: excellent for pose-graph optimization, much worse on some other perception problems. §3.3.4 · p. 95
  • It leans on the odometry. All the experiments so far assumed an odometry backbone: a chain of trusted measurements that also supplies a decent initial guess. Figure 3.10 corrupts just two odometry measurements. GNC then starts from a broken initial guess and ends in a local minimum where it labels all measurements, inliers included, as outliers. §3.3.4 · pp. 96–98

The fix the book tries is to combine the two halves of the chapter. PCM does not use an initial guess, so it can prune gross outliers first. PCM followed by GNC gives the best results on SubT and Victoria Park. On M3500 all three variants (GNC, PCM, PCM + GNC) fail in this harder setting. §3.3.4 · p. 98 Robust SLAM without a trusted backbone is an open problem.

Where the field goes from here (§3.4): §3.4 · pp. 98–100

TopicDirections the book points to
Consensus maximizationRANSAC variants that refine by local optimization, score better than by counting (MLESAC), or bias the sampling (PROSAC). Exact solvers by branch and bound: globally optimal, exponential in the worst case.
Consistency graphsGroup-\(k\) consistency, where a test involves \(k\) measurements and the graph becomes a hypergraph. Soft versions with continuous edge weights.
Robust back-endsFormulations with latent on/off variables per measurement, max-mixture noise models, expectation-maximization, a single parametrized family of robust losses, and convergence guarantees for GNC-like schemes.
Certifiable algorithmsRelax the robust problem to a convex semidefinite program that can be solved in polynomial time and can certify afterwards that a solution is globally optimal. Slower than heuristics. Chapter 6 (Weeks 9 and 10) develops the idea.

Common mistakes

  • "GNC finds the global minimum." It follows one minimum while the cost deforms. Usually that is the right one. There is no proof that it must be.
  • "μ always increases." It depends on how the surrogate is written: up for (3.24), down to 1 for (3.25).
  • "GNC replaces front-end outlier rejection." Figure 3.10 shows the two working best together, because they fail in different situations.

Check yourself

Q1. GNC with the truncated quadratic, β = 1 and μ = 1. What weight does a measurement with residual r = 1.2 get?

The band is r² ∈ [0.5, 2] and r² = 1.44 is inside it, so w = β√(μ(μ+1))/|r| − μ = 1.414/1.2 − 1 = 0.18. Without graduation the weight would be 0, since 1.2 exceeds β.

Q2. GNC with Geman-McClure, β = 1. A measurement has residual r = 2. What are its weights at μ = 4 and at the end, μ = 1?

w = (μβ²/(r² + μβ²))². At μ = 4: (4/8)² = 0.25. At μ = 1: (1/5)² = 0.04. Early on the measurement still has a say. As μ falls it is progressively shut out.

Q3. Why does starting from a nearly convex surrogate make the result less dependent on the initial guess?

The surrogate's minimizer is not the final answer, but it is a far better starting point than least squares. Each later problem is a small change of the previous one, so its minimum is nearby.

Q4. In the alternating scheme (3.22)–(3.23), which statement is true?

Each step minimizes the same joint cost over one block of unknowns, so the cost never goes up. The weight update is N closed-form formulas, and convergence is only to a stationary point.

Q5. In the book's Figure 3.10 experiment, why does GNC fail?

GNC depends on a reasonable start, which normally comes from reliable odometry. With corrupted odometry it converges to a local minimum that rejects inliers too. PCM, which needs no initial guess, helps on two of the three datasets.

Recap

  1. With weights as variables (3.16), IRLS is alternating minimization: a weighted least-squares solve (3.22), then \(N\) closed-form weight updates (3.23).
  2. The B-R weight equals \(\phi'(r^2) = \psi(r)/(2r)\), the same as rule (3.12).
  3. GNC runs the same two steps on a surrogate \(\rho_\mu\) and adds a third: move \(\mu\) from the convex end toward the original loss.
  4. For the truncated quadratic, \(\mu\) grows and \(w = \beta\sqrt{\mu(\mu+1)}/|r| - \mu\) inside the band. For Geman-McClure, \(\mu\) shrinks to 1 and \(w = (\mu\beta^2/(r^2+\mu\beta^2))^2\).
  5. GNC has no guarantee and needs a usable initial guess. Without an odometry backbone, combine it with front-end rejection such as PCM.

Sources

  1. SLAM Handbook, §3.3.3 "Alternating Minimization", §3.3.4 "Graduated Non-Convexity", §3.4 "Further Readings & Recent Trends", pp. 92–100, equations (3.21)–(3.27), Examples 3.6 and 3.7, Figures 3.8–3.10.
  2. Black and Rangarajan, On the Unification of Line Processes, Outlier Rejection, and Robust Statistics with Applications in Early Vision, 1996 (outlier processes; the relation between the weight and the derivative of the loss).
  3. Yang, Antonante, Tzoumas, Carlone, Graduated Non-Convexity for Robust Spatial Perception: From Non-Minimal Solvers to Global Outlier Rejection, 2020 (the GNC surrogates and their closed-form weights).
  4. The weight derivation, the convexity range of (3.25), and the starting values of μ used in the widget are worked out here from the book's formulas.

Week 6 · Review

Week 6 review: outliers and robust estimation

After today you can choose between RANSAC, pairwise consistency, robust losses, and graduated non-convexity for a given problem, and carry out one step of each by hand.

About 60 min · No new pages

The week in one paragraph

Least squares assumes Gaussian errors, and one grossly wrong measurement, usually a wrong data association, can move its answer arbitrarily far. Chapter 3 defends in two layers. In the front-end, RANSAC samples minimal sets and keeps the model most measurements agree with, and pairwise consistency maximization keeps the largest group of measurements that agree with each other, found as a maximum clique. In the back-end, M-estimation swaps the square for a robust loss, IRLS solves it as repeated weighted least squares, Black-Rangarajan duality explains the weights, and graduated non-convexity makes IRLS far less dependent on its starting point. None of these comes with a guarantee, and the strongest results combine the layers.

2. Mixed quiz

Check yourself

Q1. Four measurements of a distance read 10 m and a fifth reads 60 m. What does least squares return?

The mean: (4 × 10 + 60)/5 = 20 m. Equivalently, the 50 m error is divided by N = 5, a shift of 10 m.

Q2. A minimal solver needs n = 3 correspondences and half of the correspondences are inliers. What is the expected number of RANSAC iterations before an all-inlier sample?

1/ωⁿ = 1/0.5³ = 8.

Q3. 30% of the matches are correct, and 45% are wrong but all caused by the same repeated structure, so they agree with one another. What does RANSAC most likely return?

RANSAC maximizes consensus. It cannot tell a large self-consistent group of wrong matches from the truth. This is perceptual aliasing at the level of the front-end.

Q4. Two matched 3D points are 2.00 m apart in frame k − 1 and 2.05 m apart in frame k. With γ = 0.10 m, what does the consistency test (3.5) say?

|2.00 − 2.05| = 0.05 ≤ 0.10, so the pair gets an edge in the consistency graph. The test needs no motion estimate. Passing it is necessary for both to be inliers, not sufficient.

Q5. A consistency graph has edges 1–2, 1–3, 2–3, 3–4, 4–5. Which measurements does PCM keep?

{1, 2, 3} is the maximum clique: all three pairs are edges. {3, 4, 5} is not a clique because 3–5 is missing. Node 3 has the most edges, but degree alone does not decide.

Q6. Geman-McClure loss with β = 1. What IRLS weight does a residual r = 3 get?

w = (β²/(β² + r²))² = (1/10)² = 0.01. Small, but not exactly zero as it would be for the truncated quadratic.

Q7. Which of these methods needs an initial guess of the state?

RANSAC builds its own estimates from minimal samples and PCM never touches the state. IRLS and GNC run Gauss-Newton-type steps on the full problem, and GNC in particular fails when the initial guess is broken (Figure 3.10).

Q8. In GNC with the truncated quadratic surrogate (3.24), what happens to the band of residuals with weights strictly between 0 and 1 as μ grows?

The band is r² ∈ [μ/(μ+1) β², (μ+1)/μ β²]. Both ends tend to β² as μ → ∞, so the surrogate becomes min{r², β²} and the weights become binary.

3. Pen-and-paper problems

  1. A 3D-3D registration front-end uses a 3-point minimal solver. (a) With 60% outliers, find the expected number of RANSAC iterations to draw an all-inlier sample, and the number needed for 99% confidence. (b) Repeat for 90% outliers.

    Solution

    (a) \(\omega = 0.4\), \(\omega^3 = 0.064\). Expected: \(1/0.064 = 15.6\). For 99%: \(k \ge \log(0.01)/\log(1-0.064) = (-4.605)/(-0.0661) = 69.6\), so 70 iterations.

    (b) \(\omega = 0.1\), \(\omega^3 = 0.001\). Expected: 1000. For 99%: \((-4.605)/\log(0.999) = (-4.605)/(-0.0010005) = 4603\) iterations. Going from 60% to 90% outliers costs a factor of about 65, which is why the chapter turns to PCM for very high outlier rates.

  2. A robot drives down a corridor and back (treat it as one-dimensional). Five candidate loop closures each link an early pose \(a_i\) to a late pose \(b_i\). For each one you compute \(e_i\) = (loop-closure displacement) − (displacement predicted by chaining odometry from \(a_i\) to \(b_i\)), and get \(e = \{0.42,\ 0.38,\ 2.90,\ 0.45,\ -1.70\}\) m. (a) Show that the cycle test (3.6) for loop closures \(i\) and \(j\) reduces to \(|e_i - e_j|\le\gamma\). (b) With \(\gamma = 0.15\) m, build the consistency graph and find the maximum clique. (c) What do the kept loop closures say about the odometry?

    Solution

    (a) In one dimension poses compose by addition and the identity is 0. Go around the cycle \(a_i \to b_i \to b_j \to a_j \to a_i\): loop closure \(i\) forwards (\(T_i\)), odometry from \(b_i\) to \(b_j\), loop closure \(j\) backwards (\(-T_j\)), odometry from \(a_j\) to \(a_i\). Writing \(q\) for positions obtained by chaining odometry, the sum is \(T_i + (q_{b_j}-q_{b_i}) - T_j + (q_{a_i}-q_{a_j}) = [T_i-(q_{b_i}-q_{a_i})] - [T_j-(q_{b_j}-q_{a_j})] = e_i - e_j\).

    (b) There are \(5\times4/2 = 10\) pairs. \(|e_1-e_2| = 0.04\), \(|e_1-e_4| = 0.03\), \(|e_2-e_4| = 0.07\): three edges. Every pair involving closure 3 or closure 5 differs by more than 2 m: no edge. The graph is the triangle {1, 2, 4} plus two isolated nodes, so the maximum clique is {1, 2, 4}.

    (c) They agree that odometry drifted by about 0.4 m between the two passes. Closures 3 and 5 each imply a different drift that nothing else supports.

  3. Estimate a scalar \(x\) from \(z = \{0, 1, 2, 3, 19\}\) with residuals \(r_i = z_i - x\). (a) Give the least-squares estimate. (b) Run IRLS with the truncated quadratic loss, \(\beta = 3.5\), from the least-squares estimate until it stops changing. (c) Find the Huber estimate for \(\beta = 3.5\) from the condition \(\sum_i\psi(r_i) = 0\).

    Solution

    (a) The mean: \(25/5 = 5\).

    (b) Iteration 1: residuals \(-5, -4, -3, -2, 14\). Weights are 1 where \(|r|\lt3.5\): \(0, 0, 1, 1, 0\). New \(x = (2+3)/2 = 2.5\). Iteration 2: residuals \(-2.5, -1.5, -0.5, 0.5, 16.5\), weights \(1, 1, 1, 1, 0\), new \(x = 6/4 = 1.5\). Iteration 3: residuals \(-1.5, -0.5, 0.5, 1.5, 17.5\), same weights, \(x = 1.5\). Converged at the mean of the four good values. Here the bad start did not matter. Compare the Day 4 widget, where it did.

    (c) Guess that the first four residuals are within \(\beta\) and the last is beyond it. Then \(\psi = 2r\) for the first four and \(\psi = 2\beta\) for the last: \(2[(0-x)+(1-x)+(2-x)+(3-x)] + 2(3.5) = 0\), so \(12 - 8x + 7 = 0\) and \(x = 2.375\). Check the guess: the residuals are \(-2.375, -1.375, -0.375, 0.625\) (all within 3.5) and \(16.625\) (beyond). The Huber estimate is 2.375, between the truncated-quadratic answer 1.5 and the least-squares answer 5, because the outlier keeps a constant pull of \(2\beta\).

  4. (Stretch.) For GNC with the truncated quadratic, the outlier process is \(\Phi_{\rho_\mu}(w) = \dfrac{\mu(1-w)}{\mu+w}\beta^2\) and the weight inside the band is \(w^\star = \beta\sqrt{\mu(\mu+1)}/|r| - \mu\). (a) Substitute \(w^\star\) into \(w\,r^2 + \Phi_{\rho_\mu}(w)\) and show that you get the middle case of (3.24). (b) Evaluate \(w^\star\) and \(\rho_\mu\) for \(\beta = 2,\ \mu = 0.25,\ r = 3\).

    Solution

    (a) Let \(s = \beta\sqrt{\mu(\mu+1)}\), so \(w^\star = s/|r| - \mu\), \(\mu + w^\star = s/|r|\), and \(s^2 = \mu(\mu+1)\beta^2\). First term: \(w^\star r^2 = s|r| - \mu r^2\). Second term: \(\mu\beta^2\,\dfrac{1+\mu-s/|r|}{s/|r|} = \dfrac{\mu(\mu+1)\beta^2\,|r|}{s} - \mu\beta^2 = s|r| - \mu\beta^2\). The sum is \(2s|r| - \mu(\beta^2+r^2) = 2\beta|r|\sqrt{\mu(\mu+1)} - \mu(\beta^2+r^2)\), the middle case of (3.24).

    (b) The band is \(r^2\in[\tfrac{0.25}{1.25}\cdot4,\ \tfrac{1.25}{0.25}\cdot4] = [0.8, 20]\), and \(r^2 = 9\) is inside. \(\sqrt{\mu(\mu+1)} = \sqrt{0.3125} = 0.559\). \(w^\star = 2(0.559)/3 - 0.25 = 0.1227\). \(\rho_\mu = 2(2)(3)(0.559) - 0.25(4+9) = 6.708 - 3.25 = 3.458\). Check through the weight: \(0.1227\times9 + 0.25\times4\times\tfrac{0.8773}{0.3727} = 1.104 + 2.354 = 3.458\). The plain truncated quadratic would give weight 0 and loss 4.

You are ready for next week if you can

  • Explain with the \(E/N\) argument why least squares has no protection against one bad measurement.
  • Compute RANSAC iteration counts from \(\omega\), \(n\), and a confidence level.
  • Write a consistency function for a pair of measurements and find a maximum clique in a small graph.
  • Compute \(\rho\), \(\psi\), and the IRLS weight for the Huber, Geman-McClure, and truncated quadratic losses.
  • Describe IRLS as alternating a weighted least-squares solve with closed-form weight updates, and say what GNC adds.
  • Name one situation in which each method fails.

Sources

  1. SLAM Handbook, Chapter 3 "Robustness to Incorrect Data Association and Outliers", pp. 75–100.
  2. Fischler and Bolles, Random Sample Consensus: A Paradigm for Model Fitting with Applications to Image Analysis and Automated Cartography, 1981 (iteration count for a given confidence).
  3. Huber, Robust Statistics, 1981 (M-estimators and influence functions).

Week 7 · Day 1

Why differentiate through the back-end, and how autodiff does it

After today you can write SLAM with a learned front-end as a bilevel optimization problem, name the one Jacobian that makes it hard, and run forward- and reverse-mode automatic differentiation by hand on a small computation graph.

About 60 min · Read the Chapter 4 introduction, §4.1, and the start of §4.2, pp. 101–104 (4 pages) · Needs Week 2 Day 4

Read first: Chapter 4 introduction, §4.1, §4.2 up to §4.2.1, pp. 101–104

While you read, look for:

  • The sentence on p. 101 that says what "differentiating through an optimization problem" tells you, in words.
  • Equation (4.1) on p. 102, where each residual is a weight times a cost. Both the weight and the cost are places where a network can enter.
  • Equations (4.2a) and (4.2b) on p. 103: which problem is nested inside which, and which variables belong to each.
  • Equation (4.3) on p. 104 and the sentence after it that says which term is the hard one.

Today's big idea

A learned front-end produces the measurements, and the back-end turns them into the estimate \(\mathbf{x}^*\). To train the front-end on how good the final estimate is, you need to know how \(\mathbf{x}^*\) moves when the front-end's parameters \(\mathbf{y}\) move. That is the Jacobian \(\partial\mathbf{x}^*/\partial\mathbf{y}\) of an arg min, and the whole chapter is about computing it.

1. From a one-way pipeline to a loop

In Week 1 · Day 1 the front-end handed pseudo-measurements to the back-end and never heard back. Neural networks now do parts of the front-end well, such as feature detection, matching, and frame-to-frame motion estimation, while geometric optimization remains the tool that makes the result globally consistent. Ch. 4 intro · p. 101 You could train the network on its own task (say, matching accuracy), freeze it, and plug it in. But the network would then never learn which of its mistakes actually hurt the SLAM estimate.

The alternative is to let the back-end send a training signal to the front-end. For that, the error measured after the back-end must be turned into a gradient with respect to the network's weights, and the gradient has to pass through the optimizer on the way. Ch. 4 intro · pp. 101–102

2. Recap: the back-end is a nonlinear least squares problem

The back-end solves a nonlinear least squares (NLS) problem: §4.1 · p. 102

\[ \mathbf{x}^* = \argmin_{\mathbf{x}} \mathcal{L}(\mathbf{x}) = \argmin_{\mathbf{x}} \frac{1}{2}\sum_i \norm{\underbrace{w_i\,\mathbf{c}_i(\mathbf{x}_i)}_{\mathbf{r}_i(\mathbf{x}_i)}}^2 . \tag{4.1} \]

Each residual \(\mathbf{r}_i\) depends on a small subset \(\mathbf{x}_i\) of the variables (one factor of the factor graph) and is written as a scalar weight \(w_i\) times a vector cost \(\mathbf{c}_i\). The solver is the one from Week 2 · Day 4: linearize, solve the normal equations for a step \(\delta\mathbf{x}\), update, repeat. With \(\mathbf{J}_i = \partial\mathbf{r}_i/\partial\mathbf{x}\), Gauss-Newton (GN) uses \(\sum_i \mathbf{J}_i\T\mathbf{J}_i\) as an approximation of the Hessian, and Levenberg-Marquardt and dogleg modify the step to make it safer. §4.1 · pp. 102–103

Filling the gap: the sign in the normal equations

Page 102 writes the linear system compactly as \((\sum_i \mathbf{J}_i\T\mathbf{J}_i)\,\delta\mathbf{x} = \sum_i \mathbf{J}_i\T\mathbf{r}_i\). Whether a minus sign appears on the right depends on how the residual is defined. This week the residual is always "prediction minus measurement", and then minimizing \(\tfrac12\norm{\mathbf{r} + \mathbf{J}\,\delta\mathbf{x}}^2\) gives

\[ \Big(\sum_i \mathbf{J}_i\T\mathbf{J}_i\Big)\,\delta\mathbf{x} = -\sum_i \mathbf{J}_i\T\mathbf{r}_i , \]

which is the form the book itself uses later in equation (4.43) on p. 115.

The toy problem of the week. One unknown \(x\) (a position on a line), two residuals:

\[ \mathcal{L}(x, y) = \tfrac12\,(x^2 - y)^2 + \tfrac12\,(x - 1)^2 . \]

The first residual is a nonlinear sensor: it predicts the reading \(x^2\) and compares it with the measured value \(y\). The second is a prior that pulls \(x\) toward 1. The number \(y\) is what the front-end outputs. Take \(y = 2\) and start at \(x_0 = 1\). The residuals are \(\mathbf{r} = (x^2 - y,\; x - 1)\) and \(\mathbf{J} = (2x,\; 1)\T\), so one GN step is \(x \leftarrow x - \dfrac{2x(x^2-y) + (x-1)}{4x^2+1}\):

IterationxJᵀrJᵀJStep
01.0000−2.00005.00+0.4000
11.40000.28808.84−0.0326
21.36740.01158.48−0.0014
31.36610.00048.46−0.00004

It converges to \(x^* = (1+\sqrt3)/2 \approx 1.3660\). Notice that \(x^*\) is not \(\sqrt{2} \approx 1.414\) (what the sensor alone says) and not 1 (what the prior says): it is the compromise. Change \(y\) and the compromise moves. How fast it moves is the question of the week.

3. Two nested problems: bilevel optimization

Call the network's parameters \(\mathbf{y} \in \R^m\) and the back-end's variables \(\mathbf{x} \in \R^n\). Training the network on the back-end's result is a bilevel optimization (BLO) problem: §4.2 · p. 103

\[ \begin{aligned} \mathbf{y}^* & = \argmin_{\mathbf{y}\in\Theta}\; \mathcal{U}(\mathbf{y}, \mathbf{x}^*) & \quad & \text{(4.2a)} \\ \text{s.t. } \mathbf{x}^* & = \argmin_{\mathbf{x}\in\Psi}\; \mathcal{L}(\mathbf{y}, \mathbf{x}) & \quad & \text{(4.2b)} \end{aligned} \]

\(\mathcal{L}\) is the lower-level (LL) cost: the SLAM objective, minimized over \(\mathbf{x}\) with \(\mathbf{y}\) held fixed. \(\mathcal{U}\) is the upper-level (UL) cost: the training loss, minimized over \(\mathbf{y}\), and it is evaluated at the solution \(\mathbf{x}^*\) of the lower level. The constraint "s.t." is itself an optimization problem, which is what "bilevel" means. The variables \(\mathbf{x}\) usually have a physical meaning (poses, landmarks); the variables \(\mathbf{y}\) usually do not (network weights). §4.2 · p. 103

Keep to this definition of the two symbols. The sentence just before (4.2) on p. 103 uses the names of the two levels loosely; the equations and Figure 4.1 are the reference.

CaseUpper level: y and ULower level: x and L
Example 4.1, visual SLAM with learned features (p. 104)y: weights of the feature network. U: feature-matching errorx: camera poses and landmarks. L: reprojection error of bundle adjustment
Example 4.2, pose-graph optimization (p. 104)y: weights of a network that estimates relative poses. U: pose-graph errorx: the poses. L: the same pose-graph error
Our toy problemy: the measured value itself. U = ½(x* − 1.5)², the error against a ground truth of 1.5x: the position. L = ½(x² − y)² + ½(x − 1)²

In Example 4.2 both levels use the same error, and that is not a mistake: the lower level picks the poses for the given measurements, the upper level changes the network so that the measurements it produces leave less error after optimization. §4.2 · p. 104

In plain words

A cook (the front-end) prepares ingredients. A chef (the back-end) always makes the best possible dish from whatever arrives. A critic scores the dish. To improve, the cook needs to know: "if I had cut the onions a little finer, how would the chef's best dish have changed, and would the critic have liked it more?" The chef's reaction to a small change in the ingredients is \(\partial\mathbf{x}^*/\partial\mathbf{y}\).

4. The gradient the upper level needs

The upper level is trained by gradient descent, \(\mathbf{y} \leftarrow \mathbf{y} + \delta\mathbf{y}\) with \(\delta\mathbf{y}\) along the negative gradient. Because \(\mathbf{x}^*\) depends on \(\mathbf{y}\), the chain rule gives two terms: §4.2 · p. 104

\[ \nabla_{\mathbf{y}}\,\mathcal{U} = \frac{\partial\,\mathcal{U}(\mathbf{y},\mathbf{x}^*)}{\partial\mathbf{y}} + \frac{\partial\,\mathcal{U}(\mathbf{y},\mathbf{x}^*)}{\partial\mathbf{x}^*}\,\frac{\partial\mathbf{x}^*(\mathbf{y})}{\partial\mathbf{y}} . \tag{4.3} \]

Filling the gap: shapes, and which term is hard

\(\mathcal{U}\) is a scalar, \(\mathbf{y}\) has \(m\) entries, \(\mathbf{x}\) has \(n\). With gradients written as rows:

  • \(\partial\mathcal{U}/\partial\mathbf{y}\) is \(1\times m\): the direct dependence, with \(\mathbf{x}^*\) treated as a constant. Ordinary backpropagation gives it.
  • \(\partial\mathcal{U}/\partial\mathbf{x}^*\) is \(1\times n\): also ordinary.
  • \(\partial\mathbf{x}^*/\partial\mathbf{y}\) is \(n\times m\): entry \((j,k)\) says how much the \(j\)-th solution variable moves per unit change of the \(k\)-th parameter. This is the indirect part and the hard one, because \(\mathbf{x}^*\) is defined as "the result of running a solver", not by a formula.

In the toy problem \(\mathcal{U} = \tfrac12(x^*-1.5)^2\) does not contain \(y\) directly, so the first term is zero and \(\nabla_y\,\mathcal{U} = (x^* - 1.5)\cdot \dfrac{dx^*}{dy}\). You can estimate the derivative by brute force: solve the lower level at \(y = 2.01\) and \(y = 1.99\), which gives \(x^* = 1.36936\) and \(1.36269\), so

\[ \frac{dx^*}{dy} \approx \frac{1.36936 - 1.36269}{0.02} = 0.333, \qquad \nabla_y\,\mathcal{U} \approx (1.3660 - 1.5)\times 0.333 = -0.0447 . \]

The gradient is negative: raising \(y\) lowers the loss, which makes sense because \(x^* = 1.366\) is below the target 1.5. But this method needs two full solves per parameter. With a million network weights that is two million SLAM solves for one training step. The book offers two practical routes, unrolled differentiation (tomorrow) and implicit differentiation (Day 3). §4.2 · p. 104

5. The tool underneath: automatic differentiation

Both routes rest on automatic differentiation (AutoDiff). Page 105 mentions that it comes in a forward mode and a reverse mode and leaves the details to the libraries. Here they are, because the costs of the two modes decide everything tomorrow.

A program computes its output through a sequence of elementary operations (add, multiply, square, sin, …), each with a derivative you know. AutoDiff applies the chain rule to that sequence with numbers, not symbols. It is exact up to rounding: it is neither a finite-difference approximation nor a symbolic manipulation of formulas.

Filling the gap: the two modes

Write the program as intermediate values \(v_1, v_2, \dots\), each computed from earlier ones.

Forward mode picks one input, say \(x\), and carries next to every value its tangent \(\dot v = \partial v/\partial x\). The inputs are seeded with \(\dot x = 1\) and 0 for the others, and each operation updates the tangent with its own derivative rule: if \(v = a\,b\) then \(\dot v = \dot a\, b + a\, \dot b\). One pass, done together with the evaluation, gives the derivative of every output with respect to that one input.

Reverse mode first runs the program and stores every intermediate value. Then it walks the operations backward and carries for every value its adjoint \(\bar v = \partial(\text{output})/\partial v\). The output is seeded with 1, and each node passes its adjoint to the values it was computed from: if \(v = a\,b\) then \(\bar a\) receives \(\bar v\, b\) and \(\bar b\) receives \(\bar v\, a\). A value used in several places adds up what it receives. One backward pass gives the derivative of that one output with respect to every input. Applied to neural networks this is backpropagation.

Split the toy cost into elementary steps: \(v_1 = x^2\), \(v_2 = v_1 - y\), \(v_3 = x - 1\), \(v_4 = \tfrac12 v_2^2\), \(v_5 = \tfrac12 v_3^2\), \(\mathcal{L} = v_4 + v_5\). At \(x = 1.5\), \(y = 2\):

NodeValueForward tangent (seed x)Reverse adjoint ∂L/∂node
x1.51 (seed)0.25 · 2x + 0.5 · 1 = 1.25
y200.25 · (−1) = −0.25
v1 = x²2.252x · 1 = 30.25
v2 = v1 − y0.253 − 0 = 31 · v2 = 0.25
v3 = x − 10.511 · v3 = 0.5
v4 = ½v2²0.03125v2 · 3 = 0.751
v5 = ½v3²0.125v3 · 1 = 0.51
L = v4 + v50.156250.75 + 0.5 = 1.251 (seed)

Read the forward column top to bottom and the reverse column bottom to top. Both find \(\partial\mathcal{L}/\partial x = 1.25\), which agrees with the formula \(2x(x^2-y) + (x-1) = 0.75 + 0.5\). Only the reverse pass also produced \(\partial\mathcal{L}/\partial y = -0.25\).

Try it: step through each mode with the Step slider, then change x and y.

Notice that at the default x = 1.5, y = 2 the forward pass seeded on x ends with 1.250 at L and says nothing about y; seeded on y it ends with −0.250. The reverse pass delivers both numbers, at the x and y nodes, in one sweep, and its arrows run against the direction of evaluation.

For f from m inputs to p outputsForward modeReverse mode
One pass computesJacobian times a vector, J·u (one column if u is a unit vector)a vector times the Jacobian, wᵀ·J (one row if w is a unit vector)
Passes for the full Jacobianmp
Extra memorynone beyond the tangentsevery intermediate value must be kept until the backward pass
Good whenfew inputs, many outputsmany inputs, one output: a training loss

A training loss has one output and millions of inputs, so learning uses reverse mode. The price is the last-but-one row: memory proportional to the length of the computation. Tomorrow the "computation" will be every iteration of the back-end solver, and that price becomes the main problem.

Common mistakes

  • "U does not contain y, so its gradient with respect to y is zero." Only the direct term of (4.3) is zero. \(\mathcal{U}\) depends on \(\mathbf{y}\) through \(\mathbf{x}^*(\mathbf{y})\), and that indirect term is usually the whole signal.
  • "AutoDiff is finite differences done by a library." Finite differences evaluate the function at shifted inputs and have truncation error. AutoDiff propagates exact derivative rules through the same operations and has none.
  • "Reverse mode is always the faster one." It needs one pass per output and stores the whole computation. For a function with few inputs and many outputs, forward mode is cheaper.
  • "The lower level and the upper level must use different costs." Example 4.2 uses the same pose-graph error at both levels; they differ in which variables are free.

Check yourself

Q1. In Example 4.2 (a network estimates relative poses, pose-graph optimization removes the drift), what are the lower-level variables x?

The lower level is the back-end: it optimizes the poses for fixed network outputs. The network weights are the upper-level variables y.

Q2. For the toy cost L = ½(x² − y)² + ½(x − 1)², use the computation graph at x = 2, y = 3. What is ∂L/∂x?

v1 = 4, v2 = 1, v3 = 1. Reverse: the adjoints of v2 and v3 are 1 and 1, so ∂L/∂x = 1 · 2x + 1 · 1 = 4 + 1 = 5. (And ∂L/∂y = −1.)

Q3. A back-end has n = 600 variables and the network has m = 1,000,000 weights. What is the shape of ∂x*/∂y, and how many AutoDiff passes would it take to compute the single row vector ∇U in reverse mode?

Rows index solution variables, columns index parameters: n × m. The loss U is one scalar output, so one reverse pass gives its whole gradient. You never need the full 600 × 1,000,000 matrix, only its product with the row ∂U/∂x*.

Q4. In the toy problem, the solution moves from x* = 1.3660 at y = 2 to x* = 1.3991 at y = 2.1. Using this finite difference, about how much does U = ½(x* − 1.5)² change per unit of y near y = 2?

dx*/dy ≈ (1.3991 − 1.3660)/0.1 = 0.331, and ∂U/∂x* = 1.3660 − 1.5 = −0.134. Their product is about −0.044. The direct term is zero.

Recap

  1. Differentiating through the back-end tells you how the SLAM solution changes when the front-end's output changes, which lets the front-end be trained on the final accuracy.
  2. This is a bilevel problem: the upper-level cost \(\mathcal{U}\) trains \(\mathbf{y}\); the lower-level cost \(\mathcal{L}\) is the NLS problem (4.1) solved for \(\mathbf{x}^*\).
  3. The gradient (4.3) has a direct term and an indirect term. The indirect term needs \(\partial\mathbf{x}^*/\partial\mathbf{y}\), an \(n\times m\) Jacobian of an arg min.
  4. Forward-mode AutoDiff costs one pass per input; reverse mode costs one pass per output but stores the whole computation.

Sources

  1. SLAM Handbook, Chapter 4 "Differentiable Optimization" (Wang, Jatavallabhula, Mukadam), introduction, §4.1, and §4.2 up to §4.2.1, pp. 101–104; Figure 4.1; Examples 4.1 and 4.2.
  2. Griewank and Walther, Evaluating Derivatives: Principles and Techniques of Algorithmic Differentiation, 2nd ed., 2008 (forward and reverse mode, their costs).
  3. Baydin, Pearlmutter, Radul, Siskind, Automatic differentiation in machine learning: a survey, 2018.
  4. Nocedal and Wright, Numerical Optimization, 2006 (Gauss-Newton and its sign conventions). The toy problem and its numbers are this app's own.

Week 7 · Day 2

Unrolled differentiation: backpropagating through the solver's iterations

After today you can differentiate the result of T solver iterations with respect to the problem's parameters by the chain rule, say what it costs in time and memory, and quantify the bias of truncating the backward pass or of using a single step.

About 60 min · Read §4.2.1–4.2.2, pp. 104–106 (3 pages) · Needs Week 7 Day 1

Read first: §4.2.1–4.2.2, pp. 104–106

While you read, look for:

  • Equation (4.4) on p. 104 and (4.6) on p. 105: the solver written as a composition of update maps.
  • Algorithm 1 on p. 105: line 5 (unrolled) and line 6 (implicit) are two ways to fill in the same gradient.
  • The footnote on p. 105: gradient descent is only the example; the same idea covers Gauss-Newton.
  • On p. 106, what "storing only the last M iterations" buys, and what equations (4.8)–(4.10) avoid computing.

Today's big idea

An iterative solver is a program: \(T\) applications of an update rule. Unrolled differentiation treats those \(T\) updates as \(T\) layers of a network and backpropagates through them. It is exact for the program that actually ran, it works for any differentiable solver, and it pays with memory that grows with \(T\). Truncating the backward pass trades a small, predictable bias for that memory.

1. The solver as a chain of maps

Start from an initial guess \(\mathbf{x}_0 = \Phi_0(\mathbf{y})\) and apply an update map \(T\) times: §4.2.1 · pp. 104–105

\[ \mathbf{x}_t = \Phi_t(\mathbf{x}_{t-1};\, \mathbf{y}), \qquad t = 1, \dots, T . \tag{4.4} \]

The book's example of an update map is one step of gradient descent on the lower-level cost, with learning rate \(\eta_t\):

\[ \Phi_t(\mathbf{x}_{t-1};\, \mathbf{y}) = \mathbf{x}_{t-1} - \eta_t\, \frac{\partial \mathcal{L}(\mathbf{x}_{t-1}, \mathbf{y})}{\partial \mathbf{x}_{t-1}} . \tag{4.5} \]

A Gauss-Newton or Levenberg-Marquardt step is another valid \(\Phi_t\) (footnote 1, p. 105). Stop after \(T\) steps and use \(\mathbf{x}_T\) in place of the true minimizer:

\[ \mathbf{x}^* \approx \mathbf{x}_T = \Phi(\mathbf{y}) = (\Phi_T \circ \cdots \circ \Phi_1 \circ \Phi_0)(\mathbf{y}) . \tag{4.6} \]

The bilevel problem (4.2) then collapses into an ordinary single-level problem, \(\min_{\mathbf{y}} \mathcal{U}(\mathbf{y}, \Phi(\mathbf{y}))\), equation (4.7), in which \(\Phi\) is just a deep function of \(\mathbf{y}\). AutoDiff can differentiate it. §4.2.1 · p. 105

2. The chain rule along the chain

The book stops at "compute \(\partial\Phi(\mathbf{y})/\partial\mathbf{y}\) via AutoDiff". It is worth seeing what AutoDiff actually computes, because the formula explains the cost.

Filling the gap: the sensitivity recursion

Differentiate (4.4) with respect to \(\mathbf{y}\). \(\Phi_t\) depends on \(\mathbf{y}\) in two ways: directly, and through \(\mathbf{x}_{t-1}\). Name the two partial derivatives

\[ \mathbf{A}_t = \frac{\partial \Phi_t}{\partial \mathbf{x}_{t-1}} \;(n\times n), \qquad \mathbf{B}_t = \frac{\partial \Phi_t}{\partial \mathbf{y}} \;(n\times m), \]

and the quantity we are after \(\mathbf{S}_t = \partial\mathbf{x}_t/\partial\mathbf{y}\). Then

\[ \mathbf{S}_t = \mathbf{A}_t\,\mathbf{S}_{t-1} + \mathbf{B}_t, \qquad \mathbf{S}_0 = \frac{\partial\Phi_0}{\partial\mathbf{y}} \quad(\text{zero if the initial guess ignores } \mathbf{y}). \]

Running this next to the solver is forward mode. For the gradient-descent map (4.5), differentiating once more gives

\[ \mathbf{A}_t = \mathbf{I} - \eta_t\,\frac{\partial^2\mathcal{L}}{\partial\mathbf{x}\,\partial\mathbf{x}}, \qquad \mathbf{B}_t = -\eta_t\,\frac{\partial^2\mathcal{L}}{\partial\mathbf{x}\,\partial\mathbf{y}}, \qquad \text{both at } (\mathbf{x}_{t-1}, \mathbf{y}). \]

Unfolding the recursion shows the "sum over paths":

\[ \mathbf{S}_T = \mathbf{B}_T + \mathbf{A}_T\mathbf{B}_{T-1} + \mathbf{A}_T\mathbf{A}_{T-1}\mathbf{B}_{T-2} + \dots + \mathbf{A}_T\cdots\mathbf{A}_2\mathbf{B}_1 \;(+\; \mathbf{A}_T\cdots\mathbf{A}_1\mathbf{S}_0). \]

Reverse mode computes the same sum from the other end, without ever forming an \(n\times m\) matrix. Start with the adjoint \(\boldsymbol{\lambda}_T = (\partial\mathcal{U}/\partial\mathbf{x}_T)\T\) and walk back:

\[ \boldsymbol{\lambda}_{t-1} = \mathbf{A}_t\T\,\boldsymbol{\lambda}_t, \qquad \nabla_{\mathbf{y}}\,\mathcal{U} = \frac{\partial\mathcal{U}}{\partial\mathbf{y}} + \sum_{t=1}^{T} \boldsymbol{\lambda}_t\T\,\mathbf{B}_t . \]

Each backward step needs \(\mathbf{A}_t\) and \(\mathbf{B}_t\), which are evaluated at \(\mathbf{x}_{t-1}\). That is why every iterate must still be in memory when the backward pass reaches it.

Worked example. The toy problem of Day 1: \(\mathcal{L} = \tfrac12(x^2-y)^2 + \tfrac12(x-1)^2\), with \(\partial\mathcal{L}/\partial x = 2x(x^2-y) + (x-1)\), \(\partial^2\mathcal{L}/\partial x^2 = 6x^2 - 2y + 1\), and \(\partial^2\mathcal{L}/\partial x\,\partial y = -2x\). So \(A_t = 1 - \eta(6x_{t-1}^2 - 2y + 1)\) and \(B_t = 2\eta\,x_{t-1}\). Take \(y = 2\), \(x_0 = 1\), \(\eta = 0.1\):

tx at t − 1A at tB at tx at tS at t = A·S + B
11.00000.7000.20001.20000.2000
21.20000.4360.24001.31440.436 · 0.2000 + 0.2400 = 0.3272
31.31440.2630.26291.35460.263 · 0.3272 + 0.2629 = 0.3491

After two steps, forward mode gives \(\nabla_y\,\mathcal{U} = (x_2 - 1.5)\,S_2 = (-0.1856)(0.3272) = -0.0607\). Reverse mode on the same two steps: \(\lambda_2 = -0.1856\), \(\lambda_1 = A_2\lambda_2 = -0.0809\), and \(\lambda_2 B_2 + \lambda_1 B_1 = -0.0445 - 0.0162 = -0.0607\). Same number, as it must be. The true gradient from Day 1 is \(-0.0447\); with only two steps we are differentiating a solver that has not converged yet.

3. Exact for the program, not for the problem

Try it: the chart plots each estimate of dU/dy against the number of inner steps K. Raise K, then switch the inner solver to Gauss-Newton.

Notice that at the defaults (gradient descent, η = 0.1, K = 2) the unrolled gradient is −0.0607, the value from the worked example, while the reference is −0.0447. By K = 8 they agree. Lower η to 0.05 and it takes about K = 20; switch to Gauss-Newton and K = 2 is enough. The unrolled gradient is always the exact derivative of U(x_K), and it is only as good as x_K is close to x*.

The costs follow directly from the recursions: §4.2.1–4.2.2 · pp. 105–106

Way to unrollWhat it storesWork besides the T solver stepsBias
Forward modethe n × m matrix S, updated in placem tangents carried through every step: about m times the solvernone (for x at T)
Reverse modeall T iterates and whatever each step computed from themone backward sweep of T stepsnone (for x at T)
Truncated reverse, last M stepsthe last M iteratesa backward sweep of M stepsthe dropped terms, see §4 below
One step, (4.8)one iterateone second-derivative productlarge unless one step nearly solves the problem

With \(m\) in the millions, forward mode is out. Reverse mode it is, and then memory grows linearly with \(T\). The book calls this the difficulty of "long-term dependencies", and it gets worse when both \(\mathbf{x}\) and \(\mathbf{y}\) are high-dimensional. §4.2.2 · p. 106

Intuition

Reverse-mode unrolling is like auditing a calculation by replaying the tape backward. You can do it only if you kept the whole tape. A solver that needs 100 iterations produces a tape 100 states long, even though only the last state is the answer.

4. Truncated unrolling: keep only the last M steps

Truncated unrolled differentiation stops the backward walk after \(M\) steps: it uses \(t = T, T-1, \dots\) and ignores the influence that \(\mathbf{y}\) had on earlier iterates. Only the last \(M\) iterates are stored. The book reports (citing its reference [992]) that a few backward steps can perform comparably to the exact gradient with much less memory and computation. §4.2.2 · p. 106

Filling the gap: how big is the truncation bias?

Truncation keeps the first \(M\) terms of the sum for \(\mathbf{S}_T\) above and drops the rest. Every dropped term contains at least \(M\) factors \(\mathbf{A}\). Near the solution the iterates barely change, so \(\mathbf{A}_t \approx \mathbf{A}\) and \(\mathbf{B}_t \approx \mathbf{B}\) are nearly constant, and for a solver that converges, repeated multiplication by \(\mathbf{A}\) shrinks vectors (that is what convergence means). In the scalar toy problem this is a geometric series:

\[ S_{\text{full}} = B\,(1 + A + A^2 + \dots) = \frac{B}{1-A}, \qquad S_{\text{last } M} = B\,(1 + A + \dots + A^{M-1}) = \frac{B\,(1 - A^M)}{1-A} . \]

The truncated gradient is the full one times \(1 - A^M\): the fraction \(A^M\) is missing. For gradient descent with \(\eta = 0.1\) at the solution \(x^* = 1.366\), \(A = 1 - 0.1\times 8.196 = 0.18\). So \(M = 1\) loses 18%, \(M = 2\) loses 3.2%, \(M = 3\) loses 0.6%. In the widget set K = 30 and "Backprop through last M" to 1: the truncated gradient reads −0.0366, which is 82% of −0.0447.

The rule to remember: the slower the inner solver converges (the closer \(A\) is to 1), the more backward steps you need. A second-order solver such as Gauss-Newton has a small \(A\) near the solution, so short truncation works well with it.

5. The extreme case: one inner step

Under tight memory and time limits, some methods unroll a single step, \(\mathbf{x}_1(\mathbf{y}) = \Phi_1(\mathbf{x}_0;\mathbf{y})\), and use §4.2.2 · p. 106

\[ \nabla_{\mathbf{y}}\,\mathcal{U} = \frac{\partial\,\mathcal{U}(\mathbf{y},\mathbf{x}_1(\mathbf{y}))}{\partial\mathbf{y}} + \frac{\partial\,\mathcal{U}(\mathbf{y},\mathbf{x}_1(\mathbf{y}))}{\partial\mathbf{x}_1}\,\frac{\partial\mathbf{x}_1(\mathbf{y})}{\partial\mathbf{y}}, \tag{4.8} \] \[ \frac{\partial\mathbf{x}_1(\mathbf{y})}{\partial\mathbf{y}} = -\frac{\partial^2\mathcal{L}(\mathbf{x}_0,\mathbf{y})}{\partial\mathbf{x}_0\,\partial\mathbf{y}} . \tag{4.9} \]

Equation (4.9) is \(\mathbf{B}_1\) from §2 for a gradient step with the learning rate set to 1; with a general learning rate it is \(-\eta\,\partial^2\mathcal{L}/\partial\mathbf{x}_0\partial\mathbf{y}\). The matrix of mixed second derivatives is \(n\times m\) and expensive, but (4.8) needs only its product with the row vector \(\partial\mathcal{U}/\partial\mathbf{x}_1\).

Filling the gap: where the finite difference (4.10) comes from

Let \(\mathbf{v} = (\partial\mathcal{U}/\partial\mathbf{x}_1)\T\). We want \(\mathbf{v}\T\,\dfrac{\partial^2\mathcal{L}}{\partial\mathbf{x}\,\partial\mathbf{y}}\). Its transpose is \(\dfrac{\partial^2\mathcal{L}}{\partial\mathbf{y}\,\partial\mathbf{x}}\,\mathbf{v}\), and that is a directional derivative: the rate at which the gradient \(\partial\mathcal{L}/\partial\mathbf{y}\) changes when \(\mathbf{x}\) moves along \(\mathbf{v}\). A central difference estimates it from two gradient evaluations at \(\mathbf{x}_0^{\pm} = \mathbf{x}_0 \pm \epsilon\,\mathbf{v}\):

\[ \frac{\partial^2\mathcal{L}}{\partial\mathbf{y}\,\partial\mathbf{x}}\,\mathbf{v} \;\approx\; \frac{1}{2\epsilon}\left( \frac{\partial\mathcal{L}(\mathbf{x}_0^{+},\mathbf{y})}{\partial\mathbf{y}} - \frac{\partial\mathcal{L}(\mathbf{x}_0^{-},\mathbf{y})}{\partial\mathbf{y}} \right) . \]

This is the right-hand side of the book's (4.10). To get the second term of (4.8), multiply by the factor from (4.9): \(-1\), or \(-\eta\) for a general learning rate. Keep track of that sign when you implement it.

Toy check with \(x_0 = 1\), \(y = 2\), \(\eta = 0.1\): \(x_1 = 1.2\), so \(v = x_1 - 1.5 = -0.3\). Here \(\partial\mathcal{L}/\partial y = y - x^2\). With \(\epsilon = 0.01\): \(x_0^{+} = 0.997\), \(x_0^{-} = 1.003\), and

\[ \frac{(2 - 0.997^2) - (2 - 1.003^2)}{0.02} = \frac{1.005991 - 0.993991}{0.02} = 0.6 . \]

Exact value: \((-2x_0)\,v = (-2)(-0.3) = 0.6\). The gradient term is \(-\eta\times 0.6 = -0.06\), which is what the widget shows at K = 1.

One caution from the book: the perturbation \(\mathbf{x}_0 \pm \epsilon\,\mathbf{v}\) is a plain addition only for vector variables. If \(\mathbf{x}\) contains rotations or poses, the perturbation must be applied on the manifold, which is the subject of Day 4. §4.2.2 · p. 106

Common mistakes

  • "Unrolling gives the gradient of the bilevel problem." It gives the gradient of \(\mathcal{U}(\mathbf{x}_T)\). The two agree only when \(\mathbf{x}_T\) has converged.
  • "More inner steps always cost more memory." Only in reverse mode without truncation. With truncation the memory is set by \(M\), not \(T\).
  • "If the initial guess is good, no gradient is lost." With zero inner steps, \(\mathbf{x}_0\) does not depend on \(\mathbf{y}\) at all (unless the initializer does) and the indirect gradient is exactly zero, however good the guess.

Check yourself

Q1. Toy problem, gradient descent with η = 0.1 from x₀ = 1 at y = 2. The initial guess does not depend on y. What is dx₁/dy?

S₁ = B₁ = −η · ∂²L/∂x∂y = −0.1 · (−2 · 1) = 0.2. The value 0.333 is the converged sensitivity; 0.4 is what one Gauss-Newton step gives.

Q2. You unroll T = 200 solver iterations in reverse mode. Each iterate has n = 500,000 numbers stored as 8-byte floats. How much memory do the stored iterates alone need?

200 × 500,000 × 8 bytes = 800,000,000 bytes = 800 MB. One iterate is only 4 MB; the factor T is the cost of unrolling.

Q3. Near the solution, each backward step multiplies the adjoint by A = 0.5. If you truncate the backward pass to the last M = 3 steps, what fraction of the converged gradient is missing?

The truncated sum is (1 − A^M) of the full one, so the missing fraction is A^M = 0.5³ = 0.125.

Q4. In the widget at η = 0.1 and K = 2 the unrolled gradient is −0.0607 but the finite-difference reference is −0.0447. What explains the gap?

Unrolling differentiates the program that ran. Two steps of gradient descent define a different function of y than the converged solution does. Forward and reverse mode give the same −0.0607.

Q5. One-step approximation with learning rate η = 0.1. The central difference of ∂L/∂y along v = ∂U/∂x₁ returns 0.6. What is the second term of (4.8)?

The finite difference estimates (∂²L/∂y∂x)·v. The term in (4.8) multiplies it by ∂x₁/∂y's factor −η from (4.9): −0.1 × 0.6 = −0.06.

Recap

  1. Unrolling writes the solver as \(\mathbf{x}_T = (\Phi_T\circ\dots\circ\Phi_0)(\mathbf{y})\) and differentiates that composition with AutoDiff.
  2. The sensitivity obeys \(\mathbf{S}_t = \mathbf{A}_t\mathbf{S}_{t-1} + \mathbf{B}_t\); reverse mode evaluates the same sum backward with adjoints \(\boldsymbol{\lambda}_{t-1} = \mathbf{A}_t\T\boldsymbol{\lambda}_t\) and must store all iterates.
  3. The result is exact for \(\mathbf{x}_T\) and approaches the true bilevel gradient as the inner solver converges.
  4. Truncating to the last \(M\) steps drops terms of size about \(A^M\); fast inner solvers tolerate short truncation.
  5. The one-step version (4.8)–(4.10) needs only two extra gradient evaluations, at the price of a large bias when one step is far from solving the lower level.

Sources

  1. SLAM Handbook, §4.2.1 "Unrolled Differentiation" and §4.2.2 "Truncated Unrolled Differentiation", pp. 104–106; Algorithm 1; equations (4.4)–(4.10).
  2. Griewank and Walther, Evaluating Derivatives: Principles and Techniques of Algorithmic Differentiation, 2nd ed., 2008 (forward and reverse accumulation through an iteration, memory of the reverse sweep).
  3. Nocedal and Wright, Numerical Optimization, 2006 (convergence rates of gradient descent and Gauss-Newton; finite-difference directional derivatives). The sensitivity recursion, the geometric-series bias estimate, and the toy numbers are this app's own working of standard material.

Week 7 · Day 3

Implicit differentiation: the gradient from the optimality condition

After today you can derive the sensitivity of the back-end solution from its optimality condition, compute the upper-level gradient with one linear solve built from Hessian-vector products, and choose between unrolled and implicit differentiation.

About 60 min · Read §4.2.3, pp. 107–108 (2 pages) · Needs Week 7 Day 2

Read first: §4.2.3, pp. 107–108

While you read, look for:

  • The calculus reminder on p. 107: differentiating an equation that defines a function, without solving it first.
  • Equations (4.11) and (4.12) on p. 107: which fact about \(\mathbf{x}^*\) is being differentiated.
  • Example 4.3 on p. 107: 4 MB against 4 TB.
  • Equation (4.15) and Algorithm 2 on p. 108: the Hessian appears only multiplied by a vector.

Today's big idea

At the solution the gradient of the lower-level cost is zero, for every \(\mathbf{y}\). Differentiating that one equation gives \(\partial\mathbf{x}^*/\partial\mathbf{y}\) in terms of second derivatives of \(\mathcal{L}\) at the solution only. How the solver got there does not matter, nothing has to be stored along the way, and the whole upper-level gradient costs one linear solve with the Hessian.

1. A derivative without a formula

Some functions are defined by an equation, not by an explicit formula. The book's reminder uses \(x + y + 5 = 0\). §4.2.3 · p. 107 A less trivial case: let \(x(y)\) be defined by

\[ F(x, y) = x^3 + x - y = 0 . \]

For each \(y\) there is one real \(x\), but no pleasant formula for it. Differentiate the equation itself with respect to \(y\), remembering that \(x\) depends on \(y\):

\[ 3x^2\,\frac{dx}{dy} + \frac{dx}{dy} - 1 = 0 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \frac{dx}{dy} = \frac{1}{3x^2 + 1} . \]

At \(y = 2\) the solution is \(x = 1\) (check: \(1 + 1 - 2 = 0\)), so \(dx/dy = 1/4\). We needed the point on the curve, found any way we like, and derivatives of \(F\) at that point. This is implicit differentiation.

Filling the gap: the implicit function theorem

The step "remembering that \(x\) depends on \(y\)" assumes a differentiable function \(x(y)\) exists. The implicit function theorem says when. Let \(F:\R^n\times\R^m\to\R^n\) be continuously differentiable with \(F(\mathbf{x}_0,\mathbf{y}_0) = \mathbf{0}\). If the \(n\times n\) matrix \(\partial F/\partial\mathbf{x}\) is invertible at \((\mathbf{x}_0,\mathbf{y}_0)\), then near \(\mathbf{y}_0\) there is exactly one continuously differentiable function \(\mathbf{x}(\mathbf{y})\) with \(\mathbf{x}(\mathbf{y}_0)=\mathbf{x}_0\) and \(F(\mathbf{x}(\mathbf{y}),\mathbf{y}) = \mathbf{0}\), and

\[ \frac{\partial\mathbf{x}}{\partial\mathbf{y}} = -\left(\frac{\partial F}{\partial\mathbf{x}}\right)^{-1}\frac{\partial F}{\partial\mathbf{y}} . \]

The formula is what you get by differentiating \(F(\mathbf{x}(\mathbf{y}),\mathbf{y}) = \mathbf{0}\) with the chain rule, \(\frac{\partial F}{\partial\mathbf{x}}\frac{\partial\mathbf{x}}{\partial\mathbf{y}} + \frac{\partial F}{\partial\mathbf{y}} = \mathbf{0}\), and solving. The theorem is local: it describes the solution branch through \((\mathbf{x}_0,\mathbf{y}_0)\), nothing more.

2. Apply it to the optimality condition

Which equation defines \(\mathbf{x}^*(\mathbf{y})\)? The lower-level solution is a stationary point of \(\mathcal{L}\), so (assuming \(\mathcal{L}\) is twice differentiable in both arguments) §4.2.3 · p. 107

\[ \frac{\partial\mathcal{L}(\mathbf{x}^*(\mathbf{y}),\mathbf{y})}{\partial\mathbf{x}^*(\mathbf{y})} = \mathbf{0} \qquad\text{for every } \mathbf{y}. \]

Take \(F = \partial\mathcal{L}/\partial\mathbf{x}\) in the theorem. Differentiating both sides with respect to \(\mathbf{y}\) gives

\[ \frac{\partial^2\mathcal{L}(\mathbf{x}^*(\mathbf{y}),\mathbf{y})}{\partial\mathbf{x}^*(\mathbf{y})\,\partial\mathbf{y}} + \frac{\partial^2\mathcal{L}(\mathbf{x}^*(\mathbf{y}),\mathbf{y})}{\partial\mathbf{x}^*(\mathbf{y})\,\partial\mathbf{x}^*(\mathbf{y})}\cdot\frac{\partial\mathbf{x}^*(\mathbf{y})}{\partial\mathbf{y}} = \mathbf{0}, \tag{4.11} \] \[ \frac{\partial\mathbf{x}^*(\mathbf{y})}{\partial\mathbf{y}} = -\left(\frac{\partial^2\mathcal{L}(\mathbf{x}^*(\mathbf{y}),\mathbf{y})}{\partial\mathbf{x}^*(\mathbf{y})\,\partial\mathbf{x}^*(\mathbf{y})}\right)^{-1}\frac{\partial^2\mathcal{L}(\mathbf{x}^*(\mathbf{y}),\mathbf{y})}{\partial\mathbf{x}^*(\mathbf{y})\,\partial\mathbf{y}} . \tag{4.12} \]

In short: \(\partial\mathbf{x}^*/\partial\mathbf{y} = -\mathbf{H}^{-1}\,\mathbf{H}_{xy}\), where \(\mathbf{H} = \partial^2\mathcal{L}/\partial\mathbf{x}\partial\mathbf{x}\) is the \(n\times n\) Hessian of the lower-level cost and \(\mathbf{H}_{xy} = \partial^2\mathcal{L}/\partial\mathbf{x}\partial\mathbf{y}\) is the \(n\times m\) matrix of mixed second derivatives, both at the solution. The indirect gradient has become direct derivatives of \(\mathcal{L}\), at the cost of inverting a Hessian. §4.2.3 · p. 107

Toy problem. From Day 2: \(\partial^2\mathcal{L}/\partial x^2 = 6x^2 - 2y + 1\) and \(\partial^2\mathcal{L}/\partial x\,\partial y = -2x\). At \(y = 2\), \(x^* = (1+\sqrt3)/2 = 1.3660\):

\[ H = 6(1.8660) - 4 + 1 = 8.196, \qquad \frac{dx^*}{dy} = -\frac{-2(1.3660)}{8.196} = \frac{2.732}{8.196} = \frac13 . \]

That is the 0.333 that two extra solves gave by finite differences on Day 1, and the value the unrolled sensitivities 0.2000, 0.3272, 0.3491 of Day 2 were converging to. It took no extra solve and no stored iterates.

Try it: move y along the curve, then press the upper-level step button repeatedly.

Notice that at y = 2 the tangent slope is 0.3333 and dU/dy = −0.0447. Each upper-level step moves y to the right, toward y ≈ 2.417 where the curve crosses the ground-truth line and U reaches zero. Then press Reset and set the Algorithm 2 step size to 0.30: the iteration for q diverges, because 0.30 is above 2/H = 0.244 (see §4).

Intuition

Picture the lower-level cost as a valley whose floor shifts when \(\mathbf{y}\) changes. \(\mathbf{H}_{xy}\) says how hard a change in \(\mathbf{y}\) pushes the ball sideways (it is the change in the slope \(\partial\mathcal{L}/\partial\mathbf{x}\)). \(\mathbf{H}\) is the stiffness of the valley. Displacement = push divided by stiffness: a stiff, well-constrained SLAM problem moves little when a measurement changes; a floppy one moves a lot.

The theorem's condition matters: \(\mathbf{H}\) must be invertible. At a strict minimum it is positive definite, so this holds. If the lower-level problem has directions that the measurements do not constrain at all, \(\mathbf{H}\) is singular, the minimizer is not unique, and "the derivative of the solution" has no meaning until those directions are fixed.

3. Never build the big matrices

Substitute (4.12) into the gradient (4.3): §4.2.3 · p. 107

\[ \nabla_{\mathbf{y}}\,\mathcal{U} = \frac{\partial\,\mathcal{U}(\mathbf{y},\mathbf{x}^*)}{\partial\mathbf{y}} - \underbrace{\frac{\partial\,\mathcal{U}(\mathbf{y},\mathbf{x}^*)}{\partial\mathbf{x}^*}}_{\mathbf{v}\T}\; \underbrace{\left(\frac{\partial^2\mathcal{L}}{\partial\mathbf{x}^*\partial\mathbf{x}^*}\right)^{-1}}_{(\mathbf{H}\T)^{-1}}\; \frac{\partial^2\mathcal{L}}{\partial\mathbf{x}^*\partial\mathbf{y}} = \frac{\partial\,\mathcal{U}(\mathbf{y},\mathbf{x}^*)}{\partial\mathbf{y}} - \mathbf{q}\T\cdot\frac{\partial^2\mathcal{L}}{\partial\mathbf{x}^*\partial\mathbf{y}} . \tag{4.13} \]

The product of three factors can be grouped in two ways, and the choice decides the cost.

So define \(\mathbf{q}\) as the solution of \(\mathbf{H}\mathbf{q} = \mathbf{v}\), with \(\mathbf{v} = (\partial\mathcal{U}/\partial\mathbf{x}^*)\T\). (The Hessian is symmetric, so \(\mathbf{H}\T = \mathbf{H}\).) This is the same trick as reverse mode on Day 1: push the single output's sensitivity backward instead of pushing every parameter's influence forward. The vector \(\mathbf{q}\) is called the adjoint, and the procedure the adjoint method.

Even one solve can be too much if \(\mathbf{H}\) must be stored. In Example 4.3, a model with \(10^6\) parameters as 32-bit floats takes \(10^6\times 4\) bytes \(= 4\) MB, and its Hessian \((10^6)^2\times 4\) bytes \(= 4\) TB. Example 4.3 · p. 107 The way out is to solve \(\mathbf{H}\mathbf{q}=\mathbf{v}\) with a method that only ever asks for products \(\mathbf{H}\mathbf{q}\).

4. Solving Hq = v with Hessian-vector products

The book turns the linear system into a minimization, §4.2.3 · p. 108

\[ \mathbf{q}^* = \argmin_{\mathbf{q}}\; Q(\mathbf{q}) = \argmin_{\mathbf{q}}\; \tfrac12\,\mathbf{q}\T\mathbf{H}\mathbf{q} - \mathbf{q}\T\mathbf{v}, \tag{4.14} \]

and solves it by gradient descent (Algorithm 2) or conjugate gradient:

\[ \mathbf{q}_k = \mathbf{q}_{k-1} - \eta\,(\mathbf{H}\mathbf{q}_{k-1} - \mathbf{v}) . \tag{4.16} \]

The product \(\mathbf{H}\mathbf{q}\) is computed without \(\mathbf{H}\), as "the gradient of a gradient-vector product":

\[ \mathbf{H}\mathbf{q} = \frac{\partial^2\mathcal{L}}{\partial\mathbf{x}\,\partial\mathbf{x}}\cdot\mathbf{q} = \frac{\partial\left(\frac{\partial\mathcal{L}}{\partial\mathbf{x}}\cdot\mathbf{q}\right)}{\partial\mathbf{x}} . \tag{4.15} \]

Finally \(\nabla_{\mathbf{y}}\,\mathcal{U} = \partial\mathcal{U}/\partial\mathbf{y} - (\mathbf{H}_{yx}\,\mathbf{q})\T\) with \(\mathbf{H}_{yx} = \partial^2\mathcal{L}/\partial\mathbf{y}\,\partial\mathbf{x}^* = \mathbf{H}_{xy}\T\), equation (4.17), which is one more product of the same kind.

Filling the gap: three steps the book states without proof

Why minimizing Q solves the system. \(\partial Q/\partial\mathbf{q} = \mathbf{H}\mathbf{q} - \mathbf{v}\) (using the symmetry of \(\mathbf{H}\)). At a minimum the gradient is zero, so \(\mathbf{H}\mathbf{q} = \mathbf{v}\). With \(\mathbf{H}\) positive definite, \(Q\) is a bowl with exactly one minimum.

Why (4.15) holds. Hold \(\mathbf{q}\) constant. The scalar \(s(\mathbf{x}) = \frac{\partial\mathcal{L}}{\partial\mathbf{x}}\cdot\mathbf{q} = \sum_j \frac{\partial\mathcal{L}}{\partial x_j}q_j\) has \(i\)-th partial derivative \(\sum_j \frac{\partial^2\mathcal{L}}{\partial x_i\partial x_j}q_j\), which is the \(i\)-th entry of \(\mathbf{H}\mathbf{q}\). In practice: one reverse pass for the gradient, a dot product with \(\mathbf{q}\), and one more reverse pass through that computation. The cost is a small multiple of one gradient, and the memory is that of vectors.

When (4.16) converges. Subtract the exact solution \(\mathbf{q}^*\): the error obeys \(\mathbf{q}_k - \mathbf{q}^* = (\mathbf{I} - \eta\mathbf{H})(\mathbf{q}_{k-1} - \mathbf{q}^*)\). Along an eigenvector of \(\mathbf{H}\) with eigenvalue \(\lambda\) the error is multiplied by \(1 - \eta\lambda\) each step, so it shrinks if and only if \(|1-\eta\lambda| \lt 1\) for every eigenvalue, that is \(0 \lt \eta \lt 2/\lambda_{\max}\). If the eigenvalues are spread widely (an ill-conditioned Hessian), the small ones converge slowly; conjugate gradient copes with that much better.

Toy numbers. \(v = x^* - 1.5 = -0.1340\), \(H = 8.196\), \(\eta = 0.1\), \(q_0 = 0\):

\[ q_1 = -0.0134, \quad q_2 = -0.0158, \quad q_3 = -0.0163, \;\dots\;\to\; \frac{v}{H} = -0.01635 . \]

The error shrinks by the factor \(|1 - 0.1\times 8.196| = 0.18\) per step. Then \(\nabla_y\,\mathcal{U} = 0 - q\,H_{xy} = -(-0.01635)(-2.732) = -0.0447\).

Going deeper (optional): what a SLAM back-end already has

For a least-squares cost \(\mathcal{L} = \tfrac12\norm{\mathbf{r}}^2\) the Hessian is \(\mathbf{J}\T\mathbf{J}\) plus a term that multiplies the residuals by their second derivatives. Gauss-Newton drops the second term. A back-end that has just converged holds \(\mathbf{J}\T\mathbf{J}\) and usually a factorization of it, so an approximate adjoint solve \(\mathbf{J}\T\mathbf{J}\,\mathbf{q} = \mathbf{v}\) is nearly free. In the toy problem \(\mathbf{J}\T\mathbf{J} = 4x^{*2}+1 = 8.464\) against the exact \(H = 8.196\); the slope would come out as \(2.732/8.464 = 0.323\) where the exact value is 0.333. The approximation is good when the residuals at the solution are small.

5. Unrolled or implicit?

QuestionUnrolled (Day 2)Implicit (today)
What must be differentiable?every step of the solveronly the cost L, twice; the solver can be anything
Must the solver have converged?no: exact for whatever x at T it producedyes: the formula assumes ∂L/∂x = 0
Memorygrows with the number of steps T (or M)independent of T
Extra worka backward sweep through the stepsone linear solve with H
Breaks down whenT is large, or steps are not differentiableH is singular or badly conditioned, or the solver stopped early

Algorithm 1 on p. 105 applies the implicit formula at \(\mathbf{x}_T\), the iterate the solver actually returned. The widget from Day 2 shows what that does when \(T\) is small:

Notice the violet curve, the implicit formula evaluated at x_K (its values at K = 0 and 1 are far below the chart; the tile shows them). At K = 2 it reads −0.0662, further from the reference −0.0447 than the unrolled value −0.0607, because x₂ is not a stationary point and the formula's assumption fails. Once the inner solver has converged the two coincide.

Approximations. The cheapest option of all ignores the implicit part and keeps only the direct term, \(\hat\nabla_{\mathbf{y}}\,\mathcal{U} \approx \partial\mathcal{U}/\partial\mathbf{y}\,|_{\mathbf{x}_T}\). It treats the solver's output as a constant in the upper-level problem. The error is of the size of the dropped term, §4.2.3 · p. 108

\[ \epsilon \sim \left|\frac{\partial\,\mathcal{U}}{\partial\mathbf{x}^*}\,\frac{\partial\mathbf{x}^*}{\partial\mathbf{y}}\right| . \tag{4.18} \]

The book notes it is useful when the implicit part contains products of small second-order derivatives. It is useless when \(\mathcal{U}\) has no direct dependence on \(\mathbf{y}\): in the toy problem it returns exactly zero.

Common mistakes

  • "Implicit differentiation needs the inverse Hessian." It needs the solution of one linear system \(\mathbf{H}\mathbf{q}=\mathbf{v}\), and that needs only products \(\mathbf{H}\mathbf{q}\).
  • "It is exact, so it is safe to stop the inner solver early." It is exact at a stationary point. Evaluated elsewhere it is the derivative of nothing in particular.
  • "The mixed term has the same sign convention as the Hessian." Watch the minus sign in (4.12). In the toy problem \(H_{xy} = -2x\) is negative and the slope \(dx^*/dy\) is positive.

Check yourself

Q1. Let L(x, y) = ½(x − y)² + (3/2)x². Use (4.12) to find dx*/dy.

∂L/∂x = (x − y) + 3x, so H = 4 and ∂²L/∂x∂y = −1. dx*/dy = −(1/4)(−1) = 1/4. Check: the minimizer is x* = y/4.

Q2. In the toy problem at y = 1 the solution is x* = 1. What is dx*/dy there?

H = 6x² − 2y + 1 = 6 − 2 + 1 = 5 and ∂²L/∂x∂y = −2x = −2, so dx*/dy = 2/5 = 0.4.

Q3. Algorithm 2 runs on a scalar problem with H = 4. Which step size makes the iteration diverge?

The error is multiplied by 1 − ηH each step: 0.6, 0, −0.6, −1.4. Only |−1.4| exceeds 1. The limit is η = 2/H = 0.5.

Q4. With n = 600 back-end variables and m = 1,000,000 network weights, why solve Hq = v rather than first computing ∂x*/∂y = −H⁻¹·∂²L/∂x∂y?

Both groupings give the same gradient. Solving for q costs one linear solve; forming ∂x*/∂y costs one per parameter and stores a 600 × 1,000,000 dense matrix.

Q5. A lower-level problem has n = 100,000 variables. How much memory would its dense Hessian take in 8-byte floats?

(10⁵)² × 8 bytes = 8 × 10¹⁰ bytes = 80 GB. The vector itself takes 0.8 MB. This is Example 4.3 with other numbers.

Recap

  1. The solution satisfies \(\partial\mathcal{L}/\partial\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{0}\) for every \(\mathbf{y}\); differentiating this gives \(\partial\mathbf{x}^*/\partial\mathbf{y} = -\mathbf{H}^{-1}\mathbf{H}_{xy}\), equation (4.12).
  2. The implicit function theorem justifies the step and requires \(\mathbf{H}\) to be invertible.
  3. The upper-level gradient needs only \(\mathbf{q} = \mathbf{H}^{-1}\mathbf{v}\): one adjoint solve, equation (4.13).
  4. The solve uses Hessian-vector products (4.15), so \(\mathbf{H}\) is never formed; gradient descent on \(Q\) converges for \(\eta \lt 2/\lambda_{\max}\).
  5. Implicit differentiation is memory-free in the number of solver steps but assumes convergence; unrolling is the reverse.

Sources

  1. SLAM Handbook, §4.2.3 "Implicit Differentiation", pp. 107–108; Example 4.3; Algorithm 2; equations (4.11)–(4.18). Algorithm 1, p. 105.
  2. Rudin, Principles of Mathematical Analysis, 3rd ed., 1976 (the implicit function theorem).
  3. Pearlmutter, Fast exact multiplication by the Hessian, 1994 (Hessian-vector products by differentiating a gradient-vector product).
  4. Nocedal and Wright, Numerical Optimization, 2006 (quadratic minimization and linear systems, step-size condition for gradient descent, conjugate gradient, the Gauss-Newton approximation of the Hessian).
  5. Griewank and Walther, Evaluating Derivatives, 2nd ed., 2008 (the adjoint method).

Week 7 · Day 4

Derivatives on Lie groups

After today you can define the Jacobian of a function between Lie groups with the plus and minus operators, derive the Jacobians of inversion, composition, and group action, chain them, and take a gradient step on a manifold.

About 60 min · Read §4.3, pp. 109–113 (5 pages) · Needs Week 4 Days 3 and 5

Read first: §4.3, pp. 109–113

While you read, look for:

  • Equations (4.21) and (4.22) on p. 109: the right and left versions of ⊕ and ⊖, and which frame each perturbation lives in.
  • Equation (4.23) on p. 110: the definition of a Jacobian when neither input nor output is a vector.
  • The three closed forms on p. 112, equations (4.32)–(4.34). Each ends one step before the final answer; today finishes them.
  • Example 4.4 on p. 111 and Example 4.5 on p. 113: how the Jacobians are used.

Today's big idea

Poses cannot be subtracted, so the usual definition of a derivative does not apply to them. Replace "+" by ⊕ (perturb through the exponential map) and "−" by ⊖ (compare through the logarithm) and the definition works again. The result is an ordinary matrix that maps a small tangent vector at the input to a small tangent vector at the output, and it obeys the ordinary chain rule. This is what lets AutoDiff, unrolling, and implicit differentiation run on SLAM variables.

1. Plus and minus on a group

Recall from Week 4 · Day 2: a Lie group \(\mathcal{M}\) is a smooth manifold; at each element \(\boldsymbol{\chi}\) there is a tangent space, a vector space where calculus works; \(\Exp\) maps a tangent vector \(\boldsymbol{\tau}\in\R^n\) to a group element and \(\Log\) maps back, equation (4.20). §4.3.1 · p. 109 The chapter writes group elements as \(\boldsymbol{\chi}\) and composition as \(\circ\).

To measure a small change between two group elements, combine one \(\Exp\) or \(\Log\) with one composition. Because composition does not commute, there are two versions: §4.3.1 · pp. 109–110

\[ \begin{aligned} \text{right-}\oplus: \quad & \boldsymbol{\chi}_2 = \boldsymbol{\chi}_1\oplus\boldsymbol{\tau} \triangleq \boldsymbol{\chi}_1\circ\Exp(\boldsymbol{\tau}), & \qquad \text{right-}\ominus: \quad & \boldsymbol{\tau} = \boldsymbol{\chi}_2\ominus\boldsymbol{\chi}_1 \triangleq \Log(\boldsymbol{\chi}_1^{-1}\circ\boldsymbol{\chi}_2), \\ \text{left-}\oplus: \quad & \boldsymbol{\chi}_2 = \boldsymbol{\varepsilon}\oplus\boldsymbol{\chi}_1 \triangleq \Exp(\boldsymbol{\varepsilon})\circ\boldsymbol{\chi}_1, & \qquad \text{left-}\ominus: \quad & \boldsymbol{\varepsilon} = \boldsymbol{\chi}_2\ominus\boldsymbol{\chi}_1 \triangleq \Log(\boldsymbol{\chi}_2\circ\boldsymbol{\chi}_1^{-1}). \end{aligned} \]

These are equations (4.21) and (4.22). The right perturbation \(\boldsymbol{\tau}\) is expressed in the local frame at \(\boldsymbol{\chi}_1\); the left perturbation \(\boldsymbol{\varepsilon}\) is expressed in the global frame.

Example on SE(2). A planar pose at position \((2, 0)\) with heading 90°, and the tangent vector "one unit forward, no turn", \((1, 0, 0)\) (translation first, as in the book). Right-⊕ applies it in the robot's own frame: the robot moves along its heading to \((2, 1)\). Left-⊕ applies the same vector in the world frame: the pose is shifted along the world x-axis to \((3, 0)\). Same numbers, different meaning.

2. The Jacobian of a function between groups

For \(f:\mathcal{M}\to\mathcal{N}\) the book defines, with the right operators, §4.3.1 · p. 110

\[ \frac{\partial f(\boldsymbol{\chi})}{\partial\boldsymbol{\chi}} \triangleq \lim_{\boldsymbol{\tau}\to 0}\frac{f(\boldsymbol{\chi}\oplus\boldsymbol{\tau})\ominus f(\boldsymbol{\chi})}{\boldsymbol{\tau}} = \lim_{\boldsymbol{\tau}\to 0}\frac{\Log\!\big(f(\boldsymbol{\chi})^{-1}\circ f(\boldsymbol{\chi}\circ\Exp(\boldsymbol{\tau}))\big)}{\boldsymbol{\tau}} . \tag{4.23} \]

This is the right Jacobian \(\mathbf{J}_R\). It maps the tangent space at \(\boldsymbol{\chi}\) to the tangent space at \(f(\boldsymbol{\chi})\), both local. Using the left operators instead gives the left Jacobian \(\mathbf{J}_L\), equation (4.25), which maps between the global tangent spaces.

Filling the gap: what "divide by a vector" means
