You cannot divide by \(\boldsymbol{\tau}\). The notation is shorthand. Define the ordinary vector function \(g(\boldsymbol{\tau}) = \Log\big(f(\boldsymbol{\chi})^{-1}\circ f(\boldsymbol{\chi}\circ\Exp(\boldsymbol{\tau}))\big)\). It takes a vector, returns a vector, and \(g(\mathbf{0}) = \mathbf{0}\). The Jacobian is its ordinary matrix of partial derivatives at zero, which is equation (4.24):

\[ \mathbf{J}_R = \frac{\partial g(\boldsymbol{\tau})}{\partial\boldsymbol{\tau}}\bigg|_{\boldsymbol{\tau}=\mathbf{0}} \qquad\Longleftrightarrow\qquad f(\boldsymbol{\chi}\oplus\boldsymbol{\tau}) \approx f(\boldsymbol{\chi})\oplus\mathbf{J}_R\,\boldsymbol{\tau} \quad\text{for small } \boldsymbol{\tau}. \]

The second form is the one to remember: perturb the input by \(\boldsymbol{\tau}\), and the output is perturbed by \(\mathbf{J}_R\boldsymbol{\tau}\). Column \(j\) of \(\mathbf{J}_R\) is what happens to the output when you nudge the input along the \(j\)-th tangent direction. The widget below computes Jacobians exactly this way, with a nudge of \(10^{-5}\).

Sanity check: if both groups are plain vector spaces with addition, then \(\Exp\) and \(\Log\) are the identity map, ⊕ is +, ⊖ is −, and (4.23) is the usual derivative.

The two Jacobians carry the same information. A left perturbation can be moved to the right with the adjoint (Week 4 · Day 5): \(\Exp(\boldsymbol{\varepsilon})\circ\boldsymbol{\chi} = \boldsymbol{\chi}\circ\Exp(\Ad_{\boldsymbol{\chi}}^{-1}\boldsymbol{\varepsilon})\). Doing this at the input and the output gives \(\mathbf{J}_L = \Ad_{f(\boldsymbol{\chi})}\,\mathbf{J}_R\,\Ad_{\boldsymbol{\chi}}^{-1}\).

3. Closed forms: inversion, composition, and the chain rule

For the basic operations the limit can be worked out once and reused. With these blocks, derivatives of longer expressions follow from the chain rule, which holds for these Jacobians exactly as for ordinary ones: §4.3.2 · pp. 111–112

\[ \frac{\partial\mathcal{Z}}{\partial\boldsymbol{\chi}} = \frac{\partial\mathcal{Z}}{\partial\mathcal{Y}}\,\frac{\partial\mathcal{Y}}{\partial\boldsymbol{\chi}}, \qquad \mathcal{Z} = g(\mathcal{Y}),\; \mathcal{Y} = f(\boldsymbol{\chi}). \tag{4.31} \]

The book's derivations (4.32) and (4.33) stop at expressions such as \((\boldsymbol{\chi}_1^{-1}\boldsymbol{\tau}^\wedge\boldsymbol{\chi}_1)^\vee/\boldsymbol{\tau}\). One fact from Week 4 finishes them.

Filling the gap: finishing the three limits

The adjoint \(\Ad_{\boldsymbol{\chi}}\) is the matrix defined by \(\Ad_{\boldsymbol{\chi}}\boldsymbol{\tau} = (\boldsymbol{\chi}\,\boldsymbol{\tau}^\wedge\boldsymbol{\chi}^{-1})^\vee\). It moves an exponential across a group element:

\[ \boldsymbol{\chi}\circ\Exp(\boldsymbol{\tau})\circ\boldsymbol{\chi}^{-1} = \Exp(\Ad_{\boldsymbol{\chi}}\boldsymbol{\tau}) . \]

Inversion, \(f(\boldsymbol{\chi}) = \boldsymbol{\chi}^{-1}\). Put it into (4.23) and use \((\boldsymbol{\chi}\Exp(\boldsymbol{\tau}))^{-1} = \Exp(-\boldsymbol{\tau})\boldsymbol{\chi}^{-1}\):

\[ \Log\big((\boldsymbol{\chi}^{-1})^{-1}\,(\boldsymbol{\chi}\Exp(\boldsymbol{\tau}))^{-1}\big) = \Log\big(\boldsymbol{\chi}\,\Exp(-\boldsymbol{\tau})\,\boldsymbol{\chi}^{-1}\big) = \Log\big(\Exp(-\Ad_{\boldsymbol{\chi}}\boldsymbol{\tau})\big) = -\Ad_{\boldsymbol{\chi}}\,\boldsymbol{\tau} . \]

This is linear in \(\boldsymbol{\tau}\), so the Jacobian is the matrix in front: \(\dfrac{\partial\boldsymbol{\chi}^{-1}}{\partial\boldsymbol{\chi}} = -\Ad_{\boldsymbol{\chi}}\). That completes (4.32).

Composition, first factor, \(f(\boldsymbol{\chi}) = \boldsymbol{\chi}\circ\boldsymbol{\chi}_1\):

\[ \Log\big((\boldsymbol{\chi}\boldsymbol{\chi}_1)^{-1}\,\boldsymbol{\chi}\Exp(\boldsymbol{\tau})\boldsymbol{\chi}_1\big) = \Log\big(\boldsymbol{\chi}_1^{-1}\Exp(\boldsymbol{\tau})\boldsymbol{\chi}_1\big) = \Ad_{\boldsymbol{\chi}_1^{-1}}\boldsymbol{\tau} \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \frac{\partial(\boldsymbol{\chi}\circ\boldsymbol{\chi}_1)}{\partial\boldsymbol{\chi}} = \Ad_{\boldsymbol{\chi}_1^{-1}} . \]

That completes (4.33). Composition, second factor: \(\Log\big((\boldsymbol{\chi}\boldsymbol{\chi}_1)^{-1}\boldsymbol{\chi}\boldsymbol{\chi}_1\Exp(\boldsymbol{\tau})\big) = \Log(\Exp(\boldsymbol{\tau})) = \boldsymbol{\tau}\), so the Jacobian is \(\mathbf{I}\), equation (4.34).

Chain-rule check. For \(h(\boldsymbol{\chi}) = (\boldsymbol{\chi}\circ\boldsymbol{\chi}_1)^{-1}\), (4.31) gives \(-\Ad_{\boldsymbol{\chi}\boldsymbol{\chi}_1}\cdot\Ad_{\boldsymbol{\chi}_1^{-1}} = -\Ad_{\boldsymbol{\chi}}\Ad_{\boldsymbol{\chi}_1}\Ad_{\boldsymbol{\chi}_1}^{-1} = -\Ad_{\boldsymbol{\chi}}\). Directly: \(h = \boldsymbol{\chi}_1^{-1}\circ\boldsymbol{\chi}^{-1}\), a composition whose second factor is \(\boldsymbol{\chi}^{-1}\), so the Jacobian is \(\mathbf{I}\cdot(-\Ad_{\boldsymbol{\chi}})\). The two routes agree.

OperationRight JacobianWhy, in words
χ⁻¹ with respect to χ−Ad of χinverting flips the sign of the perturbation and moves it from the right of χ to the right of χ⁻¹
χ ∘ χ₁ with respect to χAd of χ₁⁻¹the perturbation sits in the middle of the product and must be carried past χ₁
χ ∘ χ₁ with respect to χ₁identitya right perturbation of the last factor is already a right perturbation of the product

Try it: a planar two-link arm on SE(2). Choose what to differentiate, then change the link and the perturbation.

Notice that the finite-difference Jacobian and the closed form agree to about ten decimals at every setting. At the defaults, the third column of the Jacobian (0.964, 1.149, 1) says that rotating the first joint moves the end-effector sideways as well as turning it: that is the lever arm, and it shrinks when you shorten the link. For "with respect to χ₁" the Jacobian is the identity for any link. For composition and inversion the prediction J·τ equals the actual change even for a large τ, because these maps are exactly linear in the tangent vector (the derivations above never needed "small"). The fourth option, the group action of §4, is different: there the linear prediction (amber) leaves the actual displacement (pink) as τ grows.

Example 4.5 is the same situation on SO(3): two joint rotations and the end-effector orientation \(\mathbf{R} = \mathbf{R}_1\circ\mathbf{R}_2\). Example 4.5 · p. 113 For rotations \(\Ad_{\mathbf{R}} = \mathbf{R}\), so

\[ \frac{\partial(\mathbf{R}_1\circ\mathbf{R}_2)}{\partial\mathbf{R}_1} = \Ad_{\mathbf{R}_2^{-1}} = \mathbf{R}_2\T, \qquad \frac{\partial(\mathbf{R}_1\circ\mathbf{R}_2)}{\partial\mathbf{R}_2} = \mathbf{I} . \tag{4.39} \]

A small rotation of the first joint reaches the end-effector re-expressed through the second joint; a small rotation of the second joint reaches it unchanged.

4. Jacobians of Exp and of the group action

Two more building blocks appear on pp. 112–113. The first is the derivative of the exponential map itself, written with a left superscript that names the perturbation type: §4.3.2 · p. 112

\[ \mathbf{J}_r(\boldsymbol{\tau}) \triangleq \frac{{}^{\boldsymbol{\tau}}\partial\,\Exp(\boldsymbol{\tau})}{\partial\boldsymbol{\tau}}, \qquad \mathbf{J}_l(\boldsymbol{\tau}) \triangleq \frac{{}^{\boldsymbol{\varepsilon}}\partial\,\Exp(\boldsymbol{\tau})}{\partial\boldsymbol{\tau}} . \]

These are (4.35) and (4.36). In the "perturb in, perturb out" form: \(\Exp(\boldsymbol{\tau}+\delta\boldsymbol{\tau}) \approx \Exp(\boldsymbol{\tau})\circ\Exp(\mathbf{J}_r(\boldsymbol{\tau})\,\delta\boldsymbol{\tau})\) and \(\Exp(\boldsymbol{\tau}+\delta\boldsymbol{\tau}) \approx \Exp(\mathbf{J}_l(\boldsymbol{\tau})\,\delta\boldsymbol{\tau})\circ\Exp(\boldsymbol{\tau})\). They answer: if I change the coordinates \(\boldsymbol{\tau}\) a little, how does the group element move, measured locally or globally? Both equal \(\mathbf{I}\) at \(\boldsymbol{\tau}=\mathbf{0}\), and on a commutative group such as SO(2) they are \(\mathbf{I}\) everywhere. Their closed forms for SO(3) were in Week 4 · Day 5.

The second is the group action, a group element applied to a vector, such as a rotation applied to a point. Equation (4.37) defines its Jacobians with respect to the group element and with respect to the vector. §4.3.2 · p. 113

Filling the gap: the action Jacobians for a rotated point

Take \(f(\mathbf{R},\mathbf{v}) = \mathbf{R}\mathbf{v}\) with \(\mathbf{R}\in\SO(3)\), \(\mathbf{v}\in\R^3\). The output is a vector, so the output ⊖ is plain subtraction. Perturb \(\mathbf{R}\) on the right and use \(\Exp(\boldsymbol{\tau}) \approx \mathbf{I} + \boldsymbol{\tau}^\wedge\) for small \(\boldsymbol{\tau}\), where \(\boldsymbol{\tau}^\wedge\mathbf{v} = \boldsymbol{\tau}\times\mathbf{v} = -\mathbf{v}^\wedge\boldsymbol{\tau}\):

\[ \mathbf{R}\,\Exp(\boldsymbol{\tau})\,\mathbf{v} - \mathbf{R}\mathbf{v} \approx \mathbf{R}\,\boldsymbol{\tau}^\wedge\mathbf{v} = -\mathbf{R}\,\mathbf{v}^\wedge\,\boldsymbol{\tau} \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \mathbf{J}^{\mathbf{R}\mathbf{v}}_{\mathbf{R}} = -\mathbf{R}\,\mathbf{v}^\wedge, \qquad \mathbf{J}^{\mathbf{R}\mathbf{v}}_{\mathbf{v}} = \mathbf{R} . \]

The second one is immediate because the action is linear in \(\mathbf{v}\). These two matrices are the core of every reprojection-error Jacobian in bundle adjustment.

The widget's fourth option is the planar version: a pose \(\boldsymbol{\chi} = (\mathbf{R}, \mathbf{t})\in\SE(2)\) acting on a point, \(\boldsymbol{\chi}\cdot\mathbf{p} = \mathbf{R}\mathbf{p} + \mathbf{t}\). The same steps give the \(2\times3\) Jacobian \(\mathbf{R}\,[\,\mathbf{I}\;\;\mathbf{p}^{\perp}\,]\) with \(\mathbf{p}^{\perp} = (-p_2, p_1)\T\). Unlike composition, the action is not exactly linear in \(\boldsymbol{\tau}\): a finite rotation moves the point along an arc, and the Jacobian predicts the tangent to that arc.

5. Using the Jacobians: a gradient step on the manifold

Example 4.4 fuses two noisy orientation measurements, from an IMU and a camera, by minimizing Example 4.4 · p. 111

\[ f(\mathbf{R}) = \norm{\Log(\mathbf{R}_{\text{IMU}}^{-1}\mathbf{R})}^2 + \norm{\Log(\mathbf{R}_{\text{Cam}}^{-1}\mathbf{R})}^2 \tag{4.28} \]

over \(\mathbf{R}\in\SO(3)\). The gradient (4.29) is \(2\,\mathbf{J}\T\mathbf{r}\) summed over the two residuals \(\mathbf{r} = \Log(\mathbf{R}_{\text{meas}}^{-1}\mathbf{R})\), with \(\mathbf{J} = \partial\mathbf{r}/\partial\mathbf{R}\) a right Jacobian. The update moves in the tangent space and maps back to the group:

\[ \mathbf{R}_{k+1} = \mathbf{R}_k\,\Exp(-\alpha\,\nabla f(\mathbf{R})) . \tag{4.30} \]

The step is applied on the right because right Jacobians produce a gradient in the local tangent space at \(\mathbf{R}_k\). By the chain rule, \(\mathbf{J}\) is the Jacobian of \(\Log\) times the Jacobian of composition with respect to the second factor, which is \(\mathbf{I}\); the Jacobian of \(\Log\) is \(\mathbf{J}_r^{-1}(\mathbf{r})\), close to \(\mathbf{I}\) when the residual is small.

The same example on SO(2), where \(\Log\) of a rotation is its angle and every Jacobian is 1. Let the IMU say 10° and the camera 30° (degrees are fine here since everything is linear in the angle). Then \(f(\theta) = (\theta-10)^2 + (\theta-30)^2\) and \(\nabla f = 2(\theta-10) + 2(\theta-30)\). From \(\theta_0 = 0\) with \(\alpha = 0.1\):

kθ (degrees)∇fNext θ = θ − 0.1·∇f
00−808
18−4812.8
212.8−28.815.68

The distance to the answer, 20°, shrinks by the factor \(1 - 4\alpha = 0.6\) each step. On SO(3) the arithmetic is the same with 3-vectors and the Jacobians above.

The same tangent-space vectors carry uncertainty. With \(\boldsymbol{\tau} = \boldsymbol{\chi}\ominus\boldsymbol{\chi}_1\), the covariance of a random group element around \(\boldsymbol{\chi}_1\) is \(\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{\boldsymbol{\chi}} \triangleq \E[\boldsymbol{\tau}\boldsymbol{\tau}\T]\), equation (4.26), and it lives in the tangent space at \(\boldsymbol{\chi}_1\). §4.3.1 · pp. 110–111 You met this in Week 4 · Day 4; to first order, a function \(f\) with Jacobian \(\mathbf{J}\) maps it to \(\mathbf{J}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{\boldsymbol{\chi}}\mathbf{J}\T\).

Common mistakes

  • "A Jacobian on SE(3) is a 4 × 4 matrix, or 12 × 12." It is 6 × 6. Its size is the dimension of the tangent spaces, not the size of the matrices that represent the group.
  • "Right and left Jacobians are interchangeable." They differ by adjoints. A gradient from right Jacobians must be applied with right-⊕, as in (4.30).
  • "J_R of a function and J_r of the group are the same thing." \(\mathbf{J}_R\) in (4.24) is the Jacobian of some function \(f\). \(\mathbf{J}_r(\boldsymbol{\tau})\) in (4.35) is the specific Jacobian of \(\Exp\).
  • "The derivative of χ⁻¹ is −I, as for −x." Only on a commutative group. In general it is \(-\Ad_{\boldsymbol{\chi}}\).

Check yourself

Q1. In Example 4.5 let R₂ be a rotation by 90° about the z-axis. The first joint R₁ is perturbed on the right by τ = (0.01, 0, 0). What perturbation does the end-effector R₁ ∘ R₂ see in its own frame?

The Jacobian is R₂ᵀ. R₂ has columns (0,1,0), (−1,0,0), (0,0,1), so R₂ᵀ·(0.01, 0, 0) = (0, −0.01, 0): the old x-axis is the new frame's negative y-axis.

Q2. What is the right Jacobian of f(χ) = χ ∘ χ₁ ∘ χ₂ with respect to χ?

Treat χ₁ ∘ χ₂ as one fixed element and apply (4.33). By the chain rule this equals Ad of χ₂⁻¹ times Ad of χ₁⁻¹.

Q3. On SO(2), the IMU reads 0° and the camera 40°. Starting from θ = 10°, take one step of (4.30) with α = 0.25. Where do you land?

∇f = 2(10 − 0) + 2(10 − 40) = −40. θ ← 10 − 0.25·(−40) = 20°, the mean of the two measurements. With α = 1/4 the factor 1 − 4α is zero, so one step suffices.

Q4. Why is ∂(χ ∘ χ₁)/∂χ₁ the identity while ∂(χ ∘ χ₁)/∂χ is not?

χ ∘ (χ₁ ∘ Exp(τ)) = (χ ∘ χ₁) ∘ Exp(τ): the output is perturbed by exactly τ. For the first factor, χ ∘ Exp(τ) ∘ χ₁ = (χ ∘ χ₁) ∘ Exp(Ad of χ₁⁻¹ times τ).

Q5. A planar pose is at (2, 0) with heading 90°. Apply the tangent vector (1, 0, 0), one unit forward and no rotation, with right-⊕. Where is the pose now?

Right-⊕ applies the increment in the robot's own frame, whose forward axis points along world y. (3, 0) is what left-⊕ would give.

Recap

  1. ⊕ and ⊖ replace + and − on a group; the right versions use the local frame, the left versions the global frame, equations (4.21)–(4.22).
  2. The Jacobian (4.23) is the matrix with \(f(\boldsymbol{\chi}\oplus\boldsymbol{\tau}) \approx f(\boldsymbol{\chi})\oplus\mathbf{J}\boldsymbol{\tau}\). Its size is set by the tangent spaces.
  3. Inversion: \(-\Ad_{\boldsymbol{\chi}}\). Composition: \(\Ad_{\boldsymbol{\chi}_1^{-1}}\) for the first factor, \(\mathbf{I}\) for the second. Rotation of a point: \(-\mathbf{R}\mathbf{v}^\wedge\) and \(\mathbf{R}\).
  4. The chain rule (4.31) combines these blocks, which is how AutoDiff differentiates through poses.
  5. A manifold gradient step moves in the tangent space and maps back with \(\Exp\), equation (4.30).

Sources

  1. SLAM Handbook, §4.3 "Differentiation on Manifold", pp. 109–113; equations (4.19)–(4.39); Examples 4.4 and 4.5.
  2. Solà, Deray, Atchuthan, A micro Lie theory for state estimation in robotics, 2018 (the ⊕/⊖ definition of Jacobians, the completed Jacobians of inversion, composition, Exp, Log, and group action, and the relation between left and right Jacobians).
  3. Barfoot, State Estimation for Robotics, 2017 (adjoints and the Jacobians of SO(3) and SE(3)). The SE(2) arm and the SO(2) numbers are this app's own examples.

Week 7 · Day 5

Numerical pitfalls, a differentiable second-order optimizer, and the libraries

After today you can explain why Lie group code switches to Taylor series near zero, write the damped linear system a differentiable Levenberg-Marquardt optimizer solves, show how a robust kernel enters it through a first-derivative correction, and place the main libraries on a map.

About 60 min · Read §4.4–4.5, pp. 113–118 (6 pages) · Needs Week 7 Day 4 and Week 6 Day 4

Read first: §4.4–4.5, pp. 113–118

While you read, look for:

  • Example 4.6 on p. 114: the two branches of equation (4.41) and the test that chooses between them.
  • Equations (4.43) and (4.44) on p. 115: the Levenberg-Marquardt step written as a linear system \(\mathbf{A}\,\boldsymbol{\delta}_t = \boldsymbol{\beta}\).
  • Equation (4.46) on p. 116 and the reason given for preferring it to Triggs' correction.
  • The three groups of libraries in §4.4.2 (pp. 116–118) and, in §4.5, what is said to be missing in systems that use bundle adjustment as "just a special layer".

Pages 116–118 are a survey. Skim the names; the table in §5 below organizes them.

Today's big idea

The mathematics of Days 1–4 becomes software only after two practical problems are solved. First, formulas that are correct on paper can produce 0/0 or lose all their digits in floating point, and AutoDiff faithfully differentiates the bad formula. Second, SLAM needs second-order, robust, manifold-aware optimizers, which deep-learning toolkits do not provide. The libraries of this section exist to close those two gaps.

1. A correct formula that still fails

Example 4.6 uses the exponential map that turns a rotation vector \(\boldsymbol{\nu}\in\R^3\) (axis times angle) into a unit quaternion. With the vector part written first, Example 4.6 · p. 114

\[ \Exp(\boldsymbol{\nu}) = \left[\, \sin\!\Big(\frac{\norm{\boldsymbol{\nu}}}{2}\Big)\frac{\boldsymbol{\nu}\T}{\norm{\boldsymbol{\nu}}},\;\; \cos\!\Big(\frac{\norm{\boldsymbol{\nu}}}{2}\Big) \right]\T . \tag{4.40} \]

(In the printed equation the argument of the cosine is written with \(\mathbf{x}\); it is the same vector \(\boldsymbol{\nu}\).) The trouble is the factor that multiplies \(\boldsymbol{\nu}\), \(\gamma = \sin(\norm{\boldsymbol{\nu}}/2)/\norm{\boldsymbol{\nu}}\). At \(\boldsymbol{\nu} = \mathbf{0}\), which is the identity rotation and the most common value of an update step near convergence, it is 0/0. The book's remedy, as implemented in PyPose's LieTensor, is to switch to a Taylor expansion for small angles: Example 4.6 · p. 114

\[ \Exp(\boldsymbol{\nu}) = \begin{cases} \big[\, \boldsymbol{\nu}\T\gamma_e,\; \cos(\norm{\boldsymbol{\nu}}/2) \,\big]\T & \text{if } \norm{\boldsymbol{\nu}} \gt \text{eps}, \\ \big[\, \boldsymbol{\nu}\T\gamma_o,\; 1 - \frac{\norm{\boldsymbol{\nu}}^2}{8} + \frac{\norm{\boldsymbol{\nu}}^4}{384} \,\big]\T & \text{otherwise,} \end{cases} \tag{4.41} \]

with \(\gamma_e = \sin(\norm{\boldsymbol{\nu}}/2)/\norm{\boldsymbol{\nu}}\) and \(\gamma_o = \frac12 - \frac{\norm{\boldsymbol{\nu}}^2}{48} + \frac{\norm{\boldsymbol{\nu}}^4}{3840}\); eps is the smallest machine number with \(1 + \text{eps} \ne 1\).

Filling the gap: where 48, 3840, 8, and 384 come from

Write \(\theta = \norm{\boldsymbol{\nu}}\) and use the series \(\sin a = a - \frac{a^3}{6} + \frac{a^5}{120} - \dots\) and \(\cos a = 1 - \frac{a^2}{2} + \frac{a^4}{24} - \dots\) with \(a = \theta/2\):

\[ \frac{\sin(\theta/2)}{\theta} = \frac{1}{\theta}\Big(\frac{\theta}{2} - \frac{\theta^3}{8\cdot 6} + \frac{\theta^5}{32\cdot 120}\Big) = \frac12 - \frac{\theta^2}{48} + \frac{\theta^4}{3840}, \qquad \cos\frac{\theta}{2} = 1 - \frac{\theta^2}{4\cdot 2} + \frac{\theta^4}{16\cdot 24} = 1 - \frac{\theta^2}{8} + \frac{\theta^4}{384} . \]

The division by \(\theta\) has been done on paper, so nothing is divided at run time. At \(\theta = 0.1\): \(\gamma_o = 0.5 - 0.000208 + 0.00000003 = 0.499792\), and the direct formula gives \(\sin(0.05)/0.1 = 0.499792\) too. The first neglected term is \(\theta^6/645120\), far below rounding for small angles.

Why does a learning library care more than a classical one? Because it also needs the derivative, and AutoDiff differentiates the operations you wrote, not the function you meant. For the naive formula the quotient rule gives

\[ \frac{d\gamma}{d\theta} = \frac{\cos(\theta/2)}{2\theta} - \frac{\sin(\theta/2)}{\theta^2} , \]

two terms of size about \(1/(2\theta)\) whose difference is the small number \(-\theta/24 + \dots\). Subtracting nearly equal numbers destroys significant digits (catastrophic cancellation), and at \(\theta = 0\) the result is NaN, which then spreads to every parameter the gradient touches. The following experiment is this app's own illustration of that mechanism.

Try it: slide the angle down from 1 toward 0, then press the button for θ = 0.

Notice that the value of γ is fine everywhere except exactly at zero, but its naive derivative is not: at θ = 1e-3 it returns −6.104e-5 where the exact value is −4.167e-5, at 1e-4 it is wrong by a factor of about 100, and below that it is rounding noise: exactly 0 at some angles, far too large or of the wrong sign at others (the chart clips errors above 100). The two-term series is accurate to about 8 digits below 0.1 and only degrades for large angles. Each formula is good where the other is bad, which is why the code needs both branches.

The same section lists what distinguishes LieTensor: gradients of any order on common hardware, batched Jacobians through a vmap operator, and support for both Lie group and Lie algebra types, so that \(\Exp\) and \(\Log\) can be called directly and differentiated. §4.4 · pp. 114–115

2. A second-order optimizer inside a learning library

Networks are trained with first-order methods such as SGD and Adam. The lower level of a SLAM bilevel problem needs more: second-order or constrained optimization, and robustness to outliers. §4.4.1 · p. 115 The book walks through Levenberg-Marquardt (LM) as PyPose organizes it. Start from weighted least squares,

\[ \min \sum_i (\mathbf{h}_i(\mathbf{x}_i) - \mathbf{z}_i)\T\,\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_i\,(\mathbf{h}_i(\mathbf{x}_i) - \mathbf{z}_i), \tag{4.42} \]

where \(\mathbf{h}\) is the model, \(\mathbf{z}_i\) the measurement, and \(\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_i\) a square information matrix (in this section \(\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_i\) multiplies the residual directly, so it plays the role of a weight). LM updates \(\mathbf{x}_t \leftarrow \mathbf{x}_{t-1} + \boldsymbol{\delta}_t\) with

\[ \sum_i \big(\boldsymbol{\Lambda}_i + \lambda\cdot\diag(\boldsymbol{\Lambda}_i)\big)\,\boldsymbol{\delta}_t = -\sum_i \mathbf{J}_i\T\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_i\mathbf{r}_i, \qquad \boldsymbol{\Lambda}_i = \mathbf{J}_i\T\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_i\mathbf{J}_i, \quad \mathbf{r}_i = \mathbf{h}_i(\mathbf{x}_i) - \mathbf{z}_i . \tag{4.43} \]

\(\boldsymbol{\Lambda}_i\) is the Gauss-Newton approximation of the Hessian and \(\lambda\) the damping factor. In short \(\mathbf{A}\,\boldsymbol{\delta}_t = \boldsymbol{\beta}\), equation (4.44). \(\mathbf{A}\) is usually positive definite, so Cholesky works (Week 1 · Day 5); for large sparse Jacobians, sparse Cholesky or preconditioned conjugate gradient. §4.4.1 · p. 115

Toy numbers. The problem of Day 1 at \(x = 1\), \(y = 2\), with \(\boldsymbol{\Sigma} = \mathbf{I}\): \(\mathbf{J} = (2, 1)\T\), \(\mathbf{r} = (-1, 0)\T\), so \(\Lambda = 5\) and \(\beta = -\mathbf{J}\T\mathbf{r} = 2\). The step is \(\delta = 2/(5 + 5\lambda)\):

Damping λA = Λ + λ·diag(Λ)Step δCharacter
050.400pure Gauss-Newton (the first row of Day 1's table)
0.15.50.364nearly Gauss-Newton
1100.200half the Gauss-Newton step
10550.036a short, cautious step along the scaled gradient

Damping with \(\diag(\boldsymbol{\Lambda})\) and not with the identity makes the step insensitive to the units of each variable; the trust-region reading of \(\lambda\) is in Week 2 · Day 5.

3. Robust kernels inside the solver

Real problems have outliers, so the quadratic is wrapped in a robust kernel \(\rho:\R\to\R\) (Chapter 3): §4.4.1 · p. 116

\[ \min \sum_i \rho\big(\mathbf{r}_i\T\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_i\mathbf{r}_i\big) . \tag{4.45} \]

The system (4.43) must change accordingly. One classical way, Triggs' correction (also used by Ceres), involves the second derivative of \(\rho\), which is negative, and that can make second-order optimizers unstable. PyPose's alternative, FastTriggs, uses only the first derivative: with \(c_i = \mathbf{r}_i\T\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_i\mathbf{r}_i\),

\[ \mathbf{r}_i^{\rho} = \sqrt{\rho'(c_i)}\;\mathbf{r}_i, \qquad \mathbf{J}_i^{\rho} = \sqrt{\rho'(c_i)}\;\mathbf{J}_i . \tag{4.46} \]

Filling the gap: why scaling by the square root of ρ′ is the right correction

Differentiate one term of (4.45) with the chain rule. Since \(\partial c_i/\partial\mathbf{x} = 2\,\mathbf{r}_i\T\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_i\mathbf{J}_i\) (for symmetric \(\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_i\)), the gradient is

\[ \nabla\rho(c_i) = \rho'(c_i)\cdot 2\,\mathbf{J}_i\T\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_i\mathbf{r}_i . \]

Now put the corrected quantities of (4.46) into the plain right-hand side of (4.43): \((\mathbf{J}_i^{\rho})\T\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_i\mathbf{r}_i^{\rho} = \rho'(c_i)\,\mathbf{J}_i\T\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_i\mathbf{r}_i\). It is the true gradient (up to the common factor 2). So the corrected problem is an ordinary weighted least-squares problem that has the same gradient as the robust cost at the current estimate. The matrix on the left becomes \(\rho'(c_i)\,\mathbf{J}_i\T\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_i\mathbf{J}_i\), which is positive semidefinite because \(\rho' \ge 0\).

This is iteratively reweighted least squares (Week 6 · Day 4) with weight \(\rho'(c_i)\), recomputed at every iteration. The exact Hessian of \(\rho(c_i)\) has one more term, proportional to \(\rho''(c_i)\). For a robust kernel \(\rho\) flattens out, so \(\rho'' \lt 0\), and that term can make the matrix indefinite. Triggs' correction keeps a version of that term; the first-order correction drops it.

Numbers. Take the Cauchy kernel \(\rho(c) = \log(1 + c)\), so \(\rho'(c) = 1/(1+c)\), with scalar residuals and \(\Sigma = 1\). An inlier \(r = 0.5\): \(c = 0.25\), \(\rho' = 0.8\), corrected residual \(0.894\times 0.5 = 0.447\). An outlier \(r = 3\): \(c = 9\), \(\rho' = 0.1\), corrected residual \(0.316\times 3 = 0.949\). A residual six times larger enters the solver only about twice as large.

4. Four pluggable parts

PyPose exposes the pieces of this loop as arguments of the optimizer: solver, kernel, corrector, and strategy. §4.4.1 · pp. 115–116

PartDecidesExamples named in the bookEquation
solverhow A·δ = β is solvedCholesky, sparse Cholesky, preconditioned conjugate gradient(4.44)
kernelthe robust loss ρthe kernels of Chapter 3(4.45)
correctorhow ρ changes r and JTriggs, FastTriggs(4.46)
strategyhow far to stepadaptive damping, dogleg, trust regionp. 116

In pseudocode (the structure described on pp. 115–116, not literal library code):

optimizer = LM(model, solver, kernel, corrector, strategy)
repeat
    r, J  = residuals and Jacobians of model at x     # J by AutoDiff, Lie groups included (Day 4)
    r, J  = corrector(kernel, r, J)                    # (4.46)
    A     = sum of JᵀΣJ + λ·diag(JᵀΣJ)                 # (4.43)
    β     = −sum of JᵀΣr
    δ     = solver(A, β)                               # (4.44)
    x, λ  = strategy(x, δ, λ)                          # accept or reject the step, adapt the damping
until converged

A plain LM run may not reach the global optimum from a poor initial guess, which is why the strategy is there to keep each step from going too far. §4.4.1 · p. 116

5. The library map, and where the field is going

§4.4.2 sorts the open-source tools into three groups. §4.4.2 · pp. 116–118

GroupWhat it providesNames in the book
Linear algebrafast vectors and matrices; the layer everything else stands onNumPy, Eigen, ArrayFire
Machine learningtensors, AutoDiff, GPU trainingTorch, Theano, Caffe, Chainer, TensorFlow, PyTorch, MXNet, JAX; gvnn for differentiable transformation layers
Machine learning with optimization insidedifferentiable optimization embedded in networks; second-order optimizers and Lie group gradientsTheseus, CvxpyLayer, PyPose
Specialized optimizationnonlinear least squares and factor graphs for SLAM; modeling and optimal-control solversCeres, g2o, GTSAM; Pyomo, JuMP, CasADi, IPOPT, OpenOCL, CT, Drake

The classical SLAM solvers (Ceres, g2o, GTSAM) are in the last row: excellent at the lower level, but not built to pass gradients to a network. The third row is the bridge this chapter is about.

§4.5 then sketches the research landscape. §4.5 · p. 118 End-to-end learned odometry comes in supervised forms (DeepVO, TartanVO), which do better but need ground truth that is laborious to collect, and unsupervised forms (UnDeepVO, Unsupervised VIO). Hybrid systems attach geometry to a network: a bundle adjustment layer (BA-Net, DROID-SLAM), a pose and code graph optimized at inference (DeepFactors), a cheirality layer (DiffPoseNet). The book's criticism is that in these systems the pose error is backpropagated through BA while the supervision still comes from ground-truth poses, so BA acts as one more layer. iSLAM instead connects front-end and back-end in both directions as a bilevel problem, so the front-end learns from the result of geometric optimization without external supervision. The same bilevel pattern appears in reinforcement learning, local and global planning, feature matching, and multi-robot routing.

Common mistakes

  • "If the value is computed accurately, so is its gradient." The widget shows the opposite: γ is accurate to 7 digits at θ = 1e-4 while its naive derivative is off by a factor of 100.
  • "The Taylor branch is an approximation, so it is less accurate." Below the switch point its truncation error is smaller than the rounding error of the exact formula.
  • "A robust kernel only changes the cost value." It changes the linear system: residuals and Jacobians are rescaled by \(\sqrt{\rho'}\) at every iteration.
  • "Any deep-learning optimizer can serve as the SLAM back-end." First-order methods converge slowly on these problems; the book's point on p. 115 is that second-order and constrained solvers are needed.

Check yourself

Q1. Using the first two terms of γₒ in (4.41), what multiplies ν in the quaternion Exp when ‖ν‖ = 0.2?

γₒ ≈ 1/2 − 0.2²/48 = 0.5 − 0.04/48 = 0.5 − 0.00083 = 0.49917. (0.09983 is sin(0.1), the size of the whole vector part.)

Q2. A scalar LM step has Λ = JᵀΣJ = 5 and β = −JᵀΣr = 2. With damping λ = 1 in (4.43), what is δ?

(Λ + λ·diag(Λ))δ = (5 + 5)δ = 2, so δ = 0.2. The value 0.333 would come from damping with λ times the identity; (4.43) scales the damping by the diagonal of Λ.

Q3. With the Cauchy kernel ρ(c) = log(1 + c) and Σ = 1, what corrected residual does (4.46) pass to the solver for r = 2?

c = r² = 4, ρ′(c) = 1/5 = 0.2, √0.2 = 0.447, and 0.447 × 2 = 0.894.

Q4. Why does the first-order correction (4.46) keep the LM matrix positive semidefinite when a correction using ρ″ may not?

The corrected matrix is a sum of ρ′(c)·JᵀΣJ terms with ρ′ ≥ 0. The exact second derivative of ρ adds a term proportional to ρ″, which is negative for robust kernels.

Q5. According to §4.5, what distinguishes iSLAM from systems that attach a bundle adjustment layer to a network?

In the BA-layer systems the supervision comes from ground-truth poses and BA is one more layer. The bilevel formulation lets the geometric optimization itself supervise the front-end.

Recap

  1. Near zero rotation, formulas such as \(\sin(\theta/2)/\theta\) give 0/0 and their AutoDiff gradients lose accuracy; Lie group code switches to Taylor series there, equation (4.41).
  2. A differentiable LM optimizer solves \(\sum_i(\boldsymbol{\Lambda}_i + \lambda\diag\boldsymbol{\Lambda}_i)\boldsymbol{\delta} = -\sum_i\mathbf{J}_i\T\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_i\mathbf{r}_i\) at each iteration, equation (4.43).
  3. A robust kernel enters by rescaling \(\mathbf{r}_i\) and \(\mathbf{J}_i\) with \(\sqrt{\rho'(c_i)}\), equation (4.46): IRLS with a matrix that stays positive semidefinite.
  4. Solver, kernel, corrector, and strategy are independent, swappable parts of the loop.
  5. Classical SLAM solvers handle the lower level; libraries such as Theseus and PyPose make it differentiable so the two levels can be trained together.

Sources

  1. SLAM Handbook, §4.4 "Numerical Challenges of Automatic Differentiation and Modern Libraries" (with §4.4.1 and §4.4.2) and §4.5 "Further Readings & Recent Trends", pp. 113–118; Example 4.6; equations (4.40)–(4.46).
  2. Goldberg, What every computer scientist should know about floating-point arithmetic, 1991 (rounding and catastrophic cancellation). The 32-bit experiment in the widget is this app's own.
  3. Nocedal and Wright, Numerical Optimization, 2006 (Levenberg-Marquardt and scaling of the damping term).
  4. Hartley and Zisserman, Multiple View Geometry, 2nd ed., 2004 (robust cost functions and iterative reweighting in geometric estimation).

Week 7 · Review

Week 7 review: gradients through an optimizer

After today you can set up a bilevel problem, compute its upper-level gradient by unrolling and by implicit differentiation on paper, differentiate simple expressions on Lie groups, and say what a differentiable optimizer library has to provide.

About 60 min · No new pages

The week in one paragraph

A learned front-end with parameters \(\mathbf{y}\) feeds a back-end that solves a nonlinear least squares problem for \(\mathbf{x}^*\). Training the front-end on the final estimate is a bilevel problem, and its gradient needs \(\partial\mathbf{x}^*/\partial\mathbf{y}\). Unrolled differentiation gets it by backpropagating through the solver's iterations: exact for the iterations that ran, with memory that grows with their number unless the backward pass is truncated. Implicit differentiation gets it from the optimality condition: one linear solve with the Hessian at the solution, no stored iterates, valid only at convergence. Both rely on AutoDiff, which on SLAM variables needs Jacobians defined with ⊕ and ⊖ on Lie groups, numerically safe \(\Exp\) and \(\Log\), and second-order robust optimizers built from differentiable parts.

1. Formula sheet

What it isFormulaWhere
Lower level: nonlinear least squares\(\mathbf{x}^* = \argmin_{\mathbf{x}} \frac12\sum_i\norm{w_i\mathbf{c}_i(\mathbf{x}_i)}^2\)(4.1), §4.1, p. 102 · Day 1
Bilevel problem\(\min_{\mathbf{y}}\,\mathcal{U}(\mathbf{y},\mathbf{x}^*)\) s.t. \(\mathbf{x}^* = \argmin_{\mathbf{x}}\mathcal{L}(\mathbf{y},\mathbf{x})\)(4.2), §4.2, p. 103 · Day 1
Upper-level gradient\(\nabla_{\mathbf{y}}\mathcal{U} = \frac{\partial\mathcal{U}}{\partial\mathbf{y}} + \frac{\partial\mathcal{U}}{\partial\mathbf{x}^*}\frac{\partial\mathbf{x}^*}{\partial\mathbf{y}}\)(4.3), p. 104 · Day 1
Unrolled solver and its sensitivity\(\mathbf{x}_t = \Phi_t(\mathbf{x}_{t-1};\mathbf{y})\), \(\;\mathbf{S}_t = \mathbf{A}_t\mathbf{S}_{t-1} + \mathbf{B}_t\)(4.4), p. 104 · Day 2
Gradient-descent step: its two partials\(\mathbf{A}_t = \mathbf{I} - \eta\,\mathbf{H}\), \(\;\mathbf{B}_t = -\eta\,\mathbf{H}_{xy}\)from (4.5), (4.9), pp. 105–106 · Day 2
Truncation to the last M steps (scalar, near convergence)fraction missing \(\approx A^M\)§4.2.2, p. 106 · Day 2
Implicit derivative\(\frac{\partial\mathbf{x}^*}{\partial\mathbf{y}} = -\mathbf{H}^{-1}\mathbf{H}_{xy}\)(4.12), p. 107 · Day 3
Adjoint form\(\mathbf{H}\mathbf{q} = \mathbf{v}\), \(\;\nabla_{\mathbf{y}}\mathcal{U} = \frac{\partial\mathcal{U}}{\partial\mathbf{y}} - \mathbf{q}\T\mathbf{H}_{xy}\)(4.13), (4.17), pp. 107–108 · Day 3
Hessian-vector product; iteration for q\(\mathbf{H}\mathbf{q} = \frac{\partial}{\partial\mathbf{x}}\big(\frac{\partial\mathcal{L}}{\partial\mathbf{x}}\cdot\mathbf{q}\big)\), \(\;\mathbf{q}_k = \mathbf{q}_{k-1} - \eta(\mathbf{H}\mathbf{q}_{k-1} - \mathbf{v})\)(4.15), (4.16), p. 108 · Day 3
Jacobian on a Lie group\(f(\boldsymbol{\chi}\oplus\boldsymbol{\tau}) \approx f(\boldsymbol{\chi})\oplus\mathbf{J}\boldsymbol{\tau}\)(4.23), p. 110 · Day 4
Inversion and composition\(\frac{\partial\boldsymbol{\chi}^{-1}}{\partial\boldsymbol{\chi}} = -\Ad_{\boldsymbol{\chi}}\), \(\;\frac{\partial(\boldsymbol{\chi}\circ\boldsymbol{\chi}_1)}{\partial\boldsymbol{\chi}} = \Ad_{\boldsymbol{\chi}_1^{-1}}\), \(\;\frac{\partial(\boldsymbol{\chi}\circ\boldsymbol{\chi}_1)}{\partial\boldsymbol{\chi}_1} = \mathbf{I}\)(4.32)–(4.34), p. 112 · Day 4
LM step; robust correction\(\sum_i(\boldsymbol{\Lambda}_i + \lambda\diag\boldsymbol{\Lambda}_i)\boldsymbol{\delta} = -\sum_i\mathbf{J}_i\T\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_i\mathbf{r}_i\); \(\;\mathbf{r}_i^\rho = \sqrt{\rho'(c_i)}\,\mathbf{r}_i\)(4.43), (4.46), pp. 115–116 · Day 5

Here \(\mathbf{H} = \partial^2\mathcal{L}/\partial\mathbf{x}\partial\mathbf{x}\), \(\mathbf{H}_{xy} = \partial^2\mathcal{L}/\partial\mathbf{x}\partial\mathbf{y}\), and \(\mathbf{v} = (\partial\mathcal{U}/\partial\mathbf{x}^*)\T\).

One experiment before the quiz. Predict first, then check: with Gauss-Newton as the inner solver, how many inner steps does the unrolled gradient need to match the reference to four decimals? And what happens to the truncated gradient at M = 1?

Notice that with Gauss-Newton two steps are enough (−0.0447), and that backpropagating through only the last step (M = 1, with K = 5) gives −0.0432, within about 3% of the full gradient. With gradient descent at η = 0.1 the same truncation loses 18%. Fast inner solvers make both unrolling and truncation cheap.

2. Mixed quiz

Check yourself

Q1. A function has 3 inputs and 500 outputs. Which AutoDiff mode computes its full Jacobian with the fewest passes, and how many?

Forward mode needs one pass per input (3); reverse mode one per output (500).

Q2. With n back-end variables and m network parameters, which factor of the upper-level gradient (4.3) is an n × m matrix?

∂U/∂y is 1 × m, ∂U/∂x* is 1 × n, and ∂x*/∂y is n × m. It is never formed in practice; only its product with ∂U/∂x* is needed.

Q3. An unrolled scalar solver has constant A = 0.5 and B = 0.3, and the initial guess does not depend on y. What is the sensitivity S₂ after two steps?

S₁ = 0.5·0 + 0.3 = 0.3 and S₂ = 0.5·0.3 + 0.3 = 0.45. The limit B/(1 − A) = 0.6 is the converged value.

Q4. Near the solution an inner solver multiplies the adjoint by A = 0.9 per backward step. About how many backward steps M keep the truncation loss below 1%?

The missing fraction is 0.9^M. 0.9^M ≤ 0.01 needs M ≥ ln(0.01)/ln(0.9) = 43.7. A slowly converging solver needs a long backward pass.

Q5. Let L(x, y) = ½(2x − y)² + ½x². What is dx*/dy by implicit differentiation?

∂L/∂x = 2(2x − y) + x = 5x − 2y, so H = 5 and ∂²L/∂x∂y = −2. dx*/dy = −(−2)/5 = 0.4. Check: x* = 2y/5.

Q6. The inner solver contains an accept-or-reject test for each step, which is not differentiable, but it does converge. Which method still gives a valid gradient?

Implicit differentiation uses only derivatives of the cost L at the solution. How the solver reached it is irrelevant.

Q7. What is the right Jacobian of f(χ) = χ⁻¹ ∘ χ₁ with respect to χ?

Chain rule: inversion gives −Ad of χ, then composition with respect to the first factor gives Ad of χ₁⁻¹. Their product is −Ad of χ₁⁻¹ times Ad of χ = −Ad of (χ₁⁻¹ ∘ χ).

Q8. With the Cauchy kernel ρ(c) = log(1 + c) and Σ = 1, a residual r = 1 enters the corrected least-squares problem (4.46) as which value?

c = 1, ρ′ = 1/2, and √(1/2) × 1 = 0.707.

3. Pen-and-paper problems

  1. Let \(f(a, b) = (ab + a)^2\). Split it into elementary operations and run reverse-mode AutoDiff by hand at \(a = 2\), \(b = 3\). Check both partial derivatives against the formula.

    Solution

    Forward evaluation: \(v_1 = ab = 6\), \(v_2 = v_1 + a = 8\), \(f = v_2^2 = 64\).

    Backward: \(\bar f = 1\); \(\bar v_2 = 2v_2\cdot\bar f = 16\); \(\bar v_1 = \bar v_2 = 16\). The input \(a\) is used twice, so its adjoint is a sum: \(\bar a = \bar v_1\cdot b + \bar v_2\cdot 1 = 48 + 16 = 64\). \(\bar b = \bar v_1\cdot a = 32\).

    Check: \(f = a^2(b+1)^2\), so \(\partial f/\partial a = 2a(b+1)^2 = 64\) and \(\partial f/\partial b = 2a^2(b+1) = 32\).

  2. Lower level \(\mathcal{L}(x, y) = \tfrac12(x-y)^2 + \tfrac12x^2\), upper level \(\mathcal{U} = \tfrac12(x-1)^2\). Run two steps of gradient descent with \(\eta = 0.25\) from \(x_0 = 0\) at \(y = 4\). Compute \(x_1, x_2\), the sensitivities \(S_1, S_2\), and the unrolled gradient \(d\,\mathcal{U}(x_2)/dy\). Compare with the gradient at the true solution, and give \(S_T\) for general \(T\).

    Solution

    \(\partial\mathcal{L}/\partial x = 2x - y\), \(H = 2\), \(H_{xy} = -1\). So \(A = 1 - 2\eta = 0.5\) and \(B = \eta = 0.25\) at every step.

    \(x_1 = 0 - 0.25(0 - 4) = 1\), \(x_2 = 1 - 0.25(2 - 4) = 1.5\). \(S_1 = 0.25\), \(S_2 = 0.5\times0.25 + 0.25 = 0.375\).

    Unrolled gradient: \((x_2 - 1)\,S_2 = 0.5\times 0.375 = 0.1875\).

    True solution: \(x^* = y/2 = 2\), \(dx^*/dy = -H^{-1}H_{xy} = 0.5\), gradient \((2-1)\times0.5 = 0.5\). Two steps give less than half of it, both because \(x_2\) is short of \(x^*\) and because \(S_2\) is short of 0.5.

    General \(T\): \(S_T = B(1 + A + \dots + A^{T-1}) = 0.5\,(1 - 0.5^T)\), which tends to 0.5.

  3. The week's toy problem at \(y = 1\): \(\mathcal{L} = \tfrac12(x^2-y)^2 + \tfrac12(x-1)^2\), \(\mathcal{U} = \tfrac12(x^*-1.5)^2\). (a) Verify that \(x^* = 1\). (b) Compute \(H\), \(H_{xy}\), \(v\), the adjoint \(q\), and \(\nabla_y\,\mathcal{U}\). (c) Run three iterations of Algorithm 2 with \(\eta = 0.1\) from \(q_0 = 0\) and state the factor by which the error shrinks. (d) Take one upper-level step with step size 2.

    Solution

    (a) \(\partial\mathcal{L}/\partial x = 2x(x^2 - y) + (x-1) = 2(0) + 0 = 0\) at \(x = 1, y = 1\).

    (b) \(H = 6x^2 - 2y + 1 = 5\), \(H_{xy} = -2x = -2\), \(v = x^* - 1.5 = -0.5\), \(q = v/H = -0.1\). \(\nabla_y\,\mathcal{U} = 0 - q\,H_{xy} = -(-0.1)(-2) = -0.2\).

    (c) \(q_k = q_{k-1} - 0.1(5q_{k-1} + 0.5)\): \(q_1 = -0.05\), \(q_2 = -0.075\), \(q_3 = -0.0875\). The error \(q_k - (-0.1)\) is \(0.05, 0.025, 0.0125\): it halves each step, the factor \(1 - \eta H = 0.5\).

    (d) \(y \leftarrow 1 - 2(-0.2) = 1.4\). The measurement is raised, which moves \(x^*\) up toward the target 1.5.

  4. A pose-graph factor between poses \(\boldsymbol{\chi}_a\) and \(\boldsymbol{\chi}_b\) with measurement \(\mathbf{Z}\) has the error element \(\mathbf{E} = \mathbf{Z}^{-1}\circ\boldsymbol{\chi}_a^{-1}\circ\boldsymbol{\chi}_b\). Using the blocks of Day 4 and the chain rule, find the right Jacobians of \(\mathbf{E}\) with respect to \(\boldsymbol{\chi}_b\) and \(\boldsymbol{\chi}_a\). Verify the second one directly from the definition, and check both on SO(2).

    Solution

    With respect to \(\boldsymbol{\chi}_b\): it is the last factor of the product, so the Jacobian is \(\mathbf{I}\) (4.34).

    With respect to \(\boldsymbol{\chi}_a\), in three stages. Inversion: \(-\Ad_{\boldsymbol{\chi}_a}\) (4.32). Then \(\boldsymbol{\chi}_a^{-1}\circ\boldsymbol{\chi}_b\) with respect to its first factor: \(\Ad_{\boldsymbol{\chi}_b^{-1}}\) (4.33). Then composing with \(\mathbf{Z}^{-1}\) on the left, where our quantity is the second factor: \(\mathbf{I}\). Product:

    \[ \frac{\partial\mathbf{E}}{\partial\boldsymbol{\chi}_a} = \mathbf{I}\cdot\Ad_{\boldsymbol{\chi}_b^{-1}}\cdot(-\Ad_{\boldsymbol{\chi}_a}) = -\Ad_{\boldsymbol{\chi}_b^{-1}\boldsymbol{\chi}_a} . \]

    Directly: \(\mathbf{Z}^{-1}(\boldsymbol{\chi}_a\Exp(\boldsymbol{\tau}))^{-1}\boldsymbol{\chi}_b = \mathbf{Z}^{-1}\Exp(-\boldsymbol{\tau})\,\boldsymbol{\chi}_a^{-1}\boldsymbol{\chi}_b\). Write \(\mathbf{D} = \boldsymbol{\chi}_a^{-1}\boldsymbol{\chi}_b\). Then \(\Exp(-\boldsymbol{\tau})\,\mathbf{D} = \mathbf{D}\,\big(\mathbf{D}^{-1}\Exp(-\boldsymbol{\tau})\mathbf{D}\big) = \mathbf{D}\,\Exp(-\Ad_{\mathbf{D}^{-1}}\boldsymbol{\tau})\), so the output is \(\mathbf{E}\circ\Exp(-\Ad_{\mathbf{D}^{-1}}\boldsymbol{\tau})\) and the Jacobian is \(-\Ad_{\mathbf{D}^{-1}} = -\Ad_{\boldsymbol{\chi}_b^{-1}\boldsymbol{\chi}_a}\), as before.

    SO(2): angles add, \(E = \theta_b - \theta_a - z\), with derivatives \(+1\) and \(-1\). The adjoint on SO(2) is 1, so the formulas give \(1\) and \(-1\).

    The residual used in the cost is \(\Log(\mathbf{E})\); its Jacobians are these times the Jacobian of \(\Log\), which is close to \(\mathbf{I}\) when the error is small.

You are ready for next week if you can

  • Say which variables and which cost belong to the upper and the lower level of a learned-front-end SLAM system.
  • Run forward and reverse AutoDiff on a five-node graph and state what one pass of each delivers.
  • Compute an unrolled sensitivity with \(\mathbf{S}_t = \mathbf{A}_t\mathbf{S}_{t-1} + \mathbf{B}_t\) and estimate the bias of truncation.
  • Derive \(\partial\mathbf{x}^*/\partial\mathbf{y} = -\mathbf{H}^{-1}\mathbf{H}_{xy}\) from the optimality condition and turn it into one adjoint solve.
  • Write the right Jacobians of inversion and composition and chain them.
  • Explain why Lie group code uses a Taylor branch near zero and how a robust kernel changes the LM system.

Sources

  1. SLAM Handbook, Chapter 4 "Differentiable Optimization", pp. 101–118.
  2. Griewank and Walther, Evaluating Derivatives, 2nd ed., 2008; Nocedal and Wright, Numerical Optimization, 2006; Solà, Deray, Atchuthan, A micro Lie theory for state estimation in robotics, 2018 (for the methods used in the problems).

Week 8 · Day 1

Range sensors, point clouds, and occupancy grids

After today you can turn a range measurement into a 3D point and update an occupancy grid cell with the log-odds rule, starting from Bayes' rule.

About 60 min · Read §5.1–5.2.1, pp. 119–124 (6 pages) · Needs Week 1 Day 2

Read first: §5.1 to §5.2.1, pp. 119–124

While you read, look for:

  • The time-of-flight formula (5.1) and the two ways a scan is stored, as a point cloud or as a range image (p. 120).
  • Equations (5.2)–(5.4) and Figure 5.2: from where each of the two angles is measured (p. 121).
  • The three questions Q1–Q3 that organize the chapter (pp. 122–123).
  • The two independence assumptions stated just before equation (5.6) (p. 124).

Today's big idea

A range sensor reports distances along known directions. Each beam says two things: the space it crossed is empty, and something solid sits where it ended. An occupancy grid keeps, for every cell, the probability that the cell is occupied, and the log-odds form reduces each new beam to one addition per cell.

Weeks 2 to 7 were about the back-end: estimating the trajectory. This chapter assumes that job is done. The poses are known, and the question is how to build a dense map from them, one that describes all the geometry the sensor saw and not only a few landmarks. Planning, obstacle avoidance, and manipulation need that detail. Ch. 5 intro · p. 119

1. Range from time of flight

A LiDAR emits a laser pulse, waits for the reflection, and measures the delay. Light travels to the surface and back, so the range is half the round trip: §5.1.1 · p. 120

\[ r = \frac{c\,(t_{\text{detect}} - t_{\text{emit}})}{2}. \tag{5.1} \]

With \(c \approx 3\times10^{8}\) m/s, a delay of 200 ns gives \(r = 3\times10^{8} \times 200\times10^{-9} / 2 = 30\) m. Turn it around: to resolve 1 cm in range the electronics must resolve \(2 \times 0.01 / (3\times10^{8}) \approx 67\) picoseconds.

One beam gives one distance. Sweep an array of \(B\) beams through a full turn with \(M\) steps and you get a range image \(\mathbf{R} \in \R^{B\times M}\): one range per beam and per step. An RGB-D camera returns the same kind of data on a pixel grid, a depth map \(\mathbf{I}_D \in \R^{H\times W}\) next to the colour image. Early RGB-D cameras project an infrared pattern and read depth from its distortion, which sunlight washes out, so they are indoor sensors. §5.1.1 · pp. 120–121

2. From ranges to points

A range is only useful with its direction. The sensor's calibration gives each beam two angles: the azimuth \(\phi\), measured around the vertical axis, and the inclination \(\theta\), measured up from the horizontal plane. The point hit by the beam, in the sensor's own frame, is §5.1.2 · p. 121

\[ x = r\cos\theta\cos\phi, \qquad y = r\cos\theta\sin\phi, \qquad z = r\sin\theta. \tag{5.2–5.4} \]

Example: \(r = 10\) m, \(\theta = 30^\circ\), \(\phi = 60^\circ\). The ground distance is \(10\cos 30^\circ = 8.66\) m, so \(x = 8.66 \times 0.5 = 4.33\), \(y = 8.66 \times 0.866 = 7.50\), \(z = 10 \times 0.5 = 5.00\) m. Check: \(4.33^2 + 7.50^2 + 5.00^2 = 100\). A planar 2D LiDAR is the case \(\theta = 0\): \((x, y) = (r\cos\phi,\; r\sin\phi)\).

Filling the gap: back-projecting a depth pixel

For an RGB-D camera the book writes the conversion in one line, \(\mathbf{p} = \mathbf{K}^{\dagger}\mathbf{x}\), equation (5.5). Unpacked for the usual pinhole camera, it reads as follows. A camera with focal lengths \(f_x, f_y\) (in pixels) and principal point \((c_x, c_y)\) projects a point \((X, Y, Z)\) in its own frame to the pixel

\[ u = f_x \frac{X}{Z} + c_x, \qquad v = f_y \frac{Y}{Z} + c_y . \]

A colour image loses \(Z\), so one pixel corresponds to a whole ray. A depth map stores \(Z\) at each pixel, and then the two equations can be solved for the other two coordinates:

\[ X = \frac{(u - c_x)\,Z}{f_x}, \qquad Y = \frac{(v - c_y)\,Z}{f_y}, \qquad Z = \mathbf{I}_D(u, v). \]

Example: \(f_x = f_y = 500\), \((c_x, c_y) = (320, 240)\), pixel \((420, 240)\), depth 2 m. Then \(X = 100 \times 2 / 500 = 0.4\) m, \(Y = 0\), \(Z = 2\) m.

The result is a point cloud \(\mathsf{P} = \{\mathbf{p}_1, \dots, \mathbf{p}_N\}\) in the sensor frame. A cloud from a depth map is organized: neighbours in the image are neighbours in the list, so finding the points next to a given one is an index lookup. A cloud from a moving LiDAR is not that simple. The sensor travels during the sweep, so each beam is fired from a slightly different pose. To undistort the cloud you need the motion during the sweep (from an IMU or odometry) and the firing time of each beam. §5.1.2 · pp. 121–122

3. What should a dense map store?

The chapter is built on three questions: which quantity to estimate, which geometric abstraction to use, and which data structure to store it in. §5.2 · pp. 122–123 For the first question there are two common answers, occupancy (today) and distance to the nearest surface (tomorrow).

An occupancy grid cuts space into cells \(m_k\). Each cell is either occupied or empty, we do not know which, and the map stores the probability \(p(m_k \mid \mathbf{z}_{1:t}, \mathbf{x}_{1:t})\) that it is occupied given all measurements \(\mathbf{z}_{1:t}\) and all sensor poses \(\mathbf{x}_{1:t}\). A value near 1 means occupied, near 0 means free, and 0.5 means the data say nothing. Mapping is then a binary classification problem, solved once per cell. §5.2.1 · pp. 123–124

4. The log-odds update

The book states the update rule directly, in terms of the odds \(o = p / (1 - p)\) and the log-odds \(l = \log o\): §5.2.1 · p. 124

\[ l(m_k \mid \mathbf{z}_{1:t}) = l(m_k \mid \mathbf{z}_{1:t-1}) + l(m_k \mid \mathbf{z}_t). \tag{5.6} \]
Probability pOdds p / (1 − p)Log-odds l
0.10.11−2.20
0.40.67−0.41
0.5 (unknown)10
0.72.33+0.85
0.99+2.20

Filling the gap: where equation (5.6) comes from

Fix one cell \(m_k\) and drop the poses from the notation, as the book does. Bayes' rule (Week 1 · Day 2), applied to the newest measurement \(\mathbf{z}_t\), gives

\[ p(m_k \mid \mathbf{z}_{1:t}) = \frac{p(\mathbf{z}_t \mid m_k, \mathbf{z}_{1:t-1})\; p(m_k \mid \mathbf{z}_{1:t-1})}{p(\mathbf{z}_t \mid \mathbf{z}_{1:t-1})}. \]

Assumption 1, conditional independence: once you know whether the cell is occupied, older measurements tell you nothing more about the new one, so \(p(\mathbf{z}_t \mid m_k, \mathbf{z}_{1:t-1}) = p(\mathbf{z}_t \mid m_k)\). Apply Bayes' rule a second time to that factor, \(p(\mathbf{z}_t \mid m_k) = p(m_k \mid \mathbf{z}_t)\,p(\mathbf{z}_t) / p(m_k)\), and substitute:

\[ p(m_k \mid \mathbf{z}_{1:t}) = \frac{p(m_k \mid \mathbf{z}_t)\; p(\mathbf{z}_t)\; p(m_k \mid \mathbf{z}_{1:t-1})}{p(m_k)\; p(\mathbf{z}_t \mid \mathbf{z}_{1:t-1})}. \]

The same steps for the opposite event "cell is free", written \(\neg m_k\), give the same formula with \(\neg m_k\) in place of \(m_k\). Divide the first by the second. The two awkward terms \(p(\mathbf{z}_t)\) and \(p(\mathbf{z}_t \mid \mathbf{z}_{1:t-1})\) appear in both and cancel:

\[ \underbrace{\frac{p(m_k \mid \mathbf{z}_{1:t})}{p(\neg m_k \mid \mathbf{z}_{1:t})}}_{o(m_k \mid \mathbf{z}_{1:t})} = \underbrace{\frac{p(m_k \mid \mathbf{z}_t)}{p(\neg m_k \mid \mathbf{z}_t)}}_{o(m_k \mid \mathbf{z}_t)} \cdot \underbrace{\frac{p(m_k \mid \mathbf{z}_{1:t-1})}{p(\neg m_k \mid \mathbf{z}_{1:t-1})}}_{o(m_k \mid \mathbf{z}_{1:t-1})} \cdot \underbrace{\frac{p(\neg m_k)}{p(m_k)}}_{1 / o(m_k)} . \]

Because \(p(\neg m_k \mid \cdot) = 1 - p(m_k \mid \cdot)\), each ratio is an odds as in equation (5.7). Take the logarithm and the product becomes a sum:

\[ l(m_k \mid \mathbf{z}_{1:t}) = l(m_k \mid \mathbf{z}_{1:t-1}) + l(m_k \mid \mathbf{z}_t) - l(m_k). \]

The last term is the log-odds of the prior. With the usual prior \(p(m_k) = 0.5\) it is \(\log 1 = 0\), and what remains is equation (5.6). Assumption 2, independent cells, is what allowed us to do all of this for one cell at a time. To read a probability back out, invert the definition: \(p = 1 / (1 + e^{-l})\).

5. The inverse sensor model, and a grid you can fill

The term \(l(m_k \mid \mathbf{z}_t)\) is the inverse sensor model: it goes from a measurement to a belief about a cell, the reverse of a model that predicts measurements. For a narrow laser beam a simple piecewise-constant model is enough. §5.4.4.1 · p. 138

Where the cell isWhat the beam saysUpdate to l
Between the sensor and the beam's end pointThe beam passed, so the cell is probably freeAdd a negative constant
Contains the end pointSomething reflected the beam hereAdd a positive constant
Beyond the end point, or off the beamNothingLeave unchanged

Worked example. Say a hit means \(p = 0.7\), so \(l = \log(0.7/0.3) = +0.847\), and a pass means \(p = 0.4\), so \(l = \log(0.4/0.6) = -0.405\). A cell that starts at \(l = 0\) and is hit three times reaches \(l = 2.542\), which is \(p = 1/(1 + e^{-2.542}) = 0.93\). Two later beams that pass through it bring it to \(l = 1.731\), \(p = 0.85\). No measurement is ever stored: the single number \(l\) summarizes all of them.

Try it: the map below already holds one scan. Press "Scan here" twice and watch the probe cell on the lower face of the box. Then press "Auto tour".

Notice the probe cell go 0.70, 0.84, 0.93 as in the worked example. Notice also what stays half-tone after the first scan: the regions hidden behind the box and behind the thin wall, the pillar included. Unknown is not the same as free, and only moving the robot resolves it.

Two limits of the grid follow from its assumptions. Treating cells as independent ignores that walls are continuous, so a grid cannot guess the occupancy of an unobserved cell from its neighbours. And the cell size is fixed before mapping starts, so the resolution is the same everywhere. §5.2.1 · p. 124 Days 4 and 5 return to both.

Common mistakes

  • "θ in (5.2)–(5.4) is measured from the z axis." Here it is measured from the horizontal plane, which is why \(z = r\sin\theta\). The physics convention (angle from the z axis) swaps the sine and cosine of \(\theta\).
  • "A cell at p = 0.5 is half full." It means no information. The cell is either occupied or free; the probability describes what we know.
  • "The inverse sensor model is the sensor's noise model." A noise model is \(p(\mathbf{z} \mid m)\), from world to measurement. The inverse model is \(p(m_k \mid \mathbf{z}_t)\), from measurement to world, and it is usually designed by hand.

Check yourself

Q1. A LiDAR must resolve 1.5 cm in range. What timing resolution does it need?

From (5.1), a range change of 0.015 m is a delay change of 2 × 0.015 / (3 × 10⁸) = 10⁻¹⁰ s = 100 ps. The factor 2 is the round trip.

Q2. A beam with azimuth 90° and inclination 30° returns r = 20 m. Where is the point in the sensor frame?

Ground distance 20 cos 30° = 17.3 m, all of it along y because the azimuth is 90°. Height z = 20 sin 30° = 10 m. The second option is what you get if you measure the inclination from the z axis.

Q3. A cell starts at p = 0.5. A hit means p = 0.7 and a pass means p = 0.4. After two hits and one pass, what is its occupancy probability?

Odds multiply: (7/3) × (7/3) × (2/3) = 3.63, so p = 3.63 / 4.63 = 0.78. In log-odds: 0.847 + 0.847 − 0.405 = 1.289. Averaging the three probabilities (0.60) is not Bayes' rule.

Q4. A beam returns r = 5 m. What does the piecewise-constant model do to a cell 7 m from the sensor in the same direction?

The beam stopped at 5 m, so it carries no information about what lies behind. The cell keeps whatever log-odds it had, which is 0 (unknown) if nothing else has observed it.

Recap

  1. Time of flight gives range, \(r = c\,\Delta t / 2\). A scan is a range image or depth map, and with the beam angles or camera intrinsics it becomes a point cloud in the sensor frame.
  2. \(x = r\cos\theta\cos\phi\), \(y = r\cos\theta\sin\phi\), \(z = r\sin\theta\), with \(\theta\) measured from the horizontal plane.
  3. An occupancy grid stores one probability per cell and treats cells as independent.
  4. Bayes' rule in log-odds form is an addition: \(l \leftarrow l + l(m_k \mid \mathbf{z}_t)\), with \(p = 1/(1 + e^{-l})\). The prior term vanishes for a prior of 0.5.
  5. A beam lowers \(l\) in the cells it crosses, raises it in the cell where it ends, and leaves the rest unknown.

Sources

  1. SLAM Handbook, Chapter 5 introduction, §5.1 "Range Sensing Preliminaries", §5.2 opening and §5.2.1 "Occupancy Maps", pp. 119–124; the piecewise-constant model is mentioned in §5.4.4.1, p. 138.
  2. Thrun, Burgard, Fox, Probabilistic Robotics, 2005 (the binary Bayes filter and the derivation of the log-odds update).
  3. Hartley and Zisserman, Multiple View Geometry in Computer Vision, 2004 (the pinhole camera model used for back-projection).

Week 8 · Day 2

Signed distance fields and the TSDF

After today you can compute a projective signed distance from a beam, fuse several of them into a TSDF voxel by weighted averaging, and locate the surface at the zero crossing.

About 60 min · Read §5.2.2–5.2.3, pp. 124–126 (3 pages) · Needs Week 8 Day 1

Read first: §5.2.2 and §5.2.3, pp. 124–126

While you read, look for:

  • The sign convention of an implicit surface, and how Figure 5.6 shows it for a disk (p. 125).
  • The two distances: Euclidean (the ESDF) and projective, and the reason the second one is used when estimating a surface from measurements (pp. 125–126).
  • What the truncation band is and why it exists (p. 126).
  • The two differences between occupancy and distance fields in §5.2.3: directness and smoothness (p. 126).

Today's big idea

Instead of asking "is this cell occupied?", ask "how far is this point from the nearest surface, and on which side?". The surface is then the set of points where the answer is zero. A range beam gives a cheap approximation of that distance for every voxel near its end point, and averaging the approximations from many beams gives a smooth field whose zero crossing locates the surface more finely than the voxel size.

1. A surface as the zero set of a function

An implicit surface is a function \(f(\mathbf{p})\) of position that is zero exactly on the surface, negative inside objects, and positive outside. §5.2.2 · pp. 124–125 The surface is never listed point by point; it is wherever \(f\) changes sign.

Example: a disk of radius 0.75 centred at the origin, as in Figure 5.6, can be described by

\[ f(x, y) = \sqrt{x^2 + y^2} - 0.75 . \]

At \((1, 0)\), \(f = +0.25\): outside. At \((0.3, 0.4)\), \(f = 0.5 - 0.75 = -0.25\): inside. At \((0.45, 0.6)\), \(f = 0.75 - 0.75 = 0\): on the surface. Testing whether a point is inside an obstacle is one function evaluation and a sign check, and there is no resolution to choose. §5.2.2 · p. 125

2. The Euclidean signed distance

Many functions have the same zero set. The most useful one is the Euclidean signed distance function (ESDF): its magnitude is the distance to the nearest surface point and its sign says inside or outside. §5.2.2 · p. 125 The disk function above is one. At \((1, 0)\) it says "0.25 from the surface", which is true.

That makes collision checking cheap. A round robot of radius \(\rho\) centred at \(\mathbf{p}\) touches nothing exactly when \(f(\mathbf{p}) \gt \rho\). And the gradient \(\nabla f\) tells a planner which way to move to gain clearance.

Filling the gap: a distance field has gradient length 1

The book speaks of "high-quality proximity gradients". The reason they are high quality is the Eikonal property: wherever a distance function \(d\) is differentiable, \(\norm{\nabla d} = 1\). Two short steps show why, for the unsigned distance outside objects.

Step 1: \(d\) cannot change faster than one metre per metre. Take two points \(\mathbf{p}\) and \(\mathbf{q}\). One way to reach the surface from \(\mathbf{p}\) is to walk to \(\mathbf{q}\) and then to the surface point nearest to \(\mathbf{q}\), so \(d(\mathbf{p}) \le \norm{\mathbf{p} - \mathbf{q}} + d(\mathbf{q})\). Swapping the roles gives \(|d(\mathbf{p}) - d(\mathbf{q})| \le \norm{\mathbf{p} - \mathbf{q}}\), hence \(\norm{\nabla d} \le 1\).

Step 2: in one direction it changes at exactly that rate. Let \(\mathbf{s}\) be the surface point nearest to \(\mathbf{p}\), and walk a distance \(\varepsilon\) straight towards it. The new point is at distance \(d(\mathbf{p}) - \varepsilon\) from \(\mathbf{s}\), and by step 1 it cannot be closer to the surface than that. So \(d\) drops by exactly \(\varepsilon\): the slope along the unit vector \(\mathbf{u}\) from \(\mathbf{s}\) to \(\mathbf{p}\) is 1.

A gradient of length at most 1 with slope 1 along \(\mathbf{u}\) must be \(\mathbf{u}\) itself: \(\nabla d = \mathbf{u}\), a unit vector pointing straight away from the nearest surface point. Check on the disk: \(\nabla f = (x, y)/\sqrt{x^2 + y^2}\), which has length 1 everywhere except at the centre, where the nearest surface point is not unique. On the surface itself, \(\nabla f\) is the surface normal.

Computing an ESDF needs, for every map point, the closest surface point. For a known surface, algorithms such as Fast Marching do this efficiently. While the surface is still being estimated from measurements, it is too expensive and too fragile. §5.2.2 · p. 125

3. What one beam gives: the projective distance

A beam from the sensor origin \(\mathbf{o}\) that returns range \(r\) says where the surface is along that beam. For a query point \(\mathbf{q}\) on the beam, the projective signed distance is the distance from \(\mathbf{q}\) to the beam's end point, measured along the beam: §5.2.2 · pp. 125–126

\[ d_{\text{proj}}(\mathbf{q}) = r - \norm{\mathbf{q} - \mathbf{o}} . \]

It is positive in front of the surface, zero at the hit, negative behind. It costs one subtraction, with no search for a closest point.

The projective distance is never smaller in magnitude than the true one: the beam's end point is itself a surface point, so the nearest surface point can only be as close or closer. For a flat wall hit at angle \(\alpha\) to its normal the factor is \(1/\cos\alpha\); at \(\alpha = 60^\circ\) the projective distance is twice the true one. What survives is the place where it is zero. The estimated surface is correct even though the distances around it are overestimates. §5.2.2 · p. 126

4. Truncate and average: the TSDF

Far from the surface the overestimate is large and useless, and behind the surface the beam knows nothing at all. So the projective distance is clamped to a truncation band of half-width \(\tau\) around the surface. The clamped field is the Truncated Signed Distance Function (TSDF). §5.2.2 · p. 126 A common convention, and the one used in this lesson: a voxel in front of the band receives \(+\tau\), which only says "free", and a voxel more than \(\tau\) behind the hit receives nothing.

Each voxel stores a value \(D\) and a weight \(W\), both starting at zero. For every new measurement \(d\) (the clamped projective distance at the voxel centre) with weight \(w\), the update of Curless and Levoy, made popular in robotics by KinectFusion, is a running weighted average: §5.2.2 · p. 126

\[ D \leftarrow \frac{W D + w\,d}{W + w}, \qquad W \leftarrow W + w . \]

Filling the gap: why an average, and why it can be done one measurement at a time

Suppose a voxel has received \(d_1, \dots, d_n\) with weights \(w_1, \dots, w_n\). The single value that fits them best in the weighted least-squares sense minimizes \(J(D) = \sum_i w_i (D - d_i)^2\). Setting the derivative to zero,

\[ \frac{dJ}{dD} = 2\sum_i w_i (D - d_i) = 0 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad D_n = \frac{\sum_i w_i d_i}{\sum_i w_i}. \]

With \(w_i = 1/\sigma_i^2\) this is the maximum-likelihood estimate under Gaussian noise (Week 1 · Day 4). Now write \(W_{n-1} = \sum_{i \lt n} w_i\). The old average satisfies \(W_{n-1} D_{n-1} = \sum_{i \lt n} w_i d_i\), so

\[ D_n = \frac{\sum_{i \lt n} w_i d_i + w_n d_n}{W_{n-1} + w_n} = \frac{W_{n-1} D_{n-1} + w_n d_n}{W_{n-1} + w_n}. \]

That is the update above. The two numbers \(D\) and \(W\) carry everything needed from the past, the same economy as the log-odds of Day 1. Averaging also removes noise: \(n\) independent measurements with standard deviation \(\sigma\) average to one with \(\sigma/\sqrt{n}\). Range noise of 5 cm becomes 1 cm after 25 scans.

Worked example, with \(w = 1\). A voxel receives \(d = 0.12, 0.08, 0.13\) m. After the first, \(D = 0.12\), \(W = 1\). After the second, \(D = (1 \times 0.12 + 0.08)/2 = 0.10\). After the third, \(D = (2 \times 0.10 + 0.13)/3 = 0.11\), \(W = 3\).

The surface lies between two neighbouring voxels whose values have opposite signs. Because the field is nearly linear there, linear interpolation places it. If the voxel at position \(x_a\) has \(D_a \gt 0\) and the next one at \(x_b\) has \(D_b \lt 0\),

\[ x^{*} = x_a + (x_b - x_a)\,\frac{D_a}{D_a - D_b}. \]

With voxels at 2.0 m and 2.1 m holding \(+0.06\) and \(-0.04\): \(x^{*} = 2.0 + 0.1 \times 0.06/0.10 = 2.06\) m. The voxels are 10 cm apart, yet the surface is placed to the centimetre.

Try it: the same room as yesterday on a finer grid, now storing a TSDF. Read the two error tiles, press "Auto tour", and read them again. Then look at the thin wall in the middle.

Notice that after one scan the zero crossing is no better than the raw end points (3.6 cm against 2.6 cm), since nothing has been averaged yet. After the 50 scans of the tour its typical error is about 1 cm: a tenth of the 12.5 cm cell, and well below the 5 cm range noise. The probe cell reads 0.40 m where the true distance is 0.19 m, the overestimate of section 3. The thin wall is the failure case: seen from both sides, it comes out about three times too thick. Set τ to 0.10 m, less than one cell, and the outline after one scan is full of gaps.

5. Occupancy or distance?

Both are volumetric: they estimate a quantity everywhere in the observed space. They differ in what they make easy. §5.2.3 · p. 126

QuestionOccupancy mapDistance field (TSDF)
How directly do beams give the quantity?Directly: a beam says free, occupied, or nothing. Few heuristics.Indirectly: the true distance is not measurable from one beam, so a proxy (projective, truncated) is used.
How smooth is the stored field?It models a yes-or-no property, so it jumps at surfaces.Smooth and differentiable: gradients, and sub-voxel accuracy by interpolation.
Thin obstaclesKept.Easily lost.

The last row is the price of estimating negative values behind a surface. If a thin object is seen from both sides, a voxel just behind it for one viewpoint is just in front of it for the other. Positive and negative values are averaged, and the zero crossing can move or vanish. §5.4.4.1 · p. 138 This is what displaced the outline of the thin wall in the widget.

Common mistakes

  • "A TSDF stores the distance to the nearest surface." It stores an average of clamped distances along beams. It is close to the true distance only near surfaces seen roughly head-on, and it overestimates elsewhere. A planner that needs true clearances should build an ESDF from it.
  • "A larger truncation band is always safer." A wide band fuses more overestimates and erases objects thinner than the band. A band narrower than a voxel leaves holes, because the voxels on the two sides of a surface are no longer both updated.
  • "Negative values mean the sensor saw inside the object." No beam goes there. The negative side is extrapolated from the hit point, which is why it is trusted only within the band.

Check yourself

Q1. A disk of radius 2 m centred at the origin has f(x, y) = √(x² + y²) − 2. What does f say about the point (1.2, 0.5)?

√(1.44 + 0.25) = 1.3, so f = 1.3 − 2 = −0.7. Negative means inside, and the magnitude is the distance to the surface.

Q2. A beam returns r = 4.00 m and τ = 0.20 m. A voxel centre lies on the beam, 3.70 m from the sensor. What does this beam contribute to that voxel?

The projective distance is 4.00 − 3.70 = +0.30 m, which is clamped to +τ = 0.20 m. A voxel at 4.50 m would have −0.50 m, deeper than τ behind the surface, and would be skipped.

Q3. A voxel holds D = 0.10 m with W = 3. A new measurement d = 0.02 m arrives with weight 1. What is the new D?

(3 × 0.10 + 1 × 0.02) / 4 = 0.08 m, and W becomes 4. The old value counts three times because it already summarizes three measurements; 0.06 would be the answer only if W were 1.

Q4. Two neighbouring voxel centres are 5 cm apart and hold D = +0.03 m and D = −0.02 m. Where is the surface?

The fraction of the way is 0.03 / (0.03 + 0.02) = 0.6, and 0.6 × 5 cm = 3 cm. The surface is closer to the voxel whose value is closer to zero.

Q5. A beam hits a flat wall at 60° to the wall's normal. At some point on the beam the projective distance is 0.40 m. How far is that point from the wall?

Euclidean distance = projective distance × cos α = 0.40 × 0.5 = 0.20 m. The projective distance overestimates, here by a factor of two.

Recap

  1. An implicit surface is the zero set of a function that is negative inside and positive outside.
  2. The Euclidean signed distance has a gradient of length 1 that points away from the nearest surface point. It gives one-lookup collision checks and useful gradients.
  3. One beam gives the projective distance \(r - \norm{\mathbf{q} - \mathbf{o}}\): cheap, an overestimate, but zero in the right place.
  4. A TSDF clamps it to a band \(\pm\tau\) and fuses by \(D \leftarrow (WD + wd)/(W + w)\), the incremental form of weighted least squares.
  5. Occupancy is direct and keeps thin obstacles. Distance fields are smooth, differentiable, and accurate below the voxel size, but can erase thin objects.

Sources

  1. SLAM Handbook, §5.2.2 "Implicit Surface and Distance Fields" and §5.2.3 "Occupancy Maps or Distance Fields?", pp. 124–126; the thin-object failure is described in §5.4.4.1, p. 138.
  2. Curless and Levoy, A Volumetric Method for Building Complex Models from Range Images, 1996 (the weighted running average).
  3. Osher and Fedkiw, Level Set Methods and Dynamic Implicit Surfaces, 2003 (signed distance functions and the property \(\norm{\nabla d} = 1\)).

Week 8 · Day 3

Points, surfels, meshes, voxels, and functions

After today you can describe the five spatial abstractions used for dense maps, interpolate a value inside a voxel grid, and turn a signed distance grid into an outline with marching squares.

About 60 min · Read §5.3.1–5.3.2, pp. 126–132 (6 pages) · Needs Week 8 Day 2

Read first: §5.3.1 and §5.3.2, pp. 126–132

While you read, look for:

  • The four categories of §5.3.1 (pp. 126–127), next to Figure 5.4 back on p. 123.
  • What a surfel stores (p. 128), and how the normal distributions transform reads a surface normal from a covariance matrix (p. 129).
  • The sentence on p. 130 that calls a voxel "merely a container", and the two different meanings a voxel value can have.
  • §5.3.2.6 on conversions, and Figure 5.8 (p. 131).

Today's big idea

Yesterday's question was which quantity to estimate. Today's is which geometric building block carries it: points, small discs, triangles, cells, or a continuous function. Each one makes some operations trivial and others awkward, so real systems convert between them. The conversion to know by heart is Marching Cubes, which turns a signed distance grid into a mesh.

1. Two ways to sort representations

The book sorts representations along two axes: whether they describe the surface or the whole volume, and whether the geometry is stored explicitly, as elements you can list, or implicitly, as a function you evaluate. §5.3.1 · pp. 126–127

Stored asSurface (the boundary of objects)Volume (all of space)
Explicit: a list of elementsPoint cloud, surfels, polygon meshPoints as used in LiDAR SLAM; voxels holding occupancy or distance
Implicit: a functionThe zero set of a signed distance functionGaussian process maps, Hilbert maps

The boxes are not sealed, as the caption of Figure 5.4 warns. A TSDF grid is the standard mix: voxels, which are explicit volume elements, hold samples of a function whose zero set is an implicit surface.

2. Points and surfels

The simplest dense map is every point ever measured. Each scan \(\mathsf{P}_t\) lives in its own sensor frame, so it is first moved into the map frame with the pose \(\mathbf{T}^1_t\) that the back-end estimated, and then added to the map cloud: §5.3.2.1 · p. 127

\[ \mathsf{P}_M = \bigcup_{t} \left\{ \mathbf{T}^1_t\,\mathbf{p} \;:\; \mathbf{p} \in \mathsf{P}_t \right\}. \]

This grows without bound, since every revisit of a place adds the same wall again. The usual cure is to keep only a few points per small cube of space, or only scans chosen as keyframes. A second weakness is that a bare point says nothing about the surface it came from: once the viewpoint is forgotten, you cannot tell which side is inside. §5.3.2.1 · p. 127

A surfel (surface element) repairs that. It is a small disc: a position \(\mathbf{p} \in \R^3\), a normal \(\mathbf{n} \in \R^3\), and a radius \(r\). Many nearby measurements are merged into one disc, which loses fine detail but saves memory: in the book's Figure 5.7 the accumulated point cloud takes 2.95 GB and the surfel map of the same drive 160 MB. §5.3.2.2 · pp. 128–129

The normal distributions transform (NDT) is a close relative. Space is cut into voxels, and each voxel stores the mean \(\boldsymbol{\mu}\) and covariance \(\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\) of the points that fell in it. If the eigenvalues of \(\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\) are \(\lambda_1 \lt \lambda_2 \lt \lambda_3\) and \(\lambda_1 \ll \lambda_2\), the points form a flat patch whose normal is the eigenvector \(\mathbf{v}_1\). §5.3.2.2 · p. 129

Filling the gap: why the smallest eigenvector is the normal

Take a unit vector \(\mathbf{u}\). The spread of the points along \(\mathbf{u}\) is the variance of their projections,

\[ \frac{1}{N}\sum_i \left(\mathbf{u}\T(\mathbf{p}_i - \boldsymbol{\mu})\right)^2 = \mathbf{u}\T \left[\frac{1}{N}\sum_i (\mathbf{p}_i - \boldsymbol{\mu})(\mathbf{p}_i - \boldsymbol{\mu})\T\right] \mathbf{u} = \mathbf{u}\T\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\,\mathbf{u}. \]

Points on a plane have almost no spread along the plane's normal, so the normal is the \(\mathbf{u}\) that minimizes \(\mathbf{u}\T\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\mathbf{u}\). Write \(\mathbf{u} = \sum_j c_j \mathbf{v}_j\) in the orthonormal eigenvectors of \(\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\), with \(\sum_j c_j^2 = 1\). Then \(\mathbf{u}\T\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\mathbf{u} = \sum_j \lambda_j c_j^2 \ge \lambda_1\), with equality when \(\mathbf{u} = \mathbf{v}_1\). The smallest eigenvalue is the variance across the patch, and its eigenvector is the normal.

A 2D example. Four points \((0, 0)\), \((1, 0.1)\), \((2, -0.1)\), \((3, 0)\) lie roughly on the x axis. Their mean is \((1.5, 0)\) and

\[ \boldsymbol{\Sigma} = \begin{bmatrix} 1.25 & -0.025 \\ -0.025 & 0.005 \end{bmatrix}, \qquad \lambda_1 = 0.0045,\quad \lambda_2 = 1.2505 . \]

Solving \((\boldsymbol{\Sigma} - \lambda_1\mathbf{I})\mathbf{v}_1 = \mathbf{0}\) gives \(\mathbf{v}_1 \propto (0.02, 1)\): the normal points along y, as it should, and the thickness of the patch is \(\sqrt{0.0045} = 0.067\) m.

3. Meshes and voxels

Points and surfels do not say which piece of surface connects to which. A mesh does: it is a set of vertices joined into polygon faces, usually triangles, since any polygon can be cut into triangles. Connectivity makes a surface watertight and lets you walk along it or interpolate on it. The element count follows the complexity of the shape, not its size: a flat wall of any extent is two triangles and four vertices. §5.3.2.3 · p. 129

Occupancy and signed distance are defined at every point of space, not only on surfaces. The direct way to store them is a regular grid of cells, called voxels in 3D. A voxel is only a container, and what its number means depends on the method. §5.3.2.4 · p. 130

GridA voxel's value meansValue at an arbitrary point
Occupancy gridThe probability that the cell contains an obstacleThe value of the voxel that contains the point
Signed distance fieldThe signed distance at the voxel's centreInterpolated from the neighbouring voxel centres

Filling the gap: interpolating between voxel centres

In 2D, let the four nearest centres hold \(f_{00}, f_{10}, f_{01}, f_{11}\) (first index along x, second along y), and let the query point sit a fraction \(a\) of the way along x and \(b\) along y, both between 0 and 1. Interpolate along x on the two rows, then along y between the results:

\[ f(a, b) = (1-b)\big[(1-a) f_{00} + a f_{10}\big] + b\big[(1-a) f_{01} + a f_{11}\big]. \]

This is bilinear interpolation. Each corner's weight is the product of two factors, the four weights sum to 1, and at a corner the formula returns that corner's value. Example: \(f_{00} = 0.10\), \(f_{10} = -0.06\), \(f_{01} = 0.14\), \(f_{11} = -0.02\), and \((a, b) = (0.5, 0.25)\). The rows give \(0.02\) and \(0.06\), and \(f = 0.75 \times 0.02 + 0.25 \times 0.06 = 0.03\). In 3D the same idea with eight corners and three factors is trilinear interpolation.

4. Continuous functions

The last abstraction drops the grid. Mapping becomes regression: fit a function to the measurements and evaluate it wherever you like. Functions with few parameters, such as lines in 2D or planes in 3D, are compact and fast but assume the world is made of them. Control-point functions such as B-splines and non-parametric ones such as Gaussian processes assume less. Their advantages are that the resolution is not fixed in advance, that they fill gaps between measurements, and that a function which is at least once differentiable provides gradients, and so surface normals. §5.3.2.5 · pp. 130–131 Day 5 builds one.

5. Conversions, and marching squares

Systems rarely stay in one representation. §5.3.2.6 · pp. 131–132

FromToHow
Points or meshSigned distanceClosest-point lookup where needed, or a wavefront over a whole grid (fast marching)
Signed distance gridMeshMarching Cubes
Mesh (also CAD and building models)Points or surfelsSample the faces
Any discrete dataContinuous functionFit its parameters by optimization

Marching Cubes visits every cube of eight neighbouring samples on its own, looks at the signs at the corners, and emits the triangles for that sign pattern from a table. Its 2D version, marching squares, shows the whole idea. A square has four corners, so there are \(2^4 = 16\) sign patterns, and they fall into four kinds:

The table only says which edges the line crosses. Where on each edge is refined by linear interpolation, the same formula as yesterday's zero crossing: on an edge whose ends hold \(f_a\) and \(f_b\) of opposite sign, the vertex sits at the fraction \(t = f_a / (f_a - f_b)\) from end \(a\). With \(f_a = 0.3\) and \(f_b = -0.1\), \(t = 0.75\). In 3D a cube has \(2^8 = 256\) sign patterns, which symmetry reduces to the 15 configurations of Figure 5.8. §5.3.2.6 · p. 131

Try it: the disk below is sampled every metre. Switch interpolation off and on. Then choose the room and step the grid spacing from 0.5 m down to 0.125 m, watching the thin wall in the middle.
