Notice that at 1 m spacing the 20 vertices lie 2.7 cm from the true circle on average with interpolation, and 21 cm without it, where the outline becomes a staircase of straight and 45° pieces. In the room, the 10 cm wall is absent down to 0.25 m spacing, because no sample falls inside it. It appears at 0.125 m, and the outline length jumps from 40.9 m to 45.3 m (true value 45.7 m).

Common mistakes

  • "A voxel is a little solid cube." It is a storage slot. In an occupancy grid its value does stand for the whole cell; in a distance field it is a sample at one point, meant to be interpolated.
  • "A point cloud is a surface." It is samples of one, with no normals, no connectivity, and no inside or outside. Turning it into a mesh or a distance field needs extra information such as the viewpoint, or assumptions.
  • "Marching Cubes can recover detail the grid missed." It only reads signs and values at the samples. If no sample falls inside an object, there is no sign change and the object is absent from the mesh.

Check yourself

Q1. An NDT voxel has covariance eigenvalues 0.0004, 0.09, and 0.12 m². What do the points in it look like?

The spread is large in two directions and tiny (2 cm standard deviation) in one, so the points lie on a plane. The direction of smallest spread is the normal. A rod would have one large eigenvalue and two small ones.

Q2. Four neighbouring voxel centres hold f₀₀ = 0.2, f₁₀ = 0.0, f₀₁ = 0.4, f₁₁ = 0.2. What is the bilinear value at a = 0.25, b = 0.5?

Along x: the lower row gives 0.75 × 0.2 + 0.25 × 0.0 = 0.15, the upper row 0.75 × 0.4 + 0.25 × 0.2 = 0.35. Along y: 0.5 × 0.15 + 0.5 × 0.35 = 0.25.

Q3. A grid edge is 10 cm long. Its ends hold +0.3 and −0.1. Where does marching squares put the vertex?

t = 0.3 / (0.3 + 0.1) = 0.75 of the way from the positive end, which is 7.5 cm. The zero is closer to the end whose value is closer to zero.

Q4. A wall 4 cm thick stands between two columns of a signed distance grid with 10 cm spacing, touching no sample. What does marching squares output for it?

The algorithm sees only the corner samples. With no negative sample there is no sign change and no line. This is the thin-obstacle weakness of sampled implicit surfaces from §5.2.3.

Recap

  1. Representations differ in what they describe (surface or volume) and how (explicit elements or an implicit function), and real systems mix them.
  2. Points are raw samples. Surfels add a normal and a radius. An NDT voxel stores a mean and covariance, whose smallest eigenvector is the surface normal.
  3. Meshes add connectivity. Voxels are containers: an occupancy value covers the cell, a distance value is a sample to interpolate (bilinear in 2D, trilinear in 3D).
  4. Continuous functions have no fixed resolution and can provide gradients.
  5. Marching Cubes converts a distance grid to a mesh: corner signs select the pattern, linear interpolation \(t = f_a/(f_a - f_b)\) places the vertices.

Sources

  1. SLAM Handbook, §5.3.1 "Explicitness of Target Spatial Structures" and §5.3.2 "Types of Spatial Abstractions", pp. 126–132; Figure 5.4, p. 123.
  2. Lorensen and Cline, Marching Cubes: A High Resolution 3D Surface Construction Algorithm, 1987 (the algorithm; marching squares is its 2D form).
  3. The eigenvector argument and bilinear interpolation are standard linear algebra and numerical analysis; see Strang, Introduction to Linear Algebra, 2016, for the eigenvalue bound on \(\mathbf{u}\T\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\mathbf{u}\).

Week 8 · Day 4

Storing a map and filling it: arrays, hashes, trees, integrators

After today you can work out what a dense voxel grid costs in memory, explain how hashing and octrees avoid that cost, and describe the two ways beams are integrated into a voxel map.

About 60 min · Read §5.3.3–5.4.4, pp. 132–141 (9 pages) · Needs Week 8 Day 3

Read first: §5.3.3 to §5.4.4, pp. 132–141

This is a longer stretch. Sections 5.4.1 to 5.4.3 (pp. 135–137) name many systems; read them for the strategies, not the names. While you read, look for:

  • What the function \(f(\cdot)\) in Figure 5.9 does (p. 132).
  • The three things to decide when a hash table stores a map (p. 133).
  • How an octant is defined, and how an octree grows when data falls outside its root (pp. 133–134).
  • The two measurement integrators and what each one needs to know about the sensor (pp. 139–140).
  • The sentence on p. 140 that says how memory grows with volume and with resolution.

Today's big idea

A room is mostly air, and the interesting part of a map is the thin layer around surfaces. A plain 3D array pays for every voxel of the bounding box. Hash tables and trees pay only for the voxels that hold something, in exchange for a more complicated lookup. Which one to use, and how to push thousands of beams per scan into it, decides whether a mapping system runs in real time.

1. The dense array and its bill

The simplest storage is one array, plus a function from a position to an array index. §5.3.3.1 · p. 132 For a grid with origin \((x_0, y_0, z_0)\), cell size \(\Delta\), and \(N_x \times N_y \times N_z\) cells, a point \((x, y, z)\) lies in the cell

\[ i = \left\lfloor \frac{x - x_0}{\Delta} \right\rfloor, \quad j = \left\lfloor \frac{y - y_0}{\Delta} \right\rfloor, \quad k = \left\lfloor \frac{z - z_0}{\Delta} \right\rfloor, \qquad n = i + N_x\,(j + N_y\,k), \]

where \(\lfloor\cdot\rfloor\) rounds down and \(n\) is the position in the array. Example: origin \((-10, -10, 0)\), \(\Delta = 0.25\) m, \(N_x = N_y = 80\). The point \((2.6, -3.1, 1.3)\) gives \(i = \lfloor 50.4 \rfloor = 50\), \(j = \lfloor 27.6 \rfloor = 27\), \(k = \lfloor 5.2 \rfloor = 5\), and \(n = 50 + 80 \times (27 + 80 \times 5) = 34{,}210\). A lookup is a handful of arithmetic operations, which is why this layout is fast.

The cost is memory. Map a 100 m × 100 m × 10 m building at 5 cm: \(2000 \times 2000 \times 200 = 8 \times 10^{8}\) voxels. At 4 bytes each that is 3.2 GB. Halving the voxel size to 2.5 cm multiplies the count by \(2^3 = 8\), to 25.6 GB. Memory grows linearly with the mapped volume and with the cube of the resolution. §5.4.4.4 · p. 140 And when the robot drives out of the box, the whole array has to be copied into a larger one. §5.3.3.1 · p. 132

2. Hash tables and voxel blocks

A hash table keeps the fast lookup and drops the bounding box. Cut the map into pieces with integer coordinates (single voxels, or voxel blocks of, say, 8 × 8 × 8 voxels), and store only the pieces that contain data in a table. §5.3.3.2 · p. 133

Filling the gap: what a hash table does

A hash function turns a key, here a block coordinate, into a slot number in a table of fixed size. To find block \((i, j)\) you compute its slot and look there; no search through the map is needed, so the cost does not depend on how large the map is. That is the \(O(1)\) of the book. Two different keys can land in the same slot, a collision. The table then stores both, for example in a short list hanging off the slot, and compares keys to pick the right one. A good hash function spreads neighbouring blocks over the table so that collisions stay rare.

The figure uses the toy function \(\text{slot} = (7i + 13j) \bmod 16\). Block \((2, 2)\) goes to \((14 + 26) \bmod 16 = 8\).

The block size is a trade. Small blocks follow the surface closely and waste few empty voxels, but there are many of them, which makes the table large and slow to insert into. Large blocks are the reverse. §5.3.3.2 · p. 133; §5.4.4.2 · p. 139

3. Trees

An octree covers space with one cube, the root octant, given by a centre \(\mathbf{c}\) and an extent \(e\). Any octant can be split into eight children of extent \(e/2\), and only the children that contain data are created. §5.3.3.3 · pp. 133–134 After \(d\) splits the cell size is \(e/2^d\): a 102.4 m root reaches 10 cm cells at depth 10. If new data falls outside the root, a larger root is put on top and the old root becomes one of its children.

What a tree adds over a hash table is hierarchy. Large uniform regions are stored as one big node, coarse versions of the map come for free, and searches such as "nearest neighbour" can discard whole branches. What it costs is that reaching a leaf takes one step per level, and that the parent-child links themselves use memory. §5.3.3.3 · p. 134

Try it: a quadtree, the 2D octree, on this week's room. Set the depth to 1, then raise it one step at a time and compare how the two cell counts grow.

Notice that up to depth 3 the tree saves almost nothing: the squares are so large that nearly every one could touch a surface. From depth 5 on, each extra level about doubles the leaves (833, 1637, 3323) while the dense grid quadruples. At depth 7 the tree holds 10% of the cells of the grid.

The reason is geometric. At depth \(d\) the cells have size \(e/2^d\). A curve of length \(L\) passes through roughly \(L \cdot 2^d / e\) of them, a number that doubles per level, while the full grid has \(4^d\) cells. In 3D a surface crosses a number of cells that grows like \(4^d\), against \(8^d\) for the full grid. Sparse structures store the surface, not the volume.

Hybrid structures combine the two. Hashed voxel blocks keep a dense array inside each block, which is simple and suits GPUs. The VDB structure hashes blocks and puts a small tree of fixed height inside each, so lookups take constant time and the map still has several resolutions. §5.3.3.4 · pp. 134–135

4. Building point, surfel, and mesh maps

Section 5.4 goes through the abstractions of Day 3 again, now asking how each map is built and kept small. §5.4.1–5.4.3 · pp. 135–137

MapHow it is kept manageableWorth remembering
PointsA voxel grid or octree that keeps only a few points per cell. LOAM instead keeps only points on corners and flat surfaces.The stored points are original measurements, not cell averages. The same grid gives the fast nearest-neighbour search that ICP scan registration needs.
SurfelsAn octree with mean and covariance statistics at several levels, or a plain list that the GPU renders to find correspondences. Outdoors, submaps of 100 m × 100 m.Loop closures are cheap to apply: ElasticFusion deforms the surfels directly; SuMa ties each surfel to a pose and lets pose-graph optimization move it.
Meshes, built directlyDelaunay triangulation of the points, keeping the triangles on the surface.Adapts to the sampling density, but is sensitive to holes and irregular sampling. Suited to dense, accurate survey data.
Meshes, through an implicit surfaceFirst fit an implicit surface (radial basis functions, moving least squares, Poisson reconstruction, or a TSDF), then extract its zero set.The implicit step does the fusing and filtering. A TSDF is updated incrementally, so this route runs on a live sensor stream.

5. Voxel maps in practice

What to estimate. Occupancy has the better recall, so few obstacles are missed, which suits collision avoidance. TSDFs give better surfaces where the world is smooth and lose thin objects (Day 2). A TSDF overestimates distances, which is unsafe for a planner, so systems such as voxblox compute a true ESDF from the TSDF with a wavefront (brushfire) algorithm, and FIESTA computes one from an occupancy map. §5.4.4.1 · p. 138

How to integrate a scan. The measurement integrator applies the sensor model to every voxel the scan observed. There are two designs. §5.4.4.3 · pp. 139–140

IntegratorLoop overNeedsStrength and weakness
Ray tracingBeams: walk each one from the sensor to its end point and update the voxels it crossesOnly the sensor's positionGeneral. But voxels near the sensor are visited by many beams, which repeats work and makes parallel code collide on the same voxel.
ProjectionVoxels: project each one into the sensor and read off the beam that sees itThe full pose and the projection modelEach voxel is written once, so it parallelizes well and dominates on GPUs. Hard to use with unorganized or motion-corrected clouds.

The occupancy widget of Day 1 traces rays. The TSDF widget of Day 2 projects: it visits each cell, computes its bearing from the robot, and looks up the beam with that bearing.

Filling the gap: which voxels does a ray cross?

Ray tracing needs the exact list of cells between two points. Sampling the ray at small steps can skip a cell that the ray only clips. The standard exact method, due to Amanatides and Woo, steps from cell to cell. For a ray \(\mathbf{o} + t\,\mathbf{d}\) with unit direction \(\mathbf{d}\), keep for each axis the ray length \(t\) at which the next cell boundary on that axis is crossed. The smallest of these tells which boundary comes first.

cell = floor(o / Δ)                      # cell that contains the origin
for each axis a:
    step[a]   = sign(d[a])               # +1 or -1: direction of travel
    tMax[a]   = t at the first boundary crossed on axis a
    tDelta[a] = Δ / |d[a]|               # t between two boundaries on axis a
while cell is not the end cell:
    a = axis with the smallest tMax
    cell[a] += step[a]
    tMax[a] += tDelta[a]
    update(cell)

Each loop turn moves to exactly one neighbouring cell with two additions and one comparison per axis, and no cell is skipped or visited twice.

How to scale. Octomap stores occupancy in an octree and merges children whose values agree with their parent, so open space collapses into a few large nodes. It still integrates every beam at the finest resolution, so the update cost stays cubic. Later systems also lower the update resolution with distance, since beams spread out, and skip updates that would change nothing; wavemap does this on a wavelet encoding of the map, which stores differences between resolution levels. §5.4.4.4 · pp. 140–141

Check yourself

Q1. A dense voxel grid takes 32 MB at 10 cm voxels. How much does the same volume take at 2.5 cm?

The voxels are 4 times smaller along each of three axes, so there are 4³ = 64 times as many: 32 MB × 64 = 2048 MB.

Q2. A 2D grid has origin (−10, −10), 0.25 m cells, and 80 cells per row, with index n = i + 80 j. Which array element holds the point (2.6, −3.1)?

i = ⌊12.6 / 0.25⌋ = 50 and j = ⌊6.9 / 0.25⌋ = 27, so n = 50 + 80 × 27 = 2210. Swapping i and j gives 4027; rounding 27.6 up instead of down gives 2290.

Q3. An octree's root octant has an extent of 51.2 m and its finest leaves are 10 cm. How many levels does a lookup descend?

Each level halves the extent: 51.2 / 2⁹ = 0.1 m, so 9 levels. The lookup time grows with this height, which is the cost of a pure tree.

Q4. Why do GPU mapping systems prefer projection-based integration?

Looping over the map gives every voxel exactly one update per scan, with no race conditions and a predictable memory pattern. The price is that it needs the full sensor pose and projection model, which is the opposite of the first option.

Recap

  1. A dense array gives the fastest lookup, \(n = i + N_x(j + N_y k)\), and the largest memory bill: linear in volume, cubic in resolution.
  2. A hash table stores only the blocks that hold data and finds each in constant time. Voxel-block hashing keeps a small dense array in each block.
  3. An octree splits space only where there is data and gives several resolutions, at the cost of a lookup that takes one step per level. Sparse structures grow with the surface area, not the volume.
  4. Point and surfel maps are thinned with grids or trees. Meshes are built directly from points or, more robustly, from an implicit surface.
  5. Ray-tracing integrators loop over beams and need only the sensor position. Projection integrators loop over voxels, need the full sensor model, and parallelize well.

Sources

  1. SLAM Handbook, §5.3.3 "Data Structures and Storage", pp. 132–135, and §5.4.1–5.4.4 "Points", "Surfels", "Meshes", "Voxels", pp. 135–141.
  2. Amanatides and Woo, A Fast Voxel Traversal Algorithm for Ray Tracing, 1987 (the grid traversal in "Filling the gap").
  3. Cormen, Leiserson, Rivest, Stein, Introduction to Algorithms, 2009 (hash tables and collision resolution).

Week 8 · Day 5

Continuous maps, and choosing a representation

After today you can predict a map value and its uncertainty with Gaussian process regression, explain how a Hilbert map learns occupancy, and choose a representation for a given environment and task.

About 60 min · Read §5.4.5–5.5, pp. 141–148 (8 pages) · Needs Week 8 Day 1 and Week 5 Day 3

Read first: §5.4.5 to §5.5, pp. 141–148

While you read, look for:

  • Equations (5.10) and (5.11): which of the two contains the measured values \(\mathbf{y}\), and which does not (pp. 141–142).
  • The cost of a Gaussian process occupancy map, and why a GP implicit surface "falls back to the mean" far from the data (pp. 142–143).
  • The three design goals of Hilbert maps (p. 143).
  • Table 5.2 (p. 147). Pick one row and say in your own words why it holds.

Today's big idea

Voxel maps fix the resolution in advance and treat neighbouring cells as unrelated. A continuous map is a function fitted to the measurements instead. It can be evaluated anywhere, it fills gaps by using the correlation between nearby places, and a Gaussian process also says how sure it is. The price is computation. No representation is best at everything, so the last section of the chapter is about matching the map to the environment and the task.

1. Mapping as regression: the Gaussian process

A Gaussian process (GP) is a probability distribution over functions. It is fixed by a mean function \(m(\mathbf{x})\) and a kernel \(\mathcal{K}(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{x}')\), which gives the covariance between the function's values at two places: §5.4.5 · p. 141

\[ f(\mathbf{x}) \sim \mathcal{GP}\big(m(\mathbf{x}),\, \mathcal{K}(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{x}')\big). \tag{5.8} \]

You met GPs over time in Week 5 · Day 3. Here the input \(\mathbf{x}\) is a position in space and \(f\) is the quantity being mapped. A common kernel is the squared exponential, \(\mathcal{K}(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{x}') = \sigma_f^2 \exp\!\big(-\norm{\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{x}'}^2 / (2\ell^2)\big)\): values at places much closer than the length-scale \(\ell\) are strongly correlated, values much farther apart are not.

The data are \(J\) noisy measurements \(y_j = f(\mathbf{x}_j) + \epsilon_j\), with \(\epsilon_j \sim \N(0, \sigma_j^2)\), at the training locations \(\mathsf{X}\). We want \(\mathbf{f}_*\), the values at the test locations \(\mathsf{X}^*\). The book's predictive equations are §5.4.5 · pp. 141–142

\[ \bar{\mathbf{f}}_* = \mathbf{K}(\mathsf{X}^*, \mathsf{X})\left[\mathbf{K}(\mathsf{X}, \mathsf{X}) + \sigma_j^2\mathbf{I}\right]^{-1}\mathbf{y}, \tag{5.10} \] \[ \cov(\mathbf{f}_*) = \mathbf{K}(\mathsf{X}^*, \mathsf{X}^*) - \mathbf{K}(\mathsf{X}^*, \mathsf{X})\left[\mathbf{K}(\mathsf{X}, \mathsf{X}) + \sigma_j^2\mathbf{I}\right]^{-1}\mathbf{K}(\mathsf{X}, \mathsf{X}^*), \tag{5.11} \]

where \(\mathbf{K}(\mathsf{A}, \mathsf{B})\) is the matrix of kernel values between every point of \(\mathsf{A}\) and every point of \(\mathsf{B}\).

Filling the gap: from the joint Gaussian (5.9) to (5.10) and (5.11)

Equation (5.9) says that \(\mathbf{y}\) and \(\mathbf{f}_*\) are jointly Gaussian. The two predictive equations are the rule for conditioning one part of a Gaussian on the other. For a zero-mean pair

\[ \begin{bmatrix} \mathbf{a} \\ \mathbf{b} \end{bmatrix} \sim \N\!\left(\mathbf{0},\; \begin{bmatrix} \mathbf{A} & \mathbf{C} \\ \mathbf{C}\T & \mathbf{B} \end{bmatrix}\right) \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \mathbf{b} \mid \mathbf{a} \;\sim\; \N\!\left(\mathbf{C}\T\mathbf{A}^{-1}\mathbf{a},\;\; \mathbf{B} - \mathbf{C}\T\mathbf{A}^{-1}\mathbf{C}\right). \]

Why: define \(\mathbf{e} = \mathbf{b} - \mathbf{C}\T\mathbf{A}^{-1}\mathbf{a}\). Its covariance with \(\mathbf{a}\) is \(\mathbf{C}\T - \mathbf{C}\T\mathbf{A}^{-1}\mathbf{A} = \mathbf{0}\), and jointly Gaussian variables that are uncorrelated are independent. So \(\mathbf{b} = \mathbf{C}\T\mathbf{A}^{-1}\mathbf{a} + \mathbf{e}\) is a part fixed by \(\mathbf{a}\) plus a part that \(\mathbf{a}\) says nothing about. The first is the conditional mean. The covariance of the second works out to \(\mathbf{B} - \mathbf{C}\T\mathbf{A}^{-1}\mathbf{C}\).

Now substitute \(\mathbf{a} = \mathbf{y}\), \(\mathbf{b} = \mathbf{f}_*\), \(\mathbf{A} = \mathbf{K}(\mathsf{X}, \mathsf{X}) + \sigma_j^2\mathbf{I}\) (kernel plus measurement noise), \(\mathbf{B} = \mathbf{K}(\mathsf{X}^*, \mathsf{X}^*)\), and \(\mathbf{C}\T = \mathbf{K}(\mathsf{X}^*, \mathsf{X})\). The formulas assume a prior mean of zero; otherwise subtract the mean from \(\mathbf{y}\) first and add it back at the end.

Worked example with one measurement: \(y_1 = 1\) at \(x_1 = 0\), with \(\sigma_f = 1\), \(\ell = 1\), and noise variance 0.1. The matrix to invert is the number \(1 + 0.1 = 1.1\).

Test point x*Kernel value K(x*, x₁)Mean (5.10)Variance (5.11)
0 (at the measurement)11 × 1 / 1.1 = 0.911 − 1 / 1.1 = 0.09
1 (one length-scale away)e−0.5 = 0.6070.607 / 1.1 = 0.551 − 0.607² / 1.1 = 0.67
5 (far away)e−12.5 ≈ 0≈ 0≈ 1

Near the data the prediction follows the data and is confident. Far away it returns to the prior: mean 0, variance \(\sigma_f^2\). Note that the variance column never used \(y_1\). Equation (5.11) depends only on where the measurements were taken, so a robot can compute how informative a measurement would be before making it. That is why GP maps are used to steer exploration. §5.4.5 · p. 142

Try it: a wall profile sampled at a few noisy points, with nothing sampled between 4.2 m and 6.6 m. Move the length-scale to its two extremes.

Notice at the default length-scale of 1 m that the band is narrow at the samples and widens in the gap, to a standard deviation of 62 cm against a prior of 70 cm. At 0.2 m each sample informs only its immediate surroundings: between samples the mean drops back to zero and the band returns to the prior. At 3 m the band is narrow everywhere (18 cm at most), yet the mean misses the true curve by 32 cm RMS. The kernel claims more smoothness than the wall has, so the map is confidently wrong.

2. GP occupancy maps and GP implicit surfaces

A Gaussian process occupancy map (GPOM) uses beam observations labelled free or occupied as training data and the map cells as test locations. The regression output is then squashed into a probability between 0 and 1. Because the kernel couples nearby places, the map can infer the occupancy of a cell no beam touched, which the independent cells of Day 1 could not. §5.4.5 · p. 142

The cost is \(O(J^3 + J^2 N)\) for \(J\) training points and \(N\) test points. The \(J^3\) comes from factorizing the \(J \times J\) matrix in the brackets (the Cholesky cost of Week 1 · Day 5), and the \(J^2 N\) from one product with that matrix per test point in (5.11). With \(J = 10{,}000\), fewer points than one sweep of a typical 3D LiDAR, \(J^3 = 10^{12}\). Practical GP maps therefore work incrementally or on local subsets. §5.4.5 · p. 142

A Gaussian process implicit surface (GPIS) applies the same machinery to distance. The training data are points on the surface, where the distance is zero, and the distance field \(d\) and its gradient \(\nabla d\) are modelled together as one zero-mean GP, equation (5.12). Differentiation is a linear operation, and a linear operation on a GP gives another GP, so the surface normal comes with its own uncertainty. §5.4.5.1 · p. 142

The zero mean has a side effect that you saw in the widget. Far from any data a GP returns to its mean, and here the mean is zero, which reads as "on the surface". A plain GPIS is trustworthy near the measured surface and wrong far from it; estimating the full distance field takes an extra non-linear step. §5.4.5.1 · p. 143

3. Hilbert maps: occupancy as a trained classifier

Hilbert maps keep the continuity of a GP occupancy map and avoid its cost. The goals were to process data online, to model the dependence between observations, and to include measurement uncertainty. The recipe is a logistic regression classifier, trained by stochastic gradient descent, on features computed from the position. §5.4.6 · p. 143

Filling the gap: the classifier and its update

Place \(M\) kernel centres \(\mathbf{c}_1, \dots, \mathbf{c}_M\) on a regular grid over the area. The feature vector of a point lists how close it is to each centre, \(\boldsymbol{\phi}(\mathbf{x}) = [k(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{c}_1), \dots, k(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{c}_M)]\T\). With a sparse kernel, which is exactly zero beyond a fixed radius, only a few entries are non-zero. The map is one weight vector \(\mathbf{w}\), and

\[ p(\text{occupied} \mid \mathbf{x}) = \frac{1}{1 + e^{-\mathbf{w}\T\boldsymbol{\phi}(\mathbf{x})}} . \]

Compare with Day 1, where \(p = 1/(1 + e^{-l})\): the number \(\mathbf{w}\T\boldsymbol{\phi}(\mathbf{x})\) is a log-odds, now a continuous function of position. If each feature were 1 inside one grid cell and 0 elsewhere, \(\mathbf{w}\) would simply hold one log-odds per cell. Overlapping kernels are what let neighbouring places share evidence.

Training data come from the beams: points sampled along a beam get the label \(y = 0\) (free), the end point gets \(y = 1\) (occupied). For one labelled point the loss is the negative log-likelihood \(-[\,y\log p + (1-y)\log(1-p)\,]\). Its gradient with respect to \(\mathbf{w}\) is \((p - y)\,\boldsymbol{\phi}(\mathbf{x})\), so a gradient step with rate \(\eta\) is

\[ \mathbf{w} \leftarrow \mathbf{w} - \eta\,(p - y)\,\boldsymbol{\phi}(\mathbf{x}). \]

Example: the map currently says \(p = 0.5\) at an end point (\(y = 1\)) and \(\eta = 0.5\). The step adds \(0.25\,\boldsymbol{\phi}(\mathbf{x})\) to \(\mathbf{w}\): the weights of the few kernels near \(\mathbf{x}\) rise and the rest stay as they were. Each sample costs a handful of operations, however large the map is.

The limit is expressiveness. Each kernel is a round bump, so fine detail needs many small kernels, which costs computation and interpolates less; few large kernels are the reverse. §5.4.6 · pp. 143–144

Learned maps go one step further and let a neural network be the function. A network can be trained to return the signed distance at any query point, and a mesh of any resolution can then be extracted from it. Recent systems store small feature vectors in a voxel grid, octree, or point set and use only a small network to decode them into distances, which scales to large scenes. Neural radiance fields and Gaussian splatting, an explicit representation related to surfels, are treated later in the book. §5.4.7 · pp. 144–145

4. Choosing: the environment

Start with where the robot works, because that settles several choices outright. §5.5.1 · pp. 145–146

Question about the environmentWhat it implies
Is it tightly controlled, like an automated factory?A custom map built around the known objects usually beats any general dense map.
Must the robot tell observed free space from space it has never seen?Points, surfels, and meshes describe only surfaces and generally cannot. Occupancy maps can. Implicit surfaces can, but often drop the information far from surfaces to save memory.
Is it large?Explicit surface maps use less memory. If free space must be stored, use a multi-resolution structure.
Do things move?Three options: ignore it (free-space updates in implicit maps erase most leftovers), detect and discard measurements of moving objects (usual with explicit maps), or model the moving objects themselves.

5. Choosing: the task

Any operation can be done on any map, but not at the same cost. The dividing line is whether the operation runs along the surface or through space. §5.5.2 · pp. 146–147, Table 5.2

OperationExplicit surface is efficient forImplicit representation is efficient for
Fusing measurementsProperties that live on the surface, such as colour and textureProperties defined in space, such as occupancy; copes with noisy depth
QueryingWalking along the surface: rendering, coverage planningAsking about a point in space: collision checking
Changing the mapGeometry: bending the surface when a loop closure corrects the trajectoryTopology: merging, cutting, and simplifying shapes

The two families can be combined. The standard example is a TSDF that filters noisy depth, followed by Marching Cubes to get a mesh for display (Days 2 and 3). The conversion has a cost, so do it locally and rarely. §5.5.2 · p. 147

Within each family the book's summary is a ladder of assumptions. Points assume the least and say the least. Surfels add a local patch. Meshes add connectivity and need the most assumptions. Among volumetric maps, occupancy is filtered with the fewest assumptions and keeps thin obstacles; distance fields give fast distances and gradients for optimization-based planning; GPs and Hilbert maps give the best uncertainty and interpolation when depth data are sparse or noisy. §5.5.3 · pp. 147–148

Common mistakes

  • "A small GP variance means the map is right." The variance in (5.11) is computed from the sample locations and the kernel alone. If the kernel is a poor description of the world, for example a length-scale that is far too long, the map can be confidently wrong.
  • "A GPIS value of zero means there is a surface." Far from all measurements zero is just the prior mean.
  • "The most accurate map is the best map." A photorealistic mesh cannot say whether unseen space is free. Choose by what the downstream task has to ask the map.

Check yourself

Q1. A zero-mean GP with prior variance 1 has one measurement, y = 2, with noise variance 0.25. What is the predicted mean at the measured location itself?

The kernel value is 1, so (5.10) gives 1 × 2 / (1 + 0.25) = 1.6. The GP does not trust a noisy sample fully and pulls it towards the prior mean of 0. The variance there is 1 − 1/1.25 = 0.2.

Q2. A GP map is built from 2,000 training points. With 20,000 points, by what factor does the J³ part of the cost grow?

Ten times the points means 10³ = 1,000 times the work for the matrix factorization. This cubic growth is why the original GP occupancy map is a batch method.

Q3. At some position a Hilbert map has wᵀφ(x) = 1.1. What occupancy probability does it report?

p = 1 / (1 + exp(−1.1)) = 1 / 1.333 = 0.75. The classifier's raw output is a log-odds, converted exactly as in the occupancy grid.

Q4. A planner must refuse to drive through space that has never been observed. Which map cannot support that on its own?

Surfels describe surfaces only. Where there is no surfel, the map does not say whether the space was seen and found empty or never seen. All occupancy-based maps keep that distinction.

Q5. After a loop closure the back-end shifts many past poses. Which map is cheapest to correct?

Explicit surface elements can simply be moved with their poses. A voxel map has fused measurements from many poses into each cell, so its geometry cannot be bent as easily.

Recap

  1. GP regression predicts a mean, (5.10), and a covariance, (5.11), at any location; both follow from conditioning a joint Gaussian. The covariance does not depend on the measured values.
  2. GP occupancy maps and GP implicit surfaces model spatial correlation and uncertainty, at a cost of \(O(J^3 + J^2 N)\). Far from data they fall back to the prior mean.
  3. A Hilbert map is logistic regression on kernel features: a continuous log-odds function trained online, one cheap gradient step per sample.
  4. Explicit surface maps are efficient along the surface (texture, rendering, deformation). Implicit maps are efficient in space (occupancy, collision checks, merging shapes).
  5. Choose by environment (free versus unobserved space, scale, dynamics) and by what the downstream task asks of the map; combine representations when one is not enough.

Sources

  1. SLAM Handbook, §5.4.5 "Gaussian Processes", §5.4.6 "Hilbert Maps", §5.4.7 "Deep Learning in Mapping", and §5.5 "Usage Considerations", pp. 141–148.
  2. Rasmussen and Williams, Gaussian Processes for Machine Learning, 2006 (the conditioning rule and the squared-exponential kernel).
  3. Bishop, Pattern Recognition and Machine Learning, 2006 (logistic regression and its gradient).

Week 8 · Review

Week 8 review: dense maps

After today you can update occupancy and TSDF voxels by hand, extract a surface from a distance grid, size a map's memory, and argue for a representation that fits a task.

About 60 min · No new pages

The week in one paragraph

With the trajectory known, dense mapping turns range measurements into a model of all the geometry. Beams become points through the sensor's angles or intrinsics. An occupancy grid stores a per-cell probability and updates it by adding log-odds. A TSDF stores an averaged, clamped distance along beams, and its zero crossing is the surface. These quantities are carried by points, surfels, meshes, voxels, or continuous functions, and Marching Cubes converts a distance grid into a mesh. Arrays, hash tables, and octrees trade lookup speed against memory. Gaussian processes and Hilbert maps drop the grid and model correlation and uncertainty, at a higher cost. The right choice depends on the environment and on what the downstream task asks of the map.

1. Formula sheet

What it isFormulaWhere
Range from time of flight\(r = c\,(t_{\text{detect}} - t_{\text{emit}})/2\)(5.1), p. 120 · Day 1
Beam to point (θ from the horizontal)\(x = r\cos\theta\cos\phi,\; y = r\cos\theta\sin\phi,\; z = r\sin\theta\)(5.2)–(5.4), p. 121 · Day 1
Depth pixel to point\(X = (u - c_x)Z/f_x,\; Y = (v - c_y)Z/f_y\)unpacks (5.5), p. 121 · Day 1
Odds, log-odds, and back\(o = p/(1-p),\; l = \log o,\; p = 1/(1 + e^{-l})\)(5.7), p. 124 · Day 1
Occupancy update\(l(m_k \mid \mathbf{z}_{1:t}) = l(m_k \mid \mathbf{z}_{1:t-1}) + l(m_k \mid \mathbf{z}_t)\)(5.6), p. 124 · Day 1
Distance field gradient\(\norm{\nabla d} = 1\)§5.2.2, p. 125 · Day 2
Projective distance, TSDF update\(d = r - \norm{\mathbf{q} - \mathbf{o}}\), clamped to \(\pm\tau\); \(D \leftarrow (WD + wd)/(W + w)\), \(W \leftarrow W + w\)§5.2.2, p. 126 · Day 2
Zero crossing on an edge\(t = f_a/(f_a - f_b)\) from end \(a\)§5.3.2.6, p. 131 · Days 2, 3
Bilinear interpolation\((1-b)[(1-a)f_{00} + a f_{10}] + b[(1-a)f_{01} + a f_{11}]\)§5.3.2.4, p. 130 · Day 3
Dense array index\(n = i + N_x(j + N_y k)\), \(i = \lfloor (x - x_0)/\Delta \rfloor\)§5.3.3.1, p. 132 · Day 4
GP prediction\(\bar{\mathbf{f}}_* = \mathbf{K}_{*}[\mathbf{K} + \sigma_j^2\mathbf{I}]^{-1}\mathbf{y}\), \(\cov(\mathbf{f}_*) = \mathbf{K}_{**} - \mathbf{K}_{*}[\mathbf{K} + \sigma_j^2\mathbf{I}]^{-1}\mathbf{K}_{*}\T\)(5.10), (5.11), pp. 141–142 · Day 5

In the last row \(\mathbf{K} = \mathbf{K}(\mathsf{X}, \mathsf{X})\), \(\mathbf{K}_* = \mathbf{K}(\mathsf{X}^*, \mathsf{X})\), and \(\mathbf{K}_{**} = \mathbf{K}(\mathsf{X}^*, \mathsf{X}^*)\).

2. Mixed quiz

Check yourself

Q1. A 2D LiDAR sits at (1, 2) in the map with heading 0. A beam at azimuth 150° returns r = 4 m. Where is the hit point in the map?

In the sensor frame the point is (4 cos 150°, 4 sin 150°) = (−3.46, 2.00). Adding the sensor position gives (−2.46, 4.00). The second option forgets the pose.

Q2. A cell has log-odds l = −1.2. One beam ends in it, and a hit means p = 0.7. What is its probability now?

l = −1.2 + log(0.7/0.3) = −1.2 + 0.847 = −0.353, and p = 1/(1 + e^0.353) = 0.41. One hit does not overturn the earlier evidence that the cell is free.

Q3. A round robot of radius 0.30 m is centred where the ESDF reads 0.25 m with gradient (0.6, 0.8). What is the smallest move that frees it?

The gradient has length 1 and points away from the nearest surface, so each centimetre along it gains one centimetre of clearance. The robot needs 0.30 − 0.25 = 0.05 m more.

Q4. Which statement about a TSDF built from projective distances is true?

The distance along a beam is at least the distance to the nearest surface point, so values are overestimates. Both distances are zero at the same place, which is why the extracted surface is still correct.

Q5. A marching-squares cell has corner values −0.2 (top left), 0.1 (top right), 0.3 (bottom right), −0.4 (bottom left). On which edges does it place vertices?

An edge gets a vertex when its two ends differ in sign: top (−0.2, 0.1) and bottom (−0.4, 0.3). The left edge is negative at both ends, the right edge positive at both. This is case 1 + 8 = 9.

Q6. Voxels are grouped in blocks of 8 × 8 × 8. Which block contains the voxel with index (37, 5, 70)?

Divide by 8 and round down: (⌊37/8⌋, ⌊5/8⌋, ⌊70/8⌋) = (4, 0, 8). The remainders (5, 5, 6) are the voxel's position inside the block.

Q7. A 3D map stores only voxels near surfaces. Going one octree level deeper (half the voxel size), by about what factor does the number of stored voxels grow?

A surface is two-dimensional, so the number of cells it crosses grows with the square of the resolution: 2² = 4. A dense grid would grow by 2³ = 8.

Q8. Why can a robot with a GP map rate a candidate measurement location before measuring there?

Equation (5.11) contains kernel matrices and the noise variance, but not y. The reduction in uncertainty from a new sample can be computed from its position alone.

3. Pen-and-paper problems

  1. An inverse sensor model assigns \(p = 0.8\) to the cell where a beam ends and \(p = 0.3\) to cells a beam passes through. A cell starts unknown and is observed as: hit, hit, pass, hit. (a) Find its log-odds and probability. (b) The object is then removed, and every later beam passes through the cell. How many passes until its probability drops below 0.5?

    Solution

    (a) A hit adds \(\log(0.8/0.2) = \log 4 = 1.386\). A pass adds \(\log(0.3/0.7) = -0.847\). So \(l = 3 \times 1.386 - 0.847 = 3.312\). The odds are \(4^3 \times 3/7 = 27.4\), and \(p = 27.4/28.4 = 0.965\).

    (b) Each pass subtracts 0.847, and \(3.312/0.847 = 3.9\), so 4 passes are needed: \(l = 3.312 - 3.389 = -0.077\), \(p = 0.48\). Had the cell been hit 100 times first, \(l\) would be 138.6 and 164 passes would be needed. This is why implementations clamp \(l\) to a fixed interval: a map of a changing world must be able to change its mind.

  2. Four voxel centres lie on one beam at 1.9, 2.0, 2.1, and 2.2 m from the sensor. Three scans from the same pose return ranges 2.06, 2.02, and 2.07 m along that beam. With \(\tau = 0.15\) m and weight 1 per measurement, find \(D\) and \(W\) for each voxel, then the surface position.

    Solution

    The projective distance is \(r\) minus the voxel's distance. Values above \(+\tau\) are clamped to 0.15, and values below \(-\tau\) are skipped.

    Voxel 1.9: 0.16, 0.12, 0.17 become 0.15, 0.12, 0.15, so \(D = 0.14\), \(W = 3\). Voxel 2.0: 0.06, 0.02, 0.07, so \(D = 0.05\), \(W = 3\). Voxel 2.1: −0.04, −0.08, −0.03, so \(D = -0.05\), \(W = 3\). Voxel 2.2: −0.14, −0.18 (skipped), −0.13, so \(D = -0.135\), \(W = 2\).

    The sign changes between 2.0 and 2.1: \(x^{*} = 2.0 + 0.1 \times 0.05/(0.05 + 0.05) = 2.05\) m. That equals the mean of the three ranges, \(6.15/3 = 2.05\) m. Inside the band nothing was clamped, so the averaging of distances is the averaging of ranges.

  3. A signed distance function \(f(x, y) = \sqrt{(x-1)^2 + (y-1)^2} - 0.8\) is sampled at the nine points with \(x, y \in \{0, 1, 2\}\). (a) Give the sign at each sample. (b) Run marching squares with linear interpolation: where are the vertices, and what shape results? (c) Compare its perimeter with the true one. (d) Where would the vertices be without interpolation?

    Solution

    (a) Centre \((1, 1)\): \(-0.8\). The four edge midpoints such as \((1, 0)\): \(1 - 0.8 = +0.2\). The four corners: \(\sqrt{2} - 0.8 = +0.61\). Only the centre is inside.

    (b) Sign changes occur on the four grid edges that leave the centre sample. On each, \(t = f_a/(f_a - f_b) = -0.8/(-0.8 - 0.2) = 0.8\) from the centre. The vertices are \((1 \pm 0.8, 1)\) and \((1, 1 \pm 0.8)\). Each of the four cells has one inside corner and contributes one segment, so the outline is a square standing on its corner.

    (c) Each side is \(0.8\sqrt{2} = 1.13\), so the perimeter is 4.53, against \(2\pi \times 0.8 = 5.03\) for the circle. The vertices lie exactly on the circle, because \(f\) is linear along a line through the centre. The 10% error comes from the straight segments between them, which a finer grid would shorten.

    (d) At the edge midpoints, 0.5 from the centre: a square of perimeter 2.83 whose vertices are 0.3 off the true outline.

  4. A zero-mean GP has kernel \(\mathcal{K}(x, x') = \exp(-(x - x')^2/2)\) and noise-free measurements \(y_1 = y_2 = 1\) at \(x_1 = 0\) and \(x_2 = 2\). (a) Find the predictive mean and variance at \(x_* = 1\). (b) What changes if both measurements are 5 instead of 1?

    Solution

    (a) With \(e^{-2} = 0.135\) and \(e^{-0.5} = 0.607\),

    \[ \mathbf{K} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0.135 \\ 0.135 & 1 \end{bmatrix}, \qquad \mathbf{K}_* = \begin{bmatrix} 0.607 & 0.607 \end{bmatrix}. \]

    By symmetry \(\mathbf{K}^{-1}\mathbf{y}\) has two equal entries \(\alpha\) with \(\alpha(1 + 0.135) = 1\), so \(\alpha = 0.881\). The mean is \(2 \times 0.607 \times 0.881 = 1.07\). In the same way \(\mathbf{K}^{-1}\mathbf{K}_*\T\) has entries \(0.607/1.135 = 0.534\), so the variance is \(1 - 2 \times 0.607 \times 0.534 = 0.35\), a standard deviation of 0.59.

    The mean sits slightly above both samples because this kernel prefers smooth curves, and the smoothest curve through two equal values one length-scale either side bulges a little. The standard deviation of 0.59 says not to rely on it.

    (b) The mean scales with the data to \(5 \times 1.07 = 5.34\). The variance stays 0.35: equation (5.11) does not contain \(\mathbf{y}\).

You are ready for next week if you can

  • Convert a range and two beam angles, or a depth pixel and camera intrinsics, into a 3D point.
  • Derive the log-odds update from Bayes' rule and name the two independence assumptions it uses.
  • Explain why a projective distance overestimates and why the TSDF zero crossing is still right.
  • Run marching squares on a small grid, with interpolation.
  • Estimate the memory of a dense grid and say what hashing and octrees save.
  • Give one task that favours an explicit surface map and one that favours an implicit map, with the reason.

Sources

  1. SLAM Handbook, Chapter 5 "Dense Map Representations", pp. 119–148.
  2. Thrun, Burgard, Fox, Probabilistic Robotics, 2005 (log-odds occupancy mapping).
  3. Hornung, Wurm, Bennewitz, Stachniss, Burgard, OctoMap: An Efficient Probabilistic 3D Mapping Framework Based on Octrees, 2013 (clamping of the log-odds).
  4. Rasmussen and Williams, Gaussian Processes for Machine Learning, 2006 (GP prediction).

Week 9 · Day 1

Local minima, certificates, and why convex problems are easy

After today you can explain why a local SLAM solver can return a wrong answer without noticing, say what a certifiably optimal solver promises, and test whether a set or a function is convex.

About 60 min · Read the Chapter 6 opening and the start of §6.1, pp. 149–152 (3 pages) · Needs Week 2 Day 4

Read first: Chapter 6 opening and §6.1 up to the heading of §6.1.1, pp. 149–152

While you read, look for:

  • The two questions the chapter sets out to answer (p. 149). This week is about the first one.
  • The three SLAM problems the book names as NP-hard (p. 150).
  • Figure 6.1 (p. 151): which panel is the global optimum, and how the other two were produced.
  • The sentence on p. 151 that says why a certifiable algorithm does not contradict NP-hardness.

Today's big idea

The solvers of Weeks 2 and 3 walk downhill from an initial guess. SLAM costs are not convex, so downhill can end in a valley that is not the lowest one, and the solver has no way to tell. A certifiably optimal solver returns an estimate together with a number that bounds how far that estimate can be from the best possible one, and often proves the gap is zero.

1. Two questions about the SLAM optimization problem

Chapters 1 to 3 turned SLAM into an optimization problem and solved it with iterative local methods: Gauss-Newton, Levenberg-Marquardt, gradient descent (Week 2 · Day 4). Chapter 6 steps back and asks two things about that problem. Ch. 6 · p. 149

QuestionWhat it is aboutWhere
Can we compute the globally best solution, possibly with no initial guess, and know that we did?Computation and reliability§6.1, this week and the first half of next week
How close is that best solution to the truth, and what controls the error?Fundamental limits of accuracy§6.2, next week

2. Local solvers can be confidently wrong

A point is a local minimum of a cost \(f\) if no nearby point has a lower cost, and a global minimum if no point at all has a lower cost. A local solver stops when the gradient is zero and the cost stops decreasing, which is true at both. Figure 6.1 shows what that means on real data: one parking-garage dataset, one cost function, and three trajectories that are all local minima. Only one is the global minimum; the other two came from random starting points. Figure 6.1 · p. 151

The book adds that this is not bad luck. Several special cases of SLAM, among them angular synchronization, rotation averaging, and pose-graph optimization (PGO), are NP-hard: unless P = NP, no algorithm solves every instance efficiently. §6.1 · p. 150 In practice SLAM often works anyway: odometry gives a good initial guess, and several optimization methods reach near-optimal solutions even from poor ones. But off-the-shelf local methods can also produce badly wrong estimates on well-posed problems. §6.1 · p. 150

You can reproduce Figure 6.1 in miniature. Ten robot poses sit on a ring and only their headings \(\theta_1,\dots,\theta_{10}\) are unknown. Each edge \((i,j)\) is a noisy measurement \(\tilde\theta_{ij}\) of the heading difference \(\theta_j-\theta_i\): ten around the ring, and one chord from pose 1 to pose 5. The cost is

\[ f(\theta_1,\dots,\theta_{10}) = \sum_{(i,j)} 4\,\bigl(1-\cos r_{ij}\bigr), \qquad r_{ij} = \theta_j-\theta_i-\tilde\theta_{ij}. \]

Each edge pays for its residual \(r_{ij}\). The payment is zero when the residual is zero, it is about \(2r_{ij}^2\) when the residual is small (because \(1-\cos r \approx r^2/2\)), and it does not change when \(r_{ij}\) grows by a full turn, as it must for angles. Day 3 shows this is exactly the rotation part of the book's PGO cost in the plane. This problem is the angular synchronization the book lists as NP-hard.

Try it: the widget starts gradient descent from random headings. Look at the cost, press "New start" a few times, then press "Run 20 starts".

Notice that the first run stops at cost 11.595 with a gradient of zero and edge residuals of up to 55°, while the next start reaches 0.091. Of the 20 starts, 16 reach 0.091 and 4 stop at 10.257 or 11.595. Nothing inside a stuck run says it is stuck.

Filling the gap: why a loop creates local minima

Take the simplest case: a ring of \(n\) headings with perfect measurements and no chord. Going once around the ring, the heading differences \(\theta_{i+1}-\theta_i\) add up to zero, and the perfect measurements add up to a whole number of turns. So the residuals \(r_1,\dots,r_n\) of any guess must add up to a whole number of turns:

\[ r_1+r_2+\dots+r_n = 2\pi k, \qquad k \in \{0,\pm1,\pm2,\dots\}. \]

Heading \(\theta_i\) enters two residuals, with a plus sign in the edge that arrives and a minus sign in the edge that leaves. So \(\partial f/\partial\theta_i = 4\sin r_{\text{in}} - 4\sin r_{\text{out}}\), and the gradient is zero when all edges have the same \(\sin r\). One way to do that is to share the total evenly, \(r_i = 2\pi k/n\) on every edge, which costs

\[ f_k = 4n\left(1-\cos\frac{2\pi k}{n}\right). \]

For \(k=0\) this is the true solution with cost 0. For \(k=\pm1\) the estimate makes one extra full turn spread around the ring. The second derivative of \(4(1-\cos r)\) is \(4\cos r\), so each edge still curves upward as long as \(\cos(2\pi k/n) \gt 0\), that is \(|k| \lt n/4\). For \(n=10\) that gives genuine local minima at \(k=\pm1\) with cost \(40(1-\cos 36^\circ) = 7.64\) and at \(k=\pm2\) with cost \(40(1-\cos 72^\circ) = 27.64\).

To get from \(k=1\) to \(k=0\), some edge has to pass through a residual of 180°, where its cost is highest. Gradient descent never goes uphill, so it stays. The widget's graph has a chord and noise, which changes the numbers (10.257 and 11.595 instead of 7.64) but not the mechanism: the two stuck solutions carry one extra turn around the loop 5–6–7–8–9–10–1 that the chord closes, one in each direction. The pink edges show where the turn is spread.

3. What a certifiably optimal solver promises

Write \(p^\star\) for the lowest cost any solution can have. A certifiably optimal (or certifiably correct) method returns an estimate \(\hat{\mathbf{x}}\) and also a lower bound \(d^\star \le p^\star\), computed by convex relaxation and not by local search. §6.1 · p. 151 The bound is the certificate:

Since \(d^\star \le p^\star \le f(\hat{\mathbf{x}})\), the estimate is at most \(f(\hat{\mathbf{x}})-d^\star\) worse than the best possible. If that difference is zero, \(\hat{\mathbf{x}}\) is a global minimum, proven.

This does not contradict NP-hardness. On a hard instance the method is allowed to return a bound with a gap and no proof of optimality. The book gives two reasons it is still worth having: for the noise levels of real SLAM problems the gap is nearly always zero, and when it is not, the failure is itself a warning the robot can act on. §6.1 · p. 151

In plain words

A local solver is a hiker in fog who stops when every direction goes up. A certifiable solver also carries an altimeter reading for the lowest point on the whole map. If the hiker's altitude matches it, the hiker is at the bottom. If not, the difference says how much lower the true bottom could be.

4. Convexity: when every local minimum is global

The book assumes you know why convex problems are the easy ones. Here is the minimum you need. A set \(\mathcal{C}\) is convex if the straight segment between any two of its points stays inside it. A function \(f\) is convex if its graph never rises above its chords: for all \(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{y}\) and all \(t\in[0,1]\),

\[ f\bigl(t\mathbf{x}+(1-t)\mathbf{y}\bigr) \le t\,f(\mathbf{x})+(1-t)\,f(\mathbf{y}). \]

A convex problem minimizes a convex function over a convex set.

Filling the gap: in a convex problem, a local minimum is a global minimum

Suppose \(\mathbf{x}\) is a local minimum but some other feasible point \(\mathbf{y}\) is better, \(f(\mathbf{y}) \lt f(\mathbf{x})\). Walk a small step \(t\) from \(\mathbf{x}\) toward \(\mathbf{y}\), to \(\mathbf{z}=(1-t)\mathbf{x}+t\mathbf{y}\). The set is convex, so \(\mathbf{z}\) is feasible. The function is convex, so

\[ f(\mathbf{z}) \le (1-t)f(\mathbf{x})+t f(\mathbf{y}) \lt (1-t)f(\mathbf{x})+t f(\mathbf{x}) = f(\mathbf{x}). \]

That holds for every \(t\in(0,1]\), however small, so there are better points arbitrarily close to \(\mathbf{x}\). Then \(\mathbf{x}\) was not a local minimum. The assumption was wrong, and no better \(\mathbf{y}\) exists.

Three quick tests you will reuse all week:

ObjectConvex?Why
\(f(x)=x^2\), or any least-squares cost \(\norm{\mathbf{A}\mathbf{x}-\mathbf{b}}^2\)YesThe second derivative, \(2\) or \(2\mathbf{A}\T\mathbf{A}\), is never negative. A twice-differentiable function is convex exactly when its Hessian is positive semidefinite everywhere.
\(f(r)=4(1-\cos r)\), the edge cost aboveNoIts second derivative \(4\cos r\) is negative for \(90^\circ \lt |r| \le 180^\circ\).
The unit circle \(\{\mathbf{x}: \norm{\mathbf{x}}=1\}\), and the rotations \(\SO(2)\)NoThe midpoint of \((1,0)\) and \((-1,0)\) is the origin, which is not on the circle. Likewise the average of the rotations by 0° and 180° is the zero matrix, which is not a rotation.
The symmetric matrices with \(\mathbf{X}\succeq 0\) (positive semidefinite, \(\mathbf{v}\T\mathbf{X}\mathbf{v}\ge 0\) for all \(\mathbf{v}\))YesIf \(\mathbf{X}\succeq0\) and \(\mathbf{Y}\succeq0\) then \(\mathbf{v}\T(t\mathbf{X}+(1-t)\mathbf{Y})\mathbf{v} = t\,\mathbf{v}\T\mathbf{X}\mathbf{v}+(1-t)\,\mathbf{v}\T\mathbf{Y}\mathbf{v} \ge 0\).

The third row is the root of the trouble: any problem whose unknowns include rotations has a non-convex feasible set (Week 4 · Day 1). The fourth row is the way out, starting tomorrow.

5. Relaxation: an easier problem that bounds the hard one

A relaxation of a minimization problem keeps the objective and enlarges the feasible set. Minimizing over more candidates can only lower the minimum, so the relaxed optimum \(d^\star\) is a lower bound on \(p^\star\). And if the relaxed minimizer happens to lie in the original feasible set, it is optimal for the original problem too, because nothing in the larger set beats it.

A one-line example. Minimize \((x-0.4)^2\) over the two points \(x\in\{0,1\}\): the best is \(x=0\) with \(p^\star=0.16\). Relax the set to the interval \([0,1]\), which is convex: the minimizer is \(x=0.4\) with \(d^\star=0\). The bound \(0\le0.16\) holds but has a gap, and \(0.4\) is not feasible. Now change the objective to \((x+0.3)^2\). The relaxed minimizer is \(x=0\), an original point, so \(p^\star=d^\star=0.09\) and the relaxation has solved the hard problem. When that happens the relaxation is called tight or exact.

Day 2 builds such a relaxation for a whole class of problems, Days 3 and 4 apply it to pose-graph optimization, and Day 5 solves it fast.

Common mistakes

  • "The solver converged, so the answer is right." Convergence means the gradient vanished. That happens at every local minimum, including the twisted ones in the widget.
  • "NP-hard means it cannot be solved." It means no efficient algorithm handles every instance. Most instances that come from real robots are among the easy ones.
  • "A certifiable solver always returns the global optimum." It always returns an estimate and a bound. The bound proves optimality only when the gap is zero.

Check yourself

Q1. A noise-free ring of 12 headings with the cost above. What is the cost of the stationary point that is twisted once (k = 1)?

Each of the 12 edges has residual 360°/12 = 30°, so the cost is 4 × 12 × (1 − cos 30°) = 48 × 0.134 = 6.43. Since 1 is less than 12/4, it is a local minimum.

Q2. A certifiable solver returns an estimate with cost 10.2 and a lower bound of 9.5. What do you know?

The optimal cost lies between 9.5 and 10.2. The gap bounds the suboptimality by 0.7 but does not say whether the true gap is zero.

Q3. Which of these sets is convex?

The segment between two points of the disk stays in the disk. For the other three, a midpoint leaves the set: 0.5, the origin, and the zero matrix.

Q4. Pose-graph optimization is NP-hard, yet certifiable solvers for it exist. Why is that not a contradiction?

They are efficient on every instance but certify optimality only when the relaxation happens to be tight. In the worst case the output is an estimate plus a suboptimality bound.

Recap

  1. SLAM costs are non-convex. Local solvers stop at any local minimum and cannot tell it from the global one.
  2. A single loop of rotation measurements already has twisted local minima, with cost \(4n(1-\cos(2\pi k/n))\) on a clean ring.
  3. A certifiable solver returns an estimate and a lower bound \(d^\star\le p^\star\); the gap \(f(\hat{\mathbf{x}})-d^\star\) bounds the suboptimality, and a zero gap proves optimality.
  4. In a convex problem every local minimum is global. Rotations form a non-convex set; positive semidefinite matrices form a convex one.
  5. A relaxation enlarges the feasible set, which gives a lower bound, and it is exact when its minimizer is feasible for the original problem.

Sources

  1. SLAM Handbook, Chapter 6 opening and §6.1 "Certifiably Optimal Solvers for SLAM", pp. 149–152, including Figure 6.1.
  2. Boyd and Vandenberghe, Convex Optimization, 2004: convex sets and functions, the second-order condition, and local-equals-global for convex problems.
  3. The twisted-ring calculation is our own worked example of the cost in equation (6.9) restricted to planar rotations.

Week 9 · Day 2

Shor's relaxation: from a QCQP to a semidefinite program

After today you can lift a quadratically constrained quadratic program to a matrix problem, drop the rank constraint to get a semidefinite program, and say what its solution proves about the original problem.

About 60 min · Read §6.1.1, pp. 152–154 (3 pages) · Needs Week 9 Day 1

Read first: §6.1.1 "Shor's Relaxation", pp. 152–154

While you read, look for:

  • The one identity, equation (6.1), that turns every quadratic expression into a linear one (p. 152).
  • The single constraint that is thrown away between problem (6.4) and problem (SDP) on p. 153.
  • Inequalities (6.5) and (6.6), and the footnote on p. 153 that explains the word "lift".
  • What follows when the SDP solution has rank 1 (p. 154).

Today's big idea

A quadratic function of a vector \(\mathbf{x}\) is a linear function of the matrix \(\mathbf{X}=\mathbf{x}\mathbf{x}\T\). Rewrite the problem in \(\mathbf{X}\) and all the non-convexity collects in one statement, "\(\mathbf{X}\) has rank 1". Delete that statement and what is left is a convex problem whose optimum bounds the original from below, and often equals it.

1. Quadratically constrained quadratic programs

A quadratically constrained quadratic program (QCQP) minimizes a quadratic function subject to quadratic equations. The book's generic form is §6.1.1 · p. 152

\[ p^\star = \min_{\mathbf{x}\in\R^n}\ \mathbf{x}\T\mathbf{C}\mathbf{x} \quad \text{s.t.}\quad \mathbf{x}\T\mathbf{A}_i\mathbf{x} = b_i,\quad i=1,\dots,m, \tag{QCQP} \]

where \(\mathbf{C},\mathbf{A}_1,\dots,\mathbf{A}_m\) are symmetric \(n\times n\) matrices (the book writes \(\mathbb{S}^n\) for that set) and \(p^\star\) is the optimal value. The constraints matter for SLAM because they can describe the sets SLAM variables live in:

RequirementAs quadratic equationsThe matrices
\(\mathbf{x}\) is a unit vector\(\mathbf{x}\T\mathbf{x}=1\)\(\mathbf{A}=\mathbf{I}\), \(b=1\)
each \(x_i\) is \(+1\) or \(-1\)\(x_i^2=1\) for every \(i\)\(\mathbf{A}_i\) has a single 1 at position \((i,i)\), \(b_i=1\)
\(\begin{bmatrix}x_1 & x_3\\ x_2 & x_4\end{bmatrix}\) has orthonormal columns\(x_1^2+x_2^2=1\), \(x_3^2+x_4^2=1\), \(x_1x_3+x_2x_4=0\)for the last one, \(\mathbf{A}\) has \(\tfrac12\) at positions \((1,3),(3,1),(2,4),(4,2)\), \(b=0\)

The third row is why QCQPs reach SLAM: the conditions that make a matrix a rotation are quadratic in its entries. Each of these feasible sets is curved or disconnected, so none is convex (Day 1), and a QCQP is hard in general.

2. The trace trick and the lift

The trace \(\tr(\mathbf{M})\) of a square matrix is the sum of its diagonal entries. Two facts: a \(1\times1\) matrix equals its own trace, and \(\tr(\mathbf{A}\mathbf{B})=\tr(\mathbf{B}\mathbf{A})\) whenever both products are defined (the cyclic property; both sides equal \(\sum_{i,j}A_{ij}B_{ji}\)). Apply them to the number \(\mathbf{x}\T\mathbf{M}\mathbf{x}\), moving the leading \(\mathbf{x}\T\) to the back: eq. (6.1) · p. 152

\[ \mathbf{x}\T\mathbf{M}\mathbf{x} = \tr\bigl(\mathbf{x}\T\mathbf{M}\mathbf{x}\bigr) = \tr\bigl(\mathbf{M}\mathbf{x}\mathbf{x}\T\bigr) = \tr(\mathbf{M}\mathbf{X}), \qquad \mathbf{X}\triangleq\mathbf{x}\mathbf{x}\T. \]

The matrix \(\mathbf{X}\) holds all products \(X_{ij}=x_ix_j\), and \(\tr(\mathbf{M}\mathbf{X})=\sum_{i,j}M_{ij}X_{ij}\) is a weighted sum of them: linear in \(\mathbf{X}\). Check with numbers. For \(\mathbf{x}=(1,2)\) and \(\mathbf{M}=\begin{bmatrix}3 & 1\\ 1 & 0\end{bmatrix}\):

\[ \mathbf{x}\T\mathbf{M}\mathbf{x} = 3\cdot1 + 2\cdot(1\cdot1\cdot2) + 0\cdot4 = 7, \qquad \mathbf{X}=\begin{bmatrix}1 & 2\\ 2 & 4\end{bmatrix},\quad \tr(\mathbf{M}\mathbf{X}) = 3\cdot1+1\cdot2+1\cdot2+0\cdot4 = 7 . \]

Moving from \(\mathbf{x}\) to \(\mathbf{X}\) is called lifting. Every lifted matrix has three properties: it is symmetric, it is positive semidefinite (written \(\mathbf{X}\succeq0\)) because \(\mathbf{v}\T\mathbf{X}\mathbf{v}=(\mathbf{x}\T\mathbf{v})^2\ge0\), and it has rank 1 because every column is a multiple of \(\mathbf{x}\). The book states that the converse also holds: eq. (6.3) · p. 152

\[ \mathbf{X}\succeq0 \ \text{ and } \ \rank(\mathbf{X})=1 \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad \mathbf{X}=\mathbf{x}\mathbf{x}\T \ \text{ for some } \mathbf{x}\in\R^n . \]

Filling the gap: why a rank-1 positive semidefinite matrix is an outer product

The book says this is "easily shown" by an eigendecomposition. Here it is. A symmetric matrix can be written \(\mathbf{X}=\sum_k\lambda_k\mathbf{u}_k\mathbf{u}_k\T\) with real eigenvalues \(\lambda_k\) and orthonormal eigenvectors \(\mathbf{u}_k\) (Week 1 · Day 5). Its rank is the number of nonzero eigenvalues, and it is positive semidefinite exactly when no eigenvalue is negative. Rank 1 and \(\mathbf{X}\succeq0\) together leave one eigenvalue \(\lambda_1\gt0\) and the rest zero, so

\[ \mathbf{X}=\lambda_1\mathbf{u}_1\mathbf{u}_1\T = \mathbf{x}\mathbf{x}\T \quad\text{with}\quad \mathbf{x}=\sqrt{\lambda_1}\,\mathbf{u}_1 . \]

This is also the recipe for getting \(\mathbf{x}\) back from \(\mathbf{X}\). Note that \(-\mathbf{x}\) gives the same \(\mathbf{X}\); the sign is lost in the lift, and it does not matter because \(\mathbf{x}\T\mathbf{M}\mathbf{x}\) cannot see it either.

3. Drop the rank constraint

Using (6.1) on the objective and on every constraint, and (6.3) to say which \(\mathbf{X}\) are allowed, (QCQP) becomes the equivalent problem (6.4). Deleting its last line gives Shor's relaxation: eq. (6.4), (SDP) · p. 153

\[ \begin{aligned} p^\star = \min_{\mathbf{X}\in\mathbb{S}^n}\ & \tr(\mathbf{C}\mathbf{X}) \\ \text{s.t.}\ & \tr(\mathbf{A}_i\mathbf{X})=b_i,\ \ i=1,\dots,m, \\ & \mathbf{X}\succeq0, \\ & \rank(\mathbf{X})=1 \end{aligned} \qquad\longrightarrow\qquad \begin{aligned} d^\star = \min_{\mathbf{X}\in\mathbb{S}^n}\ & \tr(\mathbf{C}\mathbf{X}) \\ \text{s.t.}\ & \tr(\mathbf{A}_i\mathbf{X})=b_i,\ \ i=1,\dots,m, \\ & \mathbf{X}\succeq0 . \end{aligned} \]

Look at what remains on the right. The objective is linear in \(\mathbf{X}\). The equality constraints are linear, so they cut out a flat (affine) set. The set \(\mathbf{X}\succeq0\) is convex (Day 1, section 4). An intersection of convex sets is convex, and a linear function is convex. So the right-hand problem is a convex problem. Problems of this shape are called semidefinite programs (SDPs) and can be solved in polynomial time. §6.1.1 · p. 153

The price is size. \(\mathbf{x}\) has \(n\) entries; a symmetric \(\mathbf{X}\) has \(n(n+1)/2\) free entries (footnote 1 on p. 153). For \(n=3\) that is 6 instead of 3; for \(n=3000\) it is about 4.5 million.

Filling the gap: see the relaxation for n = 2

Take the QCQP "minimize \(\mathbf{x}\T\mathbf{C}\mathbf{x}\) over unit vectors \(\mathbf{x}\in\R^2\)". Write \(\mathbf{X}=\begin{bmatrix}a & b\\ b & c\end{bmatrix}\). The constraint \(\tr(\mathbf{X})=1\) says \(a+c=1\). A symmetric \(2\times2\) matrix with positive trace is positive semidefinite exactly when its determinant is non-negative, \(ac-b^2\ge0\). Change coordinates to \(u=a-c\) and \(v=2b\). Then \(ac=\tfrac14\bigl((a+c)^2-(a-c)^2\bigr)=\tfrac14(1-u^2)\), and

\[ ac-b^2\ge0 \iff u^2+v^2\le1 . \]

So the feasible set of the SDP is a disk. Rank 1 means determinant zero, which is the boundary circle. A unit vector \(\mathbf{x}=(\cos t,\sin t)\) lifts to \(u=\cos^2t-\sin^2t=\cos2t\), \(v=2\sin t\cos t=\sin2t\): the point at angle \(2t\) on that circle. Shor's relaxation fills the circle in.

The objective becomes \(\tr(\mathbf{C}\mathbf{X}) = \tfrac12(C_{11}+C_{22}) + \tfrac12(C_{11}-C_{22})\,u + C_{12}\,v\), a linear function on the disk. A linear function on a disk takes its smallest value at a boundary point, so here the SDP always has a rank-1 solution and \(d^\star=p^\star\). Example: \(\mathbf{C}=\begin{bmatrix}3 & 2\\ 2 & 0\end{bmatrix}\) gives \(1.5+1.5u+2v\), smallest at \((u,v)=-(1.5,2)/2.5=(-0.6,-0.8)\) with value \(1.5-2.5=-1\). Then \(a=0.2\), \(c=0.8\), \(b=-0.4\), which is \(\mathbf{x}\mathbf{x}\T\) for \(\mathbf{x}=(1,-2)/\sqrt5\). And \(-1\) is indeed the smallest eigenvalue of \(\mathbf{C}\).

4. What the relaxation tells you

Every feasible \(\mathbf{x}\) of (QCQP) lifts to a feasible \(\mathbf{X}=\mathbf{x}\mathbf{x}\T\) of (SDP) with the same cost, so the SDP minimizes the same objective over a larger set: eq. (6.5), (6.6) · p. 153

\[ d^\star\le p^\star, \qquad\text{and for any feasible } \hat{\mathbf{x}}:\quad f(\hat{\mathbf{x}})-p^\star \ \le\ f(\hat{\mathbf{x}})-d^\star, \qquad f(\mathbf{x})\triangleq\mathbf{x}\T\mathbf{C}\mathbf{x}. \]

The left side of the second inequality is the suboptimality of \(\hat{\mathbf{x}}\), which nobody can compute because \(p^\star\) is unknown. The right side can be computed. This is the altimeter of Day 1.

What you findWhat it proves
The SDP minimizer \(\mathbf{X}^\star\) has rank 1Factor it as \(\mathbf{x}^\star\mathbf{x}^{\star\mathsf{T}}\). Then \(\mathbf{x}^\star\) is feasible for (QCQP) and \(f(\mathbf{x}^\star)=d^\star\le p^\star\), so \(\mathbf{x}^\star\) is a global minimizer. The relaxation is exact. p. 154
Some feasible \(\hat{\mathbf{x}}\), from any method, has \(f(\hat{\mathbf{x}})=d^\star\)\(\hat{\mathbf{x}}\) is a global minimizer, by (6.6).
\(\mathbf{X}^\star\) has rank above 1 and the best \(\hat{\mathbf{x}}\) you have costs more than \(d^\star\)Only that \(p^\star\) lies in \([d^\star,f(\hat{\mathbf{x}})]\). The relaxation may not be tight.

The disk example is always exact. Here is one that is not. Three variables, each \(\pm1\), every pair penalized for agreeing:

\[ \min\ 2(x_1x_2+x_1x_3+x_2x_3) \quad\text{s.t.}\quad x_1^2=x_2^2=x_3^2=1 . \]

Since \((x_1+x_2+x_3)^2 = 3+2(x_1x_2+x_1x_3+x_2x_3)\), the cost equals \((x_1+x_2+x_3)^2-3\). Three signs cannot sum to zero; the best is a sum of \(\pm1\), so \(p^\star=1-3=-2\). In the relaxation, \(\mathbf{X}\) is positive semidefinite with ones on its diagonal, and the cost is \(2(X_{12}+X_{13}+X_{23})=\mathbf{1}\T\mathbf{X}\mathbf{1}-3\), where \(\mathbf{1}\) is the vector of ones. Because \(\mathbf{X}\succeq0\), \(\mathbf{1}\T\mathbf{X}\mathbf{1}\ge0\), so the cost is at least \(-3\); and \(X_{12}=X_{13}=X_{23}=-\tfrac12\) reaches it with a matrix whose eigenvalues are \(0,\tfrac32,\tfrac32\). So \(d^\star=-3\lt p^\star=-2\), and \(\mathbf{X}^\star\) has rank 2.

Try it: change the three couplings and compare the two optimal values.

Notice that at (1, 1, 1) the relaxed arrows sit 120° apart, d* = −3 is below p* = −2, and X* has eigenvalues 0, 1.5, 1.5. Press "Consistent (1, 1, −1)": now all three wishes can be met, the relaxed arrows line up, d* = p* = −6, and X* has rank 1.

Intuition

Any positive semidefinite \(\mathbf{X}\) with ones on the diagonal is a table of dot products \(X_{ij}=\mathbf{y}_i\cdot\mathbf{y}_j\) of unit vectors. The QCQP forces those vectors onto a line, where a unit vector can only be \(+1\) or \(-1\). The relaxation lets them turn into extra dimensions. If the best arrangement still fits on a line, the relaxation is exact. For three variables a plane is always enough room, which is why the widget can draw the answer.

One more practical remark from the book: general-purpose SDP software becomes slow and memory-hungry on large problems, so robotics uses specialized solvers such as SE-Sync. §6.1.1 · p. 154 That is Day 5.

Common mistakes

  • "The SDP solution is a better solution of the QCQP." If its rank is above 1 it is not a solution of the QCQP at all. Its value is a bound, not an achievable cost.
  • "A relaxation that is not tight is useless." The bound \(f(\hat{\mathbf{x}})-d^\star\) still limits how wrong any candidate can be. In the three-variable example it says "at most 1 above optimal".
  • "Lifting changes the problem." Problem (6.4) with the rank constraint is exactly (QCQP). Only deleting the rank constraint changes it.

Check yourself

Q1. What is the lift X = xxᵀ of x = (2, −1)?

The entries are the products x_i x_j: 2·2 = 4, 2·(−1) = −2, (−1)·(−1) = 1. Its determinant is 4 − 4 = 0, as it must be for rank 1.

Q2. A QCQP has n = 4 unknowns. How many free numbers does the matrix variable of its Shor relaxation have?

A symmetric 4 × 4 matrix has 4 diagonal and 6 off-diagonal free entries: n(n+1)/2 = 10.

Q3. A local solver returns a feasible point with cost 12.0. The Shor relaxation of the same problem has optimal value 11.4. Which statement is certain?

d* ≤ p* ≤ f(x̂) gives 11.4 ≤ p* ≤ 12.0. Whether the point is optimal depends on whether the relaxation is tight, which these two numbers alone do not settle.

Q4. An SDP solver returns X* with eigenvalues 5, 0, 0 and eigenvector u for the eigenvalue 5. What can you do with it?

One positive eigenvalue means rank 1, so X* = xxᵀ with x = √5 · u. That x is feasible and attains the lower bound d*, so it is globally optimal.

Recap

  1. A QCQP has a quadratic objective and quadratic equality constraints; unit vectors, signs, and orthonormal columns all fit.
  2. \(\mathbf{x}\T\mathbf{M}\mathbf{x}=\tr(\mathbf{M}\mathbf{x}\mathbf{x}\T)\), so in the lifted variable \(\mathbf{X}=\mathbf{x}\mathbf{x}\T\) everything is linear.
  3. \(\mathbf{X}\) is an outer product exactly when it is positive semidefinite with rank 1. Shor's relaxation drops the rank condition and leaves an SDP, which is convex.
  4. \(d^\star\le p^\star\), and \(f(\hat{\mathbf{x}})-d^\star\) bounds the suboptimality of any feasible \(\hat{\mathbf{x}}\).
  5. If the SDP solution has rank 1, its factor is a global minimizer of the QCQP.

Sources

  1. SLAM Handbook, §6.1.1 "Shor's Relaxation", pp. 152–154, equations (QCQP), (6.1)–(6.6), (SDP).
  2. Boyd and Vandenberghe, Convex Optimization, 2004: semidefinite programs and the convexity of the positive semidefinite cone.
  3. Pataki, On the rank of extreme matrices in semidefinite programs and the multiplicity of optimal eigenvalues, 1998: an SDP with m equality constraints has a solution of rank r with r(r+1)/2 ≤ m, which is why a plane suffices for the three-variable example.
  4. The disk picture and the three-variable example are our own worked instances of (QCQP) and (SDP).

Week 9 · Day 3

Pose-graph optimization as maximum likelihood, and its rotation-only form

After today you can derive the pose-graph cost from its noise model, build the incidence and Laplacian matrices of a pose graph, and eliminate the translations to get a problem in the rotations alone.

About 60 min · Read §6.1.2 up to equation (6.18), pp. 154–160 (6 pages) · Needs Week 9 Day 2

Read first: §6.1.2 opening, §6.1.2.1, and §6.1.2.2 up to equation (6.18), pp. 154–160

While you read, look for:

  • The convention for a measurement \(\tilde{\mathbf{T}}_{ij}\) and the direction of its edge (p. 155, Figure 6.2).
  • The noise model (6.8) and the cost it leads to, Problem 6.1 (p. 156).
  • Box 6.1 (pp. 157–158): the incidence matrix and the Laplacian of the graph in Figure 6.2.
  • Equation (6.16) and Problem 6.2 (p. 159): the translations disappear.

Today's big idea

With the right noise model, pose-graph optimization has a cost that is quadratic in the entries of the rotations and translations. For fixed rotations the best translations solve a linear least-squares problem, so they can be written down and substituted away. What remains is \(\min\tr(\tilde{\mathbf{Q}}\mathbf{R}\T\mathbf{R})\) over rotations: one data matrix, a quadratic objective, and rotation constraints. That is a QCQP waiting for Shor's relaxation.

1. Poses, relative poses, and the pose graph

Pose-graph optimization (PGO) estimates \(n\) poses \(\mathbf{T}_1,\dots,\mathbf{T}_n\in\SE(d)\), with \(d=2\) or \(3\), from noisy measurements of relative poses. §6.1.2.1 · p. 154 A pose is a pair \(\mathbf{T}_i=(\mathbf{t}_i,\mathbf{R}_i)\) of a position \(\mathbf{t}_i\in\R^d\) and a rotation \(\mathbf{R}_i\in\SO(d)\), or as a matrix (Week 4 · Day 1)

\[ \mathbf{T}_i=\begin{bmatrix}\mathbf{R}_i & \mathbf{t}_i\\ \mathbf{0} & 1\end{bmatrix}, \qquad \mathbf{T}_i^{-1}\mathbf{T}_j=\begin{bmatrix}\mathbf{R}_i\T & -\mathbf{R}_i\T\mathbf{t}_i\\ \mathbf{0} & 1\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}\mathbf{R}_j & \mathbf{t}_j\\ \mathbf{0} & 1\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}\mathbf{R}_i\T\mathbf{R}_j & \mathbf{R}_i\T(\mathbf{t}_j-\mathbf{t}_i)\\ \mathbf{0} & 1\end{bmatrix}. \]

So the true relative pose "pose \(j\) seen from pose \(i\)" has rotation \(\bar{\mathbf{R}}_{ij}=\mathbf{R}_i\T\mathbf{R}_j\) and translation \(\bar{\mathbf{t}}_{ij}=\mathbf{R}_i\T(\mathbf{t}_j-\mathbf{t}_i)\). Example in the plane: pose \(i\) is at \((1,0)\) facing 90° (up), pose \(j\) is at \((1,2)\). Then \(\mathbf{t}_j-\mathbf{t}_i=(0,2)\), and rotating by \(-90^\circ\) gives \(\bar{\mathbf{t}}_{ij}=(2,0)\): two meters straight ahead, as it should be.

A measurement \(\tilde{\mathbf{T}}_{ij}=(\tilde{\mathbf{t}}_{ij},\tilde{\mathbf{R}}_{ij})\) is a noisy version of \(\mathbf{T}_i^{-1}\mathbf{T}_j\). The pose graph has one node per pose and one directed edge \(i\to j\) per measurement \(\tilde{\mathbf{T}}_{ij}\). The book assumes the graph is connected; otherwise the problem splits into independent pieces. §6.1.2.1 · p. 155

2. The noise model, and the cost it produces

To do maximum likelihood (Week 2 · Day 2) you need a probability density for the noise. For translations the book uses a Gaussian. For rotations it uses the isotropic Langevin distribution \(\mathcal{L}(\mathbf{M},\kappa)\) on \(\SO(d)\): eq. (6.7) · p. 155

\[ p(\mathbf{R};\mathbf{M},\kappa)=\frac{1}{c_d(\kappa)}\exp\bigl(\kappa\tr(\mathbf{M}\T\mathbf{R})\bigr). \]

\(\mathbf{M}\) is the most likely rotation (the mode), \(\kappa\ge0\) is the concentration, and \(c_d(\kappa)\) normalizes. In the plane, \(\mathbf{M}\T\mathbf{R}\) is a rotation by the angle \(\theta\) between the two, whose trace is \(2\cos\theta\). The density is then proportional to \(\exp(2\kappa\cos\theta)\), the von Mises distribution on the circle with concentration \(2\kappa\). p. 156 For large \(\kappa\) only small \(\theta\) matter, \(\cos\theta\approx1-\theta^2/2\), and the density is close to \(\exp(-\kappa\theta^2)\): a Gaussian with variance \(1/(2\kappa)\). So \(\kappa=50\) means a standard deviation of \(0.1\) rad, about 5.7°. With \(\kappa=0\) every rotation is equally likely.

The generative model for each edge is eq. (6.8) · p. 156

\[ \tilde{\mathbf{t}}_{ij}=\bar{\mathbf{t}}_{ij}+\mathbf{t}^\epsilon_{ij},\quad \mathbf{t}^\epsilon_{ij}\sim\N\bigl(\mathbf{0},\tau_{ij}^{-1}\mathbf{I}_d\bigr), \qquad\qquad \tilde{\mathbf{R}}_{ij}=\bar{\mathbf{R}}_{ij}\mathbf{R}^\epsilon_{ij},\quad \mathbf{R}^\epsilon_{ij}\sim\mathcal{L}(\mathbf{I}_d,\kappa_{ij}). \]

\(\tau_{ij}\) is the translation precision (one over the variance per axis). The book says "a straightforward calculation" turns this into Problem 6.1: eq. (6.9) · p. 156

\[ p^\star_{\text{MLE}}=\min_{\mathbf{t}_i\in\R^d,\ \mathbf{R}_i\in\SO(d)}\ \sum_{(i,j)}\ \kappa_{ij}\norm{\mathbf{R}_j-\mathbf{R}_i\tilde{\mathbf{R}}_{ij}}_F^2+\tau_{ij}\norm{\mathbf{t}_j-\mathbf{t}_i-\mathbf{R}_i\tilde{\mathbf{t}}_{ij}}_2^2 . \]

Filling the gap: the straightforward calculation

Maximum likelihood minimizes the sum of negative log-densities of the measurements. Do one edge.

Translation. The noise is \(\mathbf{t}^\epsilon=\tilde{\mathbf{t}}_{ij}-\mathbf{R}_i\T(\mathbf{t}_j-\mathbf{t}_i)\), and \(-\log\) of the Gaussian is \(\tfrac{\tau_{ij}}{2}\norm{\mathbf{t}^\epsilon}^2\) plus a constant. Multiplying a vector by the rotation \(\mathbf{R}_i\) does not change its length, so

\[ \norm{\tilde{\mathbf{t}}_{ij}-\mathbf{R}_i\T(\mathbf{t}_j-\mathbf{t}_i)}^2=\norm{\mathbf{R}_i\tilde{\mathbf{t}}_{ij}-(\mathbf{t}_j-\mathbf{t}_i)}^2=\norm{\mathbf{t}_j-\mathbf{t}_i-\mathbf{R}_i\tilde{\mathbf{t}}_{ij}}^2 . \]

Rotation. The noise is \(\mathbf{R}^\epsilon=\bar{\mathbf{R}}_{ij}\T\tilde{\mathbf{R}}_{ij}=\mathbf{R}_j\T\mathbf{R}_i\tilde{\mathbf{R}}_{ij}\), and \(-\log\) of the Langevin density with mode \(\mathbf{I}\) is \(-\kappa_{ij}\tr(\mathbf{R}_j\T\mathbf{R}_i\tilde{\mathbf{R}}_{ij})\) plus a constant. Now expand a squared Frobenius norm (the sum of squared entries, \(\norm{\mathbf{A}}_F^2=\tr(\mathbf{A}\T\mathbf{A})\)) of two matrices that are both orthogonal, so each has \(\norm{\cdot}_F^2=d\):

\[ \norm{\mathbf{R}_j-\mathbf{R}_i\tilde{\mathbf{R}}_{ij}}_F^2=d+d-2\tr\bigl(\mathbf{R}_j\T\mathbf{R}_i\tilde{\mathbf{R}}_{ij}\bigr) \quad\Longrightarrow\quad -\kappa_{ij}\tr\bigl(\mathbf{R}_j\T\mathbf{R}_i\tilde{\mathbf{R}}_{ij}\bigr)=\tfrac{\kappa_{ij}}{2}\norm{\mathbf{R}_j-\mathbf{R}_i\tilde{\mathbf{R}}_{ij}}_F^2-\kappa_{ij}d . \]

Add the two, drop the constants, and multiply everything by 2 (which does not move the minimizer): that is (6.9).

In the plane. For rotations by angles \(a\) and \(b\), \(\tr(\mathbf{R}(a)\T\mathbf{R}(b))=2\cos(a-b)\), so \(\norm{\mathbf{R}(a)-\mathbf{R}(b)}_F^2=4-4\cos(a-b)\). The rotation term of an edge is \(4\kappa_{ij}(1-\cos r_{ij})\) with \(r_{ij}=\theta_j-\theta_i-\tilde\theta_{ij}\). With \(\kappa=1\) this is the cost of the Day 1 widget.

The reason for choosing Langevin noise over the Gaussian-in-the-tangent-space model of Chapter 2 is this algebraic form: every term of (6.9) is a squared norm of something linear in the entries of \(\mathbf{R}_i\) and \(\mathbf{t}_i\). §6.1.2.1 · p. 156 No logarithm map appears.

3. The graph as matrices

Box 6.1 introduces two matrices. Here they are on a graph of our own with three poses and edges \(e_1=(1,2)\), \(e_2=(2,3)\), \(e_3=(1,3)\).

The incidence matrix \(\mathbf{A}\) has one row per edge, with \(-1\) in the column of the tail and \(+1\) in the column of the head. The Laplacian is \(\mathbf{L}=\mathbf{A}\T\mathbf{A}\): Box 6.1 · pp. 157–158

\[ \mathbf{A}=\begin{bmatrix}-1 & 1 & 0\\ 0 & -1 & 1\\ -1 & 0 & 1\end{bmatrix},\qquad \mathbf{L}=\mathbf{A}\T\mathbf{A}=\begin{bmatrix}2 & -1 & -1\\ -1 & 2 & -1\\ -1 & -1 & 2\end{bmatrix}. \]

The diagonal of \(\mathbf{L}\) counts the edges at each node, an off-diagonal entry is \(-1\) where an edge exists, and edge directions have disappeared. Every row sums to zero, so \(\mathbf{L}\mathbf{1}=\mathbf{0}\): zero is always an eigenvalue. A connected graph has exactly one zero eigenvalue.

Why this matrix shows up in estimation: put a number \(x_i\) on each node. Row \(e\) of \(\mathbf{A}\mathbf{x}\) is \(x_j-x_i\), so

\[ \mathbf{x}\T\mathbf{L}\mathbf{x}=\norm{\mathbf{A}\mathbf{x}}^2=\sum_{(i,j)}(x_j-x_i)^2 . \]

The Laplacian is the matrix of "sum of squared differences across edges", which is what a relative measurement penalizes. Two weighted versions are needed for PGO:

MatrixSizeDiagonal block \(i\)Off-diagonal block for an edge \(i\to j\)
\(\mathbf{L}(\mathcal{W}^\tau)\), Laplacian of the translational weight graph, eq. (6.12)\(n\times n\)\(\sum\tau\) over the edges at \(i\)\(-\tau_{ij}\)
\(\mathbf{L}(\tilde{G}^\rho)\), the connection Laplacian, eq. (6.13)\(dn\times dn\), in \(d\times d\) blocks\(\bigl(\sum\kappa\bigr)\mathbf{I}_d\) over the edges at \(i\)\(-\kappa_{ij}\tilde{\mathbf{R}}_{ij}\) at \((i,j)\) and its transpose at \((j,i)\)

With weights \(\tau=(2,5,1)\) on \(e_1,e_2,e_3\), the first is \(\begin{bmatrix}3 & -2 & -1\\ -2 & 7 & -5\\ -1 & -5 & 6\end{bmatrix}\). The second is the same pattern with the measured rotations written into the off-diagonal blocks. Stack the unknown rotations side by side, \(\mathbf{R}\triangleq(\mathbf{R}_1\ \cdots\ \mathbf{R}_n)\in\R^{d\times dn}\). Then \(\mathbf{R}\T\mathbf{R}\) has blocks \(\mathbf{R}_i\T\mathbf{R}_j\), and multiplying out block by block gives

\[ \tr\bigl(\mathbf{L}(\tilde{G}^\rho)\,\mathbf{R}\T\mathbf{R}\bigr)=\sum_{(i,j)}\kappa_{ij}\bigl(2d-2\tr(\tilde{\mathbf{R}}_{ij}\mathbf{R}_j\T\mathbf{R}_i)\bigr)=\sum_{(i,j)}\kappa_{ij}\norm{\mathbf{R}_j-\mathbf{R}_i\tilde{\mathbf{R}}_{ij}}_F^2 , \]
