the rotation half of (6.9). (Each edge puts \(\kappa_{ij}\mathbf{I}_d\) on two diagonal blocks, which gives the \(2d\), and the two off-diagonal blocks give the same trace once each.)

Common mistakes

  • "The incidence matrix in (6.17b) is the one from Box 6.1." Box 6.1 puts edges on rows, so \(\mathbf{A}\) is \(m\times n\). In (6.17b) and (6.18) the product \(\mathbf{A}\boldsymbol{\Omega}^{1/2}\) with the \(m\times m\) matrix \(\boldsymbol{\Omega}\) only has matching sizes if edges are on columns. Read \(\mathbf{A}(\overrightarrow{\mathcal{G}})\) there as the \(n\times m\) transpose of the box's matrix. We do so below.
  • "The letter L in (6.18) is a Laplacian." There it is a lower-triangular factor from an LQ decomposition.

4. Eliminating the translations

Fix the rotations. The rotation terms of (6.9) are then constants, and the translation terms \(\tau_{ij}\norm{\mathbf{t}_j-\mathbf{t}_i-\mathbf{R}_i\tilde{\mathbf{t}}_{ij}}^2\) are squared norms of expressions that are linear in the unknown \(\mathbf{t}\)'s. That is linear least squares (Week 1 · Day 4), and it has a closed-form solution: eq. (6.16) · p. 159

\[ \mathbf{t}^\star(\mathbf{R})=-\operatorname{vec}\bigl(\mathbf{R}\,\tilde{\mathbf{V}}\T\,\mathbf{L}(\mathcal{W}^\tau)^{\dagger}\bigr). \]

Here \(\tilde{\mathbf{V}}\in\R^{n\times dn}\) is built from the translation measurements (6.14), \({}^\dagger\) is the pseudo-inverse, and \(\operatorname{vec}\) stacks the columns of the resulting \(d\times n\) matrix, which are \(\mathbf{t}_1,\dots,\mathbf{t}_n\). (The book prints \(\mathbf{R}^*\) inside (6.16); it is the \(\mathbf{R}\) we fixed.) Substituting \(\mathbf{t}^\star(\mathbf{R})\) back gives Problem 6.2: eq. (6.17) · p. 159

\[ p^\star_{\text{MLE}}=\min_{\mathbf{R}\in\SO(d)^n}\tr\bigl(\tilde{\mathbf{Q}}\mathbf{R}\T\mathbf{R}\bigr),\qquad \tilde{\mathbf{Q}}=\mathbf{L}(\tilde{G}^\rho)+\tilde{\mathbf{D}}\T\boldsymbol{\Omega}^{\frac12}\boldsymbol{\Pi}\boldsymbol{\Omega}^{\frac12}\tilde{\mathbf{D}} . \]

Filling the gap: where (6.16) and (6.17b) come from

Collect the translations as columns of \(\mathbf{T}=(\mathbf{t}_1\ \cdots\ \mathbf{t}_n)\in\R^{d\times n}\), and let \(\mathbf{A}\) be the \(n\times m\) incidence matrix (column \(e\) has \(-1\) at the tail \(i\) and \(+1\) at the head \(j\)). Then column \(e\) of \(\mathbf{T}\mathbf{A}\) is \(\mathbf{t}_j-\mathbf{t}_i\). The matrix \(\tilde{\mathbf{D}}\) of (6.15) has \(-\tilde{\mathbf{t}}_{ij}\T\) in row \(e\), block \(i\), so column \(e\) of \(\mathbf{R}\tilde{\mathbf{D}}\T\) is \(-\mathbf{R}_i\tilde{\mathbf{t}}_{ij}\). With \(\boldsymbol{\Omega}=\operatorname{Diag}(\tau_{e_1},\dots,\tau_{e_m})\), the whole translation cost is one Frobenius norm:

\[ \sum_{(i,j)}\tau_{ij}\norm{\mathbf{t}_j-\mathbf{t}_i-\mathbf{R}_i\tilde{\mathbf{t}}_{ij}}^2=\norm{\bigl(\mathbf{T}\mathbf{A}+\mathbf{R}\tilde{\mathbf{D}}\T\bigr)\boldsymbol{\Omega}^{\frac12}}_F^2 . \]

Set the derivative with respect to \(\mathbf{T}\) to zero (the normal equations):

\[ \bigl(\mathbf{T}\mathbf{A}+\mathbf{R}\tilde{\mathbf{D}}\T\bigr)\boldsymbol{\Omega}\mathbf{A}\T=\mathbf{0} \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \mathbf{T}\,\underbrace{\mathbf{A}\boldsymbol{\Omega}\mathbf{A}\T}_{\mathbf{L}(\mathcal{W}^\tau)}=-\mathbf{R}\,\underbrace{\tilde{\mathbf{D}}\T\boldsymbol{\Omega}\mathbf{A}\T}_{\tilde{\mathbf{V}}\T}. \]

You can check entry by entry that \(\mathbf{A}\boldsymbol{\Omega}\tilde{\mathbf{D}}\) is the matrix \(\tilde{\mathbf{V}}\) defined in (6.14). The Laplacian is singular because \(\mathbf{L}\mathbf{1}=\mathbf{0}\): shifting every position by the same vector changes no residual. The pseudo-inverse picks the solution whose positions average to zero, \(\mathbf{T}=-\mathbf{R}\tilde{\mathbf{V}}\T\mathbf{L}(\mathcal{W}^\tau)^\dagger\), which is (6.16).

Put this \(\mathbf{T}\) back into the residual matrix and factor:

\[ \bigl(\mathbf{T}\mathbf{A}+\mathbf{R}\tilde{\mathbf{D}}\T\bigr)\boldsymbol{\Omega}^{\frac12}=\mathbf{R}\tilde{\mathbf{D}}\T\boldsymbol{\Omega}^{\frac12}\,\underbrace{\bigl(\mathbf{I}_m-\boldsymbol{\Omega}^{\frac12}\mathbf{A}\T\mathbf{L}(\mathcal{W}^\tau)^\dagger\mathbf{A}\boldsymbol{\Omega}^{\frac12}\bigr)}_{\boldsymbol{\Pi}} . \]

\(\boldsymbol{\Pi}\) is the identity minus the orthogonal projector onto the row space of \(\mathbf{A}\boldsymbol{\Omega}^{1/2}\), so it is the orthogonal projector onto the kernel of \(\mathbf{A}\boldsymbol{\Omega}^{1/2}\), exactly as the book defines it. This is least squares as you know it: the best fit removes the part of the data the model can explain and leaves the part it cannot. A projector satisfies \(\boldsymbol{\Pi}\boldsymbol{\Pi}\T=\boldsymbol{\Pi}\), so the leftover cost is

\[ \norm{\mathbf{R}\tilde{\mathbf{D}}\T\boldsymbol{\Omega}^{\frac12}\boldsymbol{\Pi}}_F^2=\tr\bigl(\mathbf{R}\tilde{\mathbf{D}}\T\boldsymbol{\Omega}^{\frac12}\boldsymbol{\Pi}\boldsymbol{\Omega}^{\frac12}\tilde{\mathbf{D}}\mathbf{R}\T\bigr)=\tr\bigl(\tilde{\mathbf{D}}\T\boldsymbol{\Omega}^{\frac12}\boldsymbol{\Pi}\boldsymbol{\Omega}^{\frac12}\tilde{\mathbf{D}}\ \mathbf{R}\T\mathbf{R}\bigr), \]

using the cyclic property of the trace. Adding the rotation half from section 3 gives \(\tilde{\mathbf{Q}}\) in (6.17b).

Try it: the widget builds all of these matrices for six poses. Choose a pose, twist its heading, and watch the positions and the cost.

Notice that the last two tiles always agree: at the start both are 17.83, and with pose 2 twisted by 30° both are 187.43. The left one needed the positions from (6.16); the right one, \(\tr(\tilde{\mathbf{Q}}\mathbf{R}\T\mathbf{R})\), never computed a position. Notice also that twisting one pose moves the other poses, and that the cost curve over a full turn is one non-convex wave.

5. What Problem 6.2 looks like

Problem 6.2 has \(n\) rotations as unknowns and a single \(dn\times dn\) data matrix \(\tilde{\mathbf{Q}}\) that is computed once from the measurements. \(\tilde{\mathbf{Q}}\) is positive semidefinite, since \(\tr(\tilde{\mathbf{Q}}\mathbf{R}\T\mathbf{R})\) is a sum of squared norms for any \(d\times dn\) matrix \(\mathbf{R}\). The book points out that the problem now has the form of rotation averaging, with a more complicated data matrix. §6.1.2.2 · p. 160

One practical point. \(\boldsymbol{\Pi}\) is a dense \(m\times m\) matrix, which would be expensive for a large graph. Equation (6.18) rewrites it using a sparse triangular factor of the (reduced) weighted incidence matrix, so that products with \(\tilde{\mathbf{Q}}\) stay cheap. eq. (6.18) · p. 160 The solver of Day 5 needs only such products.

The objective is quadratic in the entries of \(\mathbf{R}\). The only obstacle left is the constraint set \(\SO(d)^n\). Tomorrow it gets the treatment of Day 2.

Check yourself

Q1. In the plane, pose i is at (3, 1) with heading 180° and pose j is at (1, 1). What is the true relative translation of j seen from i?

t_j − t_i = (−2, 0). Multiplying by R_iᵀ, a rotation by −180°, flips both signs: (2, 0). Pose j is two meters straight ahead of a robot that faces in the −x direction.

Q2. A planar edge has κ = 10 and a rotation residual of 60°. How much does its rotation term contribute to the cost (6.9)?

In the plane the term is 4κ(1 − cos r) = 4 · 10 · (1 − 0.5) = 20.

Q3. A node has three edges with translation precisions τ = 2, 5, and 1. What is its diagonal entry in L(W^τ)?

By (6.12) the diagonal entry is the sum of the weights of the edges at that node: 2 + 5 + 1 = 8.

Q4. Why can the translations be eliminated in closed form, but not the rotations?

Translations are free vectors that enter the residuals linearly, so the normal equations solve them. Rotations enter linearly too, but must satisfy quadratic constraints, so no single linear solve gives the optimum.

Q5. A rotation measurement has concentration κ = 200. Roughly what angular standard deviation is that?

For large κ the angle is nearly Gaussian with variance 1/(2κ) = 1/400, so the standard deviation is 0.05 rad, which is 2.9°.

Recap

  1. A measurement \(\tilde{\mathbf{T}}_{ij}\) is a noisy \(\mathbf{T}_i^{-1}\mathbf{T}_j\), with rotation \(\mathbf{R}_i\T\mathbf{R}_j\) and translation \(\mathbf{R}_i\T(\mathbf{t}_j-\mathbf{t}_i)\).
  2. Gaussian translation noise and Langevin rotation noise give the cost (6.9), a sum of squared norms that are linear in the entries of the unknowns.
  3. The Laplacian \(\mathbf{A}\T\mathbf{A}\) encodes sums of squared differences across edges; its weighted and block versions carry \(\tau\), \(\kappa\), and the measured rotations.
  4. For fixed rotations the optimal translations are \(\mathbf{t}^\star(\mathbf{R})\) from (6.16); substituting them leaves \(\min\tr(\tilde{\mathbf{Q}}\mathbf{R}\T\mathbf{R})\) over \(\SO(d)^n\).

Sources

  1. SLAM Handbook, §6.1.2 and §6.1.2.1, and §6.1.2.2 "Simplifying the Maximum Likelihood Estimator" with Box 6.1, pp. 154–160, equations (6.7)–(6.18), Figure 6.2.
  2. Rosen, Carlone, Bandeira, Leonard, SE-Sync: A certifiably correct algorithm for synchronization over the special Euclidean group, 2019: the derivation of the rotation-only problem that our "Filling the gap" follows, with the incidence matrix written with one column per edge.
  3. Barfoot, State Estimation for Robotics, 2017: poses as matrices and their inverses.

Week 9 · Day 4

The semidefinite relaxation of pose-graph optimization and its certificate

After today you can write the semidefinite relaxation of rotation-only pose-graph optimization, derive the dual of a QCQP, and use the certificate matrix to prove that a candidate solution is globally optimal.

About 60 min · Read §6.1.2.2 from "Forming the Relaxation" to Theorem 6.1, pp. 160–161 (2 pages) · Needs Week 9 Day 3

Read first: §6.1.2.2 "Forming the Relaxation" and Theorem 6.1, pp. 160–161

Only two pages today, because the lesson adds the duality theory the book leaves out. While you read, look for:

  • The two relaxation steps: from \(\SO(d)\) to \(\operatorname{O}(d)\), then from \(\mathbf{R}\T\mathbf{R}\) to \(\mathbf{Z}\) (p. 160).
  • The chain of three optimal values after Problem 6.3 (p. 160).
  • The condition in Theorem 6.1 under which the relaxation is exact (p. 161).

Today's big idea

Shor's relaxation of Problem 6.2 is an SDP in a matrix \(\mathbf{Z}\) that stands for \(\mathbf{R}\T\mathbf{R}\). Its dual hands you a test: from any candidate \(\hat{\mathbf{R}}\) build a matrix \(\mathbf{S}=\tilde{\mathbf{Q}}-\boldsymbol{\Lambda}\); if \(\mathbf{S}\) has no negative eigenvalue, \(\hat{\mathbf{R}}\) is a global optimum. Theorem 6.1 says that for small enough noise the test succeeds at the true optimum.

1. Two relaxation steps

Yesterday ended with Problem 6.2, \(\min\tr(\tilde{\mathbf{Q}}\mathbf{R}\T\mathbf{R})\) over \(\mathbf{R}=(\mathbf{R}_1\ \cdots\ \mathbf{R}_n)\in\SO(d)^n\). The book relaxes it twice. §6.1.2.2 · p. 160

Step 1: allow reflections. A rotation is an orthogonal matrix, \(\mathbf{R}_i\T\mathbf{R}_i=\mathbf{I}_d\), with determinant \(+1\). The orthogonal group \(\operatorname{O}(d)\) keeps the first condition and drops the second, so it also contains reflections (determinant \(-1\)). Orthonormality is a set of quadratic equations in the entries, so the problem over \(\operatorname{O}(d)^n\) is a QCQP with no linear terms (the book says homogeneous). The map \(\operatorname{BlockDiag}_{d\times d}\) of (6.19) just reads off the \(n\) diagonal blocks of a \(dn\times dn\) matrix, and the diagonal blocks of \(\mathbf{R}\T\mathbf{R}\) are \(\mathbf{R}_i\T\mathbf{R}_i\): eq. (6.20) · p. 160

\[ p^\star_{\mathrm{O}}=\min_{\mathbf{R}\in\R^{d\times dn}}\tr\bigl(\tilde{\mathbf{Q}}\mathbf{R}\T\mathbf{R}\bigr)\quad\text{s.t.}\quad\operatorname{BlockDiag}_{d\times d}(\mathbf{R}\T\mathbf{R})=(\mathbf{I}_d,\dots,\mathbf{I}_d). \]

Step 2: lift and drop the rank. The unknown enters only through \(\mathbf{R}\T\mathbf{R}\). This is Day 2 with a matrix in place of the vector \(\mathbf{x}\): \(\mathbf{R}\T\mathbf{R}\) is symmetric, positive semidefinite, and has rank \(d\) (not 1, because \(\mathbf{R}\) has \(d\) rows). Call it \(\mathbf{Z}\), keep "positive semidefinite", delete "rank \(d\)": Problem 6.3, eq. (6.21) · p. 160

\[ p^\star_{\text{SDP}}=\min_{\mathbf{Z}\succeq0}\tr\bigl(\tilde{\mathbf{Q}}\mathbf{Z}\bigr)\quad\text{s.t.}\quad\operatorname{BlockDiag}_{d\times d}(\mathbf{Z})=(\mathbf{I}_d,\dots,\mathbf{I}_d). \]

That is the chain \(p^\star_{\text{MLE}}\ge p^\star_{\mathrm{O}}\ge p^\star_{\text{SDP}}\). And as on Day 2: if the SDP minimizer happens to be \(\mathbf{Z}^\star=\mathbf{R}^{\star\mathsf{T}}\mathbf{R}^\star\) with \(\mathbf{R}^\star\in\SO(d)^n\), then \(\mathbf{R}^\star\) is a global optimum of Problem 6.2. pp. 160–161

It helps to see what \(\mathbf{Z}\) contains. Its \((i,j)\) block is \(\mathbf{R}_i\T\mathbf{R}_j\), the relative rotation between poses \(i\) and \(j\). For two planar poses with headings \(\theta_1,\theta_2\),

\[ \mathbf{Z}=\begin{bmatrix}\mathbf{I}_2 & \mathbf{R}(\theta_2-\theta_1)\\ \mathbf{R}(\theta_1-\theta_2) & \mathbf{I}_2\end{bmatrix}. \]

Only the difference of the headings appears. Turning the whole solution by a common rotation \(\mathbf{G}\) replaces \(\mathbf{R}\) by \(\mathbf{G}\mathbf{R}\) and leaves \(\mathbf{Z}=\mathbf{R}\T\mathbf{G}\T\mathbf{G}\mathbf{R}\) unchanged. The lifted variable stores all pairwise relative rotations and has no gauge freedom. The cost is its size: for 1000 poses in 3-D, \(\mathbf{Z}\) is \(3000\times3000\).

2. Lagrangian duality for a QCQP

Day 2 got the lower bound by enlarging the feasible set. There is a second route to the same bound, and it is the one that produces certificates. Take the generic problem (QCQP): minimize \(\mathbf{x}\T\mathbf{C}\mathbf{x}\) subject to \(\mathbf{x}\T\mathbf{A}_i\mathbf{x}=b_i\). Introduce one number \(\lambda_i\) per constraint, a Lagrange multiplier, and form the Lagrangian

\[ L(\mathbf{x},\boldsymbol{\lambda})=\mathbf{x}\T\mathbf{C}\mathbf{x}-\sum_{i=1}^m\lambda_i\bigl(\mathbf{x}\T\mathbf{A}_i\mathbf{x}-b_i\bigr)=\mathbf{x}\T\mathbf{S}(\boldsymbol{\lambda})\,\mathbf{x}+\mathbf{b}\T\boldsymbol{\lambda},\qquad \mathbf{S}(\boldsymbol{\lambda})\triangleq\mathbf{C}-\sum_{i=1}^m\lambda_i\mathbf{A}_i . \]

Two observations do all the work.

  • At any feasible \(\mathbf{x}\), the brackets are zero, so \(L(\mathbf{x},\boldsymbol{\lambda})=\mathbf{x}\T\mathbf{C}\mathbf{x}\) whatever \(\boldsymbol{\lambda}\) is.
  • Minimize \(L\) over all \(\mathbf{x}\), ignoring the constraints. If \(\mathbf{S}(\boldsymbol{\lambda})\succeq0\), the quadratic term is never negative and the minimum is \(\mathbf{b}\T\boldsymbol{\lambda}\), at \(\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{0}\). If \(\mathbf{S}(\boldsymbol{\lambda})\) has a direction \(\mathbf{v}\) with \(\mathbf{v}\T\mathbf{S}\mathbf{v}\lt0\), scaling \(\mathbf{x}=s\mathbf{v}\) sends \(L\) to \(-\infty\).

The unconstrained minimum is called the dual function \(q(\boldsymbol{\lambda})\). An unconstrained minimum is at most the value at any particular point, so for every feasible \(\mathbf{x}\): \(q(\boldsymbol{\lambda})\le L(\mathbf{x},\boldsymbol{\lambda})=\mathbf{x}\T\mathbf{C}\mathbf{x}\). Hence \(q(\boldsymbol{\lambda})\le p^\star\) for every \(\boldsymbol{\lambda}\). This is weak duality. The best such bound is the dual problem:

\[ \max_{\boldsymbol{\lambda}\in\R^m}\ \mathbf{b}\T\boldsymbol{\lambda}\quad\text{s.t.}\quad\mathbf{C}-\sum_{i=1}^m\lambda_i\mathbf{A}_i\succeq0 . \]

It is again an SDP, with only \(m\) unknowns. Doing the same construction on Shor's (SDP) gives the very same dual, so the two routes meet: \(\text{dual value}\le d^\star\le p^\star\). For a convex problem with a strictly feasible point (Slater's condition; here \(\mathbf{Z}=\mathbf{I}\) is one for Problem 6.3) the first inequality is an equality, which is called strong duality.

Example: minimize \(\mathbf{x}\T\mathbf{C}\mathbf{x}\) over unit vectors. One constraint, \(\mathbf{A}=\mathbf{I}\), \(b=1\), so \(\mathbf{S}(\lambda)=\mathbf{C}-\lambda\mathbf{I}\), which is positive semidefinite exactly when \(\lambda\) is at most the smallest eigenvalue of \(\mathbf{C}\). The dual optimum is \(\lambda_{\min}(\mathbf{C})\), the same \(-1\) that the disk picture gave for \(\mathbf{C}=\begin{bmatrix}3 & 2\\ 2 & 0\end{bmatrix}\) on Day 2.

3. The certificate matrix

Filling the gap: a sufficient condition for global optimality

Claim. Let \(\hat{\mathbf{x}}\) be feasible for (QCQP). If some \(\hat{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}\) gives a matrix \(\mathbf{S}=\mathbf{S}(\hat{\boldsymbol{\lambda}})\) with

\[ \text{(i)}\ \ \mathbf{S}\hat{\mathbf{x}}=\mathbf{0}\qquad\text{and}\qquad\text{(ii)}\ \ \mathbf{S}\succeq0, \]

then \(\hat{\mathbf{x}}\) is a global minimizer.

Proof. For any feasible \(\mathbf{x}\), using \(\mathbf{C}=\mathbf{S}+\sum_i\hat\lambda_i\mathbf{A}_i\) and the constraints,

\[ \mathbf{x}\T\mathbf{C}\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{x}\T\mathbf{S}\mathbf{x}+\sum_i\hat\lambda_i\,\mathbf{x}\T\mathbf{A}_i\mathbf{x}=\underbrace{\mathbf{x}\T\mathbf{S}\mathbf{x}}_{\ge0\text{ by (ii)}}+\mathbf{b}\T\hat{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}\ \ge\ \mathbf{b}\T\hat{\boldsymbol{\lambda}} . \]

For \(\hat{\mathbf{x}}\) itself the first term is zero by (i), so \(\hat{\mathbf{x}}\T\mathbf{C}\hat{\mathbf{x}}=\mathbf{b}\T\hat{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}\). No feasible point costs less than \(\hat{\mathbf{x}}\).

Finding \(\hat{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}\). Condition (i) reads \(\sum_i\lambda_i\mathbf{A}_i\hat{\mathbf{x}}=\mathbf{C}\hat{\mathbf{x}}\): linear equations in \(\boldsymbol{\lambda}\). It says the gradient of the Lagrangian, \(2\mathbf{S}\mathbf{x}\), vanishes at \(\hat{\mathbf{x}}\), which is the first-order condition that a local solver's output satisfies. So: take the local solution, solve (i) for the multipliers, and test (ii) by computing the smallest eigenvalue of \(\mathbf{S}\). Conditions (i), (ii), and feasibility are the KKT conditions of the relaxation.

Try the test by hand on the three \(\pm1\) variables of Day 2, where \(\mathbf{A}_i\) has a single 1 at \((i,i)\), so \(\sum\lambda_i\mathbf{A}_i=\operatorname{Diag}(\boldsymbol{\lambda})\) and (i) becomes \(\lambda_i=(\mathbf{C}\hat{\mathbf{x}})_i/\hat x_i\).

Case\(\mathbf{C}\) and candidateMultipliers\(\mathbf{S}=\mathbf{C}-\operatorname{Diag}(\hat{\boldsymbol{\lambda}})\)Verdict
Consistent, couplings \((1,1,-1)\)\(\begin{bmatrix}0 & 1 & 1\\ 1 & 0 & -1\\ 1 & -1 & 0\end{bmatrix}\), \(\hat{\mathbf{x}}=(1,-1,-1)\), cost \(-6\)\(\mathbf{C}\hat{\mathbf{x}}=(-2,2,2)\), so \(\hat{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}=(-2,-2,-2)\)\(\begin{bmatrix}2 & 1 & 1\\ 1 & 2 & -1\\ 1 & -1 & 2\end{bmatrix}=3\mathbf{I}-\hat{\mathbf{x}}\hat{\mathbf{x}}\T\), eigenvalues \(0,3,3\)\(\mathbf{S}\succeq0\): certified. \(\mathbf{b}\T\hat{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}=-6\) equals the cost.
All disagree, couplings \((1,1,1)\)\(\begin{bmatrix}0 & 1 & 1\\ 1 & 0 & 1\\ 1 & 1 & 0\end{bmatrix}\), \(\hat{\mathbf{x}}=(1,1,-1)\), cost \(-2\)\(\mathbf{C}\hat{\mathbf{x}}=(0,0,2)\), so \(\hat{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}=(0,0,-2)\)\(\begin{bmatrix}0 & 1 & 1\\ 1 & 0 & 1\\ 1 & 1 & 2\end{bmatrix}\); with \(\mathbf{v}=(1,-1,0)\), \(\mathbf{v}\T\mathbf{S}\mathbf{v}=-2\)Not positive semidefinite: no certificate, although \(\hat{\mathbf{x}}\) is in fact optimal. The relaxation is not tight (\(d^\star=-3\)).

The second row shows the one-sidedness of the test. Passing proves optimality. Failing proves nothing.

For pose graphs. In (6.20) the constraints are the \(d\times d\) matrix equations \(\mathbf{R}_i\T\mathbf{R}_i=\mathbf{I}_d\). Each gets a symmetric \(d\times d\) block of multipliers \(\boldsymbol{\Lambda}_i\), and \(\boldsymbol{\Lambda}=\operatorname{Diag}(\boldsymbol{\Lambda}_1,\dots,\boldsymbol{\Lambda}_n)\) plays the role of \(\sum\lambda_i\mathbf{A}_i\). The certificate matrix is

\[ \mathbf{S}=\tilde{\mathbf{Q}}-\boldsymbol{\Lambda},\qquad\boldsymbol{\Lambda}_i=\bigl(\tilde{\mathbf{Q}}\hat{\mathbf{R}}\T\hat{\mathbf{R}}\bigr)_{ii}\ \ \text{(the } i\text{th diagonal block, symmetrized)} . \]

The formula for \(\boldsymbol{\Lambda}_i\) is condition (i), \(\mathbf{S}\hat{\mathbf{R}}\T=\mathbf{0}\): block \(i\) of \(\tilde{\mathbf{Q}}\hat{\mathbf{R}}\T\) must equal \(\boldsymbol{\Lambda}_i\hat{\mathbf{R}}_i\T\), and multiplying on the right by \(\hat{\mathbf{R}}_i\) isolates \(\boldsymbol{\Lambda}_i\). The proof is the same as above with traces: for any feasible \(\mathbf{Z}\), \(\tr(\tilde{\mathbf{Q}}\mathbf{Z})=\tr(\mathbf{S}\mathbf{Z})+\tr(\boldsymbol{\Lambda}\mathbf{Z})\ge\tr(\boldsymbol{\Lambda})\), because \(\tr(\mathbf{S}\mathbf{Z})\ge0\) for two positive semidefinite matrices and \(\tr(\boldsymbol{\Lambda}\mathbf{Z})=\sum_i\tr(\boldsymbol{\Lambda}_i\mathbf{Z}_{ii})=\tr(\boldsymbol{\Lambda})\). At \(\hat{\mathbf{R}}\) the cost equals \(\tr(\boldsymbol{\Lambda})\). So if \(\mathbf{S}\succeq0\), then \(p^\star_{\text{SDP}}=\tr(\tilde{\mathbf{Q}}\hat{\mathbf{R}}\T\hat{\mathbf{R}})\), and \(\hat{\mathbf{R}}\) is optimal for all three problems of section 1 at once.

In the plane with rotations only, the blocks come out as multiples of the identity, \(\boldsymbol{\Lambda}_i=\lambda_i\mathbf{I}_2\) with

\[ \lambda_i=\sum_{\text{edges } e \text{ at pose } i}\kappa_e\,(1-\cos r_e), \]

where \(r_e\) is the edge's angular residual from Day 1. Each pose's multiplier adds up the misfit of the edges that touch it. A pose whose two edges have residuals 60° and 90° (\(\kappa=1\)) gets \(\lambda_i=0.5+1=1.5\).

4. Try the test, and when it is guaranteed to pass

The widget runs gradient descent on the headings of the Day 1 graph, builds \(\mathbf{S}\) at the point where it stops, and plots its 20 eigenvalues.

Notice that the first run (cost 11.595) has \(\lambda_{\min}(\mathbf{S})=-0.738\): no certificate. Press "New start": cost 0.091, and the smallest eigenvalue is 0.000, a pair of zeros with everything else positive: certified. Now raise the noise, pressing "New start" a few times at each level. Up to 75° some start always earns the certificate. At 80° and above none does: there the relaxation is no longer tight.

The book's guarantee for when the relaxation is tight is Theorem 6.1. Let \(\bar{\mathbf{Q}}\) be the data matrix built from the true, noise-free relative poses. There is a constant \(\beta\gt0\), depending on \(\bar{\mathbf{Q}}\), such that if \(\norm{\tilde{\mathbf{Q}}-\bar{\mathbf{Q}}}_2\lt\beta\), then Problem 6.3 has a unique solution \(\mathbf{Z}^\star=\mathbf{R}^{\star\mathsf{T}}\mathbf{R}^\star\), where \(\mathbf{R}^\star\in\SO(d)^n\) is a global minimizer of Problem 6.2. Theorem 6.1 · p. 161 The norm is the spectral norm, the largest singular value, so the condition says "the noise has not moved the data matrix much". The global minimizer of the full Problem 6.1 then follows from (6.16).

Intuition: why small noise is enough

This is the idea, not the proof (the book refers to the SE-Sync paper for that). With perfect measurements the true rotations have cost 0, the lowest any sum of squares can go. All multipliers are zero, so \(\mathbf{S}=\bar{\mathbf{Q}}\), which is positive semidefinite: the certificate holds. For a connected graph \(\bar{\mathbf{Q}}\) has exactly \(d\) zero eigenvalues, and the rest are strictly positive. Add a little noise. The optimum and \(\mathbf{S}\) move a little. The \(d\) zeros stay at zero, because \(\mathbf{S}\hat{\mathbf{R}}\T=\mathbf{0}\) by construction, and the positive eigenvalues cannot jump below zero. So \(\mathbf{S}\) stays positive semidefinite until the noise is large enough to close that gap. You saw the pair of zeros (\(d=2\)) and the gap in the widget.

Common mistakes

  • "A negative eigenvalue of S proves the solution is a bad local minimum." It proves only that this test cannot certify it. The solution may be suboptimal, or optimal for a problem whose relaxation is not tight.
  • "S should be positive definite." It never is: \(\mathbf{S}\hat{\mathbf{R}}\T=\mathbf{0}\) gives it at least \(d\) zero eigenvalues. The test is \(\lambda_{\min}(\mathbf{S})\ge0\), in practice "not below a small negative tolerance".
  • "The SDP optimizes over rotations." It optimizes over \(\mathbf{Z}\), a table of would-be relative rotations. Only when \(\mathbf{Z}^\star\) has rank \(d\) do actual rotations come out of it.

Check yourself

Q1. A pose graph has 100 poses in 3-D. How large is the matrix Z of Problem 6.3?

Z stands for RᵀR with R of size d × dn = 3 × 300, so Z is dn × dn = 300 × 300.

Q2. Why is p*_O never larger than p*_MLE?

SO(d) is a subset of O(d). A minimum over a superset is at most the minimum over the subset. O(d) is not convex; convexity appears only after the lift.

Q3. In a planar rotation-only pose graph with κ = 1, a pose has three edges with residuals 0°, 60°, and 180°. What is its multiplier λ_i?

λ_i = (1 − cos 0°) + (1 − cos 60°) + (1 − cos 180°) = 0 + 0.5 + 2 = 2.5.

Q4. A local solver stops at R̂. You build S and find λmin(S) = −0.7. What follows?

The condition S ⪰ 0 is sufficient for optimality, not necessary. When it fails you have no certificate, and you cannot tell which of the two reasons applies without more work (Day 5).

Recap

  1. Relax \(\SO(d)\) to \(\operatorname{O}(d)\), then replace \(\mathbf{R}\T\mathbf{R}\) by a positive semidefinite \(\mathbf{Z}\) with identity diagonal blocks: Problem 6.3, with \(p^\star_{\text{MLE}}\ge p^\star_{\mathrm{O}}\ge p^\star_{\text{SDP}}\).
  2. The Lagrangian of a QCQP is \(\mathbf{x}\T\mathbf{S}(\boldsymbol{\lambda})\mathbf{x}+\mathbf{b}\T\boldsymbol{\lambda}\); its dual maximizes \(\mathbf{b}\T\boldsymbol{\lambda}\) subject to \(\mathbf{S}(\boldsymbol{\lambda})\succeq0\) and always bounds \(p^\star\) from below.
  3. If a feasible candidate has multipliers with \(\mathbf{S}\hat{\mathbf{x}}=\mathbf{0}\) and \(\mathbf{S}\succeq0\), it is globally optimal. For PGO, \(\mathbf{S}=\tilde{\mathbf{Q}}-\boldsymbol{\Lambda}\) with \(\boldsymbol{\Lambda}_i=(\tilde{\mathbf{Q}}\hat{\mathbf{R}}\T\hat{\mathbf{R}})_{ii}\).
  4. The test is one-sided: passing proves optimality, failing proves nothing.
  5. Theorem 6.1: for noise below a graph-dependent threshold the relaxation is exact and its unique solution is \(\mathbf{R}^{\star\mathsf{T}}\mathbf{R}^\star\).

Sources

  1. SLAM Handbook, §6.1.2.2 "Forming the Relaxation", pp. 160–161, equations (6.19)–(6.21), Problem 6.3, Theorem 6.1.
  2. Boyd and Vandenberghe, Convex Optimization, 2004: the Lagrangian, weak and strong duality, Slater's condition, the KKT conditions, and the dual of a QCQP.
  3. Rosen, Carlone, Bandeira, Leonard, SE-Sync: A certifiably correct algorithm for synchronization over the special Euclidean group, 2019: the certificate matrix \(\mathbf{S}=\tilde{\mathbf{Q}}-\boldsymbol{\Lambda}\) and the proof of Theorem 6.1. The certificate matrix does not appear in these pages of the book.

Week 9 · Day 5

Solving the relaxation at scale: Burer-Monteiro, the Riemannian staircase, and SE-Sync

After today you can explain how SE-Sync solves a huge semidefinite program through a small non-convex one, follow the Riemannian staircase step by step, and read the certificate that SE-Sync returns.

About 60 min · Read §6.1.2.3–6.1.2.5, pp. 161–164 (4 pages) · Needs Week 9 Day 4

Read first: §6.1.2.3 to §6.1.2.5, pp. 161–164

While you read, look for:

  • Why a general-purpose SDP solver is not an option, and the size at which it gives up (p. 161).
  • The Burer-Monteiro substitution, equation (6.22), and the definition of the Stiefel manifold, equation (6.23) (p. 162).
  • Theorem 6.2 and the paragraph after it that describes the Riemannian Staircase (p. 163).
  • Algorithm 3 and the two relations (6.26) and (6.27) (p. 164).

Today's big idea

The SDP of Day 4 is convex but enormous. Its solution, however, has low rank. So search directly for a low-rank factor \(\mathbf{Y}\) with \(\mathbf{Z}=\mathbf{Y}\T\mathbf{Y}\). That problem is small and non-convex again, but with one extra property: a local solution that does not use all the rank it was given is guaranteed to be global. Increase the rank until that happens, round the result to rotations, and compare costs to get the certificate.

1. The SDP is too big, but its solution is small

Problem 6.3 can be solved in polynomial time in principle. In practice, general-purpose interior-point solvers store and factor the dense \(dn\times dn\) matrix \(\mathbf{Z}\), which stops working when its dimension passes a few thousand, and SLAM problems are one to two orders of magnitude larger than that. §6.1.2.3 · p. 161

But look at what we expect the answer to be. When the relaxation is exact, \(\mathbf{Z}^\star=\mathbf{R}^{\star\mathsf{T}}\mathbf{R}^\star\) has rank \(d\), which is 2 or 3. Even when it is not exact, the rank of a minimizer is typically not much above \(d\). p. 161 A \(dn\times dn\) matrix of rank \(r\) can be written as \(\mathbf{Y}\T\mathbf{Y}\) with \(\mathbf{Y}\in\R^{r\times dn}\). Burer and Monteiro's idea is to substitute that factorization into the SDP: eq. (6.22) · p. 162

\[ p^\star_{\text{SDPLR}}(r)=\min_{\mathbf{Y}\in\R^{r\times dn}}\tr\bigl(\tilde{\mathbf{Q}}\mathbf{Y}\T\mathbf{Y}\bigr)\quad\text{s.t.}\quad\operatorname{BlockDiag}_{d\times d}(\mathbf{Y}\T\mathbf{Y})=(\mathbf{I}_d,\dots,\mathbf{I}_d). \]

Two things changed. The constraint \(\mathbf{Z}\succeq0\) is gone, because \(\mathbf{Y}\T\mathbf{Y}\) is positive semidefinite automatically: \(\mathbf{v}\T\mathbf{Y}\T\mathbf{Y}\mathbf{v}=\norm{\mathbf{Y}\mathbf{v}}^2\ge0\). And the number of unknowns dropped from \(dn(dn+1)/2\) to \(rdn\). For \(n=10\,000\) poses in 3-D and \(r=5\):

\[ \frac{dn(dn+1)}{2}=\frac{30\,000\cdot30\,001}{2}\approx4.5\times10^{8}\qquad\text{versus}\qquad rdn=5\cdot30\,000=1.5\times10^{5}. \]

Compare (6.22) with (6.20) from Day 4: the same problem, except that \(\mathbf{Y}\) has \(r\) rows where \(\mathbf{R}\) had \(d\). With \(r=d\) we are back at the non-convex problem over \(\operatorname{O}(d)^n\). p. 162

2. The feasible set is a product of Stiefel manifolds

Split \(\mathbf{Y}\) into \(n\) blocks of size \(r\times d\), \(\mathbf{Y}=(\mathbf{Y}_1\ \cdots\ \mathbf{Y}_n)\). The constraint says \(\mathbf{Y}_i\T\mathbf{Y}_i=\mathbf{I}_d\) for each \(i\): the \(d\) columns of \(\mathbf{Y}_i\) are orthonormal vectors in \(\R^r\). The set of all such matrices is the Stiefel manifold: eq. (6.23) · p. 162

\[ \operatorname{St}(k,p)\triangleq\bigl\{\mathbf{Y}\in\R^{p\times k}\ \big|\ \mathbf{Y}\T\mathbf{Y}=\mathbf{I}_k\bigr\}, \]

the set of \(k\) orthonormal vectors (a \(k\)-frame) in \(\R^p\).

ManifoldWhat a point isFamiliar name
\(\operatorname{St}(1,p)\)one unit vector in \(\R^p\)the unit sphere
\(\operatorname{St}(p,p)\)\(p\) orthonormal vectors in \(\R^p\)the orthogonal group \(\operatorname{O}(p)\)
\(\operatorname{St}(2,3)\)two perpendicular unit vectors in \(\R^3\)a planar frame that is free to tilt in space

So (6.22) is the same as Problem 6.4, eq. (6.24) · p. 162

\[ p^\star_{\text{SDPLR}}(r)=\min_{\mathbf{Y}\in\operatorname{St}(d,r)^n}\tr\bigl(\tilde{\mathbf{Q}}\mathbf{Y}\T\mathbf{Y}\bigr), \]

an unconstrained problem on a smooth manifold. This is the setting of Week 4 · Day 3: stay on the manifold by construction and you never have to handle the constraints separately. The book notes that manifold solvers are simpler, faster, and more accurate here than general constrained solvers. p. 162

In plain words

On Day 2, three variables that had to be \(+1\) or \(-1\) were allowed to become arrows in a plane. Here each pose's rotation, a frame of \(d\) axes in \(d\) dimensions, is allowed to become a frame of \(d\) axes in \(r\) dimensions. A planar robot's heading frame may tip out of the page. The extra room is what lets a stuck configuration get unstuck.

Filling the gap: one step of Riemannian gradient descent on Problem 6.4

The book says "apply a Riemannian optimization algorithm" and moves on. Here is the simplest one, which the widget below runs. Write \(f(\mathbf{Y})=\tr(\tilde{\mathbf{Q}}\mathbf{Y}\T\mathbf{Y})\).

Ordinary gradient. \(f\) is quadratic in \(\mathbf{Y}\) and \(\tilde{\mathbf{Q}}\) is symmetric, so \(\nabla f(\mathbf{Y})=2\mathbf{Y}\tilde{\mathbf{Q}}\), an \(r\times dn\) matrix with blocks \(\mathbf{G}_i\).

Tangent directions. A small change \(\mathbf{V}_i\) of \(\mathbf{Y}_i\) keeps \(\mathbf{Y}_i\T\mathbf{Y}_i=\mathbf{I}\) to first order when \(\mathbf{Y}_i\T\mathbf{V}_i+\mathbf{V}_i\T\mathbf{Y}_i=\mathbf{0}\), that is, when \(\mathbf{Y}_i\T\mathbf{V}_i\) is skew-symmetric. Those \(\mathbf{V}_i\) form the tangent space.

Project. Removing the symmetric part does it. With \(\operatorname{sym}(\mathbf{M})=\tfrac12(\mathbf{M}+\mathbf{M}\T)\),

\[ \operatorname{grad}_i=\mathbf{G}_i-\mathbf{Y}_i\operatorname{sym}(\mathbf{Y}_i\T\mathbf{G}_i)\qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad\operatorname{grad}f(\mathbf{Y})=2\,\mathbf{Y}\bigl(\tilde{\mathbf{Q}}-\boldsymbol{\Lambda}\bigr),\quad\boldsymbol{\Lambda}_i=\operatorname{sym}\bigl((\mathbf{Y}\T\mathbf{Y}\tilde{\mathbf{Q}})_{ii}\bigr). \]

Check: \(\mathbf{Y}_i\T\operatorname{grad}_i=\mathbf{Y}_i\T\mathbf{G}_i-\operatorname{sym}(\mathbf{Y}_i\T\mathbf{G}_i)\) is the skew part of \(\mathbf{Y}_i\T\mathbf{G}_i\), as required. And look at the result: the Riemannian gradient is \(2\mathbf{Y}\mathbf{S}\) with the certificate matrix \(\mathbf{S}=\tilde{\mathbf{Q}}-\boldsymbol{\Lambda}\) of Day 4. A point where the gradient vanishes satisfies \(\mathbf{Y}\mathbf{S}=\mathbf{0}\), which is condition (i) of the certificate, for free.

Step and retract. Move against the gradient, then push each block back onto the manifold by re-orthonormalizing its columns (Gram-Schmidt):

repeat until the gradient is tiny:
    G    = 2 * Y * Q
    grad = G - Y * SymBlockDiag(Y^T * G)       # project onto the tangent space
    Y    = orthonormalize_each_block(Y - step * grad)   # retraction; shrink step until the cost drops

SE-Sync uses a second-order (trust-region) version of this, which needs far fewer iterations, but the ingredients are the same.

3. Theorem 6.2 and the Riemannian staircase

There is an obvious objection. Problem 6.4 is non-convex, so its local solver can get stuck, and we seem to be back where we started. The answer is this result, adapted from Boumal and co-authors: Theorem 6.2 · p. 163

Suppose \(\mathbf{Y}\in\operatorname{St}(d,r)^n\) is a second-order critical point of Problem 6.4 and is (row) rank-deficient. Then \(\mathbf{Y}\) is a global minimizer of Problem 6.4, and \(\mathbf{Z}^\star=\mathbf{Y}\T\mathbf{Y}\) solves the SDP relaxation, Problem 6.3.

The terms: a first-order critical point has zero Riemannian gradient. A second-order critical point in addition has no direction of negative curvature within the tangent space; this is what a good second-order local solver converges to. Row rank-deficient means \(\rank(\mathbf{Y})\lt r\): the \(r\) rows of \(\mathbf{Y}\) are linearly dependent, so the solution fits in fewer dimensions than it was offered.

Filling the gap: why a spare dimension proves optimality (sketch)

The book cites the theorem without proof. The argument is short once Day 4 is in place.

  1. First-order critical means \(\mathbf{Y}\mathbf{S}=\mathbf{0}\) (see the box above): condition (i).
  2. For this cost, the second derivative along a tangent direction \(\mathbf{V}\) at a critical point is \(2\tr(\mathbf{V}\mathbf{S}\mathbf{V}\T)\). (We take this formula from the references.) Second-order critical means it is non-negative for every tangent \(\mathbf{V}\).
  3. Rank-deficient means there is a unit vector \(\mathbf{u}\in\R^r\) perpendicular to every column of \(\mathbf{Y}\): \(\mathbf{u}\T\mathbf{Y}=\mathbf{0}\). Take any \(\mathbf{v}\in\R^{dn}\) and set \(\mathbf{V}=\mathbf{u}\mathbf{v}\T\). It is tangent, because \(\mathbf{Y}_i\T\mathbf{V}_i=(\mathbf{Y}_i\T\mathbf{u})\mathbf{v}_i\T=\mathbf{0}\). It moves the poses into the unused dimension \(\mathbf{u}\).
  4. Insert it into step 2: \(2\tr(\mathbf{u}\mathbf{v}\T\mathbf{S}\mathbf{v}\mathbf{u}\T)=2(\mathbf{v}\T\mathbf{S}\mathbf{v})(\mathbf{u}\T\mathbf{u})=2\,\mathbf{v}\T\mathbf{S}\mathbf{v}\ge0\). This holds for every \(\mathbf{v}\), so \(\mathbf{S}\succeq0\): condition (ii).
  5. Conditions (i) and (ii) are the certificate of Day 4, so \(\mathbf{Y}\T\mathbf{Y}\) solves the SDP.

In words: an unused dimension is an escape hatch. If any feasible \(\mathbf{Z}\) had a lower cost, there would be a way down through the hatch, and a second-order critical point has no way down.

The Riemannian Staircase turns the theorem into an algorithm. §6.1.2.3 · p. 163

It must stop: \(\mathbf{Y}\) has \(dn\) columns, so its rank is at most \(dn\), and once \(r\ge dn+1\) every \(\mathbf{Y}\) is rank-deficient. In practice one or two stairs are enough. p. 163 The inner solver is the same kind of fast second-order local method SLAM already uses, so speed is kept and a global guarantee is added.

Try it: the widget solves Problem 6.4 on the graph of Days 1 and 4 for the rank \(r\) you choose. It starts at \(r=3\).

Notice that at \(r=3\) this start ends at cost 5.484 with \(\mathbf{Y}\mathbf{Y}\T/n\) having eigenvalues 1.00, 0.66, 0.34: full rank, so Theorem 6.2 is silent, and \(\lambda_{\min}(\mathbf{S})=-0.685\) confirms it is not optimal. Raise \(r\) to 4: the cost falls to 0.091, the eigenvalues become 1, 1, 0, 0 (rank-deficient), \(\lambda_{\min}(\mathbf{S})=0\), and the rounded rotations have the same cost: certified. Set \(r=2\) to see the Day 1 local minimum, 11.595. Then go back to \(r=4\) and set the noise to 80°: the SDP is solved at 5.204 but with rank 4, so it is not tight and only a bound comes out.

4. Rounding: from Y back to rotations

The staircase returns \(\mathbf{Y}^\star\in\operatorname{St}(d,r)^n\), which has \(r\) rows. The answer we want has \(d\) rows and blocks in \(\SO(d)\). If the relaxation is exact, then eq. (6.25) · p. 163

\[ \mathbf{Y}^{\star\mathsf{T}}\mathbf{Y}^\star=\mathbf{Z}^\star=\mathbf{R}^{\star\mathsf{T}}\mathbf{R}^\star, \]

so \(\mathbf{Y}^\star\) has rank \(d\) and \(\mathbf{R}^\star\) can be read off from a thin singular value decomposition (Week 1 · Day 5). Write \(\mathbf{Y}^\star=\mathbf{U}_d\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_d\mathbf{V}_d\T\), keeping the \(d\) nonzero singular values. Then \(\hat{\mathbf{R}}=\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_d\mathbf{V}_d\T\) is \(d\times dn\) and satisfies \(\hat{\mathbf{R}}\T\hat{\mathbf{R}}=\mathbf{Y}^{\star\mathsf{T}}\mathbf{Y}^\star\). Two \(d\times dn\) matrices with the same product \(\mathbf{R}\T\mathbf{R}\) differ only by an orthogonal matrix on the left, so \(\hat{\mathbf{R}}=\mathbf{G}\mathbf{R}^\star\): the optimal rotations up to one global rotation (and, if the blocks come out with determinant \(-1\), one reflection to undo). That global rotation is the gauge freedom, which no relative measurement can fix.

A small example with \(d=2\), \(r=3\), \(n=2\):

\[ \mathbf{Y}^\star=\left[\begin{array}{cc|cc}1 & 0 & 0 & -1\\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0\\ 0 & 1 & 1 & 0\end{array}\right]\quad\longrightarrow\quad\hat{\mathbf{R}}=\left[\begin{array}{cc|cc}1 & 0 & 0 & -1\\ 0 & 1 & 1 & 0\end{array}\right]. \]

Each \(3\times2\) block of \(\mathbf{Y}^\star\) has orthonormal columns, and the middle row is zero, so the rank is 2. Dropping the unused row leaves \(\hat{\mathbf{R}}_1=\mathbf{I}\) and \(\hat{\mathbf{R}}_2\), a rotation by 90°.

If the relaxation is not exact, \(\mathbf{Y}^\star\) has rank above \(d\). Then keep its \(d\) largest singular values (the best rank-\(d\) approximation), and replace each \(d\times d\) block of the result by the nearest rotation, again with an SVD. The outcome is feasible but only approximately optimal. §6.1.2.4 · pp. 163–164 All of this works on the small factor \(\mathbf{Y}^\star\); the big matrix \(\mathbf{Z}^\star\) is never formed.

5. SE-Sync, and what it hands back

SE-Sync (Algorithm 3) chains everything from Days 3 to 5. §6.1.2.5 · p. 164

Step of Algorithm 3What it doesCovered on
InputAn initial \(\mathbf{Y}\in\operatorname{St}(d,r_0)^n\) with \(r_0\ge d+1\); the data matrix \(\tilde{\mathbf{Q}}\) is built from the measurementsDay 3
Riemannian StaircaseFinds \(\mathbf{Y}^\star\) with \(\mathbf{Y}^{\star\mathsf{T}}\mathbf{Y}^\star\) solving the SDPtoday, section 3
Lower bound\(p^\star_{\text{SDP}}\) is the cost of \(\mathbf{Y}^\star\), \(\tr(\tilde{\mathbf{Q}}\mathbf{Y}^{\star\mathsf{T}}\mathbf{Y}^\star)\)Day 4
Round\(\hat{\mathbf{R}}\in\SO(d)^n\) from \(\mathbf{Y}^\star\)today, section 4
Translations\(\hat{\mathbf{t}}=\mathbf{t}^\star(\hat{\mathbf{R}})\) from (6.16)Day 3
ReturnThe poses \(\hat{\mathbf{T}}=(\hat{\mathbf{t}},\hat{\mathbf{R}})\) and the number \(p^\star_{\text{SDP}}\)

The returned number is what makes the algorithm certifiable. In the book's (6.26) and (6.27), \(F(\tilde{\mathbf{Q}}\mathbf{R}\T\mathbf{R})\) denotes the cost of a solution; read it as \(\tr(\tilde{\mathbf{Q}}\mathbf{R}\T\mathbf{R})\). Since \(p^\star_{\text{SDP}}\le p^\star_{\text{MLE}}\), for any feasible poses, from SE-Sync or from anywhere else, eq. (6.26) · p. 164

\[ \underbrace{\tr(\tilde{\mathbf{Q}}\mathbf{R}\T\mathbf{R})-p^\star_{\text{SDP}}}_{\text{computable}}\ \ge\ \underbrace{\tr(\tilde{\mathbf{Q}}\mathbf{R}\T\mathbf{R})-p^\star_{\text{MLE}}}_{\text{true suboptimality}} . \]

And if the relaxation is exact, the rounded estimate attains the bound, \(\tr(\tilde{\mathbf{Q}}\hat{\mathbf{R}}\T\hat{\mathbf{R}})=p^\star_{\text{SDP}}\) (6.27). Checking that equality after the fact is the certificate: two numbers agree, so \(\hat{\mathbf{T}}\) is a global optimum of Problem 6.1. In the widget at 10° noise and \(r=4\), both numbers are 0.091. At 80° they are 9.141 and 5.204, so the rounded estimate is at most 3.937 above optimal; the \(r=2\) run there found rotations costing 5.479, which (6.26) places within 0.275 of optimal.

The book adds that, in the experiments of the SE-Sync paper, this is as fast as or faster than traditional local solvers. p. 164

Common mistakes

  • "Problem 6.4 is non-convex, so the guarantee is lost." The guarantee moved. It no longer comes from convexity of the problem being solved, but from Theorem 6.2 plus a rank check on the answer.
  • "Full rank means the solution is wrong." It means the theorem does not apply at this \(r\). The staircase's response is to try \(r+1\).
  • "Rounding always gives the global optimum." Only when the relaxation is exact. Otherwise it gives a feasible estimate with a computable bound on its suboptimality.

Check yourself

Q1. A problem has n = 1000 poses in 3-D and is solved with r = 5. How many unknowns does Y have, compared with the free entries of Z?

Y is r × dn = 5 × 3000, so 15 000 numbers. A symmetric 3000 × 3000 matrix has 3000 · 3001 / 2 = 4 501 500 free entries.

Q2. What is St(1, 3)?

St(k, p) is the set of p × k matrices with orthonormal columns. One column of unit length in three dimensions is a point on the unit sphere.

Q3. For d = 3, the staircase runs at r = 4 and the solver returns a second-order critical point Y* of rank 4. What now?

Rank 4 with r = 4 is full row rank, so the theorem says nothing either way. The staircase climbs one step. Tightness can only be judged after the SDP is solved.

Q4. SE-Sync returns poses with cost 43.0 and p*_SDP = 41.2. What do you know?

By (6.26) the suboptimality is at most 43.0 − 41.2 = 1.8. Equality (6.27) does not hold, so there is no certificate of exact optimality.

Recap

  1. The SDP has about \((dn)^2/2\) unknowns but a solution of rank close to \(d\). Burer-Monteiro searches over a factor \(\mathbf{Y}\in\R^{r\times dn}\) with \(\mathbf{Z}=\mathbf{Y}\T\mathbf{Y}\).
  2. The constraints say each block \(\mathbf{Y}_i\) is a point of the Stiefel manifold \(\operatorname{St}(d,r)\), so the problem is unconstrained optimization on a manifold, with gradient \(2\mathbf{Y}\mathbf{S}\).
  3. Theorem 6.2: a rank-deficient second-order critical point is a global minimizer and solves the SDP. The Riemannian staircase raises \(r\) until that happens.
  4. Rounding takes the best rank-\(d\) part of \(\mathbf{Y}^\star\) and projects its blocks onto \(\SO(d)\).
  5. SE-Sync returns the estimate and \(p^\star_{\text{SDP}}\). Their difference bounds the suboptimality, and equality certifies a global optimum.

Sources

  1. SLAM Handbook, §6.1.2.3 "Efficiently Solving the Relaxation via the Riemannian Staircase", §6.1.2.4 "Rounding the Solution", §6.1.2.5 "SE-Sync: The Complete Algorithm", pp. 161–164, equations (6.22)–(6.27), Theorem 6.2, Algorithm 3.
  2. Rosen, Carlone, Bandeira, Leonard, SE-Sync: A certifiably correct algorithm for synchronization over the special Euclidean group, 2019: the Riemannian gradient and Hessian of Problem 6.4 used in the two "Filling the gap" boxes.
  3. Boumal, Voroninski, Bandeira, The non-convex Burer-Monteiro approach works on smooth semidefinite programs, 2016: the argument behind Theorem 6.2.
  4. Burer and Monteiro, A nonlinear programming algorithm for solving semidefinite programs via low-rank factorization, 2003.
  5. Absil, Mahony, Sepulchre, Optimization Algorithms on Matrix Manifolds, 2008: tangent spaces, projections, and retractions on the Stiefel manifold.

Week 9 · Review

Week 9 review: from local minima to certified optima

After today you can lift a QCQP and bound it with Shor's relaxation, reduce pose-graph optimization to its rotation-only form, test a solution with the certificate matrix, and describe how SE-Sync solves the relaxation.

About 60 min · No new pages

The week in one paragraph

SLAM costs are non-convex, so a local solver can stop at a local minimum without knowing it. For pose-graph optimization there is a way to know. With Langevin rotation noise and Gaussian translation noise the maximum-likelihood cost is quadratic; the translations can be eliminated, leaving \(\min\tr(\tilde{\mathbf{Q}}\mathbf{R}\T\mathbf{R})\) over rotations. Lifting \(\mathbf{R}\T\mathbf{R}\) to a positive semidefinite matrix \(\mathbf{Z}\) and dropping its rank constraint gives a convex semidefinite program whose optimum is a lower bound, and for small noise is exact. SE-Sync solves that program through a low-rank factor \(\mathbf{Y}\) on Stiefel manifolds, raising the rank until the solution is rank-deficient, then rounds to rotations and compares costs. Equal costs are a proof of global optimality.

1. Formula sheet

What it isFormulaWhere
Twisted local minima of a clean ring of \(n\) headings\(f_k=4n\bigl(1-\cos\tfrac{2\pi k}{n}\bigr)\), a local minimum for \(|k|\lt n/4\)Day 1 (our example)
The lift\(\mathbf{x}\T\mathbf{M}\mathbf{x}=\tr(\mathbf{M}\mathbf{X})\), \(\mathbf{X}=\mathbf{x}\mathbf{x}\T\); \(\mathbf{X}=\mathbf{x}\mathbf{x}\T\iff\mathbf{X}\succeq0,\ \rank(\mathbf{X})=1\)(6.1), (6.3), p. 152 · Day 2
Shor's relaxation\(d^\star=\min\tr(\mathbf{C}\mathbf{X})\) s.t. \(\tr(\mathbf{A}_i\mathbf{X})=b_i\), \(\mathbf{X}\succeq0\)(SDP), p. 153 · Day 2
The bound\(d^\star\le p^\star\) and \(f(\hat{\mathbf{x}})-p^\star\le f(\hat{\mathbf{x}})-d^\star\)(6.5), (6.6), p. 153 · Day 2

2. Mixed quiz

Check yourself

Q1. A clean ring of 8 headings (κ = 1, no noise) is solved from a random start and the solver stops at the once-twisted configuration. What cost does it report?

Each of the 8 edges has residual 45°, so the cost is 4 × 8 × (1 − cos 45°) = 32 × 0.293 = 9.37. Since 1 is less than 8/4, it is a local minimum.

Q2. Which statement holds for every relaxation of a minimization problem, tight or not?

A relaxation minimizes the same objective over a larger set, so its optimum cannot be higher. The other three properties hold only in special cases.

Q3. For M = [[1, 2], [2, 0]] and x = (1, 1), what is tr(M xxᵀ)?

tr(M xxᵀ) = xᵀMx = 1·1 + 2·(2·1·1) + 0·1 = 5. Directly: xxᵀ is the all-ones matrix, and the entries of M sum to 5.

Q4. Shor's relaxation of a QCQP returns X* with eigenvalues 2, 1, 0 and value d* = 7. What follows?

Two nonzero eigenvalues mean rank 2, so X* is not a lifted point. The value 7 is still a valid lower bound on p*.

Q5. A pose graph consists of two separate pieces with no measurement between them. How many zero eigenvalues does its Laplacian have?

The number of zero eigenvalues equals the number of connected components (Box 6.1). The book assumes a connected graph, which has exactly one.

Q6. After the translations are eliminated from a 3-D pose graph with n poses, what are the unknowns of Problem 6.2?

The translations are functions of the rotations through (6.16), so only R = (R_1 … R_n) remains. The 3n × 3n matrix Z appears only after the lift.

Q7. At the output R̂ of a local solver, the certificate matrix has eigenvalues 0, 0, 0.4, 0.4, 1.3, 1.3 (planar, three poses). What do you conclude?

No eigenvalue is negative, so S ⪰ 0 and R̂ is certified. The d = 2 zeros are always there, because S R̂ᵀ = 0.

Q8. For d = 3 the staircase is at r = 5 and returns a second-order critical point Y* with singular values 9.1, 9.1, 9.1, 0, 0. What is the situation?

Rank 3 is below r = 5, so Theorem 6.2 applies. Rank exactly d is the signature of an exact relaxation, equation (6.25).

3. Pen-and-paper problems

  1. Let \(\mathbf{x}=(1,-2)\) and \(\mathbf{C}=\begin{bmatrix}1 & 2\\ 2 & -1\end{bmatrix}\). (a) Compute \(\mathbf{x}\T\mathbf{C}\mathbf{x}\). (b) Form \(\mathbf{X}=\mathbf{x}\mathbf{x}\T\) and compute \(\tr(\mathbf{C}\mathbf{X})\). (c) Find the eigenvalues of \(\mathbf{X}\) and recover \(\mathbf{x}\) from them.

    Solution

    (a) \(1\cdot1+2\cdot2\cdot(1)(-2)+(-1)\cdot4=1-8-4=-11\).

    (b) \(\mathbf{X}=\begin{bmatrix}1 & -2\\ -2 & 4\end{bmatrix}\). \(\tr(\mathbf{C}\mathbf{X})=\sum_{i,j}C_{ij}X_{ij}=1\cdot1+2\cdot(-2)+2\cdot(-2)+(-1)\cdot4=-11\). The two agree, as (6.1) says.

    (c) The trace is 5 and the determinant is \(4-4=0\), so the eigenvalues are 5 and 0: rank 1. The eigenvector for 5 is \(\mathbf{u}=(1,-2)/\sqrt5\), and \(\sqrt5\,\mathbf{u}=(1,-2)\). The other sign, \((-1,2)\), gives the same \(\mathbf{X}\).

  2. Minimize \(\mathbf{x}\T\mathbf{C}\mathbf{x}\) over unit vectors \(\mathbf{x}\in\R^2\) with \(\mathbf{C}=\begin{bmatrix}2 & 1\\ 1 & 2\end{bmatrix}\). (a) Solve Shor's relaxation using the disk coordinates \(u=X_{11}-X_{22}\), \(v=2X_{12}\) of Day 2. (b) Is it exact? Give \(\mathbf{x}^\star\). (c) Write the dual and verify the certificate.

    Solution

    (a) \(\tr(\mathbf{C}\mathbf{X})=\tfrac12(C_{11}+C_{22})+\tfrac12(C_{11}-C_{22})u+C_{12}v=2+v\) on the disk \(u^2+v^2\le1\). The minimum is at \((u,v)=(0,-1)\) with \(d^\star=1\).

    (b) That point is on the boundary, so the rank is 1. \(X_{11}=X_{22}=\tfrac12\), \(X_{12}=-\tfrac12\), which is \(\mathbf{x}^\star\mathbf{x}^{\star\mathsf{T}}\) for \(\mathbf{x}^\star=(1,-1)/\sqrt2\). Check: \(\mathbf{x}^{\star\mathsf{T}}\mathbf{C}\mathbf{x}^\star=\tfrac12(2-2+2)=1\). Exact, \(p^\star=d^\star=1\).

    (c) Dual: maximize \(\lambda\) subject to \(\mathbf{C}-\lambda\mathbf{I}\succeq0\). The eigenvalues of \(\mathbf{C}\) are 1 and 3, so \(\lambda=1\) and \(\mathbf{S}=\mathbf{C}-\mathbf{I}=\begin{bmatrix}1 & 1\\ 1 & 1\end{bmatrix}\), with eigenvalues 0 and 2: positive semidefinite. And \(\mathbf{S}\mathbf{x}^\star=\mathbf{0}\). Both certificate conditions hold, and \(\mathbf{b}\T\boldsymbol{\lambda}=1\) equals the cost.

  3. One planar edge \(i\to j\) has \(\kappa=8\), \(\tau=4\), and measurement \(\tilde\theta_{ij}=60^\circ\), \(\tilde{\mathbf{t}}_{ij}=(1,0.5)\). The current estimate is \(\theta_i=0\), \(\mathbf{t}_i=(0,0)\), \(\theta_j=90^\circ\), \(\mathbf{t}_j=(1,1)\). (a) What does this edge contribute to the cost (6.9)? (b) Which \(\kappa\) corresponds to an angular standard deviation of 5°?

    Solution

    (a) Rotation: the residual is \(r=90^\circ-0^\circ-60^\circ=30^\circ\), so the term is \(4\kappa(1-\cos30^\circ)=32\times0.134=4.29\). Translation: \(\mathbf{R}_i=\mathbf{I}\), so the residual is \((1,1)-(0,0)-(1,0.5)=(0,0.5)\), with squared norm 0.25, and the term is \(4\times0.25=1\). Total: 5.29.

    (b) For small noise the angle is nearly Gaussian with variance \(1/(2\kappa)\). \(5^\circ=0.0873\) rad, so \(\kappa=1/(2\times0.0873^2)=1/0.01523\approx66\).

  4. A clean ring of \(n=8\) planar headings (\(\kappa=1\), perfect measurements) and the once-twisted critical point \(\hat{\mathbf{R}}\) with residual 45° on every edge. (a) Compute its cost and its multipliers \(\lambda_i\), and check that \(\tr(\boldsymbol{\Lambda})\) equals the cost. (b) Without computing any eigenvalue, show that \(\mathbf{S}=\tilde{\mathbf{Q}}-\boldsymbol{\Lambda}\) is not positive semidefinite. (c) What general fact does (b) prove?

    Solution

    (a) Cost: \(4\times8\times(1-\cos45^\circ)=32\times0.2929=9.37\). Each pose has two edges, so \(\lambda_i=2(1-\cos45^\circ)=0.586\) and \(\boldsymbol{\Lambda}_i=0.586\,\mathbf{I}_2\). Then \(\tr(\boldsymbol{\Lambda})=8\times2\times0.586=9.37\), the cost.

    (b) Let \(\bar{\mathbf{R}}\) hold the true rotations. They fit the perfect measurements, so \(\tr(\tilde{\mathbf{Q}}\bar{\mathbf{R}}\T\bar{\mathbf{R}})=0\). The diagonal blocks of \(\bar{\mathbf{R}}\T\bar{\mathbf{R}}\) are identities, so \(\tr(\boldsymbol{\Lambda}\bar{\mathbf{R}}\T\bar{\mathbf{R}})=\tr(\boldsymbol{\Lambda})=9.37\). Therefore

    \[ \tr\bigl(\bar{\mathbf{R}}\mathbf{S}\bar{\mathbf{R}}\T\bigr)=\tr(\tilde{\mathbf{Q}}\bar{\mathbf{R}}\T\bar{\mathbf{R}})-\tr(\boldsymbol{\Lambda}\bar{\mathbf{R}}\T\bar{\mathbf{R}})=0-9.37\lt0 . \]

    The left side is the sum of \(\mathbf{v}\T\mathbf{S}\mathbf{v}\) over the two rows \(\mathbf{v}\) of \(\bar{\mathbf{R}}\). A negative sum needs a negative term, so some \(\mathbf{v}\) has \(\mathbf{v}\T\mathbf{S}\mathbf{v}\lt0\).

    (c) The same computation with any better feasible \(\mathbf{R}\) gives \(\tr(\mathbf{R}\mathbf{S}\mathbf{R}\T)=f(\mathbf{R})-f(\hat{\mathbf{R}})\lt0\). So a critical point that is not globally optimal can never pass the test \(\mathbf{S}\succeq0\): the certificate has no false positives.

You are ready for next week if you can

  • Explain why a converged local solver may be wrong, and what a lower bound adds.
  • Lift a small QCQP, write its Shor relaxation, and interpret a rank-1 or higher-rank solution.
  • Write the incidence matrix and Laplacian of a small graph, and say what \(\mathbf{x}\T\mathbf{L}\mathbf{x}\) measures. Next week's accuracy bounds are built on the Laplacian.
  • State the chain \(p^\star_{\text{MLE}}\ge p^\star_{\mathrm{O}}\ge p^\star_{\text{SDP}}\) and what it means when the ends are equal.
  • Build \(\mathbf{S}=\tilde{\mathbf{Q}}-\boldsymbol{\Lambda}\) for a planar example and read the verdict from its smallest eigenvalue.
  • Describe the Riemannian staircase and the output of SE-Sync in three sentences.
