5. Part I quiz

Check yourself: Weeks 1–10

Q1. A prior on x is Gaussian with mean 0 and variance 4. One measurement z = 5 of x has variance 1. What is the posterior mean?

In information form: precision 1/4 + 1 = 1.25, and mean (0·1/4 + 5·1)/1.25 = 4. The estimate sits close to the more precise source.

Q2. In Levenberg-Marquardt, what happens to the step as the damping parameter grows large?

With (JᵀJ + λI)δ = −Jᵀr and large λ, δ ≈ −Jᵀr/λ: a small steepest-descent step. Small λ gives Gauss-Newton.

Q3. In a chain x₁ – x₂ – x₃, you eliminate (marginalize out) x₂ first. What appears in the remaining problem?

The Schur complement couples all neighbours of the eliminated variable. A good elimination order keeps such fill-in small.

Q4. Why does the book update a pose as T = T⁰ Exp(ξ) and not as T⁰ + Δ?

SE(3) is a group, not a vector space. Optimizing over the 6-vector ξ keeps the constraints satisfied without enforcing them.

Q5. Why is Gaussian-process regression for trajectories cheap when the prior comes from a linear stochastic differential equation such as white noise on acceleration?

Each state depends only on its neighbours in time, which gives a sparse precision matrix and a factor graph with binary factors.

Q6. RANSAC fits a model from 3 points per sample. Half the data are inliers. Roughly how many samples give a 99% chance of drawing at least one all-inlier sample?

An all-inlier sample has probability 0.5³ = 0.125. Solve (1 − 0.125)ᴺ ≤ 0.01: N ≥ ln 0.01 / ln 0.875 ≈ 34.5, so 35.

Q7. Compared with unrolling K solver iterations, what is the main advantage of implicit differentiation through an optimizer?

Unrolling stores every iterate for the backward pass. The implicit function theorem uses the optimality condition at the solution only, and assumes the solver has converged.

Q8. An occupancy cell starts at probability 0.5. Two independent range readings each say "occupied" with inverse sensor model 0.7. What is the cell's probability after the log-odds updates?

Odds multiply: (0.7/0.3)² = 5.44, and 5.44/6.44 = 0.845. In log-odds, 2 × ln(7/3) = 1.69.

Q9. Shor's relaxation of a QCQP returns an optimal matrix X* of rank 1. What follows?

A rank-1 solution is feasible for the original problem and attains the lower bound d*, so p* = d*.

Q10. A SLAM estimate is certified globally optimal, yet the far end of the trajectory is 2 m from the truth. Which explanation fits Part I?

A certificate is about the cost, not about the truth. Accuracy is limited by the data, and for a chain the variance grows with distance from the anchor.

You are ready for Part II if you can

  • Write a small SLAM problem as a factor graph and as a nonlinear least-squares cost, and say what one Gauss-Newton step solves.
  • Explain why the information matrix is sparse and what elimination order and fill-in do to the cost of solving.
  • Perturb a pose on SE(3) with \(\Exp\) and say why this replaces constraints.
  • Choose between RANSAC, a robust loss, and graduated non-convexity for a given outlier situation.
  • State what an optimality certificate proves, and what it does not.
  • Estimate the uncertainty of a pose from \(\mathbf{J}\T\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{-1}\mathbf{J}\), and predict which loop closure reduces it most.

Week 11 · Day 1

Part II begins: sensors, front-end modules, and how SLAM is scored

After today you can name the modules every SLAM front-end has, say which kind of factor each sensor adds to the graph, and compute the two standard trajectory error metrics.

About 60 min · Read Prelude II, pp. 185–192 (8 pages) · Needs Week 1 Day 1 and Week 2 Day 1

Read first: Prelude to Part II, pp. 185–192

While you read, look for:

  • The two modules that "most SLAM front-ends rely on", and the third, optional kind of measurement (p. 185, then §II.1.1–II.1.3 on pp. 186–187).
  • The two sub-problems inside loop closure (p. 186) and the two properties a place-recognition method needs (p. 187).
  • Figure II.1 on p. 188: find one unary factor and one factor that joins nodes far apart in time.
  • The two types of calibration (p. 190) and the three things that get evaluated (pp. 191–192).

Today's big idea

Part I built the back-end: a factor graph and the machinery to optimize it. Part II is about the front-end: how each sensor turns its raw data into factors. Whatever the sensor, the factors come in three kinds: odometry between consecutive states, loop closures between states far apart, and unary factors on single states.

1. Where Part II sits

For ten weeks the measurements were given. A relative pose or a landmark observation simply appeared, with a covariance, and the question was what to do with it. Part II asks where those measurements come from. The front-end handles the sensor-specific work: pre-processing, time synchronization, noise filtering, and measurement modeling. Prelude II · p. 185

The chapters are ordered by sensor, and each follows the same pattern: odometry, then place recognition, then a full system. The book recommends starting with visual SLAM because it defines the vocabulary the other chapters reuse. §II.4 · p. 192

ChapterSensorIn this course
7Cameras (visual SLAM)Weeks 11–12
8LiDARWeek 13
9RadarWeek 14
10Event camerasWeek 15
11Inertial measurement units (IMUs)Weeks 16–17
12Leg odometry (robot kinematics)Week 18

2. Three kinds of factor

Recall from Week 2 · Day 1 that a factor graph has variable nodes (the unknown states) and factors (the measurements that constrain them). A factor touching two variables is binary; a factor touching one is unary.

Odometry estimates the relative transformation between two consecutive nodes, usually a relative pose with six degrees of freedom (6-DOF: three for rotation, three for translation). There are three ways to get it. §II.1.1 · p. 186

  • By matching two consecutive sensor frames: pixel to pixel, point to point, or feature to feature. Most visual and LiDAR systems do this.
  • By integrating velocity. Radar measures radial velocity, from which the sensor's own velocity follows; a legged robot gets its motion from joint encoders, contact sensors, and its kinematics.
  • By preintegration of inertial measurements: many IMU samples between two nodes are summarized as a single factor (Week 16).

The module takes the name of its main sensor: visual odometry, LiDAR odometry, visual-inertial odometry, leg odometry.

Loop closure solves two problems in a row. §II.1.2 · pp. 186–187

  1. Detection, also called place recognition. The current measurement is a query; earlier places are stored in a database as raw data or as compact descriptors (short vectors that summarize a place). The task is retrieval: find the stored place most similar to the query.
  2. Relative pose estimation. A candidate match only says "these two places look the same". The back-end needs a number, so a fine registration between the two measurements produces a relative transformation: a binary factor between the query node and the matched node.

Detection needs two properties. Discernibility: it must tell apart places that look alike but are different. Confusing them is called perceptual aliasing, and it creates a false loop closure. Scalability: the database grows for as long as the robot runs, and the search must stay fast. §II.1.2 · p. 187

Unary factors and priors constrain one node. GPS on the ground, a depth sensor under water, and a radar's instantaneous velocity are examples. A prior can pin the first node to the origin or state that the robot stood still at certain nodes. §II.1.3 · p. 187

In plain words

Odometry says "since a moment ago I moved this much". A loop closure says "I have been here before, and I am standing this far from where I stood then". A unary factor says "something outside tells me where I am right now". The back-end does not care which sensor said it.

3. Choosing sensors, and combining them

The four exteroceptive sensors of Part II (sensors that observe the outside world) trade off as follows. §II.2.1 · pp. 188–189

SensorStrengthsLimits
RGB cameraCheap, small; captures appearance and semantic contentNeeds light; suffers from glare, reflections, motion blur, shadows, fog, smoke; no direct depth
LiDARMeasures distance directly; accurate 2D/3D geometry; works in the darkCost, size, power, memory; large point clouds; degraded by heavy rain, fog, snow
RadarRobust in extreme conditions; Doppler gives velocityNoisy and very sparse; lower accuracy than LiDAR; heavy signal processing
Event cameraMicrosecond time resolution, no motion blur, high dynamic range, low powerNoise; no fine texture and no absolute intensity

Because the weaknesses differ, systems combine sensors. The IMU is the most common partner: it is everywhere and has low size, weight, and power, and it bridges the gaps between camera, LiDAR, or radar frames. Camera plus LiDAR pairs semantics with direct range. Radar's velocity measurements detect moving objects at once. The robot's own kinematics is one more source. In factor-graph terms fusion is easy to state: each sensor adds its own factors to the same graph, and the optimizer weighs them by their covariances. §II.2.2 · pp. 189–190

4. Calibration and time synchronization

Intrinsic calibration finds the parameters of one sensor's own model, such as a camera's focal length and distortion coefficients. Extrinsic calibration finds the rigid transformation between two sensors, so that their data can be expressed in one frame. Both are usually done before deployment with a calibration target. Targetless methods use the surroundings instead, and the calibration parameters can also be added as extra variables to the SLAM factor graph and refined while the robot runs. §II.2.3 · pp. 190–191

Sensors also sample at different rates and instants, and the robot moves in between. When hardware synchronization is not available, measurements are interpolated to a common time, often with the help of a fast sensor like an IMU. §II.2.3 · p. 191

Filling the gap: how much does a timestamp error cost?

The book says synchronization "must be carefully managed" without numbers. Suppose a measurement is stamped \(\delta t\) too late. The back-end attaches it to the pose the robot had \(\delta t\) later. If the robot moves at speed \(v\) and turns at rate \(\omega\), the pose it is attached to is wrong by about

\[ \delta p \approx v\,\delta t, \qquad \delta\theta \approx \omega\,\delta t . \]

With \(v = 10\) m/s and \(\delta t = 20\) ms, \(\delta p = 0.2\) m. With \(\omega = 90^\circ\)/s, \(\delta\theta = 1.8^\circ\), and a point 20 m away then appears displaced sideways by \(20\tan 1.8^\circ \approx 0.63\) m. Rotation is the dangerous part, for the same reason heading errors dominated drift in Week 1 · Day 1: an angle error is multiplied by distance.

5. How SLAM is scored

Evaluation is done per module: odometry, place recognition, mapping. The most common score is trajectory accuracy against a ground-truth trajectory from a much better instrument, which is expensive to obtain and indoors may reduce to a few surveyed points. Place recognition is scored like a classifier, with precision and recall. Maps are the hardest to score: a reference map needs something like a terrestrial laser scanner, and memory use and fine structure count as well as global accuracy. §II.3 · pp. 191–192

Filling the gap: ATE and RPE

The book points to the literature for trajectory metrics. Two are used almost everywhere. Let \(\mathbf{P}_i\) be the estimated poses and \(\mathbf{Q}_i\) the ground-truth poses, with positions \(\mathbf{p}_i\) and \(\mathbf{q}_i\), for \(i = 1,\dots,n\).

Absolute trajectory error (ATE). The two trajectories live in different frames (the estimate starts at its own origin), so first find the rigid transformation \((\mathbf{R},\mathbf{t})\) that best lays the estimate over the ground truth, then take the root-mean-square position difference:

\[ \text{ATE} = \sqrt{\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\norm{\mathbf{q}_i - (\mathbf{R}\,\mathbf{p}_i + \mathbf{t})}^2}, \qquad (\mathbf{R},\mathbf{t}) = \argmin_{\mathbf{R},\,\mathbf{t}} \sum_{i=1}^{n}\norm{\mathbf{q}_i - (\mathbf{R}\,\mathbf{p}_i + \mathbf{t})}^2 . \]

The alignment has a closed-form solution (you will derive it in Week 13). For a monocular camera, which cannot observe scale, a scale factor is estimated too.

Relative pose error (RPE). Compare motions instead of positions. Over an interval of \(\Delta\) poses, the estimated motion is \(\mathbf{P}_i^{-1}\mathbf{P}_{i+\Delta}\) and the true motion is \(\mathbf{Q}_i^{-1}\mathbf{Q}_{i+\Delta}\). Their mismatch is the pose

\[ \mathbf{E}_i = \left(\mathbf{Q}_i^{-1}\mathbf{Q}_{i+\Delta}\right)^{-1}\left(\mathbf{P}_i^{-1}\mathbf{P}_{i+\Delta}\right), \qquad \text{RPE}_{\text{trans}} = \sqrt{\frac{1}{m}\sum_{i=1}^{m}\norm{\operatorname{trans}(\mathbf{E}_i)}^2}, \]

where \(\operatorname{trans}(\cdot)\) takes the translation part and \(m = n - \Delta\). The rotation part of \(\mathbf{E}_i\) gives a rotational RPE in the same way. No alignment is needed, because a relative motion does not depend on the frame.

ATE measures global consistency, which is what loop closures buy. RPE measures drift per unit of travel, which is what an odometry module should be judged on.

Try it: the estimate has small random noise and one sudden 10° heading error at step 10. Set the one-off error to 0° and back. Then raise the interval Δ.

Notice that at the default settings RPE over one step is about 0.03 m, because 59 of the 60 steps are almost perfect, while ATE is about 0.6 m: one bad step bends everything after it. Removing the one-off error drops ATE to about 0.24 m. With Δ = 10 the same trajectory has an RPE of about 0.5 m, so an RPE value means nothing without its interval.

For place recognition, count the proposed matches that are right (true positives, TP), proposed but wrong (false positives, FP), and real revisits that were missed (false negatives, FN). Then

\[ \text{precision} = \frac{TP}{TP+FP}, \qquad \text{recall} = \frac{TP}{TP+FN}, \qquad F_1 = \frac{2\cdot\text{precision}\cdot\text{recall}}{\text{precision}+\text{recall}} . \]

Example: 50 proposals, 45 correct, 90 real revisits. Precision is \(45/50 = 0.9\), recall is \(45/90 = 0.5\), and \(F_1 = 0.9/1.4 \approx 0.64\). A detector has a threshold; sweeping it traces the precision-recall curve, and the area under that curve (AUC) summarizes it in one number. §II.3 · p. 191

Common mistakes

  • "Place recognition gives the loop-closure factor." It gives a candidate pair. The factor comes from the second step, registering the two measurements to get a relative pose.
  • "A low RPE means the map is globally right." RPE over short intervals is blind to slow drift. A trajectory can have excellent RPE and be many meters off at the end.
  • "Fusion means averaging sensor outputs." In a factor graph each sensor contributes its own factors with its own noise model, and one optimization uses all of them.

Check yourself

Q1. Which of these enters the factor graph as a unary factor?

A GPS fix constrains the position of a single node. The other three relate two nodes, so they are binary factors.

Q2. A place-recognition module proposes 40 loop closures. 30 are correct. The robot actually revisited 60 places. What are precision and recall?

Precision = 30/40 = 0.75 (how many proposals are right). Recall = 30/60 = 0.50 (how many real revisits were found).

Q3. A visual odometry system without loop closure is very accurate from frame to frame. It runs along a 2 km path. What do you expect?

Small per-step errors keep RPE small, but they accumulate without bound, and ATE measures the accumulated error. Only loop closures or absolute measurements bound it.

Q4. A camera's timestamps are 10 ms late while the robot turns at 100°/s. Roughly how far sideways does a point 10 m away appear displaced?

The heading error is 100°/s × 0.01 s = 1°, and 10 m × tan 1° ≈ 0.17 m.

Recap

  1. Part II is the front-end, one chapter per sensor: cameras, LiDAR, radar, event cameras, IMUs, legs.
  2. Odometry gives binary factors between consecutive nodes, by matching, velocity integration, or preintegration. It drifts.
  3. Loop closure = place recognition (retrieve a candidate) + relative pose estimation (produce the factor). It needs discernibility and scalability.
  4. Unary factors and priors constrain single nodes. Calibration (intrinsic, extrinsic) and time synchronization decide whether fused factors are consistent.
  5. ATE scores global consistency after alignment; RPE scores drift over a stated interval; place recognition is scored by precision and recall.

Sources

  1. SLAM Handbook, Prelude to Part II, §II.1–II.4, pp. 185–192.
  2. ATE and RPE definitions follow Sturm, Engelhard, Endres, Burgard, Cremers, A Benchmark for the Evaluation of RGB-D SLAM Systems, 2012, and Zhang and Scaramuzza, A Tutorial on Quantitative Trajectory Evaluation for Visual(-Inertial) Odometry, 2018.
  3. Precision, recall, and F1 are the standard definitions from information retrieval.

Week 11 · Day 2

From photogrammetry to visual SLAM: the terms and the pipeline

After today you can tell photogrammetry, bundle adjustment, structure from motion, visual odometry, and visual SLAM apart, sketch the three parts of a visual SLAM system, and compute depth and its uncertainty from two views.

About 60 min · Read §7.1–7.2, pp. 193–197 (5 pages) · Needs Week 11 Day 1

Read first: §7.1–7.2, pp. 193–197

While you read, look for:

  • When bundle adjustment was formulated, and when it first ran on computers (p. 194).
  • The one-sentence difference between structure from motion and visual SLAM (p. 194), and between visual odometry and visual SLAM (p. 195).
  • The sentence on p. 196 that says why vision is harder than LiDAR.
  • The two ways to compute visual odometry, and which has the larger basin of convergence (p. 196).

Today's big idea

A camera records directions to things, not distances. Depth appears only when the same point is seen from two places, and its accuracy depends on how far apart those places are. Everything in visual SLAM, from the 19th-century surveyors to a headset tracking in real time, is a way of organizing that triangulation over many points and many views.

1. An old problem

Reconstructing the world from pictures is almost as old as photography. The mathematics the back-end runs today was written down before computers existed. §7.1.1 · pp. 193–194

WhenWhoWhat
1822–1827Nicéphore NiépcePhotography; the oldest surviving photograph dates from 1827
around 1851Aimé LaussedatTopographic maps from terrestrial photographs: the start of photogrammetry
1867Albrecht MeydenbauerPhotogrammetry for architectural surveys
from 1890Sebastian FinsterwalderAerial images to reconstruct Alpine glaciers; projective geometry
early 1900sOtto von GruberThe mathematical framework of bundle adjustment
1950sHellmut Schmid, Duane BrownMatrix methods for bundle adjustment, run on the largest computers of the time
early 1990sTomasi and KanadeMatrix factorization for static scenes under orthographic projection
2000sComputer vision communityMulti-view structure from motion: features (SIFT, SURF), matching, RANSAC, minimal solvers, then bundle adjustment
around 2000Several groupsFirst real-time structure from motion and visual SLAM

The step from offline reconstruction to SLAM needed causal methods: methods that estimate using only the images seen so far, not the whole collection. §7.1.1 · p. 194

2. Five overlapping terms

The book notes that these words are often used interchangeably. They describe similar computations with different emphasis. §7.1.2 · pp. 194–195

TermWhat it isWhat sets it apart
PhotogrammetryThe science of taking measurements and 3D reconstructions from overlapping photographsThe oldest and broadest term; camera positions are often assumed known
Bundle adjustment (BA)An optimization: adjust camera poses (optionally intrinsics) and 3D points to minimize reprojection errorIt is a solver step, not a system. It needs a good initial guess and outlier rejection
Structure from motion (SfM)Estimate the 3D structure and the camera motion together from a collection of imagesUsually offline and non-causal; images may be unordered; ends with BA
Visual odometry (VO)Estimate camera motion from consecutive video framesLocal: a sliding window of recent frames, no global map, so it drifts
Visual SLAMLocalize and map in real time in an unknown environmentAdds place recognition, relocalization, and loop closure to VO

The reprojection error in the BA row is the distance in the image between where a point was observed and where the current 3D model says it should appear. You will write it as a formula on Day 5. BA minimizes it with the Gauss-Newton or Levenberg-Marquardt methods of Week 2 · Day 4 and Week 2 · Day 5.

3. Why vision is harder than LiDAR: depth is not measured

A LiDAR returns the distance to each point. A camera returns the projection of the scene's light onto its sensor, and the 3D geometry has to be inferred. That is why the book calls the visual problem more challenging. §7.2 · p. 196

Filling the gap: depth from two views, and how uncertain it is

Take the simplest case, seen from above. Two identical cameras look along the \(z\) axis. Camera 2 sits a distance \(b\) (the baseline) to the right of camera 1. A point at sideways position \(x\) and depth \(z\) (in camera 1's frame) appears at image columns

\[ u_1 = f\,\frac{x}{z}, \qquad u_2 = f\,\frac{x-b}{z}, \]

where \(f\) is the focal length in pixels and columns are counted from the image center (tomorrow's lesson derives this). The unknown \(x\) cancels in the difference, called the disparity:

\[ d = u_1 - u_2 = \frac{f\,b}{z} \quad\Longrightarrow\quad z = \frac{f\,b}{d}. \]

Far points have small disparity. Now let the disparity be wrong by a small amount \(\delta d\). Differentiate:

\[ \frac{\partial z}{\partial d} = -\frac{f\,b}{d^2} = -\frac{z^2}{f\,b} \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \sigma_z \approx \frac{z^2}{f\,b}\,\sigma_d . \]

If each column is measured with independent noise of standard deviation \(\sigma\), then \(\sigma_d = \sqrt{2}\,\sigma\). Numbers: \(f = 500\) px, \(b = 0.5\) m, \(z = 20\) m gives \(d = 12.5\) px. With \(\sigma = 1\) px, \(\sigma_z \approx \frac{400}{250}\times 1.41 = 2.26\) m, an 11% error from one pixel of noise.

Two consequences shape every visual SLAM system. Depth error grows with the square of depth. And it shrinks in proportion to the baseline, so a camera must move sideways enough before a new point can be placed.

Try it: double the baseline, then double the depth.

Notice that the cloud of triangulated points is a thin needle along the viewing direction: sideways position is known well, depth poorly. At the defaults the predicted depth σ is 2.26 m. A baseline of 1 m halves it; a depth of 10 m divides it by four. At the far-left baseline with depth 30 m the disparity is under 2 px, the cloud smears over tens of meters, and some samples give no usable depth at all (the count of valid samples drops below 300).

A stereo rig has a fixed, known baseline. A single moving camera has to use its own motion as the baseline, and that motion is itself unknown. This is the root of two issues you will meet again: a monocular system needs a special initialization step (Day 5), and it cannot recover the absolute scale of the scene.

4. The three parts of a visual SLAM system

Like every SLAM system since Week 1 · Day 1, a visual one is split into stages. The book names three sub-functions that complement each other. §7.2 · p. 196

  • The visual odometry front-end estimates the relative motion between consecutive frames and so provides the initial estimate of the camera pose. §7.2.1 · p. 196
  • The mapping back-end refines trajectory and map with global optimization, BA or pose-graph optimization, and folds in the constraints found by place recognition. The result is long-term consistency. §7.2.2 · pp. 196–197
  • Visual place recognition and relocalization matches the current image against earlier ones, with classical descriptors or trained networks. It detects revisits, which corrects drift, and it finds the camera again when tracking is lost. §7.2.3 · p. 197

These run as parallel threads. Heavy jobs like global optimization are scheduled so that tracking stays real-time. §7.2.4 · p. 197

5. Two ways to do visual odometry

AspectFeature-based (indirect)Direct
StepsDetect feature points, match them across images, then estimate motionOne step: optimize over the images themselves
MinimizesReprojection error, over camera motion and 3D pointsA photometric loss (differences of pixel brightness), over camera motion and 3D structure
Data associationExplicit: decided by the matching stepImplicit: decided by the optimization
Closest relativeClassical BAOptical flow; "photometric BA"
Basin of convergenceLargerSmaller, at least in the basic formulation

The basin of convergence is the set of starting guesses from which the optimizer reaches the right answer. Matched features can pull a poor initial pose a long way, because the match itself says where the point went. Raw brightness only gives a useful gradient within a pixel or two of the right place. Direct methods therefore work coarse-to-fine: align heavily down-sampled images first, where a large motion is a small number of pixels, then refine at higher resolution. Some align learned feature maps instead of brightness. §7.2.1 · p. 196 Week 12 treats both alignments in detail.

Common mistakes

  • "Bundle adjustment is a kind of SLAM system." BA is the optimization problem at the core. SfM and visual SLAM are systems that call it.
  • "Visual odometry plus a map is visual SLAM." The defining addition is recognizing previously visited places and correcting the trajectory around the loop.
  • "More pixels of resolution fix depth accuracy." Depth error scales with \(z^2/(f\,b)\). Without baseline there is no depth, however sharp the image.

Check yourself

Q1. A stereo camera has f = 600 px and baseline 0.12 m. A point has disparity 9 px. How far away is it?

z = f·b/d = 600 × 0.12 / 9 = 8 m.

Q2. With the same rig and the same pixel noise, a point moves from 5 m to 10 m away. Its depth standard deviation is multiplied by about

σ_z ≈ z²·σ_d/(f·b), so doubling z quadruples the depth uncertainty.

Q3. Someone downloads 5,000 unordered tourist photos of a cathedral and computes camera poses and a 3D model overnight. Which term fits best?

Offline, non-causal, unordered images, joint estimation of structure and camera motion: that is SfM. VO and visual SLAM process a video stream as it arrives.

Q4. Why do direct methods usually start on down-sampled images?

Brightness gradients guide the optimizer only near the solution. Coarse levels bring a large displacement within reach, and finer levels then refine it.

Q5. Which component removes accumulated drift in a visual SLAM system that has no GPS?

Odometry errors accumulate no matter how good each step is. Aligning the current image to previously observed ones gives constraints across the loop, and the back-end redistributes the error.

Recap

  1. Bundle adjustment predates computers; visual SLAM is its online, causal, real-time descendant.
  2. SfM is offline reconstruction, VO is local motion estimation that drifts, and visual SLAM adds place recognition and loop closure.
  3. A camera does not measure depth. From two views, \(z = f\,b/d\) and \(\sigma_z \approx z^2\sigma_d/(f\,b)\).
  4. A visual SLAM system has an odometry front-end, a mapping back-end, and a place recognition and relocalization component, running in parallel.
  5. Feature-based odometry minimizes reprojection error with explicit matches; direct odometry minimizes a photometric loss and needs coarse-to-fine to converge.

Sources

  1. SLAM Handbook, Chapter 7, §7.1 "Historical Background and Terminology" and §7.2 "The Processing Pipeline of a Visual SLAM System", pp. 193–197.
  2. The disparity and depth-uncertainty formulas are the standard stereo relations, as in Hartley and Zisserman, Multiple View Geometry in Computer Vision, 2004, and Szeliski, Computer Vision: Algorithms and Applications, 2010.

Week 11 · Day 3

The camera model: from a 3D point to a pixel, and back to a ray

After today you can project a 3D point to a pixel with the pinhole model, unproject a pixel to a ray, apply and undo radial distortion, and say which lens needs which model.

About 60 min · Read §7.3.1, pp. 197–200 (4 pages) · Needs Week 11 Day 2

Read first: §7.3.1, pp. 197–200

While you read, look for:

  • The projection function \(\pi\) and the unprojection \(\pi^{-1}\), and the phrase "only known up to scale" (p. 198).
  • The four pinhole parameters and what each means (p. 198).
  • Why the radial-tangential model has no analytical unprojection (p. 199).
  • Which model the book suggests for lenses up to 180° and beyond 180° (p. 199), and what a rolling shutter is (p. 200).

Today's big idea

A camera model is a function \(\pi\) that maps a 3D point in the camera's frame to a pixel, using a handful of calibrated numbers. Going forward is a division by depth. Going back is impossible for a point and possible only for a ray, because the division threw the depth away. Every visual measurement model in the rest of the chapter is built on \(\pi\).

1. Projection and unprojection

A camera model has a geometric part, saying where a 3D point lands in the image, and a photometric part, saying how bright the pixel gets. §7.3.1 · p. 197 The geometric part is the projection function

\[ \mathbf{z} = \pi(\mathbf{x}^c, \boldsymbol{\xi}), \qquad \mathbf{x}^c = \begin{bmatrix} x & y & z \end{bmatrix}\T \in \R^3, \qquad \mathbf{z} = \begin{bmatrix} u & v \end{bmatrix}\T \in \Omega \subset \R^2 . \]

Here \(\mathbf{x}^c\) is the point in camera coordinates (origin at the camera, \(z\) pointing forward along the optical axis), \(\mathbf{z}\) is its pixel position in the image domain \(\Omega\), and \(\boldsymbol{\xi}\) holds the intrinsic parameters, usually calibrated beforehand. The unprojection \(\mathbf{x}^c = \pi^{-1}(\mathbf{z}, \boldsymbol{\xi})\) returns a 3D ray: the depth is unknown, so the result is known only up to scale. §7.3.1.1 · p. 198

Two notation warnings. In Part I, \(\boldsymbol{\xi}\) was a pose perturbation (Week 4 · Day 3); in Chapter 7 it is the vector of camera intrinsics. And the book uses \(z\) both for the depth coordinate and, in bold, for the measurement \(\mathbf{z}\).

2. The pinhole model

The pinhole (also rectilinear or perspective) model suits narrow-angle lenses without distortion. §7.3.1.1 · p. 198

\[ \boldsymbol{\xi}_p = \begin{bmatrix} f_u & f_v & u_0 & v_0 \end{bmatrix}\T, \qquad \pi_p(\mathbf{x}^c, \boldsymbol{\xi}) = \begin{bmatrix} f_u \dfrac{x}{z} + u_0 \\ f_v \dfrac{y}{z} + v_0 \end{bmatrix}, \qquad \pi_p^{-1}(\mathbf{z}, \boldsymbol{\xi}) \sim \begin{bmatrix} \dfrac{u-u_0}{f_u} \\ \dfrac{v-v_0}{f_v} \\ 1 \end{bmatrix}. \]

\(f_u, f_v\) are the focal lengths in pixels, horizontally and vertically; with square pixels \(f_u \approx f_v\). \((u_0, v_0)\) is the principal point, the pixel where the optical axis meets the image.

Filling the gap: where the formula comes from, and the matrix form

Similar triangles. In the figure, the ray from the point through the camera centre crosses a plane at distance \(f\). The small triangle (legs \(f\) and the image height) and the large one (legs \(z\) and \(x\)) have the same angles, so image height \(= f\,x/z\). The same holds for \(y\).

Pixels. A sensor counts pixels from a corner of the image, not from the optical axis, so the principal point is added. If the lens has focal length 4 mm and pixels are 5 µm wide, then \(f_u = 4\,\text{mm} / 0.005\,\text{mm} = 800\) pixels. This is why \(f\) is "in pixel units".

Example. \(f_u = f_v = 500\), \((u_0, v_0) = (320, 240)\), and \(\mathbf{x}^c = (0.4, -0.2, 2)\) m:

\[ u = 500\cdot\frac{0.4}{2} + 320 = 420, \qquad v = 500\cdot\frac{-0.2}{2} + 240 = 190 . \]

Unprojecting \((420, 190)\) gives \(\big(\tfrac{420-320}{500}, \tfrac{190-240}{500}, 1\big) = (0.2, -0.1, 1)\), which is \(\mathbf{x}^c/2\): the right direction, with the depth gone. The point \((4, -2, 20)\) lands on the same pixel.

Homogeneous coordinates. Represent the pixel \((u, v)\) by any triple \((\lambda u, \lambda v, \lambda)\) with \(\lambda \ne 0\), and write \(\sim\) for "equal up to a nonzero scale factor". Then the pinhole model is a matrix product:

\[ \begin{bmatrix} u \\ v \\ 1 \end{bmatrix} \sim \mathbf{K}\,\mathbf{x}^c, \qquad \mathbf{K} = \begin{bmatrix} f_u & 0 & u_0 \\ 0 & f_v & v_0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix}, \qquad \mathbf{K}\,\mathbf{x}^c = \begin{bmatrix} f_u x + u_0 z \\ f_v y + v_0 z \\ z \end{bmatrix}. \]

Dividing by the last entry, \(z\), gives back \(\pi_p\). The matrix \(\mathbf{K}\) is the calibration matrix, and \(\pi_p^{-1}(\mathbf{z}) \sim \mathbf{K}^{-1}\begin{bmatrix} u & v & 1 \end{bmatrix}\T\). The \(\sim\) in the book's unprojection formula is this same symbol. Homogeneous coordinates turn the awkward division into linear algebra, which Day 5 uses to relate two views.

Field of view. A pixel at the image edge, \(W/2\) from the principal point, sees a ray at angle \(\arctan\frac{W/2}{f_u}\) from the axis. An image 640 pixels wide with \(f_u = 500\) has a horizontal field of view of \(2\arctan(0.64) \approx 65^\circ\).

3. Lens distortion

Real lenses bend straight lines. The most common correction is the radial-tangential model, which adds four parameters, \(\boldsymbol{\xi}_{RT} = \begin{bmatrix} \boldsymbol{\xi}_p\T & k_1 & k_2 & p_1 & p_2 \end{bmatrix}\T\), and inserts one step between the division and the scaling to pixels. §7.3.1.1 · pp. 198–199

\[ \begin{aligned} x' &= \frac{x}{z}, \quad y' = \frac{y}{z}, \quad r = \sqrt{x'^2 + y'^2}, \\ x'' &= x'(1 + k_1 r^2 + k_2 r^4) + 2p_1 x'y' + p_2(r^2 + 2x'^2), \\ y'' &= y'(1 + k_1 r^2 + k_2 r^4) + p_1(r^2 + 2y'^2) + 2p_2 x'y', \\ \pi(\mathbf{x}^c, \boldsymbol{\xi}) &= \begin{bmatrix} f_u x'' + u_0 \\ f_v y'' + v_0 \end{bmatrix}. \end{aligned} \]

\((x', y')\) are normalized image coordinates: the pinhole image for \(f = 1\) and principal point at zero. The \(k\) terms are radial: they move a point along the line through the image center, by an amount that grows with the distance \(r\). The \(p\) terms are tangential, and model a lens that is slightly off-center or tilted.

Example: \(k_1 = -0.2\), all other coefficients zero, \(x' = 0.5\), \(y' = 0\). Then \(r^2 = 0.25\), the factor is \(1 - 0.05 = 0.95\), and \(x'' = 0.475\). With \(f_u = 500\) the pixel moves \(500 \times 0.025 = 12.5\) pixels toward the center.

Try it: slide \(k_1\) from negative to positive, then change the focal length.

Notice that negative \(k_1\) pulls the corners inward (barrel distortion) and positive \(k_1\) pushes them outward (pincushion). The center barely moves; the corner at \(r = 1\) moves 72 pixels at the default settings (\(0.18 \times 400\)). The last tile counts the iterations needed to undo the distortion for that corner.

Filling the gap: undoing distortion by iteration

To unproject a pixel you need \((x', y')\) from \((x'', y'')\). That means solving a polynomial of degree five in \(r\) (and worse with tangential terms), for which there is no formula. The book mentions Newton-Raphson. §7.3.1.1 · p. 199 An even simpler scheme works for moderate distortion. With radial terms only, the model says \(x' = x'' / (1 + k_1 r^2 + k_2 r^4)\), where \(r\) belongs to the unknown point. So guess, and repeat:

x', y' = x'', y''                      # first guess: no distortion
repeat until the change is tiny:
    r2 = x'*x' + y'*y'
    g  = 1 + k1*r2 + k2*r2*r2
    x', y' = x''/g, y''/g

For the example above (\(x'' = 0.475\), \(k_1 = -0.2\)) the iterates are \(0.475 \to 0.49745 \to 0.49973 \to 0.49997\), heading to the true value 0.5. Systems that need this for every pixel compute it once and store a lookup table.

4. Wide-angle and fisheye lenses

A pinhole image point lies at distance \(f\tan\theta\) from the principal point, where \(\theta\) is the angle between the ray and the optical axis. As \(\theta \to 90^\circ\) this goes to infinity, so a pinhole-based model cannot represent rays from the side, let alone from behind. The book lists the usual choices (Figure 7.1 shows the lenses). §7.3.1.1 · pp. 198–199

ModelParametersUseUnprojection
Pinhole4: \(f_u, f_v, u_0, v_0\)Narrow-angle lenses without distortionClosed form
Radial-tangential8: pinhole + \(k_1, k_2, p_1, p_2\)Ordinary lenses with some distortionIterative
Brown-Conrady (as defined in the book)6: pinhole + \(k_1, k_2\)Wide-angle lenses, fields of view up to 180°Iterative
Kannala-Brandt (KB)8: pinhole + \(k_1,\dots,k_4\)Fisheye lenses beyond 180°Iterative
Double Sphere (DS)6Fisheye and wide-angle lensesClosed form

The KB model replaces \(\tan\theta\) by a polynomial in the angle itself:

\[ \pi_{KB}(\mathbf{x}^c, \boldsymbol{\xi}) = \begin{bmatrix} f_u\, r(\theta)\cos\psi + u_0 \\ f_v\, r(\theta)\sin\psi + v_0 \end{bmatrix}, \qquad \theta = \arctan\frac{\sqrt{x^2+y^2}}{z}, \quad \psi = \arctan\frac{y}{x}, \quad r(\theta) = \theta + \sum_{n=1}^{4} k_n\theta^{2n+1}. \]

With all \(k_n = 0\), a ray at \(\theta = 90^\circ\) lands at radius \(f\cdot\tfrac{\pi}{2}\), a finite number: about 471 pixels for \(f = 300\). The DS model projects the point onto two unit spheres in turn and then applies a shifted pinhole projection; the book reports it to be around five times faster to compute than KB at comparable reprojection error. §7.3.1.1 · p. 199

The choice matters. A fisheye lens should get a spherical model and a rectilinear lens a linear one; an ill-suited model leaves systematic errors that bias the whole SLAM estimate. §7.3.1.4 · p. 200

5. Brightness and time

The photometric model \(I = f(E, T)\) maps irradiance \(E\) (the light power arriving at a pixel) to the stored intensity \(I\), given camera settings \(T\): exposure time, gain, gamma correction, de-bayering, lens vignetting. It matters for methods that compare pixel brightness across images (the direct methods of Day 2) and for textured dense reconstruction. §7.3.1.2 · pp. 199–200

Time matters too. A global shutter exposes all rows at once. A rolling shutter, found in most consumer cameras, reads the rows one after another, so each row is taken from a slightly different camera pose. Suppose read-out takes 30 ms while the camera turns at 60°/s: the last row is taken 1.8° later than the first, which at \(f = 500\) is a shift of \(500\tan 1.8^\circ \approx 16\) pixels. The remedies are a global-shutter camera, or a model with one pose per row, which becomes practical when an IMU measures the motion during the exposure. §7.3.1.3 · p. 200 The continuous-time trajectories of Week 5 · Day 1 were built for exactly this.

Common mistakes

  • "Unprojection recovers the 3D point." It recovers a direction. Every point \(\lambda\,\pi^{-1}(\mathbf{z})\) with \(\lambda \gt 0\) projects to the same pixel.
  • "The focal length is a distance in meters." In \(\boldsymbol{\xi}_p\) it is in pixels: the physical focal length divided by the pixel size.
  • "Distortion is a small cosmetic effect." At the image corners it can be tens of pixels, far more than the sub-pixel noise of a good feature detector.

Check yourself

Q1. A pinhole camera has \(f_u = f_v = 400\), \((u_0, v_0) = (320, 240)\). Where does the point \(\mathbf{x}^c = (1, 0.5, 4)\) project?

u = 400·(1/4) + 320 = 420 and v = 400·(0.5/4) + 240 = 290. (720, 440) forgets the division by depth; (100, 50) forgets the principal point.

Q2. With the same camera, which 3D point could have produced the pixel (520, 240)?

Unprojection gives the ray direction ((520−320)/400, 0, 1) = (0.5, 0, 1). The point (2, 0, 4) is 4 times that direction, so it lies on the ray.

Q3. An image is 640 pixels wide and \(f_u = 320\). What is the horizontal field of view of this pinhole camera?

Half the width is 320 pixels, so the half-angle is arctan(320/320) = 45°, and the full field of view is 90°.

Q4. A lens has \(k_1 = -0.1\) and no other distortion. A point has normalized coordinates \(x' = 1\), \(y' = 0\), and \(f_u = 400\). How does distortion move its pixel?

r² = 1, so x″ = 1·(1 − 0.1) = 0.9. The change of 0.1 in normalized units is 0.1 × 400 = 40 pixels, inward because k₁ is negative.

Q5. Why can a pinhole model with distortion terms not describe a 190° fisheye lens?

The normalized coordinate is tan θ, which diverges at 90° and has the wrong sign behind the camera. Models such as Kannala-Brandt and Double Sphere parametrize by the ray angle or by a sphere instead.

Recap

  1. \(\mathbf{z} = \pi(\mathbf{x}^c, \boldsymbol{\xi})\) maps a camera-frame point to a pixel; \(\pi^{-1}\) returns a ray, known up to scale.
  2. Pinhole: \(u = f_u x/z + u_0\), \(v = f_v y/z + v_0\), or \(\begin{bmatrix} u & v & 1 \end{bmatrix}\T \sim \mathbf{K}\mathbf{x}^c\) in homogeneous coordinates.
  3. Radial-tangential distortion acts on normalized coordinates between the division and the scaling to pixels; undoing it takes iteration.
  4. Fisheye lenses need models built on the ray angle (Kannala-Brandt) or on spheres (Double Sphere).
  5. The photometric model matters for direct methods, and a rolling shutter gives each image row its own pose.

Sources

  1. SLAM Handbook, Chapter 7, §7.3.1 "Camera Model", pp. 197–200, including Figure 7.1.
  2. Similar-triangles derivation, homogeneous coordinates, the calibration matrix, and the field-of-view formula follow Hartley and Zisserman, Multiple View Geometry in Computer Vision, 2004.
  3. The fixed-point undistortion iteration is the standard simple scheme; see Szeliski, Computer Vision: Algorithms and Applications, 2010, for lens distortion models.

Week 11 · Day 4

Keypoints: detect, describe, match

After today you can say what makes an image patch a good keypoint, compute the Harris and Shi-Tomasi corner scores from a second-moment matrix, and match binary descriptors by Hamming distance.

About 60 min · Read §7.3.2, pp. 200–204 (5 pages) · Needs Week 11 Day 3

Read first: §7.3.2, pp. 200–204

While you read, look for:

  • The definitions of a keypoint detector and a keypoint descriptor, and the three groups of desirable properties in bold (pp. 200–201).
  • How the Harris detector decides that a patch is a corner, and what Shi-Tomasi does differently (p. 201).
  • The three stages of SIFT, and the two ingredients ORB combines (p. 202).
  • What "describe-and-detect" reverses in D2-Net (pp. 203–204).

Today's big idea

Feature-based SLAM replaces each image by a few hundred points that it can find again in other images. A detector chooses locations where the image changes in every direction, so the location is well defined. A descriptor summarizes the neighbourhood as a vector, so that the same point can be recognized later. Thirty years of methods trade speed against invariance to scale, rotation, and lighting.

1. What a keypoint must do

Keypoints (or features) are salient image regions that are distinctive and can be re-detected from other viewpoints, in other runs, and under other conditions. A keypoint detector finds them. A keypoint descriptor encodes the local appearance around each one in a compact vector. §7.3.2 · p. 200 The desirable properties are: §7.3.2 · p. 201

  • Scale and rotation invariance: the same point is found, and described the same way, when the camera moves closer or rolls.
  • Repeatability and distinctiveness: it is found again, and it is not confused with other points.
  • Efficiency: all of this fits in the time between two frames.

Matching quality is measured with the precision and recall of Day 1. If two images share 100 true correspondences and a matcher returns 80 pairs of which 60 are right, precision is \(60/80 = 0.75\) and recall is \(60/100 = 0.6\). The wrong 20 are the outliers that Week 6 · Day 2 (RANSAC) and the robust kernels of Week 6 · Day 4 exist for. Strong lighting changes, textureless surfaces, and moving objects all make detection and matching worse. §7.3.2 · p. 201

2. Corners and the second-moment matrix

The Harris detector classifies a patch as a keypoint when both eigenvalues of its second-moment matrix are large, meaning the intensity varies strongly in two orthogonal directions. Shi-Tomasi uses the smaller eigenvalue directly; Harris uses a "cornerness" function that avoids computing eigenvalues. §7.3.2.1 · p. 201 The book does not define the matrix, so here it is.

Filling the gap: where the second-moment matrix comes from

Ask: if I slide a small window \(W\) by \(\boldsymbol{\Delta} = (\Delta u, \Delta v)\), how much does its content change? Measure the change by the sum of squared differences,

\[ E(\boldsymbol{\Delta}) = \sum_{(u,v)\in W}\big[I(u+\Delta u, v+\Delta v) - I(u,v)\big]^2 . \]

For a small shift, a first-order Taylor expansion gives \(I(u+\Delta u, v+\Delta v) \approx I(u,v) + I_u\,\Delta u + I_v\,\Delta v\), where \(I_u, I_v\) are the image gradients (differences between neighbouring pixels). Substituting,

\[ E(\boldsymbol{\Delta}) \approx \sum_{W}\big(I_u\,\Delta u + I_v\,\Delta v\big)^2 = \boldsymbol{\Delta}\T \mathbf{M}\,\boldsymbol{\Delta}, \qquad \mathbf{M} = \sum_{(u,v)\in W}\begin{bmatrix} I_u^2 & I_u I_v \\ I_u I_v & I_v^2 \end{bmatrix}. \]

\(\mathbf{M}\) is the second-moment matrix (also called the structure tensor). It is symmetric and positive semidefinite, with eigenvalues \(\lambda_1 \ge \lambda_2 \ge 0\). For a shift of unit length, \(E\) lies between \(\lambda_2\) (the direction of least change) and \(\lambda_1\) (the direction of most change). Three cases follow.

EigenvaluesPatchMeaning
Both smallFlatNo shift changes the patch: it cannot be localized at all
\(\lambda_1\) large, \(\lambda_2\) smallEdgeSliding along the edge changes nothing: position is known across the edge only
Both largeCornerEvery shift changes the patch: position is well defined

Shi-Tomasi scores a patch by \(\lambda_2\). Harris uses

\[ R = \det\mathbf{M} - k\,(\tr\mathbf{M})^2 = \lambda_1\lambda_2 - k\,(\lambda_1+\lambda_2)^2, \]

with \(k\) a small constant, commonly 0.04 to 0.06. \(R\) is large and positive for corners, negative for edges, and near zero for flat patches, and it needs only the entries of \(\mathbf{M}\), no square root.

Numbers. For \(\mathbf{M} = \begin{bmatrix} 10 & 2 \\ 2 & 8 \end{bmatrix}\): the eigenvalues of a symmetric \(2\times2\) matrix \(\begin{bmatrix} a & b \\ b & d \end{bmatrix}\) are \(\tfrac{a+d}{2} \pm \sqrt{\big(\tfrac{a-d}{2}\big)^2 + b^2}\), here \(9 \pm \sqrt{5}\), so \(\lambda_1 = 11.24\), \(\lambda_2 = 6.76\). Both are large: a corner. Harris with \(k = 0.04\): \(R = 76 - 0.04\cdot 18^2 = 63.0\). For \(\mathbf{M} = \begin{bmatrix} 10 & 0 \\ 0 & 0.1 \end{bmatrix}\): \(R = 1 - 0.04\cdot 10.1^2 = -3.08\). Negative: an edge.

Try it: press Flat, Edge, and Corner, then rotate the shape, then lower the contrast.

Notice that at the corner both eigenvalues are large (0.34 and 0.23 at the default settings), on the edge only one is (0.63 and 0.00, and Harris R is negative), and inside the shape both vanish. The right panel shows that \(\lambda_2\) is large only near the four corners. Rotating the shape changes the entries of \(\mathbf{M}\) but not the verdict. Halving the contrast divides the eigenvalues by four, and below a contrast of about 0.3 the fixed threshold no longer finds the corners: lighting changes are hard for hand-set thresholds.

Intuition

Look at a long straight fence through a small hole. If the fence slides sideways along its own direction you cannot tell. That is an edge, and the effect is called the aperture problem. Now put a fence post corner in the hole: any motion is visible. A good keypoint is a place where the hole pins down both directions.

One weakness remains. The window has a fixed size, so the same physical corner seen from twice as far fills the window differently. Harris is not scale invariant, and that is what SIFT and SURF set out to fix. §7.3.2.1 · p. 201

3. The classical line

Figure 7.2 (p. 201) places the methods on a timeline. In order: §7.3.2.1 · pp. 201–202

Method (year in Fig. 7.2)Detects / describesIdeaInvariant to
Harris (1988)DetectorBoth eigenvalues of the second-moment matrix largeNot scale
SIFT (2004)BothExtrema of a difference-of-Gaussians pyramid; orientation from the dominant gradient; 128-dimensional histogram of gradient orientationsScale, rotation; partly illumination
FAST (2006)DetectorCompare the pixels on a circle around the candidate with its center; reject earlyNot scale
SURF (2008)BothApproximate SIFT with integral images and box filtersScale, rotation
BRIEF (2010)DescriptorA string of bits, each the result of comparing two pixel intensitiesNeither scale nor rotation
ORB (2011)BothFAST + BRIEF, plus an image pyramid (scale) and the intensity centroid (rotation)Scale, rotation
BRISK (2011)BothFAST or Harris corners on a scale-space pyramid; binary descriptor aligned to a dominant directionScale, rotation

SIFT set the standard for precision and recall but is expensive. The binary methods are what made real-time visual SLAM practical: ORB and BRISK give up a little distinctiveness for a large gain in speed. When computation is not a constraint, SIFT and SURF may still be preferable for their robustness to lighting and perspective changes. §7.3.2.1 · p. 202

The image pyramid is how scale invariance is usually obtained: detect on the image and on copies shrunk by a constant factor, so a corner that is too big for the window at full resolution fits it a few levels up. SIFT's 128 numbers come from a \(4\times4\) grid of cells around the keypoint with an 8-bin histogram of gradient directions in each (\(4\cdot4\cdot8 = 128\)).

4. Binary descriptors and matching

A BRIEF-style descriptor is a bit string: bit \(i\) is 1 if pixel \(a_i\) of the patch is brighter than pixel \(b_i\), for a fixed list of pixel pairs. Two descriptors are compared by the Hamming distance, the number of bit positions in which they differ. §7.3.2.1 · p. 202

Filling the gap: computing and using the Hamming distance

Take the bitwise exclusive-or (XOR) of the two strings and count the ones:

a       = 1011 0010
b       = 1001 1010
a XOR b = 0010 1000      → Hamming distance 2

Processors do both steps in single instructions on 64 bits at a time, which is why binary descriptors match so fast. A SIFT comparison instead needs a 128-term sum of squared differences.

How small is "close"? ORB descriptors have 256 bits. As a rough model, treat the bits of two unrelated patches as independent coin flips. Each bit then differs with probability \(\tfrac12\), so the distance is binomial with mean \(256\cdot\tfrac12 = 128\) and standard deviation \(\sqrt{256\cdot\tfrac14} = 8\). A pair at distance 40 is eleven standard deviations below what chance produces. Real bits are correlated, so the separation is less clean, but this is why a threshold well below 128 works.

Matching. For each descriptor in image 1, find its nearest neighbour in image 2. A common safeguard is the ratio test: accept the match only if the nearest distance is clearly smaller than the second-nearest, for example below 0.8 times it. Query 11001010 against candidates 11001110 (distance 1), 01101010 (distance 2), and 00110101 (distance 8): the best is at 1, the runner-up at 2, the ratio is 0.5, so the match is accepted. If the runner-up were also at 1 the point would be ambiguous, typical of repeated texture, and dropped.

5. Learned keypoints

From the late 2010s, convolutional neural networks (CNNs) trained on large datasets took over, with the largest gains under extreme illumination change. §7.3.2.2 · pp. 203–204

Method (year in Fig. 7.2)What is new
LIFT (2016)Detection, orientation, and description in one trainable pipeline working on image patches; trained in the order descriptor, orientation, detector
SuperPoint (2018)One forward pass over the whole image yields keypoints and descriptors; self-supervised with homographic adaptation, which generates pseudo-ground-truth keypoints
HF-Net (2019)One network outputs keypoints, local descriptors, and a global image descriptor: retrieve similar images first, then match locally
D2-Net (2019)Describe-and-detect: compute dense feature maps first, then take keypoints as their local maxima; robust, but heavier than sparse methods

The pattern to keep is the pair "local descriptor for matching points, global descriptor for retrieving images". The global one is what place recognition (Day 1, and §7.3.6 on Day 5) runs on. Figure 7.2 also marks SuperGlue (2020) and MASt3R (2024) as recent developments.

Common mistakes

  • "A strong edge is a good keypoint." Its position along the edge is undetermined. One large eigenvalue is not enough; that is why Shi-Tomasi looks at the smaller one.
  • "Detector and descriptor are the same thing." FAST only detects, BRIEF only describes, and ORB is the combination. They can be mixed.
  • "Matched keypoints are correct correspondences." Matching by appearance always produces some wrong pairs. Geometry (Day 5) and robust estimation (Week 6) remove them.

Check yourself

Q1. A patch has second-moment matrix \(\mathbf{M} = \begin{bmatrix} 9 & 0 \\ 0 & 0.01 \end{bmatrix}\). What is it?

The eigenvalues are 9 and 0.01: strong change in one direction, almost none in the other. That is an edge.

Q2. Compute the Harris response for \(\mathbf{M} = \begin{bmatrix} 5 & 1 \\ 1 & 5 \end{bmatrix}\) with \(k = 0.04\).

det M = 25 − 1 = 24 and tr M = 10, so R = 24 − 0.04·100 = 20. The eigenvalues are 6 and 4, both large: a corner.

Q3. What is the Hamming distance between 11110000 and 10100101?

XOR gives 01010101, which has four ones.

Q4. The lights dim so that every image gradient is halved. What happens to the eigenvalues of the second-moment matrix?

M sums products of two gradients, so halving the gradients scales M, and its eigenvalues, by one quarter. A fixed threshold on the score then misses corners it found before.

Q5. What does ORB add to the combination of FAST detection and BRIEF description?

FAST and BRIEF alone are neither scale nor rotation invariant. ORB detects on a pyramid and orients each patch by its intensity centroid. The histogram is SIFT, the box filters are SURF, the network is SuperPoint.

Recap

  1. A detector picks repeatable locations; a descriptor makes them recognizable. Wanted: invariance, repeatability, distinctiveness, efficiency.
  2. The second-moment matrix \(\mathbf{M}\) measures how a patch changes under a small shift. Corner: both eigenvalues large. Shi-Tomasi: \(\lambda_2\). Harris: \(\det\mathbf{M} - k(\tr\mathbf{M})^2\).
  3. SIFT is the robust, expensive reference; FAST, BRIEF, ORB, and BRISK trade some distinctiveness for real-time speed.
  4. Binary descriptors are compared with the Hamming distance (XOR, then count bits); a ratio test removes ambiguous matches.
  5. Learned methods (LIFT, SuperPoint, HF-Net, D2-Net) cope better with extreme appearance change, at higher computational cost.

Sources

  1. SLAM Handbook, Chapter 7, §7.3.2 "Keypoints", pp. 200–204, including Figure 7.2.
  2. Second-moment matrix derivation and corner scores: Harris and Stephens, A Combined Corner and Edge Detector, 1988; Shi and Tomasi, Good Features to Track, 1994; Szeliski, Computer Vision: Algorithms and Applications, 2010.
  3. SIFT descriptor layout and the ratio test: Lowe, Distinctive Image Features from Scale-Invariant Keypoints, 2004.
  4. The coin-flip estimate of Hamming distances between unrelated descriptors is a binomial calculation, stated here as an idealization.

Week 11 · Day 5

Reprojection error, bundle adjustment, and the geometry of two views

After today you can derive the reprojection cost from Gaussian pixel noise, state full bundle adjustment and the ways real-time systems cut it down, and derive the epipolar constraint that ties two views together.

About 60 min · Read §7.3.3–7.3.8, pp. 204–207 (4 pages) · Needs Week 11 Days 3–4 and Week 2 Day 2

Read first: §7.3.3–7.3.8, pp. 204–207 (stop at §7.4)

While you read, look for:

  • How equation (7.1) follows from the Gaussian likelihood above it (p. 204).
  • The unknowns of equation (7.3), and what \(\mathbf{R}^i_w\mathbf{x}^w_j + \mathbf{t}^i_w\) computes (p. 205).
  • In Figure 7.4 (p. 206), why the lower-left graph is dense and the lower-right one is not.
  • Why initialization is singled out for monocular cameras in §7.3.7 (p. 207).

Today's big idea

Feature-based visual SLAM is one least-squares problem: move the cameras and the 3D points until every point, pushed through the camera model, lands on the pixel where it was observed. The mismatch is the reprojection error. Everything else is about making that problem small enough to solve in real time and giving it a good enough starting point.

1. The reprojection error

For an observed image point \(\mathbf{z}_j \in \R^2\) and a 3D point \(\mathbf{x}^c_j\) in camera coordinates, the reprojection error is §7.3.3 · p. 204

\[ \mathbf{e}_{\text{reproj}} = \mathbf{z}_j - \pi(\mathbf{x}^c_j, \boldsymbol{\xi}). \]

It is a 2-vector in pixels: observed minus predicted. With the camera of Day 3 (\(f = 500\), principal point \((320, 240)\)) and an estimated point \(\mathbf{x}^c = (0.4, -0.2, 2)\), the prediction is \((420, 190)\). If the keypoint was detected at \((423, 186)\), then \(\mathbf{e} = (3, -4)\) and its length is 5 pixels.

Filling the gap: from Gaussian noise to equation (7.1)

The book goes from the likelihood to (7.1) in two lines. Here are the steps, which repeat Week 2 · Day 2 for a camera. Assume the detected pixel is the true projection plus Gaussian noise with covariance \(\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_j\):

\[ p(\mathbf{z}_j \mid \mathbf{x}^c_j, \boldsymbol{\xi}) = \frac{1}{2\pi\sqrt{\det\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_j}}\exp\!\Big(-\tfrac12\,\mathbf{e}_j\T\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_j^{-1}\mathbf{e}_j\Big), \qquad \mathbf{e}_j = \mathbf{z}_j - \pi(\mathbf{x}^c_j, \boldsymbol{\xi}). \]

Independent observations multiply, so their logarithms add. Taking the negative logarithm,

\[ \mathcal{L} = -\sum_j \log p(\mathbf{z}_j \mid \mathbf{x}^c_j, \boldsymbol{\xi}) = \frac12\sum_j \mathbf{e}_j\T\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_j^{-1}\mathbf{e}_j + \underbrace{\sum_j \log\!\big(2\pi\sqrt{\det\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_j}\big)}_{\text{const.}} . \]

The last sum does not depend on the unknowns. Writing \(\norm{\mathbf{e}}^2_{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}} = \mathbf{e}\T\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{-1}\mathbf{e}\) for the squared Mahalanobis norm and dropping the constant gives the book's

\[ E_{\text{reproj}} = \frac12\sum_j \norm{\mathbf{z}_j - \pi(\mathbf{x}^c_j, \boldsymbol{\xi})}^2_{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_j}. \tag{7.1} \]

Maximizing the likelihood is the same as minimizing this sum. In the simplest case every keypoint has the same isotropic noise, of standard deviation \(\sigma\) pixels in each direction, and each term is \(\norm{\mathbf{e}_j}^2/(2\sigma^2)\). (The book writes this case as \(\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_j = \sigma\mathbf{I}_2\); its \(\sigma\) is then the variance.) For \(\mathbf{e} = (3, -4)\): with \(\sigma = 1\) the term is \(25/2 = 12.5\); with \(\sigma = 2\) it is \(25/8 \approx 3.1\). A keypoint detected on a coarse pyramid level is less precise, gets a larger \(\sigma\), and counts less.

Wrong matches produce huge residuals that a squared cost cannot absorb, so a robust kernel \(\rho\) such as Huber or Tukey (Week 6 · Day 4) is wrapped around each term: §7.3.3 · p. 204

\[ E_{\text{robust}} = \frac12\sum_j \rho\Big(\norm{\mathbf{z}_j - \pi(\mathbf{x}^c_j, \boldsymbol{\xi})}_{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_j}\Big). \tag{7.2} \]

2. Full bundle adjustment

Now let the camera move. Points \(j \in \mathsf{P}\) have unknown world coordinates \(\mathbf{x}^w_j \in \R^3\); images \(i \in \mathsf{C}\) have unknown poses \(\mathbf{T}^i_w \in \SE(3)\), which take world coordinates to the coordinates of camera \(i\): \(\mathbf{x}^c = \mathbf{R}^i_w\mathbf{x}^w_j + \mathbf{t}^i_w\). The observation of point \(j\) in image \(i\) is the pixel \(\mathbf{z}_{ij}\). Minimizing over everything at once is full BA: §7.3.4 · p. 205

\[ \{\mathbf{T}^{i*}_w, \mathbf{x}^{w*}_j\} = \argmin_{\mathbf{T}^i_w,\,\mathbf{x}^w_j}\ \frac12\sum_{i,j}\rho\Big(\norm{\mathbf{z}_{ij} - \pi\big(\mathbf{R}^i_w\mathbf{x}^w_j + \mathbf{t}^i_w\big)}_{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{ij}}\Big). \tag{7.3} \]

(The intrinsics \(\boldsymbol{\xi}\) are dropped from the notation from here on.) Count the sizes. Each camera has 6 unknowns and each point 3; each observation gives 2 equations. A map with 200 images and 20,000 points, each seen in 5 images, has \(200\cdot6 + 20{,}000\cdot3 = 61{,}200\) unknowns and \(2\cdot100{,}000 = 200{,}000\) equations. Solving that for every new frame is out of reach, and the book lists how systems cope. §7.3.4 · pp. 205–206

ApproachWhat it keepsConsequence
Batch optimizationAll poses, all points, all observations; Gauss-Newton or Levenberg-Marquardt on (7.3)The gold standard in SfM; too expensive to run per image
Filtering (EKF, information filter)Only the latest camera pose; older poses are marginalized outSparsity is destroyed, which limits the map to a few hundred features; past observations are never re-linearized
Keyframe-basedA few selected images, the keyframes; the frames in between and their observations are discarded for mappingThe problem stays sparse; for the same effort, longer and more accurate maps than filtering
Factor graphsA language for all of the above: variables are poses and landmarks, factors are reprojection errors and priorsPart I applies unchanged

Figure 7.4 shows why filtering loses sparsity. Marginalizing a pose is the elimination step of Week 3 · Day 3: it leaves a new factor joining everything that pose was connected to. Remove the three old poses in the figure, and all five landmarks they observed become linked to each other, 10 landmark pairs for 5 landmarks, and in general about \(n^2/2\) for \(n\). Keyframe methods avoid creating these links by throwing the in-between frames away.

3. Two views: the epipolar constraint

Problem (7.3) is non-linear and is solved iteratively, so it needs a reasonable initial guess. This matters most for a monocular camera, where a single frame does not make the state observable. §7.3.7 · p. 207 The book leaves the geometry to the literature. The classical starting point is a relation between two images of the same point that involves no 3D point at all.

Filling the gap: deriving the essential and fundamental matrices

Let a point have coordinates \(\mathbf{x}^1\) in camera 1 and \(\mathbf{x}^2\) in camera 2, related by the rigid motion \(\mathbf{x}^2 = \mathbf{R}\,\mathbf{x}^1 + \mathbf{t}\). Each camera sees it along a ray: \(\mathbf{x}^1 = \lambda_1\mathbf{b}_1\) and \(\mathbf{x}^2 = \lambda_2\mathbf{b}_2\), where \(\mathbf{b}_k = \pi^{-1}(\mathbf{z}_k)\) is the unprojected pixel of Day 3 and \(\lambda_k \gt 0\) is the unknown depth. Substituting,

\[ \lambda_2\,\mathbf{b}_2 = \lambda_1\,\mathbf{R}\,\mathbf{b}_1 + \mathbf{t}. \]

Step 1: take the cross product of both sides with \(\mathbf{t}\). Since \(\mathbf{t}\times\mathbf{t} = \mathbf{0}\),

\[ \lambda_2\,\mathbf{t}\times\mathbf{b}_2 = \lambda_1\,\mathbf{t}\times(\mathbf{R}\,\mathbf{b}_1). \]

Step 2: take the dot product of both sides with \(\mathbf{b}_2\). The left side is zero, because \(\mathbf{t}\times\mathbf{b}_2\) is perpendicular to \(\mathbf{b}_2\). Divide by \(\lambda_1\):

\[ \mathbf{b}_2\T\,[\mathbf{t}]_\times\mathbf{R}\;\mathbf{b}_1 = 0, \qquad [\mathbf{t}]_\times = \begin{bmatrix} 0 & -t_z & t_y \\ t_z & 0 & -t_x \\ -t_y & t_x & 0 \end{bmatrix}, \]

where \([\mathbf{t}]_\times\mathbf{a} = \mathbf{t}\times\mathbf{a}\) writes the cross product as a matrix. This is the epipolar constraint, and \(\mathbf{E} = [\mathbf{t}]_\times\mathbf{R}\) is the essential matrix. Both depths have dropped out. Geometrically it says that the two rays and the line joining the camera centres lie in one plane.

In pixels, with pinhole cameras and homogeneous pixels \(\mathbf{p}_k = \begin{bmatrix} u_k & v_k & 1 \end{bmatrix}\T\), we have \(\mathbf{b}_k = \mathbf{K}^{-1}\mathbf{p}_k\), so

\[ \mathbf{p}_2\T\,\mathbf{F}\,\mathbf{p}_1 = 0, \qquad \mathbf{F} = \mathbf{K}^{-\top}\mathbf{E}\,\mathbf{K}^{-1}, \]

the fundamental matrix. For a fixed pixel \(\mathbf{p}_1\), the vector \(\boldsymbol{\ell}_2 = \mathbf{F}\mathbf{p}_1 = (\alpha, \beta, \gamma)\) defines a line \(\alpha u + \beta v + \gamma = 0\) in image 2, the epipolar line: the match of \(\mathbf{p}_1\) must lie on it.

Check with stereo. Camera 2 is 1 m to the right of camera 1 with the same orientation: \(\mathbf{R} = \mathbf{I}\), \(\mathbf{t} = (-1, 0, 0)\). Then \(\mathbf{E} = \begin{bmatrix} 0 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \\ 0 & -1 & 0 \end{bmatrix}\), and for rays \(\mathbf{b}_k = (x'_k, y'_k, 1)\) the constraint reads \(y'_2 - y'_1 = 0\). Matches lie on the same image row, which is the setting of Day 2's disparity formula.

Scale. Replace \(\mathbf{t}\) by \(2\mathbf{t}\): the constraint is unchanged. Two images fix the direction of the translation but not its length. A monocular reconstruction is therefore defined only up to an overall scale. \(\mathbf{E}\) has 5 degrees of freedom (3 for \(\mathbf{R}\), 2 for the direction of \(\mathbf{t}\)), so five correspondences are the minimum to estimate it, inside a RANSAC loop (Week 6 · Day 2) because some matches are wrong.

Try it: press Next point a few times. Drag camera 2 in the top view. Then move the two error sliders one at a time.

Notice three things. The selected point always sits on its epipolar line in image 2 (0.0 px), while the other points are usually tens of pixels away, so most wrong matches violate the constraint; a few do not (after one press of Next point, another point lies only 3 px from the line). A depth error slides the prediction along the line and is invisible in image 1: +1.5 m gives a 15.6 px residual. A 1° yaw error shifts every prediction by 5 to 6 px and raises the cost from 0 to about 125. Drag camera 2 onto camera 1 and the depth slider stops having any effect: without baseline, depth is unobservable.

4. From two views to a map

The pieces chain into the standard monocular initialization. Match keypoints between two frames (Day 4). Estimate \(\mathbf{E}\) with RANSAC and split it into \(\mathbf{R}\) and the direction of \(\mathbf{t}\). Then triangulate: with \(\mathbf{R}, \mathbf{t}\) known, the ray equation \(\lambda_2\mathbf{b}_2 - \lambda_1\mathbf{R}\mathbf{b}_1 = \mathbf{t}\) is three linear equations in the two depths, solved by least squares because noisy rays do not meet exactly. Finally refine everything with BA (7.3). From then on each new frame is located against the existing 3D points, a problem called Perspective-n-Point (PnP), which you met in Week 4 · Day 3 and which opens Week 12.

The section closes with four short pointers. §7.3.5–7.3.8 · p. 207

  • Photometric error: the alternative to reprojection error used by direct methods. It compares pixel intensities, assuming that a scene point looks equally bright in consecutive frames.
  • Visual place recognition: compute one descriptor per image, \(\mathbf{d} = f(I)\), and retrieve the nearest stored descriptor. Bag-of-words methods build it by quantizing local descriptors such as ORB into clusters called visual words; learned descriptors are more invariant to appearance change.
  • Initialization: the topic of this section.
  • Map representations: a balance of accuracy, memory, and computation, treated in Chapter 5 (Week 8).

Common mistakes

  • "The reprojection error is a distance in meters." It lives in the image, in pixels. A 1-pixel error can mean a millimeter for a near point or meters for a far one.
  • "The epipolar constraint gives the match." It gives a line. Any point on that line satisfies it, at any depth.
  • "A filter is cheaper because it keeps one pose." Removing poses makes the remaining landmark block dense, and the cost grows quickly with the number of features.

Check yourself

Q1. A keypoint is observed at (212, 148). The current estimate projects the point to (209, 152). With \(\boldsymbol{\Sigma} = \mathbf{I}_2\), what does this observation contribute to \(E_{\text{reproj}}\)?

e = (3, −4), so ‖e‖² = 25 and the term is ½·25 = 12.5.

Q2. A bundle adjustment problem has 10 camera poses and 500 points. How many scalar unknowns does (7.3) have?

Each pose in SE(3) has 6 degrees of freedom and each point 3: 10·6 + 500·3 = 1,560.

Q3. Two identical pinhole cameras are related by \(\mathbf{R} = \mathbf{I}\), \(\mathbf{t} = (-1, 0, 0)\). A keypoint is at row \(v = 130\) in image 1. Where is its epipolar line in image 2?

For a sideways translation with no rotation the constraint reduces to y′₂ = y′₁, and with identical intrinsics equal y′ means equal v. Depth only decides where on that row the match is.

Q4. Why are filtering approaches limited to a few hundred features?

Eliminating a pose creates a factor over all its neighbours. After many poses are removed the landmarks are fully connected, and the cost of a dense problem grows much faster than a sparse one.

Q5. Why can two images from one moving camera not tell a small nearby scene from a large distant one?

In λ₂b₂ = λ₁Rb₁ + t, multiplying t, λ₁ and λ₂ by the same number keeps the equation true with the same rays. The images carry no information about absolute scale.

Recap

  1. Reprojection error: \(\mathbf{e} = \mathbf{z} - \pi(\mathbf{x}^c)\), in pixels. Gaussian pixel noise turns maximum likelihood into the weighted least-squares cost (7.1).
  2. Full BA (7.3) minimizes the robust reprojection error over all poses \(\mathbf{T}^i_w\) and points \(\mathbf{x}^w_j\).
  3. Batch is the reference; filtering marginalizes old poses and becomes dense; keyframe methods stay sparse; factor graphs express them all.
  4. Two views of a point satisfy \(\mathbf{b}_2\T\mathbf{E}\,\mathbf{b}_1 = 0\) with \(\mathbf{E} = [\mathbf{t}]_\times\mathbf{R}\), or \(\mathbf{p}_2\T\mathbf{F}\,\mathbf{p}_1 = 0\) in pixels. The match lies on the epipolar line \(\mathbf{F}\mathbf{p}_1\).
  5. Monocular initialization: matches, essential matrix, triangulation, then BA. The overall scale stays unknown.

Sources

  1. SLAM Handbook, Chapter 7, §7.3.3–7.3.8, pp. 204–207, equations (7.1)–(7.3) and Figure 7.4.
  2. The epipolar constraint, essential and fundamental matrices, the five-point minimal case, and triangulation follow Hartley and Zisserman, Multiple View Geometry in Computer Vision, 2004.
  3. The negative-log-likelihood derivation is the standard Gaussian maximum-likelihood argument, as in Barfoot, State Estimation for Robotics, 2017.

Week 11 · Review

Week 11 review: cameras, features, and the pipeline

After today you can project and unproject with a camera model, score a corner, match descriptors, write the reprojection cost and bundle adjustment, relate two views with the epipolar constraint, and score a trajectory.

About 60 min · No new pages

The week in one paragraph

Part II turns from the back-end to the front-end: how each sensor produces odometry factors, loop-closure factors, and unary factors, and how the result is scored (ATE, RPE, precision and recall). Visual SLAM is the first and reference case. A camera maps a 3D point to a pixel through a projection function \(\pi\) with calibrated intrinsics, and loses the depth on the way; depth returns only through a second view, with an uncertainty that grows as \(z^2\) and shrinks with the baseline. Feature-based systems reduce each image to keypoints (corners found with the second-moment matrix, described by vectors or bit strings, matched by distance), and estimate cameras and points by minimizing the reprojection error. Done over everything at once this is bundle adjustment; real-time systems keep it tractable with keyframes, and start it from two-view geometry.

1. Formula sheet

What it isFormulaWhere

Relative pose error\(\mathbf{E}_i = (\mathbf{Q}_i^{-1}\mathbf{Q}_{i+\Delta})^{-1}(\mathbf{P}_i^{-1}\mathbf{P}_{i+\Delta})\), then the RMS of its translation partDay 1 (extra)
Precision and recall\(\dfrac{TP}{TP+FP}\) and \(\dfrac{TP}{TP+FN}\)Day 1; §II.3, p. 191

Pinhole projection and unprojection\(\pi_p(\mathbf{x}^c) = \begin{bmatrix} f_u x/z + u_0 \\ f_v y/z + v_0 \end{bmatrix}\), \(\quad\pi_p^{-1}(\mathbf{z}) \sim \begin{bmatrix} (u-u_0)/f_u \\ (v-v_0)/f_v \\ 1 \end{bmatrix}\)Day 3; §7.3.1.1, p. 198
Radial distortion\(x'' = x'(1 + k_1 r^2 + k_2 r^4)\), same for \(y''\), with \(x' = x/z\), \(r^2 = x'^2 + y'^2\)Day 3; §7.3.1.1, p. 199
