Inside every BA iteration the Schur complement removes the points and leaves a small reduced camera system, whose fill-in is the covisibility graph; a power series can stand in for its inverse, and variable projection removes the need for a good start. Images alone leave a 7-parameter similarity undetermined. Depth cameras add metric depth and dense TSDF maps, and an IMU adds scale and gravity, cutting the gauge to 4.

1. Formula sheet

What it isFormulaWhere
Pose-only BA (tracking)\({\mathbf{T}^i_w}^{*} = \argmin_{\mathbf{T}^i_w} \sum_{j} \rho\big( \norm{\mathbf{z}_{ij} - \pi(\mathbf{R}^i_w\mathbf{x}^w_j + \mathbf{t}^i_w)}_{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{ij}} \big)\)(7.4), p. 208 · Day 1
Pose Jacobian of a keypoint, \(\mathbf{T} = \mathbf{T}^0\Exp(\boldsymbol{\xi})\)\(\mathbf{J} = \boldsymbol{\Pi}\,\mathbf{R}^0 [\,\mathbf{I} \;\; -(\mathbf{x}^w)^\wedge\,]\), with \(\boldsymbol{\Pi} = \partial\pi/\partial\mathbf{x}^c\)derived on Day 1; cf. (2.14)–(2.16), p. 58
Local BA(7.4) summed over \(i \in \mathsf{K}_1 \cup \mathsf{K}_2,\ j \in \mathsf{P}_1\); optimize only \(\mathbf{T}^k_w,\ k \in \mathsf{K}_1\) and \(\mathbf{x}^w_j,\ j \in \mathsf{P}_1\)(7.5), p. 209 · Day 1
Photometric loss\(E_{photo} = \sum_{i}\sum_{z \in \mathcal{P}_i}\sum_{j \in obs(z)} \rho\big( I_i(z) - I_j(\omega(z, d_z, \mathbf{T}^i_j)) \big)\)(7.6), p. 210 · Day 2
Lucas-Kanade step (1-D shift)\(\delta = -\sum_x g_x r_x \big/ \sum_x g_x^2\), \(r_x = I_2(x+s) - I_1(x)\), \(g_x = I_2'(x+s)\)derived on Day 2
BA normal equations\(\begin{pmatrix} \mathbf{H}_{cc} & \mathbf{H}_{cp} \\ \mathbf{H}_{cp}\T & \mathbf{H}_{pp} \end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix} \mathbf{d}_c \\ \mathbf{d}_p \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} \mathbf{b}_c \\ \mathbf{b}_p \end{pmatrix}\)p. 213 · Day 3
Schur complement trick\(\mathbf{H}^{red}_{cc} = \mathbf{H}_{cc} - \mathbf{H}_{cp}\mathbf{H}_{pp}^{-1}\mathbf{H}_{cp}\T\); \(\ \mathbf{H}^{red}_{cc}\mathbf{d}_c = \mathbf{b}_c - \mathbf{H}_{cp}\mathbf{H}_{pp}^{-1}\mathbf{b}_p\); \(\ \mathbf{H}_{pp}\mathbf{d}_p = \mathbf{b}_p - \mathbf{H}_{cp}\T\mathbf{d}_c\)(7.7), p. 213 · Day 3
Power series for the inverse\((\mathbf{H}^{red}_{cc})^{-1} \approx \sum_{i=0}^{m} (\mathbf{H}_{cc}^{-1}\mathbf{H}_{cp}\mathbf{H}_{pp}^{-1}\mathbf{H}_{cp}\T)^i\, \mathbf{H}_{cc}^{-1}\)(7.9), p. 213 · Day 4
Gauge freedom\(\mathbf{x}^w \mapsto s\,\mathbf{Q}\mathbf{x}^w + \mathbf{a}\) (with matching cameras) changes no pixel: 7 parameters; 4 with an IMUp. 221 · Day 4
Warp with inverse depth\(\omega = \pi\big( \mathbf{R}\,\pi^{-1}(z) + \rho_z \mathbf{t} \big)\), sideways shift \(= f\,b\,\rho_z\)derived on Day 5
Signed-distance fusion\(D(\mathbf{x}) = \sum_i \omega_i(\mathbf{x}) d_i(\mathbf{x}) \big/ \sum_i \omega_i(\mathbf{x})\)(7.12), p. 218 · Day 5

2. Mixed quiz

Check yourself

Q1. Which thread of a keypoint-based system changes the positions of map points?

Tracking solves pose-only BA with the points held constant. Local BA in the mapping thread (and full BA after a loop) updates points.

Q2. A camera at the identity pose has \(f_u = 600\) px. A map point lies on the optical axis at depth 3 m. Its keypoint is observed 4 px to the right of the prediction. Using only a translation along \(x\) in the perturbation, what does one Gauss-Newton step give?

The Jacobian entry is f_u / z = 200 px per meter. One residual, one unknown: 4 / 200 = 0.02 m.

Q3. In the photometric loss (7.6), which quantities are unknown?

The book minimizes over all camera parameters and all depth values d_z. The images are the data.

Q4. Lucas-Kanade at full resolution has a basin of about ±3 px on some image. Roughly what basin do you expect with a pyramid of three extra levels, each half the size of the one before?

At level 3 one pixel spans 2³ = 8 original pixels, so a basin of about ±3 level pixels is about ±24 original pixels.

Q5. In BA, camera \(i\) observes point \(j\). Which blocks of the Hessian receive a contribution from this one observation?

The residual depends on camera i and point j only, so JᵀJ gains AᵀA, BᵀB and AᵀB (with its transpose) and nothing else.

Q6. Five cameras in a row; each point is seen only by two neighbouring cameras, and every neighbouring pair shares some point. How many of the 10 off-diagonal block pairs \((i, k)\), \(i \lt k\), of the reduced camera system are non-zero?

A block fills in exactly when two cameras share a point. Only the neighbouring pairs (1,2), (2,3), (3,4), (4,5) do.

Q7. Which sensor setup has a gauge freedom of 6?

The known baseline fixes scale, leaving global position (3) and orientation (3). One camera has 7; with an IMU 4 remain.

Q8. Why is the weighted average (7.12) the right way to fuse signed distances?

Minimizing the sum of squared, variance-weighted differences gives the weighted mean. Watertightness needs extra steps.

3. Pen-and-paper problems

  1. A tracking step with two points. A camera sits at the identity pose with \(f_u = 500\) px. Two map points lie at \((1, 0, 5)\) m and \((-1, 0, 2.5)\) m. Their keypoints are observed \(+2\) px and \(+3\) px away from the predictions in \(u\). Allow only a translation \(\xi_x\) along \(x\) in the perturbation. Find the Gauss-Newton step and the residuals after it.

    Solution

    The \(u\)-row of the Jacobian for a translation along \(x\) is \(f_u/z\): \(J_1 = 500/5 = 100\) and \(J_2 = 500/2.5 = 200\) px per meter. The normal equation is \((J_1^2 + J_2^2)\,\xi_x = J_1 e_1 + J_2 e_2\):

    \[ \xi_x = \frac{100 \cdot 2 + 200 \cdot 3}{100^2 + 200^2} = \frac{800}{50{,}000} = 0.016 \ \text{m}. \]

    Predicted residuals after the step: \(2 - 100 \cdot 0.016 = 0.4\) px and \(3 - 200 \cdot 0.016 = -0.2\) px. One unknown cannot satisfy both observations; least squares leans towards the nearer point because its keypoint is more sensitive to translation.

  2. One Lucas-Kanade step. Let \(I_1(x) = x^2\) and \(I_2(x) = I_1(x - 0.5) = (x - 0.5)^2\). Starting from \(s = 0\) and using the pixels \(x = 1, 2, 3\), compute the update \(\delta\). Why is it not exactly 0.5?

    Solution

    Gradients \(g_x = I_2'(x) = 2(x - 0.5)\): 1, 3, 5. Residuals \(r_x = I_2(x) - I_1(x) = (x-0.5)^2 - x^2 = 0.25 - x\): \(-0.75, -1.75, -2.75\).

    \[ \delta = -\frac{\sum g_x r_x}{\sum g_x^2} = -\frac{-0.75 - 5.25 - 13.75}{1 + 9 + 25} = \frac{19.75}{35} \approx 0.564 . \]

    The true shift is 0.5. The step overshoots because the image is quadratic and Lucas-Kanade treats it as linear between \(x\) and \(x + \delta\). A second step from \(s = 0.564\) removes almost all of the remaining error; that is ordinary Gauss-Newton behaviour.

  3. Schur complement by hand. Two cameras and two points, one unknown each. Camera 1 sees point 1; camera 2 sees both points:

    \[ \mathbf{H}_{cc} = \begin{pmatrix} 4 & 0 \\ 0 & 3 \end{pmatrix}, \quad \mathbf{H}_{cp} = \begin{pmatrix} 2 & 0 \\ 1 & 1 \end{pmatrix}, \quad \mathbf{H}_{pp} = \begin{pmatrix} 2 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix}, \quad \mathbf{b}_c = \begin{pmatrix} 4 \\ 3 \end{pmatrix}, \quad \mathbf{b}_p = \begin{pmatrix} 2 \\ 1 \end{pmatrix}. \]

    Solve for \(\mathbf{d}_c\) and \(\mathbf{d}_p\) with equation (7.7). Which point created the off-diagonal entry of the reduced system?

    Solution

    \(\mathbf{H}_{cp}\mathbf{H}_{pp}^{-1} = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 0.5 & 1 \end{pmatrix}\). Then

    \[ \mathbf{H}_{cp}\mathbf{H}_{pp}^{-1}\mathbf{H}_{cp}\T = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 0.5 & 1 \end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix} 2 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} 2 & 1 \\ 1 & 1.5 \end{pmatrix}, \qquad \mathbf{H}^{red}_{cc} = \begin{pmatrix} 2 & -1 \\ -1 & 1.5 \end{pmatrix}. \]

    Right-hand side: \(\mathbf{b}_c - \mathbf{H}_{cp}\mathbf{H}_{pp}^{-1}\mathbf{b}_p = (4, 3) - (2, 2) = (2, 1)\). Solving the \(2 \times 2\) system (determinant 2): \(\mathbf{d}_c = (2, 2)\). Back-substitution: \(\mathbf{H}_{pp}\mathbf{d}_p = \mathbf{b}_p - \mathbf{H}_{cp}\T\mathbf{d}_c = (2, 1) - (6, 2) = (-4, -1)\), so \(\mathbf{d}_p = (-2, -1)\).

    Check with the first row of the full system: \(4 \cdot 2 + 2 \cdot (-2) + 0 = 4\). The entry \(-1\) comes from point 1, the only point both cameras see: \(-2 \cdot \tfrac{1}{2} \cdot 1 = -1\).

  4. Gauge and counting in the flat world (stretch). A flatland camera at position \(\mathbf{c}\) with heading \(\theta\) sees a point \(\mathbf{p}\) at \(u = f\,x_c/z_c\), where \((x_c, z_c)\) are the coordinates of \(\mathbf{p} - \mathbf{c}\) in the camera's rotated axes. (a) Show that multiplying all camera positions and all points by \(s \gt 0\), with headings unchanged, changes no observation. (b) Three cameras each observe the same \(n\) points. How large must \(n\) be before the observations can determine the solution up to gauge?

    Solution

    (a) Scaling gives \(s\mathbf{p} - s\mathbf{c} = s(\mathbf{p} - \mathbf{c})\). The rotation into the camera axes is linear, so \((x_c, z_c)\) becomes \((s x_c, s z_c)\) and \(u = f\,s x_c / (s z_c)\) is unchanged.

    (b) Unknowns: \(3 \times 3\) for the cameras and \(2n\) for the points. The gauge (2 shifts, 1 rotation, 1 scale) removes 4, leaving \(5 + 2n\) quantities to determine. Each observation is one number, and there are \(3n\). We need \(3n \ge 5 + 2n\), so \(n \ge 5\). Put differently, a point seen three times spends two observations on its own position and offers one to the cameras, and the cameras need five. With two cameras a point offers nothing (\(2n\) observations for its \(2n\) coordinates), so two flatland views never constrain the motion. In 3-D each observation is two numbers, and two views are enough.

You are ready for next week if you can

  • Explain why tracking, local mapping and loop closing run at different rates, and what each one optimizes.
  • Write a Gauss-Newton step for a residual once you have its Jacobian, for a pose (6 unknowns) or a shift (1 unknown).
  • Explain why iterative alignment needs a good initial guess and how coarse-to-fine supplies one. Next week's ICP has the same weakness.
  • Apply the Schur complement to a small block system and predict the fill-in from covisibility.
  • State what a camera alone cannot determine, and which extra sensor fixes which part.
  • Describe signed-distance fusion of depth measurements; LiDAR mapping uses the same kinds of map.

Sources

  1. SLAM Handbook, Chapter 7 "Visual SLAM", §7.4–7.9, pp. 207–223.
  2. Triggs, McLauchlan, Hartley, Fitzgibbon, Bundle Adjustment: A Modern Synthesis, 2000.
  3. Szeliski, Computer Vision: Algorithms and Applications, 2nd edition, 2022.

Week 13 · Day 1

How a LiDAR measures the world

After today you can explain how a LiDAR turns the travel time of a laser pulse into a 3D point, compare the main sensor types, and predict how point spacing changes with range and how sensor motion bends a scan.

About 60 min · Read Ch 8 intro and §8.1, pp. 224–227 (4 pages) · Needs Week 8 Day 1

Read first: Chapter 8 intro and §8.1, pp. 224–227

While you read, look for:

  • The time-of-flight principle, and what external light does to it (p. 225).
  • The three beam patterns of Figure 8.1, and which part of each sensor moves (p. 225).
  • In Figure 8.2, how the density of points changes with distance from the sensor (p. 226).
  • What a sensor can report besides range: intensity, and for FMCW sensors, velocity (pp. 226–227).

Today's big idea

A LiDAR is a laser with a stopwatch. It measures how long a pulse takes to come back, converts that to a distance, and pairs the distance with the direction the beam was pointing. The result is a point cloud: accurate in range, sparse and uneven in coverage, and collected over a tenth of a second instead of at one instant. Each of those three properties shapes an algorithm later this week.

1. Range from the travel time of light

LiDAR (light detection and ranging) sends out laser pulses and times their reflections. The basic principle is time of flight (TOF): the pulse travels to a surface and back, so a delay \(\Delta t\) between emission and detection means the surface is at distance

\[ d = \frac{c\,\Delta t}{2}, \qquad c \approx 3\times 10^{8}\ \text{m/s}. \]

The factor 2 is the round trip. §8.1 · p. 225

Filling the gap: how good must the stopwatch be?

Put numbers in. A wall at \(d = 10\) m gives \(\Delta t = 2 \times 10 / (3\times10^{8}) = 6.67\times10^{-8}\) s, or 66.7 nanoseconds. Now ask what timing error \(\delta t\) corresponds to a range error of 1 cm:

\[ \delta t = \frac{2\,\delta d}{c} = \frac{2 \times 0.01}{3\times 10^{8}} \approx 6.7\times 10^{-11}\ \text{s} = 67\ \text{picoseconds}. \]

So centimetre accuracy needs timing at the level of tens of picoseconds. Two consequences follow. The range error is set by the clock and the pulse shape, so it stays roughly the same size whether the wall is 5 m or 50 m away. And anything that makes the echo harder to time, such as sunlight raising the background level, directly costs accuracy. The book states the second point as a lower signal-to-noise ratio. §8.1 · p. 225

TOF is not the only principle. Two continuous-wave schemes borrowed from radar are also used: AMCW (amplitude-modulated continuous wave) and FMCW (frequency-modulated continuous wave). An FMCW LiDAR sweeps the frequency of its light and can read the relative velocity of the surface from the frequency shift of the return, which helps in scenes with moving objects, at a higher cost and complexity. §8.1 · pp. 225–227 Next week's radar chapter works through FMCW in detail.

2. Sensor types and their beam patterns

One laser beam measures one direction. To cover a scene the beam must be steered, and sensors are classified by how they do it. §8.1 · pp. 225–226

TypeHow the beam is steeredWhat you getTrade-off
2D mechanicalA rotating mirror sweeps one beam; an encoder disk reads the mirror angle (Figure 8.1a)One ring of (angle, range) pairs: a slice of the world in a single planeSees only that plane
3D mechanical, multi-beamSeveral emitters at different elevation angles sit on one head that spins through 360° (Figure 8.1b)One ring per emitter, all around the sensorMechanical wear and lower data rates
Scanning solid-stateMEMS mirrors or optical phased arrays, with little or no mechanical rotationA point cloud without a spinning headFewer moving parts to wear out, so longer life
Risley prismPrisms steer the beam quickly with little physical movement, tracing a spiral inside the lens window (Figure 8.1c)A cloud that gets denser the longer the sensor looksCompact, but a limited field of view
FlashNo scanning: the scene is lit at once and an array of detectors times the returnRanges on a pixel grid, and ambient channels that resemble camera images (p. 227)No moving parts; power, weight, and cost differ from scanning designs

The 3D multi-beam design came out of the DARPA Grand Challenges of the 2000s (the Velodyne HDL-64E), and sensors have since become much smaller and cheaper. §8.1 · p. 226 Whatever the mechanism, every sensor returns a set of individual range measurements, each with an intensity (also called remission): how much of the beam came back. §8.1 · p. 226

3. From ranges and angles to a point cloud

A measurement is a range \(r\) along a known direction. In 2D the direction is one angle \(\alpha\) and the point is \((r\cos\alpha,\ r\sin\alpha)\). In 3D the direction has an azimuth \(\alpha\) (around the vertical axis) and an elevation \(\epsilon\) (above the horizontal plane), and the point in the sensor frame is

\[ \mathbf{p} = r \begin{bmatrix} \cos\epsilon\,\cos\alpha \\ \cos\epsilon\,\sin\alpha \\ \sin\epsilon \end{bmatrix}. \]

Collect these for one full sweep and you have a point cloud \(\mathsf{P} = \{\mathbf{p}_i \in \R^3\}\), the object every algorithm in this chapter works on. This is the conversion you met in Week 8 · Day 1.

Try it: a 2D LiDAR sweeps a room. Change the number of beams and the range noise, and compare the near wall with the far one. Leave the speed at 0 for now.

Notice that with 120 beams the gap between neighbouring beams is 7.7 cm at the nearest wall point, 1.5 m away, and 37.6 cm at the farthest corner, 7.2 m away. The lower plot is what the sensor really outputs: one range per angle. Corners of the room show up as kinks, and the edge of the block as jumps.

Filling the gap: why far surfaces are sparse

Neighbouring beams differ in direction by a fixed angular step \(\Delta\theta\). Two rays that leave the same point with an angle \(\Delta\theta\) between them are an arc length

\[ s \approx r\,\Delta\theta \qquad (\Delta\theta \text{ in radians}) \]

apart after travelling a distance \(r\). The gap grows in proportion to range. With \(\Delta\theta = 0.2^\circ = 0.00349\) rad, points are 1.7 cm apart at 5 m and 17 cm apart at 50 m.

In 3D the same happens in both directions. Figure 8.2 shows a 64-beam sensor with a 104° vertical field of view. If its beams were evenly spaced they would be \(104/63 \approx 1.65^\circ\) apart, so at 20 m neighbouring rings would be \(20 \times 1.65 \times \pi/180 \approx 0.58\) m apart. Because both gaps scale with \(r\), the number of points per square metre on a surface facing the sensor falls like \(1/r^2\). That is the pattern in Figure 8.2: dense near the device, sparse far away. §8.1 · p. 226

In plain words

Imagine spinning in a dark room with a laser pointer and a tape measure that reads instantly. Every few degrees you write down how far the dot is. Plot those distances around a centre and you have drawn the room. Nearby walls get many dots, far walls only a few, because the same turn of your wrist moves the dot farther on a distant wall.

4. A scan is not a snapshot

One full sweep is called a scan, and scans carry time stamps so they can be processed in order. §8.2 · p. 227 But the sweep itself takes time. At a scan rate of 10 Hz it lasts 0.1 s. §8.2.2.1 · p. 231 A camera with a global shutter freezes the scene; a spinning LiDAR does not. A car at 15 m/s travels 1.5 m while its LiDAR turns once, so the first and last points of the same scan were measured from places 1.5 m apart. If the software treats them as measured from one place, straight walls come out bent and closed rooms do not close. This is motion distortion.

Go back to the widget and raise the sensor speed. The beams still hit the true walls, but the dots are drawn as if the sensor had stayed at its starting position. At 5 m/s the sensor moves 50 cm during the sweep, and the last points of the scan are drawn half a metre short of the wall they hit. Day 3 shows how odometry systems undo this.

Common mistakes

  • "A LiDAR scan is like a depth image: dense and regular." The points are spread by angle, so they are dense near the sensor and sparse far away, and a multi-beam sensor leaves wide gaps between rings.
  • "Range accuracy gets worse in proportion to distance." The timing error does not depend on distance. What degrades with distance is the spacing between points, and weak echoes from far surfaces.
  • "All points of a scan share one time stamp." They are spread over the sweep period. Ignoring that is harmless for a parked sensor and a large error for a fast one.

Check yourself

Q1. A pulse returns 200 ns after it was emitted. How far away is the surface?

d = cΔt/2 = (3×10⁸ × 200×10⁻⁹)/2 = 30 m. The pulse travelled 60 m in total, there and back.

Q2. A sensor has an angular step of 0.4°. About how far apart are neighbouring points on a wall 30 m away that faces the sensor?

s ≈ rΔθ = 30 × 0.4 × π/180 = 0.209 m, about 21 cm.

Q3. Why can a Risley-prism LiDAR that sits still produce a denser cloud than its instantaneous beam count suggests?

The beam traces a spiral inside the lens window, so accumulating measurements over time covers more directions. The cost is a limited field of view.

Q4. A LiDAR spins at 10 Hz on a vehicle driving straight at 20 m/s. How far does the sensor move between the first and last point of one scan?

One sweep takes 0.1 s, and 20 m/s × 0.1 s = 2 m. Points at the end of the scan are measured from a position 2 m ahead of the first ones.

Recap

  1. Time of flight gives range as d = cΔt/2. Centimetre accuracy needs timing to tens of picoseconds, and the range error does not grow with distance.
  2. Sensors differ in how they steer the beam: a rotating mirror (2D), a spinning multi-beam head (3D), MEMS or phased arrays, or Risley prisms. All return ranges with intensity.
  3. A range plus the beam angles is a point. Neighbouring points are about rΔθ apart, so density falls with distance.
  4. A scan is collected over about 0.1 s. If the sensor moves during that time, the scan is distorted unless the motion is compensated.

Sources

  1. SLAM Handbook, Chapter 8 introduction and §8.1 "LiDAR Sensing Preliminaries and Categorization", pp. 224–227; the definition of a scan in §8.2, p. 227; the scan period in §8.2.2.1, p. 231.
  2. Siegwart, Nourbakhsh, Scaramuzza, Introduction to Autonomous Mobile Robots, 2nd edition, 2011 (time-of-flight ranging, used in the timing arithmetic).
  3. The spacing rule s ≈ rΔθ is the arc-length formula; the 1.65° ring spacing assumes evenly spaced beams and is an illustration, not a specification of the sensor in Figure 8.2.

Week 13 · Day 2

Scan registration: ICP and the closed-form alignment

After today you can write the scan registration cost, solve it in closed form when the point pairs are known, run the ICP loop when they are not, and linearize the point-to-plane residual.

About 60 min · Read §8.2 intro and §8.2.1, pp. 227–231 (4 pages) · Needs Week 1 Day 5 and Week 4 Day 3

Read first: §8.2 (opening) and §8.2.1, pp. 227–231

While you read, look for:

  • Why Horn's closed-form method is not enough by itself, and what ICP adds (p. 227).
  • In equation (8.1), which of the two clouds the unknown \((\mathbf{R}, \mathbf{t})\) is applied to (p. 228).
  • The three distances of Figure 8.3 (p. 229), and how NDT avoids the nearest-neighbour search (p. 230).
  • Equation (8.3), and the two strategies for making the search fast (p. 230).

Today's big idea

Scan registration finds the rotation and translation that lay one scan on top of another. If you knew which point matches which, the answer would be one SVD. You do not, so ICP guesses the pairs by nearest neighbour, solves for the motion, and repeats. Each round lowers the cost, but only down to the nearest local minimum, so the starting guess matters.

1. The registration cost

Take two point clouds, a source \(\mathsf{P} = \{\mathbf{p}_i\}\) and a target \(\mathsf{Q} = \{\mathbf{q}_i\}\). We want \(\mathbf{R} \in \SO(3)\) and \(\mathbf{t} \in \R^3\) that bring them into alignment. Given a set \(\mathsf{C}\) of correspondences, pairs \((\mathbf{p}, \mathbf{q})\) believed to be the same physical spot, equation (8.1) asks for

\[ \mathbf{R}^k, \mathbf{t}^k = \argmin_{\mathbf{R},\,\mathbf{t}} \sum_{(\mathbf{p},\mathbf{q}) \in \mathsf{C}} d\big(\mathbf{p}_i,\ \mathbf{R}\mathbf{q}_i + \mathbf{t}\big), \tag{8.1} \]

where \(d\) is some distance and \(k\) counts iterations. §8.2.1 · p. 228 Two choices define a method: what \(d\) is, and how \(\mathsf{C}\) is found. Today starts with the simplest \(d\), the squared Euclidean distance \(\norm{\mathbf{p}_i - (\mathbf{R}\mathbf{q}_i + \mathbf{t})}^2\), called point-to-point (Figure 8.3a).

Filling the gap: which cloud moves, and what (R, t) means

As printed, (8.1) applies \((\mathbf{R}, \mathbf{t})\) to \(\mathbf{q}\): it takes a point written in \(\mathsf{Q}\)'s coordinates and writes it in \(\mathsf{P}\)'s. Suppose \(\mathsf{P}\) was recorded with the sensor at pose A and \(\mathsf{Q}\) at pose B, each in its own sensor frame. Then \(\mathbf{t}\) is the position of sensor B seen from A and \(\mathbf{R}\) is its orientation: the relative motion that odometry is after. Software that moves the other cloud estimates the inverse, \((\mathbf{R}\T, -\mathbf{R}\T\mathbf{t})\). In this lesson \(\mathsf{P}\) stays fixed and \(\mathsf{Q}\) moves, as in (8.1).

2. If the pairs were known: a closed form

Horn's method solves (8.1) exactly when the pairs are given. §8.2 · p. 227 The book does not derive it. Here is the SVD version, which uses only tools from Week 1 · Day 5.

Filling the gap: deriving the closed-form alignment

Minimize \(E(\mathbf{R},\mathbf{t}) = \sum_{i=1}^{N} \norm{\mathbf{p}_i - \mathbf{R}\mathbf{q}_i - \mathbf{t}}^2\).

Step 1: translation. For fixed \(\mathbf{R}\), set the gradient with respect to \(\mathbf{t}\) to zero: \(-2\sum_i (\mathbf{p}_i - \mathbf{R}\mathbf{q}_i - \mathbf{t}) = \mathbf{0}\). With the centroids \(\bar{\mathbf{p}} = \frac1N\sum_i \mathbf{p}_i\) and \(\bar{\mathbf{q}} = \frac1N\sum_i \mathbf{q}_i\) this gives

\[ \mathbf{t} = \bar{\mathbf{p}} - \mathbf{R}\,\bar{\mathbf{q}} . \]

The best translation maps centroid onto centroid, whatever the rotation is.

Step 2: remove the translation. Substitute it back and write \(\mathbf{p}_i' = \mathbf{p}_i - \bar{\mathbf{p}}\), \(\mathbf{q}_i' = \mathbf{q}_i - \bar{\mathbf{q}}\):

\[ E(\mathbf{R}) = \sum_i \norm{\mathbf{p}_i' - \mathbf{R}\mathbf{q}_i'}^2 = \sum_i \Big( \norm{\mathbf{p}_i'}^2 + \norm{\mathbf{q}_i'}^2 - 2\,\mathbf{p}_i'{}\T \mathbf{R}\,\mathbf{q}_i' \Big). \]

The middle term used \(\norm{\mathbf{R}\mathbf{q}'} = \norm{\mathbf{q}'}\): rotations keep lengths. Only the last term depends on \(\mathbf{R}\), so minimizing \(E\) means maximizing \(\sum_i \mathbf{p}_i'{}\T\mathbf{R}\mathbf{q}_i'\).

Step 3: a trace. A scalar equals its own trace, and \(\tr(\mathbf{A}\mathbf{B}) = \tr(\mathbf{B}\mathbf{A})\), so

\[ \sum_i \mathbf{p}_i'{}\T\mathbf{R}\,\mathbf{q}_i' = \sum_i \tr\big(\mathbf{R}\,\mathbf{q}_i'\mathbf{p}_i'{}\T\big) = \tr(\mathbf{R}\mathbf{H}), \qquad \mathbf{H} = \sum_i \mathbf{q}_i'\,\mathbf{p}_i'{}\T . \]

Step 4: SVD. Write \(\mathbf{H} = \mathbf{U}\mathbf{S}\mathbf{V}\T\) with \(\mathbf{S} = \diag(\sigma_1,\sigma_2,\sigma_3)\), \(\sigma_1 \ge \sigma_2 \ge \sigma_3 \ge 0\). Then \(\tr(\mathbf{R}\mathbf{U}\mathbf{S}\mathbf{V}\T) = \tr(\mathbf{S}\,\mathbf{Z})\) with \(\mathbf{Z} = \mathbf{V}\T\mathbf{R}\mathbf{U}\), which is orthogonal, so its diagonal entries satisfy \(z_{kk} \le 1\). Hence \(\tr(\mathbf{S}\mathbf{Z}) = \sum_k \sigma_k z_{kk} \le \sum_k \sigma_k\), with equality when \(\mathbf{Z} = \mathbf{I}\):

\[ \mathbf{R} = \mathbf{V}\mathbf{U}\T . \]

Step 5: no reflections. If \(\det(\mathbf{V}\mathbf{U}\T) = -1\) the result is a mirror image, not a rotation. The best proper rotation is then \(\mathbf{R} = \mathbf{V}\,\diag(1, 1, -1)\,\mathbf{U}\T\), which gives up the smallest singular value.

In 2D you can skip the SVD. With \(\mathbf{R}(\theta)\) a plane rotation, \(\sum_i \mathbf{p}_i'{}\T\mathbf{R}(\theta)\mathbf{q}_i' = A\cos\theta + B\sin\theta\) where

\[ A = \sum_i \mathbf{q}_i' \cdot \mathbf{p}_i', \qquad B = \sum_i \big(q_{i,x}'\,p_{i,y}' - q_{i,y}'\,p_{i,x}'\big), \qquad \theta = \operatorname{atan2}(B, A). \]

Worked example. Let \(\mathbf{q}_1 = (0,0)\), \(\mathbf{q}_2 = (2,0)\), \(\mathbf{q}_3 = (0,1)\) and \(\mathbf{p}_1 = (1,2)\), \(\mathbf{p}_2 = (1,4)\), \(\mathbf{p}_3 = (0,2)\). The centroids are \(\bar{\mathbf{q}} = (\tfrac23, \tfrac13)\) and \(\bar{\mathbf{p}} = (\tfrac23, \tfrac83)\). Centred, \(\mathbf{q}' = (-\tfrac23,-\tfrac13),\ (\tfrac43,-\tfrac13),\ (-\tfrac23,\tfrac23)\) and \(\mathbf{p}' = (\tfrac13,-\tfrac23),\ (\tfrac13,\tfrac43),\ (-\tfrac23,-\tfrac23)\). Then \(A = 0 + 0 + 0 = 0\) and \(B = \tfrac59 + \tfrac{17}{9} + \tfrac89 = \tfrac{10}{3}\), so \(\theta = \operatorname{atan2}(\tfrac{10}{3}, 0) = 90^\circ\). A 90° rotation sends \((x, y)\) to \((-y, x)\), so \(\mathbf{R}\bar{\mathbf{q}} = (-\tfrac13, \tfrac23)\) and \(\mathbf{t} = \bar{\mathbf{p}} - \mathbf{R}\bar{\mathbf{q}} = (1, 2)\). Check with the second point: \(\mathbf{R}\mathbf{q}_2 + \mathbf{t} = (0,2) + (1,2) = (1,4) = \mathbf{p}_2\).

3. Unknown pairs: the ICP loop

Real scans come without pairs. The iterative closest point (ICP) algorithm supplies them with a guess: for each \(\mathbf{p}\), take the point of the other cloud that is nearest under the current estimate,

\[ \mathsf{C} = \Big\{ (\mathbf{p}, \mathbf{q}) \ \Big|\ \mathbf{p} \in \mathsf{P},\ \mathbf{q} = \argmin_{\mathbf{q}' \in \mathsf{Q}} \norm{\mathbf{p} - (\mathbf{R}^{k-1}\mathbf{q}' + \mathbf{t}^{k-1})}_2 \Big\}, \tag{8.3} \]

then solve (8.1) for these pairs, and repeat with the improved estimate. §8.2.1.2 · p. 230

R, t = initial guess                      # for example "the sensor did not move"
repeat:
    C = for each p, the nearest R q + t   # equation (8.3)
    R, t = best alignment of the pairs C  # equation (8.1): closed form for point-to-point
until R, t stop changing

Try it: press Step several times and watch the two half-steps alternate, then press Run. Afterwards set "Sensor turned by" to 160° and run again.

Notice, at the default 20° turn, that point-to-point ICP needs 21 alignment steps, and the rotation error ends at 0.0°. The RMS distance falls from 68 cm to 11.5 cm but not to zero, because the two scans hit different spots on the same walls. At 160° the loop also converges, to an answer that is wrong by about 179° with an RMS of 47 cm: a room turned half-way round nearly fits itself.

Filling the gap: why ICP converges, and why only locally

Call the cost \(E(\mathbf{R}, \mathbf{t}, \mathsf{C})\). The matching step keeps \((\mathbf{R},\mathbf{t})\) and picks, for every \(\mathbf{p}\), the pair with the smallest distance, so it cannot raise \(E\). The alignment step keeps \(\mathsf{C}\) and finds the exact minimizer over \((\mathbf{R},\mathbf{t})\), so it cannot raise \(E\) either. A sequence that never increases and is bounded below by zero converges. But nothing in this argument says where. The loop stops as soon as re-matching returns the same pairs, and that can happen at a wrong alignment in which every point has found some neighbour. The pairs are only as good as the estimate that produced them, which is why the book asks for a "sufficiently good initial guess". §8.4.1 · p. 242

4. Point-to-plane: stop punishing sliding

Two scans of a wall do not contain the same points, only points on the same surface. Point-to-point distance still pulls each point toward its partner along the wall, which slows convergence. The point-to-plane distance (Figure 8.3c) fits a small plane to the fixed cloud around the matched point and measures only the offset perpendicular to it. §8.2.1.1 · p. 229 With \(\mathbf{n}_i\) the unit normal of that plane, the residual is the scalar

\[ r_i(\mathbf{R},\mathbf{t}) = \mathbf{n}_i\T\big(\mathbf{p}_i - (\mathbf{R}\mathbf{q}_i + \mathbf{t})\big), \]

and the cost is \(\sum_i r_i^2\). In 2D the plane is a line through neighbouring points, which is the point-to-line distance of Figure 8.3b. There is no closed form any more, so each alignment step is one Gauss-Newton step (Week 2 · Day 4).

Filling the gap: linearizing the point-to-plane residual

Perturb the current estimate on the right, \(\mathbf{T} = \mathbf{T}^0\Exp(\boldsymbol{\xi})\) with \(\boldsymbol{\xi} = (\boldsymbol{\rho}, \boldsymbol{\phi})\), translation part first, as in Week 4 · Day 3. To first order \(\Exp(\boldsymbol{\xi})\) maps \(\mathbf{q}\) to \(\mathbf{q} + \boldsymbol{\phi}\times\mathbf{q} + \boldsymbol{\rho}\), so

\[ \mathbf{R}\mathbf{q}_i + \mathbf{t} \approx \mathbf{R}^0\big(\mathbf{q}_i + \boldsymbol{\phi}\times\mathbf{q}_i + \boldsymbol{\rho}\big) + \mathbf{t}^0 . \]

Insert this into \(r_i\) and write \(\mathbf{m}_i = \mathbf{R}^{0\mathsf{T}}\mathbf{n}_i\) for the normal expressed in \(\mathsf{Q}\)'s frame:

\[ r_i \approx r_i^0 - \mathbf{m}_i\T\boldsymbol{\rho} - \mathbf{m}_i\T(\boldsymbol{\phi}\times\mathbf{q}_i) = r_i^0 - \mathbf{m}_i\T\boldsymbol{\rho} - (\mathbf{q}_i\times\mathbf{m}_i)\T\boldsymbol{\phi}, \]

using the triple-product identity \(\mathbf{a}\cdot(\mathbf{b}\times\mathbf{c}) = \mathbf{b}\cdot(\mathbf{c}\times\mathbf{a})\). Each pair therefore contributes one row

\[ \mathbf{J}_i = -\begin{bmatrix} \mathbf{m}_i\T & (\mathbf{q}_i\times\mathbf{m}_i)\T \end{bmatrix} \in \R^{1\times 6}, \qquad \Big(\sum_i \mathbf{J}_i\T\mathbf{J}_i\Big)\,\boldsymbol{\xi} = -\sum_i \mathbf{J}_i\T r_i^0 . \]

Solve this 6 × 6 system, update \(\mathbf{T}^0 \leftarrow \mathbf{T}^0\Exp(\boldsymbol{\xi})\), re-match, repeat. One pair gives one equation, so you need at least six, with normals that point in enough different directions. In a long corridor all normals are perpendicular to the corridor axis \(\mathbf{a}\). Then \(\mathbf{J}_i\) applied to a pure translation along \(\mathbf{a}\) is \(-\mathbf{m}_i\T\mathbf{a} = 0\) for every \(i\): the matrix is singular and the motion along the corridor cannot be estimated. That is the "structure-less corridor" failure of §8.5. §8.5 · p. 248

Switch the widget to point-to-plane and press Run. At the default settings it converges in 6 steps instead of 21, to the same answer. At a 60° turn it fails while point-to-point still succeeds: the linearization is only good near the solution.

5. Matching distributions: GICP and NDT

The book mentions methods that compare local probability distributions instead of raw points. §8.2.1.1 · pp. 229–230 Two are worth knowing by formula.

Generalized ICP (GICP) treats every point as a sample from a small Gaussian that describes the surface around it: covariance \(\mathbf{C}_i^{P}\) for \(\mathbf{p}_i\) and \(\mathbf{C}_i^{Q}\) for \(\mathbf{q}_i\). If the pair is a true match, the difference \(\mathbf{d}_i = \mathbf{p}_i - (\mathbf{R}\mathbf{q}_i + \mathbf{t})\) has zero mean and covariance \(\mathbf{C}_i^{P} + \mathbf{R}\mathbf{C}_i^{Q}\mathbf{R}\T\), and maximum likelihood gives

\[ \min_{\mathbf{R},\mathbf{t}} \sum_i \mathbf{d}_i\T\big(\mathbf{C}_i^{P} + \mathbf{R}\,\mathbf{C}_i^{Q}\,\mathbf{R}\T\big)^{-1}\mathbf{d}_i . \]

With \(\mathbf{C}_i^{P} = \mathbf{I}\), \(\mathbf{C}_i^{Q} = \mathbf{0}\) this is point-to-point; with the weight matrix \(\mathbf{n}_i\mathbf{n}_i\T\) it is point-to-plane; with flat, disk-shaped covariances on both clouds it is "plane-to-plane".

The normal distributions transform (NDT) cuts the fixed cloud into voxels and stores, for each voxel \(v\), the mean \(\boldsymbol{\mu}_v\) and covariance \(\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_v\) of its points (the voxel Gaussians of Week 8). In its original form the moving points \(\mathbf{x}_i = \mathbf{R}\mathbf{q}_i + \mathbf{t}\) are scored by the Gaussian of the voxel they fall in,

\[ \max_{\mathbf{R},\mathbf{t}} \sum_i \exp\!\Big(-\tfrac12 (\mathbf{x}_i - \boldsymbol{\mu}_{v(i)})\T \boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{v(i)}^{-1} (\mathbf{x}_i - \boldsymbol{\mu}_{v(i)})\Big). \]

Finding \(v(i)\) takes a division and a rounding, not a nearest-neighbour search, and the cost surface is smoother than one made of hard point pairs. Summarizing the moving scan by voxels as well gives the distribution-to-distribution matching the book describes. §8.2.1.1 · p. 230

Common mistakes

  • "ICP finds the best alignment." It finds a local minimum near its starting guess. With a poor guess it converges, confidently, to the wrong answer.
  • "A small final error means success." The error never reaches zero even at the truth, because the scans sample different points, and it can be modest at a wrong alignment in a symmetric scene.

Check yourself

Q1. With known pairs, the centroids are p̄ = (4, 1) and q̄ = (1, 2), and the best rotation is 90° counter-clockwise. What is t?

A 90° rotation sends (x, y) to (−y, x), so R q̄ = (−2, 1), and t = p̄ − R q̄ = (4 + 2, 1 − 1) = (6, 0).

Q2. Why does ICP need a starting guess close to the true motion?

Each step lowers the cost for the current pairs, but the pairs come from the current estimate. Far from the truth they tie together unrelated points, and the loop can stop at a wrong alignment.

Q3. A pair has p − (Rq + t) = (0.30, 0.04, −0.10) m and the plane normal is n = (0, 1, 0). What is its point-to-plane residual?

r = nᵀ(p − (Rq + t)) picks out the component along the normal, 0.04 m. The 0.30 m and −0.10 m offsets lie in the plane and are not penalized. (The point-to-point distance would be 0.32 m.)

Q4. A robot runs point-to-plane ICP in a long, straight, featureless tunnel. Which part of its motion is not determined?

All normals are perpendicular to the axis, so sliding along the axis changes no residual and the 6 × 6 system is singular in that direction. (Rotation about the axis is determined as long as the cross-section is not a perfect circle.)

Recap

  1. Registration minimizes a sum of distances between paired points over a rigid motion, equation (8.1). In the book's form (R, t) is applied to q.
  2. With known pairs the point-to-point problem has a closed form: t = p̄ − R q̄, H = Σ q′p′ᵀ = USVᵀ, R = VUᵀ (with a sign fix against reflections).
  3. ICP alternates nearest-neighbour matching, equation (8.3), with that alignment. The cost never increases, so it converges, but only to a local minimum.
  4. Point-to-plane keeps only the error along the surface normal, r = nᵀ(p − Rq − t), and is solved by Gauss-Newton with one 1 × 6 Jacobian row per pair.
  5. GICP weights each pair by local covariances; NDT replaces point pairs by per-voxel Gaussians.

Sources

  1. SLAM Handbook, §8.2 (opening) and §8.2.1 "Foundations of Scan Registration", pp. 227–231; equations (8.1)–(8.3), Figure 8.3; §8.4.1, p. 242 and §8.5, p. 248 for the two cross-references.
  2. Arun, Huang, Blostein, Least-squares fitting of two 3-D point sets, 1987, and Umeyama, Least-squares estimation of transformation parameters between two point patterns, 1991 (the SVD solution and the reflection fix).
  3. Besl and McKay, A method for registration of 3-D shapes, 1992 (the convergence argument for ICP).
  4. Chen and Medioni, Object modelling by registration of multiple range images, 1992 (point-to-plane); the linearization here uses the right perturbation of Solà, Deray, Atchuthan, A micro Lie theory for state estimation in robotics, 2018.
  5. Segal, Haehnel, Thrun, Generalized-ICP, 2009; Biber and Straßer, The normal distributions transform: a new approach to laser scan matching, 2003.

Week 13 · Day 3

From registration to odometry: motion compensation, features, local maps

After today you can name the stages of a LiDAR odometry pipeline, undo motion distortion with a constant-velocity model, classify points as edge or plane from eigenvalues, and explain why scan-to-map registration drifts less than scan-to-scan.

About 60 min · Read §8.2.2–8.2.3, pp. 231–236 (5 pages) · Needs Week 13 Day 2

Read first: §8.2.2 and §8.2.3, pp. 231–236

While you read, look for:

  • The three numbered stages of Figure 8.4 and the arrow that feeds back (p. 231).
  • Four ways to deal with motion distortion, and the weakness of each (p. 232).
  • The eigenvalue rule that separates edge points from planar points (pp. 233–234).
  • Three drawbacks of feature-based odometry, and what made direct methods practical (pp. 234–235).
  • The drift rate quoted in the summary (p. 236).

Today's big idea

LiDAR odometry is yesterday's ICP surrounded by three practical decisions: correct each point for the motion of the sensor during the sweep, decide which points to match and how to find their partners quickly, and register against a local map built from many recent scans instead of the previous scan alone. Done well, this drifts by about one metre per kilometre.

1. The pipeline

The goal of LiDAR odometry is the incremental motion of the sensor, in real time, from the current scan and past observations. §8.2 · p. 227 Figure 8.4 splits it into motion compensation, correspondence search, and relative pose estimation, with the last two iterating. §8.2.2 · p. 231 The diagram below adds the local map that the later sections introduce.

2. Motion compensation

A scan is gathered over a sweep of about 0.1 s while the sensor moves, so its points are measured from slightly different positions. Left alone, this gives a distorted cloud; the same effect in cameras is called rolling shutter. §8.2.2.1 · pp. 231–232 The fix is called motion compensation, undistortion, or deskewing.

Filling the gap: the deskewing formula

Let point \(k\) of the sweep be measured at time \(\tau_k \in [0, T]\) after the sweep started, with sensor-frame coordinates \(\mathbf{p}_k\). Let \(\mathbf{T}(\tau)\) be the sensor pose at that time. The point's world position is \(\mathbf{T}(\tau_k)\mathbf{p}_k\). To express every point in one frame, say the frame at the start of the sweep, apply

\[ \mathbf{p}_k^{\text{start}} = \mathbf{T}(0)^{-1}\,\mathbf{T}(\tau_k)\,\mathbf{p}_k . \]

Everything now depends on knowing the motion inside the sweep, \(\mathbf{T}(0)^{-1}\mathbf{T}(\tau)\). The constant-velocity model assumes the sensor keeps the velocity it had over the previous scan. If the last two estimated poses are \(\mathbf{T}_{j-1}\) and \(\mathbf{T}_j\), one scan period \(T\) apart, the body velocity (a twist, in the notation of Week 4) is

\[ \boldsymbol{\varpi} = \frac{1}{T}\,\Log\!\big(\mathbf{T}_{j-1}^{-1}\mathbf{T}_j\big), \qquad \mathbf{T}(0)^{-1}\mathbf{T}(\tau) = \Exp(\tau\,\boldsymbol{\varpi}), \qquad \mathbf{p}_k^{\text{start}} = \Exp(\tau_k\boldsymbol{\varpi})\,\mathbf{p}_k . \]

Numbers, in 2D. The sensor drives forward at \(v = 6\) m/s while turning at \(\omega = 90^\circ\)/s, and \(T = 0.1\) s. Take the point measured half-way, \(\tau_k = 0.05\) s, at range 5 m straight ahead: \(\mathbf{p}_k = (5, 0)\). By then the sensor has turned \(\theta = 4.5^\circ\) and moved along an arc of radius \(v/\omega = 3.82\) m to \(\big(3.82\sin\theta,\ 3.82(1-\cos\theta)\big) = (0.300, 0.012)\) m. Rotating \((5,0)\) by 4.5° gives \((4.985, 0.392)\); adding the position gives \(\mathbf{p}_k^{\text{start}} = (5.284, 0.404)\). Without compensation the point would sit at \((5, 0)\), wrong by 0.49 m.

Try it: the sensor of Day 1 now drives and turns. Press "Motion compensation", then make the velocity estimate wrong.

Notice that at 6 m/s and 90°/s the sensor moves 0.60 m and turns 9° during one sweep, and the raw points are 24 cm (RMS) away from the walls. With the correct velocity, compensation brings them back to under 1 cm, which is the range noise. With a velocity estimate that is 20% off, about 5 cm of distortion remains.

The book lists four ways to obtain the motion inside the sweep. §8.2.2.1 · p. 232

ApproachWhere the in-sweep motion comes fromStrengthWeakness
Constant-velocity modelThe velocity estimated at the previous stepNeeds no extra sensorInaccurate when the motion has high-frequency content
Continuous-time trajectoryA spline or Gaussian-process trajectory that gives a pose at any instant (Week 5)Corrects every point individually, without linear interpolationSlow in its conventional form, often run offline
IMU-basedGyroscope and accelerometer readings (for example at 200 Hz) integrated over the sweepHandles jerky motion; the de-facto standard on most robotsSuffers from IMU noise, bias, and poor clock synchronization
Point-wise registrationNot needed: the state is updated as each point arrivesNo distortion inside a scan to begin withA different framework from scan-based odometry

3. Features: keep the edges and the planes

A feature-based system does not match every point. It extracts a small number of informative ones and computes correspondences and residuals only for those, which cuts the cost. §8.2.2.2 · pp. 232–233 The usual features are points on edges and on planes. LOAM finds them from a curvature score computed from the differences between a point and its neighbours: high curvature marks an edge, low curvature a plane. §8.2.2.2 · p. 233 The second standard tool is principal component analysis of a point's neighbourhood. §8.2.2.2 · pp. 233–234

Filling the gap: what the eigenvalues say

Take the \(K\) points \(\mathbf{x}_j\) around a point, with mean \(\bar{\mathbf{x}}\), and form their covariance

\[ \mathbf{C} = \frac{1}{K}\sum_{j=1}^{K} (\mathbf{x}_j - \bar{\mathbf{x}})(\mathbf{x}_j - \bar{\mathbf{x}})\T . \]

\(\mathbf{C}\) is symmetric, so it has orthogonal eigenvectors, and the eigenvalue \(\lambda\) of a unit eigenvector \(\mathbf{v}\) is the variance of the points along \(\mathbf{v}\), because \(\mathbf{v}\T\mathbf{C}\mathbf{v} = \frac1K\sum_j (\mathbf{v}\T(\mathbf{x}_j-\bar{\mathbf{x}}))^2\). Sort \(\lambda_1 \ge \lambda_2 \ge \lambda_3\) and read off the shape:

For a plane, the eigenvector of the smallest eigenvalue \(\lambda_3\) is the surface normal: the direction in which the points vary least. That is where yesterday's \(\mathbf{n}_i\) comes from. The same ellipsoid, flattened into a disk, is a surfel. §8.2.2.2 · p. 234

Example in 2D. Five points on a wall: \((0, 0),\ (1, 0.02),\ (2, -0.02),\ (3, 0.01),\ (4, -0.01)\). The mean is \((2, 0)\). The variances are \(\tfrac15(4+1+0+1+4) = 2\) along \(x\) and \(\tfrac15(0 + 0.0004 + 0.0004 + 0.0001 + 0.0001) = 0.0002\) along \(y\), with covariance \(\tfrac15(-0.02 + 0.01 - 0.02) = -0.006\). The eigenvalues are close to 2 and 0.0002, a ratio of ten thousand: a clear line (a wall, in 2D), with normal almost exactly along \(y\).

The book also lists higher-level features: semantic labels that separate static from moving objects, surfels for point-to-plane distances, and intensity, which helps where the geometry has no structure. §8.2.2.2 · p. 234

4. Direct methods and fast search

Features have costs. They discard isolated points that are neither edge nor plane, which hurts among bushes and branches. Their detectors need retuning for each sensor. And the processing load still grows with the size of the scan, which becomes a problem for 64- or 128-beam sensors. §8.2.2.3 · p. 234 A direct method aligns the points themselves, ICP-style, as direct visual methods align pixels (Week 12). What held it back was the cost of the correspondence search. §8.2.2.3 · p. 235

Filling the gap: what the search costs

Equation (8.3) needs, for each of \(N\) scan points, the nearest of \(M\) map points. Checking all of them takes \(N \times M\) distance computations per ICP iteration: for \(N = 10^5\) and \(M = 10^6\) that is \(10^{11}\), far too many at 10 Hz. Two data structures fix this (see Week 8 · Day 3):

  • A k-d tree splits space recursively, so a query descends about \(\log_2 M \approx 20\) levels: roughly \(N\log_2 M = 2\times10^{6}\) steps instead of \(10^{11}\). The incremental k-d tree of Fast-LIO2 can add and remove points and rebalance itself, so the tree is not rebuilt for every scan. §8.2.2.3 · p. 235
  • A voxel grid stores points in a hash table keyed by the integer cell \(\lfloor \mathbf{x}/s \rfloor\) for voxel size \(s\). A query looks only in the cell of the point and its neighbours, a constant amount of work. It may miss the exact nearest neighbour, which the book accepts as an approximation. §8.2.1.2 · p. 230

5. Scan-to-scan or scan-to-map

The first systems registered each scan to the one before it. A single scan is sparse, so many points have no good partner in the previous scan, the registration errors add up, and the map becomes inconsistent. The modern alternative keeps a local map around the sensor and registers each scan to it. §8.2.2.4 · p. 235

AspectScan-to-scanScan-to-map
ReferenceThe previous scan onlyA local map accumulated from many scans
CorrespondencesMany points lack a suitable partnerThe map is much denser, so more pairs are true inliers
Error growthEvery registration adds its own errorEach scan is tied to a map that many scans agree on; lower drift

The starting guess for the fine registration is a motion prediction from scan-to-scan odometry or IMU pre-integration. LOAM interleaved fast scan-to-scan odometry with slower scan-to-map registration; newer systems use a single scan-to-map stage with direct point-wise correspondences in a voxelized local map. Learned LiDAR odometry exists too, with open questions about generalization. §8.2.2.4 · pp. 235–236

Put together, these systems reach drift rates on the order of 1 m per 1000 m travelled, that is 0.1%, depending on the environment and on how dynamic the scene and the sensor motion are. §8.2.3 · p. 236 After a 5 km drive that is still about 5 m of error, and it only grows. Removing it is the job of place recognition, tomorrow.

Common mistakes

  • "Deskewing needs the motion, and the motion is what we are estimating, so it is circular." It only needs a prediction of the motion inside one sweep, from the previous step or an IMU. The registration then refines the pose between sweeps.
  • "More points always give better odometry." Points that match badly, on moving objects or with no partner in the reference, hurt. Features, down-sampling, and a dense local map all aim at good pairs, not many pairs.

Check yourself

Q1. A vehicle drives straight at 10 m/s without turning. A point is measured 0.08 s after the sweep began. If the scan is not compensated, by how much is that point misplaced in the start-of-sweep frame?

The sensor has moved 10 × 0.08 = 0.8 m by then. With no rotation, the correction is exactly that translation.

Q2. The covariance of a point's neighbourhood has eigenvalues 0.50, 0.46, and 0.001 (in m²). What is the point, and what does the eigenvector of 0.001 give you?

Two similar large eigenvalues and one tiny one mean the points spread over a flat patch. They vary least along the normal, which is the eigenvector of the smallest eigenvalue.

Q3. Why does registering to a local map drift less than registering to the previous scan?

A single scan is sparse, so scan-to-scan pairs are often poor and each step's error accumulates. A local map supplies better inlier associations. It contains no loop closures and still needs an initial guess and deskewed input.

Q4. A handheld scanner is shaken while walking. Which motion-compensation method does the book recommend for such jerky motion, and what must be watched?

The constant-velocity assumption breaks for high-frequency motion. An IMU measures it directly at a high rate, but its noise, bias, and timing errors can make it worse than simpler methods if handled carelessly.

Recap

  1. A LiDAR odometry pipeline deskews the scan, searches correspondences, and estimates the pose, repeating the last two until convergence.
  2. Deskewing moves each point by the sensor motion at its own time stamp: p(start) = T(0)⁻¹ T(τ) p, with the in-sweep motion from a constant-velocity model, a continuous-time trajectory, or an IMU.
  3. Edges and planes are found from curvature or from the eigenvalues of the neighbourhood covariance; for a plane, the eigenvector of the smallest eigenvalue is the normal.
  4. Direct methods match all points and depend on fast search structures: k-d trees, incremental k-d trees, voxel grids.
  5. Scan-to-map registration against a dense local map gives drift of about 0.1% of distance travelled, which still grows without bound.

Sources

  1. SLAM Handbook, §8.2.2 "Common Components for LiDAR Odometry" and §8.2.3 "Summary of LiDAR Odometry", pp. 231–236; Figure 8.4.
  2. The deskewing formula is rigid-body kinematics with the exponential map; notation follows Solà, Deray, Atchuthan, A micro Lie theory for state estimation in robotics, 2018.
  3. Friedman, Bentley, Finkel, An algorithm for finding best matches in logarithmic expected time, 1977 (k-d tree search cost).

Week 13 · Day 4

LiDAR place recognition: describing a whole scan

After today you can state the place recognition problem, build a ring-and-sector descriptor of a scan, compare two descriptors under rotation by a column shift, and explain invariance, awareness, and structural aliasing.

About 60 min · Read §8.3, pp. 236–240 (4 pages) · Needs Week 11 Day 5

Read first: §8.3, pp. 236–240

While you read, look for:

  • The two difficulties specific to LiDAR: sparse data and structural aliasing (p. 237, Figure 8.6 on p. 236).
  • The definitions of query and database (p. 237), and the three sources of variation between them (p. 238).
  • The difference between invariance and awareness, and the two reasons awareness is worth having (p. 238).
  • The two coarse representations behind global descriptors: bird's-eye view and range image (p. 239).

Today's big idea

Odometry drifts, so a robot cannot use its own pose estimate to decide that it is back where it was. It has to recognize the place from the scan alone. Place recognition compresses each scan into a descriptor and looks for similar descriptors among those stored earlier. A good descriptor does not care how the robot was turned when it took the scan, and a better one also tells you by how much it was turned, because the next step, ICP, needs a starting guess.

1. A retrieval problem

The task is to detect loop-closure candidates. The query is the current scan. The database is the set of place descriptors collected so far. The goal is to retrieve the database entries that are similar to the query. §8.3.1 · p. 237 The same machinery serves multi-session SLAM and global localization in a prior map. §8.3 · p. 236

The query and the stored scan of the same place never look identical. The sensor may differ, time has passed (objects moved, structures changed), and above all the robot's pose differs: a shift or a turn changes how the same surroundings appear in the sensor frame. A method has to be robust to all three at once. §8.3.1 · pp. 237–238

2. What makes LiDAR different from a camera

LiDAR gives consistent metric 3D structure and is far less affected by lighting than a camera. It brings two difficulties of its own. §8.3 · pp. 236–237

DifficultyWhat it meansHow methods respond
Sparse dataPoints are not on a regular grid, their density depends on the sensor and falls with range (Day 1), and resolution is far below an image'sAvoid per-point keypoint descriptors; describe segments or the whole scan with one global descriptor
Structural aliasingDifferent places with the same geometry look the same: the corridors on two floors, two similar road junctions (Figure 8.6)Describe a place by a set of objects or segments (SegMap, InstaLoc); add a camera

A camera could tell the two corridors apart by a poster on the wall. A single LiDAR scan cannot, and a global descriptor such as Scan Context typically fails there. §8.3 · p. 237

3. A global descriptor you can compute by hand

Global descriptors summarize the coarse pattern of the entire scan. One family starts from a bird's-eye view (BEV): look at the cloud from above and lay a coarse grid over it, either polar or a sparse regular grid. Scan Context uses the polar version and aligns two descriptors in yaw to become independent of heading. §8.3.2.2 · p. 239 The book stops at this description, so here is the construction.

Filling the gap: the polar descriptor and its distance

Divide the ground plane around the sensor into \(N_r\) rings (by distance) and \(N_s\) sectors (by azimuth). A point at range \(r\) and azimuth \(\alpha\) falls into ring \(\lfloor N_r\, r / L_{\max} \rfloor\) and sector \(\lfloor N_s\, \alpha / 2\pi \rfloor\). Store one number per bin in an \(N_r \times N_s\) matrix \(\mathbf{I}\): in Scan Context, the maximum height of the points in the bin, or zero for an empty bin. The original paper uses 20 rings, 60 sectors, and \(L_{\max} = 80\) m.

Rotation becomes a shift. If the robot stands at the same spot but is turned by \(\psi\), every point's azimuth changes by \(-\psi\) and its range stays the same. Rows are unaffected; columns move sideways by \(\psi/(360^\circ/N_s)\) positions, wrapping around.

Distance. Compare column \(j\) of the query, \(\mathbf{c}^q_j\), with column \(j\) of the candidate, \(\mathbf{c}^c_j\), by the cosine distance, average over the columns, and take the best over all column shifts \(n\) of the candidate:

\[ d(\mathbf{I}^q, \mathbf{I}^c) = \frac{1}{N_s}\sum_{j=1}^{N_s}\left(1 - \frac{\mathbf{c}^q_j \cdot \mathbf{c}^c_j}{\norm{\mathbf{c}^q_j}\,\norm{\mathbf{c}^c_j}}\right), \qquad D(\mathbf{I}^q, \mathbf{I}^c) = \min_{n \in \{0,\dots,N_s-1\}} d(\mathbf{I}^q, \mathbf{I}^c_n). \]

The minimizing shift \(n^\ast\) is a by-product with a meaning: the heading difference is \(n^\ast \times 360^\circ/N_s\).

Tiny example, 2 rings by 4 sectors (each sector is 90°). Stored and query descriptors:

\[ \mathbf{I}^c = \begin{bmatrix} 2 & 0 & 1 & 3 \\ 0 & 3 & 1 & 1 \end{bmatrix}, \qquad \mathbf{I}^q = \begin{bmatrix} 3 & 2 & 0 & 1 \\ 1 & 0 & 3 & 1 \end{bmatrix}. \]

With no shift, the four column pairs have cosines \(6/(2\sqrt{10}) = 0.949\), \(0\), \(3/(3\sqrt2) = 0.707\), and \(4/\sqrt{20} = 0.894\), so \(d = \tfrac14(0.051 + 1 + 0.293 + 0.106) = 0.36\). Shift the stored columns right by one and they equal the query's exactly: \(d = 0\). So \(D = 0\) at \(n^\ast = 1\): same place, heading differs by one sector, 90°.

Try it: the stored scan and the query are taken at almost the same spot in the room, with the query turned. The toy stores the number of points in each bin (a 2D scan has no height). Change the heading, then increase the position offset.

Notice that with the query turned by 90° and 0.3 m away, the distance curve has one clear minimum at a shift of 18 columns, which gives a heading change of 90°, and that the third grid then lines up with the first. The distance there is 0.15, against 0.67 for a scan taken 4 m away. Push the offset to 1.5 m: the distance to the same place rises to 0.53 and the heading estimate becomes wrong. The column shift handles rotation, not translation.

Intuition

Unroll the view around you into a strip, like a panorama photo. Turning on the spot does not change the panorama; it only changes where the strip was cut. To compare two panoramas of the same place, slide one along the other until they agree. How far you had to slide is how much you had turned.

Trying every shift against every database entry is slow. Scan Context first searches with a short vector of one number per ring, which does not change under rotation because a row summary ignores the order of the columns, and runs the shift comparison only on the nearest few candidates.

4. Invariance and awareness

The book separates two levels of robustness to the pose difference between query and database. §8.3.1 · p. 238

PropertyMeaningIn the polar descriptor
InvarianceThe method finds the right candidate although the pose differs, but cannot say what the difference isThe per-ring vector: identical for any heading, silent about the heading
AwarenessThe method also estimates the pose differenceThe best column shift: a heading estimate with a resolution of one sector

Awareness is worth the effort for two reasons. It hands the fine registration a starting guess, and Day 2 showed what ICP does without one. And aiming at awareness tends to improve invariance too, for example by estimating heading changes or the degree of overlap between two scans. §8.3.1 · p. 238

5. The families of methods

FamilyIdeaNote from the book
Local descriptorsA descriptor per keypoint, as in visual place recognition; or histograms of local keypointsDescriptors made for dense RGB-D clouds struggle with sparse outdoor LiDAR, and lack the context of the whole scan (pp. 238–239)
Global, bird's-eye viewA coarse top-down image, polar or a sparse grid (Scan Context++, RING++)Scan Context aligns in yaw; RING++ proves invariance and awareness using the Radon transform (p. 239)
Global, range imageThe scan as a dense image of ranges, processed with CNNs or vision transformers (OverlapNet, FRAME)Suits dense multi-beam sensors and reuses computer-vision tools (p. 239)
Segmentation-basedA place as a set of objects or segments (SegMap, InstaLoc)More distinctive, less prone to aliasing than one descriptor per scan (p. 239)
Local plus globalKeep local geometry and overall structure together (BTC)Global descriptors assume a consistent viewing direction, as for vehicles on roads; this relaxes that (pp. 239–240)
Learned on raw pointsNetworks extract point-wise features without hand-made rulesTraining for place discrimination and relative pose together improved registration (p. 240)

LiDAR and visual place recognition play the same role and are judged by the same metrics, and they tend to fail in different places. Robots that carry both sensors often use both. §8.3.3 · p. 240

Common mistakes

  • "The robot can find loop closures by checking which old poses are near its current pose estimate." After a long loop the estimate may be off by more than the distance between distinct places. Place recognition must work from appearance. A pose prior can narrow the search only while the drift is small.
  • "A rotation-invariant descriptor is also translation-invariant." A polar grid is centred on the sensor. Moving the sensor sideways changes ranges and azimuths together and reshuffles the bins, as the widget shows.
  • "A descriptor match is a loop closure." It is a candidate. Two identical corridors match perfectly. The candidate still has to survive registration and verification.

Check yourself

Q1. A polar descriptor has 60 sectors. The best match with a stored descriptor is found at a shift of 9 columns. By how much do the two headings differ?

Each sector spans 360°/60 = 6°, and 9 × 6° = 54°.

Q2. A method retrieves the correct place whatever the robot's heading, but outputs nothing about the heading. In the book's terms it has

Invariance: the candidate is found despite the pose difference. Awareness would additionally estimate that difference, which is what gives ICP its starting guess.

Q3. A robot maps an office building. Its place recognition keeps matching the corridor on floor 3 to the corridor on floor 2. What is this, and what helps?

The geometry of the two corridors is the same, so one descriptor per scan cannot separate them. Object- or segment-level descriptions, or visual texture, can.

Q4. Two descriptor columns are a = (1, 0, 2) and b = (2, 0, 4). What is their cosine distance, 1 − a·b/(|a||b|)?

b = 2a, so the vectors are parallel: a·b = 10, |a||b| = √5 × √20 = 10, and the distance is 1 − 1 = 0. Cosine distance compares the pattern of a column, not its overall size.

Recap

  1. Place recognition retrieves, for a query scan, similar entries from a database of descriptors of visited places. It produces loop-closure candidates.
  2. LiDAR data is sparse and unstructured, which favours global descriptors, and geometry repeats, which causes structural aliasing.
  3. A polar bird's-eye-view descriptor turns a heading change into a column shift. The best shift gives both a distance and a heading estimate.
  4. Invariance finds the place despite the pose difference; awareness also estimates the difference and gives registration its starting guess.
  5. Families: local, global (BEV or range image), segment-based, local plus global, and learned on raw points. LiDAR and cameras complement each other.

Sources

  1. SLAM Handbook, §8.3 "LiDAR Place Recognition", pp. 236–240; Figure 8.6.
  2. Kim and Kim, Scan Context: Egocentric spatial descriptor for place recognition within 3D point cloud map, 2018 (the ring-and-sector construction, the column-shift distance, the ring key, and the 20 × 60 × 80 m configuration).
  3. The widget's descriptor stores point counts instead of maximum heights because its scans are 2D; the comparison is the same.

Week 13 · Day 5

The full LiDAR SLAM system: loop closures, pose graphs, and the map

After today you can trace a scan through the four modules of a LiDAR SLAM system, work out how a loop closure spreads a correction over the trajectory, and explain how the map is updated and how several sessions or robots are merged.

About 60 min · Read §8.4–8.5, pp. 240–249 (10 pages, mostly prose and figures) · Needs Week 13 Day 4

Read first: §8.4 and §8.5, pp. 240–249

These pages read quickly. While you read, look for:

  • The four numbered modules of Figure 8.7 and the rates they run at (pp. 241–242).
  • What turns a place-recognition candidate into a constraint, and the checks against false ones (p. 242).
  • The kinds of factor in Figure 8.8 (p. 243), and the two tricks that keep the graph small (pp. 243–244).
  • The options for updating the map after optimization (p. 244), and what an anchor node is for (pp. 245–246).
  • In §8.5, why uncertainty is called an open problem (p. 249).

Today's big idea

A LiDAR SLAM system is odometry plus memory. Odometry gives a locally consistent trajectory that drifts. Place recognition notices a revisit, registration measures it, and pose-graph optimization bends the whole past trajectory so that odometry and loop closures agree as well as they can. Then the map, which was drawn with the old poses, has to be redrawn or deformed to match.

1. Four modules at two rates

Most current systems are built from the four modules of Figure 8.7: odometry, loop closure detection, pose-graph optimization, and map update. Odometry runs at the sensor rate, for example 10 Hz, and the others more slowly, for example 1 Hz. §8.4.1 · p. 242

The odometry module sees only the surroundings of the sensor, its active local map (Day 3). It knows nothing of a place visited ten minutes ago. Global consistency, meaning that current and past observations agree in one map, is the job of the slow lane. §8.4 · pp. 240–242

2. From a candidate to a constraint

Place recognition only says that two scans look alike. A loop closure needs a number: the relative transformation between the two poses. That takes three more steps. §8.4.1 · p. 242

  1. Initial guess. In a small pose graph the current estimates of the two poses give a geometric prior. Otherwise the guess comes from the place-recognition method itself (yesterday's awareness), or from a global registration method that needs no guess and tolerates low overlap.
  2. Fine registration. ICP between the two scans, started from that guess, yields the relative pose.
  3. Verification. Heuristics reject doubtful candidates: the travel distance or time between the two visits, or the confidence of a RANSAC-based alignment (Week 6 · Day 2).

A false loop closure is worse than a missed one. It ties together two places that are not the same and bends the whole map to fit. For the ones that slip through, robust pose-graph optimization can down-weight or disable individual constraints (Week 6). §8.4.2 · p. 244

3. Pose-graph optimization

The back-end is a factor graph whose variables are sensor poses and whose factors are relative-pose constraints, hence pose graph. Figure 8.8 shows the factor types: a prior that fixes the origin, odometry factors between consecutive poses, loop-closure factors between distant ones, and optional attitude factors that constrain roll and pitch when an inertial sensor is available. §8.4.2 · p. 243 A relative-pose measurement \(\tilde{\mathbf{T}}_{ij}\) between poses \(\mathbf{T}_i\) and \(\mathbf{T}_j\) contributes the residual \(\mathbf{e}_{ij} = \Log\big(\tilde{\mathbf{T}}_{ij}^{-1}\,\mathbf{T}_i^{-1}\mathbf{T}_j\big)\), and pose-graph optimization (PGO) minimizes \(\sum \mathbf{e}_{ij}\T\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{ij}^{-1}\mathbf{e}_{ij}\) over all poses, by the methods of Weeks 2 to 4.

Filling the gap: how a loop closure spreads the correction

A one-dimensional loop shows the mechanism with no Lie groups. A robot makes \(n\) odometry steps \(u_1,\dots,u_n\) with variances \(\sigma_1^2,\dots,\sigma_n^2\). A loop closure then measures the total displacement between the first and last pose as \(z\), with variance \(\sigma_L^2\). Odometry alone says the total is \(\sum_k u_k\), so the two disagree by

\[ e = z - \sum_{k=1}^{n} u_k . \]

Let \(\delta_k\) be the correction applied to step \(k\). Least squares minimizes

\[ \sum_{k=1}^{n}\frac{\delta_k^2}{\sigma_k^2} + \frac{\big(e - \sum_k \delta_k\big)^2}{\sigma_L^2}. \]

Setting the derivative with respect to \(\delta_k\) to zero gives \(\delta_k/\sigma_k^2 = (e - \sum_m \delta_m)/\sigma_L^2\). The right side is the same for every \(k\); call it \(\mu\). Then \(\delta_k = \mu\sigma_k^2\), and summing over \(k\) and solving for \(\mu\) gives

\[ \delta_k = e\,\frac{\sigma_k^2}{\sigma_1^2 + \dots + \sigma_n^2 + \sigma_L^2}. \]

Each step absorbs a share of the disagreement in proportion to its variance. Numbers: three steps \(u = (10, 10, 10)\) m with variances \((1, 1, 4)\), and an accurate loop closure, \(z = 29.4\) m with \(\sigma_L^2 \approx 0\). Then \(e = -0.6\) and \(\delta = -0.6 \times (\tfrac16, \tfrac16, \tfrac46) = (-0.1, -0.1, -0.4)\). The corrected positions are \(0,\ 9.9,\ 19.8,\ 29.4\). Every pose moved, not only the last, and the least trusted step moved most.

This is why the book cares about the covariances on the edges: giving a high covariance to stretches where drift is likely to be high makes the optimizer put the correction there. §8.4.2 · p. 244 It is also why §8.5 lists uncertainty as unsolved. Estimated odometry uncertainty is often unreliable, so many systems fall back on fixed covariances, which spreads the error evenly whether or not that is where it arose. §8.5 · p. 249

Keeping it real-time. The graph grows for as long as the robot runs, but it is sparse, with few edges per node, and sparse factorization with good ordering and incremental relinearization (iSAM2, Week 3) updates graphs of over 1000 nodes in a fraction of a second. §8.4.2 · p. 243 Two habits keep the node count down. §8.4.2 · pp. 243–244

  • Add a node every few metres travelled, not for every scan.
  • Group the trajectory into submaps of fixed size, say 30 m of travel, with one node each, and treat the odometry inside a submap as exact.

Count it for a robot that walks at 1 m/s for one hour, 3.6 km. One node per scan at 10 Hz is 36,000 nodes. One node every 2 m is 1,800. One submap per 30 m is 120. This is how pose-graph SLAM reaches city scale.

4. Updating the map

After optimization the trajectory is globally consistent. The map is not: its points were placed using the old, drifted poses. At a revisited junction the walls appear twice, slightly apart, as on the left of Figure 8.9. §8.4.2 · p. 244

Way to update the mapHow it worksCost
RebuildRe-insert all past scans at their corrected posesSimple, but every past observation must be stored for ever, which does not scale to large environments
DeformBend the existing map representation to follow the correctionNo need to keep every raw scan
Attach map elements to posesStore each surfel or submap relative to a pose in the graphThe map follows the optimized poses; the more scalable route

§8.4.2 · p. 244 The third option is worth spelling out. If a point is stored as \(\mathbf{p}\) in the frame of pose \(\mathbf{T}_i\), its world position is \(\mathbf{T}_i\mathbf{p}\). When the optimizer changes \(\mathbf{T}_i\), the world position changes with it and nothing has to be recomputed. The price is the assumption that the points inside one submap are correct relative to each other, the same assumption that made submap nodes possible.

5. Several sessions, several robots, and what is still open

Taking the finished clouds of two separate runs and aligning them rigidly does not work well: each run keeps its own small internal errors, about a metre per kilometre, so walls double up wherever those errors differ (Figure 8.10). The sessions have to be optimized jointly. §8.4.3 · p. 245

Filling the gap: what an anchor node does

Let each session \(s\) keep its poses \(\mathbf{T}^s_i\) in its own coordinate frame, and add one extra variable per session, the anchor \(\boldsymbol{\Delta}_s \in \SE(3)\), which places that frame in a common global frame: the global pose is \(\boldsymbol{\Delta}_s\mathbf{T}^s_i\). Factors inside a session do not see the anchor, because \((\boldsymbol{\Delta}_s\mathbf{T}^s_i)^{-1}(\boldsymbol{\Delta}_s\mathbf{T}^s_j) = \mathbf{T}^{s\,-1}_i\mathbf{T}^s_j\). A loop closure between pose \(i\) of session \(a\) and pose \(j\) of session \(b\) measures

\[ \tilde{\mathbf{T}} \approx \big(\boldsymbol{\Delta}_a\mathbf{T}^a_i\big)^{-1}\big(\boldsymbol{\Delta}_b\mathbf{T}^b_j\big), \]

and is the only kind of factor that involves the anchors. Until the first such factor exists, \(\boldsymbol{\Delta}_b\) is completely free: the sessions float relative to each other. Since there is no geometric prior between disconnected sessions, that first link can only come from place recognition. §8.4.3 · pp. 245–246

Multi-robot SLAM does the same with data arriving live from several robots, so that a team can share one map and plan together. A centralized system sends measurements to a base station that computes the combined map; a decentralized (distributed) one builds a map on every robot and merges the robot maps at a base station. §8.4.3.1 · p. 246 Two competitions mark the progress. At MAGIC in 2010, the winning team ran 14 wheeled robots with 2D LiDAR in a 500 m × 500 m area; each sent pose-graph constraints to a base station that built one 2D map. At the DARPA Subterranean Challenge in 2021, robots with 3D LiDAR and further odometry sources ran pose-graph SLAM on board in tunnels with stairs and ramps, and a base station merged the maps; one system sent compressed surfel submaps, 21.5 MB per robot for a complete map. §8.4.3.1 · pp. 247–248

The hardest version is fully distributed SLAM, where every robot maintains the joint map under communication limits, and consistency is the central issue. §8.4.3.1 · p. 248 The chapter closes with four open areas. §8.5 · pp. 248–249

  • Robustness. Cluttered scenes, featureless corridors and mines, snow, fog, and dust still break systems, and performance depends on hand tuning. Day 2's singular 6 × 6 matrix is the corridor case.
  • Multi-sensor fusion. Radar in rain or smoke, cameras in tunnels. Open questions are redundancy against computation, early (tightly coupled) against late fusion, and imperfect calibration and synchronization.
  • Uncertainty. Fusing estimates needs calibrated covariances, and those from ICP-based odometry are often unreliable.
  • Deployment. Size, weight, power, and latency matter: the most accurate system is not always the right one for a car that must react quickly.

Common mistakes

  • "After a loop closure, snap the current pose to the old one." That fixes one pose and leaves a tear in the trajectory. The correction is distributed over all poses of the loop, in proportion to their uncertainty.
  • "Once the poses are optimized the map is correct." The map was built with the old poses. Without a map update the walls stay doubled.

Check yourself

Q1. A robot drives at 2 m/s for 30 minutes with a 10 Hz LiDAR. How many pose-graph nodes does it create if it adds one node every 3 m?

It travels 2 × 1800 = 3600 m, so 3600/3 = 1,200 nodes. One node per scan would be 18,000.

Q2. Place recognition reports that the current scan resembles scan 412. What has to happen before an edge is added to the pose graph?

Similarity is not a measurement. The edge needs a relative transformation, obtained by ICP from a good starting guess, and the candidate should pass checks that guard against false loop closures.

Q3. Three odometry steps have variances 1, 1, and 2. An exact loop closure shows that their sum is 0.8 m too short. How much is added to the third step?

δ₃ = e σ₃²/(σ₁² + σ₂² + σ₃²) = 0.8 × 2/4 = 0.4 m. The first two steps get 0.2 m each.

Q4. In multi-session SLAM, what does the anchor node of a session represent?

Each session keeps its own frame. The anchor places that frame in the global one, and it is constrained only by loop closures between sessions.

Recap

  1. LiDAR SLAM = odometry (fast) + loop closure detection, pose-graph optimization, and map update (slower).
  2. A place-recognition candidate becomes a constraint only after fine registration from a good initial guess and verification.
  3. PGO distributes the loop-closure correction over the trajectory in proportion to edge covariances. Sparsity, sparse node placement, and submaps keep it real-time.
  4. The map must be updated after optimization: rebuilt, deformed, or attached to poses so that it follows them.
  5. Multi-session and multi-robot SLAM add anchor nodes and inter-session loop closures. Robustness, fusion, uncertainty, and deployment remain open.

Sources

  1. SLAM Handbook, §8.4 "LiDAR SLAM" and §8.5 "Further Readings & Recent Trends", pp. 240–249; Figures 8.7–8.12.
  2. The one-dimensional loop is weighted linear least squares, as in Thrun, Burgard, Fox, Probabilistic Robotics, 2005 (graph-based SLAM).
  3. Kim, Kaess, Fletcher, Leonard, Bachrach, Roy, Teller, Multiple relative pose graphs for robust cooperative mapping, 2010 (the anchor-node formulation used in the note).

Week 13 · Review

Week 13 review: LiDAR SLAM from pulse to pose graph

After today you can go from a time-of-flight measurement to a registered scan, a place descriptor, and a loop-closed pose graph, and do the small calculations at each step by hand.

About 60 min · No new pages

The week in one paragraph

A LiDAR times laser pulses to get ranges and pairs them with beam angles to get a point cloud, dense nearby and sparse far away, gathered over a sweep of about 0.1 s. Scan registration finds the rigid motion between two clouds: in closed form by SVD when the pairs are known, and by ICP, alternating nearest-neighbour matching with alignment, when they are not. Point-to-plane, GICP, and NDT change what "distance" means. A LiDAR odometry system wraps registration with motion compensation, feature selection or fast search, and a local map, and drifts by roughly 0.1% of the distance travelled. Place recognition describes whole scans so that revisits can be detected without trusting the drifted pose. Verified loop closures enter a pose graph, whose optimization redistributes the error over the trajectory, after which the map is updated to match.

1. Formula sheet

What it isFormulaWhere
Range from time of flight; gap between neighbouring points\(d = c\,\Delta t/2\), \(\ s \approx r\,\Delta\theta\)§8.1, p. 225 · Day 1
Registration cost\(\min_{\mathbf{R},\mathbf{t}} \sum_{(\mathbf{p},\mathbf{q})\in\mathsf{C}} d(\mathbf{p}_i, \mathbf{R}\mathbf{q}_i + \mathbf{t})\)(8.1), p. 228 · Day 2
Closed form for known pairs (point-to-point)\(\mathbf{t} = \bar{\mathbf{p}} - \mathbf{R}\bar{\mathbf{q}}\), \(\ \mathbf{H} = \sum_i \mathbf{q}_i'\mathbf{p}_i'{}\T = \mathbf{U}\mathbf{S}\mathbf{V}\T\), \(\ \mathbf{R} = \mathbf{V}\mathbf{U}\T\)Horn's method, p. 227 · derived on Day 2
The same in 2D\(\theta = \operatorname{atan2}\big(\sum_i (q_{i,x}'p_{i,y}' - q_{i,y}'p_{i,x}'),\ \sum_i \mathbf{q}_i'\cdot\mathbf{p}_i'\big)\)Day 2
ICP correspondences\(\mathbf{q} = \argmin_{\mathbf{q}'\in\mathsf{Q}} \norm{\mathbf{p} - (\mathbf{R}^{k-1}\mathbf{q}' + \mathbf{t}^{k-1})}_2\)(8.3), p. 230 · Day 2
Point-to-plane residual and Jacobian row, \(\mathbf{m}_i = \mathbf{R}^{0\mathsf{T}}\mathbf{n}_i\)\(r_i = \mathbf{n}_i\T(\mathbf{p}_i - \mathbf{R}\mathbf{q}_i - \mathbf{t})\), \(\ \mathbf{J}_i = -[\,\mathbf{m}_i\T \ \ (\mathbf{q}_i\times\mathbf{m}_i)\T\,]\)Figure 8.3c, p. 229 · Day 2
Deskewing with constant velocity \(\boldsymbol{\varpi}\)\(\mathbf{p}_k^{\text{start}} = \Exp(\tau_k\boldsymbol{\varpi})\,\mathbf{p}_k\)§8.2.2.1, p. 232 · Day 3
Neighbourhood covariance; edge, plane\(\mathbf{C} = \tfrac1K\sum_j(\mathbf{x}_j-\bar{\mathbf{x}})(\mathbf{x}_j-\bar{\mathbf{x}})\T\); edge \(\lambda_1 \gg \lambda_2\); plane \(\lambda_2 \gg \lambda_3\)§8.2.2.2, pp. 233–234 · Day 3
Polar descriptor distance; heading from the best shift \(n^\ast\)\(D = \min_n \tfrac{1}{N_s}\sum_j \big(1 - \cos\angle(\mathbf{c}^q_j, \mathbf{c}^c_{j,n})\big)\), \(\ \psi = n^\ast\, 360^\circ/N_s\)§8.3.2.2, p. 239 · Day 4
Share of a loop-closure discrepancy \(e\) taken by step \(k\)\(\delta_k = e\,\sigma_k^2 / (\sum_m \sigma_m^2 + \sigma_L^2)\)§8.4.2, p. 244 · Day 5

2. Mixed quiz

Check yourself

Q1. A surface is 45 m from a time-of-flight LiDAR. How long after emission does the echo arrive?

Δt = 2d/c = 90/(3×10⁸) = 3×10⁻⁷ s = 300 ns.

Q2. A wall facing a 3D LiDAR is moved from 10 m to 20 m. What happens to the number of points per square metre on it?
