The gap between neighbours is rΔθ in both the horizontal and the vertical direction. Doubling r doubles both gaps, so the density falls by a factor of four.

Q3. In the closed-form alignment you find det(VUᵀ) = −1. What does that mean, and what do you do?

An orthogonal matrix with determinant −1 mirrors the cloud. Flipping the sign of the direction with the smallest singular value gives the best proper rotation.

Q4. Which statement about point-to-point ICP is true?

Matching picks the closest partner for the current estimate and alignment is an exact minimization, so the cost is monotone. Convergence is to a local minimum that depends on the starting guess.

Q5. A sensor turns at 20°/s without translating; one sweep takes 0.1 s. Uncompensated, about how far sideways is a point at 20 m range displaced if it was measured at the very end of the sweep?

The sensor has turned 2° = 0.0349 rad by the end of the sweep, and 20 m × 0.0349 = 0.70 m. Rotation errors grow with range.

Q6. A neighbourhood covariance has eigenvalues 0.9, 0.002, and 0.001. What kind of point is this, and which eigenvector is useful?

One dominant eigenvalue means the points lie along a line. Its eigenvector is the line direction.

Q7. A polar descriptor has 24 sectors. The robot revisits a place with its heading changed by 135°. Which column shift should give the best match?

One sector is 360°/24 = 15°, and 135°/15° = 9 columns (or 24 − 9 = 15 counted the other way round).

Q8. Four odometry steps have equal variance. An exact loop closure shows the total is 1.2 m too long. By how much does the pose reached after the second step move?

Each step is shortened by 1.2/4 = 0.3 m. The pose after two steps has accumulated two corrections: 0.6 m.

3. Pen-and-paper problems

  1. A 2D LiDAR has an angular step of 0.25° and spins at 10 Hz on a vehicle driving at 12 m/s. (a) How many points does one scan contain? (b) What is the echo delay for a wall at 60 m? (c) How far apart are neighbouring points on that wall if it faces the sensor? (d) How far does the vehicle move during one scan?

    Solution

    (a) 360/0.25 = 1440 points. (b) \(\Delta t = 2d/c = 120/(3\times10^8) = 4\times10^{-7}\) s = 400 ns. (c) \(s \approx r\Delta\theta = 60 \times 0.25 \times \pi/180 = 0.262\) m. (d) One scan takes 0.1 s, so 12 × 0.1 = 1.2 m. That is more than four times the point spacing at 60 m, which is why the scan has to be deskewed.

  2. Three pairs are given: \(\mathbf{q}_1 = (1, 0)\), \(\mathbf{q}_2 = (-1, 0)\), \(\mathbf{q}_3 = (0, 3)\) and \(\mathbf{p}_1 = (2, 0)\), \(\mathbf{p}_2 = (2, 2)\), \(\mathbf{p}_3 = (5, 1)\). Find the rotation angle \(\theta\) and translation \(\mathbf{t}\) with \(\mathbf{p}_i = \mathbf{R}(\theta)\mathbf{q}_i + \mathbf{t}\).

    Solution

    Centroids: \(\bar{\mathbf{q}} = (0, 1)\), \(\bar{\mathbf{p}} = (3, 1)\). Centred points: \(\mathbf{q}' = (1,-1),\ (-1,-1),\ (0, 2)\) and \(\mathbf{p}' = (-1,-1),\ (-1, 1),\ (2, 0)\).

    \(A = \sum \mathbf{q}'\cdot\mathbf{p}' = (-1+1) + (1-1) + (0+0) = 0\).

    \(B = \sum (q_x'p_y' - q_y'p_x') = (-1-1) + (-1-1) + (0-4) = -8\).

    \(\theta = \operatorname{atan2}(-8, 0) = -90^\circ\). A rotation by −90° sends \((x, y)\) to \((y, -x)\), so \(\mathbf{R}\bar{\mathbf{q}} = (1, 0)\) and \(\mathbf{t} = \bar{\mathbf{p}} - \mathbf{R}\bar{\mathbf{q}} = (2, 1)\). Check: \(\mathbf{R}\mathbf{q}_3 + \mathbf{t} = (3, 0) + (2, 1) = (5, 1) = \mathbf{p}_3\).

  3. A 2D scan is matched to two walls with point-to-plane ICP. The current estimate is \(\mathbf{R}^0 = \mathbf{I}\), \(\mathbf{t}^0 = \mathbf{0}\), and the rotation is known to be correct, so only the translation update \(\boldsymbol{\rho}\) is solved for. Three pairs lie on a wall with normal \((1, 0)\) and have residual \(r^0 = 0.2\) m each. Two pairs lie on a wall with normal \((0, 1)\) and have \(r^0 = -0.1\) m each. (a) Find \(\boldsymbol{\rho}\). (b) What changes if the first wall is not visible?

    Solution

    (a) With \(\mathbf{R}^0 = \mathbf{I}\), \(\mathbf{m}_i = \mathbf{n}_i\) and the translation part of the Jacobian row is \(\mathbf{J}_i = -\mathbf{n}_i\T\). The normal equations are \(\big(\sum_i \mathbf{n}_i\mathbf{n}_i\T\big)\boldsymbol{\rho} = \sum_i \mathbf{n}_i r_i^0\):

    \[ \begin{bmatrix} 3 & 0 \\ 0 & 2 \end{bmatrix}\boldsymbol{\rho} = \begin{bmatrix} 3 \times 0.2 \\ 2 \times (-0.1) \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 0.6 \\ -0.2 \end{bmatrix} \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \boldsymbol{\rho} = (0.2, -0.1). \]

    Check: the new residuals are \(r_i^0 - \mathbf{n}_i\T\boldsymbol{\rho} = 0.2 - 0.2 = 0\) and \(-0.1 + 0.1 = 0\).

    (b) The matrix becomes \(\begin{bmatrix} 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 2 \end{bmatrix}\), which is singular. The second component is still \(-0.1\), but the first is undetermined: sliding along the remaining wall changes no residual. This is the corridor degeneracy, and no number of extra points on that wall cures it.

  4. A robot makes four odometry steps \(u = (5, 5, 5, 5)\) m with variances \((0.01, 0.01, 0.04, 0.04)\) m². A loop closure measures the displacement from the first pose to the last as \(z = 19.0\) m with variance \(\sigma_L^2 = 0.02\) m². (a) Find the corrected poses. (b) How much disagreement is left on the loop-closure edge, and why is it not zero? (c) What happens as \(\sigma_L^2 \to \infty\)?

    Solution

    (a) \(e = z - \sum u_k = 19 - 20 = -1\). The denominator is \(0.01 + 0.01 + 0.04 + 0.04 + 0.02 = 0.12\), so

    \[ \delta = -1 \times \frac{(0.01, 0.01, 0.04, 0.04)}{0.12} = (-0.083, -0.083, -0.333, -0.333). \]

    The corrected steps are \(4.917, 4.917, 4.667, 4.667\), and the poses are \(0,\ 4.917,\ 9.833,\ 14.5,\ 19.167\).

    (b) The corrected total is 19.167 m, so the loop-closure edge keeps a residual of \(19.0 - 19.167 = -0.167\) m \(= e\,\sigma_L^2/0.12\). The loop closure is itself noisy, so it takes a share of the disagreement in proportion to its own variance, like every other edge.

    (c) All \(\delta_k \to 0\): a measurement with unbounded variance carries no information, and the odometry-only solution is kept. In the other limit, \(\sigma_L^2 \to 0\), the corrections sum to exactly \(e\).

You are ready for next week if you can

  • Convert a time delay to a range and a (range, angle) pair to a point, and say how point spacing scales with range.
  • Write the registration cost (8.1), solve it for known pairs, and describe the two half-steps of ICP and why it needs a good initial guess.
  • Explain what the point-to-plane residual ignores, and why a corridor makes its normal equations singular.
  • Deskew a point given its time stamp and a constant velocity.
  • Explain how a polar descriptor turns a heading change into a column shift, and what invariance and awareness mean.
  • Describe what happens between a place-recognition candidate and an updated map.

Sources

  1. SLAM Handbook, Chapter 8 "LiDAR SLAM", pp. 224–249.
  2. Arun, Huang, Blostein, Least-squares fitting of two 3-D point sets, 1987; Umeyama, Least-squares estimation of transformation parameters between two point patterns, 1991.
  3. Kim and Kim, Scan Context: Egocentric spatial descriptor for place recognition within 3D point cloud map, 2018.

Week 14 · Day 1

Radar sensors and FMCW: range from a beat frequency, speed from a phase

After today you can name the two radar types used in robotics, compute the range of a target from the beat frequency of an FMCW chirp, and compute its radial velocity from the phase change between two chirps.

About 60 min · Read §9.1.1–9.1.2.3, pp. 250–256 (7 pages) · Needs Week 13 Day 1

Read first: §9.1.1–9.1.2.3, pp. 250–256

While you read, look for:

  • Figure 9.1 (p. 250): the front-end and back-end are the ones you know. Find the two boxes that are specific to radar.
  • The main data product of each sensor type: the polar radargram and the radar datacube (p. 252).
  • Equation (9.2) on p. 255, and what the slope \(S\) is.
  • Equations (9.4) and (9.5) on p. 256, and where the limit \(v_{\max}\) comes from.

Today's big idea

An FMCW radar does not time an echo with a stopwatch. It transmits a tone whose frequency climbs steadily and compares the echo with what it is transmitting at that moment. The echo left earlier, so it is lower in frequency, and the size of that gap is proportional to the range. Velocity comes from a second comparison: how much the phase of the gap signal has turned between one chirp and the next.

1. Two kinds of radar

Radar (radio detection and ranging) sends radio waves and listens for reflections. It works in smoke, dust, rain and darkness, reaches far, and can measure velocity directly, which is why its use in SLAM is growing. Ch. 9 intro · p. 250 Robotics uses millimeter-wave (mmWave) radar: wavelengths of 1–10 mm, frequencies of 30–300 GHz, and in practice mostly the 76–81 GHz band reserved for cars. §9.1.2 · p. 253 Wavelength and frequency are tied by \(\lambda = c/f\), so a 77 GHz radar has \(\lambda = 3\times10^{8}/77\times10^{9} \approx 3.9\) mm.

Two sensor designs dominate. §9.1.1 · pp. 250–252

PropertySpinning radarSystem-on-a-chip (SoC) radar
How it covers anglesOne antenna, rotated mechanicallyA fixed array of transmit and receive antennas whose signals are combined
Main data productPolar radargram: received power for every azimuth and range binRadar datacube
Dimensions2D: azimuth and range, no elevation, although echoes come from the whole vertical beamAzimuth, elevation, range and radial velocity: "3+1D" or "4D". With few vertical antennas: "2+1D"
VelocityOften missing: one pulse per antenna angle is not enough. Recent work recovers it from neighbouring azimuthsMeasured for every return
StrengthFull 360° view, objects detected beyond 100 mLight, low power, no moving parts

A spinning 3D radar with stacked beams, built like a 3D LiDAR, is not practical: radar antennas and their focusing hardware are far larger than laser diodes. §9.1.1.1 · p. 252

How strongly an object answers is its radar cross section (RCS): the size of an imaginary sphere that would reflect the same energy. It depends on material, size and shape. A truck or a concrete wall has a high RCS, a pedestrian a low one. The echo strength, called radar intensity, depends on the transmitted power and the RCS. §9.1.2.1 · p. 253 You will meet intensity again on Day 4, where it replaces the height that LiDAR descriptors use.

2. The chirp and the beat frequency

FMCW stands for frequency-modulated continuous wave. The transmit antenna (TX) emits a chirp: a signal whose frequency rises linearly from \(f_m\) to \(f_M\) during a time \(T\). The bandwidth is \(B = f_M - f_m\) and the slope is \(S = B/T\). Repeating up chirps one after the other is called sawtooth modulation. §9.1.2.2 · pp. 253–255

The echo from a target at distance \(d\) comes back after the round-trip time \(t_0\), which is equation (9.1) read backwards:

\[ t_0 = \frac{2d}{c} \qquad\Longleftrightarrow\qquad d = \frac{c}{2}\,t_0 . \tag{9.1} \]

The receiver mixes the echo with the chirp it is transmitting at that instant. The output is the intermediate frequency (IF) signal, also called the beat signal: a sine wave of constant frequency \(f_0\).

Read the picture as geometry. At time \(t\) the transmitter is at frequency \(f_m + St\). The echo arriving at that moment left at time \(t - t_0\), so it has frequency \(f_m + S(t - t_0)\). The difference does not depend on \(t\):

\[ f_0 = S\,t_0 = \frac{B}{T}\cdot\frac{2d}{c} = \frac{2Bd}{Tc} = \frac{2Sd}{c} \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad d = \frac{c\,f_0}{2S}. \tag{9.2} \]

Worked example. Take \(B = 300\) MHz, \(T = 40\ \mu\text{s}\), and a target at \(d = 12\) m. The delay is \(t_0 = 24/(3\times10^{8}) = 80\) ns. The slope is \(S = 3\times10^{8}/(40\times10^{-6}) = 7.5\times10^{12}\) Hz/s. The beat frequency is \(f_0 = 7.5\times10^{12}\times 80\times10^{-9} = 600\) kHz. A delay of 80 billionths of a second, which is hard to time directly, has become a 600 kHz tone, which is easy to measure.

Filling the gap: why mixing gives the difference frequency

The book says the echo is "mixed with" the transmitted chirp. A mixer multiplies two signals, and the product of two cosines is

\[ \cos a \,\cos b = \tfrac12\cos(a-b) + \tfrac12\cos(a+b). \]

The sum term oscillates at about twice 77 GHz and is removed by a low-pass filter. The difference term stays. To find it, write the phase of the transmitted chirp. Frequency is the rate of change of phase divided by \(2\pi\), so a frequency \(f_m + St\) integrates to the phase

\[ \varphi_{\text{TX}}(t) = 2\pi\left(f_m t + \tfrac12 S t^2\right). \]

The echo is a delayed copy with phase \(\varphi_{\text{TX}}(t - t_0)\). Subtract and expand \((t-t_0)^2 = t^2 - 2t\,t_0 + t_0^2\):

\[ \begin{aligned} \varphi_{\text{TX}}(t) - \varphi_{\text{TX}}(t-t_0) & = 2\pi\left(f_m t_0 + S t_0\, t - \tfrac12 S t_0^2\right) \\ & = 2\pi \underbrace{(S t_0)}_{f_0}\, t + \underbrace{2\pi f_m t_0 - \pi S t_0^2}_{\phi_0} . \end{aligned} \]

So the IF signal is a sinusoid with frequency \(f_0 = S t_0\) and a constant phase \(\phi_0\). The second part of \(\phi_0\) is smaller than the first by the factor \(S t_0/(2 f_m) = f_0/(2 f_m)\), about \(4\times10^{-6}\) in the example, and the book drops it. What is left is equation (9.3):

\[ \phi_0 = 2\pi f_m t_0 = 2\pi\,\frac{c}{\lambda}\cdot\frac{2d}{c} = \frac{4\pi d}{\lambda}. \tag{9.3} \]

3. From samples to a range

The radar samples the IF signal with an analog-to-digital converter and takes a Fourier transform (FFT) of the samples of one chirp. Each target is a tone, so each target is a peak in the spectrum, and equation (9.2) converts the frequency of the peak into a range. §9.1.2.2 · p. 255 With several targets the IF signal is a sum of tones and the spectrum has several peaks. That spectrum, for one antenna direction, is one row of a radargram.

Filling the gap: range resolution and maximum range

The book does not say how close two targets may be before their peaks merge. A tone observed for a time \(T\) can be separated from another only if their frequencies differ by about \(1/T\), which is also the spacing of the FFT bins. Put \(\Delta f = 1/T\) into equation (9.2):

\[ \Delta d = \frac{c\,\Delta f}{2S} = \frac{c}{2ST} = \frac{c}{2B}. \]

Range resolution depends only on the bandwidth. For \(B = 300\) MHz it is 0.5 m, for 1 GHz it is 15 cm.

The spectrum also has an upper end. If the radar takes \(N\) complex samples per chirp, the sampling rate is \(N/T\), which is the highest beat frequency it can represent. That frequency corresponds to the range

\[ d_{\max} = \frac{c}{2S}\cdot\frac{N}{T} = N\,\frac{c}{2B} . \]

So \(N\) samples give \(N\) range bins of size \(c/(2B)\). For a fixed number of samples, more bandwidth means finer bins and a shorter reach.

Try it: the widget simulates the beat signal for two chirps and estimates range and velocity from it. Press "Add a second target", then lower the bandwidth to 50 MHz and raise it to 600 MHz.

Notice: at the start the beat frequency is 600 kHz and the peak sits at about 12.05 m. With a second target 1.5 m behind, 300 MHz shows two peaks, while at 50 MHz a range bin is 3 m and the two merge into one. At 600 MHz the bins shrink to 0.25 m and the unambiguous range drops to 32 m. The extra 5 cm at the start is not noise: it grows when you raise the velocity. Day 2 explains it.

4. Speed from the phase between two chirps

Equation (9.3) says the phase of the beat signal is \(\phi_0 = 4\pi d/\lambda\). It turns through a full circle every time the range changes by \(\lambda/2\), about 1.95 mm at 77 GHz. That makes it useless for absolute range, because the radar cannot tell how many full turns happened. It makes it very good at measuring a small change in range. §9.1.2.3 · p. 255

Send two up chirps a time \(T\) apart. A target with radial velocity \(v\) (the rate at which its range changes) moves by \(\Delta d = vT\) in between. The two beat signals have almost the same frequency, but their phases differ by

\[ \Delta\phi = \frac{4\pi\,\Delta d}{\lambda} = \frac{4\pi v T}{\lambda} . \tag{9.4} \]

Solve for the velocity:

\[ v = \frac{\lambda\,\Delta\phi}{4\pi T}. \tag{9.5} \]

§9.1.2.3 · p. 256 The book uses \(T\) both for the length of a chirp and for the time between chirps; for back-to-back chirps they are the same.

Worked example. With \(T = 40\ \mu\text{s}\) and \(v = 5\) m/s the target moves \(\Delta d = 0.2\) mm between chirps, 2500 times less than the 0.5 m range bin, so the two spectra look identical. Yet \(\Delta\phi = 4\pi \times 2\times10^{-4}/3.896\times10^{-3} = 0.645\) rad, which is 37°, and that is easy to measure.

A phase is only known up to full turns. The reading is unambiguous while \(|\Delta\phi| \lt \pi\), which gives the largest speed the pair of chirps can report:

\[ v_{\max} = \frac{\lambda}{4T}. \]

With the numbers above, \(v_{\max} = 3.896\times10^{-3}/(160\times10^{-6}) = 24.4\) m/s. In the widget, set the velocity to 28 m/s: the estimate jumps to about −20.6 m/s, which is \(28 - 2 v_{\max}\). This is velocity aliasing.

In plain words

Imagine whistling a note that slides steadily upward while standing in front of a cliff. The echo you hear is the note from a moment ago, so it is a bit lower than the note you are whistling now. The farther the cliff, the older the echo and the bigger the gap in pitch. Range is the gap. To get speed, whistle the same slide twice and check whether the echo's wave has shifted by a fraction of one ripple in between.

Going deeper (optional): many chirps and the datacube

Two chirps give a noisy velocity, as the widget shows (about 5.2 m/s for a true 5.0). Real sensors send a frame of \(N_c\) chirps. For one range bin, the phase advances by the same \(\Delta\phi\) from chirp to chirp, so the \(N_c\) complex values form a tone with frequency \(\Delta\phi/(2\pi T) = 2v/\lambda\), and a second FFT across the chirps finds it. This is what the book means by a series of FFTs over several chirps. §9.1.2.2 · p. 255 The frame lasts \(N_c T\), so by the argument of section 3 the frequency resolution is \(1/(N_c T)\) and the velocity resolution is

\[ \Delta v = \frac{\lambda}{2 N_c T}. \]

For \(N_c = 128\) and \(T = 40\ \mu\text{s}\) this is 0.38 m/s. Range FFT, then Doppler FFT, then a third transform across antennas for angle (Day 2): the result is the datacube of an SoC radar.

Common mistakes

  • "The radar measures the time of flight with a fast clock." FMCW measures a frequency difference. The chirp slope converts nanoseconds of delay into kilohertz of beat frequency.
  • "More bandwidth means more range." Bandwidth sets the size of a range bin, \(c/(2B)\). For a fixed number of samples, more bandwidth shortens the unambiguous range.
  • "The radar measures how fast the target moves." It measures only the radial part, the rate of change of range. A car crossing in front of the sensor at constant range has zero Doppler velocity.
  • "The phase gives a very precise range." It wraps every half wavelength. Only phase differences are used: between chirps for velocity, between antennas for angle.

Check yourself

Q1. A chirp has B = 600 MHz and T = 40 µs. The beat frequency of a target is 1 MHz. How far away is it? (Use c = 3 × 10⁸ m/s.)

S = B/T = 1.5 × 10¹³ Hz/s. d = c·f₀/(2S) = (3 × 10⁸ × 10⁶)/(3 × 10¹³) = 10 m.

Q2. What is the range resolution of a chirp with 1 GHz of bandwidth?

c/(2B) = 3 × 10⁸/(2 × 10⁹) = 0.15 m. It does not depend on the carrier frequency or on the chirp duration.

Q3. A radar has λ = 4 mm and sends chirps 50 µs apart. The beat phase changes by π/2 between two chirps. What is the radial velocity?

v = λΔφ/(4πT) = (0.004 × π/2)/(4π × 50 × 10⁻⁶) = 0.004/(8 × 50 × 10⁻⁶) = 10 m/s.

Q4. Why do many spinning radars give no velocity for their returns?

Velocity comes from the phase change between chirps aimed at the same target. With a single pulse per azimuth there is nothing to compare (p. 252).

Q5. You halve the time between chirps. What happens to the largest unambiguous velocity?

v_max = λ/(4T). Half the time means the target moves half as far between chirps, so twice the speed fits inside a phase change of π.

Recap

  1. Spinning radars give a 2D polar radargram over 360° and long range. SoC radars use antenna arrays, have no moving parts, and give range, angles and radial velocity.
  2. An FMCW chirp rises in frequency with slope \(S = B/T\). The echo is delayed by \(t_0 = 2d/c\), so mixing gives a beat tone \(f_0 = S t_0\) and the range is \(d = c f_0/(2S)\).
  3. An FFT of one chirp turns each target into a peak. Bins are \(c/(2B)\) wide.
  4. The beat phase is \(4\pi d/\lambda\). Its change between chirps gives \(v = \lambda\Delta\phi/(4\pi T)\), unambiguous up to \(\lambda/(4T)\).

Sources

  1. SLAM Handbook, Ch. 9 "Radar SLAM", §9.1.1 "Sensor Types" and §9.1.2.1–9.1.2.3, pp. 250–256, equations (9.1)–(9.5), Figures 9.1–9.4.
  2. Richards, Fundamentals of Radar Signal Processing, 2nd ed., 2014 (mixing and the beat signal, range resolution c/(2B), unambiguous range and velocity, velocity resolution).
  3. Skolnik, Introduction to Radar Systems, 3rd ed., 2001 (FMCW ranging).

Week 14 · Day 2

Triangular chirps, angle of arrival, and picking targets out of noise with CFAR

After today you can separate range from Doppler with an up chirp and a down chirp, compute an angle of arrival from the phase difference between two antennas, and set a CA-CFAR threshold for a chosen false alarm probability.

About 60 min · Read §9.1.2.4–9.1.4, pp. 256–261 (5 pages) · Needs Week 14 Day 1

Read first: §9.1.2.4–9.1.4, pp. 256–261

While you read, look for:

  • Equations (9.6)–(9.8) on p. 256: which of the two frequency shifts changes sign on a down chirp.
  • Figure 9.5 and equation (9.10) on p. 257: the extra path \(\ell\sin\theta\) to the second receive antenna.
  • Figure 9.6 on p. 258: find the speckle and the row of repeated multipath returns.
  • The CFAR paragraph on p. 260 and Figure 9.7 on p. 261: the cell under test, training cells and guard cells, and how the k-strongest filter differs.

Today's big idea

Radar gets every quantity by comparing two almost identical measurements: two chirp slopes separate range from Doppler, and two antennas give the angle. What comes out is a noisy power map and not a point cloud, so a filter has to decide which cells hold targets. CFAR decides by comparing each cell with its neighbours, which keeps the false alarm rate constant when the noise level changes.

1. Triangular modulation: separating range and Doppler

Day 1 treated the beat frequency as pure range. That is not exact. If the target moves, the echo is also Doppler-shifted, and the beat frequency of an up chirp is the sum of a time-of-flight part \(f_{0,t}\) and a Doppler part \(f_{0,d}\). Triangular modulation follows each up chirp with a down chirp of the same slope. On the down chirp the time-of-flight part changes sign and the Doppler part does not: §9.1.2.4 · p. 256

\[ f_{0,\text{up}} = f_{0,t} + f_{0,d}, \tag{9.6} \] \[ f_{0,\text{down}} = -f_{0,t} + f_{0,d}. \tag{9.7} \]

Two equations, two unknowns. Subtract and add:

\[ f_{0,t} = \frac{f_{0,\text{up}} - f_{0,\text{down}}}{2}, \qquad f_{0,d} = \frac{f_{0,\text{up}} + f_{0,\text{down}}}{2}. \tag{9.8} \]

The range then follows from the time-of-flight part alone, \(d = c f_{0,t}/(2S)\), which is the first half of equation (9.9). §9.1.2.4 · p. 257

Filling the gap: how large is the Doppler part, and why the signs behave this way

Equation (9.4) says the beat phase advances by \(4\pi vT/\lambda\) during a time \(T\). A phase that advances at a steady rate is a frequency: divide by \(2\pi T\) and you get

\[ f_{0,d} = \frac{2v}{\lambda} \qquad\Longleftrightarrow\qquad v = \frac{\lambda\, f_{0,d}}{2}. \]

This is the standard two-way Doppler shift. The factor 2 is there because the path to the target and back changes by \(2\,\Delta d\).

For the signs, redo the geometry of Day 1 for a down chirp with frequency \(f_M - St\). The echo that arrives at time \(t\) left at \(t - t_0\), when the frequency was higher, \(f_M - S(t - t_0)\). Transmitted minus received is now \(-S t_0\): the time-of-flight part has flipped. The Doppler shift comes from the motion of the target and does not care which way the chirp slopes.

A caution about the second half of equation (9.9). It is printed as \(v = c f_{0,d}/(2ST)\). The product \(ST\) is the bandwidth \(B\). The derivation above, which uses only the book's own equation (9.4), gives \(v = \lambda f_{0,d}/2 = c f_{0,d}/(2f)\) with the carrier frequency \(f\) in that place. We use \(v = \lambda f_{0,d}/2\) below.

Worked example. Use the radar of Day 1: \(S = 7.5\times10^{12}\) Hz/s, \(\lambda = 3.896\) mm. A target at 12 m moves away at 5 m/s. Then \(f_{0,t} = 600\) kHz and \(f_{0,d} = 2\times5/0.003896 = 2.57\) kHz.

QuantityValueWhat you conclude
Up-chirp beat, (9.6)600 + 2.57 = 602.57 kHzSawtooth range by (9.2): 3 × 10⁸ × 602 570/(1.5 × 10¹³) = 12.05 m, 5 cm too far
Down-chirp beat, (9.7)−600 + 2.57 = −597.43 kHzAlone it has the same problem
Half the difference, (9.8)600.00 kHzRange 12.00 m, free of Doppler
Half the sum, (9.8)2.57 kHzv = λ f₀,d/2 = 5.0 m/s, with no phase measurement

The 5 cm in the first row is the offset you saw in yesterday's widget. The book states the trade: the sawtooth range of (9.2) is not corrected for Doppler and the triangular one is, the triangular scheme does not need the phase, and its price is latency, because one answer needs two chirps and the first is slightly old. §9.1.2.4 · p. 257

2. Angle of arrival

A spinning radar knows the angle of a return: it is where the antenna points. An SoC radar has to compute it. Take two receive antennas (RX) a distance \(\ell\) apart, and a far target at angle \(\theta\) from the array's forward direction. The reflected wave reaches the two antennas along parallel paths, and the path to the second antenna is longer by \(\Delta d = \ell\sin\theta\) (Figure 9.5). A path difference is a phase difference: §9.1.2.5 · p. 257

\[ \Delta\phi = \frac{2\pi}{\lambda}\,\ell\sin\theta \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad \theta = \arcsin\frac{\lambda\,\Delta\phi}{2\pi\ell}. \tag{9.10} \]

The factor is \(2\pi/\lambda\) here and \(4\pi/\lambda\) in equation (9.3). In (9.3) a range change is travelled twice, out and back. Here the extra path is travelled once, on the way in.

Worked example. Antennas half a wavelength apart, \(\ell = \lambda/2\), measure \(\Delta\phi = \pi/2\). Then \(\sin\theta = (\lambda\cdot\pi/2)/(2\pi\cdot\lambda/2) = 1/2\), so \(\theta = 30°\).

Filling the gap: antenna spacing and angular resolution

As with velocity, the phase is unambiguous only while \(|\Delta\phi| \lt \pi\). From (9.10) that means \(|\sin\theta| \lt \lambda/(2\ell)\). With \(\ell = \lambda/2\) every angle from −90° to 90° is covered, which is why arrays use half-wavelength spacing. With \(\ell = \lambda\) only angles within ±30° are unambiguous.

With \(N\) antennas in a row, the phase steps by the same \(\Delta\phi\) from one antenna to the next, and an FFT across the antennas finds it, exactly like the FFT across chirps on Day 1. §9.1.2.5 · p. 257 By the same resolution argument, \(N\) samples resolve \(\Delta\phi\) to \(2\pi/N\), so two targets can be separated when

\[ \Delta(\sin\theta) \approx \frac{\lambda}{N\ell} = \frac{2}{N} \quad\text{for } \ell = \lambda/2 . \]

Eight antennas give 0.25 rad, about 14° straight ahead. This is the reason radar angles are coarse next to LiDAR, and the reason a point far away is uncertain sideways: 0.25 rad at 50 m is 12.5 m. Keep it in mind for Day 3, where registration methods give far points a larger covariance.

The two-receiver example is a single-input, multiple-output (SIMO) array. Most SLAM radars are MIMO: several TX and several RX antennas. Adding one more transmitter gives the same angular resolution as doubling the receivers, provided the receivers can tell the transmitters apart. They can if the transmitters use different frequency bands, different codes, or different time slots (TDMA). A two-dimensional array measures elevation as well, which gives 3+1D data. §9.1.2.5 · p. 258

3. What goes wrong: speckle, multipath, motion distortion

Radar data is harder to use than LiDAR data, and the reasons are physical. §9.1.3 · pp. 258–259

Speckle noise. One pulse collects energy from everything inside a wide beam. The scattered waves add up, sometimes reinforcing and sometimes cancelling. Together with thermal noise and changing RCS this produces peaks where there is no object and removes peaks where there is one. Without a way to tell them apart, the output is a scatter of spurious points.

Multipath. Part of the energy reaches the target and returns by way of the ground or a wall. The radar only knows the path length and the arrival direction, so it places a second target beyond the reflecting surface: a ghost object.

Motion distortion. A spinning radar builds one image during one rotation. The book's example sensor rotates at 4 Hz, so a scan takes 0.25 s. A car at 20 m/s moves 5 m in that time, and an object seen at the start and at the end of the rotation is recorded 5 m apart. Faster sensors exist (10 Hz, up to 50 Hz), but on a fast vehicle the effect stays significant. §9.1.3.3 · p. 259 Day 3 shows how to undo it. The book also lists biased and sparse range readings caused by the wide beam, and receiver saturation. §9.1.3 · p. 258

4. Filtering with CFAR

The obvious filter, keeping every cell above a fixed power, fails because the noise level is not fixed. It changes with range, direction and surroundings, so one threshold is too strict in one place and lets false alarms through in another. §9.1.4 · p. 259

The constant false alarm rate (CFAR) filter works along one azimuth and slides a window over the range cells. The cell being judged is the cell under test (CUT). The training cells on both sides estimate the local noise level. Optional guard cells next to the CUT are left out, so that a target that spills into its neighbours does not raise its own noise estimate. In cell-averaging CFAR (CA-CFAR) the threshold is the mean power of the training cells times a multiplier chosen from the wanted probability of false alarm. §9.1.4 · p. 260

Filling the gap: where the multiplier comes from

The book says the multiplier is "selected from the desired probability of false alarm" and stops. Here is the calculation for the standard noise model, in which the power \(x\) of a noise-only cell is exponentially distributed with mean \(\mu\): \(p(x) = \frac{1}{\mu}e^{-x/\mu}\). This is what a receiver produces when it squares the two components of complex Gaussian noise.

If \(\mu\) were known, a threshold \(\tau\) would be exceeded by noise with probability \(P(x \gt \tau) = e^{-\tau/\mu}\). Setting this equal to \(P_{fa}\) gives \(\tau = -\mu\ln P_{fa}\). For \(P_{fa} = 10^{-3}\) the threshold is \(6.91\,\mu\).

But \(\mu\) is unknown, so CA-CFAR estimates it from \(N\) training cells, \(\hat\mu = \frac1N\sum_i x_i\), and uses \(\tau = \alpha\hat\mu\). The threshold is now random, so average the false alarm probability over it. The training cells are independent, and for an exponential variable \(\E[e^{-s x}] = 1/(1 + s\mu)\):

\[ P_{fa} = \E\!\left[e^{-\alpha\hat\mu/\mu}\right] = \prod_{i=1}^{N}\E\!\left[e^{-\frac{\alpha}{N\mu}x_i}\right] = \left(1 + \frac{\alpha}{N}\right)^{-N}. \]

The unknown \(\mu\) has cancelled. Whatever the noise level, the false alarm probability is the same: that is the "constant" in CFAR. Solve for the multiplier:

\[ \alpha = N\left(P_{fa}^{-1/N} - 1\right). \]

For \(N = 20\) and \(P_{fa} = 10^{-3}\): \(\alpha = 20\,(10^{0.15} - 1) = 20 \times 0.4125 = 8.25\). That is more than 6.91, the price of having to estimate the noise. With only \(N = 4\) cells, \(\alpha = 4\,(10^{0.75} - 1) = 18.5\). As \(N\) grows, \(\alpha\) falls towards \(-\ln P_{fa}\).

Try it: the grey curve is the power along one azimuth, with five targets and a stretch of stronger clutter. Compare the adaptive threshold with the dashed fixed one, then set the training cells to 3 per side.

Notice: at the start CA-CFAR finds 4 of the 5 targets with no false alarm, while the fixed threshold finds all 5 and adds 24 false alarms inside the clutter. The target CFAR misses is the one at 31 m: the stronger target 3 m behind it lies in its training window and lifts the threshold. With 3 training cells per side the window is short enough, all 5 are found, and the multiplier has risen from 8.25 to 12.97. At "1 in 100" two false alarms appear, exactly at the two edges of the clutter, where half the window sees quiet noise.

The misses and edge effects you just saw are the known weaknesses of averaging. Ordered-statistic CFAR (OS-CFAR) replaces the mean by a robust statistic such as the median, which a single strong neighbour cannot move. BFAR (bounded false alarm rate), designed for radar odometry, applies an affine map \(T = aZ + b\) to the CFAR output \(Z\), with a learnable \(b\), so that the result blends the adaptive threshold with a fixed level. §9.1.4 · p. 260

Many odometry and SLAM pipelines use something simpler than CFAR. CFAR was built for detection, where missing a weak target is costly. Odometry wants only points that will be found again in the next scan and from another viewpoint. Two common choices are to keep the k strongest returns above a static threshold along each azimuth, or to keep every return more than one standard deviation above the mean. In Figure 9.7 CFAR reports several false alarms, and k-strongest with k = 12 keeps only points around the main targets. §9.1.4 · pp. 260–261 A third route is learned filtering: networks trained with LiDAR as ground truth that keep only the returns a LiDAR would also see. §9.1.4 · pp. 260–261

Common mistakes

  • "CFAR removes false alarms." It fixes their rate. At \(P_{fa} = 10^{-3}\), a radargram with a million cells still produces about a thousand of them per scan.
  • "More training cells are always better." They lower the multiplier, but they assume the noise is the same across the whole window. A window that reaches another target or a clutter edge gives a wrong noise estimate.
  • "Ghosts average out like noise." A multipath ghost is repeatable from the same place. It has to be rejected as an outlier, not averaged.

Check yourself

Q1. A triangular radar measures a beat of 410 kHz on the up chirp and −390 kHz on the down chirp. What are the time-of-flight and Doppler parts?

By (9.8): half the difference is (410 − (−390))/2 = 400 kHz, half the sum is (410 + (−390))/2 = 10 kHz.

Q2. Two receive antennas are half a wavelength apart and measure a phase difference of π/3. What is the angle of arrival?

sin θ = λΔφ/(2πℓ) = (π/3)/π = 1/3, so θ = arcsin(1/3) ≈ 19.5°.

Q3. A CA-CFAR filter uses N = 10 training cells and a false alarm probability of 0.01. What multiplier does it need?

α = N(P_fa^(−1/N) − 1) = 10 × (100^0.1 − 1) = 10 × 0.585 = 5.85. The value 4.61 = −ln 0.01 would be right only if the noise level were known exactly.

Q4. Why do radar odometry pipelines often keep the k strongest returns per azimuth instead of running CFAR?

CFAR was designed for detection, where a missed weak target is costly, and it passes ambiguous peaks. Odometry wants points that are detected again in later scans and from other viewpoints (p. 260).

Recap

  1. An up chirp measures \(f_{0,t} + f_{0,d}\) and a down chirp \(-f_{0,t} + f_{0,d}\). Half the difference gives range, half the sum gives the Doppler shift \(2v/\lambda\).
  2. Two antennas \(\ell\) apart see a phase difference \((2\pi/\lambda)\ell\sin\theta\), so \(\theta = \arcsin(\lambda\Delta\phi/(2\pi\ell))\). More antennas, real or virtual (MIMO), give finer angles.
  3. Radar suffers from speckle, multipath ghosts, wide beams and, for spinning sensors, motion distortion.
  4. CA-CFAR compares each cell with \(\alpha\) times the mean of its training cells, with \(\alpha = N(P_{fa}^{-1/N} - 1)\). The false alarm rate then does not depend on the noise level.
  5. SLAM pipelines often prefer conservative filters such as k-strongest, because they need repeatable points.

Sources

  1. SLAM Handbook, Ch. 9, §9.1.2.4–9.1.2.5, §9.1.3 "Challenges to Radar Applications", §9.1.4 "Radar Filtering", pp. 256–261, equations (9.6)–(9.10), Figures 9.5–9.7.
  2. Richards, Fundamentals of Radar Signal Processing, 2nd ed., 2014 (two-way Doppler shift, array spacing and angular resolution, exponential noise power and the CA-CFAR multiplier).
  3. Skolnik, Introduction to Radar Systems, 3rd ed., 2001 (triangular FMCW, CFAR).

Week 14 · Day 3

Radar odometry: ego-velocity from Doppler, and matching scans

After today you can estimate a sensor's velocity from the Doppler readings of one radar scan by least squares, reject moving objects, and compare the Doppler, direct, feature-based and registration-based families of radar odometry.

About 60 min · Read §9.2, pp. 261–268 (8 pages) · Needs Week 6 Day 2

Read first: §9.2, pp. 261–268

While you read, look for:

  • The typical drift of spinning-radar odometry and the word "correspondence-free" (p. 261).
  • The Doppler factor example on pp. 263–264: what the state vector contains, and equations (9.11)–(9.14).
  • For each of §9.2.2, §9.2.3 and §9.2.4 (pp. 265–268): what exactly is matched between two scans.
  • The size of the improvement from motion compensation (p. 268).

Today's big idea

Every static point in a radar scan reports how fast the sensor is closing in on it. That is one linear equation in the sensor's velocity, and one scan holds dozens of them, so the velocity comes out of a small least-squares problem with no matching between scans at all. Rotation is invisible to this trick and position still has to be integrated, so radar also uses the scan-matching methods you know from LiDAR, adapted to sparser and noisier data.

1. One scan, one velocity

Radar odometry estimates the sensor's own motion (its egomotion) from a sequence of radar readings. Like every odometry it drifts: methods for spinning radar accumulate on the order of 1–2% of translational drift per 100 m. §9.2 · p. 261

The radar-specific method uses the Doppler reading of each point. Let \(\mathbf{v}^s\) be the velocity of the sensor, written in the sensor frame, and \(\mathbf{r}^s\) the vector from the sensor to a target. If the target is static, its Doppler reading is the projection of the sensor velocity on the direction to the target: §9.2.1 · p. 264

\[ v = \mathbf{v}^{s\top}\!\left(\frac{\mathbf{r}^s}{\norm{\mathbf{r}^s}}\right). \tag{9.13} \]

Filling the gap: where the dot product comes from, and its sign

Let the sensor be at position \(\mathbf{s}(t)\) and a static target at \(\mathbf{p}\). The range is \(r = \norm{\mathbf{p} - \mathbf{s}}\), so \(r^2 = (\mathbf{p}-\mathbf{s})\T(\mathbf{p}-\mathbf{s})\). Differentiate both sides with respect to time, using \(\dot{\mathbf{p}} = \mathbf{0}\) and \(\dot{\mathbf{s}} = \mathbf{v}\):

\[ 2r\,\dot r = -2\,(\mathbf{p}-\mathbf{s})\T\mathbf{v} \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad \dot r = -\,\mathbf{u}\T\mathbf{v}, \qquad \mathbf{u} = \frac{\mathbf{p}-\mathbf{s}}{r}. \]

The range shrinks at the rate \(\mathbf{u}\T\mathbf{v}\). Equation (9.13) therefore describes a Doppler reading that is positive when sensor and target approach each other: a closing speed. A sensor that reports the range rate \(\dot r\) instead (positive when the range grows, the convention of Day 1) gives the same number with the opposite sign. Check which one your sensor uses before fitting anything.

In a 2D scan a point at azimuth \(\theta\) has direction \(\mathbf{u} = (\cos\theta, \sin\theta)\), so the reading of point \(i\) is

\[ y_i = v_x\cos\theta_i + v_y\sin\theta_i = \norm{\mathbf{v}}\cos(\theta_i - \beta), \]

where \(\beta\) is the direction of travel. Plotted against azimuth, the readings of all static points lie on one cosine. Its height is the speed and its peak is at the direction of travel. In 3D, with elevation \(\phi\), the direction is \(\mathbf{u} = (\cos\phi\cos\theta,\ \cos\phi\sin\theta,\ \sin\phi)\) and there are three unknowns.

Stack the directions as rows of a matrix \(\mathbf{A}\) and the readings in a vector \(\mathbf{y}\). The velocity is the least-squares solution from Week 1 · Day 4:

\[ \hat{\mathbf{v}} = \argmin_{\mathbf{v}} \norm{\mathbf{A}\mathbf{v} - \mathbf{y}}^2 = (\mathbf{A}\T\mathbf{A})^{-1}\mathbf{A}\T\mathbf{y}, \qquad \cov(\hat{\mathbf{v}}) = \sigma^2(\mathbf{A}\T\mathbf{A})^{-1}, \]

where \(\sigma\) is the standard deviation of the Doppler noise.

Worked example. Three static points at azimuths 0°, 60° and −60° read 10.000, 6.732 and 3.268 m/s. The rows of \(\mathbf{A}\) are \((1, 0)\), \((0.5, 0.866)\), \((0.5, -0.866)\).

\[ \mathbf{A}\T\mathbf{A} = \begin{bmatrix} 1.5 & 0 \\ 0 & 1.5 \end{bmatrix}, \qquad \mathbf{A}\T\mathbf{y} = \begin{bmatrix} 10 + 3.366 + 1.634 \\ 0.866\,(6.732 - 3.268) \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 15 \\ 3 \end{bmatrix}, \qquad \hat{\mathbf{v}} = \begin{bmatrix} 10 \\ 2 \end{bmatrix}. \]

The sensor moves at 10 m/s forward and 2 m/s to the left. Now squeeze the same three points into a narrow view, at 0° and ±10°. Then \(\mathbf{A}\T\mathbf{A} = \diag(1 + 2\cos^2 10°,\ 2\sin^2 10°) = \diag(2.94,\ 0.060)\). The sideways variance is \(2.94/0.060 = 49\) times the forward one, so the sideways velocity is 7 times less certain. A narrow field of view sees forward speed well and sideways speed badly.

2. Moving objects are outliers

The model assumes every target is static. A point on a moving car breaks it: its reading contains the car's velocity too, and it falls off the cosine. Least squares has no defence against such points (Week 6 · Day 1). The book names two remedies. One is RANSAC (Week 6 · Day 2) followed by least squares on the inliers; in 3D a sample is three points, because there are three unknowns and each point gives one equation. §9.2.1 · p. 262 The other is a robust loss on the Doppler residual, the Cauchy loss in the book's example (Week 6 · Day 4). §9.2.1 · p. 265

Try it: the right panel plots each point's closing speed against its azimuth. Press "Reject outliers", then narrow the field of view to 60°.

Notice: at the start the true velocity is (9.40, 3.42) m/s and plain least squares returns about (10.79, 7.36), more than 4 m/s off, because a quarter of the points sit on two moving cars. After outlier rejection 45 of the 60 points are kept and the estimate is within 0.1 m/s. With the field of view at 60°, the one-sigma uncertainty of the leftward component roughly doubles (0.029 to 0.056 m/s) while the forward one barely moves, as in the worked example.

The points RANSAC throws away are useful in their own right: they mark the moving objects. Several pipelines use the Doppler fit as a filter and remove those points before registration or place recognition. §9.2.4 · p. 268

3. What Doppler cannot see, and the factor-graph version

Spin a radar on the spot. No range to any static point changes, so every Doppler reading is zero. Rotational velocity is not observable from the per-point velocities of a single radar, unless something is assumed about how the vehicle moves. §9.2.1 · pp. 262–263 The usual fix is a gyroscope. A registration-free combination of Doppler and IMU gave the lowest error in a comparison on 3+1D radar, with drift as low as 0.3% over 4.5 km. §9.2.1 · p. 263

Filling the gap: how a mounting offset makes rotation visible

The other fix uses rigid-body kinematics. If the vehicle has velocity \(\mathbf{v}_b\) at a reference point and turns with angular velocity \(\boldsymbol{\omega}\), a sensor mounted at offset \(\boldsymbol{\ell}\) from that point moves with

\[ \mathbf{v}_s = \mathbf{v}_b + \boldsymbol{\omega}\times\boldsymbol{\ell}. \]

In the plane, with yaw rate \(\omega\) and \(\boldsymbol{\ell} = (\ell_x, \ell_y)\), the extra term is \(\omega\,(-\ell_y,\ \ell_x)\). So a radar away from the reference point does feel the rotation, as an extra velocity.

That is the idea behind estimating yaw rate from one radar on a car with Ackermann steering when the mounting point is known. §9.2.1 · p. 263 With the radar 2 m ahead of the rear axle and a fitted sideways velocity of 0.4 m/s, the yaw rate is \(\omega = 0.4/2 = 0.2\) rad/s. The same coupling appears when the radar and the IMU are not at the same place. §9.2.1 · p. 265

The book's worked example estimates velocity over a sliding window of \(K\) radar scans, with IMU measurements linking consecutive states. The state is \(\mathbf{x} = \begin{bmatrix}\mathbf{v}^{s\top} & \mathbf{q}^{w\top}_s & \mathbf{b}\T\end{bmatrix}\T\): the velocity, the orientation quaternion, and the IMU bias. §9.2.1 · pp. 263–264 The cost is

\[ J(\mathbf{x}) = \underbrace{\sum_{k=1}^{K}\sum_{d\in\mathcal{D}_k} w_{d,k}\,e_{d,k}}_{\text{Doppler term}} + \underbrace{\sum_{k=1}^{K-1}\norm{\mathbf{e}_k}^2_{\mathbf{W}_k}}_{\text{inertial term}}, \tag{9.11} \]

with the Doppler error of target \(d\) in scan \(k\) and its weight

\[ e_{d,k} = v_{d,k} - \mathbf{v}^{s\top}_k\!\left(\frac{\mathbf{r}^s_{d,k}}{\norm{\mathbf{r}^s_{d,k}}}\right), \tag{9.14} \] \[ w_{d,k} = \frac{i_{d,k}}{\sum_{j\in\mathcal{D}_k} i_{j,k}} . \tag{9.12} \]
PieceWhat it isWhy it is there
ed,k, equation (9.14)Measured Doppler minus the Doppler predicted from the velocity state: the residual of section 1Each target is a unary factor on the velocity of scan k. The book applies the Cauchy robust loss to it
wd,k, equation (9.12)The intensity of the target divided by the summed intensity of the scanStrong returns are trusted more than weak ones
Inertial termIMU error between scans k and k+1, weighted by WkIntegrated accelerometer readings connect consecutive velocities
Bias b in the stateSlowly varying offset of the IMURadar velocities have no bias, so the IMU bias becomes observable
Orientation q in the stateAttitude of the sensor: pitch and roll matterThe accelerometer also feels gravity, and removing it requires knowing which way is down

This is a factor graph in the sense of Week 2 · Day 1: a chain of states, binary IMU factors between neighbours, and many unary Doppler factors on each state (Figure 9.9).

4. Matching scans: three families

Velocity must be integrated to get position, and rotation needs help. The other families estimate the relative pose between nearby scans by finding what the scans have in common. §9.2 · pp. 261–262

FamilyWorks onHow the relative pose is foundWatch out for
Direct, §9.2.2The raw radargramCorrelation. A rotation of the sensor is a shift of the polar image along its azimuth axis, so phase correlation gives the rotation; correlating the Cartesian images then gives the translation. A learned variant masks out the parts of the radargram that are not stableAssumes the power returned from a place stays the same over time. Moving objects and noise artifacts break this
Feature-based, §9.2.3Keypoints with descriptors, as in vision (SIFT, SURF, ORB, or radar-specific ones)Match descriptors, reject outliers with RANSAC, then align the matched points in closed form with the SVD (Week 13 · Day 2)Tolerates a poor initial guess, but descriptors are harder to make repeatable in radar. Learned features need training data with ground-truth poses
Registration-based, §9.2.4A point cloud from CFAR, BFAR or k-strongest filteringICP- or NDT-style registration, usually against several previous keyframes or a submapToo few points lose information and too many bring in noise. Association by proximity needs a good initial guess

Why register against several keyframes and not just the last scan? Radar clouds are sparse and noisy, so a single pair is fragile. More keyframes give more correspondences, which adds constraints in feature-poor places, and they give redundancy in time, so a sudden occlusion or a moving object has less effect. §9.2.4 · p. 267 CFEAR is the book's main example. It keeps the k strongest returns per azimuth, registers each new cloud jointly against the \(s\) most recent keyframes with a point-to-point, point-to-line or point-to-distribution error, and weights each match by the agreement of the normal vectors, the planarity, and the number of points nearby. §9.2.4 · p. 267

For 3+1D radar the two worlds combine. The Doppler least-squares velocity of section 1 is the initial estimate and registration refines it. One method weights points by a covariance that grows with distance from the sensor, because azimuth and elevation are coarse (Day 2). Another matches each point to a weighted set of nearby distributions to cope with sparse clouds. §9.2.4 · p. 268

5. Motion compensation

Day 2 showed that a 4 Hz scan is smeared by the vehicle's own motion. Correcting it with a constant-velocity model is reported to reduce the absolute trajectory error by 29% for such a sensor. §9.2.5 · p. 268 The recipe: take the relative pose between the last two scans and their time stamps, divide to get a velocity, and move every point according to its own time stamp.

Filling the gap: the correction for one point

Let the scan be referred to the time \(t_{\text{ref}}\), and let a point \(\mathbf{p}_i\) be measured \(\Delta t_i = t_i - t_{\text{ref}}\) later, in the sensor frame of that later moment. If the sensor moves with constant velocity \(\mathbf{v}\) and yaw rate \(\omega\), then by time \(t_i\) it has turned by \(\omega\Delta t_i\) and moved by about \(\mathbf{v}\Delta t_i\). Expressed in the frame at \(t_{\text{ref}}\), the point is, to first order in \(\Delta t_i\),

\[ \mathbf{p}_i' = \mathbf{R}(\omega\,\Delta t_i)\,\mathbf{p}_i + \mathbf{v}\,\Delta t_i , \]

where \(\mathbf{R}(\cdot)\) is a 2D rotation matrix. At 4 Hz and 15 m/s straight ahead, the last point of the sweep has \(\Delta t_i = 0.25\) s and moves by 3.75 m. The same velocity also predicts where the next scan will be, which gives registration its initial guess. §9.2.5 · p. 268

This is still a discrete-pose approach. A continuous-time trajectory (a spline or a Gaussian process, Week 5 · Day 1) can be queried at the exact time of every measurement and gives a smoother result. §9.2.5 · p. 268

Common mistakes

  • "Doppler odometry needs matching between scans." It needs none. The velocity comes from a single scan, which is why the book calls it correspondence-free.
  • "More points always fix a bad fit." Not if they are moving objects. Sixty points with fifteen outliers gave an error above 4 m/s in the widget. Reject first, then fit.
  • "A radar gives the full 6-DoF motion from Doppler." Doppler gives linear velocity. Rotation needs a gyroscope, a kinematic assumption with a known mounting offset, or scan matching.
  • "CFEAR and CFAR are the same thing." CFAR is a detection filter (Day 2). CFEAR is an odometry method.

Check yourself

Q1. A sensor drives straight ahead at 12 m/s. What closing speed does it measure for a static point at azimuth 60°?

The reading is the projection on the direction to the point: 12 × cos 60° = 6 m/s.

Q2. A radar sits exactly on the vehicle's rotation centre, and the vehicle turns on the spot. Why do the Doppler readings say nothing about the turn?

Doppler measures the rate of change of range. A pure rotation about the sensor leaves every range unchanged, so every reading is zero.

Q3. All detections of a forward-looking radar lie within ±10° of straight ahead. Which part of the velocity estimate is least certain?

The sideways velocity enters each equation through sin θ, which is at most 0.17 here. The matching entry of AᵀA is small, so its inverse, the variance, is large.

Q4. Why does RANSAC on a 3+1D radar scan draw three points per sample?

A minimal sample has as many equations as unknowns. Each Doppler reading is one linear equation in the three components of the velocity.

Q5. A radar rotates at 4 Hz on a vehicle driving at 20 m/s. Without motion compensation, how far apart are the positions from which the first and last azimuth of one scan were taken?

One rotation takes 1/4 s. In that time the vehicle moves 20 × 0.25 = 5 m.

Recap

  1. A static point's Doppler reading is the sensor velocity projected on the direction to the point. Across azimuth the readings form a cosine.
  2. Stacking the directions gives a linear least-squares problem for the velocity. Its covariance \(\sigma^2(\mathbf{A}\T\mathbf{A})^{-1}\) shows which components the field of view supports.
  3. Moving objects are outliers. RANSAC or a robust loss removes them, and the rejected points identify the movers.
  4. Rotation is not observable from one radar's Doppler alone. Add a gyroscope, a kinematic model, or scan matching.
  5. Direct, feature-based and registration-based methods align scans. Radar versions register to several keyframes and compensate for motion during the scan.

Sources

  1. SLAM Handbook, Ch. 9, §9.2 "Radar Odometry", pp. 261–268, equations (9.11)–(9.14), Figures 9.8–9.9.
  2. Barfoot, State Estimation for Robotics, 2017 (linear least squares and its covariance).
  3. Lynch and Park, Modern Robotics, 2017 (velocity of a point on a rotating rigid body).
  4. Thrun, Burgard, Fox, Probabilistic Robotics, 2005 (velocity motion model used for the constant-velocity correction).

Week 14 · Day 4

Radar place recognition: why it is hard and what works

After today you can explain why a radar scan of one place changes with the viewpoint, build and compare Scan Context descriptors adapted to radar, and say which learned and hand-crafted methods suit spinning and SoC radars.

About 60 min · Read §9.3, pp. 269–273 (4 pages) · Needs Week 13 Day 4

Read first: §9.3, pp. 269–273

While you read, look for:

  • The list of what makes radar place recognition hard, and Figure 9.10 (p. 269).
  • The comparison of spinning and SoC radar for this task (p. 270).
  • How training data can be collected without knowing where each scan was taken (pp. 270–271).
  • What replaces the height value of Scan Context in the radar versions (pp. 271–272), and the remedy for a narrow field of view (pp. 272–273).

Today's big idea

Place recognition asks whether the current scan was taken somewhere the robot has been before. The LiDAR methods carry over to radar in outline, but a radar scan of the same place is less repeatable: it is coarse, noisy, and changes with the viewing angle. The radar versions therefore describe a place by intensity instead of height, build descriptors from several filtered and motion-compensated scans, and lean on odometry when the field of view is narrow.

1. What changes between two visits

Place recognition (PR) must cope with a different position, such as another lane, and a different heading, such as arriving at a junction from another street. §9.3 · p. 269 Radar adds four difficulties of its own. §9.3.1 · p. 269

DifficultyEffect on the scan
Low resolutionFewer details, so fewer features that tell places apart
Wide beamAngular ambiguity: a distant object appears as a broad patch that looks quite different from close by
Low signal-to-noise ratioWithout adequate filtering, noise hides the structure that identifies the place (Figure 9.6)
Receiver saturationA strong radial streak whose shape depends on the angle from which the target is seen. Figure 9.10 shows two scans from the same location that differ in this way

Filling the gap: how wide a beam is at a distance

A beam of angular width \(\theta_b\) (in radians) covers an arc of length \(w \approx r\,\theta_b\) at range \(r\). Suppose the beam is 2° wide, which is \(2\pi/180 = 0.035\) rad. At 100 m the arc is 3.5 m long. At 10 m it is 0.35 m. A lamp post is therefore a 3.5 m smear when seen from afar and a dot when seen from nearby, and a descriptor built from the two scans will not agree in that bin. This is the angular ambiguity the book refers to, and it is also the reason Day 2 found radar angles coarse.

The sensor type shapes the method. §9.3.1 · pp. 269–270

PropertySpinning radarSoC radar
View360°, very long range: good for capturing the surrounding structure outdoorsLimited range and field of view
Data usedThe 2D radargram treated as an image, or a point cloud after a detector such as CFARA 2D or 3D point cloud, sparser and noisier; rarely the full datacube
Borrowed fromVisual PR (image retrieval) and 2D LiDAR PRLiDAR PR
Motion distortionPresent even at low speed, because the scan is slowSmall, because nothing has to rotate
ElevationNoneAvailable in 3+1D sensors, useful indoors where a short range is enough

More PR work exists for spinning radar, partly because of the richer wide view and partly because large datasets exist for it. §9.3.1 · p. 270

2. Hand-crafted descriptors: Scan Context for radar

Recall Scan Context from Week 13 · Day 4. Divide the area around the sensor into rings (by range) and sectors (by azimuth), and store one number per bin. The result is a small matrix with one row per ring and one column per sector. For LiDAR the number is the maximum height of the points in the bin. Radar needs changes. §9.3.3 · pp. 271–272

  • No height in a spinning radar. Use the return strength instead. One adaptation stores the sum of the intensities of the points in the bin, which encodes both how strong and how many they are.
  • Sparse and noisy single scans. Keep only the k strongest returns per azimuth, which removes much of the noise, then build the descriptor from several registered scans so that it is not too sparse.
  • Slow scanning. De-skew the points first (Day 3), otherwise the same place gives different descriptors at different speeds.
  • Unreliable height in 3+1D radar. Spurious points distort the maximum height, so Intensity Scan Context stores the maximum intensity per bin, and the sum of intensities is an alternative that still encodes vertical structures.

Filling the gap: comparing two descriptors, and why a turn is a shift

Call the columns of the query descriptor \(\mathbf{q}_j\) and those of a database descriptor \(\mathbf{c}_j\), for sectors \(j = 1,\dots,N_s\). Two columns are compared by the cosine of the angle between them, and the descriptor distance is the average over the columns:

\[ d_s(\mathbf{Q},\mathbf{C}) = \frac{1}{N_s}\sum_{j=1}^{N_s}\left(1 - \frac{\mathbf{q}_j\T\mathbf{c}_{j+s}}{\norm{\mathbf{q}_j}\,\norm{\mathbf{c}_{j+s}}}\right), \qquad d(\mathbf{Q},\mathbf{C}) = \min_{s}\ d_s(\mathbf{Q},\mathbf{C}). \]

The index \(j+s\) wraps around. Why the shift \(s\)? Sectors are counted in the sensor frame. If the sensor has turned by an angle \(\psi\) since the first visit, an object that was in sector \(j+s\) is now in sector \(j\), with \(s = \psi/(360°/N_s)\). The whole matrix is shifted sideways by \(s\) columns, and the rows do not change because ranges do not change. Trying every shift and keeping the smallest distance makes the comparison independent of heading, and the best shift is an estimate of the heading change. With 36 sectors of 10°, a turn of 60° is a shift of 6 columns.

The cosine does not care about the overall scale of a column, which helps when the same wall returns more or less power on another day.

Try it: the two grids are the descriptors of the same place, the right one from a degraded scan with a different heading. Move the heading slider. Then set the field of view to 120° and move it again.

Notice: with a 360° view the best shift recovers the heading (6 sectors for 60°), and the distance to the right place stays at 0.42 for every heading, well below the 0.79 of a different place. With a 120° view the two scans share less of the scene the more the sensor has turned: the distance climbs from 0.40 at 0° to 0.63 at 60°, and at 90° the right place (0.84) scores no better than a wrong one (0.81). In the widget a sector that is empty in both scans is skipped, and a sector that is empty in only one counts as a full mismatch.

The second half of that experiment is the book's warning about SoC radars. A place looks quite different from two viewpoints when the sensor covers a small field of view, so rotation invariance is hard to achieve. One remedy is to pre-filter with odometry: compare the current descriptor only with frames whose estimated yaw is within a certain range, for example 20°. §9.3.3 · pp. 272–273

Scan Context is not the only descriptor that has been adapted. §9.3.3 · pp. 271–272

DescriptorRadar adaptation described in the book
M2DPDesigned for 3D point clouds, applied to 2D point clouds extracted from radargrams
RINGA sinogram that is invariant to rotation and translation. Plain correlation of two sinograms suffers from radar noise, and adding auto-correlation improves the result
Scan ContextSum or maximum of intensity per bin, descriptors from several filtered and motion-compensated scans

Filling the gap: the eigenvalue test for boring scans

Some scans should not be used for place recognition at all. On a highway every stretch looks like every other. The M2DP-based system detects this with principal component analysis (PCA) of the 2D points. §9.3.3 · p. 272 Compute the 2 × 2 covariance matrix of the point coordinates and its two eigenvalues \(\lambda_1 \ge \lambda_2\). Each eigenvalue is the variance of the points along one principal direction.

Example: a highway scan whose points spread 40 m (one standard deviation) along the road and 3 m across has \(\lambda_1 = 1600\ \text{m}^2\) and \(\lambda_2 = 9\ \text{m}^2\), a ratio of 178. The scan has structure in one direction only and is skipped. A junction with spreads of 30 m and 25 m has eigenvalues 900 and 625, a ratio of 1.4, and is kept.

3. Learned descriptors

The other route is to let a network turn a scan into a descriptor vector and to compare vectors. §9.3.2 · pp. 270–271

For spinning radar the radargram is an image, so image retrieval applies. An early method uses a convolutional network with cylindrical convolutions, which respect the wrap-around of the polar image, to learn a descriptor that does not change with rotation. Matching a query against a database of such descriptors gives topological place recognition: it says which stored place you are at, not your exact pose. Adding a pose refinement step turns it into a topometric system.

Where do training examples come from? A network must see pairs of scans from the same place and pairs from different places. Ground-truth positions would supply them, but they are not needed. §9.3.2 · pp. 270–271

The network is trained to give the anchor and its positives similar descriptors and to tell them apart from the negatives. No metric location is needed, so the training is unsupervised.

SoC radars need their own treatment because of the shorter range and smaller field of view. §9.3.2 · p. 271

ApproachHow it handles sparse, noisy SoC data
Spatiotemporal encoder on point clouds projected to a 2D image, followed by a NetVLAD layerFeatures are re-ranked by RCS to drop irrelevant ones, and several radars around the vehicle widen the view
Kernel point convolutions on the 3D cloud, followed by NetVLADA point importance estimator learns which points matter for recognition, and a separate network encodes the RCS values. Works from a single scan
A radar-specific backbone inspired by LiDAR PR networksRANSAC ego-velocity estimation (Day 3) keeps the static inliers and drops the rest as noise

Intuition

Both routes fight the same enemy. A descriptor is only useful if the same place gives the same numbers twice. Hand-crafted radar descriptors get there by throwing away most of the scan (k strongest), adding scans together, and undoing the motion. Learned descriptors get there by being shown many pairs that should match and learning which parts of the scan to ignore.

Common mistakes

  • "A LiDAR descriptor can be applied to radar points unchanged." A spinning radar has no height, and in 3+1D radar a single spurious point corrupts the maximum height. The radar versions store intensity.
  • "Scan Context is rotation invariant, so the field of view does not matter." The column shift only works if both scans see the same surroundings. With a narrow view, a turned sensor sees a different part of the scene.
  • "A matching descriptor is a loop closure." It is a candidate. Day 5 shows how pipelines check it against odometry and geometry before it enters the graph.

Check yourself

Q1. A Scan Context descriptor has 60 sectors. The robot returns to a place with its heading changed by 90°. By how many columns is the descriptor shifted?

Each sector spans 360°/60 = 6°, so 90° is 90/6 = 15 columns.

Q2. Why do radar versions of Scan Context store the sum of intensities in a bin?

A spinning radar has no elevation, and in 3+1D radar spurious points distort the maximum height. The sum of intensities reflects point density and return strength together (p. 272).

Q3. A 3+1D radar with a narrow field of view is used for loop detection. What does the book suggest to cope with the lack of rotation invariance?

With a small field of view a place looks different from another heading, so candidates are pre-filtered by the yaw estimated from odometry, for example within 20° (pp. 272–273).

Q4. PCA of the points of a scan gives eigenvalues 900 m² and 4 m². What does the M2DP-based system do with this scan?

Very different eigenvalues mean the points lack structure in one direction, as on a highway. Such scans are not considered for place recognition (p. 272).

Q5. How can positive training pairs for a learned radar descriptor be obtained without ground-truth positions?

Consecutive scans show almost the same place. Shifting the polar radargram simulates a different heading. Scans far apart in the sequence act as negatives (pp. 270–271).

Recap

  1. Radar scans of one place vary because of low resolution, a wide beam, noise and receiver saturation.
  2. Spinning radar offers a 360° long-range view and borrows from visual and 2D LiDAR PR. SoC radar has a narrow view and borrows from LiDAR PR.
  3. Radar Scan Context stores intensity per ring-sector bin. A heading change is a column shift, found by minimising the mean cosine distance over all shifts.
  4. With a narrow field of view the shift search fails for large heading changes, so candidates are pre-filtered by odometry yaw.
  5. Learned descriptors can be trained without positions, using sequence neighbours as positives.

Sources

  1. SLAM Handbook, Ch. 9, §9.3 "Radar Place Recognition", pp. 269–273, Figure 9.10.
  2. Kim and Kim, Scan Context: Egocentric Spatial Descriptor for Place Recognition within 3D Point Cloud Map, 2018 (the column-wise cosine distance and the column shift).
  3. Bishop, Pattern Recognition and Machine Learning, 2006 (principal component analysis: eigenvalues of the covariance matrix as variances).

Week 14 · Day 5

Complete radar SLAM: maps, pipelines, fusion and datasets

After today you can trace a radar scan through a complete SLAM pipeline, explain how loop candidates are retrieved and verified, and choose a map representation and a dataset for a radar project.

About 60 min · Read §9.4–9.6, pp. 273–281 (9 pages) · Needs Week 14 Day 4

Read first: §9.4–9.6, pp. 273–281

While you read, look for:

  • The map representations of §9.4.1 (pp. 273–274), and how the radar voxel model differs from Octomap's ray casting.
  • In the TBV-SLAM description (pp. 275–276): the keyframe rule, the finding about covariance matrices, and the formula that combines descriptor and odometry.
  • What RadarSLAM, the SoC landmark pipeline and the two 3+1D pipelines do differently (pp. 276–277).
  • Table 9.1 on p. 280. Skim it; you only need to know what kinds of datasets exist.

Today's big idea

The back-end of radar SLAM is the pose graph you already know. What is specific to radar is everything that protects the graph from bad input: conservative point selection, loop candidates that are checked against odometry, and verification of the alignment before a loop constraint is accepted.

1. Map representations

Radar maps use the representations of Week 8, with changes forced by sparse and spurious measurements. §9.4.1 · pp. 273–274

RepresentationWhat is storedRadar-specific point
Landmark mapIndividual detected targetsThe earliest approach: the map comes straight from a target detector
Occupancy gridProbability that a cell is occupiedThe detection probability of the radar can be used in the update
Point cloudSignal peaks treated like LiDAR pointsPoints can carry the distribution of their neighbours (orientation, weight), like surfels or NDT cells. Common for high-resolution 3+1D SoC radars
Power heat mapReflected power for each cell, before any peak detectionA dense map of power, not of occupancy. Maps are aligned by correlation
Voxel map with a radar sensor modelLog-odds of occupancy per voxelNo ray casting: every voxel in the field of view is updated
Learned and neural mapsAn upsampled map, or a network queried at a point in spaceLiDAR serves as ground truth for denoising. Radar fields learn geometry and reflectance from a physics-based sensor model

Filling the gap: why radar drops the ray-casting assumption

Recall the log-odds occupancy update from Week 8 · Day 2. Each voxel keeps \(l = \log\frac{p}{1-p}\), and every observation adds a constant: \(l \leftarrow l + \log\frac{p_{\text{obs}}}{1-p_{\text{obs}}}\). A LiDAR map decides which voxels to update by ray casting. The beam stops at the first surface, so voxels before the hit are observed free, the hit voxel is observed occupied, and nothing is known behind it.

Radar waves pass through some materials. A return from behind another object is then real, and "the first contact is the only occupied point" is false. The radar model in the book keeps the log-odds bookkeeping but replaces the ray: voxels inside the field of view that contain a return go up, voxels without one go down, and no assumption is made along the ray. §9.4.1 · pp. 273–274 This is how such a map can show structure behind something that blocks a camera.

A number to fix ideas. With \(p_{\text{hit}} = 0.7\) and \(p_{\text{miss}} = 0.4\), a voxel that has a return in three scans and none in a fourth ends at

\[ l = 3\ln\frac{0.7}{0.3} + \ln\frac{0.4}{0.6} = 3(0.847) - 0.405 = 2.136, \qquad p = \frac{1}{1 + e^{-2.136}} = 0.894 . \]

One missed scan does not erase the voxel. That tolerance matters for a sensor whose returns flicker.

2. One pipeline, stage by stage

All the pipelines in the book follow Figure 9.1: a front-end that filters raw data into points and recognises places, and a back-end that optimises a pose graph. §9.4.2 · p. 274 The clearest example is TBV-SLAM ("trust but verify") for 2D spinning radar. §9.4.2 · pp. 275–276

Odometry and keyframes. The pose is tracked with every scan, using CFEAR odometry (Day 3). For efficiency only some scans become nodes of the graph: a new keyframe is added once the estimated distance travelled exceeds a threshold, for example 1.5 m, together with an odometry constraint to the previous keyframe.

The covariance of a constraint. A constraint needs a relative pose and a covariance matrix. The pipeline's authors report that a predefined diagonal covariance with small values works better than one computed from the Hessian of the registration cost. §9.4.2 · p. 275

Filling the gap: what "covariance from the Hessian" means

Registration minimises a least-squares cost. Near the minimum the cost is a quadratic bowl, \(\tfrac12\,\delta\T\mathbf{H}\,\delta\), where \(\delta\) is a small change of the relative pose and \(\mathbf{H} = \mathbf{J}\T\mathbf{J}\) is the Gauss-Newton Hessian (Week 2 · Day 4). If the residuals had independent Gaussian noise of variance \(\sigma^2\), the estimate would have covariance \(\sigma^2\mathbf{H}^{-1}\): a steep bowl means a certain estimate, a flat direction means an uncertain one. In a tunnel the bowl is flat along the tunnel, and the covariance would correctly be large in that direction.

The formula is only as good as its assumptions. It takes the point matches to be correct and the errors of different points to be independent, and with radar points neither holds well. The book reports that the Hessian tends to under- or overestimate the uncertainty, and that this can make the back-end slightly misalign the keyframes. A fixed covariance is cruder, but it cannot be badly wrong in this way.

3. Retrieving and verifying loops

The loop branch of TBV-SLAM stacks several safeguards. §9.4.2 · pp. 275–276

  1. Descriptor. A Scan Context descriptor adapted to encode point density and signal strength (Day 4).
  2. Augmentation. For each keyframe, extra descriptors are made from copies of the point cloud shifted sideways, so that a revisit in another lane still matches.
  3. Several candidates, scored jointly. Instead of taking the most similar descriptor and then filtering by odometry, the candidate is chosen as \[ c = \argmin_{c}\ d_{\text{descriptor}}(q, c) + d_{\text{odometry}}(q, c), \] where \(q\) is the query and \(d_{\text{odometry}}\) comes from the likelihood that \(q\) and \(c\) are at the same place, given the accumulated odometry uncertainty.
  4. Registration. The pair is aligned with the CFEAR registration module.
  5. Verification. Overlap measures and a learned misalignment detector (CorAl) decide whether the alignment is trustworthy. Only then does the loop constraint enter the graph.

Filling the gap: an odometry term you can compute

The book describes \(d_{\text{odometry}}\) only in words. Here is one way to build such a term; it illustrates the idea and is not the exact formula of the system. Suppose that, according to odometry, candidate \(c\) lies at offset \(\mathbf{t}\) from the query, and that the accumulated position uncertainty between them is a Gaussian with covariance \(\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\). If the two frames really are at the same place, \(\mathbf{t}\) is pure drift, and its negative log-likelihood is, up to a constant,

\[ \tfrac12\,\mathbf{t}\T\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{-1}\mathbf{t} = \tfrac12 m^2 , \]

half the squared Mahalanobis distance. Take a loop of 800 m with 1.5% drift, so about \(\sigma = 12\) m in every direction.

CandidateDescriptor distanceOffset by odometrym = offset/σ½m²
A0.2060 m5.012.5
B0.2510 m0.830.35

The descriptor alone prefers A. But A would need a drift of five standard deviations, which is practically impossible, while B needs less than one. Any reasonable sum of the two terms picks B. How the terms are scaled against each other is a design choice. The benefit of scoring jointly is that a slightly worse descriptor match in a plausible location can beat a slightly better one in an implausible location.

The other pipelines make different choices at each stage. §9.4.2 · pp. 276–277

PipelineSensorOdometryGraph holdsLoop detection and checks
TBV-SLAM2D spinningCFEAR registration to keyframesKeyframe posesAdapted Scan Context, lateral augmentation, joint score with odometry, registration, alignment verification
RadarSLAM2D spinningBlob keypoints tracked with a Lucas–Kanade tracker (Week 12 · Day 2), constant-velocity motion compensationKeyframe poses, with keypoints storedM2DP on point clouds (intensity above mean plus one standard deviation). Elongated scans are excluded by the PCA test. No other verification
SoC landmark pipeline2D SoCWheel encodersPoses and individual radar featuresNo explicit place recognition. Features are matched by a compact binary descriptor with RANSAC, assuming moderate drift
4DRadarSLAM3+1D SoCDoppler filtering of moving points, then a GICP variant with range-dependent point covarianceSubmaps (keyframes)Intensity Scan Context. A candidate is rejected if the odometry distance between the frames is above a threshold
4D iRIOM3+1D SoCDoppler filtering, removal of isolated points, distribution-to-distribution matchingSubmaps (keyframes)The original Scan Context with point elevation

Two remarks on the table. The SoC landmark pipeline can afford landmarks in the graph because a 2D SoC radar returns far fewer detections than a spinning or a 3+1D radar. And in both 3+1D pipelines the sensor itself turns the datacube into points, so CFAR is not part of the SLAM software; the Doppler least-squares fit of Day 3 does the cleaning by removing points on moving objects, and the fitted ego-velocity serves as a prior for scan-to-submap registration. §9.4.2 · p. 277 Figure 9.11 shows the effect of the loop closure on a 3D radar map: the horizontal and vertical drift visible before closure is gone after it. §9.4.2 · p. 275

4. Fusion, datasets and where the field is going

Other sensors and prior maps. §9.4.3 · pp. 277–279

  • Radar with LiDAR. Use whichever is better in the current visibility: LiDAR in clear air, radar in smoke or fog. Radar scans can also be recognised against LiDAR maps.
  • Radar with cameras. Doppler ego-velocity (Day 3) is fed into a filter-based visual-inertial odometry. Thermal cameras are combined with radar for low-visibility odometry, with the radar points improving the depth estimate.
  • Radar with public maps. Building walls from OpenStreetMap, or satellite images, serve as a prior map to localise in. This is localisation more than SLAM, and the prior may be incomplete or out of date.
  • Ultra-wideband (UWB). Also radio, but its ranging differs greatly from mmWave radar. In SLAM it mostly supplies a signature of a place for detecting revisits, while distances come from wheel encoders or an IMU. Systems with fixed anchors need installed infrastructure and are not SLAM.

Datasets. Table 9.1 lists them with their ground truth and weather. §9.5 · pp. 279–280

If you needLook atWhy
Spinning radar, urban, large scaleOxford Radar RobotCarRepeated traversals of one urban route, 280 km in total, varied weather
Place recognition across sessionsMulRanDiverse environments and long gaps between sessions
Snow and rain over a yearBoreasOne route driven repeatedly for a year, 385 km
Off-roadOxford Offroad Radar DatasetAbout 154 km of unpaved roads and mountain trails
Raw ADC samples of an SoC radarColoRadarRaw samples, datacubes and point targets, indoors, outdoors and in a mine, with 6-DoF ground truth
High-resolution 3+1D radarNTU4DRadLM, MSC-RAD4R, Snail-RadarCampus, park, urban and rural roads; Snail-Radar carries two different 3+1D radars
Object labels with radarnuScenes, RadarScenesBuilt for perception. RadarScenes lacks accurate ground-truth poses

Trends. The book expects more fully 3D radar SLAM as SoC sensors improve, notably on drones; systems built from several small-view radars, with the calibration problems that brings; use of the raw radargrams and datacubes instead of point clouds, if manufacturers open access to them; semantic segmentation to support place recognition; and tighter use of other sensors and geographic priors. §9.6 · pp. 280–281

Common mistakes

  • "Radar SLAM needs a different back-end." The back-end is ordinary pose-graph optimisation. The differences are in the front-end.
  • "A better uncertainty model always helps." A covariance derived from a model whose assumptions fail can hurt more than a fixed, modest one.
  • "The most similar descriptor is the loop." Retrieval proposes; odometry gating, registration and verification dispose.
  • "UWB is just another radar." In SLAM it is mainly a place signature. It does not give the metric scans that mmWave radar gives.

Check yourself

Q1. Why does the radar voxel model update all voxels in the field of view instead of casting a ray to the first return?

The ray-cast model assumes nothing can be observed behind the first contact. Radar returns from behind an object can be real, so the model raises voxels with returns and lowers those without, without assuming anything along the ray (pp. 273–274).

Q2. A voxel starts at probability 0.5 and receives two "occupied" updates with p = 0.8 each. What is its occupancy probability?

Each update multiplies the odds by 0.8/0.2 = 4. The odds go from 1 to 16, so p = 16/17 ≈ 0.94. In log-odds: 2 ln 4 = 2.77.
