Q3. Which pipeline keeps individual radar features in the optimised graph, and why is that affordable?

A 2D SoC radar produces far fewer detections than a 360° spinning radar or a 3+1D radar, so keeping every detection as a node is feasible (pp. 276–277). TBV-SLAM and RadarSLAM optimise poses only.

Q4. Two loop candidates have descriptor distances 0.30 and 0.34. Odometry, with an accumulated uncertainty of σ = 8 m, places the first 48 m from the query and the second 4 m away. Which does a joint score favour?

48/8 = 6 standard deviations is practically impossible as drift, while 4/8 = 0.5 is ordinary. The small difference in descriptor distance does not outweigh that.

Recap

  1. Radar maps reuse landmark, grid, point-cloud and voxel representations. The radar voxel model drops ray casting because radar can see through some materials.
  2. A radar SLAM pipeline filters to few reliable points, tracks every scan, adds keyframes by distance, and optimises a pose graph.
  3. Loop closures are retrieved by descriptor, scored together with odometry uncertainty, registered, and verified before they enter the graph.
  4. 3+1D pipelines start from Doppler ego-velocity, which both seeds registration and removes moving points.
  5. Radar is fused with LiDAR, cameras and prior maps, and datasets exist for spinning radar, SoC radar, and both.

Sources

  1. SLAM Handbook, Ch. 9, §9.4 "Radar SLAM", §9.5 "Radar Datasets", §9.6 "Further Readings & Recent Trends", pp. 273–281, Figure 9.11, Table 9.1.
  2. Thrun, Burgard, Fox, Probabilistic Robotics, 2005 (log-odds occupancy update and ray-cast sensor models).
  3. Barfoot, State Estimation for Robotics, 2017 (covariance of a least-squares estimate from the Gauss-Newton Hessian; Mahalanobis distance).

Week 14 · Review

Week 14 review: radar from chirp to pose graph

After today you can compute range, velocity and angle from FMCW measurements, set a CFAR threshold, fit an ego-velocity to Doppler readings, and describe how a radar SLAM pipeline finds and verifies loop closures.

About 60 min · No new pages

The week in one paragraph

An FMCW radar sends chirps and compares each echo with the transmitted signal. The beat frequency gives range, the phase change between chirps gives radial velocity, and the phase change between antennas gives angle. The raw output is a noisy power map with speckle and multipath ghosts, so a filter such as CFAR or k-strongest picks the cells that become points. Odometry comes either from Doppler alone, by fitting the sensor velocity to the radial velocities of static points, or from matching scans as with LiDAR, usually against several keyframes and after motion compensation. Place recognition adapts LiDAR descriptors by storing intensity instead of height. A full system feeds odometry and carefully verified loop constraints into an ordinary pose graph.

1. Formula sheet

What it isFormulaWhere
Echo delay and range\(d = \tfrac{c}{2}t_0\)(9.1), p. 254 · Day 1
Beat frequency of a chirp with slope \(S = B/T\)\(f_0 = \dfrac{2Sd}{c}\), so \(d = \dfrac{c f_0}{2S}\)(9.2), p. 255 · Day 1
Range resolution and unambiguous range with \(N\) complex samples\(\Delta d = \dfrac{c}{2B}\), \(d_{\max} = N\dfrac{c}{2B}\)App · Day 1
Velocity from the phase change between chirps\(v = \dfrac{\lambda\,\Delta\phi}{4\pi T}\), \(v_{\max} = \dfrac{\lambda}{4T}\)(9.4)–(9.5), p. 256 · Day 1
Triangular modulation\(f_{0,t} = \tfrac12(f_{0,\text{up}} - f_{0,\text{down}})\), \(f_{0,d} = \tfrac12(f_{0,\text{up}} + f_{0,\text{down}})\), \(f_{0,d} = 2v/\lambda\)(9.8), p. 256 · Day 2
Angle of arrival, antennas \(\ell\) apart\(\theta = \arcsin\dfrac{\lambda\,\Delta\phi}{2\pi\ell}\)(9.10), p. 257 · Day 2
CA-CFAR threshold with \(N\) training cells\(\tau = \alpha\,\hat\mu\), \(\alpha = N\left(P_{fa}^{-1/N} - 1\right)\)§9.1.4, p. 260 and App · Day 2
Doppler residual of a static target, and the ego-velocity that minimises its squares\(e_{d,k} = v_{d,k} - \mathbf{v}^{s\top}_k \dfrac{\mathbf{r}^s_{d,k}}{\norm{\mathbf{r}^s_{d,k}}}\), \(\hat{\mathbf{v}} = (\mathbf{A}\T\mathbf{A})^{-1}\mathbf{A}\T\mathbf{y}\)(9.14), p. 264 and App · Day 3
Scan Context distance\(\min_s \dfrac{1}{N_s}\sum_j \left(1 - \dfrac{\mathbf{q}_j\T\mathbf{c}_{j+s}}{\norm{\mathbf{q}_j}\norm{\mathbf{c}_{j+s}}}\right)\)App · Day 4
Joint loop retrieval\(c = \argmin_c\ d_{\text{descriptor}}(q,c) + d_{\text{odometry}}(q,c)\)§9.4.2, p. 276 · Day 5

2. Mixed quiz

Check yourself

Q1. A chirp has slope S = 10¹³ Hz/s. What beat frequency does a target at 30 m produce? (c = 3 × 10⁸ m/s)

f₀ = 2Sd/c = 2 × 10¹³ × 30/(3 × 10⁸) = 2 × 10⁶ Hz.

Q2. You want range bins half as large. What do you change?

The bin size is c/(2B). Only the bandwidth appears in it.

Q3. A radar with λ = 4 mm sends chirps 100 µs apart. What is the largest radial speed it reports without aliasing?

v_max = λ/(4T) = 0.004/(4 × 10⁻⁴) = 10 m/s.

Q4. Two receive antennas are one full wavelength apart. For which angles of arrival is the phase difference unambiguous?

|Δφ| below π requires |sin θ| below λ/(2ℓ) = 1/2, that is, θ within ±30°.

Q5. The noise power doubles in every cell of a radargram. What happens to the false alarm probability of a CA-CFAR filter?

The threshold is a multiple of the measured local noise level, so it doubles too. P_fa = (1 + α/N)^(−N) does not contain the noise level.

Q6. A static point straight ahead (azimuth 0°) has a closing speed of 8 m/s, and a static point at azimuth 90° (to the left) has −2 m/s. What is the sensor velocity?

The reading at 0° is v_x = 8. The reading at 90° is v_y = −2: the sensor moves away from the point on its left, so it drifts to the right.

Q7. A radar Scan Context has 40 sectors. The best match with a stored descriptor is at a shift of 5 columns. What heading change does that indicate?

One sector is 360°/40 = 9°, so 5 columns are 45°.

Q8. In TBV-SLAM, what finally keeps a wrong loop candidate with a good descriptor score out of the pose graph?

Candidates are scored with odometry, then registered, and the alignment is checked by overlap measures and a misalignment detector. Only verified candidates become constraints (pp. 275–276).

3. Pen-and-paper problems

  1. An FMCW radar uses chirps with \(B = 750\) MHz and \(T = 50\ \mu\text{s}\). A target produces a beat frequency of 2 MHz. (a) How far away is it? (b) What is the range resolution? (c) With 256 complex samples per chirp, what is the largest unambiguous range? Use \(c = 3\times10^8\) m/s.

    Solution

    (a) \(S = B/T = 7.5\times10^{8}/5\times10^{-5} = 1.5\times10^{13}\) Hz/s. \(d = c f_0/(2S) = (3\times10^{8})(2\times10^{6})/(3\times10^{13}) = 20\) m.

    (b) \(\Delta d = c/(2B) = 3\times10^{8}/(1.5\times10^{9}) = 0.2\) m.

    (c) \(d_{\max} = N\,c/(2B) = 256 \times 0.2 = 51.2\) m. Check: the sampling rate is \(N/T = 5.12\) MHz, and a target at 51.2 m has \(f_0 = 2Sd/c = 5.12\) MHz.

  2. A radar has \(\lambda = 3.9\) mm and sends chirps \(T = 60\ \mu\text{s}\) apart. (a) The beat phase changes by 0.8 rad between two chirps. What is the radial velocity? (b) What is \(v_{\max}\)? (c) A target recedes at 20 m/s. What velocity does the radar report?

    Solution

    (a) \(v = \lambda\Delta\phi/(4\pi T) = (3.9\times10^{-3})(0.8)/(4\pi \times 6\times10^{-5}) = 3.12\times10^{-3}/7.54\times10^{-4} = 4.14\) m/s.

    (b) \(v_{\max} = \lambda/(4T) = 3.9\times10^{-3}/2.4\times10^{-4} = 16.25\) m/s.

    (c) The true phase change is \(4\pi v T/\lambda = 4\pi(20)(6\times10^{-5})/(3.9\times10^{-3}) = 3.867\) rad, which is more than \(\pi\). The radar sees it wrapped: \(3.867 - 2\pi = -2.416\) rad, and reports \(v = (3.9\times10^{-3})(-2.416)/(7.54\times10^{-4}) = -12.5\) m/s. Equivalently \(20 - 2v_{\max} = -12.5\). The target seems to approach.

  3. A 2D radar reports closing speeds for five points: 8.00 m/s at azimuth 0°, 1.00 m/s at 90°, −1.00 m/s at −90°, 6.36 m/s at 45°, and −2.00 m/s at 180°. (a) Fit the sensor velocity to the first four points by least squares. (b) Compute the residual of the fifth point and interpret it. (c) Fit all five points and compare.

    Solution

    (a) The rows of \(\mathbf{A}\) are \((1,0)\), \((0,1)\), \((0,-1)\), \((0.707, 0.707)\). Then

    \[ \mathbf{A}\T\mathbf{A} = \begin{bmatrix} 1.5 & 0.5 \\ 0.5 & 2.5 \end{bmatrix}, \qquad \mathbf{A}\T\mathbf{y} = \begin{bmatrix} 8 + 4.5 \\ 1 + 1 + 4.5 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 12.5 \\ 6.5 \end{bmatrix}. \]

    The determinant is \(1.5 \times 2.5 - 0.25 = 3.5\), so \(v_x = (2.5 \times 12.5 - 0.5 \times 6.5)/3.5 = 8\) and \(v_y = (1.5 \times 6.5 - 0.5 \times 12.5)/3.5 = 1\). The sensor moves at (8, 1) m/s, and all four residuals are zero.

    (b) A static point at 180° would read \(8\cos180° + 1\sin180° = -8\) m/s. The measurement is −2, so the residual is \(-2 - (-8) = 6\) m/s. The point is not static: it is something behind the sensor that follows it at 6 m/s along the line of sight.

    (c) The fifth row is \((-1, 0)\). Now \(\mathbf{A}\T\mathbf{A} = \begin{bmatrix} 2.5 & 0.5 \\ 0.5 & 2.5 \end{bmatrix}\) and \(\mathbf{A}\T\mathbf{y} = (12.5 + 2,\ 6.5) = (14.5,\ 6.5)\). The determinant is 6, so \(v_x = (2.5 \times 14.5 - 0.5 \times 6.5)/6 = 5.5\) and \(v_y = (2.5 \times 6.5 - 0.5 \times 14.5)/6 = 1.5\). One moving point out of five has pulled the forward speed from 8 to 5.5 m/s. This is why the outlier is rejected before the fit.

  4. A CA-CFAR filter uses \(N = 8\) training cells and \(P_{fa} = 10^{-4}\). (a) Compute the multiplier \(\alpha\). (b) The eight training cells have powers that sum to 12, and the cell under test has power 30. Is it a detection? (c) One training cell, of power 1.5, is replaced by a second target of power 40. Is the cell under test still detected? (d) Show that \(\alpha \to -\ln P_{fa}\) as \(N \to \infty\), and give its value here.

    Solution

    (a) \(\alpha = 8\,(10^{4/8} - 1) = 8\,(3.162 - 1) = 17.30\).

    (b) The mean is \(12/8 = 1.5\), the threshold is \(17.30 \times 1.5 = 25.9\). Since \(30 \gt 25.9\), it is a detection.

    (c) The sum becomes \(12 - 1.5 + 40 = 50.5\), the mean 6.31, the threshold \(17.30 \times 6.31 = 109.2\). Now \(30 \lt 109.2\) and the target is missed. A strong neighbour inside the training window masks a weaker target. The median of the eight cells would hardly move, which is the argument for OS-CFAR.

    (d) Write \(P_{fa}^{-1/N} = e^{-\ln P_{fa}/N}\). For large \(N\) the exponent is small and \(e^{x} \approx 1 + x\), so \(\alpha = N(e^{-\ln P_{fa}/N} - 1) \approx N \cdot (-\ln P_{fa}/N) = -\ln P_{fa}\). For \(P_{fa} = 10^{-4}\) this is 9.21: the threshold you would use if the noise level were known exactly. With 8 cells the multiplier is almost twice that.

You are ready for next week if you can

  • Explain, without formulas, how a chirp turns a delay into a frequency and why the phase between chirps gives velocity.
  • Compute range, range resolution, velocity and the aliasing limit from chirp parameters.
  • Say what speckle, multipath and motion distortion do to a radar scan, and how CFAR and k-strongest filtering differ in purpose.
  • Set up and solve the least-squares problem for ego-velocity, and explain why moving objects must be rejected and why rotation is not observable.
  • Describe how Scan Context is adapted to radar and why a narrow field of view breaks rotation invariance.
  • List the checks a loop candidate passes before it becomes a constraint in a radar pose graph.

Sources

  1. SLAM Handbook, Ch. 9 "Radar SLAM", pp. 250–281.
  2. Richards, Fundamentals of Radar Signal Processing, 2nd ed., 2014 (range and velocity resolution, CA-CFAR multiplier).
  3. Kim and Kim, Scan Context: Egocentric Spatial Descriptor for Place Recognition within 3D Point Cloud Map, 2018.

Week 15 · Day 1

How an event camera works

After today you can state the event generation model, predict how many events a brightness change produces, and explain where the sensor's speed and dynamic range come from.

About 60 min · Read §10.1, pp. 282–286 (5 pages) · Needs Week 11 Day 3

Read first: §10.1, pp. 282–286

While you read, look for:

  • Equation (10.1) on p. 283 and the three things an event carries: pixel, time, polarity.
  • The sentence on p. 284 that says a pixel "adapts its sampling rate". Ask yourself what sets that rate.
  • The four advantages on p. 285 and the number attached to each.
  • Why the authors say on p. 286 that more pixels are not automatically better.

Today's big idea

A standard camera asks every pixel "how bright are you?" at fixed times. An event camera lets every pixel speak for itself, and only when its brightness has changed by a set amount. The output is a stream of events, each saying "pixel \(\mathbf{x}\) got brighter (or darker) at time \(t\)". One short equation, (10.1), describes the whole sensor.

1. A pixel that reports only change

The cameras of Week 11 · Day 3 expose all pixels together and deliver a full image at a rate set by a clock, for example 30 Hz. Between two frames they see nothing, and if nothing moves they send the same picture again. Ch. 10 intro · p. 282

The pixels of an event camera, such as the Dynamic Vision Sensor (DVS), work independently of each other. Each one watches its own log intensity \(L = \log I\), where \(I\) is the light falling on it. It memorizes \(L\) at the moment it last sent an event and keeps comparing the current value with that memory. When the difference reaches the contrast threshold \(C\), the pixel sends a new event and memorizes the new level: §10.1.1 · p. 283

\[ \Delta L \doteq L(\mathbf{x}_k, t_k) - L(\mathbf{x}_k, t_k - \Delta t_k) = p_k\, C . \tag{10.1} \]

The event is the triple \(e_k \doteq (\mathbf{x}_k, t_k, p_k)\): the pixel location \(\mathbf{x}_k\), the time \(t_k\), and the one-bit polarity \(p_k \in \{+1, -1\}\), which says whether the brightness went up (an ON event) or down (an OFF event). \(\Delta t_k\) is the time since the previous event at the same pixel. Equation (10.1) is called the event generation model.

A worked example with \(C = 0.2\). A pixel has just fired, and the light on it then rises from 40 to 100 units. The log intensity rises by \(\ln(100/40) = \ln 2.5 = 0.916\). That is \(0.916 / 0.2 = 4.58\) thresholds, so the pixel fires 4 ON events and is left \(0.116\) above its last memorized level. If the light now falls to 50 units, \(L\) sits at \(\ln(50/40) = 0.223\) above the start, which is \(0.8 - 0.223 = 0.577\) below the memory: 2 OFF events. In general, a pixel that has just fired and then sees a change \(\Delta L\) in one direction sends

\[ n = \left\lfloor \frac{|\Delta L|}{C} \right\rfloor \ \text{events.} \]

The book does not fix the base of the logarithm. This course uses the natural logarithm; another base only rescales \(C\).

Filling the gap: why the logarithm?

The book says each event is a change of "logarithmic intensity" and leaves it there. Three consequences follow from one identity, \(\log a - \log b = \log(a/b)\).

The threshold is a ratio. \(\Delta L = \log I_\text{new} - \log I_\text{old} = \log (I_\text{new}/I_\text{old})\). An ON event with \(C = 0.3\) means the light grew by the factor \(e^{0.3} = 1.35\), that is by 35%. An OFF event means it shrank by the factor \(e^{-0.3} = 0.74\). The same 35% step triggers an event in moonlight and in sunlight.

The lighting level cancels. Model the light reaching a pixel as illumination times surface reflectance, \(I = E\,\rho\). Then \(L = \log E + \log \rho\). If the lamp is made 100 times brighter, every \(L\) shifts by the same constant \(\log 100\), and every difference \(\Delta L\) stays what it was. The events do not change. You will test this in the widget below.

Dynamic range in decibels. The dynamic range of an image sensor is the ratio of the brightest to the darkest light it can register, quoted as \(20 \log_{10}(I_{\max} / I_{\min})\) decibels (dB). The book's figures §10.1.2 · p. 285 translate to

\[ 60\ \text{dB} \Rightarrow \frac{I_{\max}}{I_{\min}} = 10^{3}, \qquad 120\ \text{dB} \Rightarrow \frac{I_{\max}}{I_{\min}} = 10^{6}. \]

So "more than 120 dB against 60 dB" means the usable brightness ratio is at least a thousand times larger. The book gives two reasons: each pixel works on its own, with no exposure setting shared by the whole image, and each pixel converts light to voltage on a logarithmic scale.

2. Events against frames

Event cameras are data-driven: how much they output depends on how much the scene changes. Faster motion gives more events per second, because each pixel samples its signal at the rate the signal changes. §10.1.1 · pp. 283–284

Try it: a bright bar crosses a row of 60 pixels. Change the speed, then the threshold, then the scene light.

Notice four things. At the start there are 593 events, 7 per pixel for each edge that passes, because \(\lfloor \ln 10 / 0.30 \rfloor = 7\). Raising the speed does not change that 7; it squeezes the same events into less time, so the rate goes up. The frame camera smears the bar over speed × exposure (7.5 px) and misses everything between frames (16.7 px of travel). And with the light 100 times dimmer or brighter the events are identical, while the frame keeps 3 or 0 grey levels of contrast out of 229.

In plain words

A frame camera is a class photo taken every so often: everyone is in it whether they moved or not. An event camera is a room where each person calls out only when something changes for them. A quiet room tells you nothing moved. A burst of calls tells you where and exactly when.

3. What the design buys

The book lists four advantages. Each follows from "independent pixels that report log changes". §10.1.2 · p. 285

AdvantageFigure in the bookWhere it comes from
High temporal resolutionEvents are timestamped with microsecond resolutionA pixel fires at the moment of the crossing, so fast motion causes no blur and there is no blind time between frames
Low latencySub-millisecondNo pixel waits for a global exposure to finish
Low power and bandwidthUnder 10 mW at the die level; embedded systems of 100 mW or lessOnly changes are sent; a static scene sends almost nothing
High dynamic rangeTypically more than 120 dB, against 60 dBIndependent pixels and logarithmic conversion

The DVS pixel has three stages that turn light into a voltage, subtract the memorized level, and compare the difference with the threshold. The book relates them to three layers of the retina (Figure 10.2). Some sensors, the ATIS and the DAVIS, also output ordinary grayscale images from the same chip. §10.1.1 · p. 284

4. Which camera for SLAM?

The book notes four trends in commercial devices. §10.1.3 · pp. 285–286

  • Smaller pixels. The pixel pitch fell from 40 µm in the DVS128 to under 5 µm. An event pixel needs more transistors than an ordinary one, so stacked chips and backside illumination are used to keep enough light-sensitive area.
  • Grayscale output is disappearing. Newer high-definition models dropped it to leave room for the event circuit.
  • Colour is rare. Motion tasks seldom need it.
  • A built-in IMU is common. It allows visual-inertial odometry, the subject of Weeks 16 and 17.

More pixels are not automatically better. A one-megapixel event camera moving fast over a textured scene can emit hundreds of millions of events per second. That can saturate the camera's output bus, and according to the book no current algorithm and hardware pair processes such a rate in real time without first converting the events to arrays or dropping some. For prototyping and for robots with little computing power, the book recommends a lower resolution such as QVGA, and adds that the choice of lens (field of view) often matters as much as the pixel count. §10.1.3 · p. 286

Common mistakes

  • "An event tells you how bright the pixel is." It tells you only that the log brightness moved by \(C\) since the last event, and in which direction. Absolute brightness is not transmitted.
  • "The number of events from an edge depends on how fast it moves." In the ideal model the count per pixel depends on the brightness ratio and on \(C\). Speed sets how close together in time they arrive.
  • "A still camera in a still scene sends a steady stream." With constant lighting it sends nothing except noise. Events need motion or changing light. §10.1.1 · p. 283

Check yourself

Q1. A pixel has just fired. The light on it then triples. With C = 0.25 (natural log), how many ON events does the ideal pixel send?

ΔL = ln 3 = 1.099, and 1.099 / 0.25 = 4.39, so 4 events fire. The remaining 0.099 stays below the threshold.

Q2. The same edge crosses the same pixel twice as fast. In the ideal model, what changes?

The count is set by the total change in log brightness divided by C. The speed only compresses the timestamps, which doubles the event rate.

Q3. A scene is filmed twice with the same camera motion, once under a lamp and once under a lamp ten times brighter. How do the ideal event streams compare?

Ten times more light adds the constant log 10 to every L. Events depend only on differences of L, and the constant cancels.

Q4. A sensor with 120 dB of dynamic range is compared with one of 60 dB. By what factor is its ratio of brightest to darkest usable light larger?

With 20 log₁₀ of the ratio, 120 dB is a ratio of 10⁶ and 60 dB is 10³. The ratio of the two is 10³ = 1000.

Recap

  1. Each pixel memorizes its log intensity at its last event and fires again when the current value differs from it by the contrast threshold \(C\): equation (10.1).
  2. An event is (pixel, time, polarity). It carries the sign of a change, not a brightness.
  3. A change \(\Delta L\) produces \(\lfloor |\Delta L| / C \rfloor\) events. Faster motion gives the same events sooner, so a higher rate.
  4. Because \(L\) is a logarithm, the threshold is a brightness ratio and the lighting level cancels. That, with independent pixels, gives the high dynamic range.
  5. For SLAM, a moderate resolution is often the practical choice: megapixel sensors can produce more events than can be transmitted or processed.

Sources

  1. SLAM Handbook, Chapter 10 introduction and §10.1 "Sensor Description", pp. 282–286.
  2. The event count \(\lfloor |\Delta L|/C \rfloor\) follows directly from (10.1). Quoting dynamic range as \(20\log_{10}\) of the intensity ratio is the usual convention for image sensors; it is the one behind the 120 dB and 60 dB figures, which also appear in Gallego et al., Event-based Vision: A Survey, 2022 (the book's reference [361]).
  3. The model \(I = E\rho\) (illumination times reflectance) is the standard Lambertian image-formation model, as in Szeliski, Computer Vision: Algorithms and Applications, 2010.

Week 15 · Day 2

Why events are hard to use, and a map of the methods

After today you can explain with the linearized event generation model why events depend on the motion, and place an event-based SLAM method on the three axes of the book's taxonomy.

About 60 min · Read §10.2–10.3, pp. 286–289 (4 pages) · Needs Week 15 Day 1

Read first: §10.2–10.3, pp. 286–289

While you read, look for:

  • The three challenges at the end of p. 286 and the top of p. 287.
  • The four questions on p. 287 that the authors say drive the research.
  • The two classes of methods by "how many events are processed simultaneously", and what the second class has to choose (p. 287).
  • How data association is usually handled (bottom of p. 287, top of p. 288).

Today's big idea

An event stream is not a fast video. It is sparse, it has no frames, each event is a single bit, and the same scene produces different events when the camera moves differently. Algorithms built for images therefore do not apply as they are. The book sorts the new algorithms along three independent axes: how many events are processed at once, whether the method is designed or learned, and whether it works on features or on all events.

1. Three challenges

The book names three properties of the data that every method has to face. §10.2 · pp. 286–287

ChallengeWhat it meansConsequence
Space-time outputEvents are asynchronous (each has its own time) and spatially sparse; images are synchronous and denseVisual SLAM written for image sequences cannot be applied directly
Motion-dependent dataAn event is one bit (brighter or darker), and whether it fires depends on the relative motion as well as on the scene textureThe "appearance" of a place is not fixed, which makes matching hard
Noise and dynamic effectsPhoton shot noise, transistor noise, dependence on the amount of light, circuit non-idealitiesSome events are spurious and some are missing, so no single event can be trusted

The first row you saw on Day 1. The third is a property of the circuit. The second is the least obvious, and one short derivation makes it exact.

2. Why events depend on motion

Filling the gap: the linearized event generation model

On p. 287 the book mentions "the event generation model (10.1) (or its linearized version)" and gives a reference instead of the formula. Here it is, in three steps.

Step 1: a short time interval. Equation (10.1) is \(L(\mathbf{x}, t) - L(\mathbf{x}, t - \Delta t) = p\,C\). If \(\Delta t\) is small, a first-order Taylor expansion in time gives

\[ L(\mathbf{x}, t) - L(\mathbf{x}, t - \Delta t) \approx \frac{\partial L}{\partial t}(\mathbf{x}, t)\, \Delta t . \]

Step 2: brightness constancy. Assume the light is constant, so a point of the scene keeps its brightness while its image moves. If the point is at \(\mathbf{x}(t)\) and moves over the image plane with velocity \(\mathbf{v} = \mathrm{d}\mathbf{x}/\mathrm{d}t\) (pixels per second), then \(L(\mathbf{x}(t), t)\) is constant in time. Differentiate with the chain rule:

\[ \frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t} L(\mathbf{x}(t), t) = \nabla L \cdot \mathbf{v} + \frac{\partial L}{\partial t} = 0 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \frac{\partial L}{\partial t} = -\nabla L \cdot \mathbf{v}, \]

where \(\nabla L = (\partial L/\partial x, \partial L/\partial y)\) is the spatial gradient of the log image: it points from dark to bright, across an edge.

Step 3: combine.

\[ \Delta L \approx -\nabla L \cdot \mathbf{v}\, \Delta t = p\, C . \]

Read three facts off this line.

  • Rate. The time between two events at a pixel is \(\Delta t \approx C / |\nabla L \cdot \mathbf{v}|\), so the pixel fires about \(|\nabla L \cdot \mathbf{v}| / C\) events per second. Strong edges and fast motion give many events.
  • Polarity. \(p = \operatorname{sign}(-\nabla L \cdot \mathbf{v})\). Reverse the motion and every ON becomes an OFF.
  • Blind direction. If \(\mathbf{v}\) is perpendicular to \(\nabla L\), the motion runs along the edge, \(\nabla L \cdot \mathbf{v} = 0\), and no event fires. Only the component of \(\mathbf{v}\) along the gradient is seen.

A check against Day 1. In the Day 1 simulator (\(v = 0.5\) px/ms, \(C = 0.3\)) the first two ON events of a pixel arrive 0.41 ms apart. The model says the edge is that steep there: \(|\partial L/\partial x| \approx C / (v\,\Delta t) = 0.3 / (0.5 \times 0.41) = 1.46\) per pixel. The exact slope of the simulated edge at that point is 1.49. Two timestamps were enough to measure a local image gradient.

A 2-D example. A vertical edge has \(\nabla L = (0.5, 0)\) per pixel, and the image moves with \(\mathbf{v} = (-200, 100)\) px/s. Then \(-\nabla L \cdot \mathbf{v} = -(0.5 \times (-200) + 0 \times 100) = +100\) per second. With \(C = 0.25\) each pixel on the edge fires \(100/0.25 = 400\) ON events per second, one every 2.5 ms. The vertical part of the motion, 100 px/s, contributes nothing.

Intuition

Run a fingertip over a ruler with raised marks. Crossing the marks, you feel each one. Sliding along a mark, you feel nothing, however fast you go. An event camera feels the image the same way, which is why the book calls a moving event camera an asynchronous edge detector. §10.4 · p. 289

3. The questions this raises

The challenges turn into four research questions: how to extract information from events for pose and depth estimation, which map and trajectory representations fit data that is nearly continuous in time and sparse in space, how to find correspondences when the data depends on motion, and how to do all of it without rebuilding the bottlenecks of frame-based processing. §10.2 · p. 287

Event-based SLAM has grown together with two neighbouring tasks. Image reconstruction recovers absolute intensity from events; by the model above, the events hold samples of \(\nabla L \cdot \mathbf{v}\), so with a known motion they constrain the image, and with a known image they constrain the motion. Optical flow estimation recovers the image velocity \(\mathbf{v}\) itself. The first event-based SLAM systems already estimated an intensity image along with the motion. §10.2 · p. 287

4. Three axes for classifying methods

The book's taxonomy has three axes, and they are independent of each other. §10.3 · p. 287

AxisOption AOption B
How many events at onceEvent-by-event: the state (map and trajectory) can change when a single event arrives; minimum latencyPackets (also called groups, batches, or slices) of events; some latency, and a packet size to choose
How the method is obtainedModel-based: designed from the sensor model and geometryData-driven: learned from data
What is extractedIndirect: first turn events into features (event corners, lines, normal flow), then run a geometric SLAM pipeline; geometric objectiveDirect: one step from all events to motion and scene parameters; photometric objective, a function of the event polarity or of the event rate

The last axis mirrors the indirect and direct methods of frame-based visual SLAM (Week 11 · Day 4). For direct methods the event generation model (10.1), or the linearized version you just derived, is the starting point of the design. §10.3 · p. 287

Choosing the packet size. The book lists three kinds of rule: a fixed number of events, a fixed duration, and hybrid criteria. Day 1 tells you what each does, because the event rate follows the motion. Take a packet of 20,000 events. If the camera moves slowly and produces 100,000 events per second, the packet spans 200 ms. If it moves fast and produces 2,000,000 per second, the packet spans 10 ms. A fixed count therefore updates more often exactly when the motion is fast, but waits indefinitely when nothing moves. A fixed duration of 10 ms gives a predictable update rate, but the slow case then has only 1,000 events to work with.

5. Data association, and the road so far

Data association means deciding which events belong to the same scene point or feature. It is a central problem, because single events carry no descriptor to match. The usual answer exploits the high temporal resolution: events that are close in time and close in pixel position are taken to come from the same edge. Both hard association (each event is assigned to one thing) and soft association (an event contributes to several things with weights) have been used. §10.3 · pp. 287–288

The field approached the full problem by raising the difficulty step by step along several axes: the number of unknowns (degrees of freedom), the type of motion (from pure rotation or planar scenes to full 6-DoF motion), the scene (from simple high-contrast patterns to natural texture), and whether the scene is static or contains independently moving objects. Early work was model-based; more recent work also explores deep learning. Because events come from moving edges, the maps these systems recover are usually edge maps: sparse or semi-dense 3D points. §10.3 · pp. 288–289, Figure 10.3

Common mistakes

  • "The same scene always produces the same events." The events sample \(\nabla L \cdot \mathbf{v}\). Change the direction of motion and different edges fire, with different polarities.
  • "Direct means event-by-event." The axes are independent. Many direct methods work on packets, and some indirect methods update with every event.
  • "A pixel with no events sees a uniform surface." It may be looking at an edge that is parallel to the motion.

Check yourself

Q1. At a pixel, ∇L = (0.4, 0) per pixel and the image velocity is v = (250, −500) px/s. With C = 0.2, what does the linearized model predict?

∇L·v = 0.4 × 250 = 100 per second. The rate is 100 / 0.2 = 500 per second, and the polarity is the sign of −100, so OFF. The speed |v| = 559 px/s is not what matters; only the component along ∇L does.

Q2. A camera pans horizontally in front of a static scene. Which edges produce the fewest events?

The image moves horizontally. A horizontal edge has a vertical gradient, so ∇L·v = 0: it slides along itself and fires nothing.

Q3. A method uses packets of 10,000 events. The event rate rises from 200,000 to 1,000,000 events per second. How does the time span of a packet change?

10,000 / 200,000 = 0.05 s and 10,000 / 1,000,000 = 0.01 s. A fixed count shortens the packet when the motion speeds up.

Q4. A system detects corners in the event stream, tracks them, and passes the tracks to a classical pipeline that minimizes reprojection error. The corner detector is hand-designed. How is it classified?

Features first and a geometric objective second make it indirect. Nothing is learned from data, so it is model-based.

Recap

  1. Event data is asynchronous and sparse, depends on motion, and is noisy. Image-based SLAM does not transfer directly.
  2. Linearized event generation model: \(-\nabla L \cdot \mathbf{v}\,\Delta t \approx p\,C\). Rate \(|\nabla L \cdot \mathbf{v}|/C\), polarity \(\operatorname{sign}(-\nabla L \cdot \mathbf{v})\), and no events for motion along an edge.
  3. Methods are classified by events per update (single or packets), by design (model-based or learned), and by what they use (indirect features or direct use of all events).
  4. Data association relies on closeness in time and in pixel position, with hard or soft assignments.
  5. Research moved from rotation-only and simple scenes toward 6-DoF motion in natural scenes, and the maps are mostly edge maps.

Sources

  1. SLAM Handbook, §10.2 "Challenges and Applications" and §10.3 "Overview and Taxonomy of Event-based SLAM Methods", pp. 286–289.
  2. The linearized event generation model follows Gallego et al., Event-based Vision: A Survey, 2022 (the book's reference [361]).
  3. Brightness constancy and the optical-flow constraint: Horn and Schunck, Determining Optical Flow, 1981.
  4. The packet-size comparison is our own arithmetic from the event rates of Day 1.

Week 15 · Day 3

The front-end: event representations, indirect and direct methods

After today you can build an event frame, a time surface, and a voxel grid from a packet of events, and explain how indirect, direct, and learned front-ends turn events into poses and a map.

About 60 min · Read §10.4, pp. 289–292 (4 pages) · Needs Week 15 Day 2

Read first: §10.4, pp. 289–292

While you read, look for:

  • What the front-end receives and what it outputs (p. 289). It is not quite the definition you met in Week 1.
  • Why "each event corresponds to a different camera pose", and the two prices paid for converting events into arrays (p. 290).
  • Why it is "natural to track features rather than to match them" (p. 291).
  • What an image of warped events is, and what "estimating motion by undoing it" means (p. 292).

Today's big idea

A single event is four numbers and may be noise, so a front-end must combine thousands of them. It makes three design choices: how to hold the events (the representation), whether to reduce them to features or use them all (indirect or direct), and whether the processing is designed or learned. Every choice trades the sensor's speed and sparsity against the convenience of mature image-based tools.

1. What the front-end does

In this chapter the front-end takes the raw events (and calibration) and outputs camera poses and a scene map. The back-end then refines both, runs more slowly, and can feed its result back to reduce drift. §10.4 · p. 289 In Week 1 · Day 1 the front-end handed the back-end pseudo-measurements; here it hands over a first full estimate. The split is the same idea: fast and rough first, slow and careful second.

With constant lighting, events come from moving contours, so the problem is posed in terms of scene edges. And since one event carries so little, thousands or millions are needed for a reliable pose or map. §10.4 · p. 289

2. Event representations

In an image, all pixels share one timestamp and therefore one camera pose. That shared pose is the assumption on which classical multi-view geometry rests. Events break it: each has its own microsecond timestamp, so each belongs to a slightly different pose. §10.4.1 · p. 290

Many methods nevertheless convert events into an array first, to reuse mature image tools or to feed a neural network. The book warns of two prices: quantization (events with similar timestamps are lumped together) and loss of sparsity (the array is mostly zeros where nothing happened). It names event images, time surfaces, and voxel grids, and sends you to a survey for the definitions. §10.4.1 · p. 290

Filling the gap: three representations, defined

Take the events \(e_k = (\mathbf{x}_k, t_k, p_k)\), \(k = 1, \dots, N_e\), that fall in a window from \(t_0\) to \(t_0 + \Delta\).

Event frame (event image). Add the polarities that landed on each pixel:

\[ F(\mathbf{x}) = \sum_{k \,:\, \mathbf{x}_k = \mathbf{x}} p_k . \]

A variant counts events and ignores polarity. Either way, all timing inside the window is gone.

Time surface. For each pixel, store how recently it fired. With \(t_\text{last}(\mathbf{x})\) the time of the pixel's latest event up to now, and a decay constant \(\tau\),

\[ T(\mathbf{x}, t) = \exp\!\left( -\frac{t - t_\text{last}(\mathbf{x})}{\tau} \right), \]

and \(T = 0\) where no event has occurred. A pixel that just fired has \(T = 1\); the value fades as the event ages.

Voxel grid. Cut the window into \(B\) time bins and let each event vote for its two nearest bins, with weights that depend linearly on its time. Rescale the event time to \(t^*_k = (B-1)(t_k - t_0)/\Delta\), which runs from 0 to \(B-1\). Then for bin \(b = 0, \dots, B-1\)

\[ V(\mathbf{x}, b) = \sum_{k \,:\, \mathbf{x}_k = \mathbf{x}} p_k \, \max\!\left(0,\; 1 - |b - t^*_k|\right). \]

A worked example. One pixel receives three events in a 20 ms window: \(+1\) at 2 ms, \(+1\) at 5 ms, \(-1\) at 16 ms. Use \(B = 3\) bins (centred at 0, 10, 20 ms) and \(\tau = 10\) ms, and evaluate at \(t = 20\) ms.

  • Event frame: \(1 + 1 - 1 = 1\).
  • Time surface: the last event is 4 ms old, so \(T = e^{-4/10} = 0.67\).
  • Voxel grid: the rescaled times are \(t^* = 0.2,\ 0.5,\ 1.6\). The first event gives 0.8 to bin 0 and 0.2 to bin 1. The second gives 0.5 and 0.5. The third gives \(-0.4\) to bin 1 and \(-0.6\) to bin 2. Totals: \(V = (1.3,\ 0.3,\ -0.6)\).

The three voxel values add up to 1, the event frame, because each event's two weights sum to one. The voxel grid is an event frame with its time axis partly restored.

Try it: the bar from Day 1 again. Lengthen the window to 50 ms, then move "Now" and the decay.

Notice that with a 20 ms window (140 events) the event frame shows each edge smeared over about 10 pixels, the distance the bar moved in that time. With a 50 ms window ending at 60 ms, 17 pixels have received both ON and OFF events and 14 of them sum to exactly zero: the event frame is blank where the whole bar passed. The voxel grid keeps the two polarities in different time bins. The time surface is a ramp that fades behind each edge, so it shows which way the edge is going.

RepresentationStored per pixelTiming keptExample of use in the book
Event frameOne number: sum or countNone inside the windowReusing frame-based feature detectors §10.5 · p. 293
Time surfaceOne number: recency of the last eventTime of the last event onlyESVO: stereo matching on time-surface patches Table 10.1 · p. 295
Voxel grid\(B\) numbersTo about \(\Delta/(B-1)\)Common input to neural networks; DEVO p. 297, Table 10.1
Raw eventsNothing is convertedAll of itEVO's mapping module §10.4.1 · p. 290

One system can mix them: EVO maps with raw events and tracks the camera with edge-like event images. The book's ideal is a representation that keeps the speed and sparsity of the sensor, and it says plainly that this is still open research. §10.4.1 · p. 290

A number shows why quantization matters. Suppose the camera turns at 300° per second (5.24 rad/s) and its focal length is 200 pixels. Near the image centre the picture then slides at about \(200 \times 5.24 \approx 1050\) pixels per second. An event frame over 10 ms smears every edge across 10 pixels, exactly the motion blur the sensor was built to avoid.

3. Indirect methods

Indirect methods work in two steps. They first extract and track features in the events (points, lines, or other primitives), then hand those to classical geometric SLAM. Features compress the stream into a few informative primitives, which saves computation. §10.4.2 · p. 291

The hard part is data association. One event is too little, and too dependent on the motion, to be matched by appearance. The sensor offers a way out: events arrive almost continuously, so a feature has barely moved when its next events arrive. Association can be made by closeness in pixel position and time, and it becomes natural to track a feature from moment to moment instead of matching it between two distant views.

The rest is the toolbox of Weeks 11 and 12. Camera tracking aligns features with a known map by minimizing the reprojection error (Week 12 · Day 1), and the 3D structure comes from triangulating corresponding features from known poses (Week 11 · Day 5). The weak link is the feature step: event features are less mature than image features because of noise, sparsity, asynchrony, and motion dependence. That limits accuracy, and some systems add grayscale images or an IMU to compensate. §10.4.2 · p. 291

4. Direct methods

Direct methods use all events, not only those that fit the definition of a feature. They align the events with a map, with an image, or with other events, in one step: the motion or scene parameters are found by optimizing an objective such as a photometric error. If the event rate exceeds what the computer can handle, events are denoised or subsampled first. §10.4.3 · p. 291

Direct methods lean on the near-continuity of the data. Since there is no blind time, the pose changes only a little from one update to the next, so each update can start from the previous pose and compute a small increment. §10.4.3 · p. 292

The most accurate subclass, according to the book, estimates motion by event alignment. The idea is to estimate the motion by undoing it. Guess the motion; move every event back along that motion to where it would have been at one reference time; add up the moved events per pixel. The result is the image of warped events (IWE). If the guess is right, events from the same edge pile onto the same pixels and the IWE is sharp. If it is wrong, the IWE is blurred. Searching for the sharpest IWE is called contrast maximization (CMax), and sharpness can be scored by variance, gradient magnitude, or other measures. Tomorrow you will run it. §10.4.3 · p. 292

Data association in direct methods is implicit and soft: events are associated because they land near each other on the pixel grid. §10.4.3 · p. 292

5. Designed or learned

Most event-based SLAM so far is model-based: hand-designed from the sensor's operating principle and the geometry of the problem. Learning-based methods use artificial neural networks instead, either on image-like representations or directly on events with spiking neural networks. §10.4.4 · p. 292

Training signalWhat it needsDifficulty
SupervisedGround-truth poses or depthGround truth is hard to collect in the real world
Self-supervisedOnly the events, or a second sensor such as grayscale frames from the same device; the loss checks temporal or photometric consistencyThe loss must be designed so that a correct answer minimizes it

A network can replace one part of the pipeline, such as feature extraction and tracking, or the whole system end to end. Learned methods cope with complicated representations and with noise without a hand-written model. In return they need large training sets, and they can fail on scenes unlike the training data, which is called domain shift. §10.4.4 · p. 292

Common mistakes

  • "Converting events to frames costs nothing." It quantizes time and fills the array with zeros, giving up two of the sensor's advantages.
  • "A time surface is a brightness image." It stores how recently each pixel fired. A bright scene region with no motion has value zero.
  • "Direct methods have no data association." They have it implicitly: events are associated by where they land on the pixel grid.

Check yourself

Q1. A window runs from 0 to 30 ms and the voxel grid has B = 4 bins. An event with polarity −1 arrives at 7 ms. What does it add to the grid at its pixel?

t* = (4 − 1) × 7 / 30 = 0.7. The weight for bin 0 is 1 − 0.7 = 0.3 and for bin 1 it is 1 − 0.3 = 0.7, both multiplied by the polarity −1.

Q2. A time surface uses τ = 20 ms. A pixel last fired 10 ms ago. What is its value?

exp(−10/20) = exp(−0.5) = 0.61.

Q3. During one window a pixel receives 6 ON events and then 6 OFF events. What does the polarity-summing event frame hold there?

6 − 6 = 0. A bright bar that passed completely leaves no trace. A voxel grid would hold positive values in early bins and negative values in late ones.

Q4. Why do indirect event-based methods track features instead of matching them between distant views?

Single events have no stable appearance to match, but the high temporal resolution keeps successive events of a feature close together in pixel space, so association by vicinity works.

Recap

  1. The front-end turns raw events into first estimates of poses and an edge map; the back-end refines them.
  2. Every event has its own timestamp and so its own camera pose. Packing events into arrays quantizes time and loses sparsity.
  3. Event frame: sum of polarities per pixel. Time surface: \(\exp(-(t - t_\text{last})/\tau)\). Voxel grid: polarity shared linearly between the two nearest of \(B\) time bins.
  4. Indirect methods extract and track features, then use classical geometry. Direct methods align all events by optimizing one objective; contrast maximization is the leading example.
  5. Learned methods handle noise and representations implicitly, but need data and can suffer from domain shift.

Sources

  1. SLAM Handbook, §10.4 "Front-end of an Event-based SLAM System", pp. 289–292; Table 10.1, p. 295.
  2. Definitions of the event representations: Gallego et al., Event-based Vision: A Survey, 2022 (the book's reference [361]).
  3. Time surfaces with exponential decay: Lagorce, Orchard, Galluppi, Shi, Benosman, HOTS: A Hierarchy of Event-Based Time-Surfaces for Pattern Recognition, 2017.
  4. The voxel grid with linear weights in time: Zhu, Yuan, Chaney, Daniilidis, Unsupervised Event-based Learning of Optical Flow, Depth, and Egomotion, 2019.
  5. The image-speed estimate uses the small-angle pinhole relation (shift ≈ focal length × angle), as in Hartley and Zisserman, Multiple View Geometry, 2004.

Week 15 · Day 4

The back-end, and contrast maximization as an optimization problem

After today you can write contrast maximization as an optimization problem, explain why variance measures alignment, and say what indirect and direct event-based back-ends optimize.

About 60 min · Read §10.5–10.6, pp. 293–295 (3 pages) · Needs Week 15 Day 3

Read first: §10.5–10.6, pp. 293–295

While you read, look for:

  • What most event-based systems do instead of a refinement step, and why (p. 293).
  • The authors' reasons why indirect back-ends "fall short" (p. 293).
  • The two objectives used by event-only direct back-ends, and the motions they have been developed for (pp. 293–294).
  • In Table 10.1 (p. 295), the columns "BA" and "Motion". Find the rows whose input is events only and that have a back-end.

Today's big idea

Bundle adjustment for events is young. Indirect back-ends reuse the reprojection error of classical visual SLAM. Direct back-ends optimize either how well the events align (contrast maximization) or a brightness error for every event. Contrast maximization deserves a close look, because it turns the vague goal "the picture should be sharp" into a function of the motion that an optimizer can climb.

1. Why back-ends are rare here

A back-end improves the agreement between all the unknowns and all the data, and stops errors from passing back and forth between tracking and mapping. In frame-based visual SLAM that job is done by bundle adjustment (BA), which you studied in Week 12 · Day 3. §10.5 · p. 293

Most event-based systems have no such step. They run parallel tracking and mapping: a tracking module estimates the pose assuming the map is right, a mapping module updates the map assuming the poses are right, and each uses the other's latest output. The book's judgement is that these systems chose simplicity and low latency over accuracy and robustness. A joint refinement is hard for events for three reasons: the data is noisy and depends on the motion, the unknowns are many and correlated so the search space is large, and the optimization is costly and has local minima. §10.5 · p. 293

2. Indirect and direct back-ends

The back-end must fit the front-end that feeds it, so the book sorts back-ends the same way. §10.5 · pp. 293–294

PropertyIndirect back-endDirect back-end
Works onCorners, lines, and other primitives detected in the events, sometimes after converting events to imagesThe sensor data itself
ObjectiveReprojection error: distance in the image plane between observed and predicted featuresA photometric error. With grayscale frames, borrowed from frame-based direct systems. With events only: event alignment, or the brightness change conveyed by each event
StrengthReuses mature, robust techniquesUses all the information. Event-only versions avoid the motion blur and low dynamic range of frames
WeaknessDiscards most of what the events contain; event corners are less accurate and stable than image cornersRecent. Event-only versions exist so far for planar or rotational motion, and need many events, which costs computation, power, and latency

The book's evidence that events hold much more than corners is image reconstruction: whole intensity images can be recovered from events alone. §10.5 · p. 293

3. Contrast maximization, step by step

The book describes contrast maximization in one paragraph (p. 292) and names it as one of the two event-only back-end objectives (p. 294). It gives no formula. Here is the method in full for the simplest case.

Filling the gap: warp, accumulate, score

The unknown. A vector of motion parameters \(\boldsymbol{\theta}\). In the simplest case the whole image slides with one constant velocity, and \(\boldsymbol{\theta}\) is that velocity in pixels per millisecond.

Step 1: warp. Pick a reference time \(t_\text{ref}\). Move each event \(e_k = (\mathbf{x}_k, t_k, p_k)\) to where its scene point would have been at \(t_\text{ref}\) if the motion were \(\boldsymbol{\theta}\):

\[ \mathbf{x}'_k = \mathbf{W}(\mathbf{x}_k, t_k; \boldsymbol{\theta}) = \mathbf{x}_k - (t_k - t_\text{ref})\,\boldsymbol{\theta} . \]

Step 2: accumulate. Count how many warped events land on each pixel \(\mathbf{x}\). This is the image of warped events:

\[ H(\mathbf{x}; \boldsymbol{\theta}) = \sum_{k=1}^{N_e} b_k \, \delta\!\left(\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{x}'_k\right), \]

where \(b_k = 1\) (count events) or \(b_k = p_k\) (sum polarities), and \(\delta\) is 1 when its argument is zero and 0 otherwise. Since \(\mathbf{x}'_k\) is rarely a whole pixel, each event is in practice shared between its nearest pixels in proportion to closeness, which also makes \(H\) change smoothly with \(\boldsymbol{\theta}\).

Step 3: score. Measure the contrast of \(H\) by its variance over the \(N_p\) pixels:

\[ f(\boldsymbol{\theta}) = \frac{1}{N_p} \sum_{i=1}^{N_p} \left( H(\mathbf{x}_i; \boldsymbol{\theta}) - \mu_H \right)^2, \qquad \mu_H = \frac{1}{N_p} \sum_{i=1}^{N_p} H(\mathbf{x}_i; \boldsymbol{\theta}). \]

The estimate is \(\boldsymbol{\theta}^\star = \argmax_{\boldsymbol{\theta}} f(\boldsymbol{\theta})\).

Why the true motion wins. A scene edge that moves at velocity \(\mathbf{v}\) fires its events along a line in space-time: at time \(t\) it is at \(\mathbf{x}_0 + (t - t_\text{ref})\mathbf{v}\). Warp with \(\boldsymbol{\theta} = \mathbf{v}\) and every one of those events lands on \(\mathbf{x}_0\). Warp with anything else and they are spread over a segment of length \(|\mathbf{v} - \boldsymbol{\theta}|\) times the duration.

Why variance rewards that. Expand the square: \(f = \frac{1}{N_p}\sum_i H_i^2 - \mu_H^2\). With \(b_k = 1\), and as long as no event is warped off the image, the total \(\sum_i H_i = N_e\) is the same for every \(\boldsymbol{\theta}\), so \(\mu_H\) is a constant. Maximizing the variance is then the same as maximizing \(\sum_i H_i^2\), and a sum of squares with a fixed total is largest when the total is concentrated in few places. Take 12 events on 4 pixels:

IWESum of squaresVariance (mean is 3)
(3, 3, 3, 3)3636/4 − 9 = 0
(6, 6, 0, 0)7272/4 − 9 = 9
(12, 0, 0, 0)144144/4 − 9 = 27

By hand. An edge fires at \((x, t) = (10, 0),\ (12, 1),\ (14, 2),\ (16, 3)\), with \(x\) in pixels and \(t\) in ms. Take \(t_\text{ref} = 0\) and an image of 8 pixels, so \(\mu_H = 4/8 = 0.5\).

  • \(\theta = 0\): the events stay at 10, 12, 14, 16. Four pixels hold 1 each. \(f = 4/8 - 0.25 = 0.25\).
  • \(\theta = 1\): they move to 10, 11, 12, 13. Still four pixels with 1 each. \(f = 0.25\).
  • \(\theta = 2\): they move to 10, 10, 10, 10. One pixel holds 4. \(f = 16/8 - 0.25 = 1.75\).

The velocity is 2 px/ms, found without ever deciding which event belongs to which edge.

function contrast(θ, events, t_ref):
    H ← image of zeros
    for each event (x, t, p):
        x' ← x − (t − t_ref)·θ            # undo the candidate motion
        add 1 to H around x'              # shared between the nearest pixels
    return variance(H)

θ* ← the θ that maximizes contrast(θ, events, t_ref)
     # any optimizer; a good start is the θ of the previous packet

Try it: 1110 events from two moving bars plus random noise. Drag the candidate speed, then press Reset and Climb.

Notice that at θ = 0 the image of warped events is only the raw event count per pixel: low and spread out (tallest column 32 events, variance 77). At θ = 0.60 the slanted streaks stand upright, the four edges of the two bars appear (tallest column 140), and the variance reaches 1023, thirteen times higher. Climb finds that peak from θ = 0 with 25 evaluations. Set the noise to 100% and the peak stays at 0.60: noise events do not line up for any θ, so they only raise the floor.

In plain words

Take a long-exposure photo of traffic at night and you get streaks. If you knew exactly how each car moved, you could slide every bit of light back along its path and the streaks would shrink to sharp headlights. Contrast maximization runs this backwards: it tries motions until the streaks become points, and the motion that does it is the answer.

4. From one speed to SLAM

The recipe does not care what \(\boldsymbol{\theta}\) is, as long as it defines a warp. Three steps lead to a back-end.

  • Rotation. For a camera that only rotates, \(\boldsymbol{\theta}\) is the angular velocity (three numbers), and the warp rotates each event's viewing direction back to the reference time. Table 10.1 lists this as "CMax-ω", for rotational motion. Table 10.1 · p. 295
  • A whole trajectory. In CMax-SLAM the unknowns are the camera's rotations over time. All events are warped onto one panorama, and the trajectory is refined until that panorama is as sharp as possible. This is bundle adjustment with contrast as the objective, and the sharp panorama is an edge map of the scene (Figure 10.3 shows one). §10.5 · p. 294; Table 10.1
  • The other objective. EMBA and EPBA instead write one residual per event from equation (10.1): the brightness change that the current map and trajectory predict at that pixel, minus the \(p_k C\) the event reported. They refine the motion together with a gradient map (EMBA) or an intensity map (EPBA). A gradient map can be turned into an intensity image by Poisson integration (Figure 10.4). §10.5 · p. 294; Table 10.1; Figure 10.4 · p. 290

All three are for rotational motion. The book states that efficient, direct, event-only BA for 6-DoF motion in natural scenes is still open. §10.5 · p. 294

Going deeper (optional): when the sharpest image is wrong

The book warns that when events can be warped onto a few pixels or a line, these methods "can suffer from undesired global optima". §10.4.3 · p. 292 The reason is visible in the table above: variance is highest when all events sit on one pixel. Our 1-D warp only shifts events, so it cannot do that. A warp family that can shrink the image, for instance one with a zoom-like parameter, can send every event toward a single point and score a huge contrast that has nothing to do with the true motion. Practical systems restrict the warp or add a penalty to rule this out.

5. Reading Table 10.1

Table 10.1 lists event-based SLAM and odometry systems in chronological order, with the labels you now know: model-based (M) or deep learning (DL), direct (D) or indirect (I), the event representation, whether there is a back-end (BA), the motion and scene handled, and the input sensors (E events, F frames, D depth, I IMU, M a given map; "2E" is a stereo pair). Table 10.1 · p. 295 The book draws these trends: §10.6 · p. 294

  • Model-based systems dominate. Only two rows, DEVO and DEIO, are marked DL. The authors expect that this may change.
  • Difficulty was raised gradually along three lines: the camera motion, the type of scene, and the extra sensors or information used to simplify the problem. A depth sensor removes the burden of estimating depth from events; an IMU supplies accurate angular velocity.
  • Good methods get extended along a standard route. Monocular becomes stereo or multi-camera, and event-only methods are made more robust by adding an IMU (ESVO led to ESVO2, DEVO to DEIO).
  • The field is still exploring. The rows use many different map representations, event representations, and loss functions; no single design has won.

Two things you can check in the table yourself: none of the first eleven systems has a back-end, and the direct, event-only systems that do have one (CMax-SLAM, EMBA, EPBA) are all rotational.

Common mistakes

  • "Contrast maximization must first decide which events belong to the same edge." It never does. Events are associated implicitly by landing on the same pixel after the warp.
  • "The sharpest image of warped events is always the right motion." Only if the warp cannot collapse the events. See the optional note.
  • "Every SLAM system has a back-end." In Table 10.1 about half of the systems have none, and the early ones never do.

Check yourself

Q1. One edge fires four events at (x, t) = (20, 0), (23, 2), (26, 4), (29, 6), with x in pixels and t in ms. With the reference time at 0, which candidate speed warps all four onto one pixel?

The edge advances 3 pixels every 2 ms, so 1.5 px/ms. Check: 23 − 2 × 1.5 = 20, 26 − 4 × 1.5 = 20, 29 − 6 × 1.5 = 20.

Q2. An image of warped events on 5 pixels is (0, 5, 0, 5, 0). What is its variance?

The mean is 10/5 = 2. The squared deviations are 4, 9, 4, 9, 4, which sum to 30, and 30/5 = 6. The flat image (2, 2, 2, 2, 2) with the same 10 events has variance 0.

Q3. Why does a higher variance of the image of warped events indicate better alignment?

With the mean fixed, variance grows with the sum of squared counts. Events of one edge piling onto one pixel raise that sum; spreading them lowers it.

Q4. Which statement about event-based back-ends agrees with the book?

§10.5 says event-only direct back-ends are recent and limited to constrained motions. Most systems lack a refinement step, indirect back-ends discard most of the event information, and reprojection error is the indirect objective.

Recap

  1. Most event-based systems run tracking and mapping in parallel with no joint refinement. Event-based BA is recent.
  2. Indirect back-ends minimize reprojection error of event features. Direct back-ends minimize a photometric error or maximize event alignment.
  3. Contrast maximization: warp events by a candidate motion, \(\mathbf{x}'_k = \mathbf{x}_k - (t_k - t_\text{ref})\boldsymbol{\theta}\), accumulate them into the image of warped events \(H\), and maximize its variance over \(\boldsymbol{\theta}\).
  4. Variance works because, for a fixed number of events, it grows with \(\sum_i H_i^2\), which is largest when events of the same edge land on the same pixel.
  5. Event-only direct BA (CMax-SLAM, EMBA, EPBA) exists for rotational motion; the 6-DoF case is open.

Sources

  1. SLAM Handbook, §10.5 "Back-end of an Event-based SLAM System" and §10.6 "State-of-the-Art Systems", pp. 293–295 with Table 10.1; §10.4.3, p. 292; Figure 10.4, p. 290.
  2. The warp, the image of warped events, and the variance objective follow Gallego, Rebecq, Scaramuzza, A Unifying Contrast Maximization Framework for Event Cameras, with Applications to Motion, Depth, and Optical Flow Estimation, 2018.
  3. The identity variance = mean of squares − square of the mean is elementary statistics. The 12-event table and the four-event example are our own arithmetic.

Week 15 · Day 5

Simulators, datasets, metrics, and open problems

After today you can explain how a simulator turns brightness samples into events and noise, choose a dataset for a task, and compute and interpret the absolute trajectory error and the relative pose error.

About 60 min · Read §10.7–10.8, pp. 294–303 (8 pages; skim the dataset descriptions) · Needs Week 15 Day 1

Read first: §10.7–10.8, pp. 294–303

This is a survey section. Read §10.7.1 and §10.7.3 with care and skim the dataset descriptions in §10.7.2. Look for:

  • How ESIM differs from "thresholding the difference between two successive frames", and the noise model for \(C\) (pp. 295–296).
  • What V2E adds, and which weakness of earlier simulators V2CE addresses (p. 297).
  • In Table 10.2 (p. 299), the resolution and sensor columns.
  • The one-sentence descriptions of ATE and RPE, and why depth errors are usually folded into trajectory errors (p. 301).

Today's big idea

A young field moves at the speed of its data and its yardsticks. Simulators give unlimited events with perfect ground truth, provided their noise is realistic. Datasets give real events with measured ground truth. Metrics compress the comparison of two trajectories into a number: ATE asks how far the whole path is off, RPE asks how wrong each step is.

1. Simulators

Event cameras are new and event data is scarce, which hurts learning-based methods most. Simulators fill the gap. §10.7.1 · pp. 295–297

SimulatorStarts fromMain idea
ESIMA rendered virtual sceneRenderer and event generator are tightly coupled, so frames are rendered adaptively, following how fast the visual signal changes
CARLA's event sensorA driving simulatorThe ESIM principle in rich driving scenes
Vid2EAny existing videoInterpolate extra frames (Super SloMo), then apply ESIM. Models an ideal sensor
V2EVideoModels the DVS circuit: temporal noise, leak events, a bandwidth that depends on intensity, Gaussian thresholds
EventGANPairs of imagesA network trained with adversarial and cycle-consistency losses; outputs a voxel grid per polarity
VISTA 2.0Real driving data, several sensor typesBuilt for learning control policies; events generated as in ESIM, with optical flow from a network
V2CEVideoA network predicts voxel grids, and a second stage recovers continuous event timestamps from them

The earliest attempts simply thresholded the difference of two consecutive frames. That gives edge-like pictures, but not the right number of events and not their times. §10.7.1 · p. 295

Filling the gap: from brightness samples to event timestamps

The book says what simulators do but not how a sample of brightness becomes an event with a microsecond timestamp. The standard construction is short.

A simulator knows a pixel's log brightness only at sample times: \(L_a\) at \(t_a\) and \(L_b\) at \(t_b\). Let \(L_\text{ref}\) be the level the pixel memorized at its last event. Assume \(L\) changes linearly between the two samples. If it rises, it crosses the levels \(L_\text{ref} + jC\) for \(j = 1, 2, \dots\) as long as they do not exceed \(L_b\), and the crossing times follow from similar triangles:

\[ t_j = t_a + \frac{L_\text{ref} + jC - L_a}{L_b - L_a}\,(t_b - t_a). \]

Each crossing is one ON event. For a falling signal use \(L_\text{ref} - jC\) and emit OFF events. Afterwards \(L_\text{ref}\) is the last level crossed. This is equation (10.1) applied between samples, and it is what the simulator behind this week's widgets does every 0.05 ms.

Example. \(L_\text{ref} = L_a = -1.0\) at \(t_a = 0\), \(L_b = -0.2\) at \(t_b = 1\) ms, \(C = 0.3\). The levels \(-0.7\) and \(-0.4\) are crossed; \(-0.1\) is not reached. So two ON events fire, at

\[ t_1 = \frac{0.3}{0.8} \times 1\ \text{ms} = 0.375\ \text{ms}, \qquad t_2 = \frac{0.6}{0.8} \times 1\ \text{ms} = 0.75\ \text{ms}, \]

and the memory ends at \(-0.4\), with \(0.2\) of change carried over to the next interval. Thresholding the frame difference would report one event at \(t_b\).

Why the sampling must adapt. The linear assumption fails if too much happens between samples. A thin bright line that crosses a pixel entirely between \(t_a\) and \(t_b\) leaves \(L_a = L_b\), and the simulator emits nothing. A reasonable rule is to sample often enough that the image moves at most about one pixel between samples. An edge moving at 2000 px/s then needs a sample every 0.5 ms, while at 20 px/s one every 50 ms is enough. A renderer can produce frames at any time, so ESIM can adapt. A recorded 30 Hz video cannot: at 2000 px/s the image jumps 67 pixels between frames. That is why Vid2E and V2E first interpolate intermediate frames, and why the book says their number needs care: too few causes aliasing, too many costs computation. §10.7.1 · p. 296

Noise. An algorithm tuned on perfect simulated events may fail on real ones; this is the simulation-to-real gap. ESIM and its descendants use a simple noise model taken from measurements: the contrast threshold is not fixed but drawn from a normal distribution \(\N(C, \sigma_C^2)\) at each simulation step, with separate thresholds \(C^+\) and \(C^-\) for the two polarities. §10.7.1 · p. 296 To see the effect, take the bar of Day 1, whose edge changes \(L\) by \(\ln 10 = 2.30\). With \(C = 0.30\) a pixel fires 7 events. If its threshold happens to be \(0.27\) it fires \(\lfloor 2.30/0.27 \rfloor = 8\), and with \(0.33\) it fires 6. Neighbouring pixels no longer agree, which is what real data looks like.

V2E goes further and models the pixel circuit, and V2CE targets the timestamps: earlier video-based simulators emit events at discrete times, which differs from real data enough to matter for methods that are sensitive to timing. §10.7.1 · p. 297

2. Datasets

Table 10.2 lists sixteen datasets. A selection, with what makes each one useful: §10.7.2 · pp. 298–301, Table 10.2

DatasetPlatformEvent pixelsWhat it offers
ECDSHand-held240 × 180The first with synchronized events, IMU, and 6-DoF ground-truth poses from motion capture; 11 real scenes and 2 synthetic ones
MVSECHand-held, drone, car, motorcycle346 × 240The first with ground-truth depth, from LiDAR; stereo events; long indoor and outdoor sequences
UZH-FPVRacing drone346 × 260Fast indoor and outdoor flight, aimed at drone racing and visual-inertial odometry
EV-IMO, EV-IMO2Hand-held346 × 260, 640 × 480Independently moving objects with pixel-wise motion masks, plus ground-truth egomotion and depth
DSECCar640 × 480Stereo events (60 cm baseline) and stereo RGB, LiDAR, RTK GPS; day, night, and direct sun; ground-truth depth maps
TUM-VIEHand-held, head-mounted1280 × 720One-megapixel stereo events with IMU at 200 Hz and grayscale frames at 20 Hz

M3EDDrone, car, quadruped robot1280 × 720High-speed motion on several platforms, with ground-truth pose, depth, and semantic labels

To choose, match three things to your task: the motion (a hand-held office sequence says little about a racing drone), the ground truth you need (poses are common, depth is rare), and the resolution (recall from Day 1 that megapixel sensors produce event rates that are hard to process).

3. Metrics

Ideally localization and mapping would be graded separately. In practice the two are intertwined, since depth errors cause pose errors and the reverse, and ground-truth poses are far easier to obtain than ground-truth depth. So the quality of the map is usually judged through the trajectory. Event-based SLAM inherits its two main metrics from classical SLAM (Week 11 · Day 1). §10.7.3 · p. 301

  • The absolute trajectory error (ATE) compares estimated and true poses in one fixed world frame. It grades long-term, global accuracy.
  • The relative pose error (RPE) compares the estimated and true motion between nearby time steps. It grades local consistency.

In both, the translational part is a Euclidean distance between positions and the rotational part is the geodesic distance in \(\SO(3)\). §10.7.3 · p. 301

Filling the gap: the formulas

The book describes the metrics in words. Let \(\mathbf{T}^\text{gt}_i\) and \(\mathbf{T}^\text{est}_i\) in \(\SE(3)\) be the true and estimated poses at the same \(n\) timestamps, with positions \(\mathbf{t}^\text{gt}_i\) and \(\mathbf{t}^\text{est}_i\).

ATE. The two trajectories usually live in different world frames, so first find the rigid transform \(\mathbf{S}\) that best maps the estimate onto the ground truth in the least-squares sense (the closed-form alignment of Week 13 · Day 2). Then take the root mean square of what remains:

\[ \text{ATE} = \sqrt{ \frac{1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^{n} \norm{ \mathbf{t}^\text{gt}_i - \mathbf{S}\,\mathbf{t}^\text{est}_i }^2 } . \]

RPE. Choose an interval of \(\Delta\) steps. Form the relative motions \(\Delta\mathbf{T}^\text{gt}_i = (\mathbf{T}^\text{gt}_i)^{-1}\mathbf{T}^\text{gt}_{i+\Delta}\) and \(\Delta\mathbf{T}^\text{est}_i = (\mathbf{T}^\text{est}_i)^{-1}\mathbf{T}^\text{est}_{i+\Delta}\), and the error

\[ \mathbf{E}_i = \left( \Delta\mathbf{T}^\text{gt}_i \right)^{-1} \Delta\mathbf{T}^\text{est}_i . \]

If the estimated step equals the true step, \(\mathbf{E}_i\) is the identity. The translational RPE is the root mean square of the lengths of the translation parts of the \(\mathbf{E}_i\); the rotational RPE uses the angles of their rotation parts. No alignment is needed, because relative motions do not depend on the world frame.

Geodesic distance in \(\SO(3)\). The distance between rotations \(\mathbf{R}_1\) and \(\mathbf{R}_2\) is the angle of the rotation that takes one to the other:

\[ d(\mathbf{R}_1, \mathbf{R}_2) = \norm{ \Log\!\left( \mathbf{R}_1\T \mathbf{R}_2 \right) } = \arccos\!\left( \frac{\tr\!\left(\mathbf{R}_1\T\mathbf{R}_2\right) - 1}{2} \right), \]

since a rotation by angle \(\theta\) about any axis has trace \(1 + 2\cos\theta\). Example: if \(\tr(\mathbf{R}_1\T\mathbf{R}_2) = 2.9696\), then \(\cos\theta = 0.9848\) and the two orientations are \(10^\circ\) apart.

Try it: the estimate below makes a single wrong turn. Move the step at which it happens.

Notice that the RPE is 0.028 steps wherever the wrong turn happens: one bad step in 40 is the same local error anywhere (its size is the chord \(2\sin 5^\circ = 0.174\), and \(0.174/\sqrt{40} = 0.028\)). The ATE is 0.29 at step 8, 0.69 at step 20, and 0.03 at step 39. A turn near either end rotates almost the whole path rigidly, and the alignment removes that; a turn in the middle bends the path, which no rigid alignment can undo. Without alignment the end point is off by 4.47 steps at step 8.

Some authors divide the position error by the mean scene depth or by the distance travelled, so that results from scenes of different size can be compared: an ATE of 0.20 m on a 50 m path is 0.4% of the distance. Further variants average the relative position and rotation errors, and for event cameras the errors in linear and angular velocity are also informative, since fast and abrupt motions are what the sensor is for. §10.7.3 · pp. 301–302

When depth is graded separately, the usual measures are the average depth error up to several cutoff distances, the root mean square distance from each estimated 3D point to the closest ground-truth surface (the preferred one), the relative error, and completion, which is the number of points recovered. §10.7.3 · p. 302

4. Open problems

The book closes with what is unsolved. §10.8 · p. 302

  • The processor does not match the sensor. The camera is asynchronous, yet most systems run on ordinary serial processors. A fully neuromorphic system would pair the event camera with asynchronous, spike-based processors and controllers, and is expected to do better in power consumption and latency. Building one means designing sensor, processor, and algorithm together, which takes expertise from several disciplines.
  • New sensors. Hybrid sensors deliver events and intensity, aligned in space and time. Foveated sensors, like the eye, keep high resolution only in part of the image to save bandwidth.
  • Fusion. Combining event cameras with frame cameras, structured light, LiDAR, or radar leaves much to explore.

Common mistakes

  • "A low RPE means the trajectory is globally accurate." Small errors at every step can add up to a large drift. RPE grades the steps, ATE grades the sum.
  • "ATE is the distance between the two trajectories as given." Without the alignment you would mostly measure the arbitrary choice of world frame.
  • "Simulated events are as good as real ones." Only as far as the noise and timing models are right. That is the reason V2E and V2CE exist.

Check yourself

Q1. A simulated pixel has just fired, so its memory equals its current level, L = 0 at t = 0. The next sample is L = 1.0 at t = 4 ms. With C = 0.4 and linear interpolation, which events does it emit?

The levels 0.4 and 0.8 are crossed; 1.2 is not reached. On a line from 0 to 1.0 over 4 ms they are crossed at 0.4 × 4 = 1.6 ms and 0.8 × 4 = 3.2 ms.

Q2. An odometry system estimates every single step accurately but has no loop closure and runs for an hour. What do you expect?

RPE looks at short intervals and stays small. The small step errors accumulate as drift, which the ATE measures in a fixed world frame.

Q3. The product of the transposed true rotation and the estimated rotation has trace 2.0. What is the rotational error?

cos θ = (2.0 − 1)/2 = 0.5, so θ = 60°.

Q4. You want to evaluate stereo depth from events on a car, at night, against ground-truth depth maps. Which dataset in the table fits best?

DSEC was recorded from a car with two event cameras, in day, night, and direct sunlight, and provides ground-truth depth maps. ECDS and EDS are hand-held with a single event camera, and UZH-FPV is a racing drone.

Recap

  1. A simulator turns brightness samples into events by finding where the interpolated log brightness crosses levels spaced \(C\) apart. Sampling must be dense when the image moves fast.
  2. Realism needs noise: at the least a randomized threshold \(\N(C, \sigma_C^2)\), and in V2E a model of the pixel circuit.
  3. Datasets differ in platform, resolution, and ground truth. Poses are common; ground-truth depth is rarer.
  4. ATE: align the estimate to the ground truth, then take the root mean square position error. RPE: compare relative motions over a short interval. ATE grades global accuracy, RPE local consistency.
  5. Open problems: asynchronous (neuromorphic) processing to match the sensor, hybrid and foveated sensors, and fusion with other sensors.

Sources

  1. SLAM Handbook, §10.7 "Datasets, Simulators, and Benchmarks" and §10.8 "Further Readings & Recent Trends", pp. 294–303, with Table 10.2.
  2. The ATE and RPE formulas follow Sturm, Engelhard, Endres, Burgard, Cremers, A Benchmark for the Evaluation of RGB-D SLAM Systems, 2012.
  3. Least-squares rigid alignment: Umeyama, Least-Squares Estimation of Transformation Parameters Between Two Point Patterns, 1991.
  4. Rotation angle from the trace, and \(\Log\) on \(\SO(3)\): Solà, Deray, Atchuthan, A micro Lie theory for state estimation in robotics, 2018.
  5. The level-crossing construction is equation (10.1) with linear interpolation between samples; the one-pixel sampling rule and the numerical examples are our own.

Week 15 · Review

Week 15 review: event-based SLAM

After today you can predict the events a brightness change produces, turn events into the common representations, run contrast maximization by hand, and evaluate a trajectory with ATE and RPE.

About 60 min · No new pages

The week in one paragraph

An event camera's pixels work independently and report only changes: when a pixel's log intensity has moved by the contrast threshold \(C\) since its last event, it sends its position, the time, and the sign of the change. That gives microsecond timing, low latency, low power, and a dynamic range above 120 dB, but the data is sparse, asynchronous, noisy, and depends on the motion, because events sample \(\nabla L \cdot \mathbf{v}\). Methods are sorted by how many events they process at once, by whether they are designed or learned, and by whether they extract features (indirect) or use all events (direct). Front-ends often repack events as event frames, time surfaces, or voxel grids. Back-ends are rare and recent; the direct, event-only ones maximize contrast or minimize a per-event brightness error, so far for rotational motion. Simulators, datasets, and the ATE and RPE metrics are how the field measures itself.

1. Formula sheet

What it isFormulaWhere
Event generation model\(\Delta L = L(\mathbf{x}_k, t_k) - L(\mathbf{x}_k, t_k - \Delta t_k) = p_k C\), event \(e_k = (\mathbf{x}_k, t_k, p_k)\)(10.1), §10.1.1, p. 283 · Day 1
Events from one change, just after a firing\(n = \lfloor |\Delta L| / C \rfloor\), where \(\Delta L = \ln(I_\text{new}/I_\text{old})\)App · Day 1
Dynamic range in decibels\(20 \log_{10}(I_{\max}/I_{\min})\); 120 dB is \(10^6\), 60 dB is \(10^3\)§10.1.2, p. 285 · Day 1
Linearized event generation model\(-\nabla L \cdot \mathbf{v}\,\Delta t \approx p\,C\); rate \(|\nabla L \cdot \mathbf{v}|/C\); polarity \(\operatorname{sign}(-\nabla L \cdot \mathbf{v})\)Named in §10.3, p. 287 · Day 2
Event frame\(F(\mathbf{x}) = \sum_{k:\,\mathbf{x}_k = \mathbf{x}} p_k\)§10.4.1, p. 290 · Day 3
Time surface\(T(\mathbf{x}, t) = \exp\!\left(-(t - t_\text{last}(\mathbf{x}))/\tau\right)\)§10.4.1, p. 290 · Day 3
Voxel grid\(V(\mathbf{x}, b) = \sum_k p_k \max(0, 1 - |b - t^*_k|)\), \(t^*_k = (B-1)(t_k - t_0)/\Delta\)§10.4.1, p. 290 · Day 3
Contrast maximization\(\mathbf{x}'_k = \mathbf{x}_k - (t_k - t_\text{ref})\boldsymbol{\theta}\); \(H(\mathbf{x}) = \sum_k b_k\,\delta(\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{x}'_k)\); maximize \(\frac{1}{N_p}\sum_i (H_i - \mu_H)^2\)§10.4.3, p. 292; §10.5, p. 294 · Day 4
Simulated event times between two samples\(t_j = t_a + \dfrac{L_\text{ref} + jC - L_a}{L_b - L_a}(t_b - t_a)\)§10.7.1, pp. 295–296 · Day 5
ATE and RPE\(\text{ATE} = \sqrt{\tfrac{1}{n}\sum_i \norm{\mathbf{t}^\text{gt}_i - \mathbf{S}\mathbf{t}^\text{est}_i}^2}\); \(\mathbf{E}_i = (\Delta\mathbf{T}^\text{gt}_i)^{-1}\Delta\mathbf{T}^\text{est}_i\); angle \(= \arccos\frac{\tr(\mathbf{R}) - 1}{2}\)§10.7.3, p. 301 · Day 5

2. Mixed quiz

Check yourself
