Q1. A pixel has just fired. The light on it then falls from 80 to 20 units. With C = 0.35, what does it send?

ΔL = ln(20/80) = −1.386. Its size is 3.96 thresholds, so 3 events fire, and they are OFF because the brightness fell.

Q2. Which of these is not contained in an event?

An event is (x, t, p). The brightness itself is never transmitted, only that its logarithm moved by C.

Q3. At a pixel, ∇L = (0, 0.6) per pixel and v = (300, 100) px/s. With C = 0.3, what event rate does the linearized model predict?

∇L·v = 0.6 × 100 = 60 per second, and 60 / 0.3 = 200. The 300 px/s along the edge adds nothing. (The events are OFF, since −∇L·v is negative.)

Q4. What makes a method "direct" in the book's taxonomy?

Direct against indirect is about features. Event-by-event against packets, and model-based against learned, are separate axes.

Q5. A voxel grid has B = 5 bins over a window from 0 to 20 ms. Where does an event at 15 ms put its weight?

t* = (5 − 1) × 15 / 20 = 3 exactly, so the weight for bin 3 is 1 and for every other bin it is 0.

Q6. An event at pixel x = 40 has time 12 ms. With reference time 2 ms and candidate speed θ = 0.5 px/ms, where does contrast maximization warp it?

x′ = x − (t − t_ref) θ = 40 − 10 × 0.5 = 35.

Q7. Most event-based systems run tracking and mapping in parallel. What do they lack compared with a system that has a back-end?

Each module trusts the other's output, so errors pass back and forth. A back-end such as bundle adjustment refines everything together.

Q8. An estimate has 50 steps. Forty-nine relative motions are exact and one has a translation error of 0.7 m. What is the translational RPE (root mean square)?

√(0.7² / 50) = 0.7 / √50 = 0.099 m. Where the bad step occurs makes no difference to the RPE, though it does to the ATE.

3. Pen-and-paper problems

  1. A pixel with \(C = 0.25\) has just fired while the light on it was 200 units. The light then goes to 600, then to 300, then to 1000. List the events in order, and give the brightness that corresponds to the pixel's final memorized level.

    Solution

    Measure everything from the starting level \(L_0 = \ln 200\). The memory starts at \(L_0\).

    To 600: \(L = L_0 + \ln 3 = L_0 + 1.099\). That is 4.39 thresholds above the memory: 4 ON. Memory is now \(L_0 + 1.0\).

    To 300: \(L = L_0 + \ln 1.5 = L_0 + 0.405\), which is \(0.595\) below the memory, 2.38 thresholds: 2 OFF. Memory is now \(L_0 + 0.5\).

    To 1000: \(L = L_0 + \ln 5 = L_0 + 1.609\), which is \(1.109\) above the memory, 4.44 thresholds: 4 ON. Memory is now \(L_0 + 1.5\).

    The final memorized level corresponds to \(200\,e^{1.5} = 896\) units. Ten events in all: 4 ON, 2 OFF, 4 ON.

  2. A pattern with log intensity \(L(x) = 2\sin(2\pi x/40)\), \(x\) in pixels, slides to the right at 400 px/s past a pixel with \(C = 0.2\). (a) Use the linearized model to find the largest event rate. (b) When is the rate zero? (c) How many events does the pixel fire per second on average? Compare with (a).

    Solution

    (a) The steepest slope is \(\max |\partial L/\partial x| = 2 \times 2\pi/40 = 0.314\) per pixel. The rate is \(|\nabla L \cdot v|/C = 0.314 \times 400 / 0.2 = 628\) events per second, at the zero crossings of the sine.

    (b) At the crests and troughs, where the slope is zero. The pixel is momentarily looking at a flat piece of the pattern.

    (c) One period passes in \(40/400 = 0.1\) s. In that time \(L\) rises by 4 (from \(-2\) to \(2\)) and falls by 4. A rise of 4 is \(4/0.2 = 20\) ON events and the fall is 20 OFF events, so 40 events per 0.1 s, or 400 per second. This is \(2/\pi = 0.64\) of the peak rate, which is the average of \(|\cos|\) over a period, as the linearized model predicts.

  3. Six events come from two edges moving at the same speed: \((x, t) = (5, 0), (7, 1), (9, 2)\) and \((12, 0), (14, 1), (16, 2)\), with \(x\) in pixels and \(t\) in ms. The image has 20 pixels and \(t_\text{ref} = 0\). (a) Compute the variance of the image of warped events for \(\theta = 0, 1, 2, 3\) px/ms. (b) Now try \(\theta = -1.5\), sharing an event that lands halfway between two pixels equally between them. What does the result tell you about the shape of the objective?

    Solution

    The mean is always \(\mu_H = 6/20 = 0.3\), so \(f = \frac{1}{20}\sum_i H_i^2 - 0.09\).

    (a) \(\theta = 0\): positions 5, 7, 9, 12, 14, 16; six pixels hold 1; \(f = 6/20 - 0.09 = 0.21\). \(\theta = 1\): positions 5, 6, 7 and 12, 13, 14; again \(f = 0.21\). \(\theta = 2\): positions 5, 5, 5 and 12, 12, 12; two pixels hold 3; \(f = 18/20 - 0.09 = 0.81\). \(\theta = 3\): positions 5, 4, 3 and 12, 11, 10; \(f = 0.21\). The maximum is at \(\theta = 2\) px/ms.

    (b) \(x' = x + 1.5\,t\): the first edge goes to 5, 8.5, 12 and the second to 12, 15.5, 19. Pixel 12 receives one event from each edge. The image is 1 at pixel 5, 0.5 at pixels 8 and 9, 2 at pixel 12, 0.5 at pixels 15 and 16, and 1 at pixel 19. \(\sum H_i^2 = 1 + 0.25 + 0.25 + 4 + 0.25 + 0.25 + 1 = 7\), so \(f = 0.35 - 0.09 = 0.26\). That is above the 0.21 of its neighbours although the motion is wrong: events of different edges met by chance. The objective can have small local maxima away from the true motion, which is why the optimizer should start near the answer, for example from the previous estimate.

  4. A robot moves along a line. The true positions at five timestamps are 0, 1, 2, 3, 4 m. An odometry estimate gives 0, 1.1, 2.2, 3.3, 4.4 m. (a) Compute the translational RPE for consecutive poses. (b) Compute the ATE, where "alignment" in one dimension is the best constant shift. (c) What happens to each metric if the run continues in the same way to 17 poses?

    Solution

    (a) Every true step is 1 m and every estimated step is 1.1 m, so each relative error is 0.1 m and the RPE is 0.1 m.

    (b) The differences true minus estimate are \(0, -0.1, -0.2, -0.3, -0.4\). The least-squares shift is their mean, \(-0.2\). The residuals are \(0.2, 0.1, 0, -0.1, -0.2\), and

    \[ \text{ATE} = \sqrt{\frac{0.04 + 0.01 + 0 + 0.01 + 0.04}{5}} = \sqrt{0.02} = 0.141\ \text{m}. \]

    Without the shift (start points matched) it would be \(\sqrt{(0 + 0.01 + 0.04 + 0.09 + 0.16)/5} = 0.245\) m.

    (c) The RPE stays 0.1 m. The residuals after the shift are \(0.1\,(i - \bar{\imath})\) for \(i = 0, \dots, n-1\), whose root mean square is \(0.1\sqrt{(n^2 - 1)/12}\). For \(n = 5\) this gives \(0.1\sqrt{2} = 0.141\) as before; for \(n = 17\) it gives \(0.1\sqrt{24} = 0.49\) m. The ATE grows with the length of the run, and the RPE does not. That is the difference between global accuracy and local consistency.

You are ready for next week if you can

  • State the event generation model (10.1) and compute how many events a given brightness change produces.
  • Derive \(-\nabla L \cdot \mathbf{v}\,\Delta t \approx pC\) from brightness constancy and use it to predict event rate and polarity.
  • Build an event frame, a time surface, and a voxel grid from a short list of events.
  • Explain contrast maximization and compute the variance of an image of warped events by hand.
  • Compute ATE and RPE for a small trajectory and say what each one grades.
  • Say why an IMU is a natural partner for an event camera: it measures angular velocity directly (p. 294). Week 16 starts there.

Sources

  1. SLAM Handbook, Chapter 10 "Event-based SLAM", pp. 282–303.
  2. Gallego et al., Event-based Vision: A Survey, 2022 (linearized model, representations).
  3. Gallego, Rebecq, Scaramuzza, A Unifying Contrast Maximization Framework for Event Cameras, with Applications to Motion, Depth, and Optical Flow Estimation, 2018.
  4. Sturm, Engelhard, Endres, Burgard, Cremers, A Benchmark for the Evaluation of RGB-D SLAM Systems, 2012 (ATE and RPE).

Week 16 · Day 1

What an IMU measures: rotation rate, specific force, bias, and noise

After today you can write the IMU measurement model, explain why an accelerometer at rest reads 9.81 m/s² upward, and say what each error term in the model stands for.

About 60 min · Read §11.1 and §11.1.1, pp. 304–306 (3 pages) · Needs Week 4 Day 1

Read first: §11.1 opening and §11.1.1, pp. 304–306

While you read, look for:

  • The difference between a strapdown and a stabilized inertial navigation system, and which one robots use (p. 305).
  • The one sentence on p. 305 that says what an accelerometer physically measures. It is not "acceleration".
  • Equations (11.1) and (11.2) on p. 306, and the remark below them about what the superscripts on \(\mathbf{b}\) and \(\boldsymbol{\eta}\) mean.
  • The three matrices \(\mathbf{T}_a\), \(\mathbf{T}_g\), \(\mathbf{T}_s\) in the extended models (11.3)–(11.5).

Today's big idea

An inertial measurement unit is two sensors in one package. The gyroscope reports how fast the body is rotating. The accelerometer reports the body's acceleration minus gravity. Both report in the body's own axes, and both are corrupted by a slowly wandering offset (the bias) and by fast random noise. The two lines of equations (11.1)–(11.2) say exactly this, and the rest of the week is built on them.

1. The sensor and its vocabulary

An inertial measurement unit (IMU) contains a 3-axis accelerometer and a 3-axis gyroscope, six numbers per sample. It needs nothing from the outside world: no light, no texture, no satellites. It is also fast, typically 200 to 1000 samples per second. §11.1 · p. 304; §11.2 · p. 308 IMUs range from large, accurate optical units in aircraft to the small, noisier micro-electromechanical (MEMS) chips in phones, which are the ones most robots carry. Ch. 11 · p. 304

TermMeaning
Inertial navigation system (INS)Estimates the current state (pose, velocity) from an initial state and the history of IMU measurements.
Strapdown systemThe IMU is bolted to the vehicle and turns with it. Nearly every robot is strapdown.
Stabilized systemThe IMU sits on gimbals that keep its orientation fixed in space while the vehicle turns around it.
Inertial odometryThe robotics name for inertial navigation. "Odometry" is a reminder that the estimate drifts.
Aided INS (AINS)An INS corrected by other sensors: GPS, cameras, LiDAR.
Visual-inertial odometry / visual-inertial SLAMCameras plus IMU for motion tracking; called SLAM once loop closures are added.

§11.1 · pp. 304–305 Many IMUs also carry a compass, but indoors and in cities it is disturbed by metal structures and electronics, so SLAM systems rarely rely on it. §11.1 · p. 304, footnote 2

2. Two frames

The model uses two coordinate frames. The world frame \(\mathcal{F}^w\) is fixed to the ground. The body frame \(\mathcal{F}^b\) is fixed to the IMU and moves with the robot (the book assumes sensor and body frames coincide). A superscript tells you in which frame a vector's coordinates are written. The rotation \(\mathbf{R}^w_b\) converts body coordinates to world coordinates, and its transpose \(\mathbf{R}^b_w = (\mathbf{R}^w_b)\T\) goes the other way. The IMU's pose at time \(t\) is the pair \(\{\mathbf{R}^w_b(t), \mathbf{p}^w(t)\}\). §11.1.1 · pp. 305–306

The physics of the sensors holds in an inertial frame, one that neither accelerates nor rotates. The ground rotates with the Earth, so strictly it is not inertial. For low-cost IMUs over small areas the Earth's rotation is far below the sensor noise, so the book treats the world frame as inertial. §11.1.1 · p. 305, footnote 3

3. The gyroscope

The gyroscope measures the angular velocity of the body. The book's model is

\[ \boldsymbol{\omega}(t) = \boldsymbol{\omega}^b_b(t) + \mathbf{b}^g(t) + \boldsymbol{\eta}^g(t). \tag{11.2} \]

The left side is the reading. On the right, \(\boldsymbol{\omega}^b_b\) is the true angular velocity of the body relative to the world, written in body coordinates: its direction is the axis of rotation and its length is the rate in rad/s. \(\mathbf{b}^g\) is the gyroscope bias and \(\boldsymbol{\eta}^g\) is zero-mean Gaussian noise. The superscript \(g\) is not a frame. It says "gyroscope", and \(a\) says "accelerometer". §11.1.1 · p. 306

Example: a robot spins on the spot at 90° per second about its vertical body axis. The true rate is \(\boldsymbol{\omega}^b_b = (0, 0, 1.571)\) rad/s. With a bias of \((0.002, -0.001, 0.003)\) rad/s the gyroscope reports about \((0.002, -0.001, 1.574)\) rad/s, plus a little noise that is different in every sample.

From equation (11.12) on, the book marks measured values with a tilde, \(\tilde{\boldsymbol{\omega}}\) and \(\tilde{\mathbf{a}}\). We use the tilde from now on so that a reading is never confused with the true quantity.

4. The accelerometer measures specific force

\[ \mathbf{a}(t) = \mathbf{R}^b_w(t)\,\big(\mathbf{a}^w(t) - \mathbf{g}^w\big) + \mathbf{b}^a(t) + \boldsymbol{\eta}^a(t). \tag{11.1} \]

Here \(\mathbf{a}^w\) is the true acceleration of the sensor in the world frame and \(\mathbf{g}^w\) is the gravity vector in the world frame. With \(z\) pointing up, \(\mathbf{g}^w = (0, 0, -9.81)\) m/s². The rotation \(\mathbf{R}^b_w\) in front converts the result into body coordinates. §11.1.1 · p. 306 The quantity \(\mathbf{a}^w - \mathbf{g}^w\) is called the specific force: acceleration with gravity taken out. The book describes it as the difference between the kinematic acceleration and the gravitational acceleration. §11.1.1 · p. 305

Filling the gap: why "minus gravity"?

The book states the minus sign without deriving it. Picture the simplest accelerometer: a small proof mass \(m\) held inside a case by a spring. The sensor can only measure how far the spring is stretched, which is the spring force \(\mathbf{F}_s\). Two forces act on the mass, the spring and gravity, so Newton's second law reads

\[ m\,\mathbf{a}^w = \mathbf{F}_s + m\,\mathbf{g}^w \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \frac{\mathbf{F}_s}{m} = \mathbf{a}^w - \mathbf{g}^w . \]

Gravity pulls on the case and on the mass equally, so it never stretches the spring by itself. The spring only responds to forces that reach the mass through the case: the floor pushing up, a motor, a collision. That is the specific force. Three cases with \(z\) up:

  • At rest on a table. \(\mathbf{a}^w = \mathbf{0}\), so the reading is \(-\mathbf{g}^w = (0,0,+9.81)\). The sensor reports the table pushing it up.
  • Free fall. \(\mathbf{a}^w = \mathbf{g}^w\), so the reading is \(\mathbf{0}\).
  • Lifting off at 2 m/s². \(\mathbf{a}^w = (0,0,2)\), so the reading is \((0,0,11.81)\).

Try it: a body in the vertical plane with a two-axis accelerometer. Press "Free fall", then "At rest", then change the pitch.

Notice that at rest the reading always has length 9.81 and points straight up in the world. Tilting the body does not change that vector, it only changes how it splits between the two body axes: at 20° pitch the sensor reads (3.36, 9.22). In free fall the reading is zero at every pitch.

In plain words

An accelerometer feels what you feel. Sitting still you feel the chair pushing up on you, and so does the sensor. Falling freely you feel nothing, and the sensor reads nothing. Gravity itself is never felt directly.

5. Bias and noise

Both readings carry the same two error terms. §11.1.1 · pp. 305–306

TermHow it behavesWhat it does once you integrateHow the estimator deals with it
Noise \(\boldsymbol{\eta}^g, \boldsymbol{\eta}^a\)Zero-mean Gaussian, independent from one sample to the next (white)Partly averages out: the integrated error grows like \(\sqrt{t}\)Modeled by a covariance (Day 4)
Bias \(\mathbf{b}^g, \mathbf{b}^a\)An offset that changes slowly, modeled as a random walkDoes not average out: the integrated error grows like \(t\)Estimated as an unknown, alongside pose and velocity (Day 5)

A worked number shows why the bias is the dangerous one. An accelerometer bias of 0.05 m/s² is about half a percent of gravity. Left uncorrected for 10 s it produces a velocity error of \(0.05 \times 10 = 0.5\) m/s and a position error of \(\tfrac12 \times 0.05 \times 10^2 = 2.5\) m. This is why the biases are part of the state that visual-inertial systems estimate. The book calls them "to-be-estimated". §11.1.1 · p. 306

6. Extended models

Real chips are not perfectly built: the three sensing axes are not exactly perpendicular, and each has its own gain. The book collects both effects in a 3×3 shape matrix that multiplies the true quantity: §11.1.1 · p. 306

\[ \mathbf{a}(t) = \mathbf{T}_a\,\mathbf{R}^b_w(t)\big(\mathbf{a}^w(t)-\mathbf{g}^w\big) + \mathbf{b}^a(t) + \boldsymbol{\eta}^a(t), \tag{11.3} \] \[ \boldsymbol{\omega}(t) = \mathbf{T}_g\,\boldsymbol{\omega}^b_b(t) + \mathbf{T}_s\,\mathbf{R}^b_w(t)\big(\mathbf{a}^w(t)-\mathbf{g}^w\big) + \mathbf{b}^g(t) + \boldsymbol{\eta}^g(t). \tag{11.5} \]

(The text introduces (11.3) as an extension of "model (11.2)"; the equation it extends is the accelerometer model (11.1).) A perfect sensor has \(\mathbf{T}_a = \mathbf{T}_g = \mathbf{I}\). Diagonal entries away from 1 are scale errors and off-diagonal entries are axis misalignment. In (11.5) the extra matrix \(\mathbf{T}_s\) models g-sensitivity: in some MEMS gyroscopes the reading shifts a little when the chip is accelerated. Equation (11.4) is (11.5) without that term. All three matrices are found by calibration.

Example: a 1% scale error on the \(z\) axis is \(\mathbf{T}_a = \operatorname{diag}(1, 1, 0.99)\). At rest and level, the reading becomes \((0, 0, 0.99 \times 9.81) = (0, 0, 9.712)\). That is 0.098 m/s² short, the same error as a bias of 0.098 m/s², but it changes as soon as the sensor tilts. For everyday SLAM the simple model (11.1)–(11.2) is usually enough, and the extended models matter when calibrating. §11.1.1 · p. 306

Common mistakes

  • "An accelerometer at rest reads zero." It reads 9.81 m/s² pointing up, because the support force is a specific force. It reads zero in free fall.
  • "The accelerometer measures gravity." Gravity is the one thing it cannot feel. At rest it measures the support force, which happens to be equal and opposite to gravity.
  • "\(\mathbf{b}^a\) is the bias expressed in frame a." The superscripts on \(\mathbf{b}\) and \(\boldsymbol{\eta}\) name the sensor. Both vectors are in body coordinates.
  • "A bias is noise, so it averages away." Averaging removes the white noise and leaves the bias untouched.

Check yourself

Q1. A robot stands level and still, with z up. Ignoring bias and noise, what does its accelerometer read?

With zero acceleration, (11.1) gives R(0 − g) = −g in body coordinates. Gravity is (0, 0, −9.81), so the reading is (0, 0, +9.81): the floor pushing up. Yaw turns the body about the vertical and leaves this vector unchanged.

Q2. A drone cuts its motors and falls freely (ignore air drag). During the fall its accelerometer reads

In free fall the acceleration equals g, so a − g = 0. No force reaches the proof mass through the case.

Q3. In the planar widget, the body is at rest with pitch 30°. What are the (x, z) readings?

The specific force is 9.81 straight up. Seen from axes pitched up by 30° it has components 9.81·sin 30° = 4.90 along body x and 9.81·cos 30° = 8.50 along body z.

Q4. A gyroscope has an uncorrected bias of 0.02°/s about its vertical axis. If you integrate its readings for 5 minutes, the heading error from the bias is about

A constant bias integrates linearly: 0.02°/s × 300 s = 6°. Only the white noise partly averages out.

Q5. What does the matrix T_s in equation (11.5) model?

T_s multiplies the specific force inside the gyroscope equation: it is the g-sensitivity. Misalignment and scale are T_a and T_g, and bias drift is a separate random-walk model.

Recap

  1. An IMU is a 3-axis gyroscope plus a 3-axis accelerometer, rigidly attached to the robot (strapdown) and sampled at hundreds of hertz.
  2. Gyroscope: reading = true body angular velocity + bias + noise, equation (11.2).
  3. Accelerometer: reading = rotation into the body frame of (acceleration − gravity), + bias + noise, equation (11.1). At rest it reads 9.81 up, in free fall zero.
  4. Noise is white and partly averages out. Bias is a slow random walk, does not average out, and must be estimated.
  5. Shape matrices and a g-sensitivity matrix extend the model for calibration, equations (11.3)–(11.5).

Sources

  1. SLAM Handbook, Chapter 11 opening, §11.1 and §11.1.1 "Sensing Principles and Measurement Models", pp. 304–306.
  2. Titterton and Weston, Strapdown Inertial Navigation Technology, 2nd ed., 2004 (specific force and the proof-mass picture of an accelerometer).
  3. Groves, Principles of GNSS, Inertial, and Multisensor Integrated Navigation Systems, 2nd ed., 2013 (inertial sensor error terms).

Week 16 · Day 2

Initial alignment and the noise parameters of an IMU

After today you can compute the gravity-aligned initial rotation from a static accelerometer reading, explain why yaw stays free, and read an IMU's noise density and bias random walk off a data sheet or an Allan plot.

About 60 min · Read §11.1.2, p. 307 (1 page) · Needs Week 16 Day 1

Read first: §11.1.2, p. 307

One dense page. While you read, look for:

  • Why the starting orientation, a free choice in ordinary SLAM, is no longer free once an IMU is used.
  • Which rotation cannot be recovered from gravity alone.
  • In equation (11.6): which column of the rotation matrix comes straight from the measurement, and which two are constructed.
  • In equation (11.7): the second physical vector a high-end IMU can sense, and the closing remark about projecting onto SO(3).

Today's big idea

Gravity is the one direction of the world that an IMU can sense directly. A robot standing still can therefore work out which way is up, which fixes two of its three orientation angles (roll and pitch). The third, yaw, is invisible to gravity. How well any of this works depends on two numbers per sensor, the white-noise density and the bias random walk, which the second half of today explains.

1. Why the first pose is no longer arbitrary

In SLAM without an IMU you may declare the first pose to be the identity. Nothing in the measurements cares how the world frame is oriented. Equation (11.1) changes that: it contains \(\mathbf{g}^w\), the gravity vector in world coordinates. To use it you must know the direction of gravity in your world frame. The usual choice is a gravity-aligned world frame, with one axis along the vertical, and then the initial rotation \(\mathbf{R}^w_b(0)\) has to be computed so that it agrees with that choice. This step is called initial alignment. §11.1.2 · p. 307

The simplest method assumes the robot starts at rest. Then \(\mathbf{a}^w = \mathbf{0}\) and, by (11.1), the accelerometer sees only gravity's reaction. One measured direction cannot fix a full 3-D orientation: turning the robot about the vertical does not change what the accelerometer reads. So yaw (rotation about gravity) cannot be recovered and is chosen freely, while roll and pitch (the two tilts away from level) can. §11.1.2 · p. 307

2. Static initialization by Gram–Schmidt

The book builds the rotation column by column: §11.1.2 · p. 307

\[ \mathbf{z}^b_w = \frac{\mathbf{g}^b}{\norm{\mathbf{g}^b}}, \qquad \mathbf{x}^b_w = \frac{\mathbf{e}_1 - \mathbf{z}^b_w\,(\mathbf{e}_1\T \mathbf{z}^b_w)}{\norm{\mathbf{e}_1 - \mathbf{z}^b_w\,(\mathbf{e}_1\T \mathbf{z}^b_w)}}, \qquad \mathbf{y}^b_w = \mathbf{z}^b_w \times \mathbf{x}^b_w, \qquad \mathbf{R}^b_w = \begin{bmatrix} \mathbf{x}^b_w & \mathbf{y}^b_w & \mathbf{z}^b_w \end{bmatrix}. \tag{11.6} \]

Here \(\mathbf{g}^b\) is the measured gravity vector in body coordinates and \(\mathbf{e}_1 = (1,0,0)\T\). The procedure of taking one vector, then removing from the next its component along the first, is Gram–Schmidt orthonormalization.

Filling the gap: why these are the columns

\(\mathbf{R}^b_w\) converts world coordinates to body coordinates. Apply it to the world's third axis \((0,0,1)\T\): the result is the third column of the matrix. So the third column is the world \(z\)-axis as seen from the body, which the book writes \(\mathbf{z}^b_w\). Likewise the first two columns are the world \(x\)- and \(y\)-axes seen from the body. Since the world \(z\)-axis is defined to be the vertical, and the static reading tells us where the vertical is, the third column is simply the normalized reading.

The other two columns only have to be perpendicular to \(\mathbf{z}^b_w\) and to each other. The construction is orthogonal by design:

\[ (\mathbf{z}^b_w)\T\big(\mathbf{e}_1 - \mathbf{z}^b_w(\mathbf{e}_1\T\mathbf{z}^b_w)\big) = \mathbf{e}_1\T\mathbf{z}^b_w - \underbrace{(\mathbf{z}^b_w)\T\mathbf{z}^b_w}_{=1}\,(\mathbf{e}_1\T\mathbf{z}^b_w) = 0 . \]

Starting from \(\mathbf{e}_1\), the body's own \(x\)-axis, is where the free yaw is spent: the world \(x\)-axis becomes the horizontal direction the robot's nose points along. Any other start vector gives another valid yaw. The recipe breaks only if \(\mathbf{e}_1\) is parallel to \(\mathbf{z}^b_w\) (a robot standing on its nose), where the numerator is zero; then start from \(\mathbf{e}_2\) instead.

Which sign? By (11.1) a static accelerometer reads \(\mathbf{R}^b_w(-\mathbf{g}^w)\), which points up. If you feed that raw reading into (11.6) as \(\mathbf{g}^b\), the world \(z\)-axis points up and \(\mathbf{g}^w = (0,0,-9.81)\). If you negate it first, world \(z\) points down. Either is consistent as long as \(\mathbf{g}^w\) in (11.1) matches. We use the raw reading and \(z\) up.

Worked example. A robot sits still and its accelerometer, averaged over a second, reads \((1.70, 0, 9.66)\) m/s². Its length is \(\sqrt{1.70^2 + 9.66^2} = 9.81\).

  • \(\mathbf{z}^b_w = (1.70, 0, 9.66)/9.81 = (0.1733, 0, 0.9849)\).
  • \(\mathbf{e}_1\T\mathbf{z}^b_w = 0.1733\), so \(\mathbf{e}_1 - 0.1733\,\mathbf{z}^b_w = (0.9700, 0, -0.1707)\), of length \(0.9849\). Dividing: \(\mathbf{x}^b_w = (0.9849, 0, -0.1733)\).
  • \(\mathbf{y}^b_w = \mathbf{z}^b_w \times \mathbf{x}^b_w = (0, 1, 0)\).
\[ \mathbf{R}^b_w = \begin{bmatrix} 0.9849 & 0 & 0.1733 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ -0.1733 & 0 & 0.9849 \end{bmatrix}, \qquad \mathbf{R}^w_b = (\mathbf{R}^b_w)\T . \]

Since \(\sin 10^\circ = 0.1736\), this is a rotation of 10° about the \(y\)-axis. The first column of \(\mathbf{R}^w_b\) is the body \(x\)-axis in world coordinates, \((0.9849, 0, 0.1733)\): the nose points 10° above the horizon. Check: \(\mathbf{R}^b_w\,(0,0,9.81)\T = (1.70, 0, 9.66)\T\), the reading we started from.

3. What can go wrong when standing still

Static alignment trusts the reading to be pure gravity. Two things break that. If the robot is accelerating, the specific force is no longer vertical. If the accelerometer has a bias \(b\) along a horizontal axis, the measured "up" is tilted by about \(b/g\) radians: a bias of 0.05 m/s² tilts it by \(0.05/9.81 = 0.0051\) rad, or 0.29°. Averaging more samples reduces the effect of white noise but does nothing to a bias.

Try it: press "At rest" and compare the inferred pitch with the true pitch. Then raise the horizontal acceleration to 1 m/s².

Notice that at rest the inferred pitch equals the true pitch (20.0°). With 1 m/s² of forward acceleration the reading tilts and the inferred pitch becomes 25.8°: an error of atan(1/9.81) = 5.8°. This is why the book's method assumes a static start.

4. Alignment with a high-end IMU

The Earth turns once a day, about 15° per hour or \(7.3 \times 10^{-5}\) rad/s. A high-end gyroscope can measure this Earth rotation rate \(\boldsymbol{\omega}_{ie}\) while standing still. That is a second known direction, not parallel to gravity, and two directions fix the full orientation including yaw. §11.1.2 · p. 307

Filling the gap: where equation (11.7) comes from

Each known vector obeys \(\mathbf{u}^b = \mathbf{R}^b_w\mathbf{u}^w\). Transposing, \((\mathbf{u}^b)\T = (\mathbf{u}^w)\T\mathbf{R}^w_b\). Write this for three vectors, gravity, the Earth rate, and their cross product (a rotation maps the cross product of two vectors to the cross product of their images), and stack the three rows:

\[ \underbrace{\begin{bmatrix} (\mathbf{g}^b)\T \\ (\boldsymbol{\omega}^b_{ie})\T \\ (\mathbf{g}^b \times \boldsymbol{\omega}^b_{ie})\T \end{bmatrix}}_{\text{measured}} = \underbrace{\begin{bmatrix} (\mathbf{g}^w)\T \\ (\boldsymbol{\omega}^w_{ie})\T \\ (\mathbf{g}^w \times \boldsymbol{\omega}^w_{ie})\T \end{bmatrix}}_{\text{known}} \mathbf{R}^w_b \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \mathbf{R}^w_b = \begin{bmatrix} (\mathbf{g}^w)\T \\ (\boldsymbol{\omega}^w_{ie})\T \\ (\mathbf{g}^w \times \boldsymbol{\omega}^w_{ie})\T \end{bmatrix}^{-1} \begin{bmatrix} (\mathbf{g}^b)\T \\ (\boldsymbol{\omega}^b_{ie})\T \\ (\mathbf{g}^b \times \boldsymbol{\omega}^b_{ie})\T \end{bmatrix}. \tag{11.7} \]

The cross product is included only to make the known matrix square and invertible. (In the book's printing the last row of the right-hand matrix carries a superscript \(w\) on \(\boldsymbol{\omega}_{ie}\); from the derivation it must be the body-frame vector.) With noisy measurements the result is not exactly a rotation matrix, so it is replaced by the nearest one, which the book calls projecting onto \(\SO(3)\). The standard way is a singular value decomposition \(\mathbf{U}\mathbf{S}\mathbf{V}\T\) of the result, keeping \(\mathbf{U}\mathbf{V}\T\) (with a sign flip of the last column of \(\mathbf{U}\) if the determinant is \(-1\)).

A MEMS gyroscope cannot do this. A bias of 0.1°/s is 360° per hour, 24 times the signal it would have to detect. So low-cost systems leave yaw free at start-up.

5. Noise parameters in practice

The model of Day 1 has two random ingredients per sensor: white noise \(\boldsymbol{\eta}\) and a bias that performs a random walk, \(\dot{\mathbf{b}} = \boldsymbol{\eta}^{b}\) (equation (11.32), Day 5). Each is described by one number, and the units of that number confuse almost everyone at first.

ParameterTypical unitStandard deviation of one sample at period ΔtAfter integrating for time t
Gyroscope noise density \(\sigma_g\)rad/s/√Hz\(\sigma_g/\sqrt{\Delta t}\)angle error \(\sigma_g\sqrt{t}\) ("angle random walk")
Accelerometer noise density \(\sigma_a\)m/s²/√Hz\(\sigma_a/\sqrt{\Delta t}\)velocity error \(\sigma_a\sqrt{t}\) ("velocity random walk")
Gyroscope bias random walk \(\sigma_{bg}\)rad/s²/√Hzbias step \(\sigma_{bg}\sqrt{\Delta t}\)bias has wandered by \(\sigma_{bg}\sqrt{t}\)
Accelerometer bias random walk \(\sigma_{ba}\)m/s³/√Hzbias step \(\sigma_{ba}\sqrt{\Delta t}\)bias has wandered by \(\sigma_{ba}\sqrt{t}\)

The two middle-column rules are the book's \(\operatorname{Cov}(\boldsymbol{\eta}^{gd}) = \tfrac{1}{\Delta t}\operatorname{Cov}(\boldsymbol{\eta}^{g})\) §11.2.1 · p. 309 and \(\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{bgd} = \Delta t_{ij}\operatorname{Cov}(\boldsymbol{\eta}^{bg})\) §11.2.2.4 · p. 316, where the extra \(d\) means "discrete-time".

Filling the gap: why divide by √Δt?

Continuous white noise has the same power at every frequency, so its instantaneous variance is infinite. Only its averages are finite. A sensor sample is roughly an average over one sampling period, and the average of white noise of density \(\sigma\) over a window \(\Delta t\) has variance \(\sigma^2/\Delta t\): a shorter window averages less, so each sample is noisier. Now integrate \(n\) samples, \(t = n\,\Delta t\). Variances of independent terms add:

\[ \operatorname{var}\Big(\sum_{k=1}^{n}\eta_k\,\Delta t\Big) = n\cdot\frac{\sigma^2}{\Delta t}\cdot\Delta t^2 = \sigma^2\,n\,\Delta t = \sigma^2 t . \]

The sampling rate has cancelled, as it should: the integrated error depends only on the density and the elapsed time. Example: \(\sigma_g = 0.01\)°/s/√Hz sampled at 100 Hz gives samples with standard deviation \(0.01 \times \sqrt{100} = 0.1\)°/s, and an angle error of \(0.01 \times \sqrt{60} = 0.077\)° after one minute. For the bias the logic runs the other way: the bias itself is the integral of white noise, so its change over \(\Delta t\) has variance \(\sigma_b^2\,\Delta t\).

How are the two numbers measured? Record the sensor at rest for a long time. Cut the record into blocks of length \(\tau\) and average each block. The Allan variance is half the mean squared difference between consecutive block averages, and its square root is the Allan deviation. For white noise of density \(N\), block averages get quieter as blocks get longer and the Allan deviation is \(N/\sqrt{\tau}\). A random-walking bias of strength \(K\) makes distant blocks disagree more, contributing \(K\sqrt{\tau/3}\). On a log-log plot these are straight lines of slope \(-\tfrac12\) and \(+\tfrac12\).

Try it: change \(N\) and \(K\) and watch the two branches move.

Notice the V shape. On the left branch you can read the noise density directly: at τ = 1 s the measured Allan deviation is 0.0200°/s against a true N of 0.020. The model's minimum, at τ = √3·N/K = 3.5 s, is the longest averaging time that still helps; averaging longer lets the wandering bias back in. Press "New noise" a few times: the rightmost points jump around the model curve, because only a dozen blocks fit in a 10-minute record. Set K to zero and the right branch disappears.

Common mistakes

  • "Averaging long enough gives a perfect gravity direction." Averaging beats white noise only. A bias \(b\) leaves a tilt error of about \(b/g\) however long you wait.
  • "A faster IMU is noisier, so it is worse." Each sample is noisier by \(\sqrt{\text{rate}}\), but there are more of them, and the integrated error \(\sigma\sqrt{t}\) is unchanged.
  • "Yaw is unknown because the gyroscope is poor." With gravity as the only reference, yaw is unobservable for any accelerometer. It takes a second reference direction, such as the Earth's rotation, to fix it.

Check yourself

Q1. Why can static alignment with a MEMS IMU not determine yaw?

The only reference is one direction, the vertical. Any rotation about that direction leaves the body-frame reading unchanged, so no amount of data can reveal it.

Q2. A static accelerometer reads (0, 4.905, 8.496) m/s², which has length 9.81. Using (11.6), what is the second column, y, of the rotation matrix?

z = (0, 0.5, 0.866). e₁ is already perpendicular to z, so x = (1, 0, 0). Then y = z × x = (0, 0.866, −0.5). Option one is z itself.

Q3. A gyroscope has noise density 0.005°/s/√Hz and is sampled at 400 Hz. The standard deviation of the noise in one sample is

Divide by √Δt, which is the same as multiplying by √rate: 0.005 × √400 = 0.005 × 20 = 0.1°/s.

Q4. During static alignment the accelerometer has a horizontal bias of 0.1 m/s². Roughly how large is the resulting tilt error, after averaging many samples?

The bias adds a horizontal component to a vertical vector of length 9.81, tilting it by 0.1/9.81 = 0.0102 rad = 0.58°. Averaging does not remove a bias.

Q5. On the white-noise branch of an Allan deviation plot, the averaging time τ is increased 100-fold. The Allan deviation

For white noise the Allan deviation is N/√τ, so 100 times more averaging gives √100 = 10 times less scatter.

Recap

  1. With an IMU the world frame is gravity-aligned, so the initial rotation must be computed, not chosen.
  2. At rest, the normalized accelerometer reading is the third column of \(\mathbf{R}^b_w\); Gram–Schmidt fills in the other two, equation (11.6). Roll and pitch are determined, yaw is free.
  3. Acceleration or accelerometer bias during alignment tilts the estimated vertical by about (horizontal error)/g.
  4. A gyroscope good enough to sense the Earth's rotation supplies a second direction and fixes yaw too, equation (11.7).
  5. White noise: per-sample deviation \(\sigma/\sqrt{\Delta t}\), integrated error \(\sigma\sqrt{t}\). Bias random walk: drift \(\sigma_b\sqrt{t}\). An Allan plot shows both.

Sources

  1. SLAM Handbook, §11.1.2 "Initial Alignment", p. 307; the discrete-noise relations on p. 309 and p. 316.
  2. Groves, Principles of GNSS, Inertial, and Multisensor Integrated Navigation Systems, 2nd ed., 2013 (levelling, gyrocompassing, and sensor noise parameters).
  3. IEEE Std 952-1997, IEEE Standard Specification Format Guide and Test Procedure for Single-Axis Interferometric Fiber Optic Gyros, 1997 (definition of Allan variance and the slopes of its noise terms).
  4. Woodman, An Introduction to Inertial Navigation, University of Cambridge technical report, 2007 (white noise and bias random walk in MEMS sensors).

Week 16 · Day 3

Motion integration: from IMU samples to a trajectory, and why it drifts

After today you can integrate IMU samples into rotation, velocity, and position with equation (11.12), predict how bias and noise grow into position error, and explain why a factor graph cannot afford to repeat that integration.

About 60 min · Read §11.2 opening and §11.2.1, pp. 308–310 (3 pages) · Needs Week 16 Day 1 and Week 4 Day 2

Read first: §11.2 opening and §11.2.1, pp. 308–310

While you read, look for:

  • The two reasons on p. 308 why putting raw IMU data into a factor graph is impractical, in discrete time and in continuous time.
  • The two assumptions made between equations (11.9) and (11.11) on p. 309, and the sentence after (11.12) about holding the orientation constant.
  • The relation between discrete-time and continuous-time noise at the bottom of p. 309.
  • The last paragraph of p. 310: what exactly must be recomputed in (11.13) when \(\mathbf{R}_i\) changes.

Today's big idea

Turn the measurement model around and you can compute motion from the readings: rotate each accelerometer sample into the world, add gravity back, and integrate twice. This is dead reckoning. It needs the starting orientation and velocity, it drifts fast because every error is integrated two or three times, and its result depends on the starting state in a way that forces a full re-integration whenever that state is revised.

1. Why not one state per IMU sample?

The models of Day 1 relate each IMU sample to the robot state at that instant, so in principle each sample could be a factor in the MAP problem of Week 2 · Day 2. The trouble is the rate. An IMU delivers 200 to 1000 samples per second, and each sample would need its own state in the graph. §11.2 · p. 308 One minute at 200 Hz is 12,000 states, each with a rotation, a position, a velocity, and two biases: 15 unknowns apiece, 180,000 in all, for a sensor that only tells you how the robot moved. A continuous-time trajectory (Week 5 · Day 1) avoids the extra states but still needs one factor per sample. §11.2 · p. 308

2. The kinematic model

Integration starts from three differential equations: §11.2.1 · p. 308

\[ \dot{\mathbf{R}}^w_b = \mathbf{R}^w_b\,(\boldsymbol{\omega}^b_b)^\wedge, \qquad \dot{\mathbf{v}}^w = \mathbf{a}^w, \qquad \dot{\mathbf{p}}^w = \mathbf{v}^w. \tag{11.8} \]

The last two are the definitions of acceleration and velocity. The wedge \((\cdot)^\wedge\) turns a 3-vector into a skew-symmetric matrix, so that \(\boldsymbol{\omega}^\wedge\mathbf{u} = \boldsymbol{\omega}\times\mathbf{u}\) (Week 4 · Day 2).

Filling the gap: where the rotation equation comes from

During a short time \(dt\) the body turns by the small rotation vector \(\boldsymbol{\omega}^b_b\,dt\), measured in its own axes. A rotation expressed in the body's axes is applied on the right:

\[ \mathbf{R}(t+dt) = \mathbf{R}(t)\,\Exp(\boldsymbol{\omega}\,dt) \approx \mathbf{R}(t)\,\big(\mathbf{I} + \boldsymbol{\omega}^\wedge dt\big). \]

Subtract \(\mathbf{R}(t)\), divide by \(dt\), and let \(dt \to 0\): \(\dot{\mathbf{R}} = \mathbf{R}\,\boldsymbol{\omega}^\wedge\). The same line read backwards is the integration rule. If \(\boldsymbol{\omega}\) is constant over a step \(\Delta t\), then \(\mathbf{R}(t+\Delta t) = \mathbf{R}(t)\Exp(\boldsymbol{\omega}\Delta t)\) exactly. The book's (11.9) only needs the direction of \(\boldsymbol{\omega}\) to stay fixed during the step.

3. One integration step

Assume \(\mathbf{a}^w\) and \(\boldsymbol{\omega}^b_b\) are constant during one sampling period \(\Delta t\). Integrating (11.8) gives §11.2.1 · p. 309

\[ \mathbf{R}(t+\Delta t) = \mathbf{R}(t)\Exp(\boldsymbol{\omega}^b_b\Delta t), \quad \mathbf{v}(t+\Delta t) = \mathbf{v}(t) + \mathbf{a}^w\Delta t, \quad \mathbf{p}(t+\Delta t) = \mathbf{p}(t) + \mathbf{v}(t)\Delta t + \tfrac12\mathbf{a}^w\Delta t^2. \tag{11.11} \]

We do not have \(\mathbf{a}^w\) and \(\boldsymbol{\omega}^b_b\); we have readings. Solve the measurement model for the true quantities. From (11.2), \(\boldsymbol{\omega}^b_b = \tilde{\boldsymbol{\omega}} - \mathbf{b}^g - \boldsymbol{\eta}^g\). From (11.1), multiply by \(\mathbf{R} = \mathbf{R}^w_b\) to undo \(\mathbf{R}^b_w\):

\[ \tilde{\mathbf{a}} = \mathbf{R}\T(\mathbf{a}^w - \mathbf{g}) + \mathbf{b}^a + \boldsymbol{\eta}^a \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \mathbf{a}^w = \mathbf{R}\,(\tilde{\mathbf{a}} - \mathbf{b}^a - \boldsymbol{\eta}^a) + \mathbf{g}. \]

Substituting into (11.11) gives the equation the rest of the chapter rests on: §11.2.1 · p. 309

\[ \begin{aligned} \mathbf{R}(t+\Delta t) &= \mathbf{R}(t)\,\Exp\!\big((\tilde{\boldsymbol{\omega}}(t) - \mathbf{b}^g(t) - \boldsymbol{\eta}^{gd}(t))\,\Delta t\big) \\ \mathbf{v}(t+\Delta t) &= \mathbf{v}(t) + \mathbf{g}\Delta t + \mathbf{R}(t)\big(\tilde{\mathbf{a}}(t) - \mathbf{b}^a(t) - \boldsymbol{\eta}^{ad}(t)\big)\Delta t \\ \mathbf{p}(t+\Delta t) &= \mathbf{p}(t) + \mathbf{v}(t)\Delta t + \tfrac12\mathbf{g}\Delta t^2 + \tfrac12\mathbf{R}(t)\big(\tilde{\mathbf{a}}(t) - \mathbf{b}^a(t) - \boldsymbol{\eta}^{ad}(t)\big)\Delta t^2 \end{aligned} \tag{11.12} \]

The frame labels are dropped from here on: \(\mathbf{R}\) is body-to-world, and \(\mathbf{v}\), \(\mathbf{p}\), \(\mathbf{g}\) are in world coordinates. The noises \(\boldsymbol{\eta}^{gd}\), \(\boldsymbol{\eta}^{ad}\) are the discrete-time versions from Day 2, with covariance \(\tfrac{1}{\Delta t}\) times the continuous one. In practice the noise is unknown, so you run (11.12) with the noise set to zero and your best bias estimate:

R, v, p = initial orientation, velocity, position      # must be given
for each IMU sample (w_meas, a_meas):
    f = R @ (a_meas - b_a)                # specific force, rotated into the world
    p = p + v*dt + 0.5*(f + g)*dt*dt      # uses the old v and the old R
    v = v + (f + g)*dt
    R = R @ Exp((w_meas - b_g)*dt)        # rotate last

Sanity check: a level robot at rest with a perfect sensor reads \(\tilde{\mathbf{a}} = (0,0,9.81)\). With \(\mathbf{R} = \mathbf{I}\) and \(\mathbf{g} = (0,0,-9.81)\), the velocity update is \(\mathbf{g}\Delta t + \tilde{\mathbf{a}}\Delta t = \mathbf{0}\). The reading and gravity cancel, and the robot stays put. That cancellation of two large numbers is the weak point, as the next section shows.

Equation (11.12) uses the orientation at the start of the step for the whole step. This is not exact when the body is rotating; a high IMU rate keeps the error small, and Day 5 returns to it. §11.2.1 · p. 309

4. Dead reckoning drifts, and gravity makes it worse

Try it: the widget runs the loop above on a simulated planar IMU (one gyroscope, two accelerometer axes) carried over two hills. Start with the default 0.1°/s gyroscope bias. Then set it to zero and try an accelerometer bias of 0.05 m/s².

Notice that a gyroscope bias of only 0.1°/s puts the estimate about 22 m off after 20 s, on a 40 m drive, and that the error follows the cubic model curve. The tilt error at the end is just 2°, but 2° of tilt turns 0.34 m/s² of gravity into false horizontal acceleration. An accelerometer bias of 0.05 m/s² alone gives roughly 10 m, following the quadratic curve. With every slider at zero about 6 cm of error remains: the rectangle rule of (11.12) on a changing acceleration.

Filling the gap: how fast does each error grow?

The book says inertial odometry drifts but does not give rates. They follow from counting integrations.

Accelerometer bias \(b_a\). A constant acceleration error, integrated twice: velocity error \(b_a t\), position error \(\tfrac12 b_a t^2\).

Gyroscope bias \(b_g\). The orientation error grows as \(\delta\theta = b_g t\). The integrator rotates the measured specific force, which is mostly the 9.81 m/s² support force, with the wrong \(\mathbf{R}\). A vertical vector of length \(g\) tilted by a small angle \(\delta\theta\) acquires a horizontal component \(g\sin\delta\theta \approx g\,\delta\theta\). After adding \(\mathbf{g}\) back, the vertical parts still nearly cancel, but the horizontal part is left over as a false acceleration \(g\,b_g\,t\). Integrate twice:

\[ \delta v(t) = \int_0^t g\,b_g\,s\,ds = \tfrac12 g\,b_g\,t^2, \qquad \delta p(t) = \int_0^t \tfrac12 g\,b_g\,s^2\,ds = \tfrac16\,g\,b_g\,t^3 . \]

With \(b_g = 0.1\)°/s \(= 1.745\times10^{-3}\) rad/s and \(t = 20\) s: \(\tfrac16 \times 9.81 \times 1.745\times10^{-3} \times 8000 = 22.8\) m, the number in the widget.

White noise. Accelerometer noise of density \(\sigma_a\) is a stream of independent kicks. A kick at time \(s\) changes the velocity for good, so by time \(t\) it has moved the position by an amount proportional to \(t-s\). Adding the variances of all kicks, \(\operatorname{var}(\delta p) = \sigma_a^2\int_0^t (t-s)^2 ds = \sigma_a^2 t^3/3\). The same argument with one more integration gives the gyroscope-noise entry in the table.

Error sourceFirst effectPosition error after time tAt t = 20 s
Accelerometer bias \(b_a\)velocity error \(b_a t\)\(\tfrac12 b_a t^2\)0.05 m/s² → 10 m
Gyroscope bias \(b_g\)tilt \(b_g t\), false acceleration \(g\,b_g t\)\(\tfrac16 g\,b_g t^3\)0.1°/s → 22.8 m
Accelerometer noise \(\sigma_a\)velocity random walk \(\sigma_a\sqrt{t}\)\(\sigma_a t^{3/2}/\sqrt{3}\) (1σ)0.005 m/s²/√Hz → 0.26 m
Gyroscope noise \(\sigma_g\)tilt random walk \(\sigma_g\sqrt{t}\)\(g\,\sigma_g t^{5/2}/\sqrt{20}\) (1σ)0.01°/s/√Hz → 0.68 m

Intuition

The integrator has to subtract gravity, a known vector of length 9.81, from a reading of about the same length. If it holds the reading at a slightly wrong angle, the subtraction leaves a sideways remainder. An IMU navigates well for exactly as long as it knows which way is down.

One more experiment: set the gyroscope bias to +0.10°/s and the accelerometer bias to about +0.11 m/s². The final error collapses to a few metres, because on this path the two errors push in opposite directions. A tilt error and an accelerometer bias look alike to the integrator. Next week's observability analysis is about telling such effects apart.

5. Keyframes, and the flaw of plain integration

Dead reckoning alone is hopeless beyond a few seconds, so the IMU is combined with a camera or LiDAR in a factor graph whose states sit at selected instants. The book calls them keyframe states, whatever sensor triggers them. §11.2.1 · p. 310 Between consecutive keyframes at times \(t_i\) and \(t_j\) there are many IMU samples, \(k = i, i+1, \dots, j-1\). Chaining (11.12) over all of them gives

\[ \begin{aligned} \mathbf{R}_j &= \mathbf{R}_i \prod_{k=i}^{j-1}\Exp\!\big((\tilde{\boldsymbol{\omega}}_k - \mathbf{b}^g_k - \boldsymbol{\eta}^{gd}_k)\Delta t\big), \\ \mathbf{v}_j &= \mathbf{v}_i + \mathbf{g}\Delta t_{ij} + \sum_{k=i}^{j-1}\mathbf{R}_k\big(\tilde{\mathbf{a}}_k - \mathbf{b}^a_k - \boldsymbol{\eta}^{ad}_k\big)\Delta t, \\ \mathbf{p}_j &= \mathbf{p}_i + \sum_{k=i}^{j-1}\Big[\mathbf{v}_k\Delta t + \tfrac12\mathbf{g}\Delta t^2 + \tfrac12\mathbf{R}_k\big(\tilde{\mathbf{a}}_k - \mathbf{b}^a_k - \boldsymbol{\eta}^{ad}_k\big)\Delta t^2\Big], \end{aligned} \tag{11.13} \]

with \(\Delta t_{ij} = \sum_{k=i}^{j-1}\Delta t\) the time between the keyframes. §11.2.1 · p. 310 This already is a relative-motion constraint between states \(i\) and \(j\). Its flaw is in how the unknowns enter. Every \(\mathbf{R}_k\) inside the sums is \(\mathbf{R}_i\) times a product of gyroscope terms, and every \(\mathbf{v}_k\) contains \(\mathbf{v}_i\). A nonlinear solver such as Gauss-Newton (Week 2 · Day 4) changes its estimate of \(\mathbf{R}_i\) and \(\mathbf{v}_i\) at every iteration, and each change invalidates every term of the sums. §11.2.1 · p. 310

Count the cost: 100 keyframe intervals, 200 samples each, 10 solver iterations is 200,000 sample integrations per solve, repeated every time the graph is re-optimized. Tomorrow's rearrangement brings it down to 20,000, done once.

Common mistakes

  • "Integrate the accelerometer twice to get position." First rotate the reading into the world with the current \(\mathbf{R}\), then add \(\mathbf{g}\), then integrate. Skip the rotation and the reading is added along the wrong axes; skip gravity and a robot at rest accelerates upward at 9.81 m/s².
  • "Position drift from a gyroscope is small because gyroscopes are accurate." Tilt error is multiplied by \(g\) and integrated twice more. It grows as \(t^3\) and usually dominates.
  • "Equation (11.13) cannot be used in a factor graph." It can. It is just wasteful, because it must be re-evaluated from the raw samples whenever the state at \(i\) changes.

Check yourself

Q1. A level robot at rest, R = I, v = 0, g = (0, 0, −9.81), perfect accelerometer reading (0, 0, 9.81), Δt = 0.01 s. What velocity does (11.12) give after one step?

v + gΔt + R·ã·Δt = 0 + (0,0,−0.0981) + (0,0,+0.0981) = 0. The reading and gravity cancel.

Q2. An uncorrected accelerometer bias of 0.02 m/s² acts for 30 s. The position error it causes is about

½·b·t² = 0.5 × 0.02 × 900 = 9 m. (0.6 m/s is the velocity error.)

Q3. With a constant gyroscope bias, the dead-reckoning time is doubled from 10 s to 20 s. The position error from that bias grows by a factor of about

The error is g·b·t³/6, cubic in time: 2³ = 8.

Q4. Why must the sums in (11.13) be recomputed when the solver changes its estimate of the rotation at keyframe i?

Each R_k = R_i·(product of Exp terms) rotates sample k into the world. Change R_i and every rotated sample, hence every term of both sums, changes. Gravity in world coordinates and Δt are fixed.

Q5. In (11.12), which orientation is used to rotate the accelerometer sample taken at time t?

The velocity and position lines use R(t). The scheme holds it constant over the step, which is an approximation whenever the body rotates.

Recap

  1. One state per IMU sample makes the factor graph far too large; the goal is one IMU factor per pair of keyframes.
  2. Kinematics (11.8) plus the measurement model give the integration step (11.12): rotate the reading into the world, add gravity, integrate.
  3. Position error grows as \(\tfrac12 b_a t^2\) for accelerometer bias and \(\tfrac16 g\,b_g t^3\) for gyroscope bias, because a tilt error leaks gravity into horizontal acceleration.
  4. Chaining the step between keyframes gives (11.13), a valid relative-motion constraint.
  5. Its sums depend on \(\mathbf{R}_i\) and \(\mathbf{v}_i\), so they must be redone from the raw samples at every solver iteration. Preintegration removes that cost.

Sources

  1. SLAM Handbook, §11.2 opening and §11.2.1 "Motion Integration", pp. 308–310.
  2. Titterton and Weston, Strapdown Inertial Navigation Technology, 2nd ed., 2004 (strapdown kinematics; how tilt errors couple gravity into position error).
  3. Woodman, An Introduction to Inertial Navigation, University of Cambridge technical report, 2007 (growth rates of position error from bias and from white noise).

Week 16 · Day 4

IMU preintegration: increments that do not depend on where you start

After today you can derive the preintegrated increments from the integration equations, show that they depend neither on the state at keyframe i nor on gravity, and explain how their noise covariance is obtained.

About 60 min · Read §11.2.2 to §11.2.2.2, pp. 311–314 (4 pages) · Needs Week 16 Day 3 and Week 4 Day 5

Read first: §11.2.2, §11.2.2.1, §11.2.2.2, pp. 311–314

These are the densest pages of the week. While you read, look for:

  • The "key insight" in the first paragraph of p. 311. It has two parts.
  • In equation (11.14): check that no right-hand side contains \(\mathbf{R}_i\), \(\mathbf{v}_i\), \(\mathbf{p}_i\), or \(\mathbf{g}\), and find the sentence warning that \(\Delta\mathbf{v}_{ij}\) and \(\Delta\mathbf{p}_{ij}\) are not physical changes.
  • On p. 312: how (11.16) and (11.17) are used to "move the noise to the end" in (11.18).
  • Equation (11.23) on p. 313, the final measurement model, and (11.28)–(11.29) on p. 314, the noise written as a sum over raw IMU noises.

Today's big idea

Rearrange yesterday's integration so that everything depending on the state at keyframe \(i\), and everything depending on gravity, sits on one side of the equation. What remains on the other side is a rotation and two vectors computed from the IMU samples alone. They are integrated once, stored, and reused however often the optimizer changes its mind about the states. These are the preintegrated IMU measurements.

1. The rotation increment

Start with the first line of (11.13): \(\mathbf{R}_j = \mathbf{R}_i\prod_{k=i}^{j-1}\Exp(\cdot)\). The unknown \(\mathbf{R}_i\) only multiplies from the left, so move it across: §11.2.2 · p. 311

\[ \Delta\mathbf{R}_{ij} \doteq \mathbf{R}_i\T\mathbf{R}_j = \prod_{k=i}^{j-1}\Exp\!\big((\tilde{\boldsymbol{\omega}}_k - \mathbf{b}^g_k - \boldsymbol{\eta}^{gd}_k)\Delta t\big). \]

The left side is the rotation of the body between the two keyframes, seen from the body at time \(i\). The right side contains gyroscope samples and nothing else. The same holds for every intermediate sample: \(\mathbf{R}_k = \mathbf{R}_i\,\Delta\mathbf{R}_{ik}\). This is the first part of the book's insight: express motion in a local frame, the body frame at \(i\), so it does not change when the global estimate changes. §11.2.2 · p. 311

2. The velocity and position increments

Filling the gap: deriving the last two lines of (11.14)

Velocity. In the second line of (11.13) put \(\mathbf{R}_k = \mathbf{R}_i\Delta\mathbf{R}_{ik}\) and move the terms with \(\mathbf{v}_i\) and \(\mathbf{g}\) to the left:

\[ \mathbf{v}_j - \mathbf{v}_i - \mathbf{g}\Delta t_{ij} = \mathbf{R}_i\sum_{k=i}^{j-1}\Delta\mathbf{R}_{ik}\big(\tilde{\mathbf{a}}_k - \mathbf{b}^a_k - \boldsymbol{\eta}^{ad}_k\big)\Delta t . \]

Multiply both sides by \(\mathbf{R}_i\T\). The left side becomes the definition of \(\Delta\mathbf{v}_{ij}\).

Position. The third line of (11.13) contains \(\mathbf{v}_k\), which depends on \(\mathbf{v}_i\). Replace it using the velocity result for the shorter interval \(i\) to \(k\): \(\mathbf{v}_k = \mathbf{v}_i + \mathbf{g}\Delta t_{ik} + \mathbf{R}_i\Delta\mathbf{v}_{ik}\). Then

\[ \mathbf{p}_j - \mathbf{p}_i = \mathbf{v}_i\Delta t_{ij} + \mathbf{g}\sum_{k=i}^{j-1}\big(\Delta t_{ik}\Delta t + \tfrac12\Delta t^2\big) + \mathbf{R}_i\sum_{k=i}^{j-1}\Big[\Delta\mathbf{v}_{ik}\Delta t + \tfrac12\Delta\mathbf{R}_{ik}\big(\tilde{\mathbf{a}}_k - \mathbf{b}^a_k - \boldsymbol{\eta}^{ad}_k\big)\Delta t^2\Big]. \]

The gravity sum is a known number. With \(N = j-i\) samples and \(\Delta t_{ik} = (k-i)\Delta t\),

\[ \sum_{m=0}^{N-1}\big(m + \tfrac12\big)\Delta t^2 = \Big(\frac{N(N-1)}{2} + \frac{N}{2}\Big)\Delta t^2 = \tfrac12 N^2\Delta t^2 = \tfrac12\Delta t_{ij}^2 . \]

Move \(\mathbf{v}_i\Delta t_{ij}\) and \(\tfrac12\mathbf{g}\Delta t_{ij}^2\) to the left and multiply by \(\mathbf{R}_i\T\).

The result is the central definition of the chapter: §11.2.2 · p. 311

\[ \begin{aligned} \Delta\mathbf{R}_{ij} &\doteq \mathbf{R}_i\T\mathbf{R}_j &&= \prod_{k=i}^{j-1}\Exp\!\big((\tilde{\boldsymbol{\omega}}_k - \mathbf{b}^g_k - \boldsymbol{\eta}^{gd}_k)\Delta t\big) \\ \Delta\mathbf{v}_{ij} &\doteq \mathbf{R}_i\T\big(\mathbf{v}_j - \mathbf{v}_i - \mathbf{g}\Delta t_{ij}\big) &&= \sum_{k=i}^{j-1}\Delta\mathbf{R}_{ik}\big(\tilde{\mathbf{a}}_k - \mathbf{b}^a_k - \boldsymbol{\eta}^{ad}_k\big)\Delta t \\ \Delta\mathbf{p}_{ij} &\doteq \mathbf{R}_i\T\big(\mathbf{p}_j - \mathbf{p}_i - \mathbf{v}_i\Delta t_{ij} - \tfrac12\mathbf{g}\Delta t_{ij}^2\big) &&= \sum_{k=i}^{j-1}\Big[\Delta\mathbf{v}_{ik}\Delta t + \tfrac12\Delta\mathbf{R}_{ik}\big(\tilde{\mathbf{a}}_k - \mathbf{b}^a_k - \boldsymbol{\eta}^{ad}_k\big)\Delta t^2\Big] \end{aligned} \tag{11.14} \]

Read each line as "definition in terms of states = recipe in terms of IMU samples". The middle expressions hold all the unknowns. The right-hand recipes hold none, apart from the biases, which Day 5 deals with. Gravity has moved to the left as well. That is the second part of the insight: gravity is a fact about the world frame, so it belongs with the states.

The increments are not physical displacements. Take a level IMU that sits still for one second, with \(\mathbf{R}_i = \mathbf{I}\) and \(\mathbf{g} = (0,0,-9.81)\). Nothing moves, yet

\[ \Delta\mathbf{v}_{ij} = \mathbf{0} - \mathbf{0} - \mathbf{g}\cdot 1 = (0,0,9.81)\ \text{m/s}, \qquad \Delta\mathbf{p}_{ij} = -\tfrac12\mathbf{g}\cdot 1^2 = (0,0,4.905)\ \text{m}. \]

The recipe side agrees: 100 readings of \((0,0,9.81)\) at \(\Delta t = 0.01\) sum to \(9.81\) m/s. The increments are the integrals of the specific force, and gravity is put back when the states are compared with them. Only \(\Delta\mathbf{R}_{ij}\) is a true physical change. §11.2.2 · p. 311

3. See it: one integration, any starting state

Try it: the sliders stand for the optimizer revising the state at keyframe \(i\). The curved pink path is naive integration (11.13), redone from scratch on every change. The three arrows are the middle column of (11.14) solved for \(\mathbf{p}_j\): \(\mathbf{p}_j = \mathbf{p}_i + \mathbf{v}_i\Delta t_{ij} + \tfrac12\mathbf{g}\Delta t_{ij}^2 + \mathbf{R}_i\Delta\mathbf{p}_{ij}\).

Notice that the stored increments (Δθ = 19.90°, Δv = (2.036, 10.787) m/s, Δp = (1.008, 5.402) m) never change, and that the arrow chain always ends exactly where the integrated path ends: the two predictions differ by about 10⁻¹⁵ m. Changing the velocity changes only the blue arrow (the other two are carried along unchanged). Changing the orientation only turns the green arrow. Meanwhile the count of IMU samples read by the naive method climbs by 100 with every change.

In plain words

Naive integration is like giving directions from a fixed street address: "from the station, go north 200 m, then east 50 m". If the starting point turns out to be wrong, every instruction must be rewritten. Preintegration writes the directions relative to the walker: "200 m ahead, then 50 m to your right". They stay valid wherever the walk starts and whichever way the walker faced. Gravity's pull is the one thing that depends on the outside world, so it is kept out of the directions and added back afterwards.

4. Separating the noise from the measurement

To use (11.14) as a factor we need it in the standard form "measurement = function of states, plus zero-mean Gaussian noise" of Week 2 · Day 2. In (11.14) the noise is buried inside products of exponentials. Assume for now that the bias is known and constant between the keyframes, equal to its value \(\mathbf{b}_i\) at \(i\) (equation (11.15)). The book then uses two properties of the exponential map of \(\SO(3)\): §11.2.2.1 · p. 312

\[ \Exp(\boldsymbol{\phi} + \delta\boldsymbol{\phi}) \approx \Exp(\boldsymbol{\phi})\,\Exp(\mathbf{J}_r(\boldsymbol{\phi})\,\delta\boldsymbol{\phi}), \tag{11.16} \] \[ \Exp(\boldsymbol{\phi})\,\mathbf{R} = \mathbf{R}\,\Exp(\mathbf{R}\T\boldsymbol{\phi}). \tag{11.17} \]

The first splits a slightly perturbed rotation into the clean rotation followed by a small one; \(\mathbf{J}_r\) is the right Jacobian of \(\SO(3)\) from Week 4 · Day 5. The second lets a small rotation hop over a large one, at the price of re-expressing its axis.

Filling the gap: moving the noise to the end, with two samples

Write \(\mathbf{A}_k = \Exp((\tilde{\boldsymbol{\omega}}_k - \mathbf{b}^g_i)\Delta t)\) for the clean rotation of sample \(k\) and \(\boldsymbol{\epsilon}_k = \mathbf{J}^k_r\,\boldsymbol{\eta}^{gd}_k\Delta t\) for its small noise rotation. By (11.16), with \(\delta\boldsymbol{\phi} = -\boldsymbol{\eta}^{gd}_k\Delta t\), each factor of the product is \(\mathbf{A}_k\Exp(-\boldsymbol{\epsilon}_k)\). For two samples:

\[ \Delta\mathbf{R} \approx \mathbf{A}_1\,\underbrace{\Exp(-\boldsymbol{\epsilon}_1)\,\mathbf{A}_2}_{\text{apply (11.17)}}\,\Exp(-\boldsymbol{\epsilon}_2) = \underbrace{\mathbf{A}_1\mathbf{A}_2}_{\text{clean}}\;\underbrace{\Exp(-\mathbf{A}_2\T\boldsymbol{\epsilon}_1)\,\Exp(-\boldsymbol{\epsilon}_2)}_{\text{all the noise}} . \]

With more samples, the noise of sample \(k\) must hop over every later clean rotation, \(\mathbf{A}_{k+1}\cdots\mathbf{A}_{j-1} = \Delta\tilde{\mathbf{R}}_{k+1\,j}\), which is why that matrix appears transposed in (11.18). Equation (11.17) itself is the adjoint identity \(\mathbf{R}\,\Exp(\boldsymbol{\phi})\,\mathbf{R}\T = \Exp(\mathbf{R}\boldsymbol{\phi})\) of Week 4 · Day 5 with \(\mathbf{R}\) replaced by \(\mathbf{R}\T\) and both sides multiplied on the left by \(\mathbf{R}\).

The outcome is a clean product times one small rotation: §11.2.2.1 · p. 312

\[ \Delta\mathbf{R}_{ij} \simeq \Delta\tilde{\mathbf{R}}_{ij}\,\Exp(-\delta\boldsymbol{\phi}_{ij}), \qquad \Delta\tilde{\mathbf{R}}_{ij} \doteq \prod_{k=i}^{j-1}\Exp\!\big((\tilde{\boldsymbol{\omega}}_k - \mathbf{b}^g_i)\Delta t\big). \tag{11.18} \]

\(\Delta\tilde{\mathbf{R}}_{ij}\) is the preintegrated rotation measurement: computable, noise-free in form. \(\delta\boldsymbol{\phi}_{ij}\) is its noise. For velocity, substitute \(\Delta\mathbf{R}_{ik} \simeq \Delta\tilde{\mathbf{R}}_{ik}(\mathbf{I} - \delta\boldsymbol{\phi}_{ik}^\wedge)\) into (11.14), using \(\Exp(-\delta\boldsymbol{\phi}) \approx \mathbf{I} - \delta\boldsymbol{\phi}^\wedge\) (11.19), drop products of two noise terms, and flip the cross product with \(\mathbf{a}^\wedge\mathbf{b} = -\mathbf{b}^\wedge\mathbf{a}\) (11.20):

\[ \Delta\mathbf{v}_{ij} \simeq \underbrace{\sum_{k=i}^{j-1}\Delta\tilde{\mathbf{R}}_{ik}(\tilde{\mathbf{a}}_k - \mathbf{b}^a_i)\Delta t}_{\Delta\tilde{\mathbf{v}}_{ij}} \;-\; \underbrace{\sum_{k=i}^{j-1}\Big[-\Delta\tilde{\mathbf{R}}_{ik}(\tilde{\mathbf{a}}_k - \mathbf{b}^a_i)^\wedge\delta\boldsymbol{\phi}_{ik}\Delta t + \Delta\tilde{\mathbf{R}}_{ik}\boldsymbol{\eta}^{ad}_k\Delta t\Big]}_{\delta\mathbf{v}_{ij}} . \tag{11.21} \]

The position works the same way (11.22). Putting the three results back into the definitions gives the preintegrated measurement model: §11.2.2.1 · p. 313

\[ \begin{aligned} \Delta\tilde{\mathbf{R}}_{ij} &= \mathbf{R}_i\T\mathbf{R}_j\,\Exp(\delta\boldsymbol{\phi}_{ij}) \\ \Delta\tilde{\mathbf{v}}_{ij} &= \mathbf{R}_i\T\big(\mathbf{v}_j - \mathbf{v}_i - \mathbf{g}\Delta t_{ij}\big) + \delta\mathbf{v}_{ij} \\ \Delta\tilde{\mathbf{p}}_{ij} &= \mathbf{R}_i\T\big(\mathbf{p}_j - \mathbf{p}_i - \mathbf{v}_i\Delta t_{ij} - \tfrac12\mathbf{g}\Delta t_{ij}^2\big) + \delta\mathbf{p}_{ij} \end{aligned} \tag{11.23} \]

Left: three quantities computed from IMU data. Right: a function of the states at \(i\) and \(j\), "plus" noise (for the rotation, "plus" means multiplying by a small rotation on the right, as in Week 4). This is a relative-motion measurement of exactly the kind a factor graph wants.

5. How noisy are the increments?

The factor needs the covariance \(\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{ij}\) of the 9-vector \(\boldsymbol{\eta}^\Delta_{ij} = [\delta\boldsymbol{\phi}_{ij}\T, \delta\mathbf{v}_{ij}\T, \delta\mathbf{p}_{ij}\T]\T\) (11.24). To first order, the rotation noise is a weighted sum of the raw gyroscope noises: §11.2.2.2 · p. 314

\[ \delta\boldsymbol{\phi}_{ij} \simeq \sum_{k=i}^{j-1}\Delta\tilde{\mathbf{R}}_{k+1\,j}\T\,\mathbf{J}^k_r\,\boldsymbol{\eta}^{gd}_k\,\Delta t . \tag{11.28} \]

\(\delta\mathbf{v}_{ij}\), shown in (11.21), and \(\delta\mathbf{p}_{ij}\) are in turn sums of accelerometer noises and of the rotation noise (11.29). A linear combination of independent zero-mean Gaussians is a zero-mean Gaussian, and its covariance follows by the rule \(\operatorname{Cov}(\mathbf{C}\boldsymbol{\eta}) = \mathbf{C}\operatorname{Cov}(\boldsymbol{\eta})\mathbf{C}\T\). The book notes that the covariance can also be built up incrementally, one sample at a time. §11.2.2.2 · p. 314

Filling the gap: the incremental form, in the plane

In the widget's planar world a rotation is one angle, \(\mathbf{J}_r = 1\), and rotations commute, so (11.28) is simply \(\delta\theta_{ij} = \sum_k\eta^{gd}_k\Delta t\). The cross-product term \(-\mathbf{f}^\wedge\delta\boldsymbol{\phi}\) becomes \(\mathbf{J}\mathbf{f}\,\delta\theta\), with \(\mathbf{J}\) the 90° rotation matrix and \(\mathbf{f}_k = \tilde{\mathbf{a}}_k - \mathbf{b}^a_i\). Each new sample updates the noise state as

\[ \begin{aligned} \delta\theta_{i,k+1} &= \delta\theta_{ik} + \eta^{gd}_k\Delta t \\ \delta\mathbf{v}_{i,k+1} &= \delta\mathbf{v}_{ik} + \Delta\tilde{\mathbf{R}}_{ik}\mathbf{J}\mathbf{f}_k\,\delta\theta_{ik}\Delta t + \Delta\tilde{\mathbf{R}}_{ik}\boldsymbol{\eta}^{ad}_k\Delta t \\ \delta\mathbf{p}_{i,k+1} &= \delta\mathbf{p}_{ik} + \delta\mathbf{v}_{ik}\Delta t + \tfrac12\Delta\tilde{\mathbf{R}}_{ik}\mathbf{J}\mathbf{f}_k\,\delta\theta_{ik}\Delta t^2 + \tfrac12\Delta\tilde{\mathbf{R}}_{ik}\boldsymbol{\eta}^{ad}_k\Delta t^2 \end{aligned} \]

This has the form \(\boldsymbol{\eta}^\Delta_{i,k+1} = \mathbf{A}_k\boldsymbol{\eta}^\Delta_{ik} + \mathbf{B}_k\boldsymbol{\eta}^d_k\), so the covariance obeys \(\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{i,k+1} = \mathbf{A}_k\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{ik}\mathbf{A}_k\T + \mathbf{B}_k\operatorname{Cov}(\boldsymbol{\eta}^d_k)\mathbf{B}_k\T\), starting from \(\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{ii} = \mathbf{0}\). It is the covariance propagation of Week 4 · Day 4, run alongside the integration. The widget does exactly this. A check by hand for the angle: \(N\) samples each contribute variance \((\sigma_g^2/\Delta t)\Delta t^2\), so \(\operatorname{var}(\delta\theta_{ij}) = \sigma_g^2\Delta t_{ij}\). With the widget's \(\sigma_g = 0.002\) rad/s/√Hz and \(\Delta t_{ij} = 1\) s the standard deviation is 0.002 rad = 0.115°, the value it displays.

Two things to remember about \(\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{ij}\). It grows with the time between keyframes, so widely spaced keyframes give weaker IMU factors. And it is not diagonal: an error in the integrated rotation mis-rotates every later accelerometer sample, so the velocity and position noises are correlated with the rotation noise.

Common mistakes

  • "\(\Delta\mathbf{p}_{ij}\) is how far the robot moved." It is the double integral of the specific force in the frame of keyframe \(i\). A robot at rest for 1 s has \(\Delta\mathbf{p}_{ij} = 4.9\) m.
  • "Preintegration is a cheaper, approximate integration." The increments are an exact regrouping of (11.13), as the 10⁻¹⁵ m in the widget shows. Approximations enter only in the first-order treatment of noise, and tomorrow in the bias correction.
  • "The increments depend on nothing but the IMU data." They still depend on the bias estimate used while integrating.

Check yourself

Q1. A level IMU (R_i = I, z up) stays perfectly still for 2 s. What is the position increment Δp_ij?

With p_j = p_i and v_i = 0, the definition gives −½·g·Δt² = −½·(0,0,−9.81)·4 = (0,0,19.62) m. The increment integrates the specific force, which points up at rest.

Q2. Which of these does NOT appear in the right-hand (recipe) sides of (11.14)?

The recipes use only IMU samples and the bias. The states at i and gravity were moved to the definition side, which is the whole point.

Q3. During optimization the estimate of R_i changes by 5°. With a preintegrated factor, what has to be redone?

The left sides of (11.23) are stored numbers. Only the state-dependent right sides are re-evaluated, with no pass over the IMU samples.

Q4. Planar case: gyroscope noise density 0.001 rad/s/√Hz and 4 s between keyframes. The standard deviation of the preintegrated angle noise is

var = σ²·Δt_ij, so the standard deviation is 0.001 × √4 = 0.002 rad. It does not depend on the IMU rate.

Q5. What is identity (11.17), Exp(φ)R = R·Exp(Rᵀφ), used for in the derivation?

After (11.16) the product alternates clean and noise rotations. (11.17) swaps a noise rotation with the clean one after it, so all noise ends up in a single factor Exp(−δφ).

Recap

  1. Moving \(\mathbf{R}_i\), \(\mathbf{v}_i\), \(\mathbf{p}_i\), and \(\mathbf{g}\) to one side of (11.13) defines \(\Delta\mathbf{R}_{ij}\), \(\Delta\mathbf{v}_{ij}\), \(\Delta\mathbf{p}_{ij}\), equation (11.14).
  2. Their recipes use only IMU samples (and the bias), so they are integrated once and never again when states change.
  3. \(\Delta\mathbf{v}\) and \(\Delta\mathbf{p}\) are integrals of specific force in the frame of keyframe \(i\), not physical changes.
  4. Pushing the noise to the end gives the measurement model (11.23): computed increment = function of states "plus" noise.
  5. The noise is a linear function of the raw IMU noises, so it is Gaussian to first order with a covariance \(\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{ij}\) propagated sample by sample.

Sources

  1. SLAM Handbook, §11.2.2 "IMU Preintegration on Manifold", §11.2.2.1, §11.2.2.2, pp. 311–314.
  2. Forster, Carlone, Dellaert, Scaramuzza, On-Manifold Preintegration for Real-Time Visual-Inertial Odometry, IEEE Transactions on Robotics, 2017 (the presentation the book follows; full derivation and the incremental covariance).
  3. Solà, Deray, Atchuthan, A micro Lie theory for state estimation in robotics, 2018 (the adjoint identity and the right Jacobian of SO(3)).

Week 16 · Day 5

Bias updates, the IMU factor, and better integration

After today you can correct preintegrated measurements for a changed bias estimate without re-integrating, write the residuals of the IMU factor and the bias factor, and say what the rectangle rule costs in accuracy.

About 60 min · Read §11.2.2.3 to §11.2.3, pp. 314–319 (5 pages) · Needs Week 16 Day 4 and Week 2 Day 2

Read first: §11.2.2.3, §11.2.2.4, §11.2.3, pp. 314–319

Start at "Incorporating Bias Updates" at the bottom of p. 314 and stop where §11.3 begins on p. 319. Look for:

  • In (11.30) on p. 315: which update is a multiplication and which are additions, and the sentence saying the Jacobians "remain constant".
  • In (11.31): match each residual to a line of yesterday's (11.23).
  • The bias model (11.32)–(11.34) on pp. 315–316, and how the discrete covariance scales with \(\Delta t_{ij}\).
  • The RMSE values in the titles of Figures 11.2 and 11.3 (pp. 317–318). Rank the four methods.
  • On p. 319, equations (11.35)–(11.36): why rotation is harder to integrate than acceleration.

Today's big idea

Yesterday's increments were free of the pose and velocity at keyframe \(i\) but still depended on the bias estimate. A first-order correction, with Jacobians accumulated during the one integration, removes that last reason to re-integrate. The corrected increments then enter the factor graph as one 9-dimensional residual per pair of keyframes, joined by a small factor that says the bias changes slowly.

1. When the bias estimate changes

The increments \(\Delta\tilde{\mathbf{R}}_{ij}, \Delta\tilde{\mathbf{v}}_{ij}, \Delta\tilde{\mathbf{p}}_{ij}\) were computed by subtracting a bias estimate \(\bar{\mathbf{b}}_i = \{\bar{\mathbf{b}}^g_i, \bar{\mathbf{b}}^a_i\}\) from every sample. The biases are unknowns of the optimization, so the solver will revise them: \(\mathbf{b} \leftarrow \bar{\mathbf{b}} + \delta\mathbf{b}\). Re-integrating would bring back the cost preintegration was meant to remove. The book instead expands to first order in \(\delta\mathbf{b}\): §11.2.2.3 · pp. 314–315

\[ \begin{aligned} \Delta\tilde{\mathbf{R}}_{ij}(\mathbf{b}^g_i) &\simeq \Delta\tilde{\mathbf{R}}_{ij}(\bar{\mathbf{b}}^g_i)\,\Exp\!\Big(\frac{\partial\Delta\bar{\mathbf{R}}_{ij}}{\partial\mathbf{b}^g}\,\delta\mathbf{b}^g\Big) \\ \Delta\tilde{\mathbf{v}}_{ij}(\mathbf{b}^g_i, \mathbf{b}^a_i) &\simeq \Delta\tilde{\mathbf{v}}_{ij}(\bar{\mathbf{b}}^g_i, \bar{\mathbf{b}}^a_i) + \frac{\partial\Delta\bar{\mathbf{v}}_{ij}}{\partial\mathbf{b}^g}\,\delta\mathbf{b}^g_i + \frac{\partial\Delta\bar{\mathbf{v}}_{ij}}{\partial\mathbf{b}^a}\,\delta\mathbf{b}^a_i \\ \Delta\tilde{\mathbf{p}}_{ij}(\mathbf{b}^g_i, \mathbf{b}^a_i) &\simeq \Delta\tilde{\mathbf{p}}_{ij}(\bar{\mathbf{b}}^g_i, \bar{\mathbf{b}}^a_i) + \frac{\partial\Delta\bar{\mathbf{p}}_{ij}}{\partial\mathbf{b}^g}\,\delta\mathbf{b}^g_i + \frac{\partial\Delta\bar{\mathbf{p}}_{ij}}{\partial\mathbf{b}^a}\,\delta\mathbf{b}^a_i \end{aligned} \tag{11.30} \]

The vectors are corrected by adding. The rotation is corrected by multiplying with a small rotation on the right, because rotations do not form a vector space (Week 4 · Day 3). The five Jacobians are evaluated at \(\bar{\mathbf{b}}_i\), computed once during preintegration, and then stay constant. The book gives no formulas for them and refers to the original paper. §11.2.2.3 · p. 315

Filling the gap: what the Jacobians look like

Accelerometer bias. Look at the recipe \(\Delta\tilde{\mathbf{v}}_{ij} = \sum_k\Delta\tilde{\mathbf{R}}_{ik}(\tilde{\mathbf{a}}_k - \mathbf{b}^a)\Delta t\). It is linear in \(\mathbf{b}^a\), so the derivative can be read off and the correction is exact:

\[ \frac{\partial\Delta\bar{\mathbf{v}}_{ij}}{\partial\mathbf{b}^a} = -\sum_{k=i}^{j-1}\Delta\bar{\mathbf{R}}_{ik}\,\Delta t, \qquad \frac{\partial\Delta\bar{\mathbf{p}}_{ij}}{\partial\mathbf{b}^a} = \sum_{k=i}^{j-1}\Big[\frac{\partial\Delta\bar{\mathbf{v}}_{ik}}{\partial\mathbf{b}^a}\Delta t - \tfrac12\Delta\bar{\mathbf{R}}_{ik}\Delta t^2\Big]. \]

If the body does not rotate these are \(-\Delta t_{ij}\mathbf{I}\) and \(-\tfrac12\Delta t_{ij}^2\mathbf{I}\): a bias of \(\delta b\) removes \(\delta b\,\Delta t_{ij}\) of velocity and \(\tfrac12\delta b\,\Delta t_{ij}^2\) of position, as for any constant acceleration.

Gyroscope bias, in the plane. The angle increment is \(\Delta\tilde\theta_{ij} = \sum_k(\tilde\omega_k - b^g)\Delta t\), so \(\partial\Delta\theta_{ij}/\partial b^g = -\Delta t_{ij}\), again exact. But a changed gyroscope bias also changes every \(\Delta\tilde{\mathbf{R}}_{ik}\) that rotates an accelerometer sample. Since \(\tfrac{d}{d\theta}\mathbf{R}(\theta) = \mathbf{J}\mathbf{R}(\theta)\) with \(\mathbf{J}\) the 90° rotation,

\[ \frac{\partial\Delta\bar{\mathbf{v}}_{ij}}{\partial b^g} = \sum_{k=i}^{j-1}\mathbf{J}\,\Delta\bar{\mathbf{R}}_{ik}(\tilde{\mathbf{a}}_k - \bar{\mathbf{b}}^a)\,\underbrace{(-\Delta t_{ik})}_{\partial\Delta\theta_{ik}/\partial b^g}\,\Delta t . \]

This one is a true first-order approximation, since \(\mathbf{R}(\theta)\) is not linear in \(\theta\). The neglected part is proportional to \((\delta b^g)^2\).

In 3-D (Forster et al.) the structure is the same: \(\partial\Delta\bar{\mathbf{R}}_{ij}/\partial\mathbf{b}^g = -\sum_k\Delta\tilde{\mathbf{R}}_{k+1\,j}\T\mathbf{J}^k_r\Delta t\), which is (11.28) with the bias error playing the role of a noise that is the same in every sample, and \(\partial\Delta\bar{\mathbf{v}}_{ij}/\partial\mathbf{b}^g = -\sum_k\Delta\bar{\mathbf{R}}_{ik}(\tilde{\mathbf{a}}_k - \bar{\mathbf{b}}^a)^\wedge\,\tfrac{\partial\Delta\bar{\mathbf{R}}_{ik}}{\partial\mathbf{b}^g}\Delta t\). All are running sums, updated with each incoming sample.

Try it: the one-second increments of Day 4 were integrated with bias estimate zero. Move the gyroscope bias update and compare three ways of responding.

Notice that for a 1°/s update, ignoring it leaves Δp wrong by 31.5 mm, while the first-order correction is within 0.14 mm of a full re-integration and reads no IMU samples. The remaining error grows like the square of the update: at 5°/s it is 3.4 mm, against 157 mm uncorrected. Set the gyroscope update to zero and move the accelerometer slider: the corrected error stays at 0.00 mm, because the increments are exactly linear in the accelerometer bias.

2. The preintegrated IMU factor

Yesterday's model (11.23) says "computed increment = function of states, plus Gaussian noise with covariance \(\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{ij}\)". As in Week 2 · Day 2, the residual is the difference between the two sides, with the bias-corrected increments of (11.30) in place of the raw ones: §11.2.2.4 · p. 315

\[ \begin{aligned} \mathbf{r}_{\Delta\mathbf{R}_{ij}} &\doteq \Log\!\Big(\Big(\Delta\tilde{\mathbf{R}}_{ij}(\bar{\mathbf{b}}^g_i)\,\Exp\!\Big(\frac{\partial\Delta\bar{\mathbf{R}}_{ij}}{\partial\mathbf{b}^g}\delta\mathbf{b}^g\Big)\Big)\T\mathbf{R}_i\T\mathbf{R}_j\Big) \\ \mathbf{r}_{\Delta\mathbf{v}_{ij}} &\doteq \mathbf{R}_i\T\big(\mathbf{v}_j - \mathbf{v}_i - \mathbf{g}\Delta t_{ij}\big) - \Big[\Delta\tilde{\mathbf{v}}_{ij}(\bar{\mathbf{b}}^g_i, \bar{\mathbf{b}}^a_i) + \frac{\partial\Delta\bar{\mathbf{v}}_{ij}}{\partial\mathbf{b}^g}\delta\mathbf{b}^g + \frac{\partial\Delta\bar{\mathbf{v}}_{ij}}{\partial\mathbf{b}^a}\delta\mathbf{b}^a\Big] \\ \mathbf{r}_{\Delta\mathbf{p}_{ij}} &\doteq \mathbf{R}_i\T\big(\mathbf{p}_j - \mathbf{p}_i - \mathbf{v}_i\Delta t_{ij} - \tfrac12\mathbf{g}\Delta t_{ij}^2\big) - \Big[\Delta\tilde{\mathbf{p}}_{ij}(\bar{\mathbf{b}}^g_i, \bar{\mathbf{b}}^a_i) + \frac{\partial\Delta\bar{\mathbf{p}}_{ij}}{\partial\mathbf{b}^g}\delta\mathbf{b}^g + \frac{\partial\Delta\bar{\mathbf{p}}_{ij}}{\partial\mathbf{b}^a}\delta\mathbf{b}^a\Big] \end{aligned} \tag{11.31} \]

Stacked, they form \(\mathbf{r}_{\mathcal{I}_{ij}} \in \R^9\), and the factor adds \(\norm{\mathbf{r}_{\mathcal{I}_{ij}}}^2_{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{ij}} = \mathbf{r}\T\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{ij}^{-1}\mathbf{r}\) to the least-squares objective. The rotation residual is the rotation vector of "measured increment inverse times predicted increment": zero when the states reproduce the measurement. The other two are plain differences. The factor touches the rotation, position, and velocity at both keyframes and the bias at \(i\).

A planar number: Day 4's widget stored \(\Delta\tilde\theta_{ij} = 19.90^\circ\) with \(\sigma = 0.115^\circ\). If the current states say the robot turned \(\theta_j - \theta_i = 20.50^\circ\), the residual is 0.60°, which is 5.2σ, and it adds \(5.2^2 \approx 27\) to the cost. The optimizer will pull the two orientations toward a 19.9° difference, or shift the gyroscope bias to explain the gap.

3. A model for the bias itself

Inside one interval the bias was treated as constant (11.15). Across intervals it is allowed to move, slowly. The book models it as integrated white noise: §11.2.2.4 · pp. 315–316

\[ \dot{\mathbf{b}}^g(t) = \boldsymbol{\eta}^{bg}, \quad \dot{\mathbf{b}}^a(t) = \boldsymbol{\eta}^{ba} \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad \mathbf{b}^g_j = \mathbf{b}^g_i + \boldsymbol{\eta}^{bgd}, \quad \mathbf{b}^a_j = \mathbf{b}^a_i + \boldsymbol{\eta}^{bad}, \tag{11.32, 11.33} \]

where the discrete noises have covariances \(\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{bgd} = \Delta t_{ij}\operatorname{Cov}(\boldsymbol{\eta}^{bg})\) and \(\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{bad} = \Delta t_{ij}\operatorname{Cov}(\boldsymbol{\eta}^{ba})\). This is the random walk of Day 2: the variance of the change grows in proportion to the elapsed time. Compare with the sample noise, whose covariance is divided by \(\Delta t\). The corresponding factor penalizes bias changes between consecutive keyframes:

\[ \norm{\mathbf{r}_{\mathbf{b}_{ij}}}^2 \doteq \norm{\mathbf{b}^g_j - \mathbf{b}^g_i}^2_{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{bgd}} + \norm{\mathbf{b}^a_j - \mathbf{b}^a_i}^2_{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{bad}} . \tag{11.34} \]

Example: a gyroscope bias random walk of \(2\times10^{-5}\) rad/s²/√Hz and keyframes 0.25 s apart give a standard deviation of \(2\times10^{-5}\times\sqrt{0.25} = 1\times10^{-5}\) rad/s for the change between keyframes. A proposed jump of \(10^{-4}\) rad/s would be a 10σ event and cost 100. Without this factor each keyframe's bias could absorb any disagreement between IMU and camera. With it, the bias has to be a slowly varying curve, which is what makes it estimable.

4. Better integration

Everything so far used the scheme (11.12), which holds each sample constant until the next one arrives: the rectangle rule, or Euler method. §11.2.3 looks at what this costs and at alternatives. §11.2.3.1 · p. 316 The book's Figures 11.2 and 11.3 integrate one example acceleration signal over 2 s in four ways and report the errors:
