Week 18 · Review

Week 18 review: leg odometry, and all of Part II

After today you can work a leg-odometry problem from joint angles to a factor, and compare the six sensing modalities of Part II by what they measure, where their odometry comes from, and how they fail.

About 75 min · No new pages

The week in one paragraph

A legged robot can read its own motion from its joints. Encoders give the joint angles; forward kinematics turns them into the foot's pose in the base frame, and the Jacobian turns joint rates into foot velocity. While a foot stands still, the foot's motion seen from the body is the body's motion seen from the ground, with the sign flipped. That gives a relative-pose measurement, \(\mathbf{f}_p(\mathbf{q}) = \mathbf{R}\T(\mathbf{c}_i - \mathbf{t})\), and a velocity measurement, \(\mathbf{v} = -\boldsymbol{\omega} \times \mathbf{f}_p - \mathbf{J}_v\dot{\mathbf{q}}\). Both depend on knowing which feet are truly stationary, which is decided by thresholding the normal force as a stand-in for the friction cone. With covariances from encoder noise and from a slip model, the measurements become factors: forward-kinematics and contact factors for bipeds, a preintegrated velocity factor for quadrupeds. Slip, soft ground, and bending legs break the assumptions and appear as biased motion.

1. Formula sheet

What it isFormulaWhere
Forward kinematics and Jacobian\(\mathbf{T}^b_f = \mathbf{fk}(\mathbf{q}) = \begin{bmatrix} \mathbf{f}_R & \mathbf{f}_p \\ \mathbf{0} & 1 \end{bmatrix}\), \(\ \begin{bmatrix} \mathbf{v}^b_f \\ \boldsymbol{\omega}^b_f \end{bmatrix} = \mathbf{J}(\mathbf{q})\,\dot{\mathbf{q}}\)(12.2), (12.3), p. 337 · Day 2

2. Mixed quiz: Week 18

Check yourself

Q1. In the state (12.1), which quantities are expressed in base coordinates?

t and R give the base pose in the world. The twist (v, ω) is written along the base's own axes.

Q2. A planar leg has l₁ = l₂ = 0.4 m and a knee angle q₂ = −30°. What is the determinant of its Jacobian J_v?

det J_v = l₁ l₂ sin q₂ = 0.16 × (−0.5) = −0.08 m². It does not depend on the hip angle, and it vanishes only for a straight leg.

Q3. A stance foot is at f_p = (0.1, 0, −0.6) m, J_v q̇ = (−0.5, 0, 0) m/s, and the gyroscope reads a pure yaw rate ω = (0, 0, 1) rad/s. What is v from (12.21)?

ω × f_p = (0 × (−0.6) − 1 × 0, 1 × 0.1 − 0, 0) = (0, 0.1, 0). Then v = −(0, 0.1, 0) − (−0.5, 0, 0) = (0.5, −0.1, 0) m/s.

Q4. Encoder noise adds an independent 5 mm (1σ) position error per footstep; slip adds 2 mm per footstep, always backward. After 100 footsteps, what are the two contributions?

Independent errors add in variance: 5 × √100 = 50 mm. A bias adds linearly: 2 × 100 = 200 mm. The smaller per-step error ends up four times larger.

Q5. A foot's force sensor shows a small force that has just begun to rise. How should leg odometry treat that leg?

A small, rising force means the foot is striking but may still slide. Contact for odometry means a stationary contact point, so the leg is not trusted until it is loaded.

Q6. In the contact factor (12.34), a stance lasts four times as long as another. By what factor does the 1σ uncertainty of the contact position grow?

The covariance is proportional to Δt, so the standard deviation is proportional to √Δt: √4 = 2.

3. Pen-and-paper problems

  1. A planar leg has \(l_1 = l_2 = 0.3\) m and joint angles \(q = (45^\circ, -90^\circ)\). (a) Find the foot position \(\mathbf{f}_p\) and the Jacobian \(\mathbf{J}_v\). (b) Check the determinant against \(l_1 l_2 \sin q_2\). (c) The joint rates are \(\dot{\mathbf{q}} = (-2,\ 1)\) rad/s, the foot is in stance, and the body does not rotate. What is the body velocity?

    Solution

    (a) \(q_1 + q_2 = -45^\circ\) and \(\sin 45^\circ = \cos 45^\circ = 0.707\). \(x = 0.3(0.707) + 0.3(-0.707) = 0\), \(z = -0.3(0.707) - 0.3(0.707) = -0.424\) m. The Jacobian is

    \[ \mathbf{J}_v = \begin{bmatrix} 0.3(0.707) + 0.3(0.707) & 0.3(0.707) \\ 0.3(0.707) + 0.3(-0.707) & 0.3(-0.707) \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 0.424 & 0.212 \\ 0 & -0.212 \end{bmatrix} \text{ m/rad}. \]

    (b) \(\det = 0.424 \times (-0.212) = -0.090\), and \(l_1 l_2 \sin q_2 = 0.09 \times (-1) = -0.09\). They agree.

    (c) Foot velocity: \(\mathbf{J}_v\dot{\mathbf{q}} = (0.424(-2) + 0.212(1),\ -0.212(1)) = (-0.636,\ -0.212)\) m/s. With no rotation, \(\mathbf{v} = -\mathbf{J}_v\dot{\mathbf{q}} = (0.636,\ 0.212)\) m/s: the body moves forward and rises.

  2. An upright planar biped starts with its base at \(\mathbf{t} = (0,\ 0.50)\) m. Leg A is in stance with \(\mathbf{f}_p^A = (0.10,\ -0.50)\) m. At the end of A's stance, \(\mathbf{f}_p^A = (-0.10,\ -0.50)\) and leg B touches down with \(\mathbf{f}_p^B = (0.12,\ -0.50)\). Later in B's stance, \(\mathbf{f}_p^B = (-0.08,\ -0.52)\). (a) Find the two contact points and the final base position. (b) If foot A in fact slid 3 cm backward during its stance, where is the base really, and does the error go away once B is planted?

    Solution

    (a) Use \(\mathbf{c} = \mathbf{t} + \mathbf{f}_p\) at touchdown and \(\mathbf{t} = \mathbf{c} - \mathbf{f}_p\) afterwards. \(\mathbf{c}_A = (0, 0.50) + (0.10, -0.50) = (0.10,\ 0)\). End of A's stance: \(\mathbf{t} = (0.10, 0) - (-0.10, -0.50) = (0.20,\ 0.50)\). Then \(\mathbf{c}_B = (0.20, 0.50) + (0.12, -0.50) = (0.32,\ 0)\). Finally \(\mathbf{t} = (0.32, 0) - (-0.08, -0.52) = (0.40,\ 0.52)\) m.

    (b) During A's stance the body really advanced \(0.20 - 0.03 = 0.17\) m, so the true final position is \(x = 0.37\) m. The error does not go away: \(\mathbf{c}_B\) was computed from the wrong \(\mathbf{t}\), so it is 3 cm too far forward, and every later estimate inherits that.

  3. The leg of problem 1 stands still (ignore \(\mathbf{h}\)) and its motors hold \(\boldsymbol{\tau} = (-8.49,\ 15.0)\) N·m. (a) Find the ground reaction force \((f_x, f_z)\). (b) Does the foot hold on a floor with \(\mu = 0.3\)? With \(\mu = 0.2\)? (c) What would a 50 N threshold on \(f_z\) conclude in each case?

    Solution

    (a) Solve \(\mathbf{J}_v\T\mathbf{f} = -\boldsymbol{\tau}\) with \(\mathbf{J}_v\T = \begin{bmatrix} 0.424 & 0 \\ 0.212 & -0.212 \end{bmatrix}\). First row: \(0.424 f_x = 8.49\), so \(f_x = 20.0\) N. Second row: \(0.212(20.0) - 0.212 f_z = -15.0\), so \(f_z = (15.0 + 4.24)/0.212 = 90.7\) N.

    (b) The cone allows \(\mu f_z\): \(0.3 \times 90.7 = 27.2\) N, which is more than 20 N, so the foot holds. With \(\mu = 0.2\) the limit is 18.1 N, less than 20 N: the foot slips.

    (c) \(f_z = 90.7\) N exceeds 50 N in both cases, so the detector reports contact both times. On the slippery floor it is wrong, and leg odometry would use a moving foot.

  4. (Stretch.) In the walking widget of Day 3, the rows of \(\mathbf{J}_v\) that map joint noise to the foot's \(x\) coordinate are \((0.65,\ 0.275)\) for the leg that lifts and \((0.65,\ 0.375)\) for the leg that lands, in m/rad. Each encoder reading has independent noise \(\sigma_q = 0.3^\circ\). (a) Find the 1σ error in \(x\) added at one foot switch. (b) The foot also slips 3 mm per step. After how many steps does slip exceed the noise-driven error? (c) Give both after 100 steps, as a fraction of the 30 m walked.

    Solution

    (a) \(\sigma_q = 0.3 \times \pi/180 = 0.00524\) rad. Each leg contributes \(\sigma_q\) times the length of its row: \(0.00524\sqrt{0.65^2 + 0.275^2} = 0.00524 \times 0.706 = 3.7\) mm and \(0.00524\sqrt{0.65^2 + 0.375^2} = 0.00524 \times 0.750 = 3.9\) mm. They are independent, so \(\sigma_{\text{step}} = \sqrt{3.7^2 + 3.9^2} = 5.4\) mm.

    (b) Noise grows as \(5.4\sqrt{n}\) mm, slip as \(3n\) mm. They are equal when \(\sqrt{n} = 5.4/3 = 1.8\), that is \(n = 3.2\). From the fourth step on, slip is the larger error.

    (c) Noise: \(5.4\sqrt{100} = 54\) mm, 0.18% of 30 m. Slip: \(300\) mm, 1%. Over long distances, the bias decides the drift rate, and no encoder upgrade changes it.

4. Part II in review: six sensors, one factor graph

Part I built the back-end: a factor graph and the tools to optimize it. Part II was about front-ends: how each sensor's raw data becomes factors. The Prelude's organizing idea is that almost every front-end has the same modules. An odometry module produces a relative measurement between consecutive nodes. A loop closure module first recognizes a place and then estimates a relative pose to an old node. Some sensors add unary factors on single nodes, such as GPS. §II.1 · pp. 185–187 Each chapter then filled in those modules for one sensor.

SensorWhat it measuresWhere odometry comes fromStrong atWeak atLessons
RGB cameraBrightness on a pixel grid: directions to scene points, no rangeMatching keypoints (reprojection error) or pixels (photometric error) across framesCheap, small; rich appearance and semanticsNeeds light; glare, blur, fog, smoke; a single camera gives no metric scaleCh 7 · Weeks 11–12
LiDARRange along laser beams: a 3-D point cloudScan registration (ICP and its variants)Direct, accurate geometry; independent of lightingCost, size, power, data volume; heavy rain, fog, snow; scans distort while movingCh 8 · Week 13
RadarRange and radial (Doppler) velocity from radio wavesEgo-velocity from Doppler, or registration of radar scansWorks in conditions that defeat cameras and LiDAR; measures velocityNoisy and sparse data; lower accuracy than LiDAR; heavy signal processingCh 9 · Week 14
Event cameraPer-pixel changes of log brightness, asynchronouslyFeatures or edges tracked in the event stream; motion compensationMicrosecond timing, no motion blur, high dynamic range, low powerNoise; no absolute intensity or fine textureCh 10 · Week 15
IMUAngular velocity and specific force, at high rateIntegration between keyframes, packaged as a preintegration factorWorks everywhere; gives the gravity direction and metric scaleBias and noise integrate into fast drift; needs another sensor; global position and yaw stay unobservableCh 11 · Weeks 16–17
LegsJoint angles, and forces or contact bitsThe stationary stance foot: forward kinematics or foot velocityHigh rate; independent of what the scene looks likeSlip, soft ground, bending legs; nothing during flight phasesCh 12 · Week 18

§II.2.1–II.2.2 · pp. 188–190, and Chapters 7–12 No row is good everywhere, which is why real systems fuse. The IMU is the common partner (visual-inertial, LiDAR-inertial, radar-inertial, legged-inertial), because it is cheap and fills the gaps between slower measurements. §II.2.2 · p. 189

SensorThe equation to rememberIn wordsWhere
Camera\(E_{\text{reproj}} = \tfrac{1}{2}\sum_j \left\lVert \mathbf{z}_j - \pi(\mathbf{x}^c_j) \right\rVert^2_{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_j}\)Observed pixel minus projected 3-D point(7.1), p. 204 · Week 11 · Day 3
LiDAR\(\mathbf{R}_k, \mathbf{t}_k = \argmin_{\mathbf{R}, \mathbf{t}} \sum_{(\mathbf{p}, \mathbf{q}) \in \mathcal{C}} d(\mathbf{p}_i, \mathbf{R}\mathbf{q}_i + \mathbf{t})\)The rigid motion that best aligns matched points; re-match and repeat(8.1), p. 228 · Week 13 · Day 2

IMU\(\mathbf{a} = \mathbf{R}^b_w(\mathbf{a}^w - \mathbf{g}^w) + \mathbf{b}^a + \boldsymbol{\eta}^a\), \(\ \boldsymbol{\omega} = \boldsymbol{\omega}^b_b + \mathbf{b}^g + \boldsymbol{\eta}^g\)Readings are the true motion plus gravity's effect, a slowly drifting bias, and noise(11.1), (11.2), p. 306 · Week 16 · Day 1

Three ideas recurred across the chapters. Odometry drifts, whatever the sensor, and only loop closures or absolute measurements bound it (Week 11 · Day 1). High-rate measurements are summarized between keyframes by preintegration, first for the IMU (Week 16 · Day 4), then for contacts and leg velocities (Day 5). And every sensor leaves some directions unobservable: scale for one camera, global position and yaw for a camera with an IMU (Week 17 · Day 2), so a second modality is added to fill them.

6. Mixed quiz: all of Part II

Check yourself

Q1. A GPS fix is added to a SLAM factor graph. What kind of factor is it?

GPS measures a property of one node, its position, and not a relation between two nodes (§II.1.3, p. 187).

Q2. A pinhole camera has focal length 500 px and principal point (320, 240). A landmark is at (0.2, −0.1, 2.0) m in camera coordinates and is observed at pixel (373, 211). How large is the reprojection error?

Projection: u = 500 × 0.2 / 2.0 + 320 = 370, v = 500 × (−0.1) / 2.0 + 240 = 215. The error is (373 − 370, 211 − 215) = (3, −4), with length 5 px.

Q3. A vision-only system has 7 unknowns that no measurement fixes. Adding an IMU leaves 4. Which 4?

The accelerometer senses gravity, which fixes roll and pitch, and gives metric scale. Where the world origin is and which way is north remain free (p. 221 and §11.3.2, p. 324).

Q4. Which two steps does ICP alternate between?

Each iteration recomputes the correspondence set from the latest transformation, then minimizes the registration error (8.1) over R and t (§8.2.1, p. 228).

Q5. A radar echo returns 1 microsecond after transmission. How far away is the target? (c = 3 × 10⁸ m/s)

d = c t₀ / 2 = 3 × 10⁸ × 10⁻⁶ / 2 = 150 m. The factor 2 is there because the wave travels out and back.

Q6. For which two modalities does the Prelude say odometry can be computed by integrating a measured velocity, with no matching of consecutive measurements?

Doppler gives radial velocities, from which ego-velocity follows; legs give body velocity from kinematics and contact (§II.1.1, p. 186). Cameras and LiDAR match pixels, points, or features between frames.

Q7. An event-camera pixel with contrast threshold C = 0.2 sees its log brightness rise steadily by 0.45. What does it output?

The pixel fires each time the change since its last event reaches C: at +0.2 and at +0.4, both with polarity +1. The remaining 0.05 is below threshold. Events carry a sign, not a magnitude.

Q8. An IMU lies still and level on a table. According to (11.1), with zero bias and noise, what does its accelerometer read?

With a = R(a^w − g^w) and a^w = 0, the reading is −g rotated into the body frame: 9.81 m/s² upward. An accelerometer measures specific force, here the table's push.

Q9. Why are IMU measurements preintegrated before they enter the factor graph?

Naive integration depends on the initial state, so it would have to be redone at every solver iteration. Preintegration separates what depends on the state from what depends only on the measurements (§11.2, p. 308).

Q10. A robot must map a tunnel filled with smoke. Which exteroceptive sensor does the Prelude single out for such conditions, and at what price?

Radar is the least affected by the environment and is one of the few sensors that keep working where LiDAR and cameras are impaired, but its data is noisy and sparse (§II.2.1, p. 189).

  • Say what "in contact" means for leg odometry and why a force threshold stands in for it.
  • Write a residual and a covariance for one leg-odometry factor.
  • For each of the six modalities, name what it measures, where its odometry comes from, and one condition in which it fails.
  • Explain why sensors are fused, and what the IMU contributes to every combination.

Week 19 · Day 1

Part III begins: Spatial AI, and where learning enters SLAM

After today you can say what Part III adds to SLAM, name four places a neural network can enter a SLAM pipeline, and compute one attention step by hand.

About 60 min · Read Prelude III, pp. 361–365, and the opening of Ch 13, pp. 366–368 (8 pages) · Needs Week 2 Day 2

Read first: Prelude III, pp. 361–365, and Chapter 13 up to §13.1, pp. 366–368

The Prelude is light reading. While you read, look for:

  • The conditions under which the editors say SLAM "could be" solved, and the settings where it is not (p. 361).
  • The three things Spatial AI adds to a map, in the last sentence of §III.1 (p. 361).
  • The chapter-by-chapter plan of Part III (p. 365).
  • In Chapter 13: the sentence about what goes wrong with the modular approach, and the three kinds of method the chapter covers (pp. 366–368).

Today's big idea

Parts I and II built SLAM from models written by hand: a measurement model, a noise model, a solver. Part III asks what happens when some of those pieces are learned from data. Chapter 13 gives the first answer. A network can replace one component, add predicted depth or pose as extra factors, be trained through the optimizer itself, or regress 3D points directly from a pair of images. In most of these, the factor graph stays.

1. Is SLAM solved? What Part III is about

The Prelude opens with a question the field keeps asking. Its answer: yes, if you restrict yourself to small, static, indoor scenes with plenty of features. The uses people actually want are underwater, on other planets, in disaster zones, and in dense city traffic, and there the answer is no. Prelude III · p. 361

The editors call the direction of travel Spatial AI. Compared with the SLAM of Parts I and II it differs in two ways. First, it uses deep learning for the parts of the problem that are hard to model by hand, which makes systems more adaptive and robust. Second, it changes what a map is: maps that can render views nobody captured (novel view synthesis), maps that carry meaning (semantic information), and maps that cope with a scene that changes. The Prelude adds two cautions: use foundation models, and do not forget that the result has to run on a real device. §III.1 · pp. 361–362

Why not skip the map and ask a large image-and-text model about the scene? The Prelude's answer is that such models give a holistic description of an image and often struggle with spatial questions. Many tasks need a persistent 3D representation that is kept up to date, a spatio-temporal memory, and building one is what SLAM does. §III.2 · p. 362

2. What the applications ask for

Section III.2 walks through eight application areas. Read them as a list of requirements. In each one, SLAM supplies the pose and the geometry, and Spatial AI adds an understanding of what the geometry is. §III.2 · pp. 362–365

ApplicationWhat SLAM suppliesWhat the added understanding is for
AR/VR glassesDevice pose and a map, so virtual objects stay fixed to real surfaces; inside-out tracking without external sensorsRecognizing walls, furniture, people; shared content for several users
AI glassesPersistent spatial awareness on a light, always-worn deviceTranslation, navigation help, task guidance, product information
Humanoid robotsMaps of homes, offices, hospitals that are updated while the robot localizesSpatial relations ("the cup is on the table") and commands in natural language
Self-driving vehiclesLocalization where GPS is unreliable (tunnels, urban canyons); detecting changesLanes, signs, pedestrians, other vehicles, for decisions
Drones3D maps and obstacle avoidance without GPS, indoors or undergroundFinding power lines, crops, structural damage
Factories and warehousesLocalization in a layout that keeps changingTask-level reasoning about shelves and aisles
Emergency responseReal-time maps of collapsed buildings or flood zonesLocating survivors, delivering supplies
Healthcare and assistive devicesSpatial cues and obstacle warnings for visually impaired users; hospital service robotsSemantic understanding, which the book calls critical for effective assistance

3. Four ways to put a network into SLAM

Chapter 13 starts from the pipeline you know from Weeks 11 and 12: detect features, match them, reject outliers, then optimize a factor graph. A deep network is a function with many parameters that is fitted to examples. The chapter sorts the ways of using one by how much of the pipeline it takes over. Ch 13 intro · pp. 366–368

  1. Replace one component. Train a network to detect features, describe them, match them, or reject outliers, then plug it back into the usual pipeline. Such networks can often beat their hand-designed counterparts. p. 366
  2. Predict 3D properties and add them as factors. A network estimates depth from one image, or relative pose from two, and the prediction enters the factor graph as an extra term. p. 366
  3. Train through the optimizer. The weakness of the modular approach is that errors made by one component feed the next and compound. The alternative is to make more of the pipeline one trainable module, with bundle adjustment as a layer of the network. This is the differentiable optimization of Week 7 · Day 1, put to work. p. 366
  4. Replace the stack. DUSt3R predicts a pointmap, one 3D point for every pixel, directly from uncalibrated images. p. 366

The chapter's own summary is that these methods combine learning with geometry: some feed network predictions into an optimization-based pipeline, some join learned components to factor graphs, and some estimate motion and structure with a network alone. pp. 366–368

4. The network vocabulary you need this week

The chapter uses a handful of network terms without defining them. Here they are, at the depth this week needs.

Filling the gap: networks, losses, and training in five lines

A neural network is a function \(f_\theta\) built by composing simple differentiable steps called layers. The vector \(\theta\) holds all its adjustable numbers, the parameters or weights. A loss \(\mathcal{L}(\theta)\) measures how far the outputs are from what we want on a set of training examples. Training lowers the loss by gradient descent:

\[ \theta \leftarrow \theta - \eta\, \nabla_\theta \mathcal{L}(\theta), \]

with a small step size \(\eta\). This is the steepest descent of Week 2 · Day 4, applied to the weights instead of the robot's state. Example with one parameter: \(\mathcal{L}(\theta) = (\theta - 3)^2\), start at \(\theta = 0\), \(\eta = 0.25\). The gradient is \(2(\theta - 3) = -6\), so \(\theta\) becomes \(0 - 0.25 \cdot (-6) = 1.5\). The next gradient is \(-3\), giving \(\theta = 2.25\). Each step halves the distance to the minimum at 3.

The gradient is computed by reverse-mode automatic differentiation (Week 7 · Day 1), which is why every layer must be differentiable. If the labels come from a sensor or a simulator (for example, true depth), the training is supervised. If the loss is built from the input data alone, it is self-supervised; you will meet one tomorrow.

Two kinds of layer appear all week.

A convolutional layer slides one small filter over the image and applies it at every position. With the 1-D filter \((-1, 0, 1)\) and the signal \((2, 2, 5, 9, 9)\), the three interior outputs are \(5 - 2 = 3\), \(9 - 2 = 7\), and \(9 - 5 = 4\): the filter responds where brightness changes. A convolutional neural network (CNN) stacks many such layers with learned filters, usually shrinking the image grid as it goes, so the output is a coarse grid of feature vectors. RAFT's encoders output features at 1/8 of the input resolution. §13.2.3 · p. 376

An attention layer lets every feature vector look at all the others, however far apart they are in the image. A transformer is a network made mostly of attention layers, and a vision transformer (ViT) is a transformer whose inputs are small image patches turned into vectors called tokens. Figure 13.6 draws attention as three boxes: MatMul, SoftMax, MatMul. Fig. 13.6 · p. 375

Filling the gap: what MatMul → SoftMax → MatMul computes

Take one query vector \(\mathbf{q}\), and a set of tokens that each offer a key \(\mathbf{k}_j\) and a value \(\mathbf{v}_j\).

\[ s_j = \mathbf{q}\T \mathbf{k}_j, \qquad a_j = \frac{e^{s_j}}{\sum_m e^{s_m}}, \qquad \text{output} = \sum_j a_j \mathbf{v}_j . \]

The first matrix product computes all scores \(s_j\) at once. The softmax turns scores into positive weights that sum to 1. The second matrix product averages the values with those weights. (Transformers also divide the scores by \(\sqrt{d}\), the square root of the vector length, and learn the linear maps that produce queries, keys, and values.)

Example: scores \((2, 1, 0)\) give \(e^2 = 7.39\), \(e^1 = 2.72\), \(e^0 = 1\), which sum to 11.11. The weights are \(0.665, 0.245, 0.090\). If the values are the numbers \(10, 20, 30\), the output is \(6.65 + 4.90 + 2.70 = 14.25\).

In self-attention the queries and the keys come from the same image. In cross-attention the queries come from one image and the keys and values from the other, which is how a network compares two views.

Try it: turn the query, then raise the sharpness β.

Notice that at the start the query points almost at key k2, which gets weight 0.73, and the output 2.15 is pulled toward the value 2. At β = 0 every key gets 1/6 and the output is the plain mean 3.5. At β = 20 the layer picks k2 alone. Attention is a soft, differentiable way of saying "find the best match".

Common mistakes

  • "Part III replaces Parts I and II." The systems in this chapter still solve least-squares problems on factor graphs. What changes is where the residuals and their weights come from.
  • "A big image-language model makes the map unnecessary." The Prelude says these models often struggle with spatial understanding and that many tasks need a persistent 3D representation. §III.2 · p. 362
  • "Learned components always help." Plugging separately trained modules together lets their errors compound. That observation is the reason for end-to-end training. p. 366

Check yourself

Q1. According to the Prelude, in which setting could SLAM be called solved?

Page 361 limits "solved" to small, static, indoor, feature-rich environments, and lists the others as the open cases.

Q2. A system trains a depth network separately and adds its output to the factor graph as an extra term. Which approach of section 3 is this?

The network predicts a 3D property (depth) and the prediction becomes a factor. The optimizer is not part of the training, so it is not end to end.

Q3. Attention scores for three keys are (1, 1, 0). What weight does the third key get? Use e = 2.72.

The exponentials are 2.72, 2.72, 1, which sum to 6.44. The third weight is 1/6.44 = 0.155, about 0.16. A softmax weight is never exactly zero.

Q4. With loss (θ − 3)², θ = 1, and step size η = 0.1, what is θ after one gradient-descent step?

The gradient is 2(1 − 3) = −4. The update is 1 − 0.1·(−4) = 1.4.

Recap

  1. SLAM is solved only for small, static, feature-rich indoor scenes. Part III is about the rest, under the name Spatial AI.
  2. Spatial AI adds learning for what is hard to model, and richer maps: renderable, semantic, and able to change.
  3. A network can replace a component, supply factors, be trained through the optimizer, or regress pointmaps directly.
  4. Training is gradient descent on a loss over the network's weights.
  5. Attention scores every key against a query, applies a softmax, and returns the weighted average of the values.

Sources

  1. SLAM Handbook, Prelude to Part III, §III.1–III.3, pp. 361–365.
  2. SLAM Handbook, Chapter 13 "Boosting SLAM with Deep Learning", introduction, pp. 366–368; Figure 13.6, p. 375.
  3. Goodfellow, Bengio, Courville, Deep Learning, 2016 (gradient descent, convolutional networks).
  4. Vaswani et al., Attention Is All You Need, 2017 (scaled dot-product attention).

Week 19 · Day 2

Learning depth and camera pose, with and without labels

After today you can explain how predicted depth and pose enter a SLAM system as factors, and write the view-synthesis loss that trains such networks without any 3D labels.

About 60 min · Read §13.1, pp. 368–373 (6 pages) · Needs Week 11 Day 3 and Week 12 Day 2

Read first: §13.1, pp. 368–373

While you read, look for:

  • The three things predicted depth does for a monocular SLAM system (p. 369).
  • The two reasons why simply stacking up per-frame depth maps gives a poor dense map, and what MonoRec adds for each (pp. 369–370).
  • Equations (13.2) and (13.3) and the word "differentiable" just after them (pp. 371–372).
  • How DVSO and D3VO connect the network to the factor graph (pp. 372–373).

Today's big idea

A network can be trained to output depth from one image or relative pose from two. Used alone, such predictions are less accurate than geometry. Used as extra factors in a factor graph, they fix what a single camera cannot: scale, robustness, and density. And the network does not need 3D labels: if depth and pose are right, one image can be re-drawn from the other, and the mismatch is a loss you can differentiate.

1. Depth from one image, and what SLAM gains from it

Give a network many pairs of an image and its depth map, from depth sensors, LiDARs, or rendering engines, and it learns to predict depth from a single image. The book describes the current recipe as a pre-trained vision transformer followed by a convolutional decoder that brings the coarse features back to image resolution, trained on a mix of more than 20 real and synthetic datasets so that it generalizes. §13.1.1 · p. 369

A monocular SLAM system gains three things from such a network. §13.1.1 · p. 369

  • Scale. One moving camera recovers the scene only up to a scale factor, and that factor drifts over time (scale drift). Depth predicted in meters pins it down.
  • Robustness. Predicted depth helps in cases that break monocular geometry: pure rotation, changing camera parameters, moving objects.
  • Density. Feature-based SLAM tracks a sparse set of points, and textureless areas barely appear in the map. A depth map has a value at every pixel.

Filling the gap: why one camera cannot see scale

A pinhole camera with focal length \(f\) and principal point \((c_x, c_y)\) projects a point \((X, Y, Z)\) in its own frame to the pixel

\[ \pi_c(X, Y, Z) = \left( f\,\frac{X}{Z} + c_x,\; f\,\frac{Y}{Z} + c_y \right). \]

Multiply the whole world by \(s\): every point and every camera translation. A point's coordinates in any camera frame become \((sX, sY, sZ)\), and the ratios \(sX/sZ = X/Z\) do not change. Every image is identical, so no amount of image data can tell \(s\). A network that has seen many scenes with metric depth knows roughly how large cars and doorways are, and that is information the geometry does not contain. (Camera model: Week 11 · Day 3.)

From depth maps to a dense map. Lifting every pixel into 3D with its predicted depth and the SLAM pose, and accumulating the points, gives a dense reconstruction. The book names two problems with doing only that, and two systems that go further. §13.1.1 · pp. 369–370

ProblemSystemWhat it does
Depth maps of neighbouring frames disagree with each otherMonoRecFeeds the depth network a cost volume: for each pixel and each of a set of candidate depths, how well the brightness agrees with the neighbouring frames
Moving objects leave trails in a static mapMonoRecA second network predicts a moving-object mask from the cost volume, and masked pixels are not lifted into 3D
Depth maps contain only visible surfacesBehind the Scenes (BTS)Predicts a volumetric density field \(\phi(\mathbf{x}): \R^3 \to \R^+\) for the whole camera frustum, including occluded regions, which can be rendered from new viewpoints (next week's topic)

MonoRec is trained with the sparse 3D points of the SLAM system as targets. Its depth and mask modules help each other, so they are trained jointly. p. 370

2. Pose from two images, and why it is not enough

The same idea works for motion. A network \(f_\theta\) takes images \(I_1\) and \(I_2\) and outputs the relative pose \(\mathbf{T}^2_1 \in \SE(3)\). With ground-truth pose \(\mathbf{T}^{2*}_1\), the book's training loss is §13.1.2 · eq. (13.1) · p. 371

\[ \mathcal{L}_{pose} = \left\| \left(\mathbf{T}^2_1\right)^{-1} \cdot \mathbf{T}^{2*}_1 \right\|, \qquad \mathbf{T}^2_1 = f_\theta(I_1, I_2). \tag{13.1} \]

Filling the gap: reading equation (13.1)

If the prediction is exact, \((\mathbf{T}^2_1)^{-1}\mathbf{T}^{2*}_1\) is the identity. Otherwise it is the leftover transformation between prediction and truth. The book does not say which norm measures its size. A standard choice, in the language of Week 4 · Day 2, is the length of its tangent vector, \(\norm{\Log\!\big((\mathbf{T}^2_1)^{-1}\mathbf{T}^{2*}_1\big)}\), which is zero exactly at the identity.

Example: the network predicts a rotation of 10° about the vertical axis, the truth is 12° about the same axis, and the translations agree. The leftover is a rotation of 2°, and its tangent vector has length \(2 \cdot \pi / 180 = 0.035\) rad. The book mentions alternatives: penalize the rotation angle, or the distance between quaternions.

Early networks stacked the two frames and regressed axis-angle or Euler-angle parameters. Chaining relative poses gives a trajectory, and chained errors compound, as with any odometry (Week 1 · Day 1). DeepVO addressed this with a recurrent network (an LSTM) that reads a sequence of feature maps and outputs a sequence of poses. TartanVO improved generalization by giving the network predicted optical flow and the camera intrinsics as inputs. §13.1.2 · p. 371

The book's verdict is plain: predicting pose directly is often less accurate than classical SfM or SLAM, where the geometry is built into the system, and these networks tend to overfit to their training data. p. 371 That is the motivation for the rest of the chapter.

3. Training without 3D labels: view synthesis

Ground-truth depth and pose are expensive. View synthesis supplies a training signal from images alone. If you know the depth of every pixel of \(I_1\) and the relative pose, you know where each pixel of \(I_1\) appears in \(I_2\), so you can rebuild \(I_1\) out of colours taken from \(I_2\). If depth and pose are right, the rebuilt image matches \(I_1\). §13.1.3 · p. 371

Let \(\pi_c^{-1}(\mathbf{x}, d)\) be the inverse projection, which returns the 3D point at depth \(d\) along the ray of pixel \(\mathbf{x}\). A pixel \(\mathbf{x}^1\) with depth \(d^1\) in \(I_1\) lands in \(I_2\) at

\[ \mathbf{x}^2 = \pi_c\!\left( \mathbf{T}^2_1\, \pi_c^{-1}(\mathbf{x}^1, d^1) \right) = \omega_{1\to2}(\mathbf{x}^1, d^1), \tag{13.2} \]

ignoring occlusions. eq. (13.2) · p. 371 The synthesized image samples \(I_2\) at those locations:

\[ \tilde{I}_2(\mathbf{x}) = I_2\big(\omega_{1\to2}(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{d}(\mathbf{x}))\big). \tag{13.3} \]

(As printed on p. 372, the right-hand side of (13.3) reads \(I_1(\cdot)\). The sentences around it describe warping \(I_2\) into the viewpoint of \(I_1\), using pixels sampled from \(I_2\), which is what is written here.) The loss compares \(\tilde{I}_2\) with \(I_1\) pixel by pixel. This is the photometric error of direct methods from Week 12 · Day 2, now used to train a network instead of to estimate a pose.

Filling the gap: (13.2) with numbers, and why interpolation makes it differentiable

Take \(f = 500\) px, \(c_x = 320\), and a pixel at \(x^1 = 420\) on the middle row with depth \(d^1 = 4\) m. Back-project: \(X = d\,(x^1 - c_x)/f = 4 \cdot 100/500 = 0.8\) m, so the point is \((0.8, 0, 4)\). Camera 2 sits \(b = 0.2\) m to the right with the same orientation, so in its frame the point is \((0.6, 0, 4)\). Project: \(x^2 = 500 \cdot 0.6/4 + 320 = 395\). The pixel moved by \(-25\) px. For this sideways motion the general rule is

\[ x^2 = x^1 - \frac{f\,b}{d}, \]

and \(500 \cdot 0.2 / 4 = 25\) checks. Had the network said \(d = 5\) m, the point would be \((1.0, 0, 5)\), then \((0.8, 0, 5)\), and \(x^2 = 400\): five pixels off.

The location \(x^2\) is rarely a whole number, so \(I_2\) is read by bilinear interpolation. In one dimension, at position \(p = a + t\) with integer \(a\) and \(0 \le t \lt 1\),

\[ I_2(p) = (1 - t)\, I_2[a] + t\, I_2[a+1], \qquad \frac{\partial I_2(p)}{\partial p} = I_2[a+1] - I_2[a]. \]

With \(I_2[395] = 0.40\), \(I_2[396] = 0.60\), and \(p = 395.25\), the value is \(0.45\) and the slope is \(0.20\) per pixel. The chain rule then reaches the depth: \(\partial x^2/\partial d = f b/d^2 = 100/16 = 6.25\) px per meter, so \(\partial \tilde{I}_2/\partial d = 0.20 \cdot 6.25 = 1.25\) per meter. Because that derivative exists, the gradient of the loss flows back into whatever produced \(d\), here a depth network, and likewise into a pose network. p. 372

Try it: move the guessed depth and watch the difference row, then press "Step downhill".

Notice that the loss has its minimum, zero, exactly at the true depth of 4 m, where the shift used for the warp equals the true shift of 6 px. From the starting guess of 2.5 m, two presses of "Step downhill" reach 4.00 m. Each press is one Gauss-Newton step on 1/d that uses the interpolation slope from the note above. The curve over candidate depths is also what one slice of a MonoRec-style cost volume holds.

The book credits Godard et al. with showing that this loss can train a depth network from stereo pairs, and later work with training a depth network and a pose network together from video. p. 372

4. DVSO and D3VO: predictions as factors

DVSO (Deep Virtual Stereo Odometry) takes a classical direct system, DSO, and adds a factor to it: a term that pulls the depth computed by DSO toward the depth map predicted by a network. That network was trained with the view-synthesis loss on stereo pairs, where the distance between the two cameras is known in meters, so its depths are metric. The result behaves as if a second camera were present, hence "virtual stereo": better reconstruction, more accurate and robust poses, and correct scale from one camera. §13.1.3 · p. 372

D3VO adds two more predictions. A pose network supplies relative motion between consecutive frames. And a network predicts uncertainty: where brightness is likely to stay constant between frames and where it is not. Direct methods assume a surface point keeps its brightness, which fails on shiny, metallic, or glass surfaces. D3VO down-weights the photometric residuals at those pixels. Depth and pose networks are trained self-supervised with view-synthesis losses, and their outputs enter the factor graph as additional terms. §13.1.3 · pp. 372–373 · Fig. 13.5

Intuition

A prediction used as a factor is advice, and a prediction used as the answer is an order. The factor graph can overrule advice when the images disagree with it. That is why "network plus factor graph" ends up more accurate than the network alone and more robust than the geometry alone.

Common mistakes

  • "Self-supervised means no geometry is used." The view-synthesis loss is built from projection, the relative pose, and depth. The geometry is in the loss, not in the labels.
  • "View synthesis from monocular video gives metric depth." The loss is unchanged if all depths and translations are scaled together. DVSO's network is metric because its training pairs came from a stereo rig with a known baseline. p. 372
  • "A pose network replaces the back-end." The book reports that direct pose prediction is often less accurate than classical methods and overfits. p. 371

Check yourself

Q1. A camera has f = 600 px. Camera 2 is 0.5 m to the right of camera 1 with the same orientation. A pixel has depth 10 m. By how many pixels does it shift between the images?

The shift is f·b/d = 600 · 0.5 / 10 = 30 px.

Q2. Image samples are I[7] = 0.2 and I[8] = 0.6. What does linear interpolation give at p = 7.75, and what is the derivative with respect to p?

0.25 · 0.2 + 0.75 · 0.6 = 0.05 + 0.45 = 0.5. The slope is I[8] − I[7] = 0.4 per pixel.

Q3. Why does MonoRec need a moving-object mask in addition to its cost volume?

Photometric consistency across frames only indicates depth if the point did not move. The mask removes moving points before they are lifted into the map (p. 370).

Q4. In D3VO, what is the predicted uncertainty used for?

The network predicts where colour is likely preserved across frames, and residuals elsewhere count less (p. 373). Scale comes from the depth predictions.

Recap

  1. Depth networks give monocular SLAM metric scale, robustness in degenerate cases, and dense maps.
  2. MonoRec adds a cost volume for consistency and a mask for moving objects. BTS predicts a density field that includes occluded space.
  3. Pose networks trained with (13.1) work, but are less accurate than geometry and overfit.
  4. View synthesis, (13.2) and (13.3), turns "depth and pose are right" into "the warped image matches", a loss that needs no 3D labels and is differentiable through bilinear interpolation.
  5. DVSO and D3VO add network predictions of depth, pose, and uncertainty to a direct SLAM system as factors and weights.

Sources

  1. SLAM Handbook, §13.1 "Deep Learning for Depth and Camera Pose", pp. 368–373, equations (13.1)–(13.3), Figures 13.3–13.5.
  2. Hartley and Zisserman, Multiple View Geometry in Computer Vision, 2004 (pinhole projection, scale ambiguity, disparity of a rectified pair).
  3. Solà, Deray, Atchuthan, A micro Lie theory for state estimation in robotics, 2018 (the Log map used to read (13.1)).

Week 19 · Day 3

Learned matching, and RAFT optical flow

After today you can describe how learned detectors and attention-based matchers produce correspondences, and trace one RAFT iteration: correlation volume, lookup, update.

About 60 min · Read §13.2.1–13.2.3, pp. 374–378 (5 pages) · Needs Week 19 Day 1 and Week 11 Day 3

Read first: §13.2 up to the end of §13.2.3, pp. 374–378

Stop at the heading "13.2.4 Optical Flow as Visual Measurements" on p. 378; that is tomorrow. While you read, look for:

  • The argument on p. 374 for predicting measurements instead of states.
  • What SuperGlue outputs, and what the extra column is for (p. 374).
  • Equation (13.4) and the shape of the correlation volume (p. 377).
  • The four inputs of RAFT's update operator (p. 378).

Today's big idea

Asking a network for the pose makes it relearn geometry. Asking it for matches lets it do what networks are good at, recognizing that two image patches show the same thing, and leaves the geometry to the factor graph. RAFT is the cleanest example: it compares every pixel of one image with every pixel of the other once, stores the result, and then refines its flow estimate by looking up that table again and again.

1. Predict the measurements, not the state

In the notation of Part I, SLAM estimates the state \(\mathbf{x}\) (poses, depths) from measurements \(\mathbf{z}\) (for example feature matches) by solving for \(\mathbf{x}^{\text{MAP}}\). Yesterday's networks went from images straight to \(\mathbf{x}\) in one forward pass. To do that well, a network has to learn multi-view geometry from scratch: how depth, pose, and intrinsics relate. The alternative is to let the network predict \(\mathbf{z}\) and keep the optimization. §13.2 · p. 374

In plain words

Finding the same corner in two photos is a recognition problem. Working out how the camera moved from a set of matched corners is a geometry problem with a known solution. Give each job to whoever is good at it.

2. Learned keypoints, descriptors, and matchers

Indirect SLAM (Week 11 · Day 3) first finds keypoints, salient image locations, then computes a descriptor vector from the neighbourhood of each, and matches keypoints by comparing descriptors. Each step can be learned. §13.2.1–13.2.2 · pp. 374–375

SystemWhat is learnedHow it works, per the book
SuperPointDetector and descriptorOne convolutional network both finds salient regions and assigns descriptors to them
Universal Correspondence NetworkDescriptorLearned descriptors improve matching accuracy downstream
SuperGlueMatcher on keypointsRepeatedly updates each keypoint's feature vector with self- and cross-attention; outputs an assignment matrix
LightGlueMatcher on keypointsArchitecture and training changes that make SuperGlue faster and more accurate
LoFTRDense matcher, no keypointsSelf- and cross-attention over a coarse feature grid, then refinement at higher resolution

Descriptor networks are typically trained with a contrastive loss: descriptors of matching points should be similar, and descriptors of non-matching points far apart. §13.2.1 · p. 374

Filling the gap: a contrastive loss you can compute

The book describes the loss in words. One standard form, for a pair of descriptors at distance \(D\), with a margin \(m \gt 0\):

\[ \ell = \begin{cases} D^2 & \text{if the pair is a true match,} \\ \max(0,\, m - D)^2 & \text{if it is not.} \end{cases} \]

Matching pairs are pulled together. Non-matching pairs are pushed apart, but only until they are \(m\) apart; after that they cost nothing. With \(m = 1\): a true match at \(D = 0.3\) costs \(0.09\); a non-match at \(D = 0.4\) costs \((1 - 0.4)^2 = 0.36\); a non-match at \(D = 1.2\) costs 0.

SuperGlue's output. For \(N\) keypoints in image 1 and \(M\) in image 2, the network outputs an assignment matrix: for each keypoint of image 1, a likelihood for each keypoint of image 2, plus one extra column meaning "no match". §13.2.2 · p. 374 A small made-up example with three keypoints on each side:

Image 1 keypoint→ B1→ B2→ B3→ unmatched
A10.020.930.010.04
A20.900.030.020.05
A30.050.020.080.85

A1 matches B2, A2 matches B1, and A3 is most likely occluded or out of view in image 2. The extra column is what lets the network decline to match, which is the outlier rejection of Week 6 · Day 1 done inside the matcher. The attention layers are the ones from Day 1: self-attention lets a keypoint consult the other keypoints of its own image, and cross-attention lets it consult the candidates in the other image.

SuperGlue and LightGlue work on a sparse set of keypoints, which is cheap but ignores most of the image and yields few good matches where texture is poor. LoFTR matches densely to avoid this. All of them plug into an indirect SLAM system as ordinary visual measurements with their factors. p. 375

3. Optical flow, and RAFT's correlation volume

Optical flow is the per-pixel motion between two frames: a vector \(\mathbf{f}(u, v)\) for every pixel, saying where that pixel went. It is dense matching, and the flow field can serve as measurements in a factor graph. Classical methods computed it by minimizing a data term (matched regions should look alike) plus a regularization term (the motion field should be plausible). §13.2.3 · pp. 375–376

RAFT (Recurrent All-Pairs Field Transforms) is the learned method the book describes, because DROID-SLAM is built on it. It has three parts. §13.2.3 · pp. 376–378 · Fig. 13.7

Feature extraction. Two encoders map an image of size \((h_{in}, w_{in}, 3)\) to a feature map of size \((h, w, c)\): an appearance encoder \(g_\theta\) applied to both images, and a context encoder \(c_\theta\). By default \(h = h_{in}/8\) and \(w = w_{in}/8\). p. 376

Correlation volume. Take the inner product of every feature vector of image 1 with every feature vector of image 2: eq. (13.4) · p. 377

\[ \mathbf{C}_{ijkl}(I_1, I_2) = \langle g_\theta(I_1)_{ij},\, g_\theta(I_2)_{kl} \rangle = \sum_m g_\theta(I_1)_{ijm} \cdot g_\theta(I_2)_{klm}. \tag{13.4} \]

\(\mathbf{C}\) has four indices and shape \(h \times w \times h \times w\). Fix a pixel \((i, j)\) of image 1, and \(\mathbf{C}_{ij\cdot\cdot}\) is a whole image: a map of how well each pixel of image 2 resembles it.

Filling the gap: (13.4) as one matrix product, and how big it is

Number the \(hw\) pixels of each feature map \(1, \dots, hw\) and stack the feature vectors as rows of two matrices \(\mathbf{F}_1, \mathbf{F}_2 \in \R^{hw \times c}\). Then

\[ \mathbf{C} = \mathbf{F}_1 \mathbf{F}_2\T \in \R^{hw \times hw}, \qquad \mathbf{C}_{pq} = \sum_m (\mathbf{F}_1)_{pm} (\mathbf{F}_2)_{qm}, \]

which is (13.4) with \(p\) standing for \((i, j)\) and \(q\) for \((k, l)\). (Which factor carries the transpose depends on whether you stack features as rows or as columns.) A tiny case with two pixels and \(c = 2\): rows \((1, 0)\) and \((0.6, 0.8)\) in \(\mathbf{F}_1\), rows \((0.8, 0.6)\) and \((0, 1)\) in \(\mathbf{F}_2\) give

\[ \mathbf{C} = \begin{bmatrix} 0.8 & 0 \\ 0.96 & 0.8 \end{bmatrix}. \]

Pixel 2 of image 1 resembles pixel 1 of image 2 most (0.96).

Size: a \(384 \times 512\) image gives a \(48 \times 64\) feature map, which is 3072 pixels. The volume has \(3072^2 \approx 9.4\) million entries. The correlation pyramid adds three coarser copies \(\mathbf{C}^1, \mathbf{C}^2, \mathbf{C}^3\), made by average-pooling the last two dimensions, so \(\mathbf{C}^l\) has shape \(h \times w \times h/2^l \times w/2^l\). Here that is \(3072 \times (3072 + 768 + 192 + 48) \approx 12.5\) million numbers in total. Only image 2's axes shrink: every pixel of image 1 keeps its own row at full resolution. p. 377

4. Lookup and update: the iteration

RAFT keeps a flow estimate \(\mathbf{f}\), starting from zero. One iteration does two things. §13.2.3 · pp. 377–378 · Fig. 13.8

Lookup. For pixel \((u, v)\) of image 1, the current guess of its match in image 2 is \((u', v') = \mathbf{f}(u, v) + (u, v)\). RAFT reads the correlation volume on a small grid around that guess,

\[ N(u', v') = \{ (u' + \Delta u,\, v' + \Delta v) \mid \Delta u, \Delta v \in \{-r, \dots, r\} \}, \tag{13.5} \]

with bilinear interpolation, since \((u', v')\) is not a whole pixel. It does the same at each coarser level around the rescaled position \((u'/2^l, v'/2^l)\), and concatenates everything into one feature vector. The fine level tells it about small displacements, and the coarse levels about large ones.

In one dimension: pixel \(u = 10\) with current flow \(3.4\) has \(u' = 13.4\). With \(r = 2\) the lookup reads positions \(11.4, 12.4, 13.4, 14.4, 15.4\) of row 10 of \(\mathbf{C}^0\); for instance the middle one is \(0.6\,\mathbf{C}^0[10][13] + 0.4\,\mathbf{C}^0[10][14]\). At level 1 it reads five positions around \(13.4/2 = 6.7\), which together span about 10 pixels of the original row. With \(r = 3\) in two dimensions, a lookup reads \(7 \times 7 = 49\) values per level, 196 in total, out of the millions stored.

Update. A convolutional GRU (a gated recurrent unit whose linear layers are replaced by convolutions) takes four inputs, each a 2-D feature map: its hidden state from the previous iteration, the context features, the current flow, and the correlation features just looked up. It outputs a new hidden state and a flow update: p. 378

\[ \mathbf{f}^{k+1} = \boldsymbol{\delta}\mathbf{f}^k + \mathbf{f}^k . \]

The same weights are used in every iteration (weight tying). The book notes that tied weights and bounded activations encourage convergence to a fixed point, and that the convolutions pass information between neighbouring pixels. RAFT is trained on synthetic data with ground-truth flow and generalizes well to real images. pp. 376, 378

Try it: press Step a few times, or Play. Then set "Pyramid levels" to 1 and run again.

Notice that with the starting settings (true shift 5 px, radius 2, three levels) the mean flow error goes 5.00 → 0.89 → 0.10 px in two iterations and stays near 0.1. The finest window (pink) cannot reach a match 5 px away, but the coarse levels (amber) can, and they pull the estimate in until the fine level takes over. With one level, the error is still about 3 px after 12 iterations: most pixels never find their match. The update rule in this widget is a fixed formula (a soft-argmax of the values read, then smoothing over neighbouring pixels), where RAFT has a learned Conv-GRU. The correlation volume, pyramid, and lookup follow the equations above.

Intuition

RAFT behaves like an optimizer whose update rule was learned. Compare it with Gauss-Newton (Week 2 · Day 4): keep an estimate, look at the local evidence around it, compute a correction, repeat. The book puts it this way: RAFT combines deep learning with traditional first-order optimization. p. 376 That design is what allows DROID-SLAM, tomorrow, to put a real Gauss-Newton step inside the same loop.

Common mistakes

  • "The correlation volume is recomputed in each iteration." It is built once. Iterations only index into it, which is why a dozen of them are affordable.
  • "The pyramid shrinks both images." Only the last two dimensions, those of image 2, are pooled. Each pixel of image 1 keeps its own full-resolution entry.
  • "The lookup returns the best match." It returns raw correlation values around the current guess. Deciding which way to move is the update operator's job.
  • "Sparse matchers are obsolete." The book lists the trade: keypoints reduce computation; dense matching helps where texture is limited. p. 375

Check yourself

Q1. RAFT's feature maps are 40 × 50. How many entries does the level-0 correlation volume have?

There are 40 · 50 = 2000 pixels in each feature map, and the volume holds one number for every pair: 2000² = 4,000,000.

Q2. In a 1-D version, pixel u = 20 has current flow −2.5 and the lookup radius is r = 1. Which positions of image 2 are read at level 0?

The guess is u′ = 20 − 2.5 = 17.5, and the neighbourhood is u′ + Δu for Δu in {−1, 0, 1}. The values are read by interpolation.

Q3. What is the extra column in SuperGlue's assignment matrix for?

A keypoint may be occluded or outside the other image. The extra column gives that outcome its own likelihood (p. 374).

Q4. A true motion is 20 pixels at feature resolution and the lookup radius is 4. Why can RAFT still find it from a zero initial flow?

Level l is pooled by 2ˡ, so one cell at level 3 covers 8 pixels and a radius of 4 cells reaches 32 pixels. Coarse levels see large displacements, fine levels refine them.

Recap

  1. Predicting matches keeps the geometry in the factor graph and gives the network a recognition task.
  2. SuperPoint learns detection and description. SuperGlue and LightGlue match keypoints with attention and can answer "no match". LoFTR matches densely.
  3. RAFT builds the all-pairs correlation volume (13.4) once, as a matrix product of feature maps, and pools it into a four-level pyramid.
  4. Each iteration looks up a \((2r+1)^2\) neighbourhood (13.5) per level around the current match and lets a Conv-GRU output a flow update.
  5. Tied weights and repeated lookups make RAFT a learned iterative optimizer for flow.

Sources

  1. SLAM Handbook, §13.2.1–13.2.3, pp. 374–378, equations (13.4)–(13.5), Figures 13.6–13.8.
  2. Hadsell, Chopra, LeCun, Dimensionality Reduction by Learning an Invariant Mapping, 2006 (the margin form of the contrastive loss).
  3. Goodfellow, Bengio, Courville, Deep Learning, 2016 (recurrent networks and gated units).

Week 19 · Day 4

Flow as a measurement, differentiable bundle adjustment, DROID-SLAM and DPVO

After today you can write optical flow as a function of pose and depth, derive the confidence-weighted Gauss-Newton step inside DROID-SLAM, and say how DPVO differs.

About 60 min · Read §13.2.4–13.3, pp. 378–386 (9 pages) · Needs Week 19 Day 3, Week 2 Day 4, Week 7 Day 2

Read first: §13.2.4–13.2.5 and §13.3, pp. 378–386

Nine pages, three of them mostly figures. Stop at the heading "13.4 DuSt3R" on p. 386. While you read, look for:

  • Equation (13.7), and which three variables each factor of (13.8) touches (pp. 378–379).
  • The two reasons why "RAFT, then least squares" does not work well (pp. 379–380).
  • Equation (13.11) and the sentence that explains it in words (pp. 381–382).
  • What the back-end adds in Figure 13.11, and what DROID-SLAM cannot do (pp. 382–383).

Today's big idea

In a static scene, the flow of a pixel is fixed by its depth and the two camera poses. So flow is a measurement of pose and depth, and a factor graph can invert it. DROID-SLAM puts that inversion inside the network: a RAFT-style update operator proposes where each pixel should go and how much to trust it, and a few Gauss-Newton steps turn those proposals into pose and depth updates. Because Gauss-Newton is differentiable, the whole loop is trained on pose error.

1. Flow is a function of pose and depth

Let \(\mathbf{T}^w_i\) and \(\mathbf{T}^w_j\) be the camera-to-world poses of images \(I_i\) and \(I_j\). A pixel \((u, v)\) of image \(i\) with depth \(d\) is back-projected to 3D, moved into frame \(j\), and projected. The difference between where it lands and where it started is the induced flow: §13.2.4 · eq. (13.6) · p. 378

\[ \hat{\mathbf{f}}(u, v) = \boldsymbol{\pi}\!\left( \mathbf{T}^j_i \cdot \boldsymbol{\pi}^{-1}(u, v, d) \right) - (u, v), \qquad \mathbf{T}^j_i = (\mathbf{T}^w_j)^{-1} \cdot \mathbf{T}^w_i . \tag{13.6} \]

This is yesterday's warp (13.2) with the starting pixel subtracted. With the numbers from Day 2, \(f = 500\) px, a pixel 100 px right of the image centre, depth 4 m, and camera \(j\) placed 0.2 m to the right of camera \(i\): the point \((0.8, 0, 4)\) becomes \((0.6, 0, 4)\) in frame \(j\), lands 75 px right of centre, and the induced flow is \((-25, 0)\) px. Applied to the whole \(h \times w\) grid of pixels with a depth map \(\mathbf{d}_i\), the same formula is the measurement function eq. (13.7) · p. 378

\[ \mathbf{h}_{ij}(\mathbf{T}^w_i, \mathbf{T}^w_j, \mathbf{d}_i) = \boldsymbol{\pi}\!\left( \mathbf{T}^j_i \cdot \boldsymbol{\pi}^{-1}(\mathbf{u}, \mathbf{v}, \mathbf{d}_i) \right) - \begin{bmatrix} \mathbf{u} \\ \mathbf{v} \end{bmatrix}. \tag{13.7} \]

Now run it backwards. Suppose a network has measured the flow \(\mathbf{z}_{ij}\) for a set of image pairs, the edges of a frame graph \(\mathcal{G}\). The unknowns \(\mathbf{x}\) are all poses and all depth maps, and the cost is §13.2.5 · eq. (13.8) · p. 379

\[ J(\mathbf{x}) \triangleq \sum_{(i,j) \in \mathcal{G}} \left\| \mathbf{z}_{ij} - \mathbf{h}_{ij}(\mathbf{T}^w_i, \mathbf{T}^w_j, \mathbf{d}_i) \right\|^2_{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{ij}} . \tag{13.8} \]

This is the nonlinear least-squares form of Week 2 · Day 2. Each edge is one factor, and it touches three variables: the source pose, the destination pose, and the source depth map. With \(48 \times 64\) feature maps, one edge contributes \(2 \cdot 3072 = 6144\) scalar residuals, and each frame brings 6 pose unknowns and 3072 depths. The book adds two practical notes: use inverse depth, because it makes the cost better approximated locally, and update poses through the local parameterization \(\exp(\boldsymbol{\xi}_i^\wedge)\, \mathbf{T}^w_i\). p. 379

2. Why "RAFT, then bundle adjustment" is not enough

Computing flow with RAFT and then minimizing (13.8) does not work particularly well, for two reasons the book gives. §13.3 · pp. 379–380

  • The flow network was trained to get flow right, not pose. Its loss does not model what SLAM cares about.
  • The flow contains outliers, and (13.8) weights every pixel equally. You know from Week 6 · Day 1 what a few outliers do to least squares.

The fix is to make the optimization a layer of the network, a differentiable bundle adjustment (DBA) layer, so that the training loss is measured after the optimizer and its gradient reaches the network through it. And to let the network output, for every residual, a confidence weight. In the general factor-graph cost

\[ J(\mathbf{x}) \triangleq \sum_i \left\| \mathbf{e}_i(\mathbf{x}_i) \right\|^2_{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_i}, \qquad \mathbf{e}_i(\mathbf{x}) = \mathbf{z}_i - \mathbf{h}_i(\mathbf{x}_i), \tag{13.9} \]

both the error and its covariance are replaced by network outputs: eq. (13.9)–(13.10) · p. 380

\[ J(\mathbf{x}) \triangleq \left\| \mathbf{e}_\theta(\mathbf{z}, \mathbf{x}) \right\|^2_{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_\theta(\mathbf{z}, \mathbf{x})} . \tag{13.10} \]

The network now shapes the cost function that the solver minimizes. BANet was among the first to do this, with a photometric error on learned feature maps. DROID-SLAM and DPVO use optical flow as the intermediate quantity. p. 380

3. One DROID-SLAM iteration

DROID-SLAM takes images \(I_1, \dots, I_n\) and a frame graph with edges between co-visible pairs. It reuses RAFT's parts: the two encoders at 1/8 resolution, and one correlation pyramid \(\mathbf{C}_{ij}\) per edge, so \(E\) edges mean \(E\) pyramids. Each edge also has a hidden state \(\mathbf{q}_{ij}\), started from the context features of frame \(i\). §13.3.1 · pp. 380–381 · Fig. 13.10

In each iteration, the current poses and depths give the induced flow of every edge through (13.7). That flow says where to look up the correlation pyramid. The Conv-GRU, one copy per edge with shared weights, takes the hidden state, the correlation features, flow features, and the residual from the previous iteration, and outputs two maps per edge: a flow revision \(\boldsymbol{\delta}\mathbf{f}_{ij}\) (how the induced flow should change) and a confidence map \(\mathbf{w}_{ij}\). p. 381 These define the cost of the DBA layer:

\[ J(\mathbf{x}) \triangleq \sum_{(i,j) \in \mathcal{G}} \left\| \boldsymbol{\delta}\mathbf{f}_{ij} - \left[ \mathbf{h}_{ij}(\mathbf{x}_{ij}) - \mathbf{h}_{ij}(\mathbf{x}^0_{ij}) \right] \right\|^2_{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{ij}}, \tag{13.11} \]

where \(\mathbf{x}^0_{ij}\) are the poses and depths at the start of the iteration. eq. (13.11) · p. 381 In words: change the state so that the induced flow changes by what the network asked for, and care most about the pixels where the network is confident. Poses and depths are then updated by a couple of Gauss-Newton steps. pp. 381–382

Filling the gap: (13.11) is a weighted Gauss-Newton step

Write the new state as the old one plus a small update \(\boldsymbol{\Delta}\) (pose increments and depth increments), and linearize as in Week 2 · Day 4:

\[ \mathbf{h}_{ij}(\mathbf{x}_{ij}) - \mathbf{h}_{ij}(\mathbf{x}^0_{ij}) \approx \mathbf{J}_{ij}\, \boldsymbol{\Delta}, \qquad \mathbf{J}_{ij} = \left. \frac{\partial \mathbf{h}_{ij}}{\partial \mathbf{x}} \right|_{\mathbf{x}^0} . \]

The book builds \(\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{ij}\) from the confidences, \(\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{ij} = \operatorname{diag} \mathbf{w}_{ij}\), and says the weights let the network place more weight where it is confident. So read \(\mathbf{w}\) as per-residual weights: with \(\mathbf{W}_{ij} = \operatorname{diag}(\mathbf{w}_{ij})\) the cost is

\[ J(\boldsymbol{\Delta}) = \sum_{(i,j)} \left( \boldsymbol{\delta}\mathbf{f}_{ij} - \mathbf{J}_{ij} \boldsymbol{\Delta} \right)\T \mathbf{W}_{ij} \left( \boldsymbol{\delta}\mathbf{f}_{ij} - \mathbf{J}_{ij} \boldsymbol{\Delta} \right). \]

Set the gradient with respect to \(\boldsymbol{\Delta}\) to zero:

\[ \Big( \sum_{(i,j)} \mathbf{J}_{ij}\T \mathbf{W}_{ij} \mathbf{J}_{ij} \Big) \boldsymbol{\Delta} = \sum_{(i,j)} \mathbf{J}_{ij}\T \mathbf{W}_{ij}\, \boldsymbol{\delta}\mathbf{f}_{ij} . \]

These are the normal equations of weighted least squares from Week 1 · Day 4. The network supplies the right-hand side's residual \(\boldsymbol{\delta}\mathbf{f}\) and the weights; geometry supplies \(\mathbf{J}\).

A scalar example. One unknown \(\Delta\), three pixels with \(J_k = 1\), requested revisions \(\delta f = (2.0,\, 2.2,\, 8.0)\). The third pixel is on a passing car. Then \(\Delta = \sum_k w_k\, \delta f_k / \sum_k w_k\).

  • Equal weights \((1, 1, 1)\): \(\Delta = 12.2 / 3 = 4.07\). The outlier drags the answer.
  • Weights \((1, 1, 0.05)\): \(\Delta = (2.0 + 2.2 + 0.4)/2.05 = 2.24\).
  • Weights \((1, 1, 0)\): \(\Delta = 2.1\).

Why it can be trained. \(\Delta\) is a smooth function of the weights. Here \(\partial \Delta / \partial w_3 = (\delta f_3 - \Delta) / \sum_k w_k = (8 - 4.07)/3 = 1.31\) at equal weights. If the training loss says \(\Delta\) is too large, the gradient says "lower \(w_3\)". In the full system the same derivative is taken through each Gauss-Newton step by the unrolled differentiation of Week 7 · Day 2. p. 382

Try it: lower the weight on the three pink matches.

Notice that with all weights equal the estimate converges to θ = 16.73°, which is 4.73° off, and the translation is off by 0.233. With weight 0.05 on the moving-object matches it is 12.55° and 0.020 off, and with weight 0 it is 12.06° and 0.004. The slider "Gauss-Newton steps" shows the convergence: one step gets within a few degrees, and after six the estimate has settled. In Week 6 · Day 4 such weights came from the size of each residual (IRLS). Here a network would output them after looking at the images, before the solver runs.

Training. DROID-SLAM is trained on the synthetic TartanAir dataset, which has ground-truth depth and pose. The loss combines a pose loss (predicted versus true poses) with a flow loss (flow induced by the predicted pose and depth versus flow induced by the true ones, both through (13.6)). p. 382

4. Running it as a SLAM system

The network is trained on a fixed set of frames. Online use needs machinery around it. §13.3.2 · pp. 382–383

StageWhat it does
Motion filteringRuns the update operator on one edge from the last keyframe to the incoming frame. If the flow revision is below a threshold, the frame is dropped.
InitializationOnce enough frames are collected, connects each frame to its temporal neighbours and runs several iterations. It fails under pure rotation.
Front-endAdds edges for each new frame: to recent frames in both directions, and to keyframes that the induced flow shows to be highly co-visible.
Global optimizationA back-end over the full frame graph. Adds long-range edges where the induced flow between two frames is small, which closes mid-range loops.

The book's Figure 13.11 shows the effect of the back-end on one EuRoC sequence (V1_02_medium): the RMSE absolute trajectory error falls from 16.5 cm with the front-end only to 1.2 cm after global optimization. Fig. 13.11 · p. 383 There is no relocalization module, so a large loop with a lot of drift cannot be closed. p. 383

Because the system is a factor graph, new sensors are new factors, with no retraining. §13.3.3 · pp. 383–384

  • RGB-D: add a term that keeps each depth \(\mathbf{d}_i\) close to the sensor depth \(\bar{\mathbf{d}}_i\), with zero weight on pixels where the sensor gave no reading: \(J(\mathbf{x}) \triangleq \sum_{(i,j) \in \mathcal{G}} \| \mathbf{z}_{ij} - \mathbf{h}_{ij}(\mathbf{x}) \|^2 + \sum_i \| \bar{\mathbf{d}}_i - \mathbf{d}_i \|^2_{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_d}\), equation (13.12).
  • Stereo: put left and right frames in the graph, add an edge between each left frame and its right partner, and hold their known relative pose fixed. Figure 13.12 shows that stereo helps considerably, partly because it removes scale drift.

5. DPVO: the same idea on sparse patches

Deep Patch Visual Odometry keeps DROID-SLAM's structure but tracks a sparse set of small patches instead of every pixel. The book says this helps accuracy as well as cost. §13.3.4 · pp. 384–386

AspectDROID-SLAMDPVO
What is trackedEvery pixel of every frame, at 1/8 resolution3 × 3 patches around randomly sampled centres, on feature maps at 1/4 resolution
Depth unknownsA dense depth map per frameOne inverse depth per patch (the patch is a fronto-parallel plane)
GraphFrame graph: edges between framesPatch graph: a bipartite graph whose edges join a patch to each frame within r time steps
Update operatorConv-GRU per edgeRecurrent, weight-tied, with temporal convolutions along a patch's lifetime and pooling across frames and patches
OptimizationA couple of Gauss-Newton steps, plus a global back-endTwo Gauss-Newton steps over an optimization window of keyframes; odometry only

The measurement function only changes its indices. Patch \(i\) was extracted from frame \(s(i)\), its source frame, and has one depth \(d_i\): eq. (13.13) · p. 385

\[ \mathbf{h}_{ij}(\mathbf{T}^w_{s(i)}, \mathbf{T}^w_j, d_i) = \boldsymbol{\pi}\!\left( \mathbf{T}^j_{s(i)} \cdot \boldsymbol{\pi}^{-1}(\mathbf{u}, \mathbf{v}, d_i) \right) - \begin{bmatrix} \mathbf{u} \\ \mathbf{v} \end{bmatrix}. \tag{13.13} \]

DPVO has no loop closure beyond its window. Its successor, Deep Patch Visual SLAM (DPVS), adds global optimization, long-range loop closure through a relocalization module, and short-range loop closure by proximity. The book notes that, unlike DROID-SLAM, it keeps real-time performance on a single GPU. p. 386

Common mistakes

  • "DROID-SLAM predicts poses with a network." The network predicts flow revisions and confidences. Poses and depths come out of Gauss-Newton steps on (13.11).
  • "δf is the optical flow." It is a correction to the flow that the current state induces. When the state is right, the network should ask for no change.
  • "Confidence weights are a robust loss." A robust loss computes weights from residuals with a fixed formula. Here the weights are a learned function of the images and the current state, trained through the solver.
  • "Dense is always more accurate than sparse." The book reports that DPVO's sparse patches bring advantages in accuracy too. p. 384

Check yourself

Q1. A camera with f = 400 px moves 0.4 m to the right without rotating. What is the induced horizontal flow of a pixel whose depth is 8 m?

The point moves 0.4 m to the left in the new camera frame, so the pixel moves by −f·b/d = −400 · 0.4 / 8 = −20 px.

Q2. Which variables does one factor of the flow cost (13.8) for edge (i, j) connect?

The flow of pixels of image i depends on their depths and on both poses. The depth map of image j is not needed to predict it (p. 379).

Q3. One unknown Δ, three residuals with J = 1: δf = (1, 1, 5) with weights (1, 1, 0.5). What is the weighted Gauss-Newton update?

Δ = (1·1 + 1·1 + 0.5·5) / (1 + 1 + 0.5) = 4.5 / 2.5 = 1.8. With equal weights it would be 7/3 = 2.33.

Q4. Why can DROID-SLAM use stereo or RGB-D input without retraining?

Sensor depth becomes one more least-squares term (13.12), and a stereo pair becomes an edge with a fixed relative pose. The learned update operator is unchanged (pp. 383–384).

Q5. How many depth unknowns does one DPVO patch contribute?

Each patch is modelled as a fronto-parallel plane in its source image, so a single (inverse) depth describes it (pp. 384–385).

Recap

  1. Induced flow (13.6)–(13.7): back-project with depth, change frame, project, subtract the pixel. It makes flow a measurement of pose and depth, with cost (13.8).
  2. Off-the-shelf flow plus least squares is weak: the flow loss is not a pose loss, and all pixels count equally.
  3. DROID-SLAM's network outputs a flow revision and a confidence per pixel. A DBA layer solves the weighted normal equations of (13.11) for pose and depth updates, and training differentiates through it.
  4. Around the network sit a motion filter, an initializer, a front-end, and a global back-end. RGB-D and stereo are extra factors.
  5. DPVO replaces dense frames with sparse patches, one inverse depth each, in a patch graph. DPVS adds loop closure.

Sources

  1. SLAM Handbook, §13.2.4–13.2.5 and §13.3, pp. 378–386, equations (13.6)–(13.13), Figures 13.9–13.13.
  2. Nocedal and Wright, Numerical Optimization, 2006 (Gauss-Newton and weighted least-squares normal equations).
  3. Hartley and Zisserman, Multiple View Geometry in Computer Vision, 2004 (pinhole projection used in the worked flow example).

Week 19 · Day 5

Pointmaps: DUSt3R, MASt3R, and the systems built on them

After today you can define a pointmap, explain DUSt3R's scale-normalized and confidence-aware losses, and say how intrinsics, relative pose, and a global map are recovered from pairwise predictions.

About 60 min · Read §13.4–13.7, pp. 386–396 (11 pages) · Needs Week 19 Days 1 and 4

Read first: §13.4–13.7, pp. 386–396

This is the longest reading of the week. The math is on pp. 387–392; pp. 393–396 are a survey and read quickly. Look for:

  • The definition of a pointmap and equation (13.14) (p. 387).
  • The coordinate frame in which the network outputs both pointmaps (p. 388).
  • Equations (13.15)–(13.17) and what the factor \(z\) is for (p. 389).
  • The constraint attached to the global alignment (13.18) (p. 391).

Today's big idea

DUSt3R drops the pipeline. One network looks at two images and outputs, for every pixel of both, a 3D point in the first camera's frame, plus a confidence. No calibration, no poses, no solver. Focal length, relative pose, depth, and matches can all be read off those points afterwards. The catch is that it handles two images at a time, so a scene with many images still needs an optimization that ties the pairs together, and that optimization looks like a factor graph again.

1. Pointmaps

The methods of Days 2 to 4 inserted networks into a pipeline that stayed hand-built: correspondences, then a factor graph, then a solver. DUSt3R asks one network to do all the steps at once, from images alone, including the intrinsics that SLAM normally assumes are given. Since it does not assume the images come in temporal order, it applies to structure from motion as well. The book is frank about the limit: reconstructing a large scene from thousands of frames in one pass is out of reach, so DUSt3R solves the problem for two images only. §13.4 · p. 386

Its output is a pointmap \(\mathbf{X} \in \R^{W \times H \times 3}\): a 3D point for every pixel of a \(W \times H\) image, under the assumption that each camera ray hits one surface point. With intrinsics \(\mathbf{K}\) and a depth map \(\mathbf{D}\), the pointmap in the camera's own frame is §13.4 · p. 387

\[ \mathbf{X}_{i,j} = \mathbf{K}^{-1} \mathbf{D}_{i,j}\, [i, j, 1]\T . \]

Example: focal length 500 px and principal point \((320, 240)\) give \(\mathbf{K}^{-1}[420, 240, 1]\T = (0.2, 0, 1)\). With depth 4 m, \(\mathbf{X}_{420,240} = (0.8, 0, 4)\). This is the back-projection \(\pi^{-1}\) of Days 2 and 4, done for all pixels. The pointmap of camera \(n\) expressed in the frame of camera \(m\) is written \(\mathbf{X}^{n,m}\): eq. (13.14) · p. 387

\[ \mathbf{X}^{n,m} = h^{-1}\!\left( \mathbf{P}_m \mathbf{P}_n^{-1}\, h(\mathbf{X}^n) \right), \tag{13.14} \]

with world-to-camera poses \(\mathbf{P}_m, \mathbf{P}_n \in \SE(3)\) and \(h\) the map to homogeneous coordinates, \((x, y, z) \to (x, y, z, 1)\).

A pointmap is more than a depth map. The book lists what it holds at once: the scene geometry, the relation between pixels and scene points, and, when two pointmaps share a frame, the relation between the two viewpoints. p. 387

2. The network

The network \(f\) takes two RGB images and returns two pointmaps \(\mathbf{X}^{1,1}, \mathbf{X}^{2,1}\) with confidence maps \(\mathbf{C}^{1,1}, \mathbf{C}^{2,1}\). §13.4.1 · p. 388 · Fig. 13.14 In the vocabulary of Day 1:

  • Encoder. One ViT encodes both images with the same weights (a Siamese arrangement), giving tokens \(F^1\) and \(F^2\).
  • Decoder. Two stacks of \(B\) transformer blocks, one per image. Each block does self-attention within its own view, cross-attention to the other view's tokens, then an MLP. The two stacks exchange information at every block, which the book calls crucial for outputting aligned pointmaps.
  • Heads. Each branch has a regression head that turns its tokens into a pointmap and a confidence map.

Nothing in this architecture enforces a camera model. The output need not correspond to any physically possible camera, although in practice it comes close. The geometry is learned from training data that contains only geometrically consistent pointmaps. The book presents the generic architecture as an advantage, because it can use strong pretraining. pp. 388–389

3. Two losses: scale-normalized regression, and confidence

Training compares predicted with ground-truth pointmaps \(\hat{\mathbf{X}}^{1,1}, \hat{\mathbf{X}}^{2,1}\) (obtained from (13.14)) on the valid pixels \(\mathcal{D}^1, \mathcal{D}^2\). For pixel \(i\) of view \(v\): §13.4.2 · eq. (13.15)–(13.16) · p. 389

\[ \ell_{\text{regr}}(v, i) = \left\| \frac{1}{z} \mathbf{X}^{v,1}_i - \frac{1}{\bar{z}} \hat{\mathbf{X}}^{v,1}_i \right\|, \qquad \operatorname{norm}(\mathbf{X}^1, \mathbf{X}^2) = \frac{1}{|\mathcal{D}^1| + |\mathcal{D}^2|} \sum_{v \in \{1,2\}} \sum_{i \in \mathcal{D}^v} \left\| \mathbf{X}^v_i \right\|, \]

with \(z = \operatorname{norm}(\mathbf{X}^{1,1}, \mathbf{X}^{2,1})\) and \(\bar{z} = \operatorname{norm}(\hat{\mathbf{X}}^{1,1}, \hat{\mathbf{X}}^{2,1})\): the mean distance of the points from the origin, for the prediction and for the truth.

Some pixels have no well-defined 3D point (sky, translucent objects) and some are simply harder. The network therefore also predicts a confidence \(\mathbf{C}^{v,1}_i\) per pixel, and the final objective is eq. (13.17) · p. 389

\[ \mathcal{L}_{\text{conf}} = \sum_{v \in \{1,2\}} \sum_{i \in \mathcal{D}^v} \mathbf{C}^{v,1}_i\, \ell_{\text{regr}}(v, i) - \alpha \log \mathbf{C}^{v,1}_i , \tag{13.17} \]

with a hyper-parameter \(\alpha\), and \(\mathbf{C}^{v,1}_i = 1 + \exp c^{v,1}_i\) so that confidence stays positive. No confidence labels are needed.

Filling the gap: what the two losses do

The division by \(z\) removes scale. Suppose the prediction is right up to a factor, \(\mathbf{X}_i = s\, \hat{\mathbf{X}}_i\). Every distance is multiplied by \(s\), so \(z = s \bar{z}\), and \(\mathbf{X}_i / z = \hat{\mathbf{X}}_i / \bar{z}\). The loss is zero for every \(s\). Two images from uncalibrated cameras cannot reveal the scene's size (Day 2), so the network is not punished for it.

The confidence term makes \(C\) track \(1/\text{error}\). For one pixel with error \(\ell\), the loss as a function of \(C\) is \(g(C) = C\ell - \alpha \log C\). Then \(g'(C) = \ell - \alpha / C = 0\) gives

\[ C^\star = \frac{\alpha}{\ell} \quad (\text{or } C \to 1 \text{ if } \alpha/\ell \le 1), \qquad g(C^\star) = \alpha \left( 1 + \log\frac{\ell}{\alpha} \right). \]

With \(\alpha = 0.2\): a pixel with \(\ell = 0.02\) wants \(C = 10\) and then costs \(0.2 - 0.2 \ln 10 = -0.26\). A pixel with \(\ell = 0.5\) wants the lowest confidence, \(C \to 1\), and costs \(0.5\). The first term alone would push every \(C\) to its minimum; the \(-\alpha \log C\) term rewards confidence, so the network is confident exactly where it expects to be accurate. As long as \(\alpha/\ell \gt 1\), the cost of a pixel at its best confidence grows like \(\log \ell\) instead of \(\ell\), so moderately hard pixels weigh less in training than their raw error would suggest.

Try it: move the scale slider, then the error on the hard points, then α.

Notice that changing the scale from × 0.5 to × 3 moves the raw error from 1.74 m to 7.57 m while the picture and the normalized mean error (0.056) do not change at all. With the starting settings, the loss prefers a confidence of about 6.5 on the seven easy points and 1.8 on the three hard ones, and the confidence-aware loss is −0.95 against 0.56 with all confidences at 1. Lower α to 0.02 and every confidence falls to its floor of 1.

4. Reading cameras and poses off the pointmaps

Everything a classical pipeline estimates can be recovered from the output. §13.4.3 · pp. 389–391

QuantityHow
Focal length of camera 1Assume a centred principal point and square pixels. Find the \(f_1\) for which \(f_1 \cdot (X, Y)/Z\) best matches the centred pixel coordinates \((i', j')\) over all pixels, weighted by confidence. A Weiszfeld-type iterative solver finds it in a few iterations.
Focal length of camera 2Run the network on the swapped pair \((I_2, I_1)\) and use \(\mathbf{X}^{2,2}\).
Relative poseEither match pixels in 2D, recover intrinsics, and go through the epipolar geometry; or align \(\mathbf{X}^{1,1}\) with \(\mathbf{X}^{1,2}\) by Procrustes alignment, a closed-form fit of scale, rotation, and translation; or, more robust to noise and outliers, RANSAC with PnP.
Depth mapsThe \(z\) coordinate of \(\mathbf{X}^{1,1}\) is the depth map of image 1.

Filling the gap: the focal length from one point

A centred pinhole camera maps \((X, Y, Z)\) to \(i' = f X / Z\). So each pixel of \(\mathbf{X}^{1,1}\) gives its own estimate \(f = i' Z / X\). The point \((0.8, 0, 4)\) at \(i' = 420 - 320 = 100\) gives \(f = 100 \cdot 4 / 0.8 = 500\) px. The book's formula fits one \(f_1\) to all pixels by minimizing a confidence-weighted sum of distances (not squared distances), which is less sensitive to bad pixels. Weiszfeld's algorithm minimizes such sums by iteratively re-weighted least squares, the idea of Week 6 · Day 4. Procrustes alignment is the closed-form rigid alignment by SVD of Week 13 · Day 2, with a scale factor added.

Global alignment. For \(N\) images, build a graph whose edges \(e = (n, m)\) are pairs that share content, found by image retrieval or by running the network on all pairs and keeping those with high average confidence.
