Run the network on each edge to get \(\mathbf{X}^{n,e}\) and \(\mathbf{X}^{m,e}\), both in the frame of that pair's first image. Then find world-frame pointmaps \(\boldsymbol{\chi}^n\), one per image, together with one rigid transform \(\mathbf{P}_e\) and one scale \(\sigma_e \gt 0\) per edge: §13.4.4 · eq. (13.18) · p. 391

\[ \boldsymbol{\chi}^* = \argmin_{\boldsymbol{\chi}, \mathbf{P}, \sigma} \sum_{e \in \mathcal{E}} \sum_{v \in e} \sum_{i=1}^{HW} \mathbf{C}^{v,e}_i \left\| \boldsymbol{\chi}^v_i - \sigma_e \mathbf{P}_e \mathbf{X}^{v,e}_i \right\| . \tag{13.18} \]

The same \(\mathbf{P}_e\) and \(\sigma_e\) must work for both pointmaps of a pair, because they share a frame. Without a further condition the minimizer is useless: set every \(\sigma_e = 0\) and every \(\boldsymbol{\chi} = \mathbf{0}\), and the cost is zero. The constraint \(\prod_e \sigma_e = 1\) rules that out. Replacing \(\boldsymbol{\chi}^n_{i,j}\) by \(\mathbf{P}_n^{-1} h(\mathbf{K}_n^{-1} \mathbf{D}^n_{i,j} [i, j, 1]\T)\) forces a pinhole model and makes the unknowns the poses, intrinsics, and depth maps of all cameras. pp. 391–392

Look at the shape of (13.18): a sum over the edges of a graph, each term tying a few unknowns together, weighted by confidence. It is a factor graph in everything but name, which is the point the book made on p. 386.

5. MASt3R: adding a matching head

DUSt3R can also give pixel correspondences, by looking for reciprocal matches between the two views. They hold up under extreme viewpoint change but are imprecise, since regression is noisy and the network was never trained to match. MASt3R adds a second head that outputs a \(d\)-dimensional descriptor for every pixel, \(\mathbf{D}^1, \mathbf{D}^2 \in \R^{H \times W \times d}\), each normalized to unit length (a two-layer MLP with a GELU activation; equations (13.19)–(13.20)). §13.5 · p. 392

It is trained with the InfoNCE loss over the ground-truth correspondences \(\hat{\mathcal{M}} = \{(i, j) \mid \hat{\mathbf{X}}^{1,1}_i = \hat{\mathbf{X}}^{2,1}_j\}\): eq. (13.21)–(13.22) · p. 392

\[ \mathcal{L}_{\text{match}} = - \sum_{(i,j) \in \hat{\mathcal{M}}} \log \frac{s_\tau(i, j)}{\sum_{k \in \mathcal{P}^1} s_\tau(k, j)} + \log \frac{s_\tau(i, j)}{\sum_{k \in \mathcal{P}^2} s_\tau(i, k)}, \qquad s_\tau(i, j) = \exp\!\left[ -\tau\, \mathbf{D}^{1\top}_i \mathbf{D}^2_j \right], \]

where \(\mathcal{P}^1, \mathcal{P}^2\) are the pixels of each image that take part in \(\hat{\mathcal{M}}\) and \(\tau\) is a temperature. The total loss is \(\mathcal{L}_{\text{total}} = \mathcal{L}_{\text{conf}} + \beta \mathcal{L}_{\text{match}}\), equation (13.23). p. 393

Filling the gap: InfoNCE is the softmax of Day 1 used as a classifier

Each fraction is a softmax over candidates: the first asks "of all pixels \(k\) in image 1, how much of the score for pixel \(j\) goes to the true partner \(i\)?", the second asks the same in the other direction. The loss is minus the log of that share. For the loss to fall as true partners become more similar, \(s_\tau\) has to grow with the similarity \(\mathbf{D}^{1\top}_i \mathbf{D}^2_j\); read the sign in the exponent of (13.22) together with the sign of \(\tau\) accordingly.

Example with three candidates. If the scores are \(s = (8, 1, 1)\) with the true partner first, its share is \(0.8\) and the term is \(-\ln 0.8 = 0.22\). If they are \((2, 1, 1)\), the share is \(0.5\) and the term is \(0.69\). There is no partial credit for landing one pixel away: the neighbour is just another wrong class. That is the contrast with regression that the book draws, and why it yields precise matches. pp. 392–393

6. From pairs to full systems, and where the field is going

SystemWhat the book says it adds
MASt3R-SfMA full SfM pipeline for unconstrained image collections. Reuses the frozen encoder for fast image retrieval, giving quasi-linear complexity in the number of images. Needs no RANSAC. Optimizes by two gradient descents on frozen pairwise outputs: a 3D matching loss, then a 2D reprojection loss.
MUSt3RA changed architecture, symmetric and with a working memory, that predicts all pointmaps in one coordinate frame at high frame rates. It is aimed at the quadratic number of pairs and the costly global alignment of the pairwise design, and serves offline SfM and online visual odometry or SLAM with the same network.
MASt3R-SLAMA real-time dense monocular SLAM system that uses MASt3R's two-view predictions for tracking, mapping, and relocalization. It filters pointmaps locally in the front-end and runs large-scale global optimization in the back-end. It assumes only that all rays of an image pass through one camera centre, so it handles generic, time-varying camera models.

§13.6 · pp. 393–394 The closing section names three trends. §13.7 · pp. 395–396

  • Bigger feed-forward networks. VGGT reconstructs hundreds of images in seconds and predicts poses, intrinsics, depths, pointmaps, and feature tracks without 3D optimization. It still gains from bundle adjustment on its tracks when high accuracy is needed, and VGGT-SLAM aligns VGGT submaps with a factor graph for long sequences.
  • Better hybrids. DROID-SLAM needs known calibration and fails in moderately dynamic scenes. MegaSAM and ViPE handle highly dynamic scenes and optimize the calibration during inference, using depth and segmentation models fused by a factor graph.
  • Pretrained vision transformers. Models trained by self-supervision give 3D reconstruction networks an excellent starting point.

Common mistakes

  • "Both pointmaps are in their own camera's frame." \(\mathbf{X}^{2,1}\) is the content of image 2 expressed in camera 1's frame. That shared frame is what encodes the relative pose.
  • "DUSt3R makes optimization unnecessary." For two images, yes. For many, (13.18) or one of the systems of §13.6 is needed, and the book stresses that factor graphs remain essential when accuracy matters. pp. 386, 395
  • "High confidence means the pixel is weighted more, so the network will claim it everywhere." Confidence multiplies the error. Claiming it on a badly predicted pixel raises the loss.

Check yourself

Q1. A camera has focal length 400 px and principal point (200, 150). The pixel (300, 150) has depth 2 m. What is its pointmap entry in the camera frame?

K⁻¹[300, 150, 1]ᵀ = ((300 − 200)/400, 0, 1) = (0.25, 0, 1). Multiply by the depth 2 to get (0.5, 0, 2).

Q2. In the confidence-aware loss with α = 0.3, which confidence minimizes the loss of a pixel whose regression error is ℓ = 0.05?

Setting the derivative ℓ − α/C to zero gives C = α/ℓ = 0.3/0.05 = 6.

Q3. A predicted pointmap is exactly twice the ground truth everywhere. What is the regression loss (13.15)?

The normalizer z is also doubled, so the normalized prediction equals the normalized truth. The loss ignores global scale by construction.

Q4. Why does the global alignment (13.18) need the constraint that the product of all σₑ equals 1?

With all σₑ = 0 and all world points at the origin every term vanishes. Fixing the product of the scales excludes that trivial solution (p. 391).

Q5. In one InfoNCE term the true partner has score 6 and the two other candidates have score 2 each. What is the term's value?

The true partner's share is 6/(6 + 2 + 2) = 0.6, and −ln 0.6 = 0.51.

Recap

  1. A pointmap stores a 3D point per pixel. DUSt3R predicts two of them, both in camera 1's frame, from an uncalibrated, unposed image pair.
  2. The regression loss divides by the mean point distance, so global scale does not matter. The confidence-aware loss makes confidence track the inverse of the expected error.
  3. Focal length, relative pose, and depth are recovered from the pointmaps afterwards. Many images are fused by the confidence-weighted global alignment (13.18).
  4. MASt3R adds per-pixel descriptors trained with InfoNCE, a classification loss, for precise matching.
  5. MASt3R-SfM, MUSt3R, and MASt3R-SLAM scale the idea up. In the book's summary, factor graphs keep an essential role wherever high accuracy is needed.

Sources

  1. SLAM Handbook, §13.4 "DuSt3R", §13.5 "MASt3R", §13.6, §13.7, pp. 386–396, equations (13.14)–(13.23), Figures 13.14–13.17.
  2. Hartley and Zisserman, Multiple View Geometry in Computer Vision, 2004 (intrinsics matrix and back-projection).
  3. Goodfellow, Bengio, Courville, Deep Learning, 2016 (softmax and cross-entropy, used to read the InfoNCE loss).

Week 19 · Review

Week 19 review: where networks meet factor graphs

After today you can compute a warp, a correlation lookup, a confidence-weighted Gauss-Newton step, and a pointmap loss by hand, and place each system of Chapter 13 on the line from "learned component" to "learned pipeline".

About 60 min · No new pages

The week in one paragraph

Part III turns SLAM toward Spatial AI, and Chapter 13 shows the first step: putting learning into the pipeline without giving up geometry. A network can predict depth or pose, trained with 3D labels or with a view-synthesis loss, and those predictions become factors (DVSO, D3VO). A network can predict matches or optical flow; RAFT does it by building an all-pairs correlation volume once and refining a flow estimate with repeated lookups. DROID-SLAM closes the loop: its network outputs flow revisions and confidences, a differentiable bundle-adjustment layer converts them into pose and depth updates by weighted Gauss-Newton, and everything is trained on pose error. DPVO does the same on sparse patches. DUSt3R goes furthest and regresses a 3D point per pixel for an uncalibrated image pair; cameras and poses are read off afterwards, and many pairs are fused by a confidence-weighted alignment. In every case a least-squares problem on a graph is still there.

1. Formula sheet

What it isFormulaWhere
Attention for one query\(a_j = e^{s_j} / \sum_m e^{s_m}\) with \(s_j = \mathbf{q}\T\mathbf{k}_j\); output \(\sum_j a_j \mathbf{v}_j\)Fig. 13.6, p. 375 · Day 1
Pose regression loss\(\mathcal{L}_{pose} = \norm{(\mathbf{T}^2_1)^{-1} \cdot \mathbf{T}^{2*}_1}\)(13.1), p. 371 · Day 2
Warp of a pixel with depth\(\mathbf{x}^2 = \pi_c(\mathbf{T}^2_1\, \pi_c^{-1}(\mathbf{x}^1, d^1))\); for a sideways baseline \(b\): \(x^2 = x^1 - f b / d\)(13.2), p. 371 · Day 2
Synthesized view\(\tilde{I}_2(\mathbf{x}) = I_2(\omega_{1\to2}(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{d}(\mathbf{x})))\), read by bilinear interpolation(13.3), p. 372 · Day 2
Correlation volume\(\mathbf{C}_{ijkl} = \sum_m g_\theta(I_1)_{ijm}\, g_\theta(I_2)_{klm}\), or \(\mathbf{C} = \mathbf{F}_1\mathbf{F}_2\T\)(13.4), p. 377 · Day 3
Lookup and updateRead \(\mathbf{C}^l\) on \(\{-r, \dots, r\}^2\) around \((u', v')/2^l\) with \((u', v') = \mathbf{f}(u,v) + (u,v)\); then \(\mathbf{f}^{k+1} = \boldsymbol{\delta}\mathbf{f}^k + \mathbf{f}^k\)(13.5), pp. 377–378 · Day 3
Induced flow\(\mathbf{h}_{ij} = \boldsymbol{\pi}(\mathbf{T}^j_i \cdot \boldsymbol{\pi}^{-1}(\mathbf{u}, \mathbf{v}, \mathbf{d}_i)) - [\mathbf{u}; \mathbf{v}]\), \(\mathbf{T}^j_i = (\mathbf{T}^w_j)^{-1}\mathbf{T}^w_i\)(13.6)–(13.7), p. 378 · Day 4
DBA layer\(J = \sum_{(i,j)} \norm{\boldsymbol{\delta}\mathbf{f}_{ij} - [\mathbf{h}_{ij}(\mathbf{x}_{ij}) - \mathbf{h}_{ij}(\mathbf{x}^0_{ij})]}^2_{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{ij}}\); step: \((\sum \mathbf{J}\T\mathbf{W}\mathbf{J})\boldsymbol{\Delta} = \sum \mathbf{J}\T\mathbf{W}\boldsymbol{\delta}\mathbf{f}\)(13.11), p. 381 · Day 4
Pointmap\(\mathbf{X}_{i,j} = \mathbf{K}^{-1}\mathbf{D}_{i,j}[i, j, 1]\T\); \(\mathbf{X}^{n,m} = h^{-1}(\mathbf{P}_m\mathbf{P}_n^{-1} h(\mathbf{X}^n))\)(13.14), p. 387 · Day 5
DUSt3R losses\(\ell_{\text{regr}} = \norm{\mathbf{X}_i / z - \hat{\mathbf{X}}_i / \bar{z}}\); \(\mathcal{L}_{\text{conf}} = \sum C_i \ell_{\text{regr}} - \alpha \log C_i\); best \(C = \alpha/\ell\)(13.15)–(13.17), p. 389 · Day 5

2. Mixed quiz

Check yourself

Q1. A system's network outputs flow corrections and per-pixel confidences, a Gauss-Newton layer turns them into poses, and the training loss is on the poses. Which kind of method is it?

The loss is measured after the optimizer and its gradient passes back through it. This is DROID-SLAM's design (§13.3).

Q2. Attention scores for two keys are 3 and 1. What weight does the first key get? (e² = 7.39)

e³/(e³ + e¹) = e²/(e² + 1) = 7.39/8.39 = 0.88. Only the difference of the scores matters.

Q3. Two cameras with f = 700 px are 0.3 m apart sideways. A pixel shifts by 14 px between the images. How far away is the point?

shift = f·b/d, so d = f·b/shift = 700 · 0.3 / 14 = 15 m.

Q4. What does DVSO add to the classical direct system DSO?

The network's metric depth acts like a virtual second camera, entering as an extra factor (p. 372).

Q5. Feature maps are 32 × 40. How many entries does level 2 of the correlation pyramid have?

Level 2 has shape 32 × 40 × 8 × 10: the 1280 pixels of image 1 times 80 pooled cells of image 2, which is 102,400.

Q6. With lookup radius r = 4 and a four-level pyramid, how many correlation values does RAFT read for one pixel in one iteration?

Each level gives a (2·4 + 1) × (2·4 + 1) = 81 grid, and there are four levels: 324.

Q7. In the DBA cost (13.11), what is the role of the confidence map w?

The weights enter the normal equations as W. Pixels the network does not trust barely influence the pose and depth update.

Q8. DUSt3R outputs X(2,1) for the second image. In which coordinate frame are its points?

Both pointmaps of a pair are expressed in the frame of the first image, which is what makes the relative pose recoverable (p. 388).

3. Pen-and-paper problems

  1. Warp and induced flow. A camera has \(f = 600\) px and principal point \((320, 240)\). Pixel \((380, 240)\) of image 1 has depth 3 m. Camera 2 is 0.3 m to the right of camera 1 with the same orientation. (a) Where does the pixel land in image 2, and what is the induced flow? (b) Where would it land if the depth were wrongly taken as 6 m?

    Solution

    (a) Back-project: \(X = d\,(x - c_x)/f = 3 \cdot 60/600 = 0.3\) m, so the point is \((0.3, 0, 3)\) in frame 1. In frame 2 it is \((0.3 - 0.3, 0, 3) = (0, 0, 3)\). Project: \(x^2 = 600 \cdot 0/3 + 320 = 320\). The pixel lands at \((320, 240)\) and the induced flow is \((-60, 0)\) px. Check: \(f b / d = 600 \cdot 0.3 / 3 = 60\).

    (b) With \(d = 6\): \(X = 6 \cdot 60/600 = 0.6\), the point is \((0.6, 0, 6)\), in frame 2 \((0.3, 0, 6)\), and \(x^2 = 600 \cdot 0.3/6 + 320 = 350\). The flow would be \(-30\) px. The view-synthesis loss compares image 1 at 380 with image 2 at 350 instead of 320, and in general finds a different brightness.

  2. Correlation and lookup. Two 1-D images have three pixels each, with 2-channel features. Image 1: \((1, 0)\), \((0, 1)\), \((0.6, 0.8)\). Image 2: \((0, 1)\), \((0.8, 0.6)\), \((1, 0)\). (a) Compute the \(3 \times 3\) correlation volume. (b) Which pixel of image 2 does each pixel of image 1 match best, and what flow does that imply? (c) Pixel 3 of image 1 currently has flow \(-0.5\). What value does a lookup with \(r = 0\) return?

    Solution

    (a) Each entry is a dot product:

    \[ \mathbf{C} = \begin{bmatrix} 0 & 0.8 & 1 \\ 1 & 0.6 & 0 \\ 0.8 & 0.96 & 0.6 \end{bmatrix}. \]

    (b) Row maxima: pixel 1 → pixel 3 (1.0), flow \(+2\). Pixel 2 → pixel 1 (1.0), flow \(-1\). Pixel 3 → pixel 2 (0.96), flow \(-1\).

    (c) The current match is at \(3 - 0.5 = 2.5\). Linear interpolation between \(\mathbf{C}[3][2] = 0.96\) and \(\mathbf{C}[3][3] = 0.6\) gives \(0.5 \cdot 0.96 + 0.5 \cdot 0.6 = 0.78\). With a larger radius the lookup would also return the values at 1.5 and 3.5, and the update operator would see that the correlation rises toward smaller positions.

  3. Confidence-weighted Gauss-Newton. A camera with \(f = 500\) px translates sideways by an unknown \(\Delta\) (meters). A pixel at depth \(d_k\) then changes its flow by \(J_k \Delta\) with \(J_k = -f/d_k\). Three pixels have depths 2, 5, and 10 m, and the network requests flow changes \(\delta f = (-5.0, -2.1, -4.0)\) px. (a) Solve for \(\Delta\) with equal weights. (b) Solve again with weights \((1, 1, 0.1)\). (c) The true motion was 0.02 m. Which pixel was the outlier, and why did it do limited damage even in (a)?

    Solution

    The Jacobians are \(J = (-250, -100, -50)\) px/m. The weighted normal equation for one unknown is \(\Delta = \sum_k w_k J_k\, \delta f_k / \sum_k w_k J_k^2\).

    (a) Numerator: \(250 \cdot 5 + 100 \cdot 2.1 + 50 \cdot 4 = 1250 + 210 + 200 = 1660\). Denominator: \(62500 + 10000 + 2500 = 75000\). \(\Delta = 0.0221\) m.

    (b) Numerator: \(1250 + 210 + 20 = 1480\). Denominator: \(62500 + 10000 + 250 = 72750\). \(\Delta = 0.0203\) m.

    (c) A motion of 0.02 m predicts flow changes \((-5, -2, -1)\). The third pixel asked for \(-4\), so it is the outlier. It is far away, so its Jacobian is small and it enters the sums with \(J^2 = 2500\) against \(62500\) for the near pixel: distant points constrain translation weakly. Down-weighting it removes most of the remaining error, from 0.0021 m to 0.0003 m.

  4. DUSt3R's losses. Work in 2-D. Ground-truth points: \((0, 2)\), \((0, 4)\), \((3, 4)\). (a) The prediction is \((0, 3)\), \((0, 6)\), \((4.5, 6)\). Compute \(\ell_{\text{regr}}\) for each point. (b) The third prediction is instead \((0, 7.5)\). Compute the three losses again. (c) With \(\alpha = 0.5\), which confidence does (13.17) prefer for the third point in (b), and for a point with \(\ell = 0.1\)? What does each then contribute to the loss?

    Solution

    (a) Ground-truth distances are 2, 4, 5, so \(\bar{z} = 11/3 = 3.667\). Predicted distances are 3, 6, 7.5, so \(z = 16.5/3 = 5.5\). Every predicted point is 1.5 times its truth and \(z = 1.5\,\bar{z}\), so the normalized points coincide and all three losses are 0.

    (b) The predicted distances are still 3, 6, 7.5, so \(z = 5.5\) again. Normalized predictions: \((0, 0.545)\), \((0, 1.091)\), \((0, 1.364)\). Normalized truths: \((0, 0.545)\), \((0, 1.091)\), \((0.818, 1.091)\). The first two losses are 0. The third is \(\sqrt{0.818^2 + 0.273^2} = \sqrt{0.669 + 0.074} = 0.862\).

    (c) For one point, \(C\ell - \alpha \log C\) is minimized at \(C = \alpha/\ell\) when that exceeds 1. Third point: \(\alpha/\ell = 0.5/0.862 = 0.58\), below 1, so the network drives \(C\) toward its floor of 1 and the point contributes about \(0.862\). The point with \(\ell = 0.1\) gets \(C = 5\) and contributes \(5 \cdot 0.1 - 0.5 \ln 5 = 0.5 - 0.805 = -0.305\).

You are ready for next week if you can

  • Explain what "differentiable" buys: a loss measured on images or poses can train whatever produced the depth, pose, or weights upstream.
  • Write the view-synthesis idea in one line: re-draw one image from another using depth and pose, and penalize the difference. Next week's maps are trained the same way.
  • Compute a softmax and a weighted average by hand.
  • Set up and solve a weighted least-squares step, and say where the weights come from in DROID-SLAM.
  • Define a pointmap and say why DUSt3R's loss ignores global scale.
  • Name, for each of DVSO, D3VO, DROID-SLAM, DPVO, and DUSt3R, what is learned and what is still optimized.

  2. Hartley and Zisserman, Multiple View Geometry in Computer Vision, 2004 (projection and disparity in the problems).
  3. Nocedal and Wright, Numerical Optimization, 2006 (weighted Gauss-Newton step).

Week 20 · Day 1

Maps you can optimize by rendering them

After today you can explain what differentiable rendering is, why it lets a 3D map be learned from ordinary 2D images, and how ray marching differs from rasterization.

About 60 min · Read Ch. 14 opening and §14.1, pp. 397–401 (5 pages) · Needs Week 8 Day 2

Read first: Chapter 14 opening and §14.1, pp. 397–401

While you read, look for:

  • The reasons p. 398 gives for why points and occupancy grids are awkward for learning, and what DeepSDF does instead.
  • The two ways a graphics pipeline can hold a 3D model, and the rendering method that goes with each (p. 399).
  • In Figure 14.2 (p. 400): what the forward arrows pass through, and where the backward arrows end.
  • The sentence on p. 400 that says what the key to high-quality view synthesis turned out to be, and the paragraph on p. 401 that says how 3DGS renders differently from NeRF.

Today's big idea

A map does not have to be assembled by hand-designed fusion rules. If an image can be rendered from the map by a procedure whose output changes smoothly when the map's parameters change, then the difference between the rendered image and a real photo has a gradient with respect to those parameters, and following it improves the map. Neural radiance fields (NeRF) and 3D Gaussian splatting (3DGS) are two map representations built for that loop.

1. From stored geometry to learned functions

The maps of Week 8 · Day 2 store geometry directly: points, or a grid of occupancy values. When deep learning moved from images to 3D, the first attempts fed those structures to networks. The book names the problem: they are discrete, and they struggle to describe a closed, continuous surface of arbitrary shape compactly, which gets in the way of gradient-based optimization. §14.1.1 · p. 398

The alternative is to let the shape be a function. A multi-layer perceptron (MLP) is a small neural network: a stack of layers, each of which multiplies its input by a matrix, adds a vector, and applies a simple nonlinearity. Its matrices and vectors are the weights. Feed it a 3D coordinate and train it to output one number: either occupancy (is this point inside something?) or the signed distance function (SDF), the distance to the nearest surface with a sign that says inside or outside. The surface is the set of points where the SDF is zero. DeepSDF does exactly this with an 8-layer MLP, optionally with an extra input vector (a latent code) that selects which shape is meant. §14.1.1 · p. 398 · Fig. 14.1

A hand-written example of what such a network has to learn: for a sphere of radius 1 centred at the origin, \(f(\mathbf{x}) = \norm{\mathbf{x}} - 1\). Then \(f(0.5, 0, 0) = -0.5\) (inside), \(f(2, 0, 0) = 1\) (outside), and \(f(0.6, 0.8, 0) = 0\) (on the surface). A trained MLP plays the role of \(f\) for shapes with no formula.

RepresentationWhat is storedWhat the book says about it
Points, occupancy gridsDiscrete samples of geometryDiscrete, not well suited to gradient-based learning
Implicit neural function (occupancy or SDF)The weights of an MLPContinuous and compact, free of topology limits and discretization error, but trained with 3D ground truth
Scene optimized by differentiable renderingAny parameters an image can be rendered fromNeeds only 2D images

The second row has a practical flaw. Training on 3D targets needs ground-truth 3D data, which is expensive to annotate and does not scale. Photos are cheap. That pushed the field toward supervising 3D with 2D images. §14.1.1 · p. 398

2. Differentiable rendering: the loop

Rendering is the computation that turns a scene description and a camera pose into an image. Differentiable rendering (DR) is rendering arranged so that gradients can flow from the 2D image back to the 3D scene parameters. §14.1.2 · p. 399

The outputs need not be colour images. The same loop renders depth maps, semantic label maps, or normal maps, and the parameters can include colour, density, semantics, and camera poses. Fig. 14.2 · p. 400

Filling the gap: the gradient of one pixel

The book says gradients "flow back" without showing one. Take the smallest possible renderer: one pixel sees one semi-transparent blob of grey level \(c\) and opacity \(\alpha\) in front of a background of grey level \(b\). The rendered pixel is the blend

\[ C = \alpha\,c + (1-\alpha)\,b , \qquad L = (C - C_{gt})^2 , \]

where \(C_{gt}\) is the pixel in the real photo ("gt" for ground truth) and \(L\) is the loss. By the chain rule,

\[ \frac{\partial L}{\partial \alpha} = 2\,(C - C_{gt})\,(c - b), \qquad \frac{\partial L}{\partial c} = 2\,(C - C_{gt})\,\alpha . \]

Numbers: \(c = 0.9\), \(b = 0.1\), \(\alpha = 0.5\) give \(C = 0.5\). The photo says \(C_{gt} = 0.7\), so \(L = 0.04\) and \(\partial L/\partial\alpha = 2(-0.2)(0.8) = -0.32\). A gradient-descent step of size 0.5 moves \(\alpha\) to \(0.5 + 0.5 \times 0.32 = 0.66\). Now \(C = 0.66 \times 0.9 + 0.34 \times 0.1 = 0.628\) and \(L = 0.0052\): the blob became more opaque because the photo was brighter than the render. A real system does the same for millions of parameters and pixels, with the derivatives produced by automatic differentiation (Week 7 · Day 1).

Intuition

You met this idea as the photometric error of direct methods (Week 11 · Day 4): predict what a pixel should look like, compare with what the camera saw, and adjust the unknowns. There the unknowns were a pose and some depths. Here they are the whole scene.

3. Two kinds of scene, two ways to render

A graphics pipeline holds a 3D model in one of two forms, and each has its own rendering method. §14.1.2 · p. 399

ModelWhat it encodesRendered byCost
Surface dataObject boundaries, as polygons or implicit surfacesRasterization: project the surface geometry onto the 2D image planeHardware-accelerated, very efficient
Volume dataContinuous fields such as density or colour throughout spaceRay marching: cast a ray through the volume for each pixel and sample values along itHigher

Early differentiable renderers softened rasterization for meshes. Volume rendering then took over as the stronger tool for gradient-based optimization, because it provides gradients over 3D space even before the exact surface position is known. §14.1.2 · p. 399

Filling the gap: why "gradients before the surface is found" matters

Put two samples on one ray, with opacities \(\alpha_1, \alpha_2\) and grey levels \(c_1, c_2\), over a black background. Light from sample 2 must pass sample 1, so

\[ C = \alpha_1 c_1 + (1-\alpha_1)\,\alpha_2 c_2 , \qquad \frac{\partial C}{\partial \alpha_1} = c_1 - \alpha_2 c_2 . \]

Suppose the current scene is wrong: sample 1 is empty (\(\alpha_1 = 0\)) and sample 2 is a solid dark wall (\(\alpha_2 = 1\), \(c_2 = 0.2\)), so \(C = 0.2\). The photo shows a bright object, \(C_{gt} = 0.8\), and sample 1 has colour \(c_1 = 0.8\). Then \(\partial C/\partial\alpha_1 = 0.8 - 0.2 = 0.6\) and \(\partial L/\partial\alpha_1 = 2(0.2 - 0.8)(0.6) = -0.72\). The derivative is not zero even though nothing is there yet: the loss asks for matter at an empty point.

A hard surface gives no such signal. If a pixel sees an opaque surface, sliding that surface slightly along the ray does not change the pixel at all, so the derivative with respect to the surface position is zero, except at object outlines where the pixel jumps. That is why mesh-based methods had to soften their rasterizers, and why volumes are easier to optimize.

4. NeRF and 3DGS at a glance

NeRF (2020) stores the scene in a single MLP and renders by ray marching: for each pixel it steps along the ray and asks the MLP for opacity and colour at each sample. The MLP takes a 3D location and a viewing direction, passed through a positional encoding so that it can represent fine detail. It is trained from posed colour images (images whose camera poses are already known) by minimizing the rendering loss, and it produces high-quality novel view synthesis: images from viewpoints that were never photographed. §14.1.3 · pp. 399–400

NeRF's bottleneck is training speed. Later work replaced or assisted the MLP with explicit volume structures, voxel grids and hash tables, and reached comparable quality without an MLP. The book draws the lesson that the key ingredient is differentiable volume rendering and not the network. Even so, marching a ray for every pixel remains slow to render. §14.1.3 · p. 400

3D Gaussian splatting (2023) keeps the idea of semi-transparent matter but changes both the storage and the renderer. The scene is a large set of semi-transparent Gaussian blobs, blended by alpha blending, and rendered by differentiable rasterization: the renderer loops over the blobs and projects each onto the image, where NeRF loops over rays. Because most of a scene is empty, this is much faster to render, with training speed similar to the fastest volumetric NeRF variants. §14.1.3 · p. 401

Both started as offline tools: given posed images, optimize a scene, originally over days. Explicit data structures brought that down to near real time, and both are now being built into SLAM systems, which is the subject of Days 3 and 5. The underlying thought is older than either: the book traces the pairing of differentiable rendering with occupancy maps back to Thrun's "forward sensor model" of the early 2000s. Ch. 14 opening · p. 397

Common mistakes

  • "NeRF works because of the neural network." Grid-based variants reach comparable quality without an MLP. The book credits differentiable volume rendering. p. 400
  • "Differentiable rendering needs 3D ground truth." Avoiding 3D ground truth is its purpose. The supervision is 2D images.
  • "Rasterization is only for surfaces, so 3DGS is a surface method." 3DGS rasterizes volume data: its primitives are semi-transparent and are blended, not depth-tested. p. 409

Check yourself

Q1. One pixel sees a blob with grey level c = 1.0 and opacity α = 0.25 over a background b = 0.2. The photo shows 0.8. With L = (C − C_gt)², what is ∂L/∂α, and what does gradient descent do?

C = 0.25 × 1.0 + 0.75 × 0.2 = 0.4. ∂L/∂α = 2(0.4 − 0.8)(1.0 − 0.2) = −0.64. Gradient descent moves against the gradient, so α goes up and the pixel gets brighter.

Q2. Why did research move from training implicit functions on 3D data to differentiable rendering?

DeepSDF-style training works but needs 3D ground truth, which does not scale. Differentiable rendering lets ordinary images supervise the 3D parameters.

Q3. Which loop structure describes splatting, as opposed to ray marching?

Rasterization iterates over primitives. That lets it skip empty space entirely, which is where its speed comes from.

Q4. A ray's first sample is empty (α₁ = 0, colour c₁ = 0.5) and its second is an opaque wall (α₂ = 1, c₂ = 0.9). With C = α₁c₁ + (1 − α₁)α₂c₂, what is ∂C/∂α₁?

∂C/∂α₁ = c₁ − α₂c₂ = 0.5 − 0.9 = −0.4. Adding matter at the empty sample would darken the pixel, and the derivative says so even though nothing is there yet.

Recap

  1. Implicit neural representations store a shape as a function (occupancy or SDF) computed by an MLP: continuous and compact, but they need 3D ground truth to train.
  2. Differentiable rendering removes that need: render, compare with real images, and send the gradient of the loss back to the scene parameters, which can include camera poses.
  3. Surfaces are rasterized, volumes are ray-marched. Volumes give useful gradients everywhere along a ray, before any surface is located.
  4. NeRF is an MLP rendered by ray marching. 3DGS is a set of semi-transparent Gaussians rendered by rasterization, which is much faster to render.

Sources

  1. SLAM Handbook, Chapter 14 opening and §14.1 "3D Scene Representation and Differentiable Rendering", pp. 397–401, Figures 14.1–14.3.
  2. The one-pixel and two-sample gradients in "Filling the gap" are direct applications of the chain rule to the alpha-blending formula, which the book states as equation (14.6).

Week 20 · Day 2

NeRF: turning density along a ray into a pixel

After today you can derive the discrete volume rendering formula from the continuous integral and compute a pixel's colour, opacity, and expected depth from samples of density along its ray.

About 60 min · Read §14.2 opening and §14.2.1, pp. 401–403 (3 pages) · Needs Week 20 Day 1

Read first: §14.2 opening and §14.2.1, pp. 401–403

While you read, look for:

  • The inputs and outputs of the NeRF function \(f_\Theta\), and the three factors under the integral in equation (14.1), p. 402.
  • The definition of the accumulated transmittance \(T(t)\), in the line below (14.1).
  • Equation (14.2) and the definitions of \(\delta_i\) and \(\alpha_i\) at the top of p. 403. The sentence that defines \(\delta_i\) is misprinted: it is the distance between neighbouring samples, \(\delta_i = t_{i+1} - t_i\).
  • The loss (14.3), and the last sentence of §14.2.1 about depth.

Today's big idea

NeRF describes a scene by two fields: a density that says how much matter is at each point, and a colour. A pixel is the average of the colours along its ray, each weighted by the probability that the ray gets that far and is stopped there. With samples, that weight is \(w_i = T_i\,\alpha_i\): what survives the samples in front, times what sample \(i\) blocks. Every step is a smooth function of the densities and colours, so the pixel is differentiable.

1. The radiance field and the camera ray

A radiance field is the function

\[ f_\Theta(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{d}) \to (\mathbf{c}, \sigma) , \]

with MLP weights \(\Theta\), a 3D position \(\mathbf{x} = (x, y, z)\), a viewing direction \(\mathbf{d} = (\theta, \phi)\), a colour \(\mathbf{c} = (r, g, b)\), and a volume density \(\sigma \ge 0\). §14.2.1 · p. 402 The colour may depend on the direction you look from, which is how a shiny surface can look different from two sides. The density depends on position only.

Each pixel defines a camera ray \(\mathbf{r}(t) = \mathbf{o} + t\,\mathbf{d}\): start at the camera centre \(\mathbf{o}\) and travel a distance \(t\) in direction \(\mathbf{d}\). Only the part between a near bound \(t_n\) and a far bound \(t_f\) is rendered. Along one ray the fields become two ordinary functions of \(t\): \(\sigma(t)\) and \(\mathbf{c}(t)\).

What does \(\sigma\) mean? Read it as a stopping rate: over a very short step \(ds\), the ray is blocked with probability \(\sigma\,ds\). Its unit is one over length, and it can be far larger than 1. Air has \(\sigma = 0\). A wall is a thin region where \(\sigma\) is huge.

2. Transmittance and the rendering integral

The accumulated transmittance \(T(t)\) is the probability that the ray travels from \(t_n\) to \(t\) without being stopped. The book states it; here is where it comes from.

Filling the gap: why the transmittance is an exponential

To survive to \(t + dt\), the ray must survive to \(t\) and then not be stopped in the next step:

\[ T(t + dt) = T(t)\,\bigl(1 - \sigma(t)\,dt\bigr) \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \frac{dT}{dt} = -\sigma(t)\,T(t) . \]

Divide by \(T\): \(\frac{d}{dt}\ln T = -\sigma(t)\). Integrate from \(t_n\), where \(T = 1\):

\[ T(t) = \exp\!\Bigl(-\int_{t_n}^{t} \sigma(s)\,ds\Bigr) . \]

Example: fog of constant density \(\sigma = 0.5\) per metre, 2 m thick. The integral is \(0.5 \times 2 = 1\), so \(T = e^{-1} = 0.368\). About 37% of the light gets through and 63% is stopped by the fog.

Now the pixel. The probability that the ray reaches \(t\) and is stopped in the next \(dt\) is \(T(t)\,\sigma(t)\,dt\). When it is stopped at \(t\) the pixel receives the colour there. The expected colour is the sum over all the places it could stop:

\[ C(\mathbf{r}) = \int_{t_n}^{t_f} T(t)\,\sigma(\mathbf{r}(t))\,\mathbf{c}(\mathbf{r}(t), \mathbf{d})\,dt . \tag{14.1} \]

§14.2.1 · p. 402 For the fog above, with one colour \(\mathbf{c}_f\) throughout, \(C = \mathbf{c}_f \int_0^2 e^{-0.5t}\,0.5\,dt = (1 - e^{-1})\,\mathbf{c}_f = 0.632\,\mathbf{c}_f\). The integral treats whatever lies beyond \(t_f\) as black.

3. From the integral to a sum

A computer cannot evaluate \(\sigma\) everywhere. NeRF divides \([t_n, t_f]\) into \(N\) equal bins, draws one sample position at random inside each bin, and queries the MLP there. §14.2.1 · p. 402 The result is equation (14.2):

\[ \hat{C}(\mathbf{r}) = \sum_{i=1}^{N} \alpha_i\,T_i\,\mathbf{c}_i , \qquad T_i = \exp\!\Bigl(-\sum_{j=1}^{i-1} \sigma_j \delta_j\Bigr) , \qquad \alpha_i = 1 - \exp(-\sigma_i \delta_i) . \tag{14.2} \]

Filling the gap: deriving equation (14.2) from (14.1)

Assume \(\sigma\) and \(\mathbf{c}\) are constant on each segment \([t_i, t_{i+1}]\), with values \(\sigma_i, \mathbf{c}_i\) and length \(\delta_i = t_{i+1} - t_i\). Split the integral (14.1) into one piece per segment.

Step 1: transmittance at the start of segment \(i\). The integral of a piecewise-constant \(\sigma\) is a sum, so \(T_i = T(t_i) = \exp\bigl(-\sum_{j \lt i} \sigma_j\delta_j\bigr)\).

Step 2: transmittance inside segment \(i\). At distance \(s\) into the segment, \(T(t_i + s) = T_i\,e^{-\sigma_i s}\).

Step 3: integrate over the segment.

\[ \int_{0}^{\delta_i} T_i\,e^{-\sigma_i s}\,\sigma_i\,\mathbf{c}_i\,ds = T_i\,\mathbf{c}_i\,\Bigl[-e^{-\sigma_i s}\Bigr]_0^{\delta_i} = T_i\,\bigl(1 - e^{-\sigma_i\delta_i}\bigr)\,\mathbf{c}_i = T_i\,\alpha_i\,\mathbf{c}_i . \]

Summing over segments gives (14.2). The quantity \(\alpha_i\) is the opacity of segment \(i\): the fraction of the light entering it that it stops. Two useful consequences:

  • Since \(e^{-\sigma_j\delta_j} = 1 - \alpha_j\), the transmittance is a product: \(T_i = \prod_{j \lt i} (1 - \alpha_j)\). This form returns on Day 4.
  • The weight \(w_i = T_i\alpha_i\) equals \(T_i - T_{i+1}\), the light lost in segment \(i\). So the weights telescope: \(\sum_{i=1}^{N} w_i = 1 - T_{N+1}\). They add up to 1 only if nothing gets through.

A worked example with three samples, all \(\delta_i = 1\), grey levels in place of colours:

Sample \(i\)Position \(t_i\)Density \(\sigma_i\)Opacity \(\alpha_i\)Transmittance \(T_i\)Weight \(w_i\)Grey level \(c_i\)
1 (fog)10.2\(1 - e^{-0.2} = 0.181\)10.1810.9
2 (air)2000.81900.5
3 (wall)33\(1 - e^{-3} = 0.950\)0.8190.7780.2

The pixel is \(\hat{C} = 0.181 \times 0.9 + 0.778 \times 0.2 = 0.319\). The light that gets through everything is \(T_4 = 0.819 \times (1 - 0.950) = 0.041\), and \(0.181 + 0.778 + 0.041 = 1\) as it must.

Try it: the widget does this computation for a ray that crosses pink fog and a blue wall. Lower "Samples N" to 8, raise it again, then turn on random sample positions.

Notice that with 16 samples the pixel is fog 0.39, wall 0.56, background 0.04, close to the exact 0.39, 0.59, 0.02. At N = 8 the wall almost disappears (weight 0.08) because the two nearest samples straddle it, while the wide fog is still measured correctly. Thin, dense structures are only seen if a sample lands on them, which is one reason sample positions are randomized during training.

4. The loss, depth, and what the gradient looks like

Training compares rendered pixels with the pixels of the real images. With \(R\) the batch of rays being rendered and \(C_{gt}(\mathbf{r})\) the true colour of the pixel that ray \(\mathbf{r}\) belongs to, the loss is the squared photometric error

\[ L = \sum_{\mathbf{r} \in R} \norm{\hat{C}(\mathbf{r}) - C_{gt}(\mathbf{r})}_2^2 . \tag{14.3} \]

§14.2.1 · p. 403 For SLAM the book adds that depth is often rendered too, by the same alpha blending, and compared with a depth sensor or a predicted depth. In symbols, the weights that average colours can average distances:

\[ \hat{D}(\mathbf{r}) = \sum_{i=1}^{N} w_i\,t_i . \]

In the example above \(\hat{D} = 0.181 \times 1 + 0.778 \times 3 = 2.52\), a little in front of the wall because the fog pulls it forward.

Filling the gap: the derivative of a pixel with respect to one density

Colours are easy: \(\partial\hat{C}/\partial\mathbf{c}_i = w_i\). A density \(\sigma_k\) appears in two places: in its own opacity, \(\partial\alpha_k/\partial\sigma_k = \delta_k(1 - \alpha_k)\), and in the transmittance of every later sample, \(\partial T_i/\partial\sigma_k = -\delta_k T_i\) for \(i \gt k\). Add the two effects and use \(T_k(1 - \alpha_k) = T_{k+1}\):

\[ \frac{\partial \hat{C}}{\partial \sigma_k} = \delta_k \Bigl( T_{k+1}\,\mathbf{c}_k \;-\; \sum_{i \gt k} w_i\,\mathbf{c}_i \Bigr) . \]

In words: more matter at sample \(k\) adds its own colour, in proportion to the light that currently passes it, and dims everything behind it. For the empty sample 2 of the example: \(1 \times (0.819 \times 0.5 - 0.778 \times 0.2) = 0.254\). It is not zero, which is the property Day 1 called "gradients before the surface is found".

In plain words

Look through a foggy window at a wall. Some of what you see is the fog, some is the wall behind it, and a sliver might be whatever is past the wall. The pixel is that mixture. The recipe walks outward from your eye and, at each step, asks two things: how much light is still travelling, and how much of it this step catches.

Common mistakes

  • "αᵢ is the density." Opacity depends on density and segment length: \(\alpha_i = 1 - e^{-\sigma_i\delta_i}\). The same fog sampled with shorter steps has smaller α per step and the same total effect.
  • "σ is a probability." It is a rate per unit length. \(\sigma = 12\) is fine. α and T are the quantities between 0 and 1.
  • "Tᵢ includes sample i." The sum in (14.2) stops at \(i - 1\): \(T_i\) is what arrives at sample \(i\).
  • "The weights always sum to 1." They sum to \(1 - T_{N+1}\). A ray that crosses only thin fog has weights that add up to much less.

Going deeper (optional): two ideas from the NeRF paper

The book mentions positional encoding in one phrase (p. 400). In the original NeRF paper each input coordinate \(p\) is replaced by the list \(\bigl(\sin(2^0\pi p), \cos(2^0\pi p), \dots, \sin(2^{L-1}\pi p), \cos(2^{L-1}\pi p)\bigr)\) before entering the MLP. A plain MLP tends to produce smooth functions, and the fast-varying inputs let it express sharp detail.

The same paper also uses the weights a second time. Normalized, the \(w_i\) form a probability distribution over where the ray stops, so a second batch of samples can be drawn from it, concentrated where the first batch found matter. The widget shows why that helps: a thin wall needs samples near it, not evenly spread.

Check yourself

Q1. A segment has density σ = 2 and length δ = 0.5. What is its opacity α?

α = 1 − exp(−σδ) = 1 − e⁻¹ = 0.632. The value 0.368 is the fraction that gets through, and 1.0 would be σδ itself, which is only a good approximation when σδ is small.

Q2. Two samples along a ray have opacities α₁ = 0.5 and α₂ = 0.8. What is the weight of the second sample?

w₂ = T₂α₂ = (1 − 0.5) × 0.8 = 0.4. The first sample has weight 0.5, and 0.5 × 0.2 = 0.1 of the light passes both.

Q3. Those two samples are at t = 2 and t = 4 (weights 0.5 and 0.4). What expected depth does alpha blending give?

D = 0.5 × 2 + 0.4 × 4 = 2.6. Dividing by the total weight 0.9 would give 2.89, but the formula blends with the weights as they are.

Q4. A segment of constant density σ and length δ is split into two halves, each with density σ and length δ/2. How does the light that gets through both halves compare with the light that got through the original segment?

Each half passes exp(−σδ/2), and the product is exp(−σδ), the same as before. This is why α must include δ: the rendered result should not depend on how finely a uniform region is sampled.

Recap

  1. NeRF is a function from position and viewing direction to colour and density, queried along camera rays \(\mathbf{r}(t) = \mathbf{o} + t\mathbf{d}\).
  2. Transmittance \(T(t) = \exp(-\int\sigma)\) is the chance of reaching \(t\). The pixel is \(\int T\sigma\mathbf{c}\,dt\), equation (14.1).
  3. With piecewise-constant samples this becomes \(\hat{C} = \sum_i T_i\alpha_i\mathbf{c}_i\) with \(\alpha_i = 1 - e^{-\sigma_i\delta_i}\) and \(T_i = \prod_{j \lt i}(1 - \alpha_j)\), equation (14.2).
  4. The weights \(w_i = T_i\alpha_i\) also render depth, and they sum to \(1 - T_{N+1}\).
  5. The loss (14.3) is the squared difference between rendered and real pixels, and its gradient reaches every density on the ray, including empty ones.

Sources

  1. SLAM Handbook, §14.2 opening and §14.2.1 "Method Overview", pp. 401–403, equations (14.1)–(14.3), Figure 14.5.
  2. Mildenhall, Srinivasan, Tancik, Barron, Ramamoorthi, Ng, NeRF: Representing Scenes as Neural Radiance Fields for View Synthesis, 2020 (the reading of density as a stopping rate, positional encoding, and sampling from the weights).
  3. Max, Optical Models for Direct Volume Rendering, 1995 (the derivation of the transmittance and of the piecewise-constant quadrature).

Week 20 · Day 3

Storing the field: MLPs, grids, points, and what SLAM needs

After today you can compare MLP, grid, and point representations of a neural field on compression, speed, scene completion, dynamic allocation, and forgetting, and say why those properties matter for SLAM.

About 60 min · Read §14.2.2–14.2.4, pp. 403–408 (6 pages) · Needs Week 20 Day 2

Read first: §14.2.2–14.2.4, pp. 403–408

While you read, look for:

  • Why a single MLP is slow, and what a voxel feature grid replaces the MLP query with (p. 403).
  • The two surface representations of §14.2.3 and how a mesh is extracted from them (pp. 404–405).
  • The three advantages of neural-field maps over classical dense SLAM (pp. 405–406), and what iMAP and NICE-SLAM each introduced (p. 406).
  • Table 14.1 on p. 407, and the four paragraphs around it that explain its rows (pp. 406–408).

Today's big idea

The rendering equation of Day 2 does not care how density and colour are stored. Put them in one network and the map is compact and fills holes, but it is slow, cannot grow, and forgets. Put them in a grid or in points and the map is fast and local, but larger. SLAM must update its map while it runs, so the book concludes that the data structure, more than any other component, decides what a neural-field SLAM system can do.

1. Why one MLP is slow, and what replaced it

The original NeRF asks one MLP for the colour and density of every sample on every ray. Each answer runs the whole network, so every weight takes part in every query, forward and backward. Training is slow as a result. Later methods moved some or all of the scene into explicit data structures with fast access. §14.2.2 · p. 403

StructureHow a query is answeredWhat the book reports
Voxel feature grid (Plenoxel, DirectVoxGo)Trainable values at grid nodes, read by index lookup and trilinear interpolationTraining time falls from days to about ten minutes
Multi-resolution hash grid (Instant-NGP)Grid features at several resolutions kept in a hash table, decoded by a tiny MLPWith an optimized GPU implementation, training in seconds
Points with features (Point-NeRF)Features attached to a point cloud, decoded by a tiny MLP, rendered by volume renderingPoints can be placed freely, so empty space is skipped: a factor of 3 over the original NeRF

§14.2.2 · pp. 403–404 Surfels (small oriented discs, Week 8 · Day 4) can carry a radiance field in the same way as points. Hash tables as a way to store a sparse grid are the idea of Week 8 · Day 3.

Filling the gap: trilinear interpolation, and why it makes updates local

A grid stores values only at its nodes. Linear interpolation fills in between. In 1D, at a fraction \(s \in [0, 1]\) of the way from node \(i\) to node \(i+1\),

\[ f = (1 - s)\,f_i + s\,f_{i+1} . \]

In 2D (bilinear) do this along \(x\), then along \(y\). The four corner values get weights that are products of 1D weights. With \(f_{00} = 1\), \(f_{10} = 3\), \(f_{01} = 2\), \(f_{11} = 6\) and \((s_x, s_y) = (0.25, 0.5)\):

\[ f = \underbrace{0.75 \cdot 0.5}_{0.375} \cdot 1 + \underbrace{0.25 \cdot 0.5}_{0.125} \cdot 3 + \underbrace{0.75 \cdot 0.5}_{0.375} \cdot 2 + \underbrace{0.25 \cdot 0.5}_{0.125} \cdot 6 = 2.25 . \]

Trilinear interpolation is the 3D version: eight corners, each weighted by a product of three such factors. Two things follow. The weights are non-negative and sum to 1, so the result is a smooth average of the corner values. And the derivative of \(f\) with respect to a node value is that node's weight, which is zero for every node outside the cell. A loss on one sample therefore changes eight numbers, not the whole map.

2. Neural fields: outputs other than radiance

A field that maps position to colour and density is one choice of output. Fields that output something else are called neural fields. §14.2.3 · p. 404

  • Surfaces. For accurate geometry from RGB images, the field can be a signed distance function (NeuS, VolSDF) or an occupancy field (UNISURF), still trained through volume rendering. A mesh is then extracted with marching cubes (Week 8 · Day 4). §14.2.3 · pp. 404–405 To use equation (14.2), such a method needs a rule that turns signed distance or occupancy into opacity. The book does not give those rules, so see the cited papers for them.
  • Semantics. Give the network an extra output for a semantic label, and train it against 2D label images from many views. The result is a labelling that is consistent in 3D. More generally a field can fuse 2D feature maps from pre-trained foundation networks, which enables scene decomposition and editing by language prompt or by clicking. §14.2.3 · pp. 405–406 · Fig. 14.9

3. Neural fields in a SLAM system

Everything so far assumed posed images and offline optimization. Visual SLAM needs the camera poses and the scene estimated together, in real time. The book lists three reasons to try it with neural fields anyway. §14.2.4 · pp. 405–406

  1. One optimization in place of several fusion steps. Differentiable rendering fuses 2D data into 3D end to end. A TSDF pipeline (Week 8 · Day 2) chains hand-designed steps whose consistency is not guaranteed.
  2. Complex light. A radiance field can model transparent objects and reflections, which helps when the error being minimized is photometric.
  3. Completion and compression. Depending on the data structure, the representation's built-in priors fill unobserved regions and keep the map small.
SystemMap representationWhat the book says about it
iMAPA single MLP, as in the original NeRFThe first neural-field SLAM system. Real-time joint estimation of camera pose and geometry from RGB-D video. The MLP's smoothness prior gives compression and scene completion.
NICE-SLAMMulti-resolution voxel feature grid plus a tiny MLPThe first hybrid representation in SLAM. Several later systems use similar grids.
NeRF-SLAMNeRFSpeeds up the reconstruction with depth from DROID-SLAM (Week 19 · Day 4).
Loopy-SLAMPoint primitivesPoints can be re-allocated, which handles loop closure more easily.
MIPS-FusionSeveral local neural-field submapsSubmaps are how grid-type fields cope with pose updates from loop closure.

§14.2.4 · pp. 406–408 · Figs. 14.10–14.12

4. Five properties, three data structures

Table 14.1 rates the three families on five properties. "Limited" marks a weakness in every row. Table 14.1 · p. 407

PropertyMLPVoxel / hashPoint / surfel
CompressionGoodModerateModerate
Inference speedLimitedGoodModerate
Scene completionGoodGoodModerate
Dynamic allocationLimitedLimitedGood
Forgetting problemLimitedModerateModerate
  • Compression against speed. An MLP packs the whole field into its weights, which is compact but hard to interpret. A grid is interpretable, fast to read, and can be updated locally, at the cost of memory. This is the usual trade of time against space, and because SLAM must run in real time, explicit structures usually win. pp. 406–407
  • Scene completion. An MLP is a continuous function, so it gives plausible values in small regions it never observed. A multi-resolution grid does the same. The smoothing reaches as far as the positional encoding's frequency or the grid's cell size allows. Points are discrete and have no such global smoothing. p. 407 · Fig. 14.11
  • Dynamic allocation. SLAM discovers the scene's extent as it goes and must move parts of the map when a loop closes (Week 1 · Day 1). An MLP or a voxel grid has fixed bounds and a fixed encoding or resolution, so such systems resort to several local models. Points can be added and moved freely. pp. 407–408 · Fig. 14.12
  • Forgetting. With a global function, a parameter update made for one place changes the output everywhere. The system must keep feeding past observations back in as a training signal, which requires an explicit keyframe database. Relying less on a global function, or removing it, reduces the problem. p. 408

Try it: the widget fits a 1D field three ways. Start with the global function, look at the gap, then press "Explore the new region". Turn on "Replay old keyframes". Then switch to the grid and to points.

Notice that the global function passes through the gap almost exactly (error 0.002) though it never saw it. After Explore it fits the new region (0.031) but its error in the old region jumps from 0.000 to 0.197. With replay it stays at 0.004. The grid at resolution 24 hardly forgets (0.003 to 0.005) but leaves a hole in the gap (0.355); at resolution 8 a cell is wide enough to bridge the gap (0.013). Points never forget and leave the gap empty.

What the widget's two learned models are: the "global function" is a sum of sines and cosines that span the whole interval. It stands in for an MLP in the one respect that matters here, that every parameter influences the output everywhere. The grid is 1D linear interpolation between node values. Explore without replay applies the least-squares fit to the new samples that changes the parameters as little as possible, which is where gradient descent on the new samples alone heads when it starts from the old parameters.

Filling the gap: why a global function forgets and a grid does not

Write either model as \(f(x) = \sum_k \theta_k\,\phi_k(x)\): parameters \(\theta_k\) times fixed basis functions \(\phi_k\). One gradient-descent step of size \(\eta\) on the squared error at a new position \(x_n\), where the residual is \(r = f(x_n) - y_n\), changes each parameter by \(\Delta\theta_k = -2\eta\,r\,\phi_k(x_n)\). The prediction at an old position \(x_o\) therefore moves by

\[ \Delta f(x_o) = \sum_k \Delta\theta_k\,\phi_k(x_o) = -2\eta\,r \sum_k \phi_k(x_n)\,\phi_k(x_o) . \]

The sum measures how much the two positions share parameters.

  • Grid. \(\phi_k(x)\) is the interpolation weight of node \(k\), which is zero unless \(x\) is in a cell next to that node. With cells 0.1 wide, \(x_n = 0.83\) and \(x_o = 0.31\) have no node in common, so the sum is 0 and the old prediction does not move.
  • Global. Take just three basis functions, \(1\), \(\sin\pi x\), \(\cos\pi x\). The sum is \(1 + \sin(0.83\pi)\sin(0.31\pi) + \cos(0.83\pi)\cos(0.31\pi) = 1 + \cos(0.52\pi) = 0.937\). With \(r = 0.5\) and \(\eta = 0.1\) the old prediction shifts by \(-2 \times 0.1 \times 0.5 \times 0.937 = -0.094\), although nothing was observed there.

Replaying old keyframes adds gradient steps that pull the old region back. That is the keyframe database the book says such maps require.

Common mistakes

  • "A finer grid is always better." A fine grid stores more and smooths less: holes smaller than a coarse cell get filled, holes larger than a fine cell do not. Multi-resolution grids keep both.
  • "Hybrid grids have no forgetting." Table 14.1 rates them "Moderate". A hybrid still decodes its features with a small shared MLP, and coarse cells are shared by neighbouring regions.
  • "Compact means fast." The MLP is the most compact and the slowest to query, because all of its weights take part in every query.

Check yourself

Q1. A 2D grid cell has corner values f₀₀ = 2, f₁₀ = 4, f₀₁ = 6, f₁₁ = 8 (first index along x). What does bilinear interpolation give at (sₓ, s_y) = (0.5, 0.25)?

Along x at the bottom: 0.5 × 2 + 0.5 × 4 = 3. Along x at the top: 0.5 × 6 + 0.5 × 8 = 7. Along y: 0.75 × 3 + 0.25 × 7 = 4.0.

Q2. After a loop closure, part of the map has to move. Which representation does the book rate best for this, and why?

MLPs and grids have fixed bounds and resolution, so they handle pose updates with several local submaps. Points can be moved, added, and removed directly.

Q3. Why does an MLP-based SLAM map need a keyframe database?

Every weight affects the whole field. Without past observations in the optimization, updates for the current view overwrite what was learned before: the forgetting problem.

Q4. In the widget, the grid fills the unobserved gap at resolution 8 but not at resolution 24. Why?

The gap is 0.12 wide. At resolution 8 a cell is 0.125 wide, so every node near the gap belongs to a cell that also contains observed samples. At resolution 24 a cell is about 0.04 wide, and some nodes have only unobserved cells around them, so nothing ever sets their values.

Recap

  1. A single MLP uses all its weights for every query. Grids answer a query by lookup and trilinear interpolation, points by reading nearby primitives.
  2. Neural fields generalize radiance fields: the output can be a signed distance, an occupancy, a semantic label, or a feature vector.
  3. For SLAM, neural fields offer end-to-end fusion, complex light modelling, and completion and compression. iMAP used one MLP, NICE-SLAM a grid with a tiny MLP.
  4. Table 14.1: MLPs compress and complete well but are slow, rigid, and forgetful. Grids are fast. Points are the easiest to re-allocate.
  5. Forgetting comes from shared parameters. The cure is replaying keyframes or making the representation local.

Sources

  1. SLAM Handbook, §14.2.2 "Data Structures in NeRF", §14.2.3 "Neural Fields", §14.2.4 "NeRF/Neural Fields for Visual SLAM", pp. 403–408, Table 14.1, Figures 14.6–14.12.
  2. Press, Teukolsky, Vetterling, Flannery, Numerical Recipes, 3rd edition, 2007 (bilinear and trilinear interpolation).
  3. The forgetting calculation is one gradient-descent step on a model that is linear in its parameters, as in Week 2 · Day 4.

Week 20 · Day 4

3D Gaussian splatting: project, sort, blend

After today you can project a Gaussian's covariance into the image through the camera Jacobian and compute a pixel by front-to-back alpha blending of the projected Gaussians.

About 60 min · Read §14.3 opening and §14.3.1, pp. 409–410 (2 pages) · Needs Week 20 Day 2

Read first: §14.3 opening and §14.3.1, pp. 409–410

While you read, look for:

  • What 3DGS takes as input besides the images, and the four things that parameterize one Gaussian (p. 409).
  • Equation (14.4): the covariance is not stored directly but built from two other matrices.
  • Equation (14.5) on p. 410, and which block of \(\boldsymbol{\Sigma}'\) is used.
  • Equations (14.6) and (14.7), then the three sentences on sorting, tiles, and frustum culling.
  • The loss (14.8) and the closing sentence on densification and pruning.

Today's big idea

3DGS keeps the blending sum of Day 2 and changes where the opacities come from. The scene is a list of semi-transparent Gaussian blobs. To render, flatten each blob onto the image, sort the blobs by depth, and blend the ones that cover a pixel from front to back. No samples are spent on empty space, and every step is differentiable, so the blobs can be fitted to photos by gradient descent.

1. What one Gaussian stores

Each primitive has a mean position \(\boldsymbol{\mu} \in \R^3\), a covariance matrix \(\boldsymbol{\Sigma} \in \R^{3\times 3}\) that sets its size, shape, and orientation, an opacity \(o\), and a colour \(\mathbf{c}\) that can vary with viewing direction, stored as spherical-harmonic (SH) coefficients. The input is a set of colour images with poses from structure from motion (SfM), together with the sparse point cloud SfM produced, which seeds the initial Gaussians. §14.3 · p. 409

The blob's strength at a point \(\mathbf{x}\) is the Gaussian function without its normalizing constant, so that it equals 1 at the centre:

\[ G(\mathbf{x}) = \exp\!\Bigl(-\tfrac{1}{2}\,(\mathbf{x} - \boldsymbol{\mu})\T\,\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{-1}(\mathbf{x} - \boldsymbol{\mu})\Bigr) . \]

The covariance is built from a diagonal scaling matrix \(\mathbf{S}\) (the blob's three radii) and a rotation \(\mathbf{R} \in \SO(3)\):

\[ \boldsymbol{\Sigma} = \mathbf{R}\,\mathbf{S}\,\mathbf{S}\T\mathbf{R}\T . \tag{14.4} \]

Filling the gap: why factor the covariance?

A covariance must be symmetric and positive semi-definite: \(\mathbf{v}\T\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\mathbf{v} \ge 0\) for every \(\mathbf{v}\). If gradient descent adjusted the six free entries of \(\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\) directly, a step could leave that set and the "Gaussian" would stop being one. The factored form cannot fail: with \(\mathbf{A} = \mathbf{R}\mathbf{S}\), \(\mathbf{v}\T\mathbf{A}\mathbf{A}\T\mathbf{v} = \norm{\mathbf{A}\T\mathbf{v}}^2 \ge 0\) for any \(\mathbf{S}\) and \(\mathbf{R}\).

A 2D example. Radii \(2\) and \(0.5\), rotated by 30°: \(\cos^2 = 0.75\), \(\sin^2 = 0.25\), \(\cos\sin = 0.433\), and \(\mathbf{S}\mathbf{S}\T = \diag(4, 0.25)\).

\[ \boldsymbol{\Sigma} = \begin{bmatrix} 0.75 \cdot 4 + 0.25 \cdot 0.25 & 0.433\,(4 - 0.25) \\ 0.433\,(4 - 0.25) & 0.25 \cdot 4 + 0.75 \cdot 0.25 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 3.06 & 1.62 \\ 1.62 & 1.19 \end{bmatrix} . \]

Check: the trace is \(4.25 = 4 + 0.25\) and the determinant is \(3.0625 \times 1.1875 - 1.6238^2 = 1.00 = 4 \times 0.25\), as rotation must preserve both.

2. Projecting a Gaussian onto the image

The book gives the covariance of the projected Gaussian in one line:

\[ \boldsymbol{\Sigma}' = \mathbf{J}\,\mathbf{W}\,\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\,\mathbf{W}\T\mathbf{J}\T , \tag{14.5} \]

where \(\mathbf{W}\) is the viewing transformation and \(\mathbf{J}\) is the Jacobian of the projective transformation, and it calls the projection "approximated". §14.3.1 · pp. 409–410 Here is what each factor does and where the approximation is.

Filling the gap: deriving equation (14.5)

Step 1: into the camera frame. A world point becomes \(\mathbf{x}_c = \mathbf{W}\mathbf{x} + \mathbf{t}\) in camera coordinates, with \(\mathbf{W}\) the rotation part of the world-to-camera transform. A linear map of a Gaussian is again a Gaussian, with covariance \(\cov(\mathbf{A}\mathbf{x} + \mathbf{b}) = \mathbf{A}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\mathbf{A}\T\). So in the camera frame the mean is \(\boldsymbol{\mu}_c = \mathbf{W}\boldsymbol{\mu} + \mathbf{t}\) and the covariance is \(\mathbf{W}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\mathbf{W}\T\). This step is exact.

Step 2: onto the plane \(z = 1\). Perspective projection (Week 11 · Day 3) is \(\pi(x, y, z) = (x/z,\; y/z)\). It divides by \(z\), so it is not linear and the true image of a Gaussian is not a Gaussian. Replace \(\pi\) by its first-order Taylor expansion around the mean, exactly as measurement functions were linearized in Week 2 · Day 3:

\[ \pi(\boldsymbol{\mu}_c + \mathbf{e}) \approx \pi(\boldsymbol{\mu}_c) + \mathbf{J}\,\mathbf{e}, \qquad \mathbf{J} = \frac{\partial \pi}{\partial \mathbf{x}_c}\bigg|_{\boldsymbol{\mu}_c} = \begin{bmatrix} 1/z & 0 & -x/z^2 \\ 0 & 1/z & -y/z^2 \end{bmatrix} , \]

with \((x, y, z) = \boldsymbol{\mu}_c\). The approximate map is linear, so the same covariance rule applies again: \(\boldsymbol{\Sigma}' = \mathbf{J}(\mathbf{W}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\mathbf{W}\T)\mathbf{J}\T\), a \(2 \times 2\) matrix, centred at \(\boldsymbol{\mu}' = \pi(\boldsymbol{\mu}_c)\). The book speaks of the upper-left \(2 \times 2\) block because the usual derivation carries a third row in \(\mathbf{J}\), which makes \(\boldsymbol{\Sigma}'\) a \(3 \times 3\) matrix whose image part is that block. To get pixel units, multiply \(\mathbf{J}\) by the focal length.

Numbers, in a 2D world (sideways \(x\), depth \(z\)) with the camera at the origin and \(\mathbf{W} = \mathbf{I}\). Here \(\mathbf{J}\) is the single row \([\,1/z \;\; -x/z^2\,]\). A Gaussian at \((x, z) = (1, 2)\) with \(\boldsymbol{\Sigma} = \diag(0.25, 0.04)\):

\[ \mu' = \tfrac{1}{2} = 0.5, \qquad \mathbf{J} = [\,0.5 \;\; -0.25\,], \qquad \sigma'^2 = 0.5^2 \cdot 0.25 + 0.25^2 \cdot 0.04 = 0.065, \qquad \sigma' = 0.255 . \]

Move it twice as far along the same ray, to \((2, 4)\): \(\mathbf{J} = [\,0.25 \;\; -0.125\,]\), \(\sigma'^2 = 0.0156 + 0.0006 = 0.0163\), \(\sigma' = 0.127\). Twice the depth, half the footprint, as perspective requires.

3. Alpha blending, front to back

At a pixel \(\mathbf{x}_{2D} = [u, v]\T\), Gaussian \(i\) has the opacity

\[ \alpha_i = o_i\,G_{2D}(\mathbf{x}_{2D}), \qquad G_{2D}(\mathbf{x}) = \exp\!\Bigl(-\tfrac{1}{2}(\mathbf{x} - \boldsymbol{\mu}'_i)\T\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_i'^{-1}(\mathbf{x} - \boldsymbol{\mu}'_i)\Bigr) , \tag{14.7} \]

its stored opacity times the value of its footprint at that pixel. With the Gaussians along the pixel's ray sorted by depth, nearest first, the pixel colour is

\[ C = \sum_{i \in \mathcal{N}} \mathbf{c}_i\,\alpha_i \prod_{j=1}^{i-1} (1 - \alpha_j) . \tag{14.6} \]

§14.3.1 · p. 410 Compare with equation (14.2) of Day 2, where \(T_i = \prod_{j \lt i}(1 - \alpha_j)\). The sum is the same. NeRF gets \(\alpha_i = 1 - e^{-\sigma_i\delta_i}\) from samples of a field along the ray. 3DGS gets \(\alpha_i\) from the primitives that happen to cover the pixel.

Filling the gap: compositing as a loop

Equation (14.6) is computed with two running quantities, the colour so far \(C\) and the transmittance \(T\). Start with \(C = 0\), \(T = 1\), and for each Gaussian from the nearest outward:

\[ C \leftarrow C + T\,\alpha_i\,\mathbf{c}_i , \qquad T \leftarrow T\,(1 - \alpha_i) . \]

Whatever \(T\) remains at the end goes to the background. The same picture results from painting back to front with the "over" rule \(C \leftarrow \alpha_i\mathbf{c}_i + (1 - \alpha_i)\,C\): for two layers over a background \(\mathbf{b}\), both give \(\alpha_1\mathbf{c}_1 + (1 - \alpha_1)\alpha_2\mathbf{c}_2 + (1 - \alpha_1)(1 - \alpha_2)\mathbf{b}\). Front to back has one advantage: once \(T\) is close to zero, nothing farther away can change the pixel and the loop can stop.

Three Gaussians with \(\alpha = 0.311,\ 0.397,\ 0.708\), nearest first: the weights are \(0.311\); \(0.689 \times 0.397 = 0.274\); \(0.689 \times 0.603 \times 0.708 = 0.294\); and \(0.689 \times 0.603 \times 0.292 = 0.121\) is left for the background. They sum to 1.

Try it: three Gaussians seen from above, a camera at the bottom, and the 1D image it renders. Drag the pink Gaussian sideways and then away from the camera. Change its opacity and rotation. Move the "Pixel u" slider and read the table.

Notice that at the default pixel u = 0.10 the table shows α = 0.311, 0.397, 0.708 and weights 0.311, 0.274, 0.294, with 0.121 left over: the calculation above. Drag a Gaussian away from the camera and its footprint on the image line shrinks. Drag the green one in front of the pink one and the table rows swap, because each weight depends on everything in front of it.

4. Making it fast, and making it learn

Sorting and culling. Blending needs the Gaussians in depth order from the viewpoint. The image is divided into tiles and the sort is done per tile with a GPU radix sort. Gaussians outside the camera's view frustum are skipped (frustum culling). §14.3.1 · p. 410

The loss. The parameters of all Gaussians are fitted by minimizing

\[ \mathcal{L} = (1 - \lambda)\,\mathcal{L}_1 + \lambda\,\mathcal{L}_{\text{SSIM}} \tag{14.8} \]

between the rendered and the real image, with a weight \(\lambda\). §14.3.1 · p. 410 \(\mathcal{L}_1\) is the mean absolute difference of pixel values. SSIM, the structural similarity index, compares small patches of the two images by their local brightness, contrast, and pattern, so the second term rewards getting local structure right and not only each pixel on its own.

Changing the number of Gaussians. Gradient descent can move, reshape, and recolour Gaussians, but it cannot create one. During optimization, adaptive densification and pruning adjust the count based on the Gaussians' gradients and opacities. §14.3.1 · p. 410 · Fig. 14.14 In the original method, a large gradient signals a region the current Gaussians cannot explain, where more are added, and a Gaussian whose opacity has fallen to almost nothing is removed.

Go back to the widget. Its lower strip is a goal image, rendered from a layout you cannot see. Press "Reset", then "10 gradient steps toward the goal" a few times.

The loss falls from 0.0382 to 0.0006 after ten steps and to about 0.0001 after twenty, and the two strips match. The widget's loss is the mean squared difference between the two images, with each Gaussian's colour as its own channel, not equation (14.8). Now open the Rotation slider for each Gaussian: the goal was drawn with pink at 29° and blue at −20°, and yours need not have ended there. A single 1D image does not pin down a 2D scene, which is why training uses many views.

Common mistakes

  • "The opacity o is the α in the blend." \(\alpha_i = o_i\,G_{2D}\) also includes the footprint's falloff. They are equal only at the footprint's centre.
  • "A sum does not care about order." Each term carries the product of \((1 - \alpha_j)\) over everything in front. Swap two Gaussians and their weights change.
  • "The projected footprint is exact." It comes from linearizing the projection at the mean. The error grows for Gaussians that are large compared with their distance from the camera.
  • "3DGS traces rays through the Gaussians." It loops over Gaussians and writes each to the pixels its footprint covers. That is rasterization.

Check yourself

Q1. In a 2D world, a Gaussian sits on the optical axis at (x, z) = (0, 4) with Σ = diag(0.16, 0.09). The camera is at the origin. What is the standard deviation σ′ of its footprint on the image line z = 1?

J = [1/z, −x/z²] = [0.25, 0]. σ′² = 0.25² × 0.16 = 0.01, so σ′ = 0.1. On the axis the depth variance 0.09 has no first-order effect.

Q2. At one pixel a red Gaussian in front has α = 0.6 and a blue one behind it has α = 0.5. What is the weight of the blue Gaussian?

Blue's weight is its α times the transmittance in front of it: 0.5 × (1 − 0.6) = 0.2. Red has 0.6, and 0.4 × 0.5 = 0.2 reaches the background.

Q3. A Gaussian has opacity o = 0.8 and a 1D footprint with standard deviation σ′. What is its α at a pixel that lies 2σ′ from the footprint's centre?

G = exp(−½ · 2²) = e⁻² = 0.135, so α = 0.8 × 0.135 = 0.108.

Q4. Why is the covariance stored as R S Sᵀ Rᵀ and not as a free symmetric matrix?

vᵀΣv = ‖SᵀRᵀv‖² ≥ 0 for every v, whatever the optimizer does to the scales and the rotation.

Q5. Equations (14.2) and (14.6) are the same blending sum. What differs?

Both are front-to-back alpha blending with transmittance ∏(1 − αⱼ). NeRF spends samples everywhere on the ray. 3DGS only visits the primitives that land on the pixel.

Recap

  1. A 3D Gaussian stores a mean, a covariance \(\boldsymbol{\Sigma} = \mathbf{R}\mathbf{S}\mathbf{S}\T\mathbf{R}\T\), an opacity, and a view-dependent colour.
  2. Its footprint in the image has covariance \(\boldsymbol{\Sigma}' = \mathbf{J}\mathbf{W}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\mathbf{W}\T\mathbf{J}\T\): rotate into the camera frame, then linearize the projection at the mean.
  3. A pixel is \(\sum_i \mathbf{c}_i\alpha_i\prod_{j \lt i}(1 - \alpha_j)\) with \(\alpha_i = o_i G_{2D}\), over the depth-sorted Gaussians that cover it.
  4. Tiles, a per-tile sort, and frustum culling make this fast. An L1 plus SSIM loss, with densification and pruning, makes it learn.

Sources

  1. SLAM Handbook, §14.3 opening and §14.3.1 "Method Overview", pp. 409–410, equations (14.4)–(14.8), Figures 14.13–14.14.
  2. Zwicker, Pfister, van Baar, Gross, EWA Volume Splatting, 2001 (projecting a 3D Gaussian by linearizing the perspective projection).
  3. Kerbl, Kopanas, Leimkühler, Drettakis, 3D Gaussian Splatting for Real-Time Radiance Field Rendering, 2023 (the factored covariance, and the triggers for densification and pruning).
  4. Porter and Duff, Compositing Digital Images, 1984 (the "over" rule). Wang, Bovik, Sheikh, Simoncelli, Image Quality Assessment: From Error Visibility to Structural Similarity, 2004 (SSIM).

Week 20 · Day 5

Gaussian splatting SLAM, and what is still hard

After today you can explain how a Gaussian splat map serves both tracking and mapping in SLAM, state the advantages the book claims over NeRF, and list the open problems of rendering-based SLAM.

About 60 min · Read §14.3.2–14.4, pp. 410–416 (7 pages, half of them figures) · Needs Week 20 Day 4

Read first: §14.3.2, §14.3.3, and §14.4, pp. 410–416

While you read, look for:

  • What SuGAR and 2DGS add to get accurate surfaces, and why editing a splat scene is easier than editing a NeRF (p. 411).
  • The two advantages of 3DGS over NeRF for SLAM (p. 412).
  • The RGB-D route and the monocular route of MonoGS, and why discrete primitives help loop closure (p. 413).
  • The systems that pair 3DGS with ORB-SLAM, ICP, or LiDAR (p. 414).
  • The four challenges of §14.4 and the remedies proposed for each (pp. 415–416).

Today's big idea

A splat map can be both the thing you render and the thing you localize against. Hold the Gaussians fixed and descend on the camera pose: that is tracking. Hold the poses fixed and descend on the Gaussians: that is mapping. The map renders fast and its primitives can be added, moved, and removed, which suits SLAM. But optimizing it is still slow, and tracking by photometric error alone is not yet as accurate as classical sparse methods.

1. Beyond view synthesis: surfaces and semantics

Like NeRF before it, 3DGS has been adapted to other 3D tasks. The book picks two. §14.3.2 · pp. 410–412

GoalProblem with plain 3DGSWhat the cited methods do
Surface reconstruction3DGS is built for photorealistic view synthesis and does not guarantee accurate geometrySuGAR adds a geometric regularizer: it defines a surface normal for each Gaussian and encourages neighbouring Gaussians to be flat, so a mesh can be extracted. 2DGS replaces the 3D Gaussians with 2D discs, which have a normal by construction, and adds normal and depth consistency losses.
Semantic understandingGaussians carry only colourGive each Gaussian a semantic feature and train it from 2D segmentations through the differentiable renderer. LangSplat and FMGS fuse 2D foundation-model features (CLIP, DINO) into the Gaussians, which enables open-vocabulary segmentation.

Because the Gaussians are explicit and discrete, editing the scene, for example moving or deleting an object, is more direct than in a continuous NeRF. §14.3.2 · p. 411

2. One loss for tracking and mapping

As with neural fields (Day 3), the appeal for SLAM is end-to-end optimization through the renderer: localization and mapping share one objective, there is no chain of hand-designed stages, and the map can represent complex light, including transparent objects. On top of that the book names two advantages specific to 3DGS. §14.3.3 · pp. 411–412

  1. Fast rendering. Rasterization is much faster than ray marching, which matters for anything that must interact with the map in real time, such as robot navigation.
  2. Flexible primitives. Discrete, point-like Gaussians can be allocated and updated freely. That fits SLAM, where the scene's boundary grows and loop closures move parts of the map. This is the "dynamic allocation" row of Table 14.1.

How does a renderer estimate a pose? Camera poses are among the parameters in Figure 14.2. The pose enters equation (14.5) through \(\mathbf{W}\) and through the camera-frame mean \(\boldsymbol{\mu}_c\), so the rendered image is a differentiable function of the pose, and the loss has a gradient with respect to it.

Filling the gap: the gradient of a pixel with respect to the camera position

Use the 2D world of Day 4: a Gaussian at \((x, z)\), a camera at sideways position \(c_x\) looking along \(z\). The footprint centre is

\[ \mu' = \frac{x - c_x}{z} \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad \frac{\partial \mu'}{\partial c_x} = -\frac{1}{z} . \]

Moving the camera to the right slides every footprint to the left, near ones more than far ones. That is parallax. Ignoring the smaller change in footprint width, the opacity at pixel \(u\) is \(\alpha = o\,\exp\bigl(-(u - \mu')^2 / 2\sigma'^2\bigr)\), so by the chain rule

\[ \frac{\partial \alpha}{\partial c_x} = \frac{\partial \alpha}{\partial \mu'}\,\frac{\partial \mu'}{\partial c_x} = \alpha\,\frac{u - \mu'}{\sigma'^2}\cdot\Bigl(-\frac{1}{z}\Bigr) . \]

Numbers: \(o = 0.8\), \(\sigma' = 0.25\), \(z = 2\). At a pixel one \(\sigma'\) from the centre, \(u - \mu' = 0.25\): \(\alpha = 0.8\,e^{-0.5} = 0.485\) and \(\partial\alpha/\partial c_x = 0.485 \times 0.25 / 0.0625 \times (-0.5) = -0.97\). At a pixel four \(\sigma'\) away, \(u - \mu' = 1\): \(\alpha = 0.8\,e^{-8} = 0.0003\) and the derivative is \(-0.002\).

The second number is the catch. A pixel tells the camera where to move only if a footprint already reaches it. If the rendered image and the recorded image do not overlap, the gradient carries almost no information, and the estimate can settle somewhere wrong.

Try it: the three Gaussians of Day 4 are now a finished map. The camera recorded one image at x = 0. Press "Run". Then set "Starting guess x" to −2.0 and run again. Then raise "Image noise".

Notice that from the default guess of 0.8 the estimate reaches 0.000 in about ten steps. From −2.0 it slides the wrong way and stops near −2.82, in a local minimum where the rendered image shares little with the recorded one. From +2.0 it still converges: the loss curve is not symmetric. With image noise at 0.30 the minimum moves to 0.015 and the loss can no longer reach zero (0.051).

3. The systems the book describes

ApproachWhat the book says
RGB-D (several early systems)A depth camera supplies dense depth that initializes the Gaussians' positions and regularizes them through a depth rendering loss. Tracking is accurate and rendering is fast, but extra hardware is needed.
Monocular (MonoGS)Colour images only. The Gaussians start at random positions and are refined by multi-view optimization, with no depth supervision.
Loop closure (LoopSplat)Discrete Gaussians act as features that can be registered across times and viewpoints, so segments of the scene can be matched and aligned.
Physical imaging (I²-SLAM)Adds motion blur and tone mapping to the rendering model, and reconstructs a high-dynamic-range map while tracking the camera.
Hybrid with keypoints or ICPPhoto-SLAM pairs ORB-SLAM's sparse tracking with a 3DGS map. GS-ICP SLAM and RTG-SLAM track with ICP, and RTG-SLAM adds a back-end optimization based on ORB keypoints.
LiDAR + 3DGSHybrid frameworks use the Gaussians as one map shared by several sensor types.

§14.3.3 · pp. 412–414 · Figs. 14.17–14.20 The hybrids work because a set of Gaussians with its extra attributes left out is a point cloud, so established point-based algorithms apply directly: ICP from Week 13 · Day 2, the ORB-SLAM pipeline from Week 12 · Day 5. p. 414

4. What is still hard

The chapter ends with four limits of NeRF- and 3DGS-based SLAM. §14.4 · pp. 414–416

ChallengeThe problemDirections the book proposes
Real-time performanceEnd-to-end systems are very slow. The book contrasts ElasticFusion, which tracked, mapped, and rendered in real time on a 2015 GPU, with most NeRF and 3DGS SLAM methods, which struggle to exceed 5 frames per second on modern GPUs. Rendering is fast; optimizing is the bottleneck.Fewer Gaussians (compact representations). A higher-order optimizer in place of first-order gradient descent. A network that predicts poses and Gaussians in one forward pass.
Tracking accuracyOften behind classical sparse SLAM. These methods assume photometric consistency across frames, which holds on synthetic data such as Replica and breaks in real scenes through unmodelled effects such as sensor noise and rolling shutter.Model the light field and the imaging process more precisely. Match in a domain other than colour. Use a robust feed-forward prediction model.
4D scenesMost methods assume a static world, and commonly mask out possibly moving objects.Build on the success of 3DGS in non-rigid and 4D reconstruction and point tracking, toward a full 4D SLAM.
Large and outdoor scenesMost methods are limited to room-scale sequences. Outdoors, illumination changes with weather and time of day.Efficient map updates such as adaptive resolution, and drift correction over long distances.

On the feed-forward direction the book is specific. PixelSplat and MVSplat predict Gaussian parameters from posed images without any optimization at test time.
