DUSt3R (Week 19 · Day 5) showed that a network can predict pointmaps without pose input, and NoPoSplat extends that to predicting Gaussians from two unposed views. Using such predictors in an incremental, multi-view SLAM setting is left as future work. §14.4 · pp. 415–416 · Fig. 14.21

Intuition

"Higher-order optimizer" is a pointer back to Week 2 · Day 4. Gradient descent knows only the slope, so on a loss that is steep in some directions and flat in others it takes many small steps, as you saw the widget do from a distant start. Gauss-Newton also uses curvature and can cover the same ground in a few steps. The price is building and solving a linear system over a very large number of Gaussian parameters.

Common mistakes

  • "3DGS renders in real time, so 3DGS SLAM runs in real time." Rendering one image is fast. SLAM must run many optimization steps per frame, and that is the slow part. p. 415
  • "A photorealistic map means accurate geometry." 3DGS optimizes appearance. Accurate surfaces need extra regularization, as in SuGAR or 2DGS. p. 411
  • "Rendering-based tracking has replaced feature-based tracking." The book says its accuracy often falls behind classical sparse SLAM, and several practical systems still track with ORB features or ICP. pp. 414–415

Check yourself

Q1. In the 2D world, the camera moves 0.2 to the right. A Gaussian at depth z = 4 stays where it is. How does its footprint centre move on the image line z = 1?

∂μ′/∂cₓ = −1/z = −0.25, so the centre moves by −0.25 × 0.2 = −0.05. A Gaussian at z = 1 would move four times as far: parallax.

Q2. In the widget, why does tracking fail from a starting guess of −2.0?

A pixel gives a useful gradient only where a footprint already has some opacity. Far from the truth the loss curve has a hump, and descent goes down its wrong side.

Q3. What lets MonoGS do monocular SLAM with no depth sensor, according to the book?

The flexibility of where Gaussians are allocated lets the positions be estimated incrementally from colour images alone.

Q4. Why can 3DGS be combined so directly with ORB-SLAM or ICP?

The Gaussian means are 3D points. Classical tracking supplies the pose, and the Gaussians supply the dense, renderable map.

Q5. Which reason does the book give for tracking accuracy falling behind classical sparse SLAM on real data?

The loss assumes a point looks the same in every frame. That holds on synthetic sequences and fails in real ones unless the imaging process is modelled.

Recap

  1. 3DGS has been extended to accurate surfaces (SuGAR, 2DGS) and to semantic maps with foundation-model features (LangSplat, FMGS).
  2. For SLAM, a splat map offers end-to-end optimization like a neural field, plus fast rendering and freely allocated primitives.
  3. Tracking is gradient descent on the pose through the renderer. It needs the rendered and recorded images to overlap.
  4. Systems range from end-to-end (RGB-D, monocular MonoGS) to hybrids that track with ORB features, ICP, or LiDAR.
  5. Open problems: optimization speed, tracking accuracy on real data, dynamic scenes, and large outdoor scenes.

Sources

  1. SLAM Handbook, §14.3.2 "Applications of 3D Gaussian Splatting", §14.3.3 "3D Gaussian Splatting for SLAM", §14.4 "Further Readings & Recent Trends", pp. 410–416, Figures 14.15–14.21.
  2. The pose gradient in "Filling the gap" is the chain rule applied to equations (14.5) and (14.7) in the 2D setting of Day 4. The tracking widget is this course's own toy, not a system from the book.

Week 20 · Review

Week 20 review: maps built by rendering

After today you can render a pixel by hand from densities or from Gaussians, project a Gaussian covariance into the image, and weigh NeRF-style and splat maps against the needs of SLAM.

About 60 min · No new pages

The week in one paragraph

Chapter 14 treats the map as whatever set of parameters an image can be rendered from by a differentiable procedure. Render, compare with the camera's image, and push the gradient of the difference back into the parameters, which may include the camera pose. NeRF stores density and colour as a field and renders by marching along each pixel's ray: a pixel is a sum of sample colours weighted by transmittance times opacity. How the field is stored (one MLP, a grid, points) decides its speed, its size, whether it fills holes, whether it can grow, and whether it forgets. 3D Gaussian splatting keeps the same blending sum but gets its opacities from explicit Gaussian primitives projected onto the image, which renders far faster and gives SLAM primitives it can add and move. Both are slow to optimize and, as trackers, still less accurate than classical sparse methods.

1. Formula sheet

What it isFormulaWhere
Radiance field and camera ray\(f_\Theta(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{d}) \to (\mathbf{c}, \sigma)\), \(\;\mathbf{r}(t) = \mathbf{o} + t\mathbf{d}\)§14.2.1 · p. 402 · Day 2
Transmittance\(T(t) = \exp\bigl(-\int_{t_n}^{t}\sigma(s)\,ds\bigr)\)p. 402 · Day 2
Volume rendering integral\(C(\mathbf{r}) = \int_{t_n}^{t_f} T(t)\,\sigma(t)\,\mathbf{c}(t)\,dt\)(14.1) · p. 402 · Day 2
Quadrature\(\hat{C} = \sum_i T_i\alpha_i\mathbf{c}_i\), \(\;\alpha_i = 1 - e^{-\sigma_i\delta_i}\), \(\;T_i = \prod_{j \lt i}(1 - \alpha_j)\)(14.2) · pp. 402–403 · Day 2
Weights and expected depth\(w_i = T_i\alpha_i = T_i - T_{i+1}\), \(\;\sum_i w_i = 1 - T_{N+1}\), \(\;\hat{D} = \sum_i w_i t_i\)Day 2 (depth in words on p. 403)
Photometric loss\(L = \sum_{\mathbf{r} \in R}\norm{\hat{C}(\mathbf{r}) - C_{gt}(\mathbf{r})}_2^2\)(14.3) · p. 403 · Day 2
Linear interpolation on a grid\(f = (1 - s)f_i + s f_{i+1}\); trilinear: products of three such weights over 8 cornersDay 3
Gaussian covariance\(\boldsymbol{\Sigma} = \mathbf{R}\mathbf{S}\mathbf{S}\T\mathbf{R}\T\)(14.4) · p. 409 · Day 4
Projected covariance\(\boldsymbol{\Sigma}' = \mathbf{J}\mathbf{W}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\mathbf{W}\T\mathbf{J}\T\), \(\;\mathbf{J} = \begin{bmatrix} 1/z & 0 & -x/z^2 \\ 0 & 1/z & -y/z^2 \end{bmatrix}\)(14.5) · p. 410 · Day 4
Splat blending\(C = \sum_i \mathbf{c}_i\alpha_i\prod_{j \lt i}(1 - \alpha_j)\), \(\;\alpha_i = o_i\,G_{2D}(\mathbf{x}_{2D})\)(14.6), (14.7) · p. 410 · Day 4
3DGS loss\(\mathcal{L} = (1 - \lambda)\mathcal{L}_1 + \lambda\mathcal{L}_{\text{SSIM}}\)(14.8) · p. 410 · Day 4

2. Mixed quiz

Check yourself

Q1. What does volume rendering give an optimizer that rendering a hard surface does not?

Every sample on the ray contributes to the pixel through its opacity, so the loss can ask for matter at an empty point. A hard surface gives zero gradient with respect to its position except at outlines.

Q2. A ray segment has density σ = 1 and length δ = 0.2. What is its opacity?

α = 1 − e^(−0.2) = 0.181. For small σδ this is close to σδ = 0.2, but never larger.

Q3. Three samples on a ray have opacities 0.2, 0.5, 1.0, nearest first. What are their weights?

w₁ = 0.2. T₂ = 0.8, so w₂ = 0.8 × 0.5 = 0.4. T₃ = 0.8 × 0.5 = 0.4, so w₃ = 0.4 × 1.0 = 0.4. They sum to 1 because the last sample is opaque.

Q4. Which two properties does Table 14.1 rate "Good" for a single MLP?

An MLP is compact and smooth, so it compresses and fills small holes. It is rated "Limited" on speed, dynamic allocation, and forgetting.

Q5. A field is stored on a 3D grid and read by trilinear interpolation. A gradient step on the loss of one sample point changes how many stored values?

The interpolated value depends only on the eight corners of the cell that contains the sample, so only those have a non-zero derivative. This locality is why grids forget less than a global function.

Q6. A Gaussian on the optical axis is moved from depth 2 to depth 6 without changing Σ. What happens to the standard deviation of its footprint?

On the axis J = [1/z, 0], so σ′ = σₓ/z. Three times the depth gives one third of the width. The variance, σ′², falls to one ninth.

Q7. At one pixel, Gaussians A and B both have α = 0.5, with A in front. Then B is moved in front of A, with both α unchanged. What is A's weight now?

Behind B, A receives only the transmittance 1 − 0.5 = 0.5, so its weight is 0.5 × 0.5 = 0.25. In front it was 0.5. Depth order matters.

Q8. What does the book name as the main obstacle to using NeRF- or 3DGS-based SLAM on a real-time robot?

3DGS renders in real time. The cost is in the many gradient steps per frame, which is why compact representations, higher-order optimizers, and feed-forward prediction are proposed.

3. Pen-and-paper problems

  1. A ray is sampled at four points with equal spacing \(\delta = 0.5\). The densities are \(\sigma = (0,\ 1,\ 0,\ 4)\), the sample positions are \(t = (0.5,\ 1.0,\ 1.5,\ 2.0)\), and the grey levels at samples 2 and 4 are \(1.0\) and \(0.2\). Compute every \(\alpha_i\), \(T_i\), and \(w_i\), the pixel value over a black background, the light that passes all four samples, and the expected depth.

    Solution

    \(\alpha_1 = \alpha_3 = 0\). \(\alpha_2 = 1 - e^{-0.5} = 0.3935\). \(\alpha_4 = 1 - e^{-2} = 0.8647\).

    \(T_1 = T_2 = 1\). \(T_3 = T_4 = 1 - 0.3935 = 0.6065\). \(T_5 = 0.6065 \times (1 - 0.8647) = 0.0821\).

    \(w_2 = 0.3935\), \(w_4 = 0.6065 \times 0.8647 = 0.5244\), the others are 0. Check: \(0.3935 + 0.5244 + 0.0821 = 1\).

    Pixel: \(0.3935 \times 1.0 + 0.5244 \times 0.2 = 0.498\). Expected depth: \(0.3935 \times 1.0 + 0.5244 \times 2.0 = 1.44\).

  2. (a) Show that \(w_i = T_i - T_{i+1}\). (b) Deduce that \(\sum_{i=1}^{N} w_i = 1 - T_{N+1}\). (c) A ray crosses fog of constant density \(\sigma = 0.4\) over a length of 5, cut into \(N\) equal segments. Show that the total weight does not depend on \(N\), and compute it.

    Solution

    (a) By definition \(T_{i+1} = T_i(1 - \alpha_i)\), so \(T_i - T_{i+1} = T_i\alpha_i = w_i\).

    (b) The sum telescopes: \((T_1 - T_2) + (T_2 - T_3) + \dots + (T_N - T_{N+1}) = T_1 - T_{N+1} = 1 - T_{N+1}\).

    (c) \(T_{N+1} = \exp(-\sum_j \sigma\delta_j) = \exp(-0.4 \times 5) = e^{-2} = 0.135\), whatever the number of segments, because the lengths always add up to 5. The total weight is \(1 - 0.135 = 0.865\). This is the reason opacity is defined as \(1 - e^{-\sigma\delta}\) and not as \(\sigma\delta\): the result must not depend on how finely a uniform region is cut.

  3. A 2D world with the camera at the origin looking along \(z\) and the image line at \(z = 1\). Gaussian A is at \((x, z) = (0.5, 2)\) with \(\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_A = \diag(0.09, 0.01)\), opacity 0.9, grey level 1.0. Gaussian B is at \((0, 4)\) with \(\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_B = \diag(0.64, 0.04)\), opacity 0.8, grey level 0. The background has grey level 0.5. Find each footprint's centre and standard deviation, then the value of the pixel at \(u = 0.25\).

    Solution

    A: \(\mu'_A = 0.5/2 = 0.25\). \(\mathbf{J} = [\,1/z \;\; -x/z^2\,] = [\,0.5 \;\; -0.125\,]\). \(\sigma'^2_A = 0.25 \times 0.09 + 0.0156 \times 0.01 = 0.0227\), so \(\sigma'_A = 0.151\).

    B: \(\mu'_B = 0\). \(\mathbf{J} = [\,0.25 \;\; 0\,]\). \(\sigma'^2_B = 0.0625 \times 0.64 = 0.04\), so \(\sigma'_B = 0.2\).

    At \(u = 0.25\): the pixel is at A's centre, so \(\alpha_A = 0.9\). For B, \(G = \exp(-0.25^2 / (2 \times 0.04)) = e^{-0.781} = 0.458\), so \(\alpha_B = 0.8 \times 0.458 = 0.366\).

    A is nearer, so it is blended first. Weights: A \(0.9\); B \(0.1 \times 0.366 = 0.037\); background \(0.1 \times 0.634 = 0.063\). Pixel: \(0.9 \times 1.0 + 0.037 \times 0 + 0.063 \times 0.5 = 0.932\).

  4. Tracking as least squares. In the same 2D world the camera's sideways position \(c\) is unknown. The centre of a Gaussian at \((1, 2)\) is observed at \(u_1 = 0.35\), and the centre of a Gaussian at \((-1, 4)\) at \(u_2 = -0.33\). (a) Write the predicted centres as functions of \(c\) and the residuals at \(c = 0\). (b) Take one Gauss-Newton step from \(c = 0\) (Week 2 · Day 4). (c) Which Gaussian influences the answer more, and why?

    Solution

    (a) \(\mu'_1(c) = (1 - c)/2\) and \(\mu'_2(c) = (-1 - c)/4\). At \(c = 0\) they are \(0.5\) and \(-0.25\), so the residuals (predicted minus observed) are \(r_1 = 0.15\) and \(r_2 = 0.08\).

    (b) The Jacobians are \(J_1 = -1/2\) and \(J_2 = -1/4\). Gauss-Newton solves \((J_1^2 + J_2^2)\,\Delta = -(J_1 r_1 + J_2 r_2)\): \(0.3125\,\Delta = 0.075 + 0.02 = 0.095\), so \(\Delta = 0.304\) and \(c = 0.304\). The predictions are linear in \(c\), so this single step is the exact least-squares answer. The residuals fall to \(-0.002\) and \(0.004\).

    (c) Gaussian 1. Alone it would give \(c = 0.30\), and Gaussian 2 alone \(c = 0.32\); the answer \(0.304\) sits close to the first. Its Jacobian is twice as large because it is half as far away, so it carries four times the weight in \(J_1^2 + J_2^2\). Nearby structure moves more in the image when the camera translates, and therefore constrains the translation more.

You are ready for next week if you can

  • Describe the differentiable rendering loop and say which quantities can sit among its parameters.
  • Compute opacities, transmittances, weights, a pixel value, and an expected depth for a short list of samples.
  • Explain the five rows of Table 14.1 and why a global function forgets.
  • Project a Gaussian's covariance with \(\mathbf{J}\mathbf{W}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\mathbf{W}\T\mathbf{J}\T\) and blend sorted Gaussians at a pixel.
  • Name the static-world assumption among the open problems of §14.4. Next week's chapter is about scenes that move and deform.

Sources

  1. SLAM Handbook, Chapter 14 "Map Representations with Differentiable Volume Rendering", pp. 397–416.
  2. Mildenhall et al., NeRF: Representing Scenes as Neural Radiance Fields for View Synthesis, 2020; Max, Optical Models for Direct Volume Rendering, 1995; Zwicker, Pfister, van Baar, Gross, EWA Volume Splatting, 2001 (the derivations added on Days 2 and 4).

Week 21 · Day 1

When the world moves: short-term, long-term, and deformable scenes

After today you can classify a changing scene as short-term dynamic, long-term dynamic, or deformable from how fast it changes relative to how often the robot observes it, and place a method on the chapter's three design axes.

About 60 min · Read Ch. 15 opening and §15.1, pp. 417–423 (7 pages, three of them mostly figures) · Needs Week 6 Day 1

Read first: Chapter 15 opening and §15.1, pp. 417–423

While you read, look for:

  • The sentence on p. 419 that says what the short-term / long-term distinction depends on, and what it does not depend on.
  • Examples A–D under Figure 15.2 (p. 420), and Figure 15.3 (p. 421): one motion, two robots, two verdicts.
  • What an offline method has that an online method cannot have (top of p. 423).

Today's big idea

Every method so far assumed that only the robot moves. Real scenes change, and the kind of change is defined by what the robot sees. If the scene changes little between two observations, the change looks smooth and can be tracked (short-term dynamics). If it changes a lot, it looks like a jump and must be re-identified (long-term dynamics). When no part of the scene is static, the problem is deformable SLAM.

1. What the static-world assumption bought us

The static-world assumption says the scene does not change and only the robot moves. Two results rest on it. A feature that is detected again constrains the robot pose, because the feature is taken to be where it was (Chapter 1, Week 2 · Day 1). A dense map can be built by fusing many posed observations, because they show the same surfaces (Chapter 5, Week 8 · Day 1). The chapter opens with three scenes where it fails: a car in city traffic, a home robot whose users rearrange the room, and a surgical robot inside the body, where there is no static background and everything deforms. Ch. 15 opening · p. 417

The oldest remedy lets outlier rejection (RANSAC, Week 6 · Day 2) separate measurements that move consistently with the sensor from those that move on their own, as the stars move together while the planets wander.

Filling the gap: how much damage does one moving object do?

A robot drives forward 1.00 m between two frames and tracks 10 features. In its own frame each static feature appears to shift by \(-1.00\) m. Three features sit on a truck that drove forward 0.60 m in the same time, so they shift by only \(-0.40\) m. Least squares picks the shift \(s\) that minimizes \(\sum_i (s_i - s)^2\), the mean:

\[ \hat{s} = \frac{7 \times (-1.00) + 3 \times (-0.40)}{10} = -0.82 \ \text{m}. \]

The robot concludes it moved 0.82 m, an 18 cm error from one frame pair, repeated for as long as the truck is in view. The median of the ten shifts is \(-1.00\) m, the right answer: the robust-estimation idea of Week 6 · Day 1.

Now let the truck cover six of the ten features. The mean is \(-0.64\) m and the median is \(-0.40\) m. The consensus is now the truck. Rejection works only while the static scene holds the majority.

2. Short-term and long-term: a ratio, not a duration

The book classifies dynamics by how they appear in the observations. Short-term dynamics give observations that change gradually (transient characteristics). Long-term dynamics give observations that change abruptly. Almost every physical process is continuous if sampled often enough, so the class does not depend on how long the process takes. It depends on the relation between the rate of change of the scene and the rate of observation of the robot. §15.1.1 · p. 419

Filling the gap: put a number on the ratio

An object moving at speed \(v\), observed \(f\) times per second, moves

\[ d = \frac{v}{f} \]

between two observations. Compare \(d\) with the distance to the nearest thing the object could be confused with. If \(d\) is much smaller, each detection is closest to its own previous position and the object is easy to follow. If \(d\) is larger, the nearest detection is often something else, and the object must be recognized again from its appearance or shape.

Example D of Figure 15.2: a tennis ball at 250 km/h is \(69.4\) m/s. At 340 Hz it moves \(69.4/340 = 0.20\) m between frames, so a very fast object still gives a smooth track. A person walking at 1.5 m/s seen by a 10 Hz LiDAR moves 0.15 m per scan; seen once a minute, up to 90 m.

The other examples of Figure 15.2 follow the same logic. Plant growth measured daily (A) is short-term although the rate is very low, because plants grow little in a day. A building patrolled daily (B) is long-term, because parts of it change completely between patrols, and so are objects rearranged while the robot was gone for a minute (C). Figure 15.2 · p. 420

In most robotics the two rates are of the same order: objects move at about \(10^{-1}\) to \(10^{2}\) m/s and sensors run at about \(10^{0}\) to \(10^{3}\) Hz. The sensor then sees motion as continuous whenever the object is in view, and the distinction becomes simple: short-term is motion within view, long-term is change that happened out of view. §15.1.1 · p. 419

Try it: eight identical objects, one observer. Lower the observation rate step by step.

Notice: at 1.5 m/s and 10 Hz each object moves 0.15 m between observations, about an eighth of the distance to its nearest neighbour, and 99% of the nearest-neighbour matches are right. At 0.5 Hz it moves 3 m, twice that distance, and 15% are right, close to the 12.5% of a blind guess among eight. Then set 3 m/s and 20 Hz: the picture is the same as at the start, because only \(v/f\) matters.

3. The observer decides

Since the class depends on the observations, it is not a property of the object or of the environment. The same physical motion can be short-term for one robot and long-term for another. §15.1.1 · pp. 419–421, Figure 15.3

The book's example is a bottle that a person picks up and puts down next to where it stood: a robot that sees the table only before and after sees a bottle that jumped. Mapping a place in several sessions is the extreme case, with the scene static during each visit and the changes piling up in between. §15.1.1 · p. 419 Both classes assume some static background. In endoscopic surgery the whole scene moves and deforms around the sensor; this setting with no static part is deformable SLAM (Day 5). §15.1.1 · p. 420

Papers use other words. Dynamic or high-dynamic means short-term. Semi-static, quasi-static, or low-dynamic means long-term: objects that could move but stand still while observed, or changes between visits. Spatio-temporal or 4D models keep the history of the scene, 3D plus time (not radar's 4D, whose fourth dimension is velocity). Lifelong, persistent, or continuous systems cope with a varying environment over long time spans. §15.1.1.1 · pp. 420–421

The classes also mix: one rigid moving object, a person who moves and deforms, a building that changes only between patrols, a home with all of these. Estimating every effect jointly gets, in the book's words, exponentially more complex, so knowing which effects to expect allows a narrower system that works better. §15.1.1.2 · pp. 421–422

4. Three axes for placing a method

Figure 15.1 organizes the chapter along three questions. §15.1 · pp. 418–419

AxisThe questionValues
1. Observation characteristicsWhich dynamic effects appear in the observations?Short-term, long-term
2. Level of reconstructionHow much must the robot understand for its task?Pose → scene geometry → temporal scene understanding
3. Time criticalityWhen, and how fast, must the answer be ready?Online, offline

Ordinary pose-graph SLAM sits at one corner: pose only, online, moving parts rejected as outliers. Multi-session change detection sits far from it: a detailed account of how a scene evolved, from a few sessions. Figure 15.1 · p. 418

Axis 2. If the application needs only the robot state, it is often adequate to treat dynamic observations as outliers and localize against the static background. If a dense map is wanted, the robot must detect and represent the motion and change. §15.1.2 · p. 422

Axis 3. Robots mostly must act at once, so the chapter concentrates on real-time methods. Offline processing has more computation and all the data: to decide whether something in frame \(F_t\) moved, it can use the later frames \(F_{t+1}, \dots, F_T\), which an online method has not seen yet. §15.1.3 · pp. 422–423

The week follows the chapter: short-term dynamics on Day 2, long-term on Days 3 and 4, deformable SLAM on Day 5.

Common mistakes

  • "Long-term means slow, or a long time ago." A bottle moved during the minute the robot looked away is long-term. Plant growth measured daily is short-term. Only the ratio of the two rates counts.
  • "Robust estimation always finds the static scene." It finds the largest consistent group. When a moving object fills most of the view, that group is the object.

Check yourself

Q1. A 10 Hz LiDAR watches a cyclist riding at 6 m/s. How far does the cyclist move between two scans?

d = v / f = 6 / 10 = 0.6 m, small next to the spacing of road users, so the cyclist can be followed from scan to scan.

Q2. A camera photographs a glacier once a day. Between photos the ice moves 30 cm, and its distinctive features are about 20 m apart. How do these dynamics appear to the camera?

The change between observations (0.3 m) is small compared with the feature spacing (20 m), as in example A. Neither the low rate nor the duration decides it.

Q3. A robot tracks 10 features. Eight are static and appear to shift by −0.50 m. Two are on a moving cart and appear to shift by −0.10 m. What forward motion does plain least squares report?

The mean shift is (8 × (−0.50) + 2 × (−0.10)) / 10 = −0.42 m, so the robot reports 0.42 m instead of 0.50 m.

Q4. What can an offline method use to decide whether a point in frame t belongs to a moving object, that an online method cannot?

Offline, frames t+1 … T are already recorded. Online methods cannot use the future.

Recap

  1. The static-world assumption lets a re-detected feature constrain the pose and posed observations be fused. Moving things break both.
  2. Short-term dynamics look smooth to the robot, long-term dynamics look like jumps. The class is set by rate of change against rate of observation: \(d = v/f\) against the spacing of confusable things.
  3. In practice short-term means motion in view and long-term means change out of view; the same motion can be either. Deformable SLAM is the case with no static part.
  4. A method is placed by three axes: which dynamics it sees, how much it reconstructs, and whether it runs online or offline.

Sources

  1. SLAM Handbook, Chapter 15 opening and §15.1 "Characterizing the Dynamic SLAM Problem", pp. 417–423, Figures 15.1–15.3.
  2. The mean-versus-median example and \(d = v/f\) are arithmetic added by this course; robust estimation is Week 6 (SLAM Handbook, Chapter 3).

Week 21 · Day 2

Short-term dynamics: discard moving objects, track them, or reconstruct them

After today you can name the cues used to reject moving objects, write the factors that add a rigidly moving object to a SLAM factor graph, and outline how dense dynamic SLAM tracks and reconstructs objects.

About 60 min · Read §15.2, pp. 423–432 (9 pages, five of them half figures) · Needs Week 4 Day 2 and Week 11 Day 5

Read first: §15.2, pp. 423–432

While you read, look for:

  • The six families of cues for removing dynamic objects (pp. 424–426), and the weakness named for RANSAC and for semantic segmentation.
  • Figure 15.6 and equations (15.1)–(15.4), pp. 427–428. For each factor, find which variables it touches.
  • The four steps of simultaneous tracking and reconstruction (pp. 430–431).

Today's big idea

A moving object in view can be handled at three levels. Throw its measurements away and localize on the rest. Or keep them and add the object to the factor graph as a rigid body with its own pose and velocity at every time step. Or build a dense model of it.

1. Three levels of ambition

The first methods found the measurements explained by the sensor's own motion, with statistical tests, RANSAC, or the Hough transform, and discarded the rest as outliers. Later work also filled in what the moving object had hidden, because a map without holes localizes better. The alternative is to track the objects inside SLAM, which computer vision calls multi-body structure from motion; it was first judged too expensive, has recently become feasible, and may be needed to avoid collisions. Beyond tracking lies dense reconstruction of the objects, which manipulation needs. §15.2 · pp. 423–424

2. Removing dynamic objects

Discarding is simple and still effective: the persistent parts of the scene are usually what the map is for, and geometric estimation assumes rigidity, so moving parts show up as measurements that do not fit a rigid model. The book groups the cues into six families; current systems combine several. §15.2.1 · pp. 424–426

CueHow it separates robot motion from object motionCaveat
Proprioceptive sensingAn IMU or odometry does not observe the scene, so scene motion cannot affect itMust be fused with the other sensors (Chapters 11, 12)
Robust estimationMeasurements are redundant. RANSAC takes the largest consensus set at initialization; robust losses damp large residuals afterwards (Week 6 · Day 4)For low rates of dynamic content: under large occlusion the largest consensus set may be a moving object
Multi-view motion cuesA state is removed once its count of high-residual measurements passes a threshold (Figure 15.4)Decides only after evidence has accumulated
Semantic informationA segmentation network masks classes that can moveClosed-set networks miss objects, and "can move" is not "is moving" (parked cars); combine with geometric checks
Domain knowledgeA car cannot slide sideways, so features implying sideways motion are outliersOnly where such knowledge exists
Motion-aware sensorsEvent cameras; radars and some LiDARs measure point velocity by DopplerStill under active investigation

3. Tracking: one rigid body per object in the factor graph

Tracking objects alongside SLAM is also called multi-object tracking (MOT). The central modelling decision is that each dynamic object is a rigid moving body. The front-end extracts features as before and uses semantic masks to assign points to objects. §15.2.2 · pp. 426–427

VariableMeaning
\(\mathbf{T}^w_i \in \SE(3)\)Camera pose at time \(t_i\) in the world frame \(\mathcal{F}^w\)
\(\mathbf{x}^w_l \in \R^3\)Static map point \(l\), in the world frame
\(\mathbf{T}^w_{k,i} \in \SE(3)\)Pose of object \(k\) at \(t_i\): object frame \(\mathcal{F}^k\) to world frame
\(\mathbf{v}^k_i,\ \boldsymbol{\omega}^k_i \in \R^3\)Linear and angular velocity of object \(k\) at \(t_i\), in the object frame
\(\mathbf{x}^k_j \in \R^3\)Point \(j\) on object \(k\), in the object frame; no time index

The reprojection error of an object point is §15.2.2 · p. 427

\[ \mathbf{e}^{i,j,k}_{\text{reproj}} = \mathbf{z}^i_j - \pi\!\left( \left(\mathbf{T}^w_i\right)^{-1} \mathbf{T}^w_{k,i}\, \tilde{\mathbf{x}}^k_j \right), \tag{15.1} \]

with \(\tilde{\mathbf{x}}^k_j\) the point in homogeneous coordinates, \(\mathbf{z}^i_j\) its pixel in image \(i\), and \(\pi\) the projection. Read it right to left: the object pose takes the point to the world frame, the inverse camera pose takes it to the camera frame, and \(\pi\) takes it to a pixel. Compared with the static reprojection error of Week 11 · Day 5 there is one extra transform, and it is an unknown that changes with time. The problem stays solvable because the points \(\mathbf{x}^k_j\) are shared by all frames.

Two more factors tie the object's poses together over time. Velocity is assumed constant between consecutive observations, and velocity is coupled to pose by comparing where a point is under the next pose with where the motion model puts it: §15.2.2 · pp. 427–428

\[ \mathbf{e}^{i,k}_{\text{vcte}} = \begin{bmatrix} \mathbf{v}^k_{i+1} - \mathbf{v}^k_i \\ \boldsymbol{\omega}^k_{i+1} - \boldsymbol{\omega}^k_i \end{bmatrix}, \tag{15.2} \] \[ \mathbf{e}^{i,j,k}_{\text{vcte},\mathbf{x}} = h^{-1}\!\left( \left( \mathbf{T}^w_{k,i+1} - \mathbf{T}^w_{k,i}\, \Delta\mathbf{T}^{k,i}_{k,i+1} \right) \tilde{\mathbf{x}}^k_j \right), \tag{15.3} \] \[ \Delta\mathbf{T}^{k,i}_{k,i+1} = \begin{bmatrix} \Exp\!\left( \boldsymbol{\omega}^k_i\, (t_{i+1} - t_i) \right) & \mathbf{v}^k_i\, (t_{i+1} - t_i) \\ \mathbf{0} & 1 \end{bmatrix}, \tag{15.4} \]

where \(h^{-1} : (x, y, z, \lambda) \mapsto (x/\lambda,\ y/\lambda,\ z/\lambda)\) and \(\Exp\) is the rotation exponential of Week 4 · Day 2.

Filling the gap: equations (15.3) and (15.4) with numbers

Why the increment multiplies on the right. The velocities are expressed in the object frame, and a motion described in a body's own frame is applied after the current pose: the predicted pose is \(\mathbf{T}^w_{k,i}\, \Delta\mathbf{T}\).

How to read \(h^{-1}\). Both \(\mathbf{T}^w_{k,i+1}\tilde{\mathbf{x}}\) and \(\mathbf{T}^w_{k,i}\Delta\mathbf{T}\tilde{\mathbf{x}}\) are homogeneous points with last entry 1, so their difference has last entry 0. Read (15.3) as the difference of the two Euclidean points: a 3-vector, zero when the pose estimate and the motion model agree.

A planar example. An object is at world position \((4, 2)\) m, heading \(90^\circ\). In its own frame \(\mathbf{v} = (2, 0)\) m/s and \(\omega = 0.5\) rad/s; the time step is 0.2 s. Then \(\Delta\mathbf{T}\) is a rotation by \(0.1\) rad with translation \((0.4, 0)\) m, and the predicted pose has

\[ \text{position } \begin{bmatrix} 4 \\ 2 \end{bmatrix} + \begin{bmatrix} 0 & -1 \\ 1 & 0 \end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix} 0.4 \\ 0 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 4 \\ 2.4 \end{bmatrix}, \qquad \text{heading } 90^\circ + 5.73^\circ = 95.73^\circ . \]

The object point \(\mathbf{x}^k_j = (1, 0)\) is then predicted at \((4 + \cos 95.73^\circ,\ 2.4 + \sin 95.73^\circ) = (3.900,\ 3.395)\). If the current estimate of \(\mathbf{T}^w_{k,i+1}\) is position \((4.05, 2.38)\), heading \(96^\circ\), it puts the point at \((3.945,\ 3.375)\). The residual (15.3) is the difference, \((0.045,\ -0.020)\) m. The optimizer reduces it by changing the two poses, the velocity, or all three.

The widget is the same graph reduced to a plane without rotation: positions \(\mathbf{p}_i\) and velocities \(\mathbf{v}_i\), a velocity factor \(\mathbf{v}_{i+1} - \mathbf{v}_i\) as in (15.2), a coupling factor \(\mathbf{p}_{i+1} - \mathbf{p}_i - \mathbf{v}_i \Delta t\) as in (15.3), and position measurements standing in for reprojection. All are linear, so one solve of the normal equations (Week 2 · Day 3) gives the answer.

Try it: lower "velocity change allowed per step", then switch the motion factors off.

Notice: with the default settings the measurements are off by 0.36 m (RMS) and the estimate by 0.19 m, and through the six hidden steps the estimate stays within 0.10 m of the truth with no measurement there. Set the allowed velocity change to 0.02 m/s: the estimate straightens, and its error (0.43 m) is worse than the raw measurements. Constant velocity is a prior, and its weight has to match how the object really moves. With the motion factors off there is no estimate in the gap at all.

The book's examples: Multimotion Visual Odometry (MVO) segments tracklets into clusters that each move rigidly. VDO-SLAM, Dynamic SLAM, and DynaSLAM II introduce the factor-graph approach. AirDOS extends it to articulated objects, connected rigid bodies such as a human skeleton. §15.2.2 · p. 428

4. Dense dynamic SLAM

Dense dynamic SLAM also wants a dense reconstruction that includes the moving things. Most systems split the work into a localization step, which tracks the robot against the static background with the methods above, and a mapping step, which represents the background and the dynamic entities. §15.2.3 · p. 428

ApproachIdeaNotes from the book
Moving object segmentation (MOS)Label every point or pixel as moving or not; ignore the moving ones or keep them as a low-level recordDetection must be dense. Geometric cues: tracking residuals (StaticFusion) or consistency with the fused map (Dynablox). Semantic cues: mask classes such as people. Learned classifiers may not generalize out of domain.
Parametric modelsIf the kind of object is known, estimate the parameters of a shape model as factor-graph variablesUsed most for people: skeletons or SMPL meshes
Simultaneous tracking and reconstructionA separate dense model per moving object, usually assumed rigid, plus one for the backgroundNeeds no prior model. Objects are mostly TSDF volumes (Week 8 · Day 2).

Simultaneous tracking and reconstruction mostly follows four steps per image: detect the objects (segmentation refined by geometry and motion cues), track the camera against the background, track each object against the current image (usually with direct methods), and fuse each object's pixels into its own model. §15.2.3.3 · pp. 430–431 The price is computation, and a feedback loop: a tracking error fuses misaligned measurements into the object's model, and the worse model degrades later tracking. The rigid assumption can be relaxed to articulated and deformable objects (Day 5). Finally, the reconstructed objects improve the robot's own pose only in corner cases, for example when more than 70% of the view is occluded and good motion models of the objects exist. §15.2.3.3 · pp. 431–432

Common mistakes

  • "Mask every car and person and the problem is solved." A parked car is a good landmark, and a closed-set network does not know every movable thing. Semantics says what could move; geometry says what did.

Check yourself

Q1. In equation (15.1), which product takes a point from the frame of object k to the camera frame at time i?

Read right to left: object frame to world, then world to camera.

Q2. An object is at world position (10, 5) m and faces along world −x. In its own frame v = (3, 0) m/s and ω = 0. Where does the constant-velocity model put it 0.1 s later?

The increment is 0.3 m along the object's own x axis, which points along world −x: (10, 5) + (−0.3, 0) = (9.7, 5).

Q3. A bus stops in front of the camera and fills 80% of the image, then pulls away. Which cue is least affected?

RANSAC's largest consensus set is now the bus, and a robust loss damps whatever disagrees with it. Proprioceptive sensing is not influenced by scene motion.

Q4. Why does an object point carry no time index, while the object's pose does?

Rigidity means the shape is constant in the object's own frame. All the motion is carried by the pose.

Recap

  1. Moving objects can be removed, tracked, or reconstructed, depending on what the task needs.
  2. Removal uses six kinds of cue: proprioception, robust estimation, multi-view residuals, semantics, domain knowledge, motion-aware sensors. Each has a failure case, so systems combine them.
  3. Tracking models each object as a rigid body: a pose and velocity per time step, points fixed in the object frame, and the factors (15.1), (15.2), and (15.3)–(15.4).
  4. Dense dynamic SLAM localizes against the background and maps background and objects, by segmentation, parametric models, or per-object dense models.

Sources

  1. SLAM Handbook, §15.2 "Short-term Dynamics and Dynamic SLAM", pp. 423–432, equations (15.1)–(15.4), Figures 15.4–15.9.
  2. Solà, Deray, Atchuthan, A micro Lie theory for state estimation in robotics, 2018 (right composition of body-frame increments).

Week 21 · Day 3

Long-term change: staying localized, cleaning the map, detecting what changed

After today you can explain how a lifelong SLAM system keeps localizing while a place changes, clear a ghost trail from a map with free-space evidence, and decide from two volumetric maps what appeared and what disappeared.

About 60 min · Read §15.3 opening, §15.3.1, and §15.3.2 up to Figure 15.11, pp. 432–439 (7 pages) · Needs Week 8 Day 1 and Week 3 Day 3

Read first: §15.3 opening to §15.3.2.2, pp. 432–439

While you read, look for:

  • The three reasons long-term dynamics are harder than short-term ones (p. 432).
  • When an experience-based map adds new data (p. 433), and what marginalization "bakes in" (p. 435).
  • The chair in the corner (p. 435).
  • Why change detection prefers occupancy or TSDF maps (p. 437), and the half-removed table (p. 438).

Today's big idea

Change that happens out of view cannot be tracked. The robot must keep localizing although the place looks different, remove from the map what should not be there, and work out what changed between visits. All three depend on telling "I did not look there" apart from "I looked and it was gone", and that is the information a volumetric map keeps as free space.

1. Why long-term change is harder

The book gives three reasons. §15.3 · p. 432 First, changes are abrupt and can be arbitrarily large, so data association can no longer be done by tracking and may need global re-identification; perceptual aliasing gets worse, because one landmark that has moved is seen in several positions. Second, effects that were negligible now matter: objects added, moved, or removed, structural change (a construction site), and appearance change from weather, time of day, and season. Third, more time and travel mean large viewpoint changes and degraded or replaced sensors.

2. Staying localized for a lifetime

Localizing in a changed place is close to place recognition, which also asks whether two views show the same place despite changes. The book describes three groups of ideas. §15.3.1 · p. 433

Parallel and summary maps. Each visit is an experience (or session), short enough that the robot can track through it. When the current experience localizes well against the stored ones, nothing is added. When localization is weak or fails, the new data is added, so the map grows only where the place's appearance varies. Experiences can be chained: if \(E_A\) cannot localize against \(E_C\) but both can against \(E_B\), then \(E_C \to E_B \to E_A\) still ties them together. Maps are sometimes summarized offline: a full bundle adjustment over all experiences, keeping only the features most likely to help later. §15.3.1.1 · p. 433

Appearance-invariant representations. Learned detectors, descriptors, and matchers let one feature match across appearances; they train on many conditions and use context up to the whole image. Semantics is a special case: a chair stays a chair, so the arrangement of objects can localize the robot even between aerial and ground views. Matches on moved objects must still be rejected. §15.3.1.2 · p. 434

Memory, scaling, and marginalization. A robot that never stops collects data without bound. §15.3.1.3 · pp. 434–435

StrategyHow it worksCost
ForgettingEach map point has a weight or persistence probability that decays with time; old points are pruned. Summarization ranks points, so the top N fit a memory budget.Information is discarded
Memory managementMap data moves in and out of the part being processed; RTAB-Map uses short-term, working, and long-term memoryExtra computation; capacity may still run out
MarginalizationOld nodes are replaced by one node carrying their marginal distributionThe marginalized part can no longer be changed

Filling the gap: what "baking in" means, with two numbers

Take two scalar poses. The new pose \(x_n\) has information 1 of its own, the old pose \(x_o\) has 3, and a loop closure between them has 2. In the order \((x_n, x_o)\):

\[ \boldsymbol{\Lambda} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 + 2 & -2 \\ -2 & 3 + 2 \end{bmatrix}, \qquad \Lambda'_{n} = 3 - \frac{(-2)(-2)}{5} = 2.2 . \]

The second expression marginalizes \(x_o\) with the Schur complement of Week 3 · Day 3. The graph now has one node with information 2.2: its own 1 plus 1.2 that arrived through the loop closure. If a later measurement shows the loop closure was a false match, the correct value is 1, but the factor no longer exists as a separate thing to switch off. Marginalization keeps information and loses the freedom to revise inlier and outlier decisions; when to do it is an open question. §15.3.1.3 · p. 435

3. Absence of evidence, and cleaning the map

A detector that fires is evidence that something is there. The reverse does not hold. The robot saw a chair in a corner; on the next visit it does not see it. §15.3.2 · p. 435

What happenedNameRight conclusion
The robot did not look into the cornerAbsence of evidenceNone; the chair may still be there
The robot looked and saw the corner emptyEvidence of absence (a negative detection)The chair is gone
The robot looked and the detector missed the chairA detector error"Gone" would be wrong

Maps built from positive detections therefore pile up outdated measurements. Map cleaning removes dynamic and spurious measurements so that only the static, persistent part of the scene remains, most often to filter the traces of moving objects out of one session. It is mostly done offline in two stages: first, globally consistent poses from robust bundle adjustment, with dynamic points ignored as outliers; second, with the poses fixed, every measurement is re-checked for consistency. Volumetric methods fuse everything by ray-casting into an occupancy or TSDF grid and test each cell, at a cost in memory and time. Visibility-based methods compare a subset of nearby measurements, often directly on the sensor data. §15.3.2.1 · p. 436

Filling the gap: how ray-casting erases a trail

Recall the log-odds update of Week 8 · Day 1: the cell where a beam ends gains \(l_{\text{hit}}\), and every cell the beam crossed loses \(l_{\text{miss}}\). The second half is the evidence of absence. A beam that reaches the far wall proves every cell on its path is empty now, whatever was recorded there before.

Use the widget's numbers: \(l_{\text{hit}} = 0.85\), \(l_{\text{miss}} = 0.40\), log-odds kept between \(-2\) and \(+3.5\), and a cell is solid when its log-odds is above 0.

  • A cell seen free for a long time sits at \(-2\). An object arrives: \(-2 \to -1.15 \to -0.30 \to +0.55\). It takes 3 hits to turn solid.
  • The object leaves: \(+0.55 \to +0.15 \to -0.25\). Free again after 2 misses.
  • Had the object stayed until the cell saturated at \(+3.5\), clearing would take \(\lceil 3.5 / 0.40 \rceil = 9\) misses.

So an object moving one cell per scan leaves a tail about one cell long, and a visitor that covers a cell for fewer than three scans never enters the map. A map that stores every hit point has neither mechanism: its trail is permanent.

Try it: press Play. Then set "Miss update" to 0, and after that slow the object down.

Notice: after 30 scans the point map holds 30 ghost cells along the object's path, and the occupancy grid holds 1, the cell the box left one scan ago. Both contain the same 86 wall and pillar cells, so clearing cost nothing. With the miss update at 0 the grid keeps all 30 ghosts: without free-space evidence it is the point map. At 0.2 cells per scan the box saturates its cells and drags a short pink tail, part of it in the box's own shadow where no beam can pass yet. The wedge behind the pillar stays "never observed": the grid does not claim it is free.

4. Change detection between sessions

Change detection establishes negative observations and other differences. A mapping robot can do it in 3D between submaps or sessions. Typically a robot scans a room in the morning and again in the evening, each session gives an internally consistent map, and the goal is what changed in between. The useful unit is the object, a piece of the scene that changes coherently: added, removed, or moved. §15.3.2.2 · p. 437

Occupancy and TSDF maps have proven most useful, because unlike a bare surface model they distinguish unobserved space from space observed to be free. Comparing two of them is called scene differencing. §15.3.2.2 · pp. 437–438

MorningEveningVerdict
Observed freeSurfaceSomething appeared
SurfaceObserved freeSomething disappeared
SurfaceSurfaceUnchanged; fuse the two for accuracy
Surface or freeNot observedNo verdict (absence of evidence); keep the morning data
Not observedSurface or freeNo verdict; the evening data completes the map

The sessions must first be registered into one frame. Each has its own drift, so one rigid alignment is often not enough; the best results come from jointly optimizing the alignment with inter-session constraints and bundle adjustment. §15.3.2.2 · p. 438

Semantics is added for three reasons. A label does not change with appearance (the appearance problem is handed to the detection network). It carries what geometry lacks: a sheet of paper taken from a table changes no surface. And objects, the things that move as a unit, largely coincide with detector classes such as mugs and chairs. §15.3.2.2 · p. 438

Semantic consistency is the problem that scenes change in coherent units but the robot sees parts. A table has been removed, and on the second visit half of its place is occluded. Differencing per cell removes the observed half and leaves half a table floating in the map. The options: rebuild the map from scratch each time, which is consistent but never accumulates a more complete model; detect change per object or semantic class, the usual choice; or wait for later observations to remove the leftovers. §15.3.2.2 · p. 438, Figure 15.11

Common mistakes

  • "I do not see it, so it is gone." Only if you looked. A cell or object outside the field of view, or occluded, has produced no evidence either way.
  • "A point cloud map can be cleaned by adding more scans." More scans add more points. Removal needs free-space reasoning: a ray passing through a stored point contradicts it.

Check yourself

Q1. An occupancy cell has log-odds +2.55. Each beam that passes through it subtracts 0.40. After how many passes is the cell no longer solid (log-odds at or below 0)?

2.55 / 0.40 = 6.4: six passes leave +0.15 and the seventh brings it to −0.25.

Q2. Region 1 is observed free in the morning and contains a surface in the evening. Region 2 has a surface in the morning and was not observed in the evening. What does scene differencing conclude?

Free then surface is a new surface. Surface then unobserved is absence of evidence, so the old surface is kept.

Q3. An experience-based map has five stored experiences of a corridor. Today the robot localizes well against them. What is added to the map?

New data is added only when localization is weak or fails, so the map grows with the variation of the place, not with the number of visits.

Q4. A node with information 4 is linked to an old node (own information 6) by a factor of information 3. The old node is marginalized. What information does the remaining node have?

The matrix is [[4+3, −3], [−3, 6+3]], and the Schur complement is 7 − 9/9 = 6: the node's own 4 plus 2 that came through the factor.

Recap

  1. Long-term change is abrupt and large, so it needs re-identification where short-term motion needs tracking.
  2. Lifelong localization stores several experiences of a place or uses appearance-invariant features, and bounds its memory by forgetting, memory management, or marginalization, which freezes earlier decisions.
  3. Not seeing something is evidence of absence only if the robot looked. Free-space ray-casting records exactly that, and it erases the trails of moving objects.
  4. Change detection compares registered volumetric maps: free-then-surface appeared, surface-then-free disappeared. Reasoning per object keeps the result semantically consistent.

Sources

  1. SLAM Handbook, §15.3 opening, §15.3.1 "Lifelong SLAM for Localization", §15.3.2.1–15.3.2.2, pp. 432–439, Figures 15.10–15.11.
  2. Thrun, Burgard, Fox, Probabilistic Robotics, 2005 (the log-odds occupancy update along a beam, used in the ray-casting note and the widget).

Week 21 · Day 4

Objects through time: re-localization, change-aware SLAM, and temporal patterns

After today you can explain how a moved object is found again, how change-aware SLAM tells real change from noise and pose error while the robot is running, and how a map can model when things change.

About 60 min · Read §15.3.2.3, §15.3.3, and §15.3.4, pp. 439–445 (7 pages) · Needs Week 21 Day 3 and Week 6 Day 5

Read first: §15.3.2.3 to §15.3.4, pp. 439–445

While you read, look for:

  • What makes object instance re-localization harder than place recognition (pp. 439–440), and the chairs-and-mug example.
  • The two extreme solutions and "local consistency" (p. 442).
  • How NeuSE, POV-SLAM, and Khronos each decide which object observations belong together (p. 443).
  • The three families of temporal models (p. 445).

Today's big idea

The object is the natural unit of long-term change. Finding a moved object again is a small place-recognition problem with few features and many look-alikes. Online, a mismatch between map and view can mean change, noise, or a wrong pose. Change-aware systems trust only short stretches of data that cannot have changed, reason per object, and keep for each object a probability that it is still there.

1. Objects from change, and finding them again

Change and objects explain each other. Object detection from changes clusters the surfaces that changed in a dense reconstruction into likely objects. It needs no semantic detector, but partial views mislead it: two touching objects removed together come out as one, and one object seen through occlusions comes out as several. §15.3.2.3 · p. 439

Object instance re-localization tracks an object through long-term changes: given an earlier and a later scan, decide which instances correspond and estimate each one's 6-DoF motion. It resembles place recognition, with four added difficulties. §15.3.2.3 · pp. 439–440

DifficultyDetail
Arbitrary motionAn object can move any distance between observations
Few featuresAn object is far smaller than a scene, and small objects seen from afar give few measurements
Perceptual aliasingA seminar room holds a hundred identical chairs. Which is which may not matter; one shared chair model could do. A mug among identical mugs matters to its owner. A remedy: accept unique matches, and keep several hypotheses when candidates look alike.
Closed or open setWith a fixed set of objects this is an optimal matching problem. If objects can be added and removed, a new, similar object is always an alternative explanation.

Solutions extract and match descriptors. One family puts several keypoints with descriptors on each object and solves for the 6-DoF transform from correspondences. The keypoints can be visual features or 3D descriptors such as FPFH and SHOT, which ignore appearance but describe only a local patch, so matches often need geometric verification; learned shape descriptors perform best. A second family computes a single descriptor per object. The networks are built \(\SE(3)\)-invariant, for matching across viewpoints, or \(\SE(3)\)-equivariant, for registering the matched objects. §15.3.2.3 · pp. 440–441

Filling the gap: invariant and equivariant, with three points

Let \(f\) turn a point set \(X\) into a descriptor and \(\mathbf{T}\) be a rigid motion. \(f\) is invariant if \(f(\mathbf{T}X) = f(X)\). It is equivariant if \(f(\mathbf{T}X) = \rho(\mathbf{T})\, f(X)\) for a known action \(\rho\): the descriptor moves with the object in a predictable way.

Take \(X = \{(0,0),\ (2,0),\ (0,1)\}\) and the same object rotated by \(90^\circ\) and shifted by \((5,5)\): \(Y = \{(5,5),\ (5,7),\ (4,5)\}\). The sorted pairwise distances are \(\{1,\ 2,\ \sqrt5\}\) for both: an invariant descriptor, which says "same object" and not where it went. The centroid is \((\tfrac23, \tfrac13)\) for \(X\) and \((\tfrac{14}{3}, \tfrac{17}{3})\) for \(Y\), which is the first centroid rotated by \(90^\circ\) to \((-\tfrac13, \tfrac23)\) and shifted by \((5,5)\): an equivariant descriptor, which reveals part of the motion. Hence invariance for matching, equivariance for registration.

2. Change-aware SLAM: change, noise, or a wrong pose?

Long-term change does not wait for the next session: a robot back from the kitchen after two minutes may find the living room changed. Change-aware SLAM detects and represents such changes during online operation. §15.3.3 · p. 441

This is harder than multi-session mapping. Changes can happen at any moment, so stationarity holds only over a short window, with little data to average out noise. And a pose error looks like change: with the pose estimate off by a metre, mapped surfaces seem absent although nothing moved. Localization and change detection need each other's answer. If every measurement is treated as an unchanged inlier, the registration averages true and false matches. If the whole old scene is declared changed, the open-loop estimate is trivially optimal and the map is neither complete nor consistent. §15.3.3 · p. 442

Two ideas keep the problem manageable. Object-level reasoning: measurements are first summarized locally into rigid semantic objects, and localization and change decisions are made per object, a much smaller problem that is semantically consistent by construction. Local consistency: detecting change on every raw frame lets a few noisy points mark an object as changed, while cautious rules fuse different things into one corrupted model. The way out is to find stretches of data guaranteed free of change. The minimum is data tracked from frame to frame, since the scene cannot change unobserved while the robot observes it; with assumptions on the rate of change and on odometry error this extends to a sliding or active window. §15.3.3 · p. 442

Filling the gap: a persistence probability

Several systems keep, for each object, a probability that it is still where the map says. The book gives no formula. The simplest model is a two-state Bayes filter, the mathematics of the occupancy cell of Week 8 · Day 1. Let \(p\) be the probability that the object is present and \(o = p/(1-p)\) its odds. The detector fires on a present object with probability \(P_D\) (recall) and on an empty spot with probability \(P_F\). Dividing Bayes' rule for "present" by Bayes' rule for "absent":

\[ o \leftarrow o \cdot \frac{P_D}{P_F} \ \ \text{(detected)}, \qquad o \leftarrow o \cdot \frac{1 - P_D}{1 - P_F} \ \ \text{(in view, not detected)}, \qquad o \leftarrow o \ \ \text{(not in view)}. \]

The third case is Day 3's absence of evidence: no measurement, no update. Forgetting is a separate step: before each visit \(p \leftarrow s\,p\), with \(s\) the probability that the object stayed put.

With \(P_D = 0.8\), \(P_F = 0.05\), \(s = 1\), starting at \(p = 0.5\): one detection multiplies the odds by 16, so \(p = 16/17 = 0.94\). Each look without a detection multiplies them by \(0.2/0.95 = 0.21\): odds \(16 \to 3.37 \to 0.71 \to 0.15\), so \(p = 0.77,\ 0.41,\ 0.13\). One miss does not remove the object, because the detector misses a fifth of the time. Three in a row do.

Try it: add your own sequence of visits with the three buttons.

Notice: in the example, two detections lift the probability to 0.99. Three visits with the object out of view lower it only to 0.85, and only because of the 0.95 survival factor. Two looks without a detection then take it to 0.47 and 0.15, and the object is removed. Raise the recall to 0.99 and a single miss is almost conclusive. The filter is this course's illustration, not any one system's model.

The systems the book describes: §15.3.3 · pp. 443–444, Figure 15.13

SystemWhat the book says it does
Panoptic Multi-TSDFsA first real-time change-aware mapping system, given consistent poses. Only active submaps, tracked frame to frame, are updated. Overlapping inactive submaps are discarded whole if they disagree and merged if they agree.
POCDSegments frames into objects and registers them against the current map, tolerating some odometry noise. A probabilistic persistence model per object is updated when the object is observed and when it should have been observed but was not.
NeuSELearns \(\SE(3)\)-equivariant neural object representations from partial views. Associations serve as loop-closure constraints; inconsistent or missing ones signal change.
POV-SLAMExpectation-maximization: alternates between poses given the associations, and associations and persistence probabilities given the layout
KhronosCreates candidate association factors between nearby objects and lets graduated non-convexity (Week 6 · Day 5) pick the inliers. A first dense spatio-temporal metric-semantic SLAM method: it also estimates when each change happened.
Changing-SLAMA first unified short- and long-term formulation, on top of ORB-SLAM. Object points are tracked frame to frame (short-term); untracked ones are associated globally to nearby objects of the same class (long-term). A persistence score lets undetected objects be forgotten.

3. Temporal scene understanding

A map can also capture the patterns behind the changes and predict how the scene will evolve. §15.3.4 · pp. 444–445

FamilyIdeaNotes from the book
Maps of dynamicsEstimate the typical motion patterns of a place from object trajectoriesConstant (a one-way road) or time-dependent (into the office in the morning, out in the evening)
Periodic eventsAssume a hidden periodic process drives the scene and estimate itFrequency maps (Krajnik et al.) keep only the dominant Fourier modes: compact, and able to predict future states
Learning-based methodsLearn to predict object-level change, typically on scene graphsFlexible; combine semantic priors with observations. Need more data, and change data is scarce.

Filling the gap: a door as a sum of cosines

A door is open every day from 08:00 to 18:00. Its state \(s(t)\) is 1 when open, with period 24 h, open fraction \(D = 10/24\), centred on 13:00. The Fourier series of this rectangular pulse train is

\[ s(t) = D + \sum_{n \ge 1} \frac{2}{n\pi} \sin(n\pi D)\, \cos\!\left( \frac{2\pi n\,(t - 13)}{24} \right). \]

Keep the mean and the first mode, whose amplitude is \(\tfrac{2}{\pi}\sin(75^\circ) = 0.615\):

\[ p(t) \approx 0.417 + 0.615 \cos\!\left( \frac{2\pi\,(t - 13)}{24} \right). \]

Predict "open" when \(p(t) \gt 0.5\). That needs \(\cos(\cdot) \gt 0.135\), which holds for \(|t - 13| \lt 5.48\) h: from 07:31 to 18:29. Three stored numbers predict the door on any future day to within half an hour.

Common mistakes

  • "The map and the view disagree, so the scene changed." A wrong pose produces the same disagreement. Change must be judged together with localization, or inside a locally consistent window.

Check yourself

Q1. An object's prior probability of being present is 0.5. The detector has recall 0.9 and fires on empty spots 10% of the time. The robot detects the object once, then looks again and does not detect it. What is the probability now (no forgetting)?

Odds start at 1. The detection multiplies them by 0.9/0.1 = 9, the miss by 0.1/0.9 = 1/9. The odds are back at 1, so p = 0.5.

Q2. You have matched a mug in two scans and now need the rigid transform between its two positions. Which kind of object descriptor helps with that step?

An invariant descriptor has discarded the pose. An equivariant one transforms with the object, so comparing two of them recovers the motion.

Q3. A robot returns to a room with a pose estimate that is 1 m off. Nothing has moved. What does per-frame change detection against the old map tend to report?

Pose error and scene change look alike.

Q4. A frequency map stores p(t) = 0.3 + 0.4 cos(2π(t − 14)/24) for a shop's shutter being open, t in hours. What does it predict at 20:00?

At 20:00 the argument is 2π·6/24 = 90°, whose cosine is 0, so p = 0.3, below 0.5: closed.

Recap

  1. Changed surfaces can be clustered into objects, and moved objects re-localized by matching descriptors: invariant ones to match, equivariant ones to register.
  2. Online, a mismatch can be change, noise, or pose error. Change-aware SLAM reasons per object and trusts only locally consistent data, at minimum what was tracked frame to frame.
  3. A persistence probability goes up with a detection, down with a look that finds nothing, and is untouched when the object was not in view.
  4. Temporal models go further: maps of dynamics, periodic models stored as a few Fourier modes, and learned predictors on scene graphs.

Sources

  1. SLAM Handbook, §15.3.2.3, §15.3.3 "Change-aware SLAM", §15.3.4 "Temporal Scene Understanding", pp. 439–445, Figures 15.12–15.13.
  2. Thrun, Burgard, Fox, Probabilistic Robotics, 2005 (the binary Bayes filter in odds form).
  3. Oppenheim and Willsky, Signals and Systems, 1997 (the Fourier series of a periodic rectangular pulse).

Week 21 · Day 5

Deformable SLAM: when nothing in the scene stands still

After today you can explain why reconstructing a deforming scene from one camera needs priors, evaluate an as-rigid-as-possible regularizer on a small deformation graph, and describe the tracking and mapping threads of a deformable SLAM system.

About 60 min · Read §15.4 and §15.5, pp. 446–453 (8 pages) · Needs Week 12 Day 1 and Week 8 Day 2

Read first: §15.4 and §15.5, pp. 446–453

While you read, look for:

  • The three panels of Figure 15.14 (p. 447): in each, what moves and what is fixed?
  • The template and the isometric deformation model (p. 447), and the "Floating Map Ambiguity" (p. 448).
  • The open questions under "Deformable SLAM" in §15.5 (p. 452).

Today's big idea

If every point may move freely in every frame, one camera does not provide enough equations to locate the points, let alone the camera. Deformable SLAM becomes solvable by assuming how surfaces deform: smoothly in time, like their neighbours, and without stretching. The rigid part of what the camera sees is then assigned to the camera's own motion and the rest to the scene.

1. The problem, and why it is under-constrained

If only part of the scene deforms, the robot localizes against the static background as on Day 2, and what remains is reconstruction of a deforming object with known sensor poses. Deformable SLAM is the general case with no visible rigid part. The motivating application is minimally invasive surgery, where a monocular camera sees only deforming organs. The related vision problem is non-rigid structure from motion (NRSfM): a point has a different 3D position in every frame, so the map stores a 3D trajectory per point. §15.4 · p. 446

Filling the gap: count the unknowns

Take \(N\) points seen in \(F\) images. Each observation is a pixel, two numbers.

ProblemUnknownsEquationsN = 100, F = 10
Rigid scene, moving camera (Week 11 · Day 5)\(3N + 6F - 7\), the 7 being the gauge freedom of Week 12 · Day 4\(2NF\)353 against 2000
Deforming scene, one fixed camera\(3NF\)\(2NF\)3000 against 2000
Deforming scene, depth camera\(3NF\)\(3NF\)3000 against 3000

In the middle row every point in every frame can slide along its viewing ray without changing any pixel: \(NF = 1000\) free depths. More data does not help, because each frame brings as many new unknowns as it removes. The missing equations must come from priors. The book names temporal smoothness (a point's trajectory is smooth over time) and spatial smoothness (a point deforms like its neighbours). §15.4.1.1 · p. 446 With depth the counts already balance and the priors over-constrain the problem, which is why the book treats that case first. §15.4.2 · p. 449

2. From NRSfM to deformable SLAM

Classical NRSfM assumes a fixed camera and a moving object with no static background: a hand, a waving flag, a jumping person. Most frames show the whole object. Each point's motion mixes a rigid motion of the object with a local deformation; the rigid part is never computed separately, but it supplies parallax, which makes the estimation well conditioned. §15.4.1.1 · pp. 446–447

Shape from template (SfT) adds a strong prior: the textured 3D shape of the object at rest, the template, is known, and only the deformation is recovered. One model is isometric deformation: the geodesic distance between surface points, the shortest path within the surface, is preserved. Paper bends this way; rubber does not. It is well-posed and led to stable real-time solutions; the alternative jointly minimizes a deformation energy and the reprojection error. Without a template, early NRSfM assumed an orthographic camera, valid only for distant objects, and a low-dimensional basis for the trajectories. Close-ups need a perspective camera, where isometry has also worked well. §15.4.1.1 · pp. 447–448

AspectClassical NRSfMDeformable SLAM
CameraFixedMoving; its trajectory is estimated too
Rigid part of the observed motionLeft inside each point's motionAssigned to the camera trajectory
Field of viewMost frames see the whole objectClose-up and exploratory: frames see different regions
ProcessingBatch, over all imagesCausal, real-time: at time \(k\) only frames \(1 \dots k\)

The second row is a hypothesis, not a fact. With no static background the images cannot tell "the tissue drifted right" from "the camera moved left". Separating the rigid from the non-rigid component is ill-posed in general, which the book calls the floating map ambiguity; priors on the displacements of the deformable object make the separation possible. §15.4.1.2 · p. 448

3. With depth: a canonical map and a deformation graph

RGB-D and stereo cameras measure depth. DynamicFusion, which the book calls the seminal work on deformable 3D SLAM from RGB-D data, builds a canonical map, the scene's shape at rest, and deforms it to explain the current depth image, combining a form of embedded deformation (ED) graph with an as-rigid-as-possible regularizer. An ED model discretizes the space of deformations as a graph, which speeds up dense reconstruction. §15.4.2 · p. 449

Filling the gap: what a deformation graph and "as rigid as possible" compute

A deformation graph is a sparse set of nodes spread over the surface. Node \(i\) has a rest position \(\mathbf{q}_i\), a current position \(\mathbf{p}_i\), and a rotation \(\mathbf{R}_i\); edges join nearby nodes. Each dense surface point follows a blend of the transforms of the nodes near it, so a few hundred node transforms stand in for millions of points.

The as-rigid-as-possible energy asks every node's neighbourhood to move as a rigid piece:

\[ E_{\text{ARAP}} = \sum_i \sum_{j \in \mathcal{N}(i)} \norm{ (\mathbf{p}_i - \mathbf{p}_j) - \mathbf{R}_i\, (\mathbf{q}_i - \mathbf{q}_j) }^2 . \]

The energy is zero exactly when every neighbourhood has only rotated and translated, so bending is cheap and stretching or shearing is expensive.

One node by hand, in the plane. Rest edges \(\mathbf{e}_1 = (1, 0)\), \(\mathbf{e}_2 = (0, 1)\); current edges \(\mathbf{e}'_1 = (0.8, 0.6)\), \(\mathbf{e}'_2 = (-0.6, 0.8)\). With \(\mathbf{a} \times \mathbf{b} = a_x b_y - a_y b_x\), the best rotation angle is

\[ \theta_i = \operatorname{atan2}\Big( \sum_j \mathbf{e}_j \times \mathbf{e}'_j,\ \sum_j \mathbf{e}_j \cdot \mathbf{e}'_j \Big) = \operatorname{atan2}(0.6 + 0.6,\ 0.8 + 0.8) = 36.9^\circ . \]

Rotating the rest edges by \(36.9^\circ\) gives exactly the current edges, so this node contributes 0. The simpler prior "neighbours move alike", \(\sum \norm{(\mathbf{p}_i - \mathbf{p}_j) - (\mathbf{q}_i - \mathbf{q}_j)}^2\), gives \(\norm{(-0.2, 0.6)}^2 + \norm{(-0.6, -0.2)}^2 = 0.8\): it punishes a pure rotation that deforms nothing.

Minimizing \(E_{\text{ARAP}}\) alternates two easy steps. With positions fixed, each \(\mathbf{R}_i\) has the closed form above (in 3D, an SVD as in Week 13 · Day 2). With rotations fixed, the energy is quadratic in the positions, and its gradient vanishes when \(\sum_{j}(\mathbf{p}_i - \mathbf{p}_j) = \sum_{j} \tfrac12(\mathbf{R}_i + \mathbf{R}_j)(\mathbf{q}_i - \mathbf{q}_j)\) at every free node, a linear system.

Try it: drag the round handle, and switch the regularizer.

Notice: at the start the handle has been pulled down and to the left. With no regularizer only the handle moves, and the strip's departure from rigid motion is 89%. "Neighbours move alike" spreads the displacement but shears every cell: 25%. As-rigid-as-possible lets each piece rotate, and the strip bends like a ruler: 6%. Now drag the handle far beyond the strip's length. No rigid solution exists, and the regularizer spreads the stretch over all edges.

After DynamicFusion, VolumeDeform added photometric information, and KillingFusion enforced smooth, nearly isometric deformations (Figure 15.16). All three store the map as an SDF, which scales poorly and limits exploration; SurfelWarp uses surfels instead. For stereo in surgery, MIS-SLAM combines as-rigid-as-possible deformation with the ED model. §15.4.2 · p. 449

4. One camera: the tracking and mapping threads

A monocular deformable SLAM system keeps the two threads of visual SLAM (Week 12 · Day 1): tracking at frame rate, mapping at keyframe rate. Tracking resembles shape from template: a shape at rest is assumed available for the area being explored, and each frame estimates the camera pose and the deformation of that local template. Mapping takes point tracks and recomputes the templates. §15.4.3–15.4.4 · pp. 450–451

StageDefSLAMNR-SLAM
TrackingDeformation energy inspired by a physics-based elastic modelSpatial as-rigid-as-possible and viscous temporal regularizers
MappingIsometric NRSfM on covisible keyframes gives a template per keyframe; assumes planar topologyA dynamic deformable graph copes with any topology; a visco-elastic model inside a deformable bundle adjustment
Feature matchingORB proved inadequate for close-frame tracking in medical scenes; Lucas-Kanade flow (Week 12 · Day 2) does better, being invariant to affine lighting changes. ORB with a bag of words still relocalizes.Lucas-Kanade tracking
InitializationIsometric NRSfM computes the first templates from scratch; initial matches assume a planar sceneRigid structure from motion gives the initial guess
Extending the mapHandled by isometric NRSfM once matches for the new points are foundNew points are triangulated with a rigid and a non-rigid algorithm, and the fitting model is selected

5. Where the field stands

§15.5 closes with open problems. §15.5 · pp. 451–453 Tracking objects helps state estimation under large occlusions and many moving objects, at higher cost. NeRF and 3D Gaussian splatting (Week 20) show promise for dynamic scenes, with real-time cost and map management unsolved. Data association is still hard, and the trend is toward learned priors. Lifelong operation needs memory management: what to keep, how to summarize or marginalize, when to forget. For deformable SLAM the basic questions are open: under what conditions can camera trajectory and deformation both be estimated, can the object's rigid motion be told from the camera's, are there local minima? The stated goal is spatio-temporal AI, a world model that gives a consistent history and predicts what comes next.

Common mistakes

  • "As rigid as possible means the object stays rigid." Each small neighbourhood should move rigidly, each with its own rotation. The whole can bend a great deal.

Check yourself

Q1. A fixed monocular camera observes 50 points on a deforming surface in 20 frames. With no priors, how many unknowns and equations are there?

Every point has its own 3D position in every frame: 3 × 50 × 20 = 3000. Each observation is a pixel: 2 × 50 × 20 = 2000. One depth per observation is undetermined.

Q2. A node has rest edges (1, 0) and (0, 1) and current edges (0, 1) and (−1, 0). What are its as-rigid-as-possible energy and its "neighbours move alike" energy?

The current edges are the rest edges rotated by 90°, so the best rotation fits exactly: ARAP energy 0. Without a rotation the differences are (−1, 1) and (−1, −1), with squared lengths 2 + 2 = 4.

Q3. In deformable SLAM, part of the observed motion could be explained by a rigid transformation. Where does the working hypothesis put it?

Whatever a rigid transformation can explain is included in the camera trajectory.

Q4. Why did Lucas-Kanade optical flow replace ORB matching for frame-to-frame tracking in medical scenes?

The book credits LK's better performance there to its invariance to affine lighting changes.

Recap

  1. A deforming scene seen by one camera has \(3NF\) unknowns and \(2NF\) equations. Temporal and spatial priors, or a depth sensor, supply the rest.
  2. Shape from template assumes a known rest shape; isometry, preserving distances within the surface, is the prior that works under perspective.
  3. Deformable SLAM moves the camera too, sees the scene in close-up pieces, runs causally, and assigns the rigid part of the motion to the camera.
  4. With depth, a canonical map is warped by a deformation graph regularized to be as rigid as possible: neighbourhoods may rotate, not stretch.

Sources

  1. SLAM Handbook, §15.4 "Deformable SLAM" and §15.5 "Further Readings & Recent Trends", pp. 446–453, Figures 15.14–15.16.
  2. Sorkine and Alexa, As-Rigid-As-Possible Surface Modeling, 2007 (the energy and its alternating local and global steps).
  3. Sumner, Schmidt, Pauly, Embedded Deformation for Shape Manipulation, 2007 (deformation graphs); Hartley and Zisserman, Multiple View Geometry, 2004 (the 7-parameter gauge).

Week 21 · Review

Week 21 review: SLAM in a world that changes

After today you can classify a changing scene, write the factors that track a moving object, clear and compare maps with free-space evidence, update an object's persistence, and say what makes deformable SLAM solvable.

About 60 min · No new pages

The week in one paragraph

Chapter 15 drops the static-world assumption. Motion in view is short-term: it can be rejected as outliers, tracked as rigid bodies in the factor graph, or reconstructed densely. Change out of view is long-term: it needs re-identification, maps that record free space so that "gone" differs from "not looked at", and per-object persistence estimates. When nothing is static, one camera leaves the problem under-constrained (\(3NF\) unknowns, \(2NF\) equations), and deformation priors make it solvable.

1. Formula sheet

What it isFormulaWhere
Motion between two observations\(d = v / f\), against the spacing of confusable things§15.1.1, p. 419 · Day 1
Reprojection error, point on moving object \(k\)\(\mathbf{e}^{i,j,k}_{\text{reproj}} = \mathbf{z}^i_j - \pi\big( (\mathbf{T}^w_i)^{-1} \mathbf{T}^w_{k,i} \tilde{\mathbf{x}}^k_j \big)\)(15.1), p. 427 · Day 2
Constant velocity\(\mathbf{e}^{i,k}_{\text{vcte}} = \begin{bmatrix} \mathbf{v}^k_{i+1} - \mathbf{v}^k_i \\ \boldsymbol{\omega}^k_{i+1} - \boldsymbol{\omega}^k_i \end{bmatrix}\)(15.2), p. 427 · Day 2
Pose-velocity coupling\(h^{-1}\big( ( \mathbf{T}^w_{k,i+1} - \mathbf{T}^w_{k,i} \Delta\mathbf{T} ) \tilde{\mathbf{x}}^k_j \big)\), \(\Delta\mathbf{T} = \begin{bmatrix} \Exp(\boldsymbol{\omega}^k_i \Delta t) & \mathbf{v}^k_i \Delta t \\ \mathbf{0} & 1 \end{bmatrix}\)(15.3)–(15.4), p. 428 · Day 2
Occupancy update along a beamend cell \(l \leftarrow l + l_{\text{hit}}\); crossed cells \(l \leftarrow l - l_{\text{miss}}\)§15.3.2.1, p. 436 · Day 3
Persistence, in odds \(o = p/(1-p)\)detected: \(o \leftarrow o\,P_D/P_F\); in view, missed: \(o \leftarrow o\,(1-P_D)/(1-P_F)\); not in view: unchanged§15.3.3, p. 443 · Day 4
As-rigid-as-possible energy\(\sum_i \sum_{j \in \mathcal{N}(i)} \norm{ (\mathbf{p}_i - \mathbf{p}_j) - \mathbf{R}_i (\mathbf{q}_i - \mathbf{q}_j) }^2\)§15.4.2, p. 449 · Day 5

2. Mixed quiz

Check yourself

Q1. What decides whether a robot experiences a change as short-term or long-term?

Fast motion sampled fast enough is short-term; a small rearrangement while the robot looked away is long-term.

Q2. A 5 Hz radar watches drones flying at 20 m/s, 2 m apart. Can nearest-neighbour matching between scans be trusted?

d = 20 / 5 = 4 m, so the nearest detection is usually another drone.

Q3. A visual SLAM system masks every pixel labelled "car". What goes wrong in a full car park?

Labels mark potentially dynamic classes; combine them with geometric checks.

Q4. Which variables does the coupling factor (15.3) connect?

It compares the point under the pose at i+1 with the point under the pose at i advanced by (15.4). No camera appears.

Q5. A long-free grid cell sits at the lower clamp, log-odds −2. A hit adds 0.7. How many hits make it solid (above 0)?

−2 → −1.3 → −0.6 → +0.1: three hits.

Q6. After a second visit the map shows half a table floating in the room. What happened, and what is the usual remedy?

Semantic consistency: scenes change in units, the robot sees parts.

Q7. During a visit, a mapped object is outside the camera's field of view. With no forgetting, how does its persistence probability change?

No observation, no update: absence of evidence.

Q8. Why is deformable SLAM much easier with a depth camera than with a monocular one?

3NF equations for 3NF unknowns; the priors no longer have to supply the depth.

3. Pen-and-paper problems

  1. A security robot has a 10 Hz LiDAR. People walk at 1.2 m/s and stay at least 0.8 m apart. (a) How far does a person move between scans, as a fraction of the spacing? (b) The robot passes each corridor once every 5 minutes. How far can a person move between passes?

    Solution

    (a) \(d = 1.2/10 = 0.12\) m, 15% of the spacing: short-term, track from scan to scan. (b) \(1.2 \times 300 = 360\) m: long-term, nothing can be tracked across the gap.

  2. A planar object is at position \((2, 1)\) m with heading 0. In its own frame \(\mathbf{v} = (1.5, 0)\) m/s and \(\omega = 1\) rad/s; \(\Delta t = 0.1\) s. (a) Give the increment (15.4) and the predicted pose. (b) Where does the model put the object point \((0, 1)\)? (c) The estimate of the next pose is position \((2.20, 1.00)\), heading 0.1 rad. Evaluate (15.3) for that point.

    Solution

    (a) Rotation by 0.1 rad, translation \((0.15, 0)\). The heading is 0, so the predicted pose is position \((2.15, 1)\), heading 0.1 rad. (b) \((0,1)\) rotated by 0.1 rad is \((-\sin 0.1, \cos 0.1) = (-0.100, 0.995)\); adding the position gives \((2.050, 1.995)\).
