(c) The estimate has the same heading, so it puts the point at \((2.100, 1.995)\). The residual is \((0.050, 0)\) m.

  3. An occupancy grid uses \(l_{\text{hit}} = 0.85\), \(l_{\text{miss}} = 0.40\), and clamps log-odds to \([-2, 3.5]\). A forklift parks on a long-free cell, is hit in 10 consecutive scans, and drives away. (a) What is the cell's log-odds when it leaves? (b) How many scans until the cell is free again? (c) How many without the upper clamp?

    Solution

    (a) \(-2 + 10 \times 0.85 = 6.5\), clamped to 3.5 (reached at the seventh hit). (b) \(3.5 - 0.40\,n \le 0\) needs \(n \ge 8.75\): 9 scans. (c) \(6.5/0.40 = 16.25\): 17 scans. The clamp bounds how long the map takes to accept a change.

  4. (Stretch.) A fixed camera tracks \(N = 100\) points on a deforming surface through \(F = 50\) frames. (a) Count unknowns and equations with no prior. (b) Assume every frame's shape is a weighted sum of \(K = 3\) basis shapes shared by all frames, \(\mathbf{S}_f = \sum_{k} c_{f,k} \mathbf{B}_k\). Count again. (c) What is the largest \(K\) with no more unknowns than equations, and why is a larger \(K\) not simply better?

    Solution

    (a) \(3NF = 15000\) unknowns, \(2NF = 10000\) equations. (b) \(3NK + KF = 900 + 150 = 1050\) unknowns for the same 10000 equations. (c) \(3NK + KF \le 2NF\) gives \(K \le 10000/350 = 28.6\), so \(K = 28\). The basis is the prior: few basis shapes allow only a small family of deformations, which is what fixes the depths. At \(K = F\) every frame can have its own shape and the prior says nothing. This is the low-dimensional basis of early NRSfM (p. 448).

You are ready for next week if you can

  • Decide from speed, sensor rate, and spacing whether an object can be tracked.
  • Write equations (15.1)–(15.4) and say which variables each factor connects.
  • Update a persistence probability for a detection, a miss, and a visit without a view.
  • Say why monocular deformable SLAM needs priors and what the as-rigid-as-possible energy penalizes.

Sources

  1. SLAM Handbook, Chapter 15 "Dynamic and Deformable SLAM", pp. 417–453.
  2. Thrun, Burgard, Fox, Probabilistic Robotics, 2005; Sorkine and Alexa, As-Rigid-As-Possible Surface Modeling, 2007.

Week 22 · Day 1

Maps that know what things are: objects as landmarks

After today you can say what a metric-semantic map adds to a geometric one, define an object landmark, and write the residual that compares projected semantic landmarks with detected keypoints.

About 60 min · Read Ch. 16 intro, §16.1, §16.2 to §16.2.1.1, pp. 454–458 (5 pages) · Needs Week 11 Day 5

Read first: Chapter 16 opening, §16.1, and §16.2 up to equation (16.3), pp. 454–458

While you read, look for:

  • What a vision front-end can output beyond keypoints (pp. 454–455), and what "closed-set" means (p. 455).
  • The four parts of an object landmark in Definition 16.1 (p. 456).
  • In equation (16.2) on p. 457: what is learned offline and what is estimated online.
  • In equation (16.3) on p. 458: the transformations a semantic landmark goes through to become a pixel.

Today's big idea

A metric-semantic map stores what things are together with where they are. In its sparse form, the landmarks stop being anonymous 3D points and become objects with a category, a pose, a scale, and a shape. The back-end stays the same least-squares machine; only the residual changes.

1. What geometry alone cannot do

A geometric map answers "is this space free?". That is enough for collision checking, but not for "go to the laptop in the office", and not for a planner that should prefer road over sidewalk over vegetation. Those need labels on the map. Ch. 16 intro · p. 454

Semantics also help SLAM itself. An object is recognizable from many viewpoints and is more distinctive than a corner, which makes data association and loop closure less ambiguous. Labels also flag things that may move (Week 21 · Day 2). Ch. 16 intro · p. 454

The labels come from learned vision models in the front-end: Ch. 16 intro · pp. 454–455

Front-end outputWhat it gives
Object detectionA class and a bounding box per object
Semantic keypoints or edgesImage locations of named parts (a wheel, a door)
Semantic segmentationA class for every pixel
Instance segmentationA mask per object, separating two objects of one class
Panoptic segmentationBoth: background classes and separate instances

This chapter assumes closed-set semantics: the labels come from a fixed dictionary of typically 100 to 1000 words such as "chair", "table", "office". Open-set semantics (language embeddings) is Chapter 17, next week. Ch. 16 intro · p. 455

Section 16.1 names three places to put the labels: on sparse landmarks, which become objects (§16.2, Days 1–3); on every point, surfel, voxel, or mesh face of a dense map (§16.3, Day 4); and on regions of free space such as rooms (§16.4, Day 5). Each needs a model of what a detector should report for a given map, and a way to fuse many noisy reports. §16.1 · pp. 455–456

2. The object landmark

Landmark-based SLAM minimizes a sum of squared residuals, one per measurement. The book writes the residual of factor \(i\) as

\[ r_i(\mathbf{x}_i) = \norm{\mathbf{z}_i - h_i(\mathbf{T}_i, \boldsymbol{\ell}_i)}_{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_i}, \qquad \mathbf{x}_i = (\mathbf{T}_i, \boldsymbol{\ell}_i), \tag{16.1} \]

with measurement \(\mathbf{z}_i\), robot pose \(\mathbf{T}_i\), landmark \(\boldsymbol{\ell}_i\), measurement model \(h_i\), and the Mahalanobis norm \(\norm{\mathbf{e}}_{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}^2 = \mathbf{e}\T\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{-1}\mathbf{e}\) of Week 2 · Day 2. In visual SLAM \(\boldsymbol{\ell}_i\) is a 3D point and \(\mathbf{z}_i\) a pixel. Sparse metric-semantic SLAM keeps (16.1) and changes what \(\boldsymbol{\ell}\), \(\mathbf{z}\), and \(h\) are. §16.2 · p. 456

An object landmark is a tuple \(\boldsymbol{\ell} = (\sigma, \mathbf{q}, \lambda, \mathbf{s})\). Definition 16.1 · p. 456

PartLives inMeaning
Category \(\sigma\)\(\mathbb{N}\)"car", "chair", "table": the only discrete part
Pose \(\mathbf{q}\)\(\SE(3)\)The object's own frame, expressed in the world frame
Scale \(\lambda\)\(\R_{\gt 0}\)Size relative to the category's canonical model
Shape \(\mathbf{s}\)\(\R^d\)The surface in the object frame (today keypoints; tomorrow ellipsoid, mesh, latent code)

A point landmark has 3 unknowns. An object landmark has \(6 + 1 + d\) and a discrete label. The scale is kept apart so that a car and a toy car can share one shape and differ only in \(\lambda\). §16.2.1 · p. 457

3. Shape as a set of semantic landmarks

The first shape model is a short list of 3D points \(\{\mathbf{s}_j\}_j\), called semantic landmarks, placed on named parts of the object: for a car, the wheels, mirrors, and plate. Their projections into an image are semantic keypoints \(\mathbf{z}_j \in \R^2\). A network detects them by producing, for each part, a heatmap with a bump at the part's pixel. §16.2.1.1 · p. 457

If every \(\mathbf{s}_j\) were free, the optimizer could move the left wheel to the roof. The deformable shape model prevents that by building the points from a category template:

\[ \mathbf{s}_j = \mathbf{b}_{j,0} + \sum_k c_k\, \mathbf{b}_{j,k}. \tag{16.2} \]

Here \(\mathbf{b}_{j,0}\) is the position of part \(j\) on the average car, each \(\mathbf{b}_{j,k}\) is one way cars differ from the average (a mode of variability), and the deformation coefficients \(c_k \in \R_{\ge 0}\) say how much of each mode this car has. The \(\mathbf{b}\)'s are fixed per category. The \(c_k\) are estimated per object. §16.2.1.1 · p. 457

Try it: the pink rings are detected keypoints of one car. Press "Fit shape only", then press "Gauss-Newton step" four times.

Notice that shape alone cannot explain the detections: with the wrong scale and yaw, \(c_1\) runs into its upper limit and the error stays above 130 cm. Three Gauss-Newton steps on all four unknowns bring it to about 6 cm, the noise level, at \(c_1 \approx 0.80\), \(c_2 \approx 0.53\), \(\lambda \approx 1.29\), yaw 25°; the fourth changes nothing.

Filling the gap: where the modes \(\mathbf{b}_{j,k}\) come from

The book says the modes are obtained by PCA. The recipe: take \(N\) CAD models of the category, each annotated with the same \(J\) parts. Stack the \(J\) part positions of model \(n\) into one vector \(\mathbf{m}_n \in \R^{3J}\). Then

\[ \bar{\mathbf{m}} = \frac{1}{N}\sum_{n=1}^{N} \mathbf{m}_n, \qquad \mathbf{C} = \frac{1}{N}\sum_{n=1}^{N} (\mathbf{m}_n - \bar{\mathbf{m}})(\mathbf{m}_n - \bar{\mathbf{m}})\T . \]

The mean \(\bar{\mathbf{m}}\), cut back into \(J\) triples, gives the \(\mathbf{b}_{j,0}\). The eigenvectors of \(\mathbf{C}\) with the largest eigenvalues are the directions in which the training cars differ most; cutting eigenvector \(k\) into triples gives the \(\mathbf{b}_{j,k}\).

Count the unknowns. With \(J = 12\) parts, free points cost \(36\) numbers per car. With \(K = 5\) modes the shape costs \(5\), and the estimate stays car-shaped even when half the keypoints are hidden.

4. The keypoint residual

With the shape fixed in the object frame, the residual between object \(\boldsymbol{\ell}_i\) and the keypoints \(\{\mathbf{z}_{i,j}\}_j\) detected from camera pose \(\mathbf{T}_i\) is a sum of reprojection errors, one per part:

\[ r_i(\mathbf{x}_i)^2 = \sum_j \norm{\mathbf{z}_{i,j} - \pi\!\left(\mathbf{q}_i^{-1}\mathbf{T}_i,\; \lambda_i\, \mathbf{s}_{i,j}\right)}^2_{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_i}. \tag{16.3} \]

\(\pi(\mathbf{T}, \mathbf{s})\) is the perspective projection of point \(\mathbf{s}\) into a camera with pose \(\mathbf{T}\). §16.2.1.1 · p. 458

Filling the gap: reading \(\pi(\mathbf{q}^{-1}\mathbf{T}, \lambda\mathbf{s})\), with numbers

Both \(\mathbf{T}\) (camera) and \(\mathbf{q}\) (object) map their own frame to the world frame. So \(\mathbf{q}^{-1}\mathbf{T}\) maps camera coordinates to object coordinates: it is the pose of the camera as seen from the object. To project a point given in object coordinates you need the opposite direction, \((\mathbf{q}^{-1}\mathbf{T})^{-1} = \mathbf{T}^{-1}\mathbf{q}\), followed by the pinhole model of Week 11 · Day 3.

Take a camera at the world origin with \(\mathbf{T} = \mathbf{I}\), focal length 500 px, principal point \((320, 240)\). The object frame is not rotated and sits at \((1, 0, 8)\) m. Its scale is \(\lambda = 2\), and one semantic landmark is \(\mathbf{s} = (0.5, 0.25, 0)\).

\[ \lambda\mathbf{s} = (1, 0.5, 0) \;\xrightarrow{\ \mathbf{q}\ }\; (2, 0.5, 8) \;\xrightarrow{\ \mathbf{T}^{-1} = \mathbf{I}\ }\; (2, 0.5, 8) \;\xrightarrow{\ \div\, z\ }\; (0.25,\ 0.0625) \;\xrightarrow{\ \text{intrinsics}\ }\; (445,\ 271.25)\ \text{px}. \]

If the detector reports \(\mathbf{z} = (448, 270)\), the error is \(\mathbf{e} = (3, -1.25)\) px. With \(\boldsymbol{\Sigma} = 2^2\mathbf{I}\) px² this part contributes \((3^2 + 1.25^2)/4 = 2.64\) to \(r_i^2\). The optimizer can lower it through \(\mathbf{T}\), \(\mathbf{q}\), \(\lambda\), or the shape coefficients.

Common mistakes

  • "\(\mathbf{q}\) takes world coordinates to object coordinates." It is the pose of the object frame in the world, so it takes object coordinates to world coordinates. That is why (16.3) contains \(\mathbf{q}^{-1}\mathbf{T}\) and not \(\mathbf{q}\mathbf{T}\).

Check yourself

Q1. An image shows two chairs on a carpet. Which output gives a separate mask for each chair and also labels the carpet pixels?

Semantic segmentation does not separate the two chairs. Panoptic segmentation separates instances and labels the background.

Q2. The camera is at the world origin with identity pose. An object frame is unrotated at (0, 0, 10) m with scale λ = 3. Where does the semantic landmark s = (1, 0, 0) land in normalized image coordinates (x/z, y/z)?

Scale first: λs = (3, 0, 0). Move to the world: (3, 0, 10). Divide by depth: (0.3, 0).

Q3. A category model has J = 10 semantic landmarks and K = 4 modes. How many continuous unknowns does one object add to the problem if its shape is optimized through the coefficients?

Pose 6, scale 1, coefficients 4: 11 in total. Ten free points would cost 6 + 1 + 30 = 37.

Q4. In equation (16.3), what is the transformation q⁻¹T?

T maps camera coordinates to the world and q⁻¹ maps the world to the object, so q⁻¹T is the camera's pose seen from the object.

Recap

  1. A metric-semantic map holds labels as well as geometry, on sparse objects, on dense map elements, or on regions. Labels serve tasks and also help data association and loop closure.
  2. An object landmark is \((\sigma, \mathbf{q}, \lambda, \mathbf{s})\): category, pose, scale, shape.
  3. The deformable model (16.2) is a category mean plus a few learned modes, so a shape costs a handful of coefficients.
  4. The residual (16.3) scales each semantic landmark, moves it object → world → camera, projects it, and compares it with the detected keypoint.

Sources

  1. SLAM Handbook, Chapter 16 introduction, §16.1, §16.2 to §16.2.1.1, pp. 454–458.
  2. Cootes, Taylor, Cooper, Graham, Active Shape Models: Their Training and Application, 1995 (the mean-plus-modes model and its PCA); Hartley and Zisserman, Multiple View Geometry in Computer Vision, 2004 (the pinhole projection).

Week 22 · Day 2

Ellipsoids, meshes, and learned shapes

After today you can turn an ellipsoid into a dual quadric, project it to an image conic and read off its bounding box, and write the residuals that fit a mesh to a segmentation mask and a signed distance function to depth points.

About 60 min · Read §16.2.1.2–16.2.1.4, pp. 458–466 (9 pages, 5 of them mostly figures) · Needs Week 22 Day 1

Read first: §16.2.1.2 to §16.2.1.4, pp. 458–466

While you read, look for:

  • The same ellipsoid written three ways in (16.4), (16.5), and (16.6), pp. 458–459.
  • The two conics that the residual (16.10) compares: (16.8) from the map, p. 460, and (16.9) from the detector, p. 461.
  • On p. 466: what is optimized when the SDF decoder is trained, and what when it is used.

Today's big idea

Every shape model is paired with a detector output: an ellipsoid with a bounding box, a mesh with a segmentation mask, a signed distance function with depth points. The residual always has the same form: predict what the detector would report for the current object and camera, and compare.

1. An ellipsoid as a quadric

The coarsest useful shape is an ellipsoid with semi-axis lengths \(\mathbf{s} \in \R^3\), centred at the origin of the object frame:

\[ \mathcal{E}_{\mathbf{s}} = \{\mathbf{x} \in \R^3 \mid \mathbf{x}\T \diag(\mathbf{s})^{-2}\, \mathbf{x} \le 1\}. \tag{16.4} \]

Appending a 1 to \(\mathbf{x}\) (homogeneous coordinates) moves the "\(\le 1\)" into a matrix:

\[ \begin{bmatrix}\mathbf{x}\\ 1\end{bmatrix}\T \mathbf{Q}_{\mathbf{s}} \begin{bmatrix}\mathbf{x}\\ 1\end{bmatrix} \le 0, \qquad \mathbf{Q}_{\mathbf{s}} = \diag\!\left(s_1^{-2},\, s_2^{-2},\, s_3^{-2},\, -1\right). \tag{16.5} \]

A surface that is the zero set of such a quadratic form, with a symmetric \(4\times 4\) matrix, is a quadric. Its attraction is that its outline in an image has a closed form. §16.2.1.2 · pp. 458–459

2. The dual quadric: describe the surface by its tangent planes

The book switches to the dual description: the set of planes that touch the ellipsoid.

\[ \mathcal{E}^*_{\mathbf{s}} = \{\mathbf{y} \in \R^3 \mid \mathbf{y}\T \diag(\mathbf{s})^{2}\, \mathbf{y} \le 1\} = \big\{\mathbf{y} \mid [\mathbf{y}; 1]\T\, \mathbf{Q}^*_{\mathbf{s}}\, [\mathbf{y}; 1] \le 0\big\}, \tag{16.6} \]

with \(\mathbf{Q}^*_{\mathbf{s}}\) the adjugate of \(\mathbf{Q}_{\mathbf{s}}\). A quadric does not change when its matrix is multiplied by a constant, so the adjugate \(\det(\mathbf{Q}_{\mathbf{s}})\mathbf{Q}_{\mathbf{s}}^{-1}\) can be replaced by \(\mathbf{Q}_{\mathbf{s}}^{-1} = \diag(s_1^2, s_2^2, s_3^2, -1)\). An image outline is made of rays that touch the object, so the tangent description is the one a camera sees. §16.2.1.2 · pp. 459–460

Filling the gap: why \(\mathbf{Q}^* = \mathbf{Q}^{-1}\), and why duals are easy to project

Tangent planes. Write a plane as \(\{\mathbf{x} : \mathbf{y}\T\mathbf{x} + 1 = 0\}\), which is the homogeneous vector \([\mathbf{y}; 1]\). Every point of the ellipsoid is \(\mathbf{x} = \diag(\mathbf{s})\,\mathbf{u}\) with \(\norm{\mathbf{u}} \le 1\). Then \(\mathbf{y}\T\mathbf{x} = (\diag(\mathbf{s})\mathbf{y})\T\mathbf{u}\), and as \(\mathbf{u}\) runs over the unit ball this takes every value between \(-\norm{\diag(\mathbf{s})\mathbf{y}}\) and \(+\norm{\diag(\mathbf{s})\mathbf{y}}\). The plane needs the value \(-1\). It misses the ellipsoid if \(\norm{\diag(\mathbf{s})\mathbf{y}} \lt 1\), cuts through it if \(\gt 1\), and touches it at one point exactly when

\[ \norm{\diag(\mathbf{s})\mathbf{y}}^2 = \mathbf{y}\T\diag(\mathbf{s})^2\mathbf{y} = 1 \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad \begin{bmatrix}\mathbf{y}\\ 1\end{bmatrix}\T \begin{bmatrix}\diag(\mathbf{s})^{2} & \mathbf{0}\\ \mathbf{0}\T & -1\end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix}\mathbf{y}\\ 1\end{bmatrix} = 0 . \]

The matrix in the middle is \(\mathbf{Q}_{\mathbf{s}}^{-1}\), and the tangent planes are the boundary of the set in (16.6).

Moving the object. If points move by a \(4\times4\) matrix \(\mathbf{H}\) (\(\mathbf{x}' = \mathbf{H}\mathbf{x}\)), a plane \(\boldsymbol{\pi}\) moves to \(\boldsymbol{\pi}' = \mathbf{H}^{-\top}\boldsymbol{\pi}\), since then \(\boldsymbol{\pi}'^{\top}\mathbf{x}' = \boldsymbol{\pi}\T\mathbf{H}^{-1}\mathbf{H}\mathbf{x} = 0\) still holds. Substituting \(\boldsymbol{\pi} = \mathbf{H}\T\boldsymbol{\pi}'\) into \(\boldsymbol{\pi}\T\mathbf{Q}^*\boldsymbol{\pi} = 0\) gives \(\boldsymbol{\pi}'^{\top}(\mathbf{H}\mathbf{Q}^*\mathbf{H}\T)\boldsymbol{\pi}' = 0\): the dual moves as \(\mathbf{H}\mathbf{Q}^*\mathbf{H}\T\), with no inverse.

Projecting. An image line \(\mathbf{l}\) and the camera centre span a plane, \(\boldsymbol{\pi} = \mathbf{M}\T\mathbf{l}\), where \(\mathbf{M}\) is the \(3\times4\) camera matrix. The line touches the object's outline exactly when that plane touches the object: \(\mathbf{l}\T(\mathbf{M}\mathbf{Q}^*\mathbf{M}\T)\mathbf{l} = 0\). So the outline is the conic whose dual is \(\mathbf{M}\mathbf{Q}^*\mathbf{M}\T\). The point form \(\mathbf{Q}\) would need the inverse of \(\mathbf{M}\), which a \(3\times4\) matrix does not have.

3. From the object to a bounding-box residual

Apply the two rules. Scaling by \(\lambda\) and placing the object with pose \(\mathbf{q}\) gives the dual quadric in the world frame (the book writes \(\mathbf{H}\) out as two matrices), and the camera at pose \(\mathbf{T}\) turns it into a dual conic, a symmetric \(3\times3\) matrix: §16.2.1.2 · p. 460

\[ \mathbf{Q}^*_{\boldsymbol{\ell}} \propto \mathbf{H}\,\mathbf{Q}^*_{\mathbf{s}}\,\mathbf{H}\T, \qquad \mathbf{H} = \mathbf{q}\,\diag(\lambda, \lambda, \lambda, 1), \tag{16.7} \] \[ \mathbf{C}^*_{\mathbf{x}} \propto \frac{1}{\beta}\,\mathbf{P}\,\mathbf{T}^{-1}\mathbf{Q}^*_{\boldsymbol{\ell}}\mathbf{T}^{-\top}\mathbf{P}\T, \qquad \mathbf{P} = \begin{bmatrix}\mathbf{I}_3 & \mathbf{0}\end{bmatrix}. \tag{16.8} \]

The detector reports a box \(\mathbf{z} = [u\ v\ w\ h]\T\) in normalized image coordinates: a corner, a width, and a height. The book turns it into the dual conic of the axis-aligned ellipse that fits inside the box, with centre \((c_u, c_v) = (u + w/2,\ v + h/2)\). Multiplying out the three matrices of (16.9) gives

\[ \mathbf{C}^*_{\mathbf{z}} \propto \begin{bmatrix} (w/2)^2 - c_u^2 & -c_u c_v & -c_u\\ -c_u c_v & (h/2)^2 - c_v^2 & -c_v\\ -c_u & -c_v & -1 \end{bmatrix}. \tag{16.9} \]

This also tells you how to read a box off any dual conic: scale it so the bottom-right entry is \(-1\); the centre is minus the last column, and the half-width is \(\sqrt{C^*_{11} + c_u^2}\). The residual compares the two conics, §16.2.1.2 · p. 461

\[ r_i(\mathbf{x}_i) = \norm{\mathbf{C}^*_{\mathbf{z}_j} - \mathbf{C}^*_{\mathbf{x}_i}}_{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_i} = \norm{\mathbf{b}_j - \tfrac{1}{\beta_i}\mathbf{A}\,\mathbf{v}(\mathbf{T}_i, \boldsymbol{\ell}_i)}_{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_i}. \tag{16.10, 16.11} \]

The second form flattens each symmetric matrix into the vector of its distinct entries (\(\operatorname{vech}\)): 6 in \(\mathbf{b}_j\) for the box conic, 10 in \(\mathbf{v}\) for \(\mathbf{T}_i^{-1}\mathbf{Q}^*_{\boldsymbol{\ell}_i}\mathbf{T}_i^{-\top}\). The constant \(6\times10\) matrix \(\mathbf{A}\) applies \(\mathbf{P}\) on both sides.

A sphere, by hand. Radius 1, centre \(\mathbf{t} = (0, 0, 5)\), camera at the origin with \(\mathbf{T} = \mathbf{I}\). Then \(\mathbf{Q}^*_{\mathbf{s}} = \diag(1,1,1,-1)\), and moving it by \(\mathbf{t}\) gives a matrix whose upper-left block is \(\mathbf{I}_3 - \mathbf{t}\mathbf{t}\T\). \(\mathbf{P}\) keeps exactly that block:

\[ \mathbf{P}\mathbf{Q}^*_{\boldsymbol{\ell}}\mathbf{P}\T = \mathbf{I}_3 - \mathbf{t}\mathbf{t}\T = \diag(1, 1, -24) \;\propto\; \diag\!\left(\tfrac{1}{24}, \tfrac{1}{24}, -1\right). \]

Here \(\beta = 24\). The centre is \((0, 0)\) and the half-width is \(1/\sqrt{24} = 0.204\). Check: a ray that grazes the sphere makes an angle \(\alpha\) with the axis where \(\sin\alpha = 1/5\), so \(\tan\alpha = 1/\sqrt{24}\). "Radius over depth", 0.2, is slightly too small, because grazing rays touch the sphere in front of its centre.

Try it: turn the yaw to 90°, then back to 30°. Then set the scale to 1.5 and the distance to 9 m.

Notice that the box depends on orientation: its width drops from 0.76 to 0.39 when the long axis points at the camera. And at \(\lambda = 1.5\), \(d = 9\) m the residual is exactly zero again: one box cannot separate a large far object from a small near one.

4. A mesh, compared with a segmentation mask

A triangle mesh with vertices \(\mathcal{V} = \{\mathbf{s}_j\}_j\) and faces \(\mathcal{F}\) can follow the real surface. It is compared with a segmentation mask \(\mathbf{z}_i \subset \R^2\), the set of pixels the detector assigns to the object. A rasterization function \(\rho(\mathcal{V}, \mathcal{F})\) fills in the pixels the mesh covers once its vertices are projected as in (16.3). Call that rendered set \(\hat{\mathbf{z}}_i = \rho(\{\pi(\mathbf{q}_i^{-1}\mathbf{T}_i, \lambda_i\mathbf{s}_{i,j})\}_j, \mathcal{F})\). The residual is the reciprocal of the intersection-over-union: §16.2.1.3 · pp. 461–462

\[ r_i(\mathbf{x}_i) = \frac{\hat{\mathbf{z}}_i \cup \mathbf{z}_i}{\hat{\mathbf{z}}_i \cap \mathbf{z}_i}. \tag{16.12} \]

If the rendering covers 500 pixels, the mask 400, and they share 300, the union is \(500 + 400 - 300 = 600\) and \(r = 600/300 = 2\). A perfect match gives the minimum, \(r = 1\).

The catch is the gradient. A pixel is either covered or not, so \(\rho\) is piecewise constant in the vertex positions and its derivative is zero almost everywhere. Differentiable rendering replaces it with an approximate gradient, as in Week 20 · Day 1. The vertices can be optimized directly or through the coefficients of (16.2). §16.2.1.3 · pp. 461–462

5. Implicit shapes: a function instead of a surface

The models so far are explicit: they list the surface. An implicit model is a function of space whose level set is the surface: an occupancy function, \(-1\) inside the object \(\mathcal{S}\) and \(+1\) outside (16.13), or a signed distance function, §16.2.1.4 · pp. 464–465

\[ d_{\mathcal{S}}(\mathbf{x}) = \begin{cases} -\inf_{\mathbf{y}\in\partial\mathcal{S}} \norm{\mathbf{x}-\mathbf{y}}, & \mathbf{x}\in\mathcal{S},\\ \phantom{-}\inf_{\mathbf{y}\in\partial\mathcal{S}} \norm{\mathbf{x}-\mathbf{y}}, & \mathbf{x}\notin\mathcal{S}. \end{cases} \tag{16.14} \]

For a unit sphere, \(d_{\mathcal{S}}(\mathbf{x}) = \norm{\mathbf{x}} - 1\): \(-0.5\) at \((0.5, 0, 0)\) and \(2\) at \((3, 0, 0)\). You met SDFs as maps in Week 8 · Day 2. Here one SDF describes one object, and a network \(d_\theta(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{s})\) produces it: a decoder with weights \(\theta\) shared by a whole category, and a shape code \(\mathbf{s} \in \R^d\) that selects one shape within it.

A depth sensor at pose \(\mathbf{T}_i\) gives points \(\mathbf{y}_{i,j}\) near the object with measured distances \(z_{i,j}\) to its surface. The residual asks the decoder for the distance at each point: §16.2.1.4 · p. 465

\[ r_i(\mathbf{x}_i)^2 = \sum_j \left| z_{i,j} - d_\theta\!\left(\lambda_i^{-1}\mathbf{q}_i\mathbf{T}_i^{-1}\mathbf{y}_{i,j},\ \mathbf{s}_i\right)\right|^2_{\sigma_i}. \tag{16.15} \]

The argument of \(d_\theta\) takes the point from the robot frame to the world, then to the object frame, then divides by \(\lambda_i\), so the decoder is always queried in its canonical frame. Trust that description in words: with yesterday's conventions for \(\mathbf{T}\) and \(\mathbf{q}\) the same chain reads \(\lambda^{-1}\mathbf{q}^{-1}\mathbf{T}\mathbf{y}\).

Training, offline and once per category, holds the poses and scales fixed and optimizes \(\theta\) with one code per training object. Testing, online inside SLAM, freezes \(\theta\) and optimizes \(\mathbf{T}_i\), \(\mathbf{q}_i\), \(\lambda_i\), \(\mathbf{s}_i\) for an object never seen before. §16.2.1.4 · p. 466

Check yourself

Q1. A sphere of radius 2 m is centred on the optical axis at depth 4 m. What is the half-width of its outline in normalized image coordinates?

With radius ρ the block is ρ²I − t tᵀ = diag(4, 4, −12) ∝ diag(1/3, 1/3, −1). The half-width is √(1/3) = 0.58.

Q2. A detection is z = (u, v, w, h) = (0.1, −0.2, 0.4, 0.2). With the bottom-right entry scaled to −1, what is the top-left entry of its dual conic (16.9)?

The centre is c_u = 0.1 + 0.2 = 0.3. The entry is (w/2)² − c_u² = 0.04 − 0.09 = −0.05.

Q3. A rendered mesh covers 300 pixels, the segmentation mask covers 300 pixels, and 200 pixels are in both. What is the residual (16.12)?

Union = 300 + 300 − 200 = 400, intersection = 200, so the residual is 2 (the IoU is 0.5).

Q4. A robot meets a chair it has never seen, with a chair SDF decoder already trained. What does minimizing (16.15) adjust?

Online, θ is frozen. The state is x = (T, q, λ, s).

Recap

  1. An ellipsoid is a quadric. Its dual \(\mathbf{Q}^* \propto \mathbf{Q}^{-1}\) describes it by tangent planes, moves as \(\mathbf{H}\mathbf{Q}^*\mathbf{H}\T\), and projects to the dual conic (16.8).
  2. A bounding box becomes the dual conic (16.9), and the residual (16.10) is the difference of the two conics. One box leaves size and distance tied together.
  3. A mesh is fitted to a segmentation mask through the reciprocal IoU (16.12), with a differentiable rasterizer.
  4. An implicit shape is a decoder \(d_\theta(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{s})\): weights trained offline; code, pose, and scale estimated online with (16.15).

Sources

  1. SLAM Handbook, §16.2.1.2 "Object Shape Representation as Quadric Surface", §16.2.1.3 "…as Mesh", §16.2.1.4 "Implicit Object Shape Representations", pp. 458–466.
  2. Hartley and Zisserman, Multiple View Geometry in Computer Vision, 2004 (dual quadrics, how planes transform, and the projection of a quadric to a conic).
  3. Magnus and Neudecker, Matrix Differential Calculus with Applications in Statistics and Econometrics, 1988 (vec, vech, and the Kronecker-product identity).

Week 22 · Day 3

Discrete and continuous unknowns together: hybrid solvers

After today you can write metric-semantic SLAM as a discrete-continuous factor graph, explain why alternating between associations and geometry is tractable, and compute hard, max-mixture, and EM association weights by hand.

About 60 min · Read §16.2.2, pp. 466–471 (5 pages) · Needs Week 6 Day 5

Read first: §16.2.2 "Hybrid Solvers for Sparse Metric-Semantic SLAM", pp. 466–471

While you read, look for:

  • The four ways discrete variables enter the problem (p. 466).
  • The condition (16.20) on p. 469 under which the discrete problem falls apart into small ones.
  • What the E-step and the M-step each hold fixed (p. 470).

Today's big idea

Semantic SLAM has unknowns you can differentiate (poses, shapes) and unknowns you can only enumerate (classes, associations). Fix either kind and the other becomes easy: least squares for the continuous ones, a small choice per measurement for the discrete ones. Hybrid solvers alternate, with hard choices or soft weights.

1. Where the discrete unknowns come from

Discrete variables enter in four ways: the class \(\sigma\) of each object, which is tied to its shape; symmetries (a square table looks the same every 90°); several pose hypotheses from a learned front-end; and data association, the question of which mapped object produced a detection (Week 6 · Day 1). §16.2.2 · p. 466

Put together, the estimation problem is a MAP problem over robot poses \(X\), landmarks \(L\), and associations \(D\), given all measurements \(Z\): §16.2.2 · p. 467

\[ \hat{X}, \hat{L}, \hat{D} = \argmax_{X, L, D}\; p(X, L, D \mid Z). \tag{16.16} \]

Classes and associations belong in one problem because they inform each other: a detection labelled "table" is unlikely to be a chair. The price is a search space that is combinatorial as well as nonconvex. If 6 detections can each come from any of 6 objects there are \(6^6 = 46{,}656\) assignments, and in the worst case each needs its own continuous optimization. §16.2.2 · p. 468

2. The hybrid factor graph

Group the continuous variables into \(\Theta\) and the discrete ones into \(D\). The posterior factors as before, and taking the negative logarithm turns the product into a sum: §16.2.2 · p. 468

\[ p(\Theta, D \mid Z) \propto \prod_k \phi_k(V_k), \qquad \Theta^*, D^* = \argmin_{\Theta, D} \underbrace{\sum_k -\log \phi_k(V_k)}_{\mathcal{L}(\Theta, D)}. \tag{16.17, 16.18} \]

\(V_k\) is the set of variables factor \(k\) touches. There are three kinds of factor: discrete \(\phi_k(D_k)\), continuous \(\phi_k(\Theta_k)\), and discrete-continuous \(\phi_k(\Theta_k, D_k)\). The last kind is assumed to be a squared residual once the discrete value is fixed: §16.2.2 · p. 469

\[ -\log \phi_k(\Theta_k, D_k) = \norm{r_k(\Theta_k, D_k)}_2^2 . \tag{16.19} \]

A detection factor is the typical case. Its discrete variable \(d_k \in \{1, \dots, J\}\) picks which landmark the residual is computed against: \(r_k = \boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{-1/2}\left(\mathbf{z}_k - h(\mathbf{T}, \boldsymbol{\ell}_{d_k})\right)\).

3. Alternating minimization: fix one kind, solve the other

Two observations make a local method possible. §16.2.2 · p. 469

  • With \(D\) fixed, only continuous variables remain, and the Gauss-Newton tools of Week 2 · Day 4 apply.
  • With \(\Theta\) fixed, what remains is a discrete factor graph. If the discrete variables split into small groups \(D_j\) that are conditionally independent given \(\Theta\), \[ p(D \mid \Theta, Z) \propto \prod_j p(D_j \mid \Theta, Z) \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \max_D\, p(D \mid \Theta, Z) \propto \prod_j \Big[\max_{D_j} p(D_j \mid \Theta, Z)\Big], \tag{16.20, 16.21} \] each group can be optimized on its own.

DC-SAM turns this into a loop, repeated until \(\mathcal{L}\) stops decreasing: §16.2.2 · p. 470

\[ D^{(i+1)} = \argmin_D\, \mathcal{L}(\Theta^{(i)}, D), \qquad \Theta^{(i+1)} = \argmin_\Theta\, \mathcal{L}(\Theta, D^{(i+1)}). \tag{16.22} \]

Filling the gap: why the maximum of a product splits, and what it saves

Take two groups. Each factor is non-negative and depends on its own group only, so

\[ \max_{D_1, D_2}\, f_1(D_1)\, f_2(D_2) = \max_{D_1}\Big[f_1(D_1)\,\max_{D_2} f_2(D_2)\Big] = \Big[\max_{D_1} f_1(D_1)\Big]\Big[\max_{D_2} f_2(D_2)\Big]. \]

The inner maximum is a non-negative constant as far as \(D_1\) is concerned, so it comes out of the outer one. For data association, one group is one detection's variable \(d_k\): with poses and landmarks fixed, what detection 1 saw says nothing more about detection 2. The discrete step then costs \(K \times J\) likelihood evaluations (36 for 6 detections and 6 objects) in place of \(J^K\) (46,656).

Neither step of (16.22) can increase \(\mathcal{L}\), so the loop settles, but at a local minimum: a wrong association can pull the geometry to where that association still looks best.

Max-mixture factors are the same idea folded into the factor. Maximize over \(d_k\) inside it:

\[ \phi_k(\Theta) = \max_j\; w_{kj}\, \N\!\big(\mathbf{z}_k;\, h(\Theta, \boldsymbol{\ell}_j),\, \boldsymbol{\Sigma}\big) \quad\Longrightarrow\quad -\log\phi_k = \min_j \Big[\tfrac12 \norm{\mathbf{z}_k - h(\Theta, \boldsymbol{\ell}_j)}^2_{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}} - \log w_{kj}\Big] + \text{const}. \]

At every iteration the solver keeps the smallest branch at the current estimate and linearizes it like any Gaussian factor. Semantics enter through \(w_{kj}\), the probability of the reported label if the object were \(j\).

4. Expectation-maximization: soft associations

Bowman et al. keep a probability for every candidate where alternating minimization commits to one. §16.2.2 · p. 470

  • E-step. Fix poses and landmarks. For each detection \(k\) compute the probability that it came from object \(j\): \[ w_{kj} = \frac{\pi_{kj}\; \N\!\big(\mathbf{z}_k;\, h(\Theta, \boldsymbol{\ell}_j),\, \boldsymbol{\Sigma}\big)}{\sum_{j'} \pi_{kj'}\; \N\!\big(\mathbf{z}_k;\, h(\Theta, \boldsymbol{\ell}_{j'}),\, \boldsymbol{\Sigma}\big)}, \qquad \pi_{kj} = p(\text{label of } k \mid \text{class of } j). \]
  • M-step. Fix the weights. Optimize poses and landmarks with every detection-object pair counted in proportion to its weight: \[ \Theta \leftarrow \argmin_\Theta \sum_k \sum_j w_{kj}\, \norm{\mathbf{z}_k - h(\Theta, \boldsymbol{\ell}_j)}^2_{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}} + (\text{other factors}). \]

The loop converges gradually to a local optimum. The E-step probabilities can be computed exactly through a matrix permanent, or more cheaply by approximating it. §16.2.2 · p. 470

Filling the gap: one detection, three answers

A robot in a corridor believes it is at \(p = 2.5\) m. The map has a table at \(4.0\) m and a chair at \(5.2\) m. A detection says "a chair, \(z = 2.0\) m ahead", which puts the object at \(4.5\) m: \(0.5\) m from the table and \(0.7\) m from the chair. Take \(\sigma = 0.3\) m, and a detector whose label is right 90% of the time.

The geometry term \(e^{-d^2/2\sigma^2}\) is \(e^{-1.389} = 0.249\) for the table and \(e^{-2.722} = 0.066\) for the chair. The label term \(\pi\) is \(0.1\) for the table and \(0.9\) for the chair. The products are \(0.0249\) and \(0.0592\), which normalize to weights \(0.30\) and \(0.70\).

  • Nearest neighbour looks at distance only and picks the table. The detection then says the robot is at \(4.0 - 2.0 = 2.0\) m.
  • Max-mixture picks the largest product, the chair: \(5.2 - 2.0 = 3.2\) m.
  • EM uses both: \(0.30 \times 2.0 + 0.70 \times 3.2 = 2.84\) m. Without the label the weights would be \(0.79\) and \(0.21\), and the answer \(2.25\) m.

Why the M-step is a weighted least squares: EM maximizes the log-likelihood averaged over the associations, \(\sum_k\sum_j w_{kj} \log\big[\pi_{kj}\,\N(\mathbf{z}_k; h(\Theta, \boldsymbol{\ell}_j), \boldsymbol{\Sigma})\big]\), and its only part that depends on \(\Theta\) is \(-\tfrac12\sum_k\sum_j w_{kj}\norm{\mathbf{z}_k - h(\Theta, \boldsymbol{\ell}_j)}^2_{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}\). It is the "weights, then weighted least squares" loop of IRLS (Week 6 · Day 4) with probabilities as weights.

5. The three methods on one problem

Try it: a robot returns to a mapped room with four chairs and two tables. Its odometry has drifted 0.8 m, more than half the spacing of the row. Press Step three times. Then switch the class labels off and repeat. Then try EM with the labels still off.

Notice that with max-mixture and labels, three steps take the error from 0.62 to 0.23 to 0.03 m and the wrong associations from 3 to 1 to 0, although detection z4 carries a wrong label. Without labels the same method stays at 0.82 m with four wrong associations, and so does nearest neighbour. EM without labels still escapes, in about six steps, because each wrong pairing leaves some weight on the right object. At \(\sigma = 0.15\) m all three are stuck: an overconfident noise model turns soft weights into hard ones. At \(\sigma = 0.8\) m the wrong label on z4 outvotes the geometry.

The book names three more families. Multi-hypothesis solvers (MH-iSAM2, iMHS) keep several assignments alive and prune the search. Continuous relaxations replace a label by a probability vector on the simplex and optimize it as a continuous variable. Marginalization sums the discrete variables out, which leaves a non-Gaussian mixture over \(\Theta\) for specialized solvers. §16.2.2 · pp. 470–471

Check yourself

Q1. Ten detections can each come from one of four mapped objects. How many likelihood evaluations does one discrete step of (16.22) need when (16.20) holds, and how many joint assignments exist?

Each detection is decided on its own: 10 × 4 = 40 evaluations. The joint space has 4¹⁰ = 1,048,576 assignments.

Q2. A detection is at distance 0.3 m from candidate A and 0.6 m from candidate B, with σ = 0.3 m and no label information. What is the EM weight of A?

Geometry terms: exp(−0.09/0.18) = 0.607 for A and exp(−0.36/0.18) = 0.135 for B. Weight of A = 0.607/(0.607 + 0.135) = 0.82.

Q3. In the same situation the detection is labelled "table", A is a chair, B is a table, and the label is right 90% of the time. Which candidate does a max-mixture factor select?

Products: A 0.1 × 0.607 = 0.061, B 0.9 × 0.135 = 0.122. Max-mixture keeps the single largest, B. EM would keep both, with weights 0.33 and 0.67.

Q4. Why can alternating minimization end with wrong associations even though every step lowers the cost?

Block coordinate descent stops when neither block can improve alone, as in the widget with labels off.

Recap

  1. Classes, symmetries, pose hypotheses, and associations are discrete unknowns. With poses and shapes they form the MAP problem (16.16), a hybrid factor graph with cost \(\mathcal{L}(\Theta, D)\).
  2. Fixing \(D\) leaves least squares. Fixing \(\Theta\) leaves a discrete problem that splits into conditionally independent groups.
  3. Alternating minimization and max-mixtures make hard choices, re-made every iteration. EM keeps weights \(w_{kj}\) and solves a weighted least squares.
  4. All of them are local. Labels and a sensible noise model decide whether the local answer is the right one.

Sources

  1. SLAM Handbook, §16.2.2 "Hybrid Solvers for Sparse Metric-Semantic SLAM", pp. 466–471.
  2. Dempster, Laird, Rubin, Maximum Likelihood from Incomplete Data via the EM Algorithm, 1977; Bishop, Pattern Recognition and Machine Learning, 2006, Chapter 9 (the E-step weights and the weighted M-step).
  3. Olson and Agarwal, Inference on Networks of Mixtures for Robust Robot Mapping, 2013 (max-mixture factors).

Week 22 · Day 4

Dense semantic maps: fusing labels into surfels and voxels

After today you can explain how noisy per-frame labels are fused into surfel and voxel maps, derive the multi-class log-odds update, and run it by hand for one voxel.

About 60 min · Read §16.3.1–16.3.2, pp. 471–478 (8 pages, 3 of them mostly figures) · Needs Week 8 Day 1

Read first: §16.3.1 and §16.3.2, pp. 471–478

While you read, look for:

  • Why SuMa++ does not simply delete every point labelled "car" (p. 472).
  • The definition of a range-category observation (p. 473).
  • The log-odds vector, the softmax that undoes it, and the update (16.24), pp. 474–475.
  • The three cases of the model (16.26), p. 475, and the pruning rule, pp. 476–477.

Today's big idea

A dense semantic map keeps, for every small piece of space, a probability for each class. One segmented image is noisy, so the map fuses many with Bayes' rule. Written in log-odds, that fusion is an addition: each observation adds a fixed vector to the cell it touches.

1. Labels on points and surfels

Segmentation networks can label every point of a LiDAR scan. The labels of one scan are noisy and disagree with the next scan's, so the mapping problem is to integrate them over time. SuMa++ stores a class and a confidence in each surfel. Conflicting labels lower the confidence, and surfels with low confidence are filtered out. §16.3.1 · p. 471

The same mechanism handles moving objects. Deleting every point of a movable class throws away parked cars, which are good references for scan registration in a city. Deleting only the surfels whose stored label conflicts with the current scan worked better. §16.3.1 · p. 472

Labels also feed back into SLAM: registration can match only points of compatible classes (compare ICP in Week 13 · Day 2), and place descriptors such as Scan Context (Week 13 · Day 4) can be extended with class information for loop closure. §16.3.1 · p. 472

2. Voxels: what is observed and what is estimated

Split the environment into classes \(\mathcal{K} = \{0, \dots, K\}\), where 0 is free space and the others are object classes. A range-category observation is, for each sensor ray \(b\), a pair \(z = (r_{t,b}, y_{t,b})\): the range at which the ray stopped and the class of what it hit. An RGB-D camera produces one per pixel by pairing the depth image with a segmentation of the colour image. §16.3.2 · p. 473

The map \(\mathbf{m}\) is a grid of cells \(i = 1, \dots, N\), each with an unknown class \(m_i \in \mathcal{K}\). With the robot poses known, Bayes' rule updates the map's probability mass function \(p_t(\mathbf{m})\) with each new observation set \(\mathcal{Z}_{t+1}\):

\[ p_{t+1}(\mathbf{m}) \propto p(\mathcal{Z}_{t+1} \mid \mathbf{m})\, p_t(\mathbf{m}), \qquad p_t(\mathbf{m}) = \prod_{i=1}^{N} p_t(m_i). \tag{16.23} \]

The second equation is an approximation chosen for cost: cells are treated as independent, so the map stores \(N\) small distributions and not one distribution over \((K+1)^N\) maps. §16.3.2 · pp. 473–474

3. Multi-class log-odds

Each cell stores its distribution as a multi-class log-odds vector, the log of each class probability relative to "free": §16.3.2 · p. 474

\[ \mathbf{h}_{t,i} = \begin{bmatrix} \log\frac{p_t(m_i=0)}{p_t(m_i=0)} & \cdots & \log\frac{p_t(m_i=K)}{p_t(m_i=0)} \end{bmatrix}\T \in \R^{K+1}, \qquad p_t(m_i = k) = \frac{e^{h_k}}{\sum_{j=0}^{K} e^{h_j}} . \]

The first entry is always 0. The second formula, the softmax, recovers the probabilities. In these coordinates the Bayesian update is a sum:

\[ \mathbf{h}_{t+1,i} = \mathbf{h}_{t,i} + \sum_{z \in \mathcal{Z}_{t+1}} \mathbf{l}_i(z), \qquad \mathbf{l}_i(z) = \begin{bmatrix} \log\frac{p(z \mid m_i=0)}{p(z \mid m_i=0)} & \cdots & \log\frac{p(z \mid m_i=K)}{p(z \mid m_i=0)} \end{bmatrix}\T . \tag{16.24, 16.25} \]

Filling the gap: deriving (16.24) and the softmax

Bayes' rule for one cell and one observation, with \(\eta\) a normalizer that does not depend on \(k\):

\[ p_{t+1}(m_i = k) = \eta\; p(z \mid m_i = k)\; p_t(m_i = k). \]

Write the same line for \(k = 0\), divide, and take logarithms. \(\eta\) cancels:

\[ \underbrace{\log\frac{p_{t+1}(m_i=k)}{p_{t+1}(m_i=0)}}_{\text{entry } k \text{ of } \mathbf{h}_{t+1,i}} = \underbrace{\log\frac{p(z \mid m_i=k)}{p(z \mid m_i=0)}}_{\text{entry } k \text{ of } \mathbf{l}_i(z)} + \underbrace{\log\frac{p_t(m_i=k)}{p_t(m_i=0)}}_{\text{entry } k \text{ of } \mathbf{h}_{t,i}} . \]

If the observations are independent given the cell's class, their likelihoods multiply and their logs add, which gives the sum over \(z\). For the softmax, \(h_k = \log[p(k)/p(0)]\) means \(p(k) = p(0)\,e^{h_k}\). The probabilities sum to one, so \(p(0)\sum_j e^{h_j} = 1\), and substituting \(p(0)\) back gives the formula. With \(K = 1\) the vector is \([0,\ \log(p_{\text{occ}}/p_{\text{free}})]\): the occupancy log-odds of Week 8 · Day 1.

4. The observation model, with numbers

A ray says three different things to three kinds of cell, and the book's model is piecewise constant along the ray: §16.3.2 · p. 475

\[ \mathbf{l}_i((r, y)) = \begin{cases} \boldsymbol{\phi}^+ + \mathbf{E}_{y+1}\boldsymbol{\psi}^+, & r \text{ indicates } m_i \text{ is occupied},\\ \boldsymbol{\phi}^-, & r \text{ indicates } m_i \text{ is free},\\ \mathbf{0}, & \text{otherwise}. \end{cases} \tag{16.26} \]

\(\mathbf{E}_k = \mathbf{e}_k\mathbf{e}_k\T\) keeps only entry \(k\) of a vector, and the first entries of \(\boldsymbol{\phi}^+, \boldsymbol{\psi}^+, \boldsymbol{\phi}^-\) are 0. So a hit raises every object class against "free" (\(\boldsymbol{\phi}^+\)) and raises the reported class \(y\) a little more (\(\boldsymbol{\psi}^+\)); a pass-through lowers every object class (\(\boldsymbol{\phi}^-\) has negative entries).

Filling the gap: where the parameter vectors come from, and three updates by hand

The entries are log likelihood ratios, as (16.25) says. Take classes {free, chair, table} and this sensor: a ray passes through a free cell with probability 0.9 and reports a false hit of either class with probability 0.05 each; it passes through an occupied cell without stopping with probability 0.2, and when it stops the label is right with probability 0.75, so a chair cell gives "hit, chair" with probability 0.6 and "hit, table" with 0.2. Then

\[ \mathbf{l}(\text{hit, chair}) = \begin{bmatrix} 0 & \ln\frac{0.6}{0.05} & \ln\frac{0.2}{0.05} \end{bmatrix} = [0,\ 2.48,\ 1.39], \qquad \mathbf{l}(\text{pass}) = \begin{bmatrix} 0 & \ln\frac{0.2}{0.9} & \ln\frac{0.2}{0.9} \end{bmatrix} = [0,\ -1.50,\ -1.50], \]

which is (16.26) with \(\boldsymbol{\phi}^+ = [0, 1.39, 1.39]\), \(\boldsymbol{\psi}^+ = [0, 1.10, 1.10]\), \(\boldsymbol{\phi}^- = [0, -1.50, -1.50]\). Start a cell at \(\mathbf{h} = [0, 0, 0]\) (all classes equally likely) and fuse three hits labelled chair, table, chair:

\[ \mathbf{h} = [0,\ 2.48 + 1.39 + 2.48,\ 1.39 + 2.48 + 1.39] = [0,\ 6.36,\ 5.26], \qquad e^{\mathbf{h}} = [1,\ 576,\ 192]. \]

The softmax gives \(p = [1, 576, 192]/769 = [0.001,\ 0.749,\ 0.250]\). The cell is almost surely occupied, and chair leads table three to one: two votes against one, each worth a factor \(0.6/0.2 = 3\).

Try it: press "Sample 1" once. Reset and press "Sample 10". Then set the label accuracy to 50% and sample again.

Notice that one hit already gives chair 71%, table 24%, free 6%. Ten samples (eight labelled chair, one labelled table, one pass-through) put chair at 99.95%. At 50% accuracy the labels carry no information: chair and table stay tied, yet "free" is still ruled out, because that part of the evidence comes from the range.

5. Storing it: the multi-class octree

A regular grid wastes memory on large empty volumes. An octree (Week 8 · Day 4) divides space recursively into eight octants; a node has either 8 children or none, and a node without children is a leaf. In a multi-class octree every node stores a log-odds vector. §16.3.2 · pp. 475–476

  • Update. Cast the ray through the tree, expand each observed leaf down to the finest resolution, and apply (16.24).
  • Prune. If the 8 children of a node are leaves with equal log-odds, delete them and make the parent a leaf. A free block of \(16^3 = 4096\) finest cells collapses to one node. Occupied regions rarely prune, since only their surfaces are observed.
  • Clamp. Noise keeps equal cells from reaching exactly equal values. Limiting each entry of \(\mathbf{h}\) to a fixed interval lets cells settle at the same value and prune, at the price of losing information near certainty.
  • Keep few classes. Cost grows linearly with \(K\) and the chance of pruning falls quickly, so a cell may store only its \(\bar{K}\) most likely classes and lump the rest into "others".

A parent's vector can be the average of its children's, or, conservatively, that of the child most likely to be occupied. Several robots can build one such map by agreeing on their local octrees over one-hop communication (ROAM). §16.3.2 · pp. 476–478

Check yourself

Q1. With classes {free, 1, 2}, a cell has h = [0, 1.1, −0.7]. What is the probability of class 1?

e^0 = 1, e^1.1 = 3.00, e^−0.7 = 0.50. Softmax: 3.00/(1 + 3.00 + 0.50) = 0.67.

Q2. A sensor reports "hit, class 1" with probability 0.6 if the cell is class 1, 0.1 if it is class 2, and 0.02 if it is free. What does this observation add to the class-2 entry of h?

Entry 2 of l(z) is ln[p(z | class 2)/p(z | free)] = ln(0.1/0.02) = ln 5 = 1.61. Even a hit with the other label is evidence that the cell is not free.

Q3. In a city, which rule for handling movable objects in a semantic surfel map worked better according to the chapter?

Parked vehicles are common and useful for registration. Removing all of them discards good constraints, so only surfels with conflicting labels are filtered.

Q4. Why does free space compress much better than occupied space in a multi-class octree?

Pruning needs 8 equal children. Rays cross free volumes everywhere and clamping makes their values equal. The inside of an object is never observed, so its cells differ from the surface cells.

Recap

  1. Surfel maps keep a class and a confidence per surfel; conflicting labels lower the confidence.
  2. A range-category observation gives a range and a class per ray. The voxel map keeps an independent class distribution per cell.
  3. In log-odds relative to "free", Bayes' rule is \(\mathbf{h} \leftarrow \mathbf{h} + \mathbf{l}(z)\), and the softmax returns probabilities.
  4. The model (16.26) adds \(\boldsymbol{\phi}^+ + \mathbf{E}_{y+1}\boldsymbol{\psi}^+\) at the ray's end point and \(\boldsymbol{\phi}^-\) along the way. The entries are log likelihood ratios of the sensor.
  5. A multi-class octree prunes equal children; clamping and keeping few classes make pruning likely.

Sources

  1. SLAM Handbook, §16.3.1 "Point-based and Surfel-based Metric-Semantic SLAM" and §16.3.2 "Voxel-based Metric-Semantic SLAM", pp. 471–478.
  2. Thrun, Burgard, Fox, Probabilistic Robotics, 2005 (the log-odds form of the binary Bayes filter, generalized here to several classes); Hornung, Wurm, Bennewitz, Stachniss, Burgard, OctoMap: An Efficient Probabilistic 3D Mapping Framework Based on Octrees, 2013.
  3. The sensor probabilities in the worked example are made up for illustration; they are the ones the widget uses.

Week 22 · Day 5

Meshes that bend, hierarchies, and 3D scene graphs

After today you can explain how a mesh is corrected after a loop closure by optimizing a deformation graph, count the memory a hierarchical map saves, and define a 3D scene graph and say what makes inference on it cheap.

About 60 min · Read §16.3.3, §16.4, §16.5, pp. 479–489 (11 pages, about 3 of them figures and 3 a survey) · Needs Week 13 Day 5

Read first: §16.3.3, §16.4, and §16.5, pp. 479–489

While you read, look for:

  • The two drawbacks of voxel maps that open §16.3.3 (p. 479).
  • The three sums of (16.27) on p. 481, and which graph edges each runs over.
  • Where the factor \(L\) goes between (16.34) and (16.35), p. 484.
  • The three properties in Definition 16.2 and the bound (16.37), p. 485.

Today's big idea

A loop closure moves the trajectory, and the dense map has to follow. A mesh can: tie a few of its vertices to the pose graph, optimize both as one pose graph, and drag the rest along. The same graph then grows upward into objects, places, and rooms: a 3D scene graph, where each symbol is stored once and a query touches only the branch it needs.

1. A mesh tied to the pose graph

Voxel maps fuse information well but are expensive to store and hard to edit: after a loop closure, past observations have to be removed and integrated again at their corrected poses. A mesh, usually extracted from a voxel map kept in a window around the robot, stores only surfaces and can be deformed in place. The method is pose-graph and mesh optimization (PGMO). §16.3.3 · p. 479

PGMO builds a deformation graph whose nodes each carry a rigid transformation: §16.3.3 · pp. 479–480

  • Pose vertices \(\mathbf{X}_i = [\mathbf{R}^X_i, \mathbf{t}^X_i]\), the nodes of the robot's pose graph, joined by its odometry and loop-closure edges.
  • Mesh vertices \(\mathbf{M}_k = [\mathbf{R}^M_k, \mathbf{t}^M_k]\), the vertices of a downsampled mesh, joined by its edges. Before any deformation \(\mathbf{R}^M_k = \mathbf{I}_3\) and \(\mathbf{t}^M_k = \mathbf{g}_k\), the vertex's original position.
  • An edge between pose \(i\) and mesh vertex \(k\) whenever the vertex was visible from that pose.

2. The cost, and why it is a pose graph

When a loop closure arrives, all transformations are re-estimated by minimizing §16.3.3 · p. 481

\[ \sum_{\mathbf{Z}_{ij}} \norm{\mathbf{X}_i\mathbf{Z}_{ij} - \mathbf{X}_j}^2_{\boldsymbol{\Omega}_{ij}} + \sum_{k}\sum_{l \in \mathcal{N}^M(k)} \norm{\mathbf{R}^M_k(\mathbf{g}_l - \mathbf{g}_k) + \mathbf{t}^M_k - \mathbf{t}^M_l}^2_{\boldsymbol{\Omega}_{kl}} + \sum_{i}\sum_{l \in \mathcal{N}^M(i)} \norm{\mathbf{R}^X_i\tilde{\mathbf{g}}_{il} + \mathbf{t}^X_i - \mathbf{t}^M_l}^2_{\boldsymbol{\Omega}_{il}}. \tag{16.27} \]

The first sum is ordinary pose-graph optimization over the relative-pose measurements \(\mathbf{Z}_{ij}\). The second keeps the mesh locally rigid: if the patch around node \(k\) moved as a rigid body, neighbour \(l\) would be at \(\mathbf{R}^M_k(\mathbf{g}_l - \mathbf{g}_k) + \mathbf{t}^M_k\), and the term penalizes its distance from where \(l\) actually is. The third does the same between a pose and the mesh nodes it saw, with \(\tilde{\mathbf{g}}_{il} = \tilde{\mathbf{R}}_i\T(\mathbf{g}_l - \mathbf{g}_i)\) the original position of node \(l\) in the frame of pose \(i\). Before deformation every rigidity term is zero.

Filling the gap: from (16.27) to the pose-graph form (16.30)

The book defines \(\mathbf{G}_{kl} = \begin{bmatrix}\mathbf{I}_3 & \mathbf{g}_l - \mathbf{g}_k\\ \mathbf{0} & 1\end{bmatrix}\) and claims the second sum equals \(\sum \norm{\mathbf{M}_k\mathbf{G}_{kl} - \mathbf{M}_l}^2_{\boldsymbol{\Omega}}\). Multiply out, writing \(\mathbf{M}_k\) as a \(4\times4\) matrix:

\[ \mathbf{M}_k\mathbf{G}_{kl} - \mathbf{M}_l = \begin{bmatrix}\mathbf{R}_k & \mathbf{R}_k(\mathbf{g}_l - \mathbf{g}_k) + \mathbf{t}_k\\ \mathbf{0} & 1\end{bmatrix} - \begin{bmatrix}\mathbf{R}_l & \mathbf{t}_l\\ \mathbf{0} & 1\end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix}\mathbf{R}_k - \mathbf{R}_l & \mathbf{R}_k(\mathbf{g}_l - \mathbf{g}_k) + \mathbf{t}_k - \mathbf{t}_l\\ \mathbf{0} & 0\end{bmatrix}. \]

The last column is exactly the rigidity residual. The weighted Frobenius norm of (16.28), \(\norm{\mathbf{A}}^2_{\boldsymbol{\Omega}} = \tr(\mathbf{A}\boldsymbol{\Omega}\mathbf{A}\T)\) with \(\boldsymbol{\Omega} = \diag(\omega_R\mathbf{I}_3, \omega_t)\), weights the squared entries of the first three columns by \(\omega_R\) and those of the last column by \(\omega_t\). Setting \(\omega_R = 0\) on mesh edges leaves \(\omega_t\) times the squared rigidity residual, and the third sum works the same way. So every term has the form \(\norm{\mathbf{T}_i\mathbf{E}_{ij} - \mathbf{T}_j}^2_{\boldsymbol{\Omega}_{ij}}\), equation (16.31): one pose graph over \(n + m\) nodes, for the solvers of Week 13 · Day 5.

3. Moving every other vertex

The optimization moved only the control nodes. Each vertex \(\mathbf{v}_i\) of the full mesh is then carried by its \(m\) nearest control nodes: §16.3.3 · p. 482

\[ \tilde{\mathbf{v}}_i = \sum_{j=1}^{m} w_j(\mathbf{v}_i)\left[\mathbf{R}^M_j(\mathbf{v}_i - \mathbf{g}_j) + \mathbf{t}^M_j\right], \qquad w_j = \frac{\bar{w}_j}{\sum_k \bar{w}_k}, \quad \bar{w}_j(\mathbf{v}_i) = \left(1 - \frac{\norm{\mathbf{v}_i - \mathbf{g}_j}}{d_{\max}}\right)^2 . \tag{16.32, 16.33} \]

Each bracket is "where \(\mathbf{v}_i\) would go if it were glued to node \(j\)", and \(d_{\max}\) is the distance to the furthest of the \(m\) nodes. Take \(m = 3\) nodes at distances 1, 2, and 4 m. Then \(\bar{w} = (0.75^2, 0.5^2, 0) = (0.5625, 0.25, 0)\) and \(w = (0.69, 0.31, 0)\). If the nodes only translated, by \((0.4, 0)\), \((0.1, 0)\), and \((-2, 0)\) m, the vertex moves by \(0.69 \times 0.4 + 0.31 \times 0.1 = 0.31\) m in \(x\). The furthest node has weight zero.

4. Symbols, and what hierarchy saves

Symbol grounding is tying a symbol that means something to a person, such as "chair" or "kitchen", to a location in the map. Raw images are too bulky to ground symbols in, so they are attached to a compact sub-symbolic representation such as voxels or a mesh. §16.4.1 · p. 483

The naive way stores in every voxel which of the \(L\) symbols apply to it (a voxel can belong to a chair and to a kitchen). For volume \(V\) and resolution \(\delta\): §16.4.1 · p. 484

\[ m = O\!\left(L \cdot V/\delta^3\right). \tag{16.34} \]

Organizing the symbols by containment gives instead

\[ m = O\!\left(V/\delta^3 + N_{\text{objects}} + N_{\text{rooms}} + \dots + N_{\text{buildings}}\right). \tag{16.35} \]

Each symbol is now stored once, as a node of a graph whose edges mean "contains". Nothing is lost; the per-voxel labels can be regenerated. For a flat of 150 m³ at \(\delta = 0.1\) m with 15 symbols, (16.34) is \(15 \times 150{,}000 = 2{,}250{,}000\) entries and (16.35) is \(150{,}000 + 14 + 4 + 1\). Replacing the voxel grid by an octree or by a graph of places shrinks the first term to \(N_{\text{sub-sym}}\) (16.36), now with some loss. §16.4.1 · p. 484

5. Hierarchical graphs and 3D scene graphs

A graph is hierarchical if its nodes split into layers \(1, \dots, l\) such that (1) a node has at most one parent in the layer above, (2) edges between layers join consecutive layers only, and (3) children of different parents are never connected. Then the descendants of two nodes of the same layer never mix, and the treewidth of the whole graph is bounded by Definition 16.2, §16.4.1 · p. 485

\[ \max_{v \in \mathcal{V}}\; tw\big[\mathcal{G}[\mathcal{C}(v)]\big] + 1, \tag{16.37} \]

where \(\mathcal{G}[\mathcal{C}(v)]\) is the subgraph formed by the children of \(v\).

Filling the gap: what treewidth buys

Treewidth measures how far a graph is from a tree: a tree has treewidth 1, a fully connected graph on \(n\) nodes has \(n - 1\). With the best elimination order (Week 3 · Day 3), the largest clique created has treewidth \(+\,1\) variables, and exact inference over discrete variables costs exponentially in that number but only linearly in the number of nodes. So (16.37) says the cost is set by the most tangled group of siblings, such as the objects of one cluttered room, and not by the size of the building.

A 3D scene graph is a graph \(\mathcal{G} = (\mathcal{V}, \mathcal{E})\) whose nodes carry features that always include a position, and whose edges carry features too. Its layers are typically objects, places (a sparse model of free space), rooms, and buildings. Edges between layers mean containment. Edges inside a layer mean relations such as "on top of" or "nearby", some of them directed. Relations such as "left of", common in 2D scene graphs, depend on the viewpoint and mean little in 3D. §16.4.2 · pp. 486–487

Try it: run each of the four queries and compare the first two counters.

Notice that "the mug in the kitchen" examines 9 of 19 nodes and never opens the living room, which has a mug of its own. "Go to the living room" examines 5 and no object at all. The last two queries examine all 19, more than the 14 entries of a flat object list: hierarchy pays when the query names a level above the answer.

Going deeper (optional): loop closures and where §16.5 points

To keep a scene graph consistent, one approach adds the places layer to the deformation graph of (16.27) and re-interpolates the other layers; another puts factors between all layers, which is no longer a plain pose graph. §16.4.2 · p. 487 The trends: maps that store language-aligned features in place of a fixed label set (next week), scene graphs for outdoor scenes with task-driven layers, uncertainty over mixed discrete and continuous variables, and multi-robot semantic mapping. §16.5 · pp. 487–489

Check yourself

Q1. In the pose-graph form (16.30), why is the rotation weight ω_R set to zero on mesh edges?

The rigidity terms are 3-vectors equal to the last column of the matrix difference, so the other three columns must get weight zero.

Q2. A mesh vertex has m = 3 nearest control nodes at distances 1, 3, and 4 m. What is the normalized weight of the nearest node in (16.33)?

d_max = 4. Unnormalized weights: (1 − 1/4)² = 0.5625, (1 − 3/4)² = 0.0625, and 0. Normalized: 0.5625/0.625 = 0.90.

Q3. A floor of 200 m³ is stored at δ = 0.1 m with L = 50 symbols, 300 objects, and 12 rooms in 1 building. Roughly how much smaller is the hierarchical count (16.35) than the flat count (16.34)?

V/δ³ = 200,000 voxels. Flat: 50 × 200,000 = 10,000,000. Hierarchical: 200,000 + 313. The ratio is about 50, the number of symbols.

Q4. Which of these breaks Definition 16.2?

Two parents violate the single-parent property. Edges between siblings are allowed; they only raise the treewidth of that group.

Recap

  1. PGMO joins the pose graph and a downsampled mesh in a deformation graph and optimizes (16.27): pose-graph terms plus local-rigidity terms. With \(\omega_R = 0\) on mesh edges it is a standard pose graph.
  2. The full mesh follows by blending the motions of each vertex's nearest control nodes (16.32).
  3. Storing each symbol once in a hierarchy cuts memory from \(L \cdot V/\delta^3\) to \(V/\delta^3 + N\), without loss.
  4. A 3D scene graph is a layered graph of positioned nodes. Single parents, locality, and disjoint children bound its treewidth by that of one group of siblings, plus one.

Sources

  1. SLAM Handbook, §16.3.3 "Mesh-based Metric-Semantic SLAM", §16.4 "Hierarchical Metric-Semantic Representations and 3D Scene Graphs", §16.5 "Further Readings & Recent Trends", pp. 479–489.
  2. Sumner, Schmid, Pauly, Embedded Deformation for Shape Manipulation, 2007 (the deformation graph and its blending weights); Koller and Friedman, Probabilistic Graphical Models, 2009 (treewidth and the cost of exact inference).

Week 22 · Review

Week 22 review: metric-semantic SLAM

After today you can write the residual for each object shape model, run one step of hard and soft data association, fuse class labels in a voxel, and explain how meshes and scene graphs stay consistent after a loop closure.

About 60 min · No new pages

The week in one paragraph

A metric-semantic map stores what things are as well as where they are. Sparse maps turn landmarks into objects with a class, pose, scale, and shape, and compare each shape model with the matching detector output: keypoints, boxes, masks, or depth. Classes and data associations are discrete, so the back-end alternates between choosing them (hard, or softly with EM) and solving least squares. Dense maps keep a class distribution per voxel and fuse labels by adding log-odds. Meshes follow a loop closure through a deformation graph, and scene graphs stack objects, places, and rooms on top, storing each symbol once.

1. Formula sheet

What it isFormulaWhere
Object landmark; keypoint shape\(\boldsymbol{\ell} = (\sigma, \mathbf{q}, \lambda, \mathbf{s})\), \(\ \mathbf{s}_j = \mathbf{b}_{j,0} + \sum_k c_k\mathbf{b}_{j,k}\)Def. 16.1, (16.2), pp. 456–457 · Day 1
Keypoint residual\(r_i^2 = \sum_j \norm{\mathbf{z}_{i,j} - \pi(\mathbf{q}_i^{-1}\mathbf{T}_i, \lambda_i\mathbf{s}_{i,j})}^2_{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_i}\)(16.3), p. 458 · Day 1
Dual quadric, projected\(\mathbf{Q}^*_{\mathbf{s}} \propto \mathbf{Q}_{\mathbf{s}}^{-1}\), \(\ \mathbf{C}^*_{\mathbf{x}} \propto \mathbf{P}\mathbf{T}^{-1}\mathbf{Q}^*_{\boldsymbol{\ell}}\mathbf{T}^{-\top}\mathbf{P}\T\)(16.6)–(16.8), pp. 459–460 · Day 2
Hybrid cost and alternation\(\mathcal{L}(\Theta, D) = \sum_k -\log\phi_k(V_k)\); minimize over \(D\), then over \(\Theta\)(16.18), (16.22), pp. 468–470 · Day 3

2. Mixed quiz

Check yourself

Q1. A real car and a 1:10 toy of the same model are both in the map. Which component of their object landmarks differs, apart from the pose?

Same category and same canonical shape. Only the scale differs.

Q2. Camera at the world origin with identity pose. An unrotated object frame sits at (2, 0, 10) m with λ = 1. Where does the semantic landmark s = (0, 1, 0) appear in normalized image coordinates?

World point: (2, 1, 10). Dividing by depth gives (0.2, 0.1).

Q3. A sphere of radius 3 m is centred on the optical axis at depth 5 m. What is the half-width of its outline in normalized image coordinates?

ρ²I − t tᵀ = diag(9, 9, 9 − 25) ∝ diag(9/16, 9/16, −1). Half-width = 3/4 = 0.75, not 3/5.

Q4. Which pairing of shape model and detector output does the chapter use?

Ellipsoid with bounding box (16.10), mesh with mask (16.12), SDF with depth points (16.15).

Q5. A detection labelled "chair" is equally far from object A (a chair) and object B (a table). The label is right 80% of the time. What is the EM weight of A?

The geometry terms cancel. The label likelihoods, normalized, give 0.8/(0.8 + 0.2) = 0.8.

Q6. With the continuous variables fixed, why can each detection's association be chosen on its own?

This is (16.20) and (16.21): K searches over J candidates replace one search over J^K assignments.

Q7. A voxel with classes {free, A, B} has h = [0, 2, 2]. A ray passes through it, with φ⁻ = [0, −1.5, −1.5]. What is the probability of "free" afterwards?

h becomes [0, 0.5, 0.5]. Softmax: 1/(1 + 2e^0.5) = 1/4.30 = 0.23. Before the pass it was 1/(1 + 2e²) = 0.06.

Q8. In a scene graph, the room nodes of the building form a subgraph of treewidth 2, and the objects of any one room form a subgraph of treewidth at most 3. What bound does (16.37) give for the whole graph?

The largest treewidth among groups of siblings, plus one: max(2, 3) + 1 = 4, however many rooms there are.

3. Pen-and-paper problems

  1. A dual conic, scaled so that its bottom-right entry is \(-1\), is \(\begin{bmatrix}0.05 & 0.02 & -0.2\\ 0.02 & 0 & 0.1\\ -0.2 & 0.1 & -1\end{bmatrix}\). Find the bounding box \((u, v, w, h)\) it represents.

    Solution

    Compare with (16.9) multiplied out. The centre is minus the last column: \((c_u, c_v) = (0.2, -0.1)\). Then \((w/2)^2 = C^*_{11} + c_u^2 = 0.05 + 0.04 = 0.09\), so \(w = 0.6\), and \((h/2)^2 = C^*_{22} + c_v^2 = 0 + 0.01\), so \(h = 0.2\). Check the off-diagonal: \(-c_uc_v = 0.02\). The corner is \((u, v) = (0.2 - 0.3,\ -0.1 - 0.1) = (-0.1, -0.2)\).

  2. A robot moves along a line. The map has two chairs, A at 2.0 m and B at 3.0 m. The robot believes it is at \(p = 0.4\) m and receives two detections of objects ahead, \(z_1 = 1.9\) m and \(z_2 = 2.7\) m, with \(\sigma = 0.5\) m and no useful labels. Do one EM iteration for \(p\). Compare with a hard nearest-neighbour step.

    Solution

    E-step. The detections are predicted at \(2.3\) and \(3.1\) m. With \(e^{-d^2/2\sigma^2} = e^{-2d^2}\): for \(z_1\), distances \(0.3\) and \(0.7\) give \(0.835\) and \(0.375\), so \(w_{1A} = 0.69\), \(w_{1B} = 0.31\). For \(z_2\), distances \(1.1\) and \(0.1\) give \(0.089\) and \(0.980\), so \(w_{2A} = 0.08\), \(w_{2B} = 0.92\).

    M-step. Minimizing \(\sum_{k,j} w_{kj}(z_k + p - \ell_j)^2\) gives the weighted mean of the values \(\ell_j - z_k\), with weights summing to 2: \(p = \tfrac12[0.69(0.1) + 0.31(1.1) + 0.08(-0.7) + 0.92(0.3)] = 0.31\) m.

    Nearest neighbour assigns \(z_1\) to A and \(z_2\) to B: \(p = \tfrac12(0.1 + 0.3) = 0.2\) m. EM differs because it still gives 31% to the first detection being chair B.

  3. A voxel has classes {free, wall, door} and starts with all three equally likely. The sensor reports "hit, wall" with probability 0.04, 0.64, 0.16 when the cell is free, wall, door; "hit, door" with 0.04, 0.16, 0.64; and passes through with 0.92, 0.2, 0.2. The cell receives: hit wall, hit wall, hit door, pass. Find the class probabilities.

    Solution

    Log-odds increments relative to "free": \(\mathbf{l}(\text{hit wall}) = [0, \ln 16, \ln 4]\), \(\mathbf{l}(\text{hit door}) = [0, \ln 4, \ln 16]\), \(\mathbf{l}(\text{pass}) = [0, \ln 0.217, \ln 0.217]\). Adding logs is multiplying ratios: wall \(16 \cdot 16 \cdot 4 \cdot 0.217 = 222.6\), door \(4 \cdot 4 \cdot 16 \cdot 0.217 = 55.7\), free \(1\). So \(\mathbf{h} = [0, 5.41, 4.02]\) and \(p = [1, 222.6, 55.7]/279.3 = [0.004, 0.797, 0.199]\). Wall leads door four to one: a net of one label vote, worth \(0.64/0.16\).

  4. Mesh control nodes \(k\) and \(l\) start at \(\mathbf{g}_k = (0,0,0)\) and \(\mathbf{g}_l = (2,0,0)\). After a loop closure both have rotated by 90° about the \(z\)-axis; \(\mathbf{t}_k = (0,0,0)\) and \(\mathbf{t}_l = (0, 2, 0.3)\). (a) Compute the rigidity residual of edge \((k, l)\) in (16.27) and its cost for \(\omega_t = 4\). (b) A third node \(j\) at \(\mathbf{g}_j = (1, 2, 0)\) did not move. Where does the mesh vertex \(\mathbf{v} = (1, 0, 0)\) go under (16.32) with \(m = 3\)?

    Solution

    (a) A 90° rotation about \(z\) maps \((x, y, z)\) to \((-y, x, z)\). So \(\mathbf{R}_k(\mathbf{g}_l - \mathbf{g}_k) + \mathbf{t}_k - \mathbf{t}_l = (0, 2, 0) + (0,0,0) - (0, 2, 0.3) = (0, 0, -0.3)\). Cost: \(4 \times 0.09 = 0.36\).

    (b) Distances from \(\mathbf{v}\): 1 to \(k\), 1 to \(l\), 2 to \(j\), so \(d_{\max} = 2\), \(\bar{w} = (0.25, 0.25, 0)\), and \(w = (0.5, 0.5, 0)\). Node \(k\) sends \(\mathbf{v}\) to \(\mathbf{R}_k(1,0,0) + \mathbf{t}_k = (0, 1, 0)\). Node \(l\) sends it to \(\mathbf{R}_l(-1, 0, 0) + \mathbf{t}_l = (0, -1, 0) + (0, 2, 0.3) = (0, 1, 0.3)\). The blend is \(\tilde{\mathbf{v}} = (0, 1, 0.15)\).

Week 23 · Day 1

Foundation models, contrastive learning, and what open-world means

After today you can say what a foundation model is, write the contrastive loss that trains models such as CLIP, and tell an open-world map from a closed-set one.

About 60 min · Read Ch. 17 opening and §17.1, pp. 490–495 (6 pages, one of them figures) · Needs Week 22

Read first: Chapter 17 opening and §17.1, pp. 490–495

While you read, look for:

  • What "closed-set" means for the semantic maps of Chapter 16 (p. 490), and the two ingredients a foundation model needs (p. 491).
  • How BERT gets labels without human annotators (p. 492), and what "positives" and "negatives" are in contrastive learning (pp. 492–493, Figure 17.2).
  • The two ways "open-world" could enter a SLAM system, and why the first one still gives a closed map (pp. 494–495).

Today's big idea

The semantic maps of last week could only name things from a list fixed when the detector was trained. Models trained on internet-scale data without human labels produce feature vectors that are not tied to any list. If the map stores those vectors, the choice of what to look for moves from the day the map is built to the moment someone asks.

1. From a fixed dictionary to an open one

Every map so far stored geometry, and sometimes appearance. Chapter 16 added semantics, but the perception models it used were trained closed-set: the dictionary of classes was decided when the model was trained, so it is fixed and finite. Ch. 17 · p. 490 A detector trained on 80 classes will never report an 81st.

A foundation model is a machine-learning model trained on a dataset so vast that we can reasonably expect it to generalize to a wide variety of operating conditions. It needs two things: an architecture that can efficiently update a very large number of parameters, and a very large dataset, for example one of internet scale. §17.1.1 · p. 491 Such models can learn open-world representations (the book treats open-set and open-vocabulary as synonyms): representations that may generalize to any class, object type, or concept one might meet. Ch. 17 · p. 490

2. How labels stopped being the bottleneck

The history in §17.1.1 is a sequence of obstacles removed. Read it as a table.

Step (book's example)What it removedHuman labels?
AlexNet, a convolutional network trained on ImageNet (3.2 million labeled images, the book's figure)Showed that a big network plus a big labeled dataset worksYes, every image
Residual networks (ResNets)Vanishing gradients in deep networks; these encoders became the base of closed-vocabulary detectors such as YOLO and RCNNYes
BERT: hide a word, predict it (English Wikipedia, about 2.5 billion words; BookCorpus, about 800 million)The need for annotators: the data supplies its own labelsNo
Transformer and attention (used by BERT and by the first GPT model)Difficulty capturing long-range dependencies in the inputNo
Contrastive learning (SimCLR) and the vision transformer (ViT)The lack of a "hide a word" task for imagesNo
DINO (teacher–student distillation), CLIP (image–caption pairs)Strong visual features; one shared feature space for images and textNo

§17.1.1 · pp. 491–494 The book calls every method that needs no human annotation unsupervised, and does not separate "self-supervised" from it (footnote, p. 492). The vision transformer cuts an image into fixed-size patches, turns each into a vector, and feeds the sequence to a standard Transformer, the same way text is fed as a sequence of tokens. Figure 17.3 · p. 493

Filling the gap: why gradients vanish, and what a residual connection does

Training adjusts each parameter along the gradient of the loss. For a chain of layers \(\mathbf{x}_{l+1} = F_l(\mathbf{x}_l)\), the chain rule gives the gradient at the first layer as a product of one factor per layer:

\[ \frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial \mathbf{x}_1} = \frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial \mathbf{x}_{L}}\, \frac{\partial \mathbf{x}_{L}}{\partial \mathbf{x}_{L-1}} \cdots \frac{\partial \mathbf{x}_{2}}{\partial \mathbf{x}_{1}} . \]

If each factor shrinks a vector by about half, 20 layers shrink it by \(0.5^{20} \approx 10^{-6}\). The early layers get almost no signal: that is the vanishing gradient the book mentions on p. 492. A residual layer computes \(\mathbf{x}_{l+1} = \mathbf{x}_l + F_l(\mathbf{x}_l)\) instead, so each factor becomes \(\mathbf{I} + \partial F_l / \partial \mathbf{x}_l\). The identity term is the "direct pathway from one layer to the next": through it the gradient reaches early layers unshrunk, whatever \(F_l\) does.

3. Contrastive learning: pull the pair together, push the rest away

Text has an obvious self-made task: hide a word. A random image patch carries no such specific meaning, so images needed another idea. §17.1.1 · p. 492 Contrastive learning takes an input and a second version of it that should mean the same thing (a positive), and writes a loss that moves their representations together while moving all other inputs in the batch (the negatives) away. In SimCLR the positive is the same image after an augmentation such as flipping or removing patches. §17.1.1 · pp. 492–493 In CLIP the positive pair is an image and its caption, collected from the internet, which puts the two modalities in one feature space. §17.1.1 · p. 494

Filling the gap: the loss itself (InfoNCE)

The book describes the loss in words. Here it is. Take a batch of \(N\) image–caption pairs. Encode image \(i\) as a unit vector \(\mathbf{u}_i\) and caption \(j\) as a unit vector \(\mathbf{v}_j\), and let \(s_{ij} = \langle \mathbf{u}_i, \mathbf{v}_j \rangle\) be their cosine similarity. For image \(i\), treat "which of the \(N\) captions is mine?" as a classification problem and take its cross-entropy:

\[ \ell_i = -\log \frac{\exp(s_{ii}/\tau)}{\sum_{j=1}^{N} \exp(s_{ij}/\tau)} . \]

\(\tau \gt 0\) is the temperature: a small \(\tau\) makes the comparison sharper. CLIP-style training averages this over all images and adds the mirror-image term for captions choosing among images. SimCLR uses the same form with two augmented views in place of image and caption.

Numbers. \(N = 4\), \(\tau = 0.2\), true pair \(s_{ii} = 0.8\), three wrong captions at \(0.2\). Then \(\exp(0.8/0.2) = e^{4} = 54.60\) and \(\exp(0.2/0.2) = e = 2.718\), so

\[ \ell_i = -\log \frac{54.60}{54.60 + 3 \times 2.718} = -\log 0.870 = 0.139 . \]

If all four similarities were equal, the fraction would be \(1/4\) and the loss \(\log 4 = 1.386\). That is the value for a model that has learned nothing.

Which way does it push? Write \(p_{ij}\) for the fraction inside the log with \(s_{ij}\) on top (a softmax over row \(i\)). Since \(\ell_i = -s_{ii}/\tau + \log \sum_j \exp(s_{ij}/\tau)\),

\[ \frac{\partial \ell_i}{\partial s_{ij}} = \frac{1}{\tau}\left(p_{ij} - \delta_{ij}\right), \]

with \(\delta_{ij} = 1\) if \(i = j\) and 0 otherwise. For the true pair the derivative is \((p_{ii} - 1)/\tau \le 0\): gradient descent raises \(s_{ii}\). For a wrong pair it is \(p_{ij}/\tau \ge 0\): descent lowers \(s_{ij}\), and hardest for the wrong captions that currently look most similar.

Try it: press Play and watch the similarity matrix. Then press New start once and play again.

Notice that the loss falls from 5.22 to about 0.01 in 120 steps while the diagonal of the matrix goes to 1 and the four pairs spread around the circle. The first New start stalls near 0.35 with two pairs on the same spot: a circle has very little room, which is one reason real feature spaces have hundreds of dimensions.

In plain words

Shuffle four photos and four captions on a table. The training game is to slide each photo next to its own caption and away from the other three. Nobody ever says what a "dog" is. After hundreds of millions of rounds, photos and captions about the same thing end up in the same place.

4. Open-world at query time, not at mapping time

There are at least two ways to bring this into SLAM. §17.1.2 · pp. 494–495

QuestionParadigm 1: open-vocabulary detector in the front-endParadigm 2: open-world features in the map
What runs during mappingA detector prompted with a word list (the book names YOLO-World and OV-DETR)A feature encoder, with no word list
What the map storesLabels from that listA feature vector per map element
When the vocabulary is fixedAt map constructionAt query time
The map isClosed-worldOpen-world

The detector of paradigm 1 accepts any text, but the text must be supplied when the detector runs, which in SLAM is while the map is being built. What gets stored is decided then. The chapter is about paradigm 2, where the question is asked when the map is used. §17.1.2 · pp. 494–495

Two limits on scope. First, most methods in the chapter are pure mapping: they assume posed camera frames from an upstream SLAM system, so the problem becomes how to embed foundation-model features into the map. Foundation features are also used for place recognition (the book cites AnyLoc, built on DINO features), but that is not this chapter's subject. §17.1.2 · p. 495 Second, the power of these models comes from internet-scale data, and as of the book's April 2026 edition sensors such as LiDAR and radar have no readily available data at that scale. §17.1.1 · p. 494

Common mistakes

  • "An open-vocabulary detector gives an open-vocabulary map." Only if you could re-run it on the original images for every new query. The map itself kept just the words chosen during mapping.
  • "Unsupervised means the model learns from nothing." There is still a target: the hidden word, or the identity of the matching caption. It is made from the data instead of by an annotator.

Check yourself

Q1. A batch has two image–caption pairs. For image 1 the similarity to its own caption is 1.0 and to the other caption 0.0, with τ = 0.5. What is its loss?

The loss is −log(e² / (e² + e⁰)) = log(1 + e⁻²) = log(1.135) = 0.127. It is 0.693 = log 2 only when both similarities are equal.

Q2. A team builds a map with an open-vocabulary detector prompted with 50 words while mapping. Later a user asks for a 51st word. According to §17.1.2 the map is

The detector is open-vocabulary, but its text conditioning happened at map construction. The stored map can only answer for those 50 words.

Q3. In the gradient of the contrastive loss, which wrong caption is pushed away from image i the hardest?

The derivative with respect to a wrong pair's similarity is p divided by τ, and p (the softmax weight) is largest for the wrong caption that currently scores highest.

Q4. A plain 30-layer network scales the gradient by 0.5 at every layer. Roughly what fraction of it reaches the first layer, and what changes with residual connections?
