0.5³⁰ ≈ 9 × 10⁻¹⁰. A residual layer's factor is the identity plus the layer's own derivative, so the product always contains a path of pure identities.

Recap

  1. Closed-set perception has a dictionary fixed at training time. Foundation models, trained on vast data, aim at open-world representations.
  2. Self-made training tasks (predict a hidden word, match two views, match image and caption) removed the need for human labels.
  3. The contrastive loss is a cross-entropy over "which item in the batch is my partner"; its gradient raises the true pair's similarity and lowers the others in proportion to how confusing they are.
  4. A map is open-world only if the vocabulary is chosen at query time. Storing features, not detections, is what makes that possible.

Sources

  1. SLAM Handbook, Chapter 17 "Towards Open-World Spatial AI", opening and §17.1 "Background and Terminology", pp. 490–495.
  2. The loss in "Filling the gap" follows van den Oord, Li, Vinyals, Representation Learning with Contrastive Predictive Coding, 2018 (InfoNCE); Chen, Kornblith, Norouzi, Hinton, A Simple Framework for Contrastive Learning of Visual Representations, 2020; and Radford et al., Learning Transferable Visual Models From Natural Language Supervision, 2021.
  3. Vanishing gradients and residual connections: Goodfellow, Bengio, Courville, Deep Learning, 2016; He, Zhang, Ren, Sun, Deep Residual Learning for Image Recognition, 2016.

Week 23 · Day 2

Features, generators, and masks: three model families a map builder uses

After today you can compute a cosine similarity, build a zero-shot classifier from text prompts, and say what a feature model, a generative model, and a class-agnostic segmenter each return.

About 60 min · Read §17.2, pp. 495–499 (5 pages) · Needs Week 23 Day 1

Read first: §17.2, pp. 495–499

While you read, look for:

  • The definition of a feature as the output of an encoder, \(\mathbf{f}_x = f_{\mathcal{X}}(x) \in \R^d\) (p. 496).
  • Equation (17.1), the zero-shot classifier, and the sentence after it about redefining the class set (p. 497).
  • The caveat about patch-level CLIP features at the end of §17.2.1 (p. 497).
  • What the function \(\texttt{Seg}(\cdot)\) returns, and why its masks must be class-agnostic (p. 499).

Today's big idea

Open-world mapping uses three kinds of pretrained model. A feature-based model turns an image or a text into a vector, and everything is done by comparing vectors. A generative model produces new text from a prompt. A class-agnostic segmenter cuts an image into object-shaped regions without naming them. Tomorrow's maps are built by combining the three.

1. A feature is a vector, and similarity is an angle

A feature (also called an embedding, representation, or code) is the real-valued vector a deep network outputs for one input. The book hides the network behind a function: an encoder \(f_{\mathcal{X}}\) for inputs of modality \(\mathcal{X}\) (text, image, sound) maps an input \(x\) to a \(d\)-dimensional feature \(\mathbf{f}_x = f_{\mathcal{X}}(x) \in \R^d\). The property that matters is that distances in feature space measure meaningful similarity, so that "how similar is this caption to this image?" becomes a calculation. §17.2.1 · p. 496

The standard measure is cosine similarity, the cosine of the angle between two features drawn as arrows from the origin: §17.2.1 · p. 496

\[ \cos\theta = \frac{\langle \mathbf{a}, \mathbf{b} \rangle}{\norm{\mathbf{a}}\,\norm{\mathbf{b}}}, \qquad \langle \mathbf{a}, \mathbf{b} \rangle = \sum_{i=1}^{d} a_i b_i . \]

Numbers. \(\mathbf{a} = (3, 4)\), \(\mathbf{b} = (4, 3)\): \(\langle \mathbf{a}, \mathbf{b} \rangle = 12 + 12 = 24\), both norms are 5, so \(\cos\theta = 24/25 = 0.96\), an angle of about 16°. It ranges from 1 (same direction) through 0 (perpendicular, unrelated) to −1 (opposite), and ignores length.

Filling the gap: unit vectors, dot products, and distances

CLIP outputs unit-norm features, \(\norm{\mathbf{f}} = 1\). §17.2.1 · p. 497 Then the denominator above is 1 and cosine similarity is just the inner product \(\langle \mathbf{a}, \mathbf{b} \rangle\). That is why every formula in this chapter is written with \(\langle \cdot, \cdot \rangle\).

For unit vectors, "close in angle" and "close in distance" are the same statement. Expand the squared distance:

\[ \norm{\mathbf{a} - \mathbf{b}}^2 = \norm{\mathbf{a}}^2 - 2\langle \mathbf{a}, \mathbf{b} \rangle + \norm{\mathbf{b}}^2 = 2 - 2\langle \mathbf{a}, \mathbf{b} \rangle . \]

Check with the example: \(\mathbf{a}/5 = (0.6, 0.8)\), \(\mathbf{b}/5 = (0.8, 0.6)\), difference \((-0.2, 0.2)\), squared length \(0.08 = 2 - 2 \times 0.96\). So ranking by largest cosine and ranking by smallest Euclidean distance give the same order. Vectors that are not unit length (after averaging, as tomorrow) must be divided by their norm first.

2. Three feature extractors

Model (as described in the book)InputHow it is trainedWhat you get
BERT, SentenceBERTTextPredict masked words; SentenceBERT adds pooling and fine-tuningBERT: one feature per token. SentenceBERT: one per sentence, compared by cosine similarity
DINO, DINOv2ImageA student network matches a teacher's predictions. The teacher sees global crops (more than 50% of the image); the student sees local crops (less than 50%) too. DINOv2 adds a curated set of 142M imagesAn image-level feature, and a patch-level feature for each small patch (for example every 8×8 pixels)
CLIPImage and textContrastive loss on 400M image–caption pairs from the internetUnit features \(\mathbf{f}_I = f_{\text{image}}(\mathbf{I})\) and \(\mathbf{f}_T = f_{\text{text}}(T)\) in one aligned space

§17.2.1 · pp. 496–497 DINO's features serve vision tasks directly: nearest neighbours in its feature space classify or retrieve images. But DINO has no text encoder, so you cannot type a word at it. CLIP's defining property is the aligned feature space: two encoders, trained so that an image and its caption land close together (yesterday's loss).

How many patch features is that? For a 224×224 image and 8×8 patches (our example sizes), \(224/8 = 28\) patches per side, so \(28 \times 28 = 784\) vectors instead of one. One warning the book gives: you can pull patch-level features out of CLIP's image encoder too, but you should not expect them to be language-aligned, and studies have found them weaker than DINO's for vision and 3D tasks. §17.2.1 · p. 497

3. A classifier made of sentences

With aligned features, a classifier needs no training. Write each class as text, possibly in a template ("a picture of a dog", "a picture of a cat"), encode each prompt to get \(\mathbf{f}_c\), and predict

\[ \argmax_{c \in \mathsf{C}} \; \langle \mathbf{f}_I, \mathbf{f}_c \rangle . \tag{17.1} \]

This is a zero-shot classifier: it never saw a labeled example of these classes. Changing the problem means changing the list \(\mathsf{C}\). §17.2.1 · p. 497

Try it: the image is an armchair and the class set has no "chair". Add "chair". Then choose the soda can and see what the classifier says before and after you add "drink".

Notice that with {sofa, television, plant} the armchair is called a sofa (0.95), and adding "chair" (0.99) flips the answer with no retraining. The soda can scores 0.00 against all three starting classes, yet arg max still returns one of them: a class set is a closed set, however you obtained the classifier.

4. Generative models: one token at a time

A large language model (LLM) is a transformer trained to generate text. Text is first cut into tokens (words, sub-words, characters, or bytes from a fixed vocabulary), each with a learnable embedding. The training objective is next-token prediction: given the first \(T-1\) tokens, output the probabilities \(p(w_T \mid w_{1:T-1})\) of the next one. §17.2.2 · p. 498

Filling the gap: why predicting one token is enough to write paragraphs

The chain rule of probability factors any joint distribution into next-item conditionals:

\[ p(w_1, \dots, w_T) = \prod_{t=1}^{T} p(w_t \mid w_{1:t-1}) . \]

So a model of the next token is a model of whole texts. Generation runs the factorization forward, which the book calls autoregressive:

context = tokens(prompt)
repeat:
    probs = model(context)        # p(next token | context)
    w     = choose_from(probs)
    context.append(w)
until w is a stop token or a length limit is hit

Each new token costs one pass through a very large network. Compare CLIP: one pass per image, then dot products. This is the book's remark that generative inference "tends to be more computationally expensive than extracting features". §17.2 · p. 495

An LLM can be applied to any task whose instructions, inputs, and outputs fit in text, and the wording of the prompt matters. The book names two prompt techniques: chain-of-thought (ask the model to reason step by step) and in-context learning (put input–output examples in the prompt). §17.2.2 · p. 498 A vision language model (VLM) is an LLM that also accepts image tokens. The book's example, LLaVA, connects the CLIP vision encoder to an LLM and trains on vision-and-language data. Given the right prompt a VLM can classify, caption, or answer questions about an image. §17.2.2 · p. 499 As of the book's April 2026 edition it lists the LLaMa family and the GPT models as widely used, and notes that newer models appear frequently.

5. Masks without names

The third tool answers "which pixels belong together?" For an RGB image \(\mathbf{I}\) of width \(W\) and height \(H\), a segmenter returns a set of binary masks \(\mathbf{Z}_i \in \{0,1\}^{H \times W}\), one per likely object: \(\mathbf{Z}_i[u,v] = 1\) where pixel \((u,v)\) belongs to region \(i\). The book writes this function \(\texttt{Seg}(\cdot)\). The masks must be class-agnostic, meaning proposed without any class list, or the segmenter would bring the closed set back in. §17.2.3 · p. 499

The main tool is the Segment Anything Model (SAM). It is promptable: give it pixel coordinates, a bounding box, or another mask, and it predicts a mask. It can also process a whole image and return masks for the instances in it. Unlike the models above, SAM is trained by large-scale supervised learning. It can also refine the boxes of an open-vocabulary detector, which gives better object outlines and shorter inference time. §17.2.3 · p. 499

Common mistakes

  • "CLIP gives a language-aligned feature for every pixel." Its aligned feature describes the whole image. Patch features can be extracted, but the book warns not to expect them to be language-aligned.
  • "A higher dot product always means more similar." Only for unit vectors. Without normalizing, a long vector wins by length alone.

Check yourself

Q1. What is the cosine similarity of a = (1, 2, 2) and b = (2, 1, 2)?

The inner product is 2 + 2 + 4 = 8 and both norms are √9 = 3, so the cosine is 8/9 = 0.89.

Q2. An image has unit feature (0.6, 0.8). The class prompts encode to dog (1, 0), cat (0, 1), fox (0.8, 0.6). What does equation (17.1) predict?

Scores: dog 0.6, cat 0.8, fox 0.48 + 0.48 = 0.96. Arg max picks the largest, whatever its size.

Q3. Two unit features are at squared Euclidean distance 0.5. What is their cosine similarity?

For unit vectors the squared distance is 2 − 2·cos, so cos = (2 − 0.5)/2 = 0.75.

Q4. Why does the book require the segmentation masks to be class-agnostic?

The masks decide which regions get features at all. If only listed classes get masks, everything else never enters the map.

Recap

  1. An encoder maps an input to a feature vector; cosine similarity (the inner product, for unit features) measures how related two inputs are.
  2. DINO gives strong vision-only features, including per-patch ones. CLIP aligns images and text in one space.
  3. Equation (17.1) builds a classifier from text prompts: encode the class names and take the arg max of the similarities.
  4. LLMs generate text by repeated next-token prediction; VLMs also take images. They are more capable and more expensive than feature extraction.
  5. \(\texttt{Seg}(\cdot)\), usually SAM, returns class-agnostic binary masks.

Sources

  1. SLAM Handbook, §17.2 "Foundation Models for Spatial AI" (§17.2.1–17.2.3), pp. 495–499, including equation (17.1) and Figure 17.4.
  2. Cosine similarity, the unit-vector distance identity, and the chain rule of probability are standard; see Goodfellow, Bengio, Courville, Deep Learning, 2016.
  3. The widget's 8-dimensional features are hand-built for this lesson and are not outputs of CLIP.

Week 23 · Day 3

Open-vocabulary maps: features on points, then features on objects

After today you can fuse per-pixel features into map elements with a confidence-weighted average, answer a text query by cosine similarity, and build an object map by associating masks.

About 60 min · Read §17.3 up to "Language Descriptions" in §17.3.2, pp. 499–506 (7 pages) · Needs Week 23 Day 2

Read first: §17.3 opening, §17.3.1, and §17.3.2 up to "Language Descriptions", pp. 499–506

While you read, look for:

  • The definition of a map element \(m_k \triangleq \{\mathbf{p}_k, \mathbf{f}_k\}\) (p. 501).
  • The four bullets that build a pixel-level feature in ConceptFusion (pp. 501–502), and the update (17.2)–(17.3) on p. 502.
  • Equation (17.4) and the sentence saying the prompt list need not be known when the map is built (p. 503).
  • The two similarity scores used to match a mask to an object, and the fusion update (p. 505).

Today's big idea

Replace the class label stored in each map element by a feature vector from a foundation model. Building the map is then averaging: every view contributes a feature for each element it sees. Using the map is comparing: encode the question, take inner products with the stored features, and keep the elements that score high. Storing one vector per object instead of per point makes the map thousands of times smaller.

1. Swap the label for a feature

A class label is a coarse description. The book's toolbox example makes the point: "tool" is true but useless, "hammer" is better, and colour, material, use, or the sound an object makes do not fit in one label at all. Rare objects are missing from any list. §17.3 · pp. 499–500 So an open-vocabulary map keeps the geometry of Week 8 and changes what is attached to it. The map is a set \(\mathcal{M} \triangleq \{m_k\}\) of map elements

\[ m_k \triangleq \{\mathbf{p}_k, \mathbf{f}_k\}, \]

where \(\mathbf{p}_k\) is the geometric part (a 3D point, a voxel location, a mesh face) and \(\mathbf{f}_k\) is a feature vector. The geometry comes from an upstream SLAM system. §17.3.1 · p. 501 The book assumes posed RGB-D frames of a static scene, processed one after another. §17.3 · p. 500 The features can sit on the cells of a 2D grid (VLMaps, which suits navigation), on an unordered set of 3D points (ConceptFusion, OpenScene), or in a TSDF volume (Open-Fusion; see Week 8 · Day 2). §17.3.1 · p. 501

2. A feature for every pixel

CLIP describes a whole image with one vector, but a map needs a vector per pixel. There are two routes. §17.3.1 · p. 501

Route A: a model that outputs dense features. Fine-tune a model like CLIP on a segmentation dataset so that it emits pixel-level features (LSeg, used by OpenScene and VLMaps) or region-level ones (SEEM, used by Open-Fusion for speed). The cost: evidence suggests these fine-tuned features lose some of the rare, long-tail concepts the original CLIP features hold.

Route B: keep CLIP untouched and do arithmetic. ConceptFusion combines whole-image context with object crops: §17.3.1 · pp. 501–502

  1. Global feature \(\mathbf{f}^G = f(\mathbf{I})\): encode the entire image.
  2. Local features: run \(\texttt{Seg}(\mathbf{I})\), turn each mask into a bounding box, crop the image to it, and encode the crop: \(\mathbf{f}^L_i = f(\mathbf{I}_i)\).
  3. Merge per mask: \(\mathbf{f}^P_i = w_i \mathbf{f}^G + (1 - w_i)\,\mathbf{f}^L_i\) with \(w_i \in [0,1]\). The weights are set to emphasize local features that differ from the global one and from the other local ones.
  4. Per pixel: \(\mathbf{f}^P_{u,v}\) is the sum of the mask features over all masks with \(\mathbf{Z}_i[u,v] = 1\), scaled to unit length.

(On p. 502 this last bullet prints \(\mathbf{f}^L_i\) in the sum; its own description means \(\mathbf{f}^P_i\).) Back-project each pixel with its depth, as in Week 8 · Day 1, and you have a point cloud in which every point carries a feature. The book calls this a range-feature observation. §17.3.1 · p. 502

3. Fusing many views into one feature

The same 3D point is seen in many frames, so its features must be combined. VLMaps simply averages all features that fall in the same grid cell. ConceptFusion keeps a feature \(\mathbf{f}_k\) and a confidence \(c_k\) per point and updates both with each new pixel feature: §17.3.1 · p. 502

\[ \mathbf{f}_k \leftarrow \frac{c_k \mathbf{f}_k + \alpha\, \mathbf{f}^P_{u,v}}{c_k + \alpha} \tag{17.2} \] \[ c_k \leftarrow c_k + \alpha \tag{17.3} \]

with \(\alpha = e^{-\gamma^2/2\sigma^2}\), where \(\gamma\) is the radial distance to the camera center and \(\sigma\) a scale. Small \(\gamma\) gives \(\alpha\) near 1; large \(\gamma\) gives a small \(\alpha\).

Numbers (two dimensions, to keep it readable). A point has \(c_k = 2\), \(\mathbf{f}_k = (1, 0)\). A new view gives \(\mathbf{f}^P = (0, 1)\) at \(\gamma = \sigma\), so \(\alpha = e^{-1/2} = 0.607\). Then \(\mathbf{f}_k \leftarrow (2 \cdot (1,0) + 0.607 \cdot (0,1))/2.607 = (0.767, 0.233)\) and \(c_k \leftarrow 2.607\).

Filling the gap: the update is a weighted mean, and averaging removes noise

Unrolling. Start a point at \(c_k = 0\) and feed it features \(\mathbf{f}_1, \dots, \mathbf{f}_n\) with weights \(\alpha_1, \dots, \alpha_n\). Claim: after \(n\) updates \(c_k = \sum_t \alpha_t\) and \(c_k \mathbf{f}_k = \sum_t \alpha_t \mathbf{f}_t\). It holds after one update. If it holds after \(n-1\), then (17.2) times its denominator reads \(c_k^{\text{new}} \mathbf{f}_k^{\text{new}} = c_k \mathbf{f}_k + \alpha_n \mathbf{f}_n = \sum_{t \le n} \alpha_t \mathbf{f}_t\). So

\[ \mathbf{f}_k = \frac{\sum_{t=1}^{n} \alpha_t \mathbf{f}_t}{\sum_{t=1}^{n} \alpha_t} . \]

The map never stores the individual views, only this running weighted mean and the sum of weights. It is the same trick as the TSDF weight in Week 8 · Day 2.

Why average. Model each view's feature as the true one plus an independent error, \(\mathbf{f}_t = \mathbf{f} + \mathbf{e}_t\), each of the \(d\) components of \(\mathbf{e}_t\) having variance \(s^2\). With equal weights the mean's error has variance \(s^2/n\) per component, so its squared length is about \(d s^2 / n\). That error is mostly perpendicular to \(\mathbf{f}\) (length 1), so

\[ \cos(\mathbf{f}_k, \mathbf{f}) \approx \frac{1}{\sqrt{1 + d s^2 / n}} . \]

For \(d = 8\), \(s = 0.6\): one view gives \(1/\sqrt{3.88} = 0.51\), twenty views give \(1/\sqrt{1.144} = 0.93\).

One caution. A mean of unit vectors is shorter than 1 (the example above has length 0.80). The arg max in (17.4) below does not care, but a threshold on \(\langle \mathbf{f}_k, \mathbf{f}_T \rangle\) does: normalize \(\mathbf{f}_k\) first.

Averaging is not the only choice. To avoid averaging high-dimensional vectors and to resist outliers, the book lists alternatives: keep a buffer of features per element and store its medoid (the member closest to all the others); cluster the buffer and keep a few centroids, or the member nearest the centroid of the majority cluster; or, in Open-Fusion, store in each voxel only a key into a dictionary of features. §17.3.1 · pp. 502–503

4. Asking the map a question

To label the map with classes chosen today, encode a prompt list \(\mathsf{C}\) with the text encoder and give each element its best-matching prompt: §17.3.1 · p. 503

\[ y_k = \argmax_{C \in \mathsf{C}} \; \langle \mathbf{f}_k, \mathbf{f}_C \rangle, \qquad \mathbf{f}_C = f_{\text{text}}(C). \tag{17.4} \]

This is yesterday's classifier (17.1) with a map feature in place of an image feature. \(\mathsf{C}\) plays no part in building the map and can be changed at will. The main use, though, is the open-ended query: encode any text \(T\), score every element by \(\langle \mathbf{f}_k, \mathbf{f}_T \rangle\), keep those above a threshold, and cluster the kept points in space to separate instances.

Try it: the query is "a comfy place to sit" with one noisy view. Slide "Views fused" up to 20. Then try the other queries and move the threshold.

Notice that with one view only 4 cells pass the threshold, one of them wrong, and 11 are missed. With 20 views all 14 sofa and armchair cells are retrieved and nothing else, and the mean cosine to the clean features rises from 0.49 to 0.93, as the formula above predicts.

The query need not be text. Any modality with an aligned encoder works; ConceptFusion shows a click on a map point (use that point's own \(\mathbf{f}_k\)), an image, and an audio clip. A map built from vision-only features such as DINO loses text queries but still supports image and click queries. §17.3.1 · pp. 503–504

5. One feature per object

Dense feature maps scale poorly because the vectors are large. Count it: a million points, each with a 768-number feature (the size the book quotes for one CLIP model on p. 510) at 4 bytes per number, is about 3 GB. Nearby points usually belong to the same object and share semantics, so store the feature once per object. §17.3.2 · p. 504 Two hundred objects need 200 × 768 × 4 bytes, about 0.6 MB.

The object map is a set \(\mathsf{V}_O = \{o_j\}_{j=1}^{J}\). Each object has a point cloud \(\mathsf{P}_{o_j}\), a feature \(\mathbf{f}_{o_j}\), and a detection count \(n_{o_j}\). For each new frame: §17.3.2 · pp. 504–505

  1. Extract. For each mask from \(\texttt{Seg}(\mathbf{I})\), encode its crop to get \(\mathbf{f}^M_i\) and back-project its pixels to a point cloud \(\mathsf{P}^M_i\) in the map frame.
  2. Associate. Compare each mask with existing objects. Geometric similarity \(\phi_{geo} \in [0,1]\) is the fraction of mask points that have a neighbour in the object's cloud within a distance \(\delta_{nn}\). Semantic similarity is \(\phi_{sim} = \tfrac{1}{2}(\langle \mathbf{f}_i, \mathbf{f}_{o_j} \rangle + 1) \in [0,1]\). Combine or threshold them. An unmatched mask starts a new object.
  3. Fuse. On a match, \(\mathbf{f}_{o_j} \leftarrow (n_{o_j}\mathbf{f}_{o_j} + \mathbf{f}_i)/(n_{o_j}+1)\), \(\mathsf{P}_{o_j} \leftarrow \mathsf{P}_{o_j} \cup \mathsf{P}^M_i\), \(n_{o_j} \leftarrow n_{o_j}+1\). This is (17.2) with \(\alpha = 1\) and the count as confidence.
  4. Clean up. Now and then merge duplicate objects, and drop those with a low count.

Numbers. A mask cloud has 200 points; 150 have an object point within \(\delta_{nn}\), so \(\phi_{geo} = 0.75\). The features have inner product 0.6, so \(\phi_{sim} = 0.8\). If both pass your thresholds and the object had \(n = 4\), its feature becomes \((4\mathbf{f}_o + \mathbf{f}_i)/5\) and \(n = 5\).

Queries now return whole objects: \(o^* = \argmax_{o \in \mathsf{V}_O} \langle \mathbf{f}_o, \mathbf{f}_T \rangle\). In the book's example, "something to drink" scores high on a soda can, whose point cloud can go straight to a motion planner. §17.3.2 · p. 506

Common mistakes

  • "The prompt list must be chosen before mapping." Neither \(\mathsf{C}\) nor the query enters the map. Only features do.
  • "A retrieved element is a detection." Arg max always returns something, and a threshold is a setting you chose. Neither says the object exists.

Check yourself

Q1. A point has c = 3 and f = (0.8, 0.6). A new pixel feature (0, 1) arrives with α = 1. What does (17.2)–(17.3) give?

f = (3·(0.8, 0.6) + 1·(0, 1))/4 = (2.4, 2.8)/4 = (0.6, 0.7), and c = 3 + 1 = 4.

Q2. With equal weights, how many views must you average to halve the per-component noise of a fused feature?

The variance of a mean of n independent errors is s²/n, so the standard deviation is s/√n. Halving it needs n = 4.

Q3. A mask has 40 back-projected points, 10 of which have a neighbour in object A within δ. The inner product of the features is 0.9. What are the two similarities?

Geometric: 10/40 = 0.25. Semantic: ½(0.9 + 1) = 0.95.

Q4. Why does ConceptFusion mix a global image feature with features of mask crops instead of using a fine-tuned pixel-level model?

The book reports evidence that dense features from fine-tuned models capture fewer long-tail concepts than unaltered CLIP features.

Recap

  1. A map element is geometry plus a feature: \(m_k = \{\mathbf{p}_k, \mathbf{f}_k\}\).
  2. Per-pixel features come from a fine-tuned dense model, or from mixing global and mask-crop CLIP features.
  3. Equations (17.2)–(17.3) keep a running confidence-weighted mean; averaging \(n\) views cuts feature noise by \(\sqrt{n}\).
  4. Labels (17.4) and queries are inner products with encoded text, chosen after the map is built.
  5. Object maps store one feature per object, built by mask association (\(\phi_{geo}\), \(\phi_{sim}\)) and fusion.

Sources

  1. SLAM Handbook, §17.3 opening, §17.3.1 "Dense Representations", and §17.3.2 "Object Maps and 3D Scene Graphs" up to the Inference paragraph, pp. 499–506, equations (17.2)–(17.4).
  2. The unrolling of the running mean and the variance of an average are standard; see Thrun, Burgard, Fox, Probabilistic Robotics, 2005. The cosine estimate and the memory figures are our own.
  3. The widget's map and 8-dimensional features are hand-built and are not outputs of CLIP.

Week 23 · Day 4

Captions, scene graphs, feature fields, and maps shaped by the task

After today you can say when captions beat feature vectors, score a query down a hierarchical scene graph, compute a LERF relevancy score, and run one merge of task-driven clustering.

About 60 min · Read §17.3.2 from "Language Descriptions" through §17.3.4, pp. 506–514 (8 pages, three with large figures) · Needs Week 23 Day 3

Read first: §17.3.2 from "Language Descriptions", §17.3.3, §17.3.4, pp. 506–514

While you read, look for:

  • The query that feature retrieval gets wrong (p. 506), and the layers of equation (17.5) (p. 508).
  • The relevancy score (17.7), and why LangSplat can shrink a 512-number feature to 3 (pp. 510–511).
  • The piano example and the two terms of equation (17.8) (pp. 511–512).

Today's big idea

A set of objects with one vector each is a start. Today adds four things: words in place of vectors when the question is complicated, edges and layers so that a query can be resolved step by step, features stored inside a radiance field, and a rule for what counts as one object. The rule is that the task decides.

1. When a vector is not enough: describe the object in words

Object features work best against short descriptive queries. They miss negation and affordances: "something to drink other than a soda can" still lands on the soda can. A feature also cannot be read by a person or an LLM. The alternative is a caption: keep the best image crops of each object, ask a VLM to describe the central object, and let an LLM merge the per-view captions. To answer a query, give an LLM the caption list and ask for the most relevant object. This handles complex queries that defeat feature retrieval, but is much slower than inner products. Some methods keep both. §17.3.2 · pp. 506–507

2. Scene graphs: edges between objects, layers above them

An object scene graph \(\mathcal{G} = (\mathsf{V}_O, \mathsf{E}_O)\) adds edges for pairwise relations. In ConceptGraphs an LLM reads object captions and positions and infers relations such as "a on b". §17.3.2 · p. 507 A hierarchical scene graph (Week 22) groups nodes into ordered layers. Following HOV-SG, indoors: §17.3.2 · pp. 507–508

\[ \mathsf{V} = \mathsf{V}_E \cup \mathsf{V}_F \cup \mathsf{V}_R \cup \mathsf{V}_O, \qquad \mathsf{E} = \mathsf{E}_{EF} \cup \mathsf{E}_{FR} \cup \mathsf{E}_{RO}, \tag{17.5} \]

one root node \(\mathsf{V}_E\), then floors, regions, and objects, with edges only between consecutive layers. Every node carries at least one CLIP feature, so every layer can be queried in words.

HOV-SG finds floors as peaks in a histogram of point heights. For each region it takes the CLIP embeddings of the camera views inside it and reduces them to \(K\) representatives \(\mathbf{f}_{r_k}\) by k-means. Each representative votes for a category from a candidate list \(\mathsf{C}_R\), and the majority names the region: §17.3.2 · pp. 508–509

\[ c^*_{r_k} = \argmax_{c \in \mathsf{C}_R} \; \langle \mathbf{f}_{r_k}, \mathbf{f}_{R,c} \rangle . \tag{17.6} \]

Numbers. \(K = 5\), votes kitchen, kitchen, living room, kitchen, corridor: a kitchen, 3 of 5. For a query, a generative model splits the sentence into one concept per layer, and each is scored from the top layer down. With 2 floors, 5 regions per floor, and 30 objects per region (our numbers), a flat search compares the query with 300 objects; the layered search compares 2 + 5 + 30 = 37 features.

3. Features inside a radiance field

The radiance fields of Week 20 can carry language too. LERF gives a NeRF a second output, a semantic embedding at point \(\mathbf{x}\) and scale \(s\), rendered along a ray the way colour is and trained on CLIP embeddings of image crops at many scales. To query, it converts similarities into a relevancy score for each rendered embedding: §17.3.3 · p. 510

\[ \min_i \; \frac{\exp(\langle \mathbf{f}_{\text{render}}, \mathbf{f}_{\text{text}} \rangle)}{\exp(\langle \mathbf{f}_{\text{render}}, \mathbf{f}^i_{\text{canonical}} \rangle) + \exp(\langle \mathbf{f}_{\text{render}}, \mathbf{f}_{\text{text}} \rangle)} , \tag{17.7} \]

where the canonical embeddings come from generic phrases such as "object", "things", "stuff", "texture".

Filling the gap: what (17.7) computes

Write \(a\) for the similarity with the text and \(b_i\) for the similarity with canonical phrase \(i\). Dividing top and bottom by \(e^{a}\) gives \(1/(1 + e^{\,b_i - a})\), which grows with \(a - b_i\). So the minimum is set by the largest \(b_i\): the score is \(1/(1 + e^{\,b_{\max} - a})\), and it exceeds 0.5 exactly when the query beats every generic phrase. A raw cosine cannot say that, because "object" is somewhat similar to everything.

Numbers. \(a = 0.30\) and \(b = 0.20, 0.25, 0.10, 0.28\): the score is \(1/(1 + e^{-0.02}) = 0.505\). With \(a = 0.22\) it is \(1/(1 + e^{0.06}) = 0.485\): the point looks more like a generic phrase than like the query.

LangSplat attaches language features to the Gaussians of a splat map, using CLIP vectors of SAM segments at three levels of granularity. A 512-number vector per Gaussian is too much memory, so it trains a scene-specific network that compresses each vector to 3 numbers, and a decoder that restores it. One scene varies far less than CLIP's training corpus, so 3 numbers suffice. §17.3.3 · pp. 510–511

4. The task decides what an object is

With no class list, what is one object? The book's piano is one object if the task is to move it, more than 90 if the task is to play it (keys and pedals), hundreds if the task is to tune it. §17.3.4 · pp. 511–512 Clio poses the problem: given tasks in natural language, such as "clean backpacks" and "get condiment packets", build a map whose objects have the granularity the tasks need. It uses the Information Bottleneck. Let \(X\) be fine-grained primitives (over-segmented 3D pieces), \(\tilde{X}\) the clusters, \(Y\) the tasks. Find the assignment \(p(\tilde{x} \mid x)\) that solves §17.3.4 · p. 512

\[ \min_{p(\tilde{x} \mid x)} \; I(X; \tilde{X}) - \beta\, I(\tilde{X}; Y) . \tag{17.8} \]

Filling the gap: mutual information, and the cost of one merge

The mutual information measures how much knowing one variable tells you about another:

\[ I(X;Y) = \sum_x p(x)\, D_{\mathrm{KL}}\big(p(y \mid x) \,\|\, p(y)\big), \qquad D_{\mathrm{KL}}(p \,\|\, q) = \sum_y p(y) \log \frac{p(y)}{q(y)} . \]

It is zero when the two are independent. In (17.8), a small \(I(X;\tilde{X})\) means strong compression (a single cluster gives 0); a large \(I(\tilde{X};Y)\) means the clusters still tell you which task a piece matters for; \(\beta\) sets the exchange rate.

Clio solves it greedily (Agglomerative Information Bottleneck): every primitive starts as its own cluster, neighbours are connected, and the pair with the smallest weight is merged, again and again: §17.3.4 · p. 513

\[ d_{ij} = \big(p(\tilde{x}_i) + p(\tilde{x}_j)\big) \cdot D_{\mathrm{JS}}\big[p(y \mid \tilde{x}_i),\, p(y \mid \tilde{x}_j)\big] . \tag{17.9} \]

\(D_{\mathrm{JS}}\) is the Jensen–Shannon divergence. With \(\pi_i = p(\tilde{x}_i)/(p(\tilde{x}_i) + p(\tilde{x}_j))\), \(\pi_j = 1 - \pi_i\), and the mixture \(\bar{p} = \pi_i\, p(y \mid \tilde{x}_i) + \pi_j\, p(y \mid \tilde{x}_j)\),

\[ D_{\mathrm{JS}} = \pi_i\, D_{\mathrm{KL}}\big(p(y \mid \tilde{x}_i) \,\|\, \bar{p}\big) + \pi_j\, D_{\mathrm{KL}}\big(p(y \mid \tilde{x}_j) \,\|\, \bar{p}\big) . \]

The merged cluster has probability \(p(\tilde{x}_i) + p(\tilde{x}_j)\) and task distribution \(\bar{p}\), and \(d_{ij}\) is exactly the drop in \(I(\tilde{X};Y)\).

Numbers. Two clusters, each with \(p = 1/12\). Same \(p(y \mid x)\): \(D_{\mathrm{JS}} = 0\), merging is free. Distributions \((1, 0)\) and \((0, 1)\): \(\bar{p} = (\tfrac12, \tfrac12)\), each KL term is \(\log 2\), so \(d = \tfrac{2}{12} \times 0.693 = 0.116\) nats.

For \(p(y \mid x)\) Clio uses the cosine score between a primitive's averaged CLIP embedding and the task text as a proxy. §17.3.4 · pp. 512–513 Try it: press "Merge 5 times", then merge twice more. Then switch the task list to "clean backpacks only".

Notice that seven merges turn 12 primitives into 5 clusters (wall; backpack; chair and table; the two packets; napkin, wall and poster) and keep 97.0% of the task information. The eighth merge would cost 0.097 nats, eight times the seventh. With only the backpack task the cheap merges continue down to 3 clusters (99.6% kept): the packets are no longer objects. The toy adds a "neither task" outcome so each row sums to 1.

Clio clusters regions of free space the same way. As of the book's April 2026 edition, the book flags two weak points (the cosine proxy, and aggregating semantics across views), cites Bayesian Fields as a more grounded treatment, and notes that tasks must still be phrased specifically, mostly because of CLIP's limits. §17.3.4 · pp. 513–514

Check yourself

Q1. A rendered embedding has similarity 0.4 with the query and 0.1, 0.4, 0.2 with three canonical phrases. What is its relevancy score (17.7)?

The largest canonical similarity, 0.4, ties the query: 1/(1 + e⁰) = 0.50. The value 0.57 is the score against the weakest phrase alone, but (17.7) takes the minimum.

Q2. Which query does the book use to show where object features fail and captions read by an LLM do better?

The feature of the negated sentence is still close to the soda can's feature. An LLM reading captions can apply "other than".

Q3. Clusters A, B, C lie in a row with equal probability. Their task distributions are A = (0.9, 0.1), B = (0.9, 0.1), C = (0.1, 0.9). Which merge comes first?

A and B have identical task distributions, so the Jensen–Shannon divergence and the weight (17.9) are zero. Merging B with C would mix different distributions and lose task information.

Q4. A building has 3 floors, 4 regions per floor, and 20 objects per region. How many features does a layered query compare, against how many objects for a flat search?

Layered: 3 floors, then the 4 regions of the winning floor, then the 20 objects of the winning region: 27. Flat: 3 × 4 × 20 = 240 objects.

Recap

  1. Captions from a VLM, searched by an LLM, handle negation and complex queries that features miss, at a much higher cost.
  2. Scene graphs add relations and layers (17.5); regions are named by a vote (17.6); queries are resolved layer by layer.
  3. LERF and LangSplat put language features in a radiance field; the relevancy score (17.7) asks whether the query beats generic phrases.
  4. Task-driven mapping (17.8) merges primitives while the merge cost (17.9) is small, so the task list sets the granularity.

Sources

  1. SLAM Handbook, §17.3.2 (from "Language Descriptions"), §17.3.3, §17.3.4, pp. 506–514, equations (17.5)–(17.9).
  2. Mutual information and KL divergence: Cover and Thomas, Elements of Information Theory, 2006. The weighted Jensen–Shannon merge cost: Slonim and Tishby, Agglomerative Information Bottleneck, 1999.
  3. The widget's relevance numbers are hand-set; the search counts are our arithmetic.

Week 23 · Day 5

Do robots still need maps? Language models, maps, and robot foundation models

After today you can describe two ways to connect a language model to a map, report what the book says about replacing maps with large models, and explain how a vision-language-action policy differs from a mapping pipeline.

About 60 min · Read §17.4, pp. 514–520 (7 pages) · Needs Week 23 Day 4

Read first: §17.4, pp. 514–520

While you read, look for:

  • The two ways to integrate an LLM with a map, "map prompting" and "map API" (pp. 514–515).
  • The two experiments with long-context VLMs, and the italic sentence that states the book's position (p. 515).
  • The form of robot data, \(\mathcal{D} = \{\mathbf{z}_t, \mathbf{u}_t\}_{t=1}^{T}\), and what a VLA model outputs (pp. 517–518).
  • The last paragraph of the chapter (p. 520).

Today's big idea

Two efforts pull in opposite directions. One connects language models to maps, so that their knowledge is tied to a real place. The other trains very large models on images or robot data in the hope of doing without an explicit map. This section is a snapshot of fast-moving work. Everything below is what the book reports as of its April 2026 edition; expect the details to date.

1. Handing a map to a language model

An LLM knows a great deal about the world but nothing about this room. Grounding means tying its reasoning to the physical scene. The book highlights two ways to do it with a map. §17.4.1 · pp. 514–515

# 1. Map prompting: the map is text inside the prompt
{"objects": [
  {"id": 3, "caption": "red soda can", "on": 7, "center": [2.1, 0.4, 0.9]},
  {"id": 7, "caption": "wooden dining table", "center": [2.0, 0.5, 0.4]}]}

# 2. Map API: the map stays outside; the LLM calls functions on it
exists("soda can")               → true
where_is("soda can")             → [2.1, 0.4, 0.9]
distance("soda can", "fridge")   → 3.2

Our illustration; the function names are the book's examples (p. 515), the contents are made up.

QuestionMap promptingMap API
What the LLM receivesThe whole map as structured text (JSON or YAML), which a scene graph with captions already nearly isA few function signatures, then the results of the calls it makes
What answers a callNothing: the LLM readsThe query mechanisms of Day 3, for example \(\argmax_o \langle \mathbf{f}_o, \mathbf{f}_T \rangle\)
Limits the book statesCannot convey detailed geometry; needs a sparse, text-compatible map; how well LLMs use coordinates in text is unclearThe LLM sees only what it asks for

A system that passes a VLM-built map as text to an LLM is an instance of what the book calls a Socratic model: pretrained models composed as modules. With a map API, map calls can be interleaved with LLM calls and robot commands. This is the pattern of tool calling, in which an LLM is free to call external functions and use their outputs while it generates an answer. The book's example, NLMap, has an LLM break a user request into proposed objects and check that each exists, and where, by querying an open-vocabulary map. §17.4.1 · p. 515

2. Could a large model replace the map?

The book returns here to a question from its first pages: is an explicit map needed at all? §17.4.2 · p. 515

Evidence the book citesWhat was doneWhat was found
OpenEQA (embodied question answering)Compared ways of combining VLMs and scene graphsPrompting GPT-4V directly with 50 frames beat an explicit scene-graph prompt on that benchmark
Mobility VLA (navigation)Gave a VLM a full office tour of 948 frames and asked for the goal image matching a user requestWorked when the goal image was handed to a map-based navigation pipeline. A map-free variant, with the VLM outputting actions directly, was ineffective
Geometry-aware VLMsModels enhanced with awareness of geometry and physics, which most VLMs lack out of the boxImpressive 3D reasoning from a single image, but still a gap to the embodied intelligence shown with SLAM in the pipeline

So one benchmark favours raw frames, and one robot still needed a map to move. The book's reading, at present: whether an LLM- or VLM-based agent needs an explicit map appears to depend largely on the spatial and temporal horizons of its tasks, and the question is open. §17.4.2 · pp. 515–516 It adds that it is unclear how far long-context VLMs have a coherent understanding of the spatial structure behind the images.

Intuition

Fifty photos of a flat are enough to answer "what colour is the sofa?" Walking from the bedroom to the front door of an office you toured an hour ago is a different kind of problem: many steps, each depending on where the last one left you. The first has a short horizon, the second a long one.

3. A foundation model for robots needs robot data

Text and images had the internet. The book's example of the recipe working in a new domain is DUSt3R for 3D vision (Week 19 · Day 5). A robotics foundation model would be a base generalist policy: one model performing many skills on many robot bodies, representing the world only implicitly. Its training data are trajectories of sensor–action pairs \(\mathcal{D} = \{\mathbf{z}_t, \mathbf{u}_t\}_{t=1}^{T}\), which must be collected on robots or in simulation. §17.4.3 · pp. 516–517

DatasetSize the book gives
RT1 (Robotics Transformer)130k trajectories, a fleet of 13 robots, 700 tasks, collected over 17 months
BridgeData V2Over 50k demonstrations of 13 skills in 24 environments
DROIDA multi-institution dataset of diverse robot interaction, mainly for manipulation policies
Open-X-EmbodimentThe above and others combined: over 1M episodes, 22 robot embodiments, 527 skills, 34 laboratories

Compare the scale with Day 2: CLIP was trained on 400M image–caption pairs. Much of the effort therefore goes into making demonstration cheap: teleoperation with a VR headset (DROID), ALOHA's paired low-cost manipulators that mirror a human's motion, and the handheld gripper of the Universal Manipulation Interface, which matches a robot gripper and its eye-in-hand sensor. §17.4.3 · p. 517 These datasets mainly teach skills such as grasping; longer tasks are meant to come from longer demonstrations or by chaining short ones.

4. Policies that act without an explicit map

The simplest learner is behaviour cloning: supervised learning of the mapping from observation to action. The book calls it brittle, because the demonstrations contain little sub-optimal data and small deviations take the model out of distribution. §17.4.3 · p. 517

Filling the gap: why small errors compound

Suppose the cloned policy errs with probability \(\epsilon\) per step while it is in states like those in the demonstrations. An expert never shows how to recover from a mistake, so in the worst case one error puts the robot in unfamiliar states where it keeps erring for the rest of a \(T\)-step episode. A first error at step \(t\) then costs \(T - t + 1\) bad steps, and the expected number of bad steps is at most

\[ \sum_{t=1}^{T} \epsilon\,(T - t + 1) = \epsilon\,\frac{T(T+1)}{2} \approx \frac{\epsilon T^2}{2} . \]

If errors did not compound it would be \(\epsilon T\). With \(\epsilon = 0.01\) and \(T = 100\): 1 bad step against a worst case of about 50. The bound grows with the square of the horizon, which is the same horizon the book pointed to in section 2. An explicit map and planner behave differently: after a slip the robot relocalizes and replans.

FamilyIdeaExamples the book names
Vision-language-action (VLA)A transformer like those of Day 2, whose output tokens are read directly as control actionsGATO, PaLM-E, RT1, RT2, RT1-X and RT2-X (trained on Open-X-Embodiment), OpenVLA, π0
Action chunkingOutput a sequence of actions, not one; the book says this has proved important for generalizationACT, designed for ALOHA
Diffusion policyA generative model learns to undo a gradual noising process; here it denoises random noise into actions, conditioned on what the robot seesDiffusion Policy; Octo feeds a transformer's output to a diffusion action head
Reinforcement learningLearn from rewards. The datasets above contain none, so it suits simulation and fine-tuning of the other policies(none named)

§17.4.3 · pp. 517–519 One number gives a sense of cost: the book reports that OpenVLA, built from open-source vision and language components, was fine-tuned for 15 days on a cluster of 64 A100 GPUs. §17.4.3 · p. 518 The book also observes that as these models grow, their ability to encode some representation of the environment implicitly seems to improve, which may change where an explicit map is still needed. §17.4.3 · p. 519

5. Where the chapter lands

The book does not pick a winner. Scaling robot datasets and models, combined with internet-scale VLMs and LLMs, could conceivably make explicit maps obsolete. Against that, it cites evidence that transformers struggle with compositional or chain-of-thought reasoning, which is why neural memory mechanisms with a notion of state (it names structured state space models) are re-emerging, with limits still unclear. It judges it equally likely, or more so, that generalization to compositional tasks in large, complex environments will come from explicit structure learned through a process such as SLAM. And it suggests the two are complementary: perceiving, representing, and understanding the world comes before acting, and an explicit world model should only help. §17.4.4 · pp. 519–520

Common mistakes

  • "The book says VLMs have made maps unnecessary." It reports one benchmark where frames beat a scene-graph prompt and one robot where the map-free variant failed, and concludes that it depends on the task's horizons.
  • "A VLA model contains no representation of the world." It has no explicit one that you can inspect or query. Whatever it knows is implicit in its weights and context.
  • "These model lists are the state of the art." The book itself says the section is not exhaustive and that new models appear very frequently.

Check yourself

Q1. A user asks, "How far is the mug from the sink, in metres?" The map is a dense metric map with object features. Which integration fits, according to §17.4.1?

Map prompting is restricted to sparse, text-compatible maps and conveys geometry poorly. A map API leaves the geometry in the map and returns only the answer.

Q2. What does the Mobility VLA result, as the book reports it, suggest?

The VLM chose the goal image from the tour. The map-free variant, in which it output actions directly, was found ineffective.

Q3. A cloned policy errs with probability 0.02 per step on a 50-step task. Using the worst-case argument, about how many bad steps should you expect, against how many if errors did not compound?

Worst case εT²/2 = 0.02 × 2500 / 2 = 25. Without compounding, εT = 0.02 × 50 = 1.

Q4. What makes a model a vision-language-action model in the book's description?

A VLA keeps the structure of the language and vision-language models of Day 2 and changes what the output tokens mean: robot actions.

Recap

  1. An LLM can be grounded by putting a text map in its prompt, or by letting it call functions on a map that stays outside.
  2. As of the book's April 2026 edition, large VLMs answer some questions from raw frames, but the robot example still needed a map to navigate. The need depends on spatial and temporal horizons.
  3. Robot foundation models learn policies from sensor–action trajectories, which are far scarcer than internet text and images.
  4. Behaviour cloning compounds errors; VLA models, action chunking, diffusion policies, and reinforcement learning are the current families.
  5. The book's closing view: explicit world modelling through SLAM and generalist policies are complementary.

Sources

  1. SLAM Handbook, §17.4 "Further Readings & Recent Trends" (§17.4.1–17.4.4), pp. 514–520. All statements about named models, datasets, and results are as given there.
  2. The compounding-error argument follows Ross and Bagnell, Efficient Reductions for Imitation Learning, 2010.

Week 23 · Review

Week 23 review: open-world maps and foundation models

After today you can compute the contrastive loss, fuse and query feature maps, match masks to objects, and compute a LERF relevancy and a task-driven merge cost by hand.

About 60 min · No new pages

The week in one paragraph

Models trained on internet-scale data without human labels produce features tied to no class list. CLIP's contrastive training puts images and text in one space where similarity is an inner product. An open-vocabulary map stores such features on points, objects, graph nodes, or in a radiance field, fuses them over views by a weighted average, and is questioned afterwards by encoding text and comparing. Captions and LLMs handle complex questions; a task list can decide what an object is. Whether large models will replace explicit maps is open as of the book's April 2026 edition.

1. Formula sheet

What it isFormulaWhere
Contrastive (InfoNCE) loss\(\ell_i = -\log \dfrac{\exp(s_{ii}/\tau)}{\sum_{j} \exp(s_{ij}/\tau)}\); gradient \((p_{ij} - \delta_{ij})/\tau\)Added to pp. 492–494 · Day 1
Cosine similarity; unit vectors\(\dfrac{\langle \mathbf{a}, \mathbf{b} \rangle}{\norm{\mathbf{a}}\norm{\mathbf{b}}}\); \(\norm{\mathbf{a}-\mathbf{b}}^2 = 2 - 2\langle \mathbf{a}, \mathbf{b} \rangle\)p. 496 · Day 2
Feature fusion\(\mathbf{f}_k \leftarrow \dfrac{c_k \mathbf{f}_k + \alpha \mathbf{f}^P_{u,v}}{c_k + \alpha}\), \(c_k \leftarrow c_k + \alpha\), \(\alpha = e^{-\gamma^2/2\sigma^2}\) (17.2)–(17.3)p. 502 · Day 3
Zero-shot classifier (17.1), map labels (17.4), query score\(\argmax_{c} \langle \mathbf{f}_I, \mathbf{f}_c \rangle\); \(y_k = \argmax_{C \in \mathsf{C}} \langle \mathbf{f}_k, \mathbf{f}_C \rangle\) (17.4); \(\langle \mathbf{f}_k, \mathbf{f}_T \rangle\)pp. 497, 503 · Days 2–3
Object maps\(\phi_{sim} = \tfrac12(\langle \mathbf{f}_i, \mathbf{f}_{o_j} \rangle + 1)\); \(\mathbf{f}_{o_j} \leftarrow \dfrac{n_{o_j}\mathbf{f}_{o_j} + \mathbf{f}_i}{n_{o_j}+1}\); \(o^* = \argmax_o \langle \mathbf{f}_o, \mathbf{f}_T \rangle\)pp. 505–506 · Day 3
LERF relevancy\(\min_i \dfrac{e^{a}}{e^{b_i} + e^{a}} = \dfrac{1}{1 + e^{\,b_{\max} - a}}\) (17.7)p. 510 · Day 4
Task-driven clustering\(\min I(X;\tilde{X}) - \beta I(\tilde{X};Y)\) (17.8); \(d_{ij} = (p_i + p_j)\, D_{\mathrm{JS}}\) (17.9)pp. 512–513 · Day 4

2. Mixed quiz

Check yourself

Q1. In a batch of 8 pairs, every image is equally similar to all 8 captions. What is the contrastive loss per image?

Every softmax weight is 1/8, so the loss is log 8.

Q2. Why does §17.1.1 say foundation models are harder to build for LiDAR or radar?

Internet-scale data is a key ingredient, and these modalities lack it.

Q3. An image has unit feature (0.6, 0.8, 0). Prompts encode to A = (1, 0, 0), B = (0, 0.8, 0.6), C = (0, 0, 1). What does (17.1) return?

A: 0.6. B: 0.8 × 0.8 = 0.64. C: 0.

Q4. A language model gives the three tokens of a sentence conditional probabilities 0.5, 0.2, 0.1. What is the probability of the sentence?

The chain rule multiplies them: 0.5 × 0.2 × 0.1 = 0.01.

Q5. A map point has c = 1, f = (1, 0). A view adds (0, 1) with α = 1. After normalizing, what is its similarity to the query (0, 1)?

The fused feature (0.5, 0.5) normalizes to (0.707, 0.707).

Q6. A dense map has 2 million points, each with a 512-number feature of 4-byte numbers. How much memory is that?

2 × 10⁶ × 512 × 4 bytes = 4.1 × 10⁹ bytes.

Q7. In task-driven clustering, a task is added that cares about the individual keys of a piano. What changes?

The cost (17.9) grows with how differently two clusters relate to the tasks.

Q8. Which statement matches the book's position, as of its April 2026 edition?

§17.4.2 says so; §17.4.4 calls maps and generalist policies complementary.

3. Pen-and-paper problems

  1. \(N = 3\), \(\tau = 0.5\). Image 1 has similarities \(0.9\) (own caption), \(0.1\), \(0.5\). Compute its loss and the derivative with respect to each similarity.

    Solution

    \(e^{1.8} = 6.050\), \(e^{0.2} = 1.221\), \(e^{1.0} = 2.718\), sum \(9.989\). Softmax \(p = (0.606, 0.122, 0.272)\), loss \(-\log 0.606 = 0.502\). Derivatives \((p_{1j} - \delta_{1j})/\tau\): \(-0.789\), \(0.244\), \(0.544\).

  2. A map point starts with \(c_k = 0\). View 1 gives \((1, 0, 0)\) at \(\gamma = 0\); view 2 gives \((0.6, 0.8, 0)\) at \(\gamma = \sigma\). Fuse them with (17.2)–(17.3). Does a query with \(\mathbf{f}_T = (0.8, 0.6, 0)\) and threshold 0.9 retrieve the point?

    Solution

    \(\alpha_1 = 1\), \(\alpha_2 = e^{-1/2} = 0.607\). Fused: \(((1,0,0) + 0.607\,(0.6, 0.8, 0))/1.607 = (0.849, 0.302, 0)\), \(c_k = 1.607\). Length \(0.901\), unit feature \((0.942, 0.335, 0)\). Similarity \(0.942 \times 0.8 + 0.335 \times 0.6 = 0.955\): retrieved. Unnormalized it would be \(0.860\) and wrongly rejected.

  3. In one dimension, a mask's points are at \(0.0, 0.1, 0.2, 0.3, 1.0\) m. An object has points at \(0.05, 0.15, 0.25\) m, feature \((0.6, 0.8)\), count 3. The mask's feature is \((1, 0)\) and \(\delta_{nn} = 0.08\) m. Compute \(\phi_{geo}\) and \(\phi_{sim}\); if both exceed 0.5, update the object.

    Solution

    Four mask points are 0.05 m from an object point; the one at 1.0 is 0.75 m away. \(\phi_{geo} = 4/5 = 0.8\). Inner product \(0.6\), so \(\phi_{sim} = 0.8\). Match. \(\mathbf{f}_o \leftarrow (3\,(0.6, 0.8) + (1, 0))/4 = (0.7, 0.6)\), count 4, and the mask points join the cloud.

  4. Primitives A, B, C in a row, each with probability \(1/3\), have \(p(y \mid A) = p(y \mid B) = (0.9, 0.1)\) and \(p(y \mid C) = (0.1, 0.9)\). (a) Compute \(d_{AB}\) and \(d_{BC}\). (b) Merge the cheaper pair and cost the last merge. (c) Check that the costs add up to \(I(X;Y)\).

    Solution

    (a) \(d_{AB} = 0\). For B, C: \(\bar{p} = (0.5, 0.5)\), \(D_{\mathrm{KL}} = 0.9 \log 1.8 + 0.1 \log 0.2 = 0.368\) for each, so \(D_{\mathrm{JS}} = 0.368\), \(d_{BC} = \tfrac23 \times 0.368 = 0.245\) nats.

    (b) AB has probability \(\tfrac23\) and distribution \((0.9, 0.1)\). With C: \(\bar{p} = (0.633, 0.367)\), and the same formula gives \(D_{\mathrm{KL}} = 0.186\) for AB and \(0.624\) for C. \(D_{\mathrm{JS}} = \tfrac23(0.186) + \tfrac13(0.624) = 0.332\), so \(d = 0.332\) nats.

    (c) \(p(y) = (0.633, 0.367) = \bar{p}\), so \(I(X;Y) = \tfrac13(0.186 + 0.186 + 0.624) = 0.332 = 0 + 0.332\).

You are ready for next week if you can

  • Write the contrastive loss and say which way its gradient moves each similarity.
  • Apply (17.2)–(17.3) by hand, and normalize before thresholding.
  • Compute a relevancy score (17.7) and a merge cost (17.9).
  • Say why storing features, not detections, makes a map open-vocabulary.

Sources

  1. SLAM Handbook, Chapter 17, pp. 490–520.
  2. Extra math as cited on Days 1–5.

Week 24 · Day 1

From SLAM to Spatial AI: representation and the closed loop

After today you can say what a Spatial AI system is, state the chapter's two hypotheses, and explain why a persistent world model in a closed loop beats frame-to-frame estimation.

About 60 min · Read §18.1–18.2, pp. 521–526 (6 pages) · Needs Week 1 Day 1 and Week 19 Day 1

Read first: §18.1 and §18.2, pp. 521–526

While you read, look for:

  • The two example products, and the numbers attached to the second: 65 g and under 1 W (pp. 521–522).
  • The definition of a representation (p. 522) and the two hypotheses in italics (p. 523).
  • The six numbered properties of a Spatial AI system and the sentence naming its "key computational quality" (p. 525).

Today's big idea

The chapter treats Spatial AI as SLAM grown up: a device keeps a persistent, close-to-metric model of its surroundings and checks every new piece of sensor data against it. The hard part is doing this within the size, cost, and power budget of a real product.

1. The gap between the task and the budget

Chapter 18, by Andrew Davison, has no equations and argues for a position. Spatial AI is the capability of a device to build rich but efficient representations of its surroundings that let it act intelligently. The aim is the right representation for real-time interpretation and action; scene understanding in the abstract is not the goal. §18.1.1 · p. 521 A design is squeezed between what the task needs and what the device can carry. §18.1.1 · pp. 521–522

DeviceThe task requiresThe setting allows
Household robotClean and know when it is clean; recognize, move, and tidy objects; make way for peopleConsumer price, size, safety, limited power
AR glasses ("IA", intelligence augmentation)Remember every place, object, and person met; find lost things; pin notes to real thingsThe form of ordinary spectacles, 65 g, a full day per charge, under 1 W

A waking day of 16 hours at 1 W is \(16\ \text{Wh} = 57.6\ \text{kJ}\) for cameras, processing, and display together. Today's robot-vision processors are far from that, and robust performance is hard even with bulky sensors and unlimited computing. §18.1.1 · p. 522

2. Representation, also called a world model

A representation is the set of values in memory that stand for the state of the device and the world around it. It persists, it changes as information arrives or the world changes, and parts of it may be abstracted or forgotten to save resources. §18.1.2 · p. 522 Machine learning calls this a world model. The idea looks new there because most networks are stateless: input in, output out, nothing kept. Networks trained end to end from sensor to action do well on short tasks and struggle on long ones. A map is the oldest fix: a robot vacuum can guarantee full coverage because it remembers where it has been. §18.1.2 · pp. 522–523

Hypothesis 1. A device that must run for a long time, do many tasks (some unknown at design time), and communicate with people should keep a scene representation that is general, persistent, close to metric 3D geometry at least locally, and understandable by a human. This excludes single-task representations and opaque learned states. The reasons given are efficiency, composability, interpretability, and generality. §18.1.2 · p. 523

Hypothesis 2. The usefulness of such a system across many tasks is captured by a small number of performance measures, so a drone, a tidying robot, and an AR display would run largely the same system, tuned by a few numbers. §18.1.2 · pp. 523–524 Day 5 returns to this.

A Spatial AI system, for the chapter, is a module that builds and maintains such a representation incrementally, in real time, from mainly visual input, with quantifiable performance. §18.1.2 · p. 524

3. SLAM has been walking this road already

Real-time visual SLAM has grown richer in steps, and you have met each one. §18.1.3 · p. 524

LevelWhat the map holdsWhere you studied it
1. Sparse localizationCamera poses and 3D pointsWeek 11 · Day 5
2. Dense mappingSurfaces: distance fields, surfels, GaussiansWeek 8 · Day 2, Week 20 · Day 4
3. Semantic labelingA class or feature on every map elementWeeks 22 and 23

Beyond these the chapter expects scene graphs of segmented, physically simulated objects (Week 22). The levels describe progress; they are no recipe. A new representation is almost never bolted onto a working system. It changes the whole system: once a dense map exists the tracker can align whole images against it (Week 12 · Day 2), and labels can improve the reconstruction. §18.1.3 · pp. 524–525 Hence the chapter's working assumption: today's SLAM systems are the best guide to the structure of tomorrow's Spatial AI.

4. The overall computational structure

Section 18.2 lists six properties of any such system. §18.2 · p. 525

  1. Embedded: cameras and supporting sensors such as an IMU, with low-power processing, in a mobile body.
  2. Real-time model and pose, with geometry and semantics, mainly from on-board sensors.
  3. What is where: ideally the identity, position, shape, and motion of everything nearby.
  4. Close to metric, at least locally.
  5. Focused quality: full detail only where the device looks and will act; the rest at lower quality, upgradable on a revisit.
  6. Alert: every incoming piece of visual data is checked against a prediction from the model.

The quality the chapter singles out is the closed loop: the model is persistent, updated incrementally, and used inside the real-time loop for data association and tracking. The contrast is incremental estimation such as pure visual odometry, which estimates motion frame to frame and keeps no long-term structure. Closed loop does not mean one fixed rate for everything. It means each result is available when needed, so the whole never pauses. §18.2 · pp. 525–526

Try it: a camera sweeps a corridor four times, and two estimators get the same measurements.

Notice that the curves are similar for the first 42 frames, while the map is being built. After that the map-based error stays near 0.04, while the odometry error wanders and averages 0.14 over the last sweep. Press New noise: odometry sometimes wanders back toward zero, but nothing holds it there.

Filling the gap: why the stored map bounds the error

In the widget, a landmark at \(l_j\) seen from position \(x_k\) gives \(z_{kj} = l_j - x_k + n_{kj}\), with independent noise of variance \(\sigma^2\).

Odometry sums frame-to-frame motions, each the average change in \(z\) over the landmarks two frames share. While the shared set is unchanged the noise cancels in the sum. Each time a landmark enters or leaves the view, a term fails to cancel and a fresh error, a fraction of \(\sigma\) in size, is added for good. After \(h\) hand-overs the error variance has grown in proportion to \(h\): the random walk of Week 1 · Day 1.

The stored map holds landmark \(j\) as \(\hat{l}_j = l_j + e_j\), where \(e_j\) is the error at the moment it was stored. On any later frame with \(m\) landmarks in view,

\[ \hat{x}_k = \frac{1}{m}\sum_{j}\bigl(\hat{l}_j - z_{kj}\bigr) = x_k + \frac{1}{m}\sum_j e_j - \frac{1}{m}\sum_j n_{kj}. \]

The first error term is frozen: it is the same on every return to those landmarks. The second is fresh noise of variance \(\sigma^2/m\). Neither depends on how long the system has run. With \(\sigma = 0.05\) and \(m \approx 6\) the fresh part is \(0.05/\sqrt{6} \approx 0.02\); the rest of the 0.04 is map error frozen in during the first sweep.

Section 18.2 ends with the route to efficiency: find the graphs of computation and data movement in the algorithms, and use hardware with the same graph so that data moves as little as possible. Three questions organize the rest of the week: what is stored where, what is processed where, and what is transmitted where and when. §18.2 · p. 526

Check yourself

Q1. Which system satisfies the chapter's first hypothesis about representation?

The hypothesis asks for a general, persistent representation, close to metric at least locally and understandable by a human. It excludes task-specific and opaque ones.

Q2. AR glasses must run 16 hours per charge at no more than 1 W. How much energy may the device use in a day?

16 h × 3600 s/h = 57 600 s at 1 J per second: 57.6 kJ, or 16 Wh.

Q3. A camera tracks against a stored map with 4 landmarks in view and measurement noise σ = 0.08. What is the standard deviation of the fresh, frame-to-frame part of the position error?

The fresh part averages 4 independent noises: σ/√m = 0.08/2 = 0.04.

Q4. A system estimates camera motion between consecutive frames very accurately and stores nothing else. What does it most clearly lack?

This is pure visual odometry. With no model to predict from, it cannot detect change or bound its drift.

Recap

  1. Spatial AI builds representations for real-time action, within a product's limits on size, cost, and power.
  2. Hypothesis 1: keep a general, persistent, close-to-metric, human-readable scene representation. Hypothesis 2: a few performance measures describe its usefulness.
  3. The defining structure is a closed loop: every measurement is compared with a prediction from a persistent model, which is then updated.

Sources

  1. SLAM Handbook, Chapter 18 (A. J. Davison), §18.1 "From SLAM to Spatial AI" and §18.2 "Overall Computational Structure", pp. 521–526.
  2. The error model in "Filling the gap" is this app's own illustration.

Week 24 · Day 2

Learning and estimation together, and the hardware that must run them

After today you can explain why the chapter expects hybrid systems of learned and designed parts, why single-core speed stopped growing, and why efficient Spatial AI means many simple processors and little data movement.

About 60 min · Read §18.3–18.4, pp. 526–532 (7 pages) · Needs Week 1 Day 3 and Week 19

Read first: §18.3 and §18.4, pp. 526–532

While you read, look for:

  • The three forms that learned components take inside the geometric loop (p. 527).
  • The question about a network that builds a scene from 100 images (p. 528).
  • The difference between Moore's law and Dennard scaling, and the clock speed where the "power wall" sits (pp. 528–529).
  • What is free about the cloud and what is not (p. 532).

Today's big idea

Machine learning is taking over more of the pipeline, but a system that must keep and update a model over time still needs probabilistic fusion, so the future is hybrid. And processors no longer get faster by raising the clock, so performance per watt has to come from parallel, specialized hardware in which data stays close to where it is processed.

1. Where learning sits in SLAM today

SLAM is unusual within AI: machine learning has not taken it over. The best systems for localization and sparse mapping are still mostly hand-designed state estimation, meaning algorithms built on probability theory, while dense and semantic systems mix the two. §18.3 · pp. 526–527

At first a network sat beside the estimator: SemanticFusion pasted CNN labels onto ElasticFusion's dense map. Then learned parts moved into the geometric loop, in three forms. §18.3 · p. 527

FormWhat the network outputsExample in the bookWhere you studied it
1. Single-image predictionDepth, surface normals, or object masks from one imageDepth networksWeek 19 · Day 2
2. Learned update stepsMatches, or an optimization step on poses and pointsDROID-SLAMWeek 19 · Day 4
3. Multi-image predictionGeometry directly from several imagesDUSt3R, VGGTWeek 19 · Day 5

Form 1 has a known weakness: a depth map predicted from one image often carries large systematic errors, and its uncertainty is poorly understood, so it is hard to fuse. One answer is to predict something weaker than depth, such as a depth code (CodeSLAM) or a depth covariance, and let a small multi-view optimization produce consistent geometry. §18.3 · p. 527

2. Why the chapter bets on hybrids

Learning has two attractions. Networks can do jobs nobody managed to design by hand, such as labeling a scene or guessing depth from one picture. And a network compresses an iterative computation into one feed-forward pass that runs fast on current processors. §18.3 · pp. 527–528

Will one network do all of SLAM end to end? Work in that direction keeps improving, from DeepVO to VGGT. The chapter still expects hybrids to win for the foreseeable future, for two connected reasons: the uncertainty of a network's output is poorly understood, and a long-lived system must be able to update its model. Its example: a network builds a scene from 100 images, and then image 101 arrives. Running everything again on 101 images cannot be the answer. Accept that, and you need long-term representation and fusion, which is what probabilistic state estimation provides. §18.3 · p. 528

Filling the gap: what "fuse one more" costs

The book asks the question and leaves the arithmetic to you. Take the simplest estimation problem: \(n\) measurements \(z_1,\dots,z_n\) of one quantity, each with noise variance \(\sigma^2\). In information form (Week 1 · Day 3) the estimate is stored as an information value \(\Lambda\) and an information vector \(\eta\), and fusing a measurement is two additions:

\[ \Lambda \leftarrow \Lambda + \frac{1}{\sigma^2}, \qquad \eta \leftarrow \eta + \frac{z_{n+1}}{\sigma^2}, \qquad \mu = \frac{\eta}{\Lambda}. \]

After 100 measurements, \(\Lambda = 100/\sigma^2\) and \(\mu\) is their average. Measurement 101 changes the mean to

\[ \mu_{101} = \frac{100\,\mu_{100} + z_{101}}{101} = \mu_{100} + \frac{z_{101} - \mu_{100}}{101}. \]

With \(\mu_{100} = 2.00\) and \(z_{101} = 3.01\), the new mean is \(2.00 + 1.01/101 = 2.01\). The cost did not depend on the 100 earlier measurements: the pair \((\eta, \Lambda)\) is a sufficient summary of them.

Now count work over a whole run of \(n\) images. Recursive fusion touches each image once: \(n\) units. A method that must reprocess everything whenever an image arrives does \(1 + 2 + \dots + n = n(n+1)/2\) units. For \(n = 1000\) that is 500 500 against 1000. A factor graph does the same at full scale: each measurement adds one factor (Week 3 · Day 4).

The chapter's forecast is that learned and designed parts will become so interleaved that you cannot tell them apart, reached either by adding learned modules to a designed system or by adding structure to a learned one. What stays important either way is the storage and computational structure of the whole. §18.3 · p. 528

3. Why processors stopped getting faster the easy way

For decades SLAM researchers could count on single-core speed doubling every one to two years. That ended, although Moore's law (the transistor count per chip keeps doubling) has continued. The rule that failed is Dennard scaling: as transistors shrink, their power density stays constant. At nanometre sizes transistors leak current and heat up, and the resulting power wall holds clock speeds near 4 GHz. §18.4.1 · pp. 528–529

Filling the gap: where Dennard scaling comes from, and how it breaks

The power a transistor spends switching is \(P = C V^2 f\): its capacitance \(C\), the supply voltage \(V\) squared, and the switching frequency \(f\). Shrink every length by a factor \(k\) (so \(k = 2\) halves all dimensions) and, as Dennard proposed, shrink the voltage by \(k\) as well.

  • Capacitance is area over thickness, \((1/k^2)/(1/k)\), so \(C \to C/k\).
  • The transistor switches \(k\) times faster, so the clock can go to \(kf\).
  • Power per transistor becomes \(\dfrac{C}{k}\cdot\dfrac{V^2}{k^2}\cdot kf = \dfrac{CV^2f}{k^2}\).
  • Each transistor occupies \(1/k^2\) of the area, so \(k^2\) times as many fit per square millimetre.
\[ \text{power density} \;\propto\; \underbrace{k^2}_{\text{transistors per mm}^2} \times \underbrace{\frac{1}{k^2}}_{\text{power each}} = 1. \]

The catch is the voltage. Below a certain voltage a transistor no longer turns off properly and leaks, which is the leakage the book mentions, so \(V\) stopped shrinking. Hold \(V\) fixed and repeat the sum: power per transistor is \((C/k)\,V^2\,(kf) = CV^2f\), unchanged, and power density grows as \(k^2\). Freeze the clock as well and it still grows as \(k\).

Try it: step through transistor generations under the three regimes.

Notice that under Dennard scaling six generations give 64 times the transistors and 8 times the clock at the same power per square millimetre. Switch the regime to "voltage stuck, clock still rising": the same six generations multiply the heat per square millimetre by 64. Freezing the clock reduces that to 8, which is still not flat.

4. What efficient processing looks like

If the clock cannot rise, performance must come from doing many things at once. The chapter's recipe: divide the computation among a large number of simple, low-clock-rate cores and minimize the movement of data between them. §18.4.1 · p. 529 A CPU does the reverse. It pulls small pieces of data one at a time from a separate main memory and pushes results back, with a cache as the only relief. That makes a CPU easy to program, but the piece-by-piece traffic has a large power cost. §18.4.1 · pp. 529–530

ProcessorHow it computesWhat the chapter says about it
CPUSequential steps on one central memoryFlexible and easy to program; heavy data traffic, limited by the power wall
GPUSIMT (single instruction, multiple threads): one operation applied to every element of a regular arrayEnabled dense SLAM and deep learning; built for graphics, and a full system still shuttles data between CPU and GPU
Custom vision chipsCPU-like, DSP-like, and custom blocks in one low-power packageMovidius Myriad, the HoloLens HPU, Apple's R1; details confidential
Graph processorsThousands of independent cores, each with local memory, joined by a programmable interconnectSpiNNaker (up to a million ARM cores), Graphcore's IPU; not yet ready for embedded vision, large long-term potential

§18.4.1 · pp. 529–531 The graph that matters is also larger than one chip: it includes cameras, actuators, other robots, and the cloud. §18.4.1 · p. 531

5. Sensors, and the cloud

For this chapter a camera is any device that captures an array of light measurements, and each design trades information quality against size and power. §18.4.2 · p. 531 Two sensors point at the future:

  • The event camera (Week 15 · Day 1) sends only intensity changes, so it carries the content of video at a much lower bit rate.
  • The SCAMP5 vision chip puts a small analog processor at every pixel of a 256 × 256 array and runs at 1.2 W. Pixels can add, subtract, divide, square, and pass values to neighbours, so a useful amount of vision is computed on the sensor itself. §18.4.2 · p. 532

The purpose of processing near the sensor is to cut the bit rate on the link to the main processor. To see what is at stake, a plain 640 × 480 camera at 8 bits and 30 frames per second produces \(640 \times 480 \times 8 \times 30 \approx 73.7\) million bits every second, most of them repeating what the previous frame already said.

The cloud changes the sums less than you might hope. From the device's side, cloud compute and memory are close to infinite and free. Communication is neither: sending video costs power, and the round trip adds a delay of a significant fraction of a second. Some places (space, undersea, underground) have no link at all. §18.4.2 · p. 532 A robot moving at 1 m/s travels 30 cm during a 0.3 s delay, so the tight loop has to stay on board.

Common mistakes

  • "Moore's law ended, so chips stopped improving." Transistor density kept growing. What ended is Dennard scaling, the ability to switch those transistors faster without more heat per area.

Check yourself

Q1. An estimate is the average of 49 equally good measurements and equals 10.0. The 50th measurement is 12.5. What is the updated estimate?

μ ← μ + (z − μ)/n with n = 50: 10.0 + 2.5/50 = 10.05. Nothing about the first 49 is needed except their mean and count.

Q2. All lengths on a chip shrink by k = 2, the supply voltage stays fixed, and the clock is doubled. By what factor does power per square millimetre change, using P = C·V²·f?

Per transistor: C halves and f doubles, V is fixed, so power per transistor is unchanged. Four times as many transistors fit per mm², so power density is ×4.

Q3. A 320 × 240 sensor outputs 8-bit pixels at 100 frames per second. What is its raw bit rate?

320 × 240 = 76 800 pixels, × 8 bits = 614 400 bits per frame, × 100 frames = 61.4 million bits per second.

Q4. Why does the chapter doubt that a single feed-forward network will replace the whole SLAM system soon?

Networks do predict geometry, and fast. The objections concern uncertainty and updating a long-term model.

Recap

  1. The chapter expects hybrids: a long-lived system must fuse new data into a persistent model with known uncertainty, and fusion in information form costs the same however much came before.
  2. Moore's law continued; Dennard scaling failed. With voltage stuck, power density rises as transistors shrink, and the clock stays near 4 GHz.
  3. Efficient processing uses many simple cores and moves little data. CPUs, GPUs, custom vision chips, and graph processors are successive steps toward matching hardware to the algorithm.
  4. Processing near the sensor cuts the bit rate. Cloud compute is nearly free, but the link costs power and a fraction of a second.

Sources

  1. SLAM Handbook, Chapter 18, §18.3 "State Estimation and Machine Learning in Spatial AI" and §18.4 "The Future Landscape of Processor and Sensor Hardware", pp. 526–532.
  2. Dennard, Gaensslen, Yu, Rideout, Bassous, LeBlanc, Design of ion-implanted MOSFET's with very small physical dimensions, 1974 (the scaling rules in "Filling the gap").
  3. Hennessy and Patterson, Computer Architecture: A Quantitative Approach, 6th edition, 2017 (dynamic power \(CV^2f\), the end of Dennard scaling).

Week 24 · Day 3

Mapping Spatial AI graphs to hardware: map store, real-time loop, and the image plane

After today you can sketch the chapter's design for a Spatial AI processor, say which computations belong in the map store, the real-time loop, and the sensor, and show how purely local message passing reaches a global estimate.

About 60 min · Read §18.5, pp. 532–540 (8 pages) · Needs Week 3 Day 3 and Week 24 Day 2

Read first: §18.5, pp. 532–540

While you read, look for:

  • The blocks of Figure 18.1, and why the bulk of the computation stays in one central processor (p. 533).
  • Why features observed together end up strongly correlated, and how that gives a sparse graph (p. 535).
  • The five maintenance jobs inside the map store (p. 536) and the five elements of the real-time loop (p. 537).
  • Local against global regularization in tracking, and the proposal that follows (p. 539).

Today's big idea

The algorithms of Spatial AI already have graph structure: the map is a graph of features, the real-time loop is a fixed processing graph, and an image is a grid of pixels. The chapter's design gives each graph hardware of the same shape, so that most computation happens where its data already sits, and connects the pieces with as few bits as possible.

1. The design in one picture

The chapter considers one device working with on-board resources only, since that works anywhere. §18.5 · pp. 532–533 Its claim is that long-term efficiency comes from matching the graph structures of the algorithms to the physical layout of the hardware. That argues for pushing work out toward the sensors. Yet most of the computation stays central, for one reason: the world model. Every new piece of data is in the end compared with it, and then either updates it or is discarded. §18.5 · p. 533 Figure 18.1 draws the result as a "Spatial AI brain". §18.5.1 · p. 534

BlockJobWorks on
Close-to-sensor processor, one per cameraReduce the image stream before it leaves the sensorEvery pixel, all the time
Camera interface (in the main processor)Model and predict the data arriving from its cameraEvery frame
Real-time loopConnect the image stream to the world modelEvery frame
Map storeHold the world model and maintain itIn the background
Sensor and actuator interfacesOther inputs, and outputs to the taskAs the task demands

The last column is this app's reading; the book gives no rates. The central unit is not a CPU with RAM. A CPU reaches any memory cell at about the same cost, but spatial data is local, and so is the work of adding to it. The design asks for storage and processing combined in one graph-shaped unit, like Graphcore's IPU, where a program is compiled into a layout of operations, data, and communication channels over the cores. §18.5.1 · p. 534

2. The map store: a graph that maintains itself
