A "feature" here is any abstraction of a scene entity, from a point to an object. Each can be measured only from some region of camera positions, so as the camera moves, features come into view in overlapping groups. Features measured at the same time become strongly correlated through the uncertain camera state, features a short motion apart less so, and distant ones only weakly. Join strongly correlated features, cut edges below a threshold, and a sparse graph of nearby features is left. §18.5.1.1 · p. 535

Filling the gap: "correlated through the camera state", with numbers

In one dimension, let the camera's position have error variance \(\sigma_x^2\). It measures two landmarks, each with independent noise of variance \(\sigma_z^2\), and places them at \(\hat{l}_i = \hat{x} + z_i\). Each landmark's error is the camera's error plus its own noise:

\[ \hat{l}_i - l_i = (\hat{x} - x) + n_i, \qquad \operatorname{var}(\hat{l}_i) = \sigma_x^2 + \sigma_z^2, \qquad \cov(\hat{l}_1,\hat{l}_2) = \sigma_x^2 . \]

The shared term \(\hat{x}-x\) is the covariance, so the correlation is \(\rho = \sigma_x^2/(\sigma_x^2 + \sigma_z^2)\). With \(\sigma_x = 0.1\) and \(\sigma_z = 0.02\): \(\rho = 0.01/0.0104 = 0.96\). The camera does not know where it is, but it knows well where the landmarks are relative to each other.

Now let the camera take \(n\) odometry steps, each adding error variance \(\sigma_o^2\), before it measures landmark 2. Then \(\operatorname{var}(\hat{l}_2) = \sigma_x^2 + n\sigma_o^2 + \sigma_z^2\) while the shared part is still \(\sigma_x^2\). With \(n\sigma_o^2 = 0.09\):

\[ \rho = \frac{0.01}{\sqrt{0.0104 \times 0.1004}} = \frac{0.01}{0.0323} = 0.31 . \]

More motion between two observations means a weaker edge. In the language of Week 3 · Day 3: eliminating a pose links every pair of features seen from it, so the feature graph follows co-visibility.

A pose graph has the same shape with poses in place of features, and the chapter sees no fundamental difference. Its conclusion: represent space by a graph of features, linked in multi-scale patterns that follow camera motion, and able to generate dense predictions. §18.5.1.1 · pp. 535–536 That graph is laid out across many cores whose connections mirror it. Much of large-scale SLAM can then run inside the store as maintenance: clustering features and segmenting objects, detecting loop closures, optimizing after them, smoothing the map, and discovering new semantic categories. Smoothing and segmentation act on each part separately; global optimization can use message passing (tomorrow). Memory sets a deadline: an IPU has about 1 MB per tile, about 1 GB over 1000 tiles, so dense data should be abstracted quickly toward a compact object-level form. §18.5.1.1 · p. 536

3. The real-time loop, and the problem of a moving window

The chapter expects the tightest loop to look like today's dense SLAM (Week 12 · Day 5): model the world in enough generative detail that every new pixel can be compared with a prediction. Its elements are labeling (pixels to features, usually by a network), rendering (a dense predicted image from the map), tracking (aligning prediction and image, finding outliers and independent motion), fusion (writing geometry and labels back), and self-supervised learning. Rendering reads the map and fusion writes it. §18.5.2 · p. 537

These are fixed blocks of massively parallel work and suit a fixed processing graph. The hard part is the link to the map: the part in view changes constantly with motion, so no fixed data path leads to "the relevant memory". The proposed answer is a set of interface nodes, communication specialists wired to the loop on one side and to many sites of the map graph on the other. If the store has a small-world topology, where any two nodes are a few hops apart, they can copy any needed part of the map in a few operations. §18.5.2 · pp. 537–538

4. Processing close to the image plane

Pixels form a grid, and neighbouring pixels usually see the same object, so a graph linking each pixel to its four neighbours underlies smoothing in dense matching and optical flow. §18.5.3 · p. 538 A chip like SCAMP5 can do such bottom-up work itself. Optical flow fits well: its parallel form alternates a per-pixel data step with smoothing between neighbours. §18.5.3 · pp. 538–539

SLAM tracking is harder because it wants one set of global motion parameters. On ordinary hardware, dense tracking alternates a parallel step (an error at every pixel) with a reduction step (sum all errors, update the parameters). The reduction is a global regularizer, and a grid of pixel processors cannot do it without sending everything to one place. The chapter's way out is to give up guaranteed global consistency and converge toward it: each pixel keeps its own estimate of the global parameters and shares it with its neighbours every iteration. After enough rounds any pixel can be asked for a usable answer, and longer links, or a small-world pattern, would speed this up. §18.5.3 · p. 539

Try it: 64 pixels each hold a local estimate of one global number. The Rounds slider runs neighbour-to-neighbour averaging; the second slider adds long links.

Notice that with grid links only, the numbers smooth out locally within a few rounds but a left-to-right slope survives: after 20 rounds the spread is still 1.34, and it takes 100 rounds before every pixel is within 0.05 of the global mean, 2.045. Add 16 long-range links: the longest shortest path drops from 14 hops to 7, and the same agreement takes 32 rounds. No pixel ever computed a global sum.

Filling the gap: why local averaging finds the global mean

The book expects convergence and gives no rule. The simplest one: give every link \((i,j)\) a weight \(w_{ij} = w_{ji}\), and in each round let every pixel move toward each neighbour,

\[ x_i \leftarrow x_i + \sum_{j \in \text{nbrs}(i)} w_{ij}\,(x_j - x_i), \qquad w_{ij} = \frac{1}{1 + \max(d_i, d_j)}, \]

where \(d_i\) is the number of neighbours of pixel \(i\).

The sum never changes. Link \((i,j)\) adds \(w_{ij}(x_j - x_i)\) to pixel \(i\) and the opposite to pixel \(j\).

The only resting state is agreement. With these weights each new value is a weighted average of a pixel and its neighbours, so the largest value can only fall and the smallest only rise until all are equal. The sum is fixed, so the common value is the mean of the starting values, which is what the reduction step would have computed.

Check on three pixels in a row holding 1, 2, 6. The degrees are 1, 2, 1, so both links have weight \(1/3\). One round gives \(1 + \tfrac13(2-1) = 1.33\), \(2 + \tfrac13(1-2) + \tfrac13(6-2) = 3\), and \(6 + \tfrac13(2-6) = 4.67\). The sum is still 9, and the values head for 3.

Information moves one hop per round, so the shape of the graph sets the speed. Averaging treats all pixels as equally reliable; Gaussian belief propagation, tomorrow, passes uncertainty along with the estimate.

The flow need not be one-way. If the main processor sends its prediction to the camera, the camera needs to report only what differs. An event camera reports a pixel when its brightness changes, which amounts to predicting that nothing changes; a model-based event camera would report a pixel when it departs from the model's prediction. §18.5.1 · p. 535; §18.5.3 · p. 540 The aim throughout is fewer bits on the link, and with them less communication power. §18.4.2 · p. 532

Check yourself

Q1. Three pixels in a row hold 0, 3, 9 and average with the weights from "Filling the gap". What does the middle pixel hold after one round?

Both links have weight 1/3. The middle pixel becomes 3 + (0 − 3)/3 + (9 − 3)/3 = 4. The ends become 1 and 7, and the sum stays 12.

Q2. Two landmarks are measured from the same camera pose. The pose error variance is 0.04 and each measurement has noise variance 0.01. What is the correlation between the two landmark estimates?

ρ = σx² / (σx² + σz²) = 0.04 / 0.05 = 0.8. The shared camera error is the covariance.

Q3. Which job does the chapter place inside the map store and not in the real-time loop?

Loop-closure detection and optimization, smoothing, and clustering are maintenance the store performs on itself. Rendering, tracking, and fusion connect the live image to the map.

Q4. Why does the design need interface nodes between the real-time loop and the map store?

Motion changes which map nodes the loop needs. Interface nodes linked to many sites of a small-world map graph can fetch any part in a few hops.

Recap

  1. The design matches hardware to the graphs in the algorithms, but keeps most computation central because all data is compared with one world model.
  2. The map is a sparse graph: features seen together are strongly correlated through the camera state. The store holds it across many cores and maintains it in place.
  3. The real-time loop labels, renders, tracks, and fuses. Interface nodes and a small-world map topology connect it to a map whose relevant part keeps moving.
  4. Near the image plane a global estimate can be reached by local message passing, at a cost in rounds that depends on the graph. Two-way links let a sensor send only what the model did not predict.

Sources

  1. SLAM Handbook, Chapter 18, §18.5 "Mapping Spatial AI Graphs to Hardware", pp. 532–540, Figure 18.1.
  2. Xiao and Boyd, Fast linear iterations for distributed averaging, 2004 (averaging over a graph with symmetric weights).
  3. Xiao, Boyd, Lall, A scheme for robust distributed sensor fusion based on average consensus, 2005 (the Metropolis weights used in the widget).

Week 24 · Day 4

Gaussian belief propagation: estimation by local messages, and learning in the same graph

After today you can derive the message rules of Gaussian belief propagation in information form, run them by hand on a small pose chain, relate them to variable elimination, and say what GBP Learning proposes.

About 60 min · Read §18.6–18.7, pp. 540–545 (5 pages) · Needs Week 1 Day 3, Week 3 Days 2–3, Week 6 Day 4

Read first: §18.6 and §18.7, pp. 540–545

While you read, look for:

  • What the chapter calls the "purest representation" of a Spatial AI problem, and what each node in belief propagation is allowed to know (pp. 540–541).
  • The four properties wanted of learning (p. 543) and the key idea of GBP Learning (p. 545, Figure 18.4).

Today's big idea

The book gives no equations for Gaussian belief propagation, so today supplies them. There are three rules, each using only what one node and its neighbours hold: a variable adds up the messages it receives, tells each factor everything it knows except what that factor told it, and a factor answers by eliminating its other variables. On a tree this is variable elimination done in parallel. On a graph with loops you repeat it, and the means converge to the least-squares solution.

1. What the chapter asks of an algorithm

If computing and storage are spread over many small units (Day 3), estimation must live there too. The chapter's brief: keep the factor graph itself as the master representation, and work on it in place by local message passing with no "god's eye view", letting messages keep "bubbling" as the graph grows. §18.6 · pp. 540–541

Belief propagation (BP) has this character and tolerates arbitrary, asynchronous schedules. Gaussian belief propagation (GBP) is BP when every factor and variable is Gaussian, which covers least-squares estimation (Week 2 · Day 2). The book adds that it converges well on loopy graphs, those with cycles. §18.6 · p. 541

2. Two operations on Gaussians in information form

Write a Gaussian as \(\exp(-\tfrac12\mathbf{x}\T\boldsymbol{\Lambda}\mathbf{x} + \boldsymbol{\eta}\T\mathbf{x})\) up to a constant, with information matrix \(\boldsymbol{\Lambda}\) and information vector \(\boldsymbol{\eta} = \boldsymbol{\Lambda}\boldsymbol{\mu}\) (Week 1 · Day 3). Multiplying is adding: a product of Gaussians over the same variable has \(\boldsymbol{\Lambda} = \boldsymbol{\Lambda}_1 + \boldsymbol{\Lambda}_2\) and \(\boldsymbol{\eta} = \boldsymbol{\eta}_1 + \boldsymbol{\eta}_2\). Marginalizing is a Schur complement (Week 3 · Day 3): to keep part \(a\) and remove part \(b\),

\[ \boldsymbol{\Lambda}_{a}^{\text{marg}} = \boldsymbol{\Lambda}_{aa} - \boldsymbol{\Lambda}_{ab}\boldsymbol{\Lambda}_{bb}^{-1}\boldsymbol{\Lambda}_{ba}, \qquad \boldsymbol{\eta}_{a}^{\text{marg}} = \boldsymbol{\eta}_{a} - \boldsymbol{\Lambda}_{ab}\boldsymbol{\Lambda}_{bb}^{-1}\boldsymbol{\eta}_{b}. \]

A factor is written the same way. A linear measurement \(\mathbf{z} = \mathbf{J}\mathbf{x} + \text{noise}\) with covariance \(\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\) contributes \(\exp(-\tfrac12(\mathbf{z}-\mathbf{J}\mathbf{x})\T\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{-1}(\mathbf{z}-\mathbf{J}\mathbf{x}))\). Expand the square and drop the term without \(\mathbf{x}\):

\[ \boldsymbol{\Lambda}_f = \mathbf{J}\T\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{-1}\mathbf{J}, \qquad \boldsymbol{\eta}_f = \mathbf{J}\T\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{-1}\mathbf{z}. \]

For a one-dimensional odometry factor \(x_j - x_i = z\) with variance \(\sigma^2\), \(\mathbf{J} = \begin{bmatrix} -1 & 1 \end{bmatrix}\) on \((x_i, x_j)\). With \(w = 1/\sigma^2\):

\[ \boldsymbol{\Lambda}_f = w\begin{bmatrix} 1 & -1 \\ -1 & 1 \end{bmatrix}, \qquad \boldsymbol{\eta}_f = wz\begin{bmatrix} -1 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix}. \]

3. The three rules

Every edge of the factor graph carries two messages, one each way. A message is a Gaussian over the variable on that edge, stored as \((\boldsymbol{\eta}, \boldsymbol{\Lambda})\). All start at zero, meaning "no information".

Rule 1, belief. A variable's estimate is the product of its incoming messages, a sum in information form:

\[ \boldsymbol{\Lambda}_{b(x)} = \sum_{f \ni x} \boldsymbol{\Lambda}_{f\to x}, \qquad \boldsymbol{\eta}_{b(x)} = \sum_{f \ni x} \boldsymbol{\eta}_{f\to x}, \qquad \boldsymbol{\mu}_x = \boldsymbol{\Lambda}_{b(x)}^{-1}\boldsymbol{\eta}_{b(x)}. \]

Rule 2, variable to factor. A variable tells factor \(f\) what it has heard from its other factors, which is its belief minus what \(f\) sent:

\[ \boldsymbol{\Lambda}_{x\to f} = \boldsymbol{\Lambda}_{b(x)} - \boldsymbol{\Lambda}_{f\to x}, \qquad \boldsymbol{\eta}_{x\to f} = \boldsymbol{\eta}_{b(x)} - \boldsymbol{\eta}_{f\to x}. \]

Without the subtraction, a factor's own information would be echoed back to it and counted twice.

Rule 3, factor to variable. To send to \(x_i\), the factor takes its own \((\boldsymbol{\eta}_f, \boldsymbol{\Lambda}_f)\), adds the incoming message from every other variable \(x_j\) to that variable's diagonal block and to its part of \(\boldsymbol{\eta}\), and marginalizes all the \(x_j\) out by the Schur complement. A Gaussian over \(x_i\) alone is left.

Filling the gap: rule 3 worked out for an odometry factor

Let the message arriving from \(x_i\) be \((\eta_{\text{in}}, \Lambda_{\text{in}})\), and send to \(x_j\). Adding it to the \(x_i\) entries of the factor gives

\[ \boldsymbol{\Lambda}' = \begin{bmatrix} w + \Lambda_{\text{in}} & -w \\ -w & w \end{bmatrix}, \qquad \boldsymbol{\eta}' = \begin{bmatrix} -wz + \eta_{\text{in}} \\ wz \end{bmatrix}. \]

Remove \(x_i\) (part \(b\)) and keep \(x_j\) (part \(a\)):

\[ \Lambda_{f\to x_j} = w - \frac{w^2}{w + \Lambda_{\text{in}}} = \frac{w\,\Lambda_{\text{in}}}{w + \Lambda_{\text{in}}}, \qquad \eta_{f\to x_j} = wz + \frac{w(\eta_{\text{in}} - wz)}{w + \Lambda_{\text{in}}} = \frac{w\,(z\Lambda_{\text{in}} + \eta_{\text{in}})}{w + \Lambda_{\text{in}}}. \]

In covariance form the variance is \(1/\Lambda_{f\to x_j} = 1/\Lambda_{\text{in}} + 1/w = \sigma_{\text{in}}^2 + \sigma^2\) and the mean is \(\eta/\Lambda = \mu_{\text{in}} + z\). The message says: "\(x_j\) is where \(x_i\) thinks it is, plus the measured step, and the uncertainties add." The other direction gives mean \(\mu_{\text{in}} - z\). If nothing has arrived, \(\Lambda_{\text{in}} = 0\) and the outgoing message is zero too.

4. A full example by hand

Two poses. A prior says \(x_0 = 2\) with variance \(\tfrac14\). Odometry says \(x_1 - x_0 = 3\) with variance \(\tfrac12\), so \(w = 2\). A position fix says \(x_1 = 6\) with variance \(\tfrac14\).

StepMessage or belief\((\eta, \Lambda)\)Mean, variance
1prior → \(x_0\)\((8,\ 4)\)2, 1/4
2fix → \(x_1\)\((24,\ 4)\)6, 1/4
3odometry → \(x_1\), using \(x_0\)'s message \((8, 4)\)\(\left(\tfrac{2(3\cdot 4 + 8)}{6},\ \tfrac{2\cdot 4}{6}\right) = \left(\tfrac{20}{3},\ \tfrac43\right)\)5, 3/4
4odometry → \(x_0\), using \(x_1\)'s message \((24, 4)\)\(\left(4,\ \tfrac43\right)\)3, 3/4
5belief of \(x_0\) = step 1 + step 4\(\left(12,\ \tfrac{16}{3}\right)\)2.25, 3/16
6belief of \(x_1\) = step 2 + step 3\(\left(\tfrac{92}{3},\ \tfrac{16}{3}\right)\)5.75, 3/16

In step 4, \(x_1\) sends the odometry factor its belief minus that factor's message, which leaves the fix, \((24, 4)\). The factor reports mean \(6 - 3 = 3\) and variance \(\tfrac14 + \tfrac12\). Check against the direct solution:

\[ \boldsymbol{\Lambda} = \begin{bmatrix} 6 & -2 \\ -2 & 6 \end{bmatrix}, \quad \boldsymbol{\eta} = \begin{bmatrix} 8 - 6 \\ 6 + 24 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 2 \\ 30 \end{bmatrix}, \quad \boldsymbol{\Lambda}^{-1} = \frac{1}{32}\begin{bmatrix} 6 & 2 \\ 2 & 6 \end{bmatrix}, \]

so \(\boldsymbol{\mu} = (72/32,\ 184/32) = (2.25,\ 5.75)\) and both variances are \(6/32 = 3/16\). The messages reproduced the means and the marginal variances exactly.

5. How this relates to elimination

Rule 3 is one step of variable elimination (Week 3 · Day 2): absorb what is known about a factor's other variables, then eliminate them. On a graph without loops, messages sent from the leaves inward are elimination in some order, and messages sent back outward are back-substitution that also delivers every marginal, so the result is exact. Elimination needs a global ordering and creates fill-in. GBP needs neither and never changes the graph, but on a loopy graph it must iterate.

In a loop, a variable's own message comes back round as if it were independent evidence. For Gaussian models this double counting distorts the variances but cancels in the means: Weiss and Freeman proved that whenever GBP converges, its means are exact.

Try it: press Step, then try each toggle.

Notice that at iteration 3 only five poses have a belief: information has travelled two hops from the prior, both ways round the loop. At iteration 5 every pose has one, but the largest mean error is still 0.29 m. By iteration 20 it is under 0.0001 m. The blue bars stay slightly short: at x4 GBP reports σ = 0.433 where the exact value is 0.439. Switch off the loop closure: the graph is a chain, and after 9 iterations the means and the σ values are both exact.

GBP also takes the nonlinear and robust factors of real problems. §18.6 · p. 541 Both are local changes to a factor: a nonlinear factor is re-linearized about the current belief means (Week 2 · Day 4), and a robust factor shrinks its own \(w\) when its residual is large. The widget uses the Huber weight of Week 6 · Day 4: with the residual in standard deviations \(m\), multiply \(w\) by \(\beta/m\) when \(m \gt \beta = 1.5\). Turn on the outlier, a false loop closure claiming \(x_6 - x_2 = 2.5\) when the truth is 0. Least squares, and GBP with it, drags \(x_6\) to 2.66. With robust factors the outlier's weight falls to 0.27 and \(x_6\) settles at 2.22.

Two systems show the scale: bundle adjustment as GBP on a Graphcore IPU, 30 times faster than a CPU on small real problems, and Robot Web, where many robots shared one localization graph and stayed accurate despite asynchronous and dropped messages. §18.6 · pp. 541–542

6. Learning inside the factor graph

Section 18.7 wants learning that runs alongside probabilistic inference, is mainly self-supervised, is continual with no divide between training and test time, and is interpretable at the level of modules. §18.7 · p. 543 The chapter's answer is Bayesian machine learning: estimate a model's parameters by the same laws as any other unknown. In its words, state estimation and model learning differ only in structure and scale. §18.7 · p. 544

A weight is then just another variable. For a model with one weight, each observed input-output pair is a linear measurement of that weight and adds one term to its information pair, exactly as a sensor reading would. Nothing separates training from use.

GBP Learning (Nabarro and colleagues) scales this up with a factor graph shaped like a neural network. The parameters are variables shared across all observations; inputs, outputs, and activations are variables copied per observation; nonlinear factors between layers switch softly, as neurons do. Learning is then inference by ordinary GBP; the book reports a version that learned image denoising and classification. §18.7 · pp. 544–545, Figure 18.4

Check yourself

Q1. A pose sends an odometry factor a message with mean 4 and variance 0.5. The factor measured a step of 2 with variance 0.25. What does the factor send to the next pose?

The mean is the incoming mean plus the step, 4 + 2 = 6, and the variances add, 0.5 + 0.25 = 0.75.

Q2. A variable's belief is (η, Λ) = (10, 5). Factor f sent it (4, 2). What does the variable send back to f?

Rule 2: the belief minus what f itself sent, (10 − 4, 5 − 2) = (6, 3).

Q3. A chain of nine poses has a prior on the first pose and odometry between neighbours. With a synchronous schedule, after which iteration does the last pose first hold its exact marginal?

Iteration 1 delivers the prior to the first pose, and each later iteration carries information one pose further. A chain has no loops, so the result at iteration 9 is exact.

Q4. GBP has converged on a pose graph with several loop closures. Which statement is correct?

For Gaussian models, convergence implies exact means (Weiss and Freeman). Marginal variances are exact only on graphs without loops.

Recap

  1. The chapter wants the factor graph as master representation, updated in place by local messages.
  2. GBP has three rules: belief = sum of incoming messages; variable to factor = belief minus that factor's message; factor to variable = add incoming messages, then Schur-complement away the other variables.
  3. On a tree GBP is elimination plus back-substitution and is exact. With loops it iterates: the means converge to the least-squares solution and the variances are approximate.
  4. GBP Learning treats network weights as variables in the same graph, so learning becomes continual inference.

Sources

  1. SLAM Handbook, Chapter 18, §18.6 and §18.7, pp. 540–545, Figures 18.2–18.4.
  2. Davison and Ortiz, FutureMapping 2: Gaussian Belief Propagation for Spatial AI, 2019, and Ortiz, Evans, Davison, A visual introduction to Gaussian Belief Propagation, 2021 (the message rules).
  3. Weiss and Freeman, Correctness of belief propagation in Gaussian graphical models of arbitrary topology, 2001 (exact means at convergence).

Week 24 · Day 5

Measuring a Spatial AI system, and the editors' closing words

After today you can list the chapter's twelve proposed performance metrics, explain why one accuracy benchmark is not enough, pick a system from a Pareto front, and summarize where the book says the field is heading.

About 60 min · Read §18.8–18.9 and the Epilogue, pp. 545–549 (5 pages) · Needs Week 11 Day 1

Read first: §18.8, §18.9, and the Epilogue, pp. 545–549

While you read, look for:

  • How ground truth is obtained for poses, for dense geometry, and for semantic labels (p. 545).
  • The specific complaints about benchmarks, including the one about which test sequences get reported (p. 546).
  • What SLAMBench measured, and the two words "Pareto fronts" (p. 546).
  • The twelve metrics (pp. 546–547), and in the Epilogue (pp. 548–549) the advice you most want to keep.

Today's big idea

A Spatial AI system produces many outputs under several resource limits, so no single number ranks two systems. The chapter proposes a short list of metrics covering accuracy, robustness, latency, scene understanding, and resources, and it expects choices to be made by looking at trade-off curves. It also trusts a live demo more than any table.

1. What is measured today, and against what

Section 18.8 returns to the hypothesis of Day 1 that a few measures capture usefulness. Most evaluation today is of localization accuracy: a motion-capture system provides an external pose that is treated as ground truth, and the SLAM estimate is compared with it. §18.8 · p. 545 That is the absolute and relative trajectory error of Week 11 · Day 1. Everything else is harder to check.

OutputWhere ground truth comes fromExample in the bookThe difficulty
Camera poseMotion captureBenchmark trajectory datasetsCovers one output of many
Dense scene modelLaser scanning of the real scene, or synthetic scenes rendered by computer graphicsICL-NUIM (synthetic)Scanning is slow and expensive; is a rendered world like the real one?
Semantic labelsSynthetic scenesSceneNet RGB-DSame doubt
Geometry and labels at scaleCrowdsourced real capturesScanNetReal data, but hard to gather at scale

The chapter accepts the suspicion about synthetic data and still expects it to grow in importance as rendering improves. §18.8 · p. 545

2. Why the chapter distrusts benchmarks, and keeps them anyway

The criticism is blunt. Too much effort goes into squeezing a few percentage points out of a dataset. A SLAM benchmark fixes the scene type, the sensors and their placement, the frame rate, and the resolution, and then scores mostly accuracy, while efficiency and robustness, which matter at least as much, go unmeasured. Papers often report only the sequences on which their method basically works. §18.8 · p. 546

Against this the chapter sets the live demo. Playing with a visual SLAM system for a minute, watching its visualization and pushing it around, tells you more than its score. Progress is better read from the line of open real-time systems people could try for themselves: MonoSLAM, PTAM, KinectFusion, LSD-SLAM, ORB-SLAM, OKVIS, SVO, ElasticFusion, DROID-SLAM, Gaussian Splatting SLAM, MASt3R-SLAM. §18.8 · p. 546

Should we benchmark at all? The answer given is yes, with two changes: broaden what a benchmark measures, and trust it less. §18.8 · p. 546

3. Several objectives at once: the Pareto front

SLAMBench was a first step toward judging a whole system. It took one algorithm, KinectFusion, and measured both its accuracy and its computational cost across processor platforms and language implementations. The chapter wants benchmarks to move toward measures that predict performance on real tasks. That gives a set of objectives that pull against each other, and it says the analysis of Pareto fronts will let a designer choose for a particular application. §18.8 · p. 546

Filling the gap: what a Pareto front is and how to find it

The book uses the term without defining it. Score every candidate system on each metric, with lower being better. Candidate \(A\) dominates candidate \(B\) if \(A\) is at least as good as \(B\) on every metric and strictly better on at least one. Nobody should ever pick a dominated candidate. The Pareto front is the set of candidates that nothing dominates. Among those, improving one metric always costs you on another, so the choice depends on the application.

Five configurations, scored as (power in W, drift in %):

\[ A = (1,\ 3.0), \quad B = (2,\ 2.0), \quad C = (3,\ 2.5), \quad D = (5,\ 1.0), \quad E = (6,\ 1.5). \]

\(C\) is dominated by \(B\): \(B\) uses less power (2 against 3) and drifts less (2.0 against 2.5). \(E\) is dominated by \(D\) in the same way. \(A\), \(B\), and \(D\) survive: going from \(A\) to \(B\) to \(D\) buys accuracy with watts each time. The front is \(\{A, B, D\}\).

To choose, add a constraint from the product. With a budget of 4 W the candidates are \(A\) and \(B\), and \(B\) has the lower drift. For two metrics the front is found by sorting by power and keeping each candidate whose drift is lower than every cheaper one's.

Try it: forty synthetic configurations of one system, scored on power and drift. Move the power budget.

Notice that only 10 of the 40 configurations are on the front; each of the other 30 is beaten on both metrics by something else. At a 1 W budget the best choice uses 0.49 W and drifts 1.73%. Raise the budget to 2 W and it drops to 1.06%. From there the curve is nearly flat: at 20 W the best is 0.61%. Where the front bends tells you what a watt is worth.

4. The twelve metrics

The chapter's candidate list, grouped here by what each one protects. §18.8 · pp. 546–547

GroupMetric (book's number)Where the course met it
Localization(1) Local pose accuracy in newly explored areas, the visual odometry drift rate. (2) Long-term metric pose repeatability in well-mapped areas.Drift: Week 1 · Day 1. The two regimes are the two curves of the Day 1 widget.
Robustness(3) Tracking robustness percentage. (4) Relocalisation robustness percentage.Outliers, Week 6; place recognition, Weeks 11, 13, 14.
Timing(5) SLAM system latency.Incremental solving, Week 3 · Day 5.
Geometry(6) Dense distance prediction accuracy at every pixel.Dense maps, Weeks 8 and 20.
Semantics(7) Object segmentation accuracy. (8) Object classification accuracy.Weeks 22 and 23.
Display(9) Pixel registration accuracy for augmented reality.Reprojection error, Week 11 · Day 5.
Change(10) Scene change detection accuracy.Week 21.
Resources(11) Power usage. (12) On-device data movement, in bits × millimetres.Day 2, Day 3.

The book names these without formulas. Three small calculations show what they would look like. The definitions are natural ones chosen for this lesson; the book does not fix them.

  • Drift rate. End-point error divided by distance travelled, with no loop closures. An error of 0.5 m after 100 m is 0.5%.
  • Tracking robustness. The share of frames on which the tracker held. Tracked on 5 820 of 6 000 frames is 97%.
  • Data movement. Bits sent times the distance they travel. A camera that sends a 1 Mbit frame along a 50 mm link moves \(10^6 \times 50 = 5\times10^7\) bit·mm per frame. If pixel-level processing lets it send 10 kbit of differences, that is \(5\times10^5\), a hundred times less.

5. Where the book says the field is going

Section 18.9 closes the chapter in two moves. First, capability has to rise while the resources it needs fall, and that takes joined-up thinking about algorithms, processors, and sensors: find the computational structure, design for sparse graph patterns in both algorithms and storage, and fit them to the new hardware. Second, hand-designed estimation and machine learning will both stay, and will converge. Estimation systems are gaining learned parts and learned networks are gaining structure and domain knowledge, and the chapter expects both routes to arrive at the same place with the same questions about computational structure. §18.9 · p. 547

The book then ends with an Epilogue: two pages of short, unattributed remarks from its authors. Epilogue · pp. 548–549 Read them in the original. Grouped by theme, with the part of this course where you practised each:

ThemeThe advice, paraphrasedIn this course
RigorTrust the math. Keep notation clear in your math, your code, and your papers, because that is how modeling errors get caught. Keep SLAM's formulation as an optimization problem rigorous as it grows.Certificates, Week 9 · Day 4; observability, Week 17 · Day 3
PracticeTheory sinks in when you apply it on a robot. Start from a toy problem with perfectly controlled synthetic data and build up. Plug in a live camera and visualize: five minutes of that teaches more than many dataset results.Every widget in the app is such a toy problem
The core skillExtracting the truth from measurements that conflict is the most important thing in SLAM.Robust estimation, Week 6 · Day 4
AmbitionDo not accept that SLAM is solved. Work on a problem two or three steps beyond the state of the art. New sensors are waiting to be used, event cameras being one example.Open problems at the end of each chapter; Week 15
PurposeSLAM is about letting machines perceive, understand, and reason about the world, and it is the backbone of robot autonomy and the interface to decision-making. Differentiable optimization is expected to play a key part.Week 7; Part III

Common mistakes

  • "The system with the lowest trajectory error is the best system." It may use ten times the power, fail on half the sequences nobody reported, or respond too late. Accuracy is one of twelve.
  • "A point on the Pareto front is the optimum." Every point on the front is optimal for some trade-off. The application's constraints pick one.

Check yourself

Q1. Four configurations are scored as (power, drift): P = (1 W, 4%), Q = (2 W, 2%), R = (3 W, 3%), S = (4 W, 1%). Which one is dominated?

Q uses less power than R and drifts less, so Q dominates R. P, Q, and S each beat the others on one metric and lose on the other, so they form the front.

Q2. With no loop closures, a visual odometry system is 1.2 m from the truth after travelling 300 m. What is its drift rate?

1.2 / 300 = 0.004, which is 0.4% of the distance travelled.

Q3. A sensor sends 500 kbit per frame over a 40 mm link. Near-sensor processing cuts that to 5 kbit. What is the data movement per frame afterwards?

5 000 bits × 40 mm = 2 × 10⁵ bit·mm. Before, it was 500 000 × 40 = 2 × 10⁷, a hundred times more.

Q4. Why does the chapter rate a one-minute live demo above a benchmark score?

Datasets capture limited aspects of performance, mostly accuracy, under fixed assumptions. Interacting with a running system shows how it behaves when pushed.

Recap

  1. Pose accuracy against motion capture is the usual benchmark. Ground truth for dense geometry and semantics is costly, so synthetic data and crowdsourcing fill in.
  2. Benchmarks fix too many assumptions and reward accuracy over robustness and efficiency. The chapter keeps them, broadened, and trusts a live demo more.
  3. With several objectives there is no single winner. The Pareto front is the set of undominated candidates, and the application's limits choose among them.
  4. The twelve proposed metrics span localization, robustness, latency, geometry, semantics, AR registration, change detection, power, and data movement in bits × millimetres.
  5. The book's closing view: design algorithms, processors, and sensors together around sparse graph structure, expect estimation and learning to converge, trust the math, and test on real systems.

Sources

  1. SLAM Handbook, Chapter 18, §18.8 "Performance Metrics" and §18.9 "Further Readings & Recent Trends", pp. 545–547; Epilogue, pp. 548–549.
  2. Boyd and Vandenberghe, Convex Optimization, 2004 (Pareto optimality in multi-criterion problems, §4.7).
  3. The metric definitions in Section 4 and the widget's configurations are this app's own illustrations.

Week 24 · Review

Week 24 review: the computational structure, Part III, and the whole course

After today you can work Gaussian belief propagation and the week's other calculations by hand, place every chapter of Part III in one table, and draw the path from a factor graph to a Spatial AI system from memory.

About 60 min · No new pages

The week in one paragraph

Chapter 18 argues that Spatial AI is SLAM continued: a device keeps a persistent, close-to-metric world model and checks every measurement against it in a closed loop. Because products limit size, cost, and power, and because single-core speed stopped rising when Dennard scaling failed, the computation has to be spread over many simple units with little data movement. The design gives each graph in the problem matching hardware: a self-maintaining map store, a real-time loop, and processing at the sensor. Gaussian belief propagation is the estimation algorithm that fits, since it needs only local messages and tolerates any schedule, and it can carry learning in the same factor graph. Success is to be judged on a dozen metrics at once, read as trade-offs.

1. Formula sheet

What it isFormulaWhere

Switching power and Dennard scaling\(P = CV^2f\). Shrink by \(k\): power density \(\times 1\) if \(V \to V/k\); \(\times k^2\) if \(V\) fixed and \(f \to kf\)Concept in §18.4.1, pp. 528–529 · Day 2

2. Mixed quiz: Week 24

Check yourself

Q1. Which of these is not one of the six properties of a Spatial AI system in §18.2?

Property 5 says the opposite: full quality only where the device is looking and about to act, with the rest stored at lower quality levels that can be upgraded on a revisit.

Q2. A camera tracks against a stored map with 9 landmarks in view and measurement noise σ = 0.06. What is the standard deviation of the fresh noise in its position estimate?

Averaging 9 independent measurements divides σ by √9: 0.06/3 = 0.02.

Q3. An estimate is stored as (η, Λ) = (40, 20). A new measurement z = 5 with variance 0.2 arrives. What is the new mean?

The measurement adds Λ = 1/0.2 = 5 and η = 5/0.2 = 25. New pair: (65, 25), mean 65/25 = 2.6.

Q4. Under ideal Dennard scaling with k = 3, by what factor does the switching power of one transistor change?

C → C/3, V² → V²/9, f → 3f, so P → P × (1/3)(1/9)(3) = P/9. Nine times as many transistors fit per area, so power density is unchanged.

Q5. Two pixel processors are linked only to each other and hold 2 and 8. With the averaging rule of Day 3, what do they hold after one round?

Each has one neighbour, so the weight is 1/(1 + 1) = 1/2. The first becomes 2 + (8 − 2)/2 = 5 and the second 8 + (2 − 8)/2 = 5.

Q6. An odometry factor has w = 1/σ² = 3. The message arriving from one pose has Λ = 6. What is Λ of the message the factor sends to the other pose?

Λ = wΛin/(w + Λin) = 18/9 = 2. In variances: 1/6 + 1/3 = 1/2.

Q7. In GBP Learning, what plays the part of a neural network's weights?

Parameters are variables like any others; inputs, outputs, and activations are variables copied per observation. Inference on the graph is the learning.

Q8. Four configurations, as (power, drift): A = (1 W, 3.0%), B = (2 W, 2.2%), C = (4 W, 1.4%), D = (8 W, 1.3%). With a 5 W budget, which do you pick for the lowest drift?

All four are on the Pareto front. D is over budget, and among A, B, C the lowest drift is C at 1.4%.

3. Pen-and-paper problems

  1. Three poses on a line. Prior: \(x_0 = 0\), variance 0.04. Odometry: \(x_1 - x_0 = 1.0\) and \(x_2 - x_1 = 1.2\), each with variance 0.09. Run GBP by hand and give the mean and variance of each belief. Why do the messages travelling back toward \(x_0\) carry nothing?

    Solution

    The prior gives \(x_0\): mean 0, variance 0.04. Through the first odometry factor the mean gains the step and the variances add: \(x_1\) has mean 1.0, variance \(0.04 + 0.09 = 0.13\). Through the second: \(x_2\) has mean 2.2, variance \(0.13 + 0.09 = 0.22\).

    The message from \(x_2\) to the second odometry factor is \(x_2\)'s belief minus what that factor sent, and \(x_2\) has no other factor, so it is zero. A factor that receives zero information sends zero onward (\(\Lambda = w\cdot 0/(w+0) = 0\)). With no measurement downstream there is nothing to report upstream.

  2. Add a position fix to Problem 1: \(x_2 = 2.0\) with variance 0.02. Compute the new beliefs of \(x_2\) and \(x_1\).

    Solution

    Belief of \(x_2\). Two incoming messages: from odometry (mean 2.2, variance 0.22), so \((\eta,\Lambda) = (10,\ 4.545)\); from the fix, \((100,\ 50)\). Sum: \((110,\ 54.545)\). Mean \(110/54.545 = 2.017\), variance \(1/54.545 = 0.0183\).

    Message back to \(x_1\). \(x_2\) sends the second odometry factor its belief minus that factor's message, which leaves the fix: mean 2.0, variance 0.02. The factor passes it on with the step subtracted and the variances added: mean \(2.0 - 1.2 = 0.8\), variance \(0.02 + 0.09 = 0.11\).

    Belief of \(x_1\). Forward message (mean 1.0, variance 0.13) is \((7.692,\ 7.692)\); backward message (mean 0.8, variance 0.11) is \((7.273,\ 9.091)\). Sum: \((14.965,\ 16.783)\). Mean \(0.892\), variance \(0.0596\). Solving the \(3\times3\) system \(\boldsymbol{\Lambda}\boldsymbol{\mu} = \boldsymbol{\eta}\) directly gives the same numbers, because the graph has no loop.

  3. Four pixel processors sit in a ring, each linked to its two neighbours, and hold 0, 4, 8, 4. Using the averaging rule with \(w_{ij} = 1/(1+\max(d_i,d_j))\), find the values after one round, and the number of rounds until every pixel is within 0.05 of the mean.

    Solution

    Every pixel has degree 2, so every weight is \(1/3\). The mean is \(16/4 = 4\).

    Round 1: pixel 1 becomes \(0 + \tfrac13(4-0) + \tfrac13(4-0) = 2.67\). Pixel 3 becomes \(8 + \tfrac13(4-8) + \tfrac13(4-8) = 5.33\). Pixels 2 and 4 see one neighbour 4 below and one 4 above and stay at 4. The values are 2.67, 4, 5.33, 4, and the sum is still 16.

    The deviations from the mean went from \((-4, 0, 4, 0)\) to \((-1.33, 0, 1.33, 0)\): each round multiplies them by \(1/3\). After \(t\) rounds the largest deviation is \(4/3^t\). It is \(4/27 = 0.148\) at \(t = 3\) and \(4/81 = 0.049\) at \(t = 4\). Four rounds.

  4. (Stretch.) Show with numbers that one forward step of GBP on a pose chain is one predict-and-update step of a Kalman filter. Prior: \(x_0\) has mean 0, variance 1. Odometry: \(x_1 - x_0 = 1\), variance 1. A position fix: \(x_1 = 3\), variance 1.

    Solution

    Kalman filter. Predict: mean \(0 + 1 = 1\), variance \(1 + 1 = 2\). Update with the fix: gain \(K = 2/(2+1) = 2/3\), mean \(1 + \tfrac23(3 - 1) = 2.33\), variance \((1 - \tfrac23)\cdot 2 = 0.667\).

    GBP. The odometry factor's message to \(x_1\) is the prediction: mean 1, variance 2, so \((\eta,\Lambda) = (0.5,\ 0.5)\). The fix sends \((3,\ 1)\). The belief is the sum, \((3.5,\ 1.5)\): mean \(3.5/1.5 = 2.33\), variance \(1/1.5 = 0.667\).

    The factor-to-variable message is the predict step, and adding the fix's message is the update step written in information form. Messages sent backward along the chain then turn the filter into a smoother. Compare Week 1 · Day 3.

4. Part III in review: Weeks 19–24

Part III opened by asking whether SLAM is solved, and answered: only for small, static, feature-rich indoor scenes. Prelude III · p. 361 Each chapter removed one restriction or added one capability.

WeekChapterWhat it adds to the SLAM of Parts I and IIThe idea to keep
1913. Boosting SLAM with deep learningLearned depth, matching, and optical flow; differentiable bundle adjustment; pointmapsA network can supply the measurements and their confidence. A factor graph still fuses them.
2014. NeRF and Gaussian splattingMaps that are optimized by rendering them and comparing with the imagesIf rendering is differentiable, the photometric error can train the map and the pose together.
2115. Dynamic and deformable SLAMMoving objects, scenes that change between visits, surfaces that deformWithout a static world, the system must decide what to remove, what to track, and what to update.
2216. Metric-semantic SLAMObjects as landmarks, labels on dense maps, hierarchical 3D scene graphsSemantics adds discrete unknowns to the factor graph and layers of abstraction to the map.
2317. Open-world Spatial AIFeatures from foundation models stored in the map; open-vocabulary queriesThe map grounds a language model in a place; the model gives the map a vocabulary not fixed in advance.
2418. Computational structureHow all of the above can run on a real deviceFind the graph in the computation and give it hardware of the same shape.

5. The whole course on one page

Read the map as a sentence. A factor graph states what depends on what (Week 2); Gaussian noise turns it into least squares, and sparsity makes that solvable at scale (Week 3). Each sensor of Part II adds its own residual to the same graph, from reprojection error (Week 11) to preintegrated IMU increments (Week 16). Part III keeps the graph and changes what hangs on it. This week asks the graph to run itself, by passing messages.

6. Course quiz: Weeks 1–24

Check yourself: the whole course

Q1 (Week 2). With Gaussian noise on every factor, what is MAP inference on a factor graph equivalent to?

The negative log of a product of Gaussians is a sum of squared Mahalanobis distances, which is a nonlinear least-squares problem.

Q2 (Week 3). Why can a poor elimination order make sparse Cholesky slow?

Each elimination produces a factor on the variable's separator. A bad order makes separators large, so the triangular factor fills with nonzeros. The answer itself is the same in any order.

Q3 (Week 4). In the book's convention, how does Gauss-Newton apply a computed step ξ to a pose T?

Poses are not vectors. The step is computed in the tangent space and applied by the exponential map on the right, which keeps T a valid pose.

Q4 (Week 6). Half of the matches are inliers and a minimal sample needs 3 matches. About how many RANSAC iterations give a 99% chance of drawing at least one all-inlier sample?

An all-inlier sample has probability 0.5³ = 0.125. N = log(0.01)/log(1 − 0.125) = 4.605/0.1335 ≈ 34.5, so 35.

Q5 (Week 9). Shor's relaxation of a pose-graph problem returns the value d*. The true optimum is p*. What is guaranteed?

A relaxation enlarges the feasible set, so its minimum is a lower bound. If the relaxed solution is rank one it is feasible for the original problem, so it is the global optimum.

Q6 (Week 12). In bundle adjustment, why are the landmarks eliminated first with the Schur complement?

No factor joins two landmarks, so the landmark part of the information matrix is block diagonal. Eliminating it gives the reduced camera system.

Q7 (Week 13). What does one iteration of point-to-point ICP do?

ICP alternates data association by nearest neighbour with a closed-form alignment (by SVD), and repeats until the transform stops changing.

Q8 (Week 15). When does a pixel of an event camera emit an event?

Each pixel works independently and asynchronously and reports the time and sign of a brightness change. A static scene seen by a static camera produces almost no data.

Q9 (Week 17). How many directions of the state are unobservable for visual-inertial odometry in general motion?

The accelerometer sees gravity, which fixes roll and pitch, and makes scale observable. Global position and yaw are never measured and remain free.

Q10 (Week 20). In what order does 3D Gaussian splatting produce a pixel?

Splatting rasterizes: project, sort, blend. Sampling an MLP along each ray is NeRF's volume rendering.

Q11 (Week 23). What makes a map "open-vocabulary"?

A closed-set map holds labels from a list chosen at training time. An open-vocabulary map holds embeddings that can be compared with any text query later.

Q12 (Weeks 3 and 24). What do variable elimination and Gaussian belief propagation have in common?

The factor-to-variable message is a local elimination. Elimination applies it once in a global order and is exact; GBP applies it everywhere repeatedly, with exact means at convergence.

7. Where to go next

  1. Build one toy system end to end. This is the Epilogue's advice. A good first one: a 2D pose graph with simulated odometry and loop closures, solved by Gauss-Newton (Week 2 · Day 4), then given outliers and a robust loss (Week 6 · Day 4), then solved again by GBP (Day 4) and compared.
  2. Use a real library. The book points to GTSAM in Chapter 1, and to Theseus and PyPose for differentiable optimization in Chapter 4. Rebuild your toy system in one of them.
  3. Run a full system on a live camera. §18.8 lists open real-time systems, from ORB-SLAM to MASt3R-SLAM (p. 546). Push it until it fails and write down how it failed.
  4. Follow the pointers in the "Further Readings & Recent Trends" section that ends almost every chapter.
  5. Pick an open problem. The Part III prelude lists where SLAM is not solved: underwater, on other planets, in disaster zones, in dense city traffic (p. 361).

You have finished the course if you can

  • Write a SLAM problem as a factor graph and turn it into whitened least squares.
  • Explain why sparsity, elimination order, and incremental updates decide whether it runs in real time.
  • Give the residual each sensor of Part II contributes, and say what each cannot observe.
  • Say what a learned component adds in Part III and what the estimator still does.
  • Derive a GBP message through an odometry factor and say when the result is exact.
  • Name the metrics you would report for a system beyond trajectory error.
